Advanced Shell Scripting Mastery

How bash reads a line, and everything that follows from it: quoting, expansion, redirection, errors, processes, security, portability, tests, performance and style. Every claim was produced by running the code, on two machines, under two versions of bash; the ones that contradicted what the manuals say were kept and corrected.

How to use this course

  • This course is about what a shell script does, as opposed to what it looks like. It assumes you can already use a terminal and have written a few shell scripts, and it does not assume you have ever read the manual. §1 begins with why the script's runtime is one you do not control, and §2 with how a single line is read before anything runs.
  • Every example was run. Each block that shows output was run under bash 5.3.20 on macOS and again under bash 5.2.37 on Debian 13, twice each, and the two runs compared; a difference between the machines is stated where it appears, and no example prints a duration, since a duration belongs to a machine. §1.7 says how the examples are produced, and §21 shows how speed is claimed without a stopwatch: by counts and by ratios.
  • The tools are named and versioned. ShellCheck 0.11.0, bats-core 1.14.0, shunit2 2.1.8, shfmt 3.14.1, hyperfine 1.20.0, dash 0.5.12 and strace 6.13 (Linux only). Where a tool's own message is quoted, it was copied from a run.
  • The course follows the order in which a script is read and then run. §1–§4 are how bash reads a line: when shell is the right tool, the grammar, quoting and word splitting, and the order of expansions. §5–§8 are the language: parameter expansion, arrays, conditionals and arithmetic, and control flow. §9–§12 are how a script is built to behave: functions and scope, redirection, exit status and errexit, and traps and cleanup. §13–§15 are its edges: a command-line interface, input and output, and text processing. §16–§17 are processes and concurrency. §18–§19 are hostile input and other shells. §20–§22 are the discipline: static analysis and tests, performance, and style, architecture and a capstone.
  • Each section has numbered subsections, examples with their real output, and exercises with worked solutions. The exercises are the part that makes a rule stick: most ask you to find the fault in a script, predict what it prints, and then run it.

Check what you have before starting, because several sections use features that only recent versions have:

bash --version | head -n 1     # GNU bash, version 5.2 or later; 5.3 for a few labelled examples
shellcheck --version | head -n 2

macOS ships bash 3.2 as /bin/bash, twenty years behind, and §1.2 explains why the course never uses it. Install a current bash (brew install bash) and run the examples with that.

What you are actually learning

Not a list of builtins. Five skills that carry over to scripts in any environment:

  1. Reading a line the way bash does. Tokens before meaning, the seven expansions in their fixed order, why quoting is the only protection, and what one pass means (§1–§4). With that, you can say what a line does before running it, and most of the rest follows.
  2. Writing a script that fails loudly and cleans up after itself. Exit status, set -e and the ways it does not do what its users believe, pipefail, traps, and correct exit after a signal (§9–§12).
  3. Treating input as hostile. Where data becomes code: an unquoted variable, an arithmetic context, a file name that starts with a dash, eval, PATH, the environment (§18), and writing for a shell you did not choose (§19).
  4. Establishing that a script works, and how fast. ShellCheck as a gate, bats tests, stubs, and tracing (§20); then counting processes, reading with the right tool, and measuring instead of guessing (§21).
  5. Structuring a script so someone else can keep it, and knowing when to stop. Functions and libraries, a style a machine can check, layers with the logic apart from the I/O, and the point at which the work is no longer shell's (§22, with §1.6 and §21.7).

By the end you should be able to read an unfamiliar script and say what it does and where it will fail, write one that is safe on hostile input and on a re-run, prove it with a test and a linter, and decide, on evidence, when a shell script has done as much as a shell script should.

SECTION 1

When Shell Is the Right Tool

The shell is the only programming language guaranteed to be on the far end of every machine you will ever log into. That is its whole claim, and it is a larger claim than it sounds. A Python script needs Python, a Go binary needs to have been cross-compiled for the architecture, a container needs a runtime; a shell script needs a shell, and if there is no shell there is also no way for you to have got there in the first place.

That guarantee is why shell scripting refuses to die, and it is also why it is written so badly. A language you never chose is a language you never learned. Almost every professional has written a few hundred lines of shell without once reading what the shell does with a line before running it, and the result is the genre of bug this course exists to remove: scripts that work on the author's machine, on the author's filenames, with the author's arguments, and fail the first time any of those change.

This section is about the decision that comes before any of that: whether to write the script at all, which shell will run it, and what "which shell" turns out to mean in practice. That last question has an answer that should genuinely alarm you, and it is measured rather than asserted below.

What this course assumes you already have. The linux course teaches the shell as a place you work — its §2 covers quoting, the environment, PATH and startup files, and its §4 covers the three streams, redirection, pipes and exit status at the prompt. This course does not repeat that. It starts where a command line becomes a program: a file that someone else runs, on inputs you did not choose, with consequences if it is wrong. Where a topic genuinely belongs to both, this course assumes the interactive half and teaches the scripting half.

1.1 A Script Is a Program Whose Runtime You Do Not Control

A shell script is a text file the shell reads one command at a time. There is no compilation step, no link step, and — this is the part that shapes everything else — no separation between parsing and running. The shell reads a line, expands it, runs it, and only then looks at the next line. A syntax error halfway down a script is discovered halfway down the script, after everything above it has already happened.

That single property explains most of what makes shell scripting different from programming in any other language:

Property
Consequence for the way you write
No parse-before-run
A typo on line 200 does not stop lines 1–199 from executing. Half-completed work is the default failure mode, so cleanup has to be arranged explicitly (§12).
Everything is a string
There are no types to disagree with you. rm -rf $dir where dir is empty is not a type error; it is a valid command with a different meaning.
Whitespace is syntax
A word boundary is a semantic boundary. This is why quoting (§3) is the single largest source of defects, and why it is a whole section rather than a paragraph.
Failure is opt-in
A command that fails sets a status nobody is obliged to read. The default script continues cheerfully past its own failure (§11).
The runtime is not yours
The script runs under whatever shell, version and settings the target machine has. This section is about that sentence.

The last one is the theme. In every other language you ship the runtime or pin it: a package.json names a Node version, a pyproject.toml names a Python. A shell script names its interpreter in a single line of text at the top and hopes.

1.2 There Are Two Shells Named Bash, and They Are Twenty Years Apart

Here is the measurement promised above. This is run on macOS, and every claim in this course is produced by running it rather than by remembering it.

cat > a.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
echo "  /bin/bash          -> $BASH_VERSION"
EOF
cat > b.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "  /usr/bin/env bash  -> $BASH_VERSION"
EOF
chmod +x a.sh b.sh
./a.sh
./b.sh

  /bin/bash          -> 3.2.57(1)-release
  /usr/bin/env bash  -> 5.3.20(1)-release

Two scripts, differing only in their first line, run on one machine, get shells released nineteen years apart. Bash 3.2 is from 2007. Bash 5.3 is current.

This is not a macOS quirk you can dismiss. Apple froze /bin/bash at 3.2 because bash 4.0 moved to GPLv3, and that freeze is permanent — the version in /bin will never advance. Meanwhile the bash you install yourself lands in /opt/homebrew/bin or /usr/local/bin. Both are on the machine. Which one runs your script is decided entirely by the line you wrote at the top of it.

What is actually missing from 3.2 is not exotic. Asking each shell for its builtin list, and taking the difference, gives:

/bin/bash            -c 'compgen -b' | sort > old.txt
/opt/homebrew/bin/bash -c 'compgen -b' | sort > new.txt
echo "in bash 5 but not in bash 3.2:"
comm -13 old.txt new.txt | sed 's/^/  /'
echo "reserved words added since 3.2:"
comm -13 <(/bin/bash -c 'compgen -k' | sort) \
         <(/opt/homebrew/bin/bash -c 'compgen -k' | sort) | sed 's/^/  /'

in bash 5 but not in bash 3.2:
  compopt
  mapfile
  readarray
reserved words added since 3.2:
  coproc

mapfile and readarray are how you read a file into an array without a loop (§14.7). compopt is part of writing completions (§13.12). coproc is the coprocess keyword (§17.11). Beyond the builtins, 3.2 has no ${var^^} case conversion, no ${var@Q} quoting transformation, no associative arrays, and no declare -n namerefs — that is §5 and §6 of this course, mostly absent.

The rule this produces: decide which bash you are targeting, write it down, and make the script prove it rather than assume it. A three-line guard costs nothing and turns a baffling mapfile: command not found on someone else's laptop into a sentence that says what to do:

if (( BASH_VERSINFO[0] < 4 )); then
  printf 'This script needs bash 4.0 or newer; found %s at %s.\n' \
         "$BASH_VERSION" "${BASH:-unknown}" >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "running under bash $BASH_VERSION"

running under bash 5.3.20(1)-release

BASH_VERSINFO is an array of the version's components, so BASH_VERSINFO[0] is the major number as an integer and the comparison is arithmetic rather than string juggling. BASH_VERSION is the human-readable string, which is what you want in the message and not what you want in the test — "5.3.20(1)-release" < "4.0" compares as text and is nonsense.

The bourne-again shell, the dash shell and the ksh shell

The name bash is an acronym for the Bourne-Again shell: the bourne-again shell is a pun on Stephen Bourne, whose Bourne shell (sh, from 1979) it replaced in the GNU system. Two other shells matter to anyone who writes bash, because scripts move between them. The dash shell, the Debian Almquist shell, is small and fast and is /bin/sh on Debian and Ubuntu, so a script run as sh there is run by the dash shell, and §19 measures what breaks. The ksh shell, the Korn shell, is where much of bash's syntax comes from — [[ ]], $( ), (( )) and arrays all appeared in the ksh shell first — and it is the shell whose behaviour the POSIX standard was largely written from. The rest of the course says "bash" when it means the Bourne-Again shell and "sh" when it means whatever the system calls sh, and §19 is where the difference starts to cost something.

1.3 The Shebang Line, Precisely

The first two bytes of an executable file are read by the kernel, not by the shell. If they are #!, the kernel treats the rest of that line as the interpreter to run, and hands it the script's path as an argument. This is the mechanism, and it is worth seeing directly rather than described. /bin/echo is a real program that prints its arguments, so putting it in a shebang shows exactly what the kernel passed:

printf '#!/bin/echo ARGS:\n' > show.sh
chmod +x show.sh
./show.sh

ARGS: ./show.sh

So ./show.sh ran /bin/echo ARGS: ./show.sh. The interpreter, then the text after it, then the path of the script itself. Nothing else happens: the kernel does not look at the file's extension, does not care that it is called .sh, and does not read any further into the file.

Three consequences follow, and each is a real bug people hit:

The interpreter path is absolute and literal. There is no PATH search. #!/bin/bash means that exact file; if the target machine keeps bash somewhere else — NixOS, a BSD, an Alpine container — the script fails with a message that names the script rather than the interpreter, which is why it reads so confusingly:

printf '#!/bin/nosuchshell\necho hi\n' > bad.sh
chmod +x bad.sh
./bad.sh
echo "exit status: $?"

example.sh: ./bad.sh: /bin/nosuchshell: bad interpreter: No such file or directory
exit status: 126

Read that message carefully once and you will never lose ten minutes to it again. It names three things: example.sh, the script that tried to run something; ./bad.sh, the thing it tried to run; and /bin/nosuchshell, the thing that is actually missing. The missing file is the one nobody looks at, because the eye stops at the first filename.

The status is worth noting too. 126 means "found it, could not execute it"; 127 means "could not find it". Here bad.sh exists and is executable, so the failure is 126 even though the underlying cause is a missing file — the missing file is the interpreter, and the kernel reports the failure against the thing you asked to run. A command not found for a name that is not on PATH gives 127 instead. §11.4 uses both numbers.

Arguments in the shebang are not portable. How the kernel splits the text after the interpreter differs between systems. On macOS it splits on whitespace into separate arguments; on Linux the entire remainder is passed as a single argument. The difference is visible:

printf '#!/bin/echo one two three\n' > show2.sh
chmod +x show2.sh
./show2.sh

one two three ./show2.sh

That is macOS, showing three separate words. Linux would hand /bin/echo a single argument "one two three", which for echo looks identical but for env does not: #!/usr/bin/env bash -eu works on macOS and fails on Linux with env: 'bash -eu': No such file or directory, because env is asked for a program whose name contains spaces. Never put options in a shebang. Put them on the first line of the script instead, where they behave the same everywhere:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -eu

A file with no shebang has no interpreter of its own. It is run by whatever is already running, which means the same file behaves differently depending on how it was invoked:

cat > c.sh <<'EOF'
echo "  BASH_VERSION=${BASH_VERSION:-<not bash>}"
EOF
chmod +x c.sh
echo "./c.sh   :"; ./c.sh
echo "bash c.sh:"; bash c.sh
echo "sh c.sh  :"; sh c.sh

./c.sh   :
  BASH_VERSION=5.3.20(1)-release
bash c.sh:
  BASH_VERSION=5.3.20(1)-release
sh c.sh  :
  BASH_VERSION=3.2.57(1)-release

Three invocations of one file, two different shells. Note the third line especially: on macOS /bin/sh is bash 3.2 running in POSIX mode, not a separate shell. POSIX mode is a switch inside bash, not a different program — it turns off the extensions the standard does not describe, so a bash invoked as sh refuses declare -A and process substitution even though the same binary supports both under its own name. On Ubuntu and Debian /bin/sh is dash, a different program entirely. Either way sh is not bash, and §19 is about the gap.

1.4 Choosing the Interpreter Line

Given the above, there are exactly two defensible shebangs and one common mistake.

Shebang
Use it when
#!/usr/bin/env bash
The default for anything you write. Finds the first bash on PATH, so it picks up a modern bash installed anywhere. This is what gets 5.3 rather than 3.2 on macOS.
#!/bin/bash
When the script runs somewhere you control completely and where PATH is itself untrusted — a sudoers-invoked script, a setuid context, a minimal container image whose contents you pin.
#!/bin/sh
Only when the script is genuinely POSIX and you have checked it with shellcheck -s sh (§19). Writing bash under this shebang is the mistake: it works on macOS, where sh is bash, and breaks on Debian, where it is dash.

One rule belongs here regardless of which row you pick, and it is the Google Shell Style Guide's flattest prohibition: never make a shell script setuid or setgid. The sgid bit on a script asks the kernel to run it with the group privileges of its owner, and suid asks the same for the user; both are honoured inconsistently across systems and are trivially subvertible on the ones that do honour them, because a shell script's behaviour depends on PATH, IFS and a dozen environment variables the caller controls. A script carrying suid or sgid is a way of handing your privileges to whoever can set an environment variable. Where a script genuinely must cross a privilege boundary, sudo with a narrowly written rule is the mechanism, because the rule lives somewhere the caller cannot edit — §18.20 works through what such a rule has to pin down.

The trade in the first two rows is worth stating plainly rather than leaving as folklore. env searches PATH, and searching PATH is exactly what you want on a developer machine (it finds the good bash) and exactly what you do not want in a privileged context (an attacker who controls PATH chooses your interpreter). §18.7 returns to this with the concrete attack. For the overwhelming majority of scripts — the ones in your repository, run by you and your colleagues — #!/usr/bin/env bash is right.

1.5 Execute, Source, or Invoke

There are three ways to run a script and they differ in which shell process ends up doing the work. This matters far more than it appears to, because it decides which variables survive, which directory you end up in, and whether exit kills your terminal.

printf 'v=set_by_script\n' > e.sh
v=original
bash e.sh   ; echo "after 'bash e.sh': v=$v"
source e.sh ; echo "after 'source'   : v=$v"

after 'bash e.sh': v=original
after 'source'   : v=set_by_script

bash e.sh starts a child process. It gets a copy of the exported environment, and anything it changes dies with it. source e.sh (or . e.sh) does not start a process at all — the current shell reads the file and runs its lines as if you had typed them, so assignments, cd, function definitions and exit all affect the shell you are sitting in.

Invocation
New process?
What it is for
./script.sh
Yes
The normal case. Needs the executable bit and a shebang.
bash script.sh
Yes
Overrides the shebang. Useful for bash -x script.sh when debugging (§20.12) and for running a bash script that is not executable.
source script.sh
No
Loading a function library or a settings file into the current shell (§9.13). Anything else is usually a mistake.

Note what the middle row buys you: because the shebang is only consulted when the kernel launches the file, naming an interpreter explicitly overrides it entirely. That is the escape hatch when a bash script arrives without the executable bit, or when you want to run one under a different bash than its first line names — /opt/homebrew/bin/bash ./deploy.sh runs a bash script written for 3.2 under 5.3 without editing it, which is the cheapest way to find out whether a version guard is the real problem.

The practical rule: a script that is meant to be executed and a file that is meant to be sourced are different kinds of file, and should look different. A sourced file defines things and sets variables; it must not call exit, because that exits the caller's shell. An executed script does work. §9.14 shows the guard that lets one file safely be both.

An invocation option belongs to whoever starts the shell

An invocation option is a flag given to the shell when it starts: bash -c 'string' runs a string as the script, bash -n file parses without running (§2.7), bash -x file traces (§20.12) and bash --posix changes the language (§19.1). An invocation option is chosen by the person or program that starts the shell, not by the script, which is why a script cannot rely on the options its own shebang line names: naming the interpreter on the command line overrides the shebang entirely. A script that needs an option sets it inside the file, with set -o or shopt (§22.5), and an invocation option is what a caller uses to change how a script that does not object runs, which is why bash -x script works on scripts written years ago.

1.6 When Not to Write It in Shell

The Google Shell Style Guide gives the clearest version of the rule, and it is worth taking seriously because it comes from an organisation with an enormous shell codebase and every incentive to like it: shell should be used for small utilities and for wrapper scripts around other programs, and if you are writing something longer than about a hundred lines, or that does anything non-trivial with data, rewrite it in a language with data structures.

The reasoning is not that shell is inelegant. It is that the things shell is bad at are exactly the things that grow:

It has one and a half data types. Strings, and arrays of strings. No nested structures, no records, no maps of lists. The moment your data has two dimensions you are encoding structure into delimiters and parsing it back out, which is where the quoting bugs live.
Error handling is bolted on. §11 is an entire section about the ways set -e does not do what its users believe. There is no exception mechanism, no stack trace by default, and no way to attach context to a failure.
It has no integer arithmetic worth the name and no floating point at all. §7.9 shows $(( )) silently truncating; anything numeric beyond counting wants a different language.
Every operation is a process. §21 measures this: a loop that calls one external command per line is about two thousand times slower, over ten thousand lines, than the equivalent single command, and the difference is not constant-factor tuning, it is the cost of fork().

What shell is unbeatably good at is the thing it was designed for: running other programs, wiring their inputs and outputs together, and reacting to their exit statuses. A ninety-line script that runs six tools in order, checks each one, and cleans up after itself is a better shell script than it would be a Python program, because in Python that same script is mostly subprocess.run boilerplate.

The honest test: if the script's interesting content is which commands to run in what order, shell is right. If the interesting content is what to do with the data those commands produced, it is time to leave. Recognising the crossing is a skill this course returns to in §21.8, once you know enough to see it coming.

The decision to rewrite in another language

The honest test ends in one of two decisions: keep it shell, or rewrite in another language. To rewrite in another language is not a failure of the script. It is the same design decision as choosing a data structure, made when the requirements show that the data has structure. It is rarely all-or-nothing: §21.8 shows a shell wrapper at the seam and one program behind it, and §22.11 applies the test to a tool as it grows. The reason to put the decision this early is that it is cheapest before the script has callers: to rewrite in another language a script that a hundred cron jobs and three teams depend on is a migration, not a rewrite.

1.7 How the Examples in This Course Are Produced

One methodological note, because it changes how much you should trust what follows.

Every claimed output in this course was produced by running the code that precedes it under bash 5.3.20, twice, with the results compared. That is not a figure of speech: the fragments are generated from a template that executes each example and pastes its real standard output, so a claim and the code that produced it cannot drift apart. When this course says a command prints something, it printed it.

Two things fall out of that discipline which you should adopt yourself. Examples run with LC_ALL=C, because bash localises its diagnostics and an error message is part of what a script does — on the machine this was written on, the ambient locale prints bash: linha 1: where the course needs bash: line 1:. And no example prints a duration, because timings are properties of a machine under a load, not of a program; where §21 makes a performance claim it prints a count or a ratio, and the numbers live in the prose where they can be labelled as measurements rather than guarantees.

Exercises

1. The version guard. Write a guard that requires bash 4.4 or newer — not just a major version — and prints the version it found. Why is [[ $BASH_VERSION > 4.4 ]] wrong?

Solution

Compare the components numerically. BASH_VERSINFO is an array whose first two elements are the major and minor versions as plain integers:

if (( BASH_VERSINFO[0] < 4 || (BASH_VERSINFO[0] == 4 && BASH_VERSINFO[1] < 4) )); then
  printf 'need bash >= 4.4, found %s\n' "$BASH_VERSION" >&2
  exit 1
fi
printf 'ok: bash %s.%s\n' "${BASH_VERSINFO[0]}" "${BASH_VERSINFO[1]}"

ok: bash 5.3

[[ $BASH_VERSION > 4.4 ]] is wrong for two independent reasons. First, > inside [[ ]] is a string comparison using the current locale's collation order, so it compares "5.3.20(1)-release" against "4.4" character by character; it happens to give the right answer here and gives the wrong one for "10.0", which sorts before "4.4" as text. Second, the version string carries a suffix ((1)-release) that is not part of any number, so there is no arrangement of string comparison that is correct in general. §7.4 covers the [[ ]] comparison operators and exactly which of them are numeric.

2. Reading the error. A colleague reports that running ./deploy.sh gives ./deploy.sh: /bin/bash^M: bad interpreter: No such file or directory. The file exists and /bin/bash exists. What happened, and how would you confirm it?

Solution

The file has Windows line endings. The shebang line is #!/bin/bash\r\n, so the kernel takes the interpreter to be /bin/bash\r — a filename ending in a carriage return, which does not exist. The ^M in the message is that carriage return being displayed.

Confirm it by looking at the bytes rather than the characters:

printf '#!/bin/bash\r\necho hi\r\n' > crlf.sh
head -1 crlf.sh | od -c | head -2

0000000    #   !   /   b   i   n   /   b   a   s   h  \r  \n            
0000015

The \r before the \n is the whole problem. file crlf.sh will also say with CRLF line terminators. Fix it with sed $'s/\r$//' crlf.sh > fixed.sh, or better, stop it recurring: set * text=auto eol=lf in .gitattributes so the repository stores LF endings regardless of who commits.

This failure mode is worth memorising because the error message points at the script and the missing file is the interpreter — the same misdirection as §1.3's bad interpreter example, with an invisible character on top.

3. Sourced or executed? You are given a file lib.sh that ends with exit 0. It works when run as ./lib.sh and closes the user's terminal when they source lib.sh. Explain precisely why, and give two ways to make the file safe to source.

Solution

source does not create a process. The current shell reads lib.sh and executes its lines itself, so exit 0 exits that shell — which, at an interactive prompt, is the terminal's login shell. A login shell is the one started for you when you sign in or open a terminal, and it is the process the window belongs to; killing it closes the window, which is why a stray exit in a sourced file is so much worse than a stray exit in a script. Executed as ./lib.sh, the exit ends the child process, which is exactly what it is for.

The two fixes:

Remove the exit. A file intended to be sourced should define functions and set variables and then simply end. Use return instead if you need to stop early — return is legal at the top level of a sourced file and is an error in an executed script.

Detect how it was loaded. BASH_SOURCE[0] is the path of the file currently being read, and $0 is the name the shell was invoked as. They are equal when the file is being executed and differ when it is being sourced:

cat > lib.sh <<'EOF'
greet() { echo "hello from the library"; }
if [[ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} == "$0" ]]; then
  echo "executed directly: running main"
  greet
else
  echo "sourced: only defining functions"
fi
EOF
chmod +x lib.sh
./lib.sh
source lib.sh
greet

executed directly: running main
hello from the library
sourced: only defining functions
hello from the library

This is the main guard, the shell counterpart of Python's if __name__ == "__main__":. §9.14 develops it into the standard layout for a file that is both a library and a command.

4. The hundred-line rule, applied. You are asked to write a script that reads a CSV of servers, groups them by datacentre, and for each datacentre with more than three servers, calls an API and merges the JSON responses into a report. Should this be a shell script? Argue both ways, then decide.

Solution

For shell: the work is mostly invoking other programs — curl for the API, and the CSV is a text file, which is shell's native input. If the tooling around it is already shell and the report is a one-off, a script that shells out to jq for the JSON is a legitimate ninety lines.

Against, and decisive: three of the four verbs are data manipulation, not process orchestration. Grouping by datacentre needs a map from string to list, which bash cannot represent — an associative array (§6.9) holds one string per key, so the list has to be encoded into a delimited string and split back out, and the delimiter must be a character no datacentre name can contain, which is an assumption about data you do not control. Merging JSON means either shelling out to jq for every merge or doing it in shell, and doing it in shell is how you get a parser written in sed. And a CSV cannot be split on commas — quoted fields may contain commas and newlines — so IFS=, is wrong on the first row that has an address in it.

The decision: not shell. The tell is that the interesting content is what happens to the data, not which commands run in what order. The middle path is often right, though: keep a short shell wrapper that handles arguments, credentials and cleanup, and have it call one Python program that does the data work. That plays to what each is good at, and it is exactly the boundary §21.8 teaches you to find.

SECTION 2

The Grammar: How Bash Reads a Line

Almost every confusing shell bug is a disagreement between what you thought a line meant and what the shell decided it meant. Resolving those arguments by experiment is slow and produces superstition — a colleague who "always puts quotes there because it broke once" has learned a ritual rather than a rule.

The alternative is to know the procedure. Bash reads a line in a fixed order: it splits the text into words, it decides what kind of command those words form, it expands them (§3 and §4), and only then does it run anything. Every rule in this section comes from that order, and the order never changes. Once you can run it in your head, the surprising cases stop being surprising — not because you have memorised them, but because you can derive them.

This section is the grammar half: how the shell gets from characters to a command. §3 and §4 are the expansion half: how it gets from a command to the arguments a program actually receives.

2.1 Words First, Meaning Second

The shell's first act is to break input into tokens, and it does this before it knows or cares what any of them mean. A token is either a word or an operator, and the boundary between them is decided by a small fixed set of characters.

Class
Characters, and what they do
Blank
Space and tab. Separates words, and is not part of any word. This is why x = 5 is not an assignment: it is the command x with two arguments.
Control operator
| |& & && || ; ;; ;& ;;& ( ) and newline. These separate commands and say how they relate.
Redirection operator
< > >> << <<- <<< <& >& <> >|, optionally preceded by a digit. These attach files to file descriptors (§10).
Metacharacter
The union of the above plus " ' and \. Unquoted, any of these ends the word it appears in.

Those four classes are worth holding onto, because the rest of the language refers back to them constantly. A control operator is what ends one command and begins the next, so it is what decides where a command boundary falls; a redirection operator never ends a command, it attaches a file to it, which is why echo hi > out.txt is one command and not two; and a metacharacter is simply any character that ends a word when it is unquoted, so the set of metacharacters is exactly the set of characters you must quote to use literally. Every quoting rule in §3 is a consequence of that last sentence, and every redirection in §10 is a consequence of the second.

The consequence that matters is that tokenisation happens before interpretation, and it is purely mechanical. Here is the sharpest demonstration in the whole grammar:

if=5
echo "a variable named 'if' now holds: ${if}"

a variable named 'if' now holds: 5

if is a reserved word. if=5 contains it. And yet this is a perfectly ordinary variable assignment, because the tokeniser produced the single word if=5 — which is not the word if, and reserved-word recognition compares whole words. The shell never had the opportunity to think of this as a conditional.

The same rule read from the other direction explains why keywords can be ordinary arguments:

# shellcheck disable=SC1010  # keywords as data is the point of this example
echo if then fi done esac
printf '[%s]' for in do done; echo

if then fi done esac
[for][in][do][done]

The directive on the first line is not decoration. ShellCheck flags every one of these words with SC1010 — "use a semicolon or linefeed before then" — because in code anyone actually means, a bare then in argument position is a missing semicolon rather than a deliberate string. That is a fair warning and the disable comment is the right response to it: the example is exercising a property of the grammar on purpose. §20.3 covers directives properly, including why a bare # shellcheck disable=SC1010 with no explanation is worse than the warning it silences.

Both lines are unambiguous to the shell and look alarming to a human. In the second, the four words that build every loop in the language are passed to printf as ordinary strings, and the shell has no difficulty at all — because it decides what a word means from where the word is, which is the subject of the next subsection. The same words would be loop syntax if any of them stood at the start of a command, and that is the entire difference.

Shell token, shell word and blank as a delimiter

The manual has exact names for the pieces, and later sections use them. A shell token is a sequence of characters that the shell treats as a single unit, and it is either a shell word or an operator. A shell word is a token that is not an operator: a command name, an argument, an assignment, a file name. What separates one word from the next is a delimiter, and the ordinary one is a blank — a space or a tab — which is a blank as a delimiter only when it is unquoted: inside quotes a blank is a character like any other, which is the whole of §3. A newline separates commands, not words. The metacharacters — the blank, the tab, the newline and | & ; ( ) < > — end a word when they are unquoted, and no other character does.

Shell grammar and parsing a line

The rules that say how tokens combine into commands are the shell grammar, and the manual gives it as a set of definitions — a simple command, a pipeline, a list, a compound command — that §2.3 to §2.6 take in turn. Parsing a line is applying them: the shell reads a line, breaks it into tokens, works out which commands and lists they form, and only then expands and runs anything (§4). Because parsing a line happens before any expansion, an expansion can never change the shape of a command; it can only change the words in it, and §3 and §4 are about how. It is also why a syntax error is found in a whole line, or a whole compound command, before any of it runs (§2.7).

2.2 Reserved Words Are Recognised by Position

Bash has 22 reserved words. They are not "keywords" in the way a compiled language has keywords, because they are only special in one place: the position where a command name would go.

compgen -k | sort | tr '\n' ' '; echo

! [[ ]] case coproc do done elif else esac fi for function if in select then time until while { }

A reserved word is recognised when it is the first word of a command, and ignored everywhere else. That is why echo done prints done while a bare done is a syntax error:

echo done
bash -c 'echo done; done' 2>&1 | head -1

done
bash: -c: line 1: syntax error near unexpected token `done'

In the first, done is an argument to echo, so no reserved word is involved. In the second, the ; ended the previous command, so done is in command position — and there is no loop for it to close.

Why this design, and why it matters to you. The shell's job is running programs, and programs have arbitrary names. If reserved words were reserved everywhere, you could not have a file called test or pass the argument in to a command. The cost of that flexibility is that the shell's grammar is context-sensitive: the same characters are syntax or data depending on position, and you cannot tell which by looking at them in isolation. This is exactly why an unquoted variable is so dangerous (§3.4) — the shell decides what the expanded text means, and expansion happens after the grammar has already been settled, which is the subject of §4.8.

Two of these reserved words are worth a note now because they surprise people:

time is a reserved word, not a program. That is precisely why it can time a whole pipeline rather than a single command — a program could only ever time one child, but a keyword is part of the grammar:

printf '  type -t time        -> %s\n' "$(type -t time)"
printf '  type -t /usr/bin/time -> %s\n' "$(type -t /usr/bin/time)"

  type -t time        -> keyword
  type -t /usr/bin/time -> file

[[ is also a reserved word, and [ is not — [ is a builtin command whose last argument must be ]. That single difference is the source of every behavioural gap between them, and §7.2 spends a subsection on it.

The time keyword

time is a reserved word, the time keyword, and not a program. Like the other reserved words it is recognised by position, only where a command may start, and it times the whole pipeline that follows it, which a program named time (/usr/bin/time) cannot do: that would see only its own single command. Its report is formatted by TIMEFORMAT, and §21.1 uses the time keyword to tell a script that is waiting from one that is working.

2.3 The Simple Command, and the Assignment Prefix

A simple command is the base case of the whole grammar: an optional sequence of assignments, then a command name, then arguments, with redirections allowed anywhere among them.

LC_ALL=C
assignment prefix
sort
command name
-u names.txt
arguments
> out.txt
redirection

The assignment prefix has a property that is genuinely useful and widely misunderstood: an assignment written before a command name applies only to that command, and does not change the shell running it.

v=outer
v=inner env | grep '^v='
echo "after the prefixed command, v=$v"

v=inner
after the prefixed command, v=outer

The child saw v=inner; the shell still has v=outer. This is the correct way to run one command in a modified environment — LC_ALL=C sort, TZ=UTC date, DEBUG=1 ./script.sh — and it is better than export-ing because it cannot leak into anything else. Note that the variable is placed in the environment of the child, which is why env can see it; §16.3 covers the difference between a shell variable and an environment variable, which is exactly what this construct exploits.

The trap is that this only works when there is a command. v=inner alone is an ordinary assignment to the current shell, and v=inner; env is two separate commands, so the prefix form and the semicolon form mean entirely different things despite looking similar.

An assignment preceding a command

An assignment preceding a command — LC_ALL=C sort file, or GREETING=hello bash -c 'echo "$GREETING"' — puts the variable in that one command's environment and leaves the shell's own variables alone:

GREETING=hello bash -c 'echo "inside: $GREETING"'
echo "afterwards: ${GREETING-unset}"

inside: hello
afterwards: unset

The child saw the variable and the shell never set it. That is the difference between an assignment preceding a command and an assignment on a line of its own, which does set the variable in the shell, and it is why IFS= read -r line (§14.1) changes IFS for the read alone.

2.4 Pipelines

A pipeline is one or more commands separated by |, with the standard output of each connected to the standard input of the next. Optionally preceded by !, which inverts its exit status.

The rule people get wrong is which status a pipeline reports. It is the last command's, and nothing else:

false | true ; echo "false | true  -> $?"
true  | false; echo "true  | false -> $?"

false | true  -> 0
true  | false -> 1

The first line is the dangerous one. A pipeline whose first command failed completely reports success, because true succeeded. This is why curl ... | tar xz reports success when curl 404s and pipes an HTML error page into tar — and why set -o pipefail exists:

set -o pipefail
false | true; echo "with pipefail -> $?"

with pipefail -> 1

pipefail makes a pipeline report the rightmost non-zero status, or zero if all succeeded. §11.7 covers it properly, including the cases where it makes things worse; for now, know that the default is last command wins and that it is rarely what you want.

! inverts the status of the whole pipeline, and it is a reserved word, so it needs to be its own word:

if ! false; then echo "! inverted the status"; fi

! inverted the status

This is the idiomatic way to test for failure, and it matters under set -e in a way §11.3 makes precise.

A bash pipeline

A bash pipeline is one or more commands separated by |, or by |&, which also sends the left command's standard error into the pipe. Its status is the last command's unless pipefail is set (§11.7), each stage runs in its own subshell unless lastpipe says otherwise (§16.6), and the whole pipeline can be negated with ! or timed with the time keyword. A bash pipeline is also where the shell's first performance fact lives: every stage is a fork, so : | : is two forks per execution even though both commands are builtins (§21.2 counted them).

2.5 Lists, and the Precedence Trap

A list is a sequence of pipelines joined by ;, &, && or ||. The first two say when to run the next thing; the second two say whether. Each of the four is a command separator — it ends one command and starts another — and a newline is a command separator too, which is why a script needs no punctuation at the end of its lines.

a ; b — run a, wait for it, then run b regardless of how it went. A newline means the same thing.
a & b — start a in the background and move to b immediately, without waiting. The status of a & is 0, because it reports that the launch succeeded, not the program (§17.3).
a && b — run b only if a succeeded (exit status 0).
a || b — run b only if a failed (any non-zero status).

Now the trap, and it is worth real attention because it is invisible in review. && and || have equal precedence and associate left to right. They do not behave like && and || in C, Python, JavaScript or any other language you know, where && binds tighter.

false || echo "first ran" && echo "second also ran"

first ran
second also ran

Read as a C programmer would — false || (echo A && echo B) — this output is impossible to explain. Read left to right, it is obvious: false || echo "first ran" is a list that succeeded (because echo succeeded), and && echo "second also ran" therefore runs.

This produces a specific, common, real bug. The pattern command || echo "failed" >&2 && exit 1 looks like it means "if the command fails, complain and exit". It means nothing of the sort: when command succeeds, the || branch is skipped, the list's status is the command's success, and && exit 1 runs anyway. The script exits 1 on the happy path.

The fix is to group explicitly, which also documents the intent:

run() { return "$1"; }
run 0 || { echo "failed" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "reached the end with status $?"

reached the end with status 0

The rule to carry: && and || chains longer than two elements should be braces or an if. A three-element chain is already ambiguous to every reader, including the one who wrote it.

Sequential list, asynchronous list, an and-list and an or-list

The manual names four kinds of list, and every script is made of them. A sequential list is commands separated by ; or a newline, run one after another. An asynchronous list is a command terminated by &, which the shell starts and does not wait for. An and-list, a && b, runs b only if a succeeded, and an or-list, a || b, runs b only if a failed; an and-list and an or-list have equal precedence and group from the left, which is the precedence trap above.

echo one; echo two
true && echo "and-list ran"
false || echo "or-list ran"
{ sleep 0.2; echo "background done"; } & echo "foreground first"; wait

one
two
and-list ran
or-list ran
foreground first
background done

The sequential list printed in order. The and-list and the or-list each ran their second command because the first did what the operator was waiting for. And the asynchronous list — the braces, started with & — let the foreground echo run first and finished afterwards, which is why the wait is there.

The newline separator

The newline separator ends a command exactly as ; does, and the two are interchangeable at the end of a command. The exceptions are the places where the shell is sure the command is not finished: after an operator such as &&, || or |, after a backslash, and inside an open quote, where the shell keeps reading. So echo one && followed by a newline and echo continued is one and-list, and this is what makes the pipeline layout of §22.2 legal.

2.6 Grouping: { } and ( )

Two constructs group a list into one unit, and the difference between them is one of the most consequential in the language.

( list ) runs the list in a subshell — a forked copy of the shell. Changes inside it are discarded.

{ list; } runs the list in the current shell. It is pure grouping, with no process created.

# shellcheck disable=SC2030,SC2031  # the lost modification is the demonstration
v=original
( v=changed; echo "  inside ( ): $v" )
echo "  after   ( ): $v"
{ v=changed; echo "  inside { }: $v"; }
echo "  after   { }: $v"

  inside ( ): changed
  after   ( ): original
  inside { }: changed
  after   { }: changed

§16 is devoted to what a subshell inherits and what it cannot give back, because the "variable set inside a loop is empty after it" bug is the most reported problem in all of shell scripting and this is its root.

The syntax of { } has two requirements that trip everyone, and both follow from §2.1's tokenisation rule rather than being arbitrary:

bash -c '{echo no-space; }' 2>&1 | head -1
bash -c '{ echo no-terminator }' 2>&1 | head -1

bash: -c: line 1: syntax error near unexpected token `}'
bash: -c: line 2: syntax error: unexpected end of file from `{' command on line 1

{ needs a space after it, because { is a reserved word and not an operator — {echo tokenises as the single word {echo, which is a command name, not a brace. And the list needs a terminator before } — a ; or a newline — because } is likewise a reserved word that must appear in command position, and echo no-terminator } puts it in argument position where it is just a word. ( ) has neither requirement, because parentheses are control operators and therefore self-delimiting.

2.7 When a Syntax Error Is Found

§1.1 claimed that a script does not get parsed before it runs. Here is the demonstration, because the consequence is severe enough to deserve one:

cat > mid.sh <<'EOF'
echo "line 1 ran"
echo "line 2 ran"
for x in a b c
  echo "missing do"
done
echo "line 6"
EOF
bash mid.sh
echo "status=$?"

line 1 ran
line 2 ran
mid.sh: line 4: syntax error near unexpected token `echo'
mid.sh: line 4: `  echo "missing do"'
status=2

Two lines of work happened before the shell noticed that line 4 could not possibly be valid. If those lines had deleted a directory or started a deployment, they would still have done so.

Bash reads and parses one complete command at a time, where "complete command" means a whole compound structure — an entire if, an entire function definition, an entire loop. That is why the error appeared at line 4 rather than line 3: the for was incomplete until the parser hit a word where do should be.

The mitigation is free and belongs in every commit. bash -n parses without executing:

cat > mid.sh <<'EOF'
for x in a b c
  echo "missing do"
done
EOF
bash -n mid.sh
echo "bash -n status=$?"

mid.sh: line 2: syntax error near unexpected token `echo'
mid.sh: line 2: `  echo "missing do"'
bash -n status=2

bash -n catches only syntax. It has no opinion about whether git swtich is a real command or whether $dir might be empty when you rm -rf it — that is what ShellCheck is for, and §20 makes it a gate. But it is instant, it is built in, and there is no reason for a script with a syntax error to ever reach a colleague.

2.8 Comments

A # begins a comment only when it starts a word. In the middle of a word it is an ordinary character:

echo hello # this is a comment
echo not#a#comment
echo "a # inside quotes is literal"

hello
not#a#comment
a # inside quotes is literal

This is the same positional rule as reserved words, applied to a character instead of a word, and it explains why echo foo#bar needs no escaping while echo foo #bar loses everything after foo. It also explains a real annoyance: a URL fragment like https://example.com/page#section is safe as a bare word, but the moment there is a space before the # — as in a comment-looking string built by expansion — the meaning changes.

Comments run to the end of the line and there is no block-comment syntax. The usual substitute is a quoted heredoc sent nowhere, which the shell parses but never executes:

: <<'NOTES'
Anything here is read as a here-document and discarded.
It is not executed, and $variables are not expanded because
the delimiter is quoted (§10.9).
NOTES
echo "the script continues"

the script continues

: is the null command — a builtin that does nothing and succeeds. §11.9 uses it again for a different purpose.

A shell comment

A shell comment starts at a # that begins a word and runs to the end of the line. A # in the middle of a word is an ordinary character, and only the start of a word is special:

echo a#b # a comment

a#b

The # inside a#b stayed, and the one after the space started a shell comment that was discarded during tokenisation, so nothing in it is expanded or run. Comments work the same in a script and, by default, in an interactive bash (the interactive_comments option is on).

Exercises

1. Predict the output. Without running it, say what each line prints and why:

echo a && echo b || echo c
echo a || echo b && echo c
false && echo b || echo c
Solution 
echo a && echo b || echo c
echo ---
echo a || echo b && echo c
echo ---
false && echo b || echo c

a
b
---
a
c
---
c

Evaluate strictly left to right, tracking the status of the list so far.

Line 1: echo a succeeds → && echo b runs, succeeds → || echo c is skipped. Prints a, b.

Line 2: echo a succeeds → || echo b is skipped, and the list's status is still 0 → && echo c runs. Prints a, c. This is the surprising one, and it is the shape of the command || echo failed && exit 1 bug from §2.5: the || branch being skipped does not make the list fail.

Line 3: false fails → && echo b is skipped, list status still non-zero → || echo c runs. Prints c.

The general rule: && and || are not expression operators, they are list separators that inspect the running status. There is no precedence to remember because there is no precedence.

2. Why does this fail? Explain the error, then fix it two ways. ❌ counter-example:

# ❌ deliberately broken — this is the exercise
if [ -f /etc/hosts ] { echo "exists" }
Solution

It contains three separate errors, all of them instances of §2.1's tokenisation rule.

if requires the reserved word then, not a brace — bash is not C. { needs a space after it to be a reserved word rather than the first characters of the word {echo. And the list before } needs a terminator.

The direct fix:

if [ -f /etc/hosts ]; then echo "exists"; fi

exists

Note the ; after ]: then is a reserved word and must be in command position, so the test command has to be terminated first. Written across lines, the newline does that job and the semicolon disappears — which is why the multi-line form has no semicolons and the one-line form has two.

The second fix uses the fact that [ is just a command with a status, so && works directly:

[ -f /etc/hosts ] && echo "exists"

exists

This form is idiomatic for a single guarded command. It is not a general replacement for if, because its own status is that of the last thing it ran — which under set -e at the end of a function is a genuine trap that §11.5 covers.

3. The keyword that is not. time and [[ are reserved words; [ and test are builtins. Demonstrate one behaviour that is only possible because time is a reserved word, and one that is only possible because [ is a command.

Solution

Because time is part of the grammar, it takes a pipeline as its operand, so it can time several processes at once. A program could never do this — by the time /usr/bin/time is running, it is a single process that can only fork one child:

time_report=$( { time { sleep 0.01 | cat ; } ; } 2>&1 )
echo "timed a whole pipeline; report has $(printf '%s\n' "$time_report" | grep -c .) lines"
printf '%s\n' "$time_report" | grep -o '^real' || true

timed a whole pipeline; report has 3 lines
real

Because [ is an ordinary command, its arguments are subject to every normal expansion, and it can be looked up, aliased and even replaced:

type -t '['
printf '  argument count seen by [ : '
[ -f /etc/hosts ] && echo "and it needs a literal ] as its last argument"

builtin
  argument count seen by [ : and it needs a literal ] as its last argument

That last property is the whole story of [ versus [[. Since [ receives its operands as ordinary expanded words, an empty or word-split variable changes the number of arguments and therefore changes which test is being performed — [ $x = y ] with an empty x becomes [ = y ], a syntax error. Inside [[ ]], which the parser handles itself, no word splitting or globbing occurs and the same expression is safe. §7.2 measures the difference across the full operator set.

4. A block comment that bites. This is intended to comment out a block, and it destroys the script instead. Say what happens and why.

: <<NOTES
The old implementation used $(rm -rf "$tmpdir") here.
NOTES
Solution

The heredoc delimiter is unquoted, so the body is subject to parameter expansion, command substitution and arithmetic expansion exactly like a double-quoted string. $(rm -rf "$tmpdir") is therefore executed while the "comment" is being read.

tmpdir=$(mktemp -d)
touch "$tmpdir/important.txt"
echo "before: $(ls "$tmpdir" | wc -l | tr -d ' ') file(s)"
: <<NOTES
The old implementation used $(rm -rf "${tmpdir:?}"/*) here.
NOTES
echo "after:  $(ls "$tmpdir" | wc -l | tr -d ' ') file(s)"

before: 1 file(s)
after:  0 file(s)

The file is gone, and nothing in the script looks like it deleted anything.

The fix is one character: quote the delimiter, : <<'NOTES'. A quoted delimiter — 'NOTES', "NOTES" or \NOTES — makes the entire body literal, which is what a comment must be. §10.9 covers the rule in full, and it is the same rule that decides whether a heredoc used to generate a config file interpolates the shell's variables or the target program's.

This is worth internalising beyond the comment case: an unquoted heredoc delimiter means the body is live code. It is the reason a heredoc that writes an awk script or a systemd unit mangles every $1 and ${VAR} in it unless the delimiter is quoted.

SECTION 3

Quoting, Word Splitting and IFS

If you fix only one habit from this course, make it this section. Unquoted expansions are the single largest source of shell defects — not because they usually break, but because they usually work, right up until a filename has a space in it, a variable is empty, or a value arrives from somewhere you do not control. The bug is latent by construction, which is why it reaches production.

The mistake most people make is thinking of quotes as string delimiters, the way they are in every other language. They are not. In shell, a bare word is already a string; echo hello needs no quotes and gains nothing from them. What quotes actually do is switch off steps of the expansion pipeline. "$file" is not "the string $file" — it is the value of file with word splitting and pathname expansion disabled. Once you read quotes as disabling machinery rather than marking strings, the rules stop needing to be memorised.

The linux course covers quoting at the prompt in its §2.2. This section is the scripting half: the exact algorithm, the cases that surprise, and the rules you can apply without thinking.

3.1 The Three Quoting Mechanisms, and What Each Switches Off

Form
What it disables
\c
Everything, for exactly one character. Outside quotes, a backslash makes the next character literal — including a newline, where it removes the line break entirely.
'…'
Everything. No expansion of any kind happens inside single quotes, and there is no escape character, so a single quote cannot appear inside them at all.
"…"
Word splitting and pathname expansion. Parameter expansion, command substitution and arithmetic expansion still happen — which is what makes double quotes the useful default.
$'…'
Everything, like single quotes, but after interpreting C-style escapes: \n, \t, \xNN, \uNNNN, \NNN octal.

Single quotes are absolute, and it is worth seeing how absolute:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # an inert $ is exactly what is being shown
printf '%s\n' 'a$b`c\d'

a$b`c\d

A dollar, a backtick and a backslash, all inert. This is why single quotes are correct for anything you want the shell to leave alone: an awk program, a sed expression, a password, a regex.

The cost is that a single quote cannot be escaped inside single quotes — there is no mechanism, because no character is special. The idiom is to close, escape, and reopen:

echo 'it'\''s done'
echo "it's easier in double quotes"

it's done
it's easier in double quotes

Read 'it'\''s done' as four pieces glued together with no spaces: 'it', then \', then 's done'. The shell concatenates adjacent quoted and unquoted fragments into one word, which is the same rule that makes "$dir"/file.txt work.

$'…' is the escape-interpreting form, and it is the right way to get a tab or a newline into a variable:

printf '%s' $'a\tb\n'
v=$'line1\nline2'
echo "the variable holds ${#v} characters"

a	b
the variable holds 11 characters

Eleven characters: line1 is five, line2 is five, and the \n between them is one. Had that been written 'line1\nline2' it would be twelve, with a literal backslash and n.

Locale translation: $"..."

$"..." is a double-quoted string that also asks for locale translation: if the current locale has a message catalogue with a translation of the string, the translation is used. Where there is none, and in the C locale, it is the same as a plain double-quoted string:

echo $"hello, world"

hello, world

Locale translation is a poor fit for a script that has to behave the same everywhere, since the result depends on the machine's locale and installed catalogues, and it is a hazard when the string is later compared or parsed. It is worth recognising when it appears in someone else's script, and worth not writing.

The backslash escape

A backslash escape quotes the single character after it: the character keeps its plain meaning and loses any special one. It is the tool for one character, where single and double quotes are for a run of them:

echo a\ b\ \ c
echo \$HOME
echo one \
  two

a b  c
$HOME
one two

Each escaped space stayed part of the word, so a\ b\ \ c was one word with three spaces in it; the backslash escape in \$HOME stopped the expansion; and a backslash at the end of a line is a backslash escape of the newline, which the shell removes, so the two lines were one command. The other quoting forms handle the backslash differently (§3.2), and inside double quotes it is special only before $, `, ", \ and a newline.

3.2 Inside Double Quotes, Backslash Is Almost Never Special

This one catches people who arrive from C or Python, where "\n" in a string is a newline. In shell it is not:

printf '%s\n' "a\$b"
printf '%s\n' "a\\b"
printf '%s\n' "a\nb"
printf '%s\n' "a\tb"

a$b
a\b
a\nb
a\tb

Inside double quotes a backslash is special before exactly five characters — $, `, ", \, and a newline — and is an ordinary backslash before anything else. So "a\nb" is a four-character string containing a literal backslash, and the only reason printf turns it into a newline in other examples is that printf interprets escapes in its format string itself. That is a property of printf, not of quoting, and it is why printf '%s\n' "$x" is safe while printf "$x" is a bug: in the second form the data is being read as a format string, which §14.11 shows being exploited.

3.3 Word Splitting Happens Only to Expansions

Here is the rule that makes the whole thing tractable, and it is narrower than most people assume. The shell does not split your source code into words at whitespace and then expand. It splits the results of expansions, and only those.

# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # the unquoted expansion is the subject of this section
printf '[%s]\n' a\ b
x='a b'
printf '[%s]\n' $x
printf '[%s]\n' "$x"

[a b]
[a]
[b]
[a b]

Three lines, three results. The first has a literal escaped space and is one word — the shell never reconsiders it. The second is an unquoted expansion, so the value a b is split into two words after substitution. The third is quoted, so splitting is off and the value stays one word.

The order matters and it is the subject of §4: the shell substitutes the value first, then splits what came out. That is why a variable's contents can change how many arguments a command receives, and why no amount of care at the assignment site helps. x='a b' is a perfectly ordinary assignment; the damage happens at the point of use.

Splitting only applies to expansions

Splitting only applies to expansions. The results of a parameter expansion, a command substitution and an arithmetic expansion are split at the characters of IFS; text written in the script is never split, and a quoted expansion is not split either. So the same two words behave differently depending on where they came from:

# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # the unquoted expansion is the point
words='a b'
printf '[%s]' $words; echo
printf '[%s]' 'a b'; echo

[a][b]
[a b]

The variable's value was split into two arguments and the literal was not. Splitting only applies to expansions, which is why quoting the expansion is the whole cure and why no quoting is needed on a literal.

3.4 IFS: the Field Separator, and Its Two Kinds of Character

Splitting is governed by IFS — the internal field separator. Its default value is space, tab and newline. What is not obvious is that IFS characters come in two classes with different rules, and the difference is visible only in the edge cases that break scripts.

# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # every $s here is unquoted on purpose
show() { printf 'fields=%d ' "$#"; printf '[%s]' "$@"; echo; }
s='  a  b  '   ; t='a::b:' ; u='a: :b'
IFS=' '  ; set -- $s ; show "$@"
IFS=':'  ; set -- $t ; show "$@"
IFS=' :' ; set -- $u ; show "$@"
IFS=':'  ; set -- $u ; show "$@"
IFS=''   ; set -- $s ; show "$@"
unset IFS; set -- $s ; show "$@"

fields=2 [a][b]
fields=3 [a][][b]
fields=3 [a][][b]
fields=3 [a][ ][b]
fields=1 [  a  b  ]
fields=2 [a][b]

Read those six lines carefully, because every rule is in them.

IFS whitespace is greedy and edge-trimming. Line 1: ' a b ' with IFS=' ' gives two fields, not six. Runs of IFS whitespace collapse into a single separator, and leading and trailing runs produce no empty fields at all.

Non-whitespace IFS is literal and every occurrence counts. Line 2: 'a::b:' with IFS=':' gives three fields, a, empty, b. The :: produces a genuine empty field. But the trailing : does not produce a fourth — a single trailing delimiter terminates the last field rather than starting a new one. That asymmetry is the detail people get wrong when hand-parsing /etc/passwd or a CSV line, and it is worth checking rather than assuming: a trailing empty field is invisible, and a script that counts fields will disagree with one that iterates them.

The two classes mix. Line 3 sets IFS=' :', so space is whitespace-class and : is not; 'a: :b' gives a, empty, b, because the space around the colon is absorbed as whitespace. Line 4 sets IFS=':' only, so the space is now ordinary data and the middle field is [ ] — one space. Same input, same field count, different contents.

IFS='' disables splitting entirely (line 5), which is exactly why while IFS= read -r line preserves leading and trailing whitespace — §8.8 returns to this idiom, which is the correct way to read a file line by line (§14.4 explains its -r) and the reason is right here.

Unsetting IFS restores the default (line 6) rather than disabling splitting. IFS= and unset IFS are not the same thing, and confusing them is a real bug: the first switches splitting off, the second switches it back to space-tab-newline.

A null field

With IFS set to a comma, the input x,,z has three fields, and the middle one is a null field: empty but present. A whitespace IFS behaves differently, since adjacent whitespace characters count as one delimiter:

IFS=, read -r a b c <<< 'x,,z'
printf '[%s]' "$a" "$b" "$c"; echo
IFS=' ' read -r a b c <<< 'x  z'
printf '[%s]' "$a" "$b" "$c"; echo

[x][][z]
[x][z][]

The comma kept the null field and put z in the third variable. The two spaces collapsed, so there was no null field at all and the third variable was left empty. A null field is what makes a non-whitespace IFS a real field splitter for delimited data, and whitespace IFS only a word splitter.

3.5 "$@" and "$*"

These two look interchangeable and are not. "$@" expands to one word per positional parameter; "$*" joins them into a single word using the first character of IFS.

# shellcheck disable=SC2068  # pass_bare's unquoted $@ is the counter-example
count() { printf 'saw %d: ' "$#"; printf '[%s]' "$@"; echo; }
pass_at()   { count "$@"; }
pass_star() { count "$*"; }
pass_bare() { count $@; }
pass_at   'a b' 'c  d'
pass_star 'a b' 'c  d'
pass_bare 'a b' 'c  d'

saw 2: [a b][c  d]
saw 1: [a b c  d]
saw 4: [a][b][c][d]

Two arguments went in. "$@" delivered exactly two, with their internal spaces intact — including c d's two spaces. "$*" delivered one. Bare $@ delivered four, having split on whitespace and destroyed the distinction between the arguments and the spaces inside them.

"$@" — with the quotes — is the only correct way to pass arguments through. A wrapper script, a function that forwards to a command, a main "$@" at the bottom of a file: all of them need the quoted form, every time. The unquoted $@ is never what you want, and neither is unquoted $*.

"$*" has exactly one good use: producing a human-readable joining of the arguments, usually with IFS set deliberately.

set -- alpha beta gamma
( IFS=', '; echo "joined: $*" )
( IFS=$'\n'; echo "one per line:"; echo "$*" )

joined: alpha,beta,gamma
one per line:
alpha
beta
gamma

Look closely at the first line: IFS=', ' was set to a comma and a space, and the output has no spaces. "$*" joins using only the first character of IFS, not the whole string. To get alpha, beta, gamma you cannot go through "$*" at all — the join string has to be applied some other way, such as printf '%s, ' "$@" and trimming the tail, which §15.9 works through.

Note the subshell around each. IFS is a global, and setting it for one command is worth doing in a way that cannot leak — §3.7 covers the safe patterns.

The empty case is worth knowing because it differs. With no positional parameters, "$@" expands to nothing at all — zero words, not one empty word — while "$*" expands to one empty word:

set --
count() { printf 'got %d argument(s)\n' "$#"; }
count "$@"
count "$*"

got 0 argument(s)
got 1 argument(s)

This is why cmd "$@" with no arguments runs cmd cleanly, and cmd "$*" runs cmd with one empty argument — which for many programs means "operate on the file named empty string" and fails confusingly.

$@ unquoted and $* unquoted

$@ unquoted and $* unquoted are the same thing: each is split at the characters of IFS after expansion, and empty arguments disappear. Only the quoted forms differ, and only they are useful:

# shellcheck disable=SC2048,SC2068,SC2086  # the unquoted forms are the point
set -- 'two words' '' last
printf '[%s]' $@; echo
printf '[%s]' $*; echo
printf '[%s]' "$@"; echo

[two][words][last]
[two][words][last]
[two words][][last]

Unquoted, $@ and $* both broke two words into two arguments and lost the empty one. Only "$@" kept all three arguments as they were, so an unquoted $@ or $* is a bug wherever it appears, and ShellCheck reports it as one.

The shift builtin

The shift builtin discards $1 and renumbers the rest, and shift n discards n of them. It is how a hand-written option parser consumes what it has handled (§13.2), and it fails, changing nothing, when asked to shift more than there are:

set -- a b c
shift
echo "after shift: $* ($# left)"
shift 2
echo "after shift 2: ($# left)"
set -- a
shift 2
echo "status $? left $#"

after shift: b c (2 left)
after shift 2: (0 left)
status 1 left 1

shift removed a, shift 2 removed the remaining two, and the shift builtin asked for two of one parameter left it alone and returned 1. A parser that shifts by two for an option with an argument checks first that two are there (§13.6).

Special parameters: $#, $0, $?, $$ and $!

A special parameter is one whose name is a single punctuation character or digit, and which the shell sets and you cannot assign to. $# is the number of positional parameters, $0 the name the script was run as, $? the status of the last command, $$ the shell's own process ID and $! the process ID of the last background job. The others in the family, $@, $* and $-, have their own subsections:

set -- a b c
echo "arguments: $#"
echo "script name: ${0##*/}"
true; echo "last status: $?"
false; echo "after false: $?"
echo "shell PID is a number: $([[ $$ =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] && echo yes)"
sleep 0.1 & echo "background PID is a number: $([[ $! =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] && echo yes)"; wait

arguments: 3
script name: example.sh
last status: 0
after false: 1
shell PID is a number: yes
background PID is a number: yes

The values of $$ and $! differ on every run, which is why the example tests their shape and does not print them. $? changes with every command, so it has to be read at once or saved (§11.1). A special parameter is read like any variable and needs the same quoting, though the numeric ones ($#, $$, $?) can never contain a space.

3.6 What an Unquoted Expansion Actually Costs

An unquoted expansion is subject to two further steps, not one: word splitting and pathname expansion. The second is the one people forget.

mkdir -p demo && cd demo
touch a.txt b.txt
v='* a.txt'
echo "quoted:   [$v]"
# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # the glob and the split are the demonstration
set -- $v; printf 'unquoted field: [%s]\n' "$@"

quoted:   [* a.txt]
unquoted field: [a.txt]
unquoted field: [b.txt]
unquoted field: [a.txt]

The variable held two words. Unquoted, it produced three — because after splitting into * and a.txt, the * was expanded against the directory and matched every file in it. The value of a variable became a directory listing, and a.txt appears twice: once from the glob, once from the literal second word. In a directory with a hundred files it would have produced a hundred and one arguments.

This is not a contrived example. It is what happens when a filename, a search pattern, or a command-line argument containing *, ? or [ passes through an unquoted expansion — and * is a completely ordinary character in a search pattern.

set -f (equivalently set -o noglob) disables pathname expansion, and it isolates the two effects:

mkdir -p demo && cd demo
touch a.txt b.txt
v='* a.txt'
set -f
# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # deliberately unquoted, to isolate what set -f changes
set -- $v; printf 'with set -f: [%s]\n' "$@"

with set -f: [*]
with set -f: [a.txt]

Two fields now — split, but not globbed. set -f is a real tool for the case where you genuinely want splitting and genuinely do not want globbing, and §18.13 uses it defensively. But it is a global switch on a global behaviour, and the far better answer in almost every case is a quote.

3.7 Changing IFS Without Breaking Everything Downstream

IFS is one shell variable shared by everything, so changing it is a global act. Three patterns are safe and one common one is not.

The assignment prefix — best when it applies to a single command. §2.3's rule applies: the assignment lasts exactly as long as the command:

line='root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash'
IFS=: read -r user pass uid gid gecos home sh <<< "$line"
printf 'user=%s pass=%s uid=%s gid=%s gecos=%s home=%s shell=%s\n' \
       "$user" "$pass" "$uid" "$gid" "$gecos" "$home" "$sh"
printf 'IFS afterwards is still the default: %s\n' "$(printf '%q' "$IFS")"

user=root pass=x uid=0 gid=0 gecos=root home=/root shell=/bin/bash
IFS afterwards is still the default: $' \t\n'

IFS=: read ... splits that one line on colons and leaves IFS untouched for everything after it. %q prints the value in a form you could paste back — here $' \t\n', confirming space, tab and newline are intact. This is the single most useful IFS idiom in the language.

A subshell — best when several commands need it, and you do not need their variables afterwards:

set -- alpha beta
( IFS='|'; echo "inside:  $*" )
echo "outside: $IFS is unchanged (printed as $(printf '%q' "$IFS"))"

inside:  alpha|beta
outside:  	
 is unchanged (printed as $' \t\n')

Note the ugly second line: $IFS was expanded unquoted into the message, printing an actual space, tab and newline. That is the correct output for what was written and a good reminder that IFS holds real control characters — which is why printf '%q' is the only sane way to display it.

Save and restore — necessary when the change must persist across commands in the current shell:

old_ifs=$IFS
csv='a,b,c'
IFS=,
# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # splitting on IFS is the point
set -- $csv
printf 'split into %d fields\n' "$#"
IFS=$old_ifs
printf 'restored: %s\n' "$(printf '%q' "$IFS")"

split into 3 fields
restored: $' \t\n'

The pattern that is not safe is IFS=, followed by a bare unset IFS to "restore" it. unset restores the default, not whatever the caller had — if your function was called from code that had deliberately set IFS=$'\n', you have silently changed its behaviour. Save the old value and put it back.

3.8 The Rules, Applied Mechanically

Everything above reduces to a short list you can follow without thinking about it, which is the point — quoting decisions made by reasoning are quoting decisions made inconsistently.

Quote every expansion. "$var", "$(cmd)", "${arr[@]}", "$@". The default is quotes; leaving them off is the decision that needs justifying, not the other way round.
The exceptions are few and deliberate. Inside [[ ]] and (( )) no splitting occurs, so quotes are optional there (§7.2). And when you want a string split into words, leave it unquoted on purpose and set IFS to say how — with a comment, because a reader must be able to tell the deliberate case from the forgotten one.
Single-quote anything meant for another program. An awk script, a sed expression, a regex, a jq filter. Those languages have their own $, and double quotes hand it to the shell first.
Put quotes around the whole word, not the variable. "$dir/$name.txt", not "$dir"/"$name".txt. Both work — adjacent fragments concatenate — but the first is what everyone reads.
Let ShellCheck enforce it. SC2086 is the unquoted-expansion warning and it is the most valuable single check the tool has. §20 makes it a gate; until then, run shellcheck on anything you are about to commit.

The last one deserves emphasis. Every rule in this section is mechanically checkable, and a tool that checks it does not get tired, does not make exceptions at 6pm, and does not assume that this particular filename will never contain a space.

Exercises

1. Count the arguments. For each line, say how many arguments count receives. Assume x='a b', y='', and the current directory holds exactly one.txt and two.txt.

# shellcheck disable=SC2086,SC2035  # each unquoted form is the question
count $x
count "$x"
count $y
count "$y"
count *.txt
count "*.txt"
Solution 
# shellcheck disable=SC2086,SC2035  # each unquoted form is the question
count() { printf '%d\n' "$#"; }
mkdir -p d && cd d
touch one.txt two.txt
x='a b'; y=''
count $x
count "$x"
count $y
count "$y"
count *.txt
count "*.txt"

2
1
0
1
2
1

The interesting pair is lines 3 and 4. An unquoted expansion of an empty variable produces zero words, not one empty word. After substitution the field is empty, and word splitting discards empty fields that did not come from a quoted expansion — so count $y calls count with no arguments at all.

That is the mechanism behind a whole family of real bugs. rm -rf $dir/ with an empty dir does not run rm -rf ''; it runs rm -rf /. And [ $y = "" ] with an empty y becomes [ = "" ], which is a syntax error rather than a false — the reason [ -z "$y" ] is the correct emptiness test and why §7.2 prefers [[ ]], where the expansion is not re-split at all.

Line 5 versus 6 is the globbing half: unquoted *.txt is expanded against the directory into two words; quoted, it is one literal word that no program will match against anything.

2. The trailing delimiter. Write a function that splits a colon-separated string into an array and reports the count, then explain why 'a:b:' and 'a:b' give the same answer while ':a:b' does not.

Solution 
split_count() {
  local IFS=':'
  # shellcheck disable=SC2206  # deliberate word splitting is the point here
  local parts=( $1 )
  printf '%-8s -> %d fields: ' "$1" "${#parts[@]}"
  printf '[%s]' "${parts[@]}"
  echo
}
split_count 'a:b'
split_count 'a:b:'
split_count ':a:b'
split_count 'a::b'

a:b      -> 2 fields: [a][b]
a:b:     -> 2 fields: [a][b]
:a:b     -> 3 fields: [][a][b]
a::b     -> 3 fields: [a][][b]

A non-whitespace IFS character terminates a field rather than beginning one. A trailing : therefore ends the field b and adds nothing after it, so 'a:b:' and 'a:b' are indistinguishable. A leading : is different: it terminates a field that started at the beginning of the string and is empty, so a real empty field appears.

This asymmetry is why hand-splitting structured data is risky.
