If the format's trailing field can legitimately be empty — and in /etc/passwd, PATH and most colon-separated formats it can — splitting on IFS loses the information that it was there. read -d with an explicit delimiter, or a real parser, is the answer when the distinction matters. §14.9 covers null-delimited data, which is the version of this that has no ambiguity at all.

Note local IFS=':' rather than a bare assignment: making IFS local to the function means it is restored automatically when the function returns, which is the fourth safe pattern and the best one inside a function (§9.4).

3. Fix the script. This deploys a build to a server and breaks on a directory containing a space. ❌ Find every defect and fix them.

deploy() {
  local src=$1
  local dest=$2
  local files=$(ls $src)
  for f in $files; do
    scp $src/$f user@host:$dest/
  done
}
Solution

There are five distinct defects, and four of them are this section's.

$(ls $src) parses the output of ls. Filenames may contain spaces and newlines, so there is no delimiter that safely separates them in that output. linux §4.9 states the rule; the fix is to let the shell produce the names directly with a glob, which never loses a character.

$src is unquoted in three places, so a directory with a space becomes two arguments.

$files is unquoted in the for, splitting names on whitespace and then globbing whatever comes out.

$dest is unquoted, with the same consequence at the far end.

The failure of scp is ignored. The loop continues after an error and the function reports success regardless — §11 is about this, but the fix belongs here too.

deploy() {
  local src=$1 dest=$2 f
  for f in "$src"/*; do
    [[ -e $f ]] || continue          # an unmatched glob stays literal; skip it
    scp -- "$f" "user@host:$dest/" || return 1
  done
}
type deploy >/dev/null && echo "defined; globbing replaces the ls parse"

defined; globbing replaces the ls parse

Three details worth naming. for f in "$src"/* quotes only the variable and leaves the * unquoted, which is exactly right: the directory name must not be split, and the glob must still expand. The [[ -e $f ]] || continue guard handles the empty directory — an unmatched glob expands to itself by default, so without the guard the loop body would run once with a literal * in the name; shopt -s nullglob is the other answer and §4.7 compares them. And -- ends option parsing, so a file called -rf is treated as a filename rather than a flag (§18.6).

4. Why does this print nothing? ❌ Predict and explain.

files="report 2024.txt"
if [ -f $files ]; then echo "found"; else echo "not found"; fi
Solution

The unquoted $files splits into two words, so the command that actually runs is [ -f report 2024.txt ] — the [ builtin receives four arguments (-f, report, 2024.txt, ]) where it expected three. That is not a false result; it is a usage error.

# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # the unquoted test is the bug being demonstrated
touch 'report 2024.txt'
files="report 2024.txt"
if [ -f $files ]; then echo "found"; else echo "not found"; fi
echo "---"
if [ -f "$files" ]; then echo "found"; else echo "not found"; fi

example.sh: line 4: [: report: binary operator expected
not found
---
found

The message names the real problem, and it is easy to miss because the script carries on and prints a plausible-looking not found. A quoting bug that produces a wrong answer is worse than one that crashes, and this is the shape of it: the file exists, the test says it does not, and nothing stops the script.

Two fixes, and they are not equivalent. [ -f "$files" ] quotes the expansion, which is the direct repair. [[ -f $files ]] also works — and works even unquoted, because [[ ]] is parsed by the shell rather than receiving expanded words, so no splitting happens inside it. That is a genuine advantage of [[ ]] and the reason §7.2 recommends it, but relying on it makes the quoting habit inconsistent: quote it anyway, and the same line is correct in both forms.

SECTION 4

The Expansion Pipeline

Between the moment the shell has parsed a command and the moment a program starts, the words of that command are rewritten — sometimes several times over, sometimes into a different number of words than you wrote. That rewriting is the expansion pipeline, and it runs in a fixed order that never varies.

Knowing the expansion order is worth more than knowing any individual expansion. Almost every question that begins "why doesn't this work" has the same answer — because that step runs before the one you were relying on — and once you can name the steps in order you can answer those questions yourself instead of experimenting until something works.

§3 covered two of the steps in detail because they cause the most damage. This section is the whole sequence, the four expansions §3 did not cover, and the rule that ties it together: the shell makes one pass, and does not look at its own output again.

4.1 The Order

#
Step
What it turns into what
1
Brace
{a,b} → a b. Purely textual, unconditional, and done before any variable exists.
2
Tilde
~ → a home directory, ~+ → $PWD. Only at the start of a word, only unquoted.
3
Parameter
$var, ${var#x} → a value. The whole of §5.
3
Command substitution
$(cmd) → the command's stdout, minus trailing newlines.
3
Arithmetic
$((expr)) → an integer.
3
Process substitution
<(cmd) → a filename that reads the command's output.
4
Word splitting
The results of step 3, unquoted, are cut on IFS (§3.4).
5
Pathname
*.txt → matching filenames, if any exist.
6
Quote removal
The quotes you typed are deleted. They never reach the program.

Steps 3 through 6 are the ones to hold onto, and they are the half of the expansion order that decides how many words a command receives. The four kinds of substitution all happen at the same stage, left to right, and everything they produce is then subject to splitting and globbing — which is why quoting matters and why it is applied at the point of use rather than the point of assignment.

Two structural facts are worth stating before the details.

Brace expansion is first, before variables exist. So a variable cannot supply the endpoints of a range. This is the single most common surprise in the whole pipeline:

# shellcheck disable=SC2051,SC2175  # a variable in a brace range is the lesson
a=1; b=3
echo "literal braces with variables: $(echo {$a..$b})"
echo "brace with literals:           $(echo {1..3})"
echo "forced through a second pass:  $(eval echo {$a..$b})"

literal braces with variables: {1..3}
brace with literals:           1 2 3
forced through a second pass:  1 2 3

Read the first line carefully: the output is {1..3}, not 1 2 3 and not {$a..$b}. Brace expansion ran first and found {$a..$b}, which is not a valid range because $a is not a number yet; it declined and left the text alone. Then parameter expansion replaced $a and $b, producing the string {1..3} — a perfectly good range that nothing will ever expand, because that step is over. The correct way to build a range from variables is seq or a C-style loop (§8.6), not eval; eval is shown here to demonstrate the mechanism, and §18.10 explains why reaching for it is usually the wrong instinct.

Quote removal is last. The quotes are not passed to the program; they are instructions to the shell about which steps to skip, and they are deleted once those steps are done.

v='hello world'
printf '[%s]\n' "$v"
printf '[%s]\n' "'$v'"

[hello world]
['hello world']

The first has no quotes in its output — they did their job and vanished. The second does, because those single quotes were inside a double-quoted string and so were ordinary characters rather than syntax.

Left to right expansion

Within the stage that holds tilde expansion, parameter expansion, arithmetic expansion and command substitution, the manual says expansion is done "in a left-to-right fashion": left to right expansion. A side effect in one word is therefore visible to the words after it on the same line:

i=0
echo $((i++)) $((i++)) $((i++))

0 1 2

Each $((i++)) saw the i the one before it left. Left to right expansion is a guarantee, and relying on it is still poor style: a reader has to hold the whole line in mind to know what each word will be, and §4.8's one-pass rule means the results cannot be reordered.

4.2 Brace Expansion

Brace expansion generates text. It is the only expansion that can make more words out of nothing, and it does not consult the filesystem, the environment, or anything else.

echo {1..3}{a,b}
echo {01..10..3}
echo {a..e}
echo nosuch{1,2}.txt

1a 1b 2a 2b 3a 3b
01 04 07 10
a b c d e
nosuch1.txt nosuch2.txt

Adjacent braces multiply, giving a Cartesian product. A sequence expression {x..y..incr} counts, and it preserves zero padding when the endpoints are padded — {01..10..3} gives 01 04 07 10, not 1 4 7 10, which is what makes it useful for filenames that must sort correctly. A sequence expression also runs backwards when the first endpoint is the larger ({5..1} gives 5 4 3 2 1) and works over single characters as well as integers, which is the {a..e} on the third line; those are the only two kinds it understands, so there is no sequence over words.

The last line is the important contrast with globbing. Brace expansion is unconditional: it produced nosuch1.txt nosuch2.txt although neither file exists. A glob is conditional on matching something:

mkdir -p bd && cd bd
echo "brace, nothing exists: $(echo nosuch{1,2}.txt)"
echo "glob,  nothing exists: $(echo nosuch*.txt)"

brace, nothing exists: nosuch1.txt nosuch2.txt
glob,  nothing exists: nosuch*.txt

The glob found no match and — by default — was left as literal text. That default is a trap worth naming now, because a loop over an unmatched glob runs once with the pattern as its value. §4.7 covers the switch that changes it.

The idiomatic use of braces is making a backup without repeating a long path:

mkdir -p etc && touch etc/nginx.conf
cp etc/nginx.conf{,.bak}
ls etc

nginx.conf
nginx.conf.bak

nginx.conf{,.bak} expands to two words — the empty alternative gives the original name, the second gives the name with .bak appended. It is compact and it guarantees the two paths cannot drift apart, which is exactly the mistake it exists to prevent.

4.3 Tilde Expansion

~ is replaced with a home directory, but only under conditions narrow enough to be worth stating exactly. It must be unquoted and it must be at the start of a word.

echo '"~" quoted            :' "~"
echo "a~ not at word start  : a~"
echo "~nosuchuser1234       : ~nosuchuser1234"

"~" quoted            : ~
a~ not at word start  : a~
~nosuchuser1234       : ~nosuchuser1234

Three cases, three times the tilde survives untouched. The third is the most useful to know: ~name means that user's home directory, and when no such user exists the word is left alone rather than becoming an error. So a typo in a username produces a literal ~alice path that fails much later, at the point something tries to open it.

Two forms have nothing to do with home directories at all:

echo "~+ and ~- : $(cd /usr && cd /etc && echo ~+ ~-)"
echo "~+ keeps a suffix : $(cd /usr && echo ~+/lib)"

~+ and ~- : /etc /usr
~+ keeps a suffix : /usr/lib

~+ is $PWD and ~- is $OLDPWD — the directory you were in before the last cd. They are genuinely useful in a script that moves around, and unlike $OLDPWD they can be followed by a path suffix directly.

Do not use ~ in a script where the path matters. Use $HOME, which is an ordinary variable you can quote, test and print. ~ is unquotable by definition — quoting it stops it expanding — so a home directory containing a space cannot be passed safely through a tilde, while "$HOME" handles it without thought.

4.4 Command Substitution, and the Newlines It Eats

$(...) runs the command inside it and replaces itself with that command's standard output. One detail of that sentence causes real defects: every trailing newline is removed, not just one. The older spelling is a pair of backticks, and the modern $(...) form nests without escaping, which is the whole reason it replaced them.

v=$(printf 'a\n\n\n')
echo "captured ${#v} character(s): $(printf '%q' "$v")"
w=$(printf 'a\nb\n')
echo "internal newlines survive: $(printf '%q' "$w")"

captured 1 character(s): a
internal newlines survive: $'a\nb'

Three trailing newlines became none; the newline between a and b survived. That asymmetry is deliberate and almost always what you want — dir=$(pwd) should not end in a newline — but it means command substitution cannot tell you whether the output ended in a newline, which matters when you are checking whether a file is well-formed. The idiom for preserving it is to append a sentinel and strip it yourself:

out=$(printf 'a\n\n\n'; printf 'X')
out=${out%X}
echo "with a sentinel: ${#out} characters"

with a sentinel: 4 characters

The sentinel X stops the newlines being trailing, and ${out%X} (§5.6) removes it afterwards. Four characters: a and three newlines.

The older backtick form `cmd` means the same thing and should not be used. It cannot nest without escaping, and it treats backslashes differently, so $( ) is both more capable and more predictable. ShellCheck reports backticks as SC2006.

Command substitution runs in a subshell, which is why a variable set inside one does not survive. That is §16.8's subject and one of the most reported problems in shell scripting.

Backtick substitution

Backtick substitution, `command`, is the older spelling of $(command). Both produce the command's output with the trailing newlines removed. They differ in the details: inside backticks a backslash before $, ` or \ is special, and nesting needs the inner backticks escaped, where $( ) nests without any change:

# shellcheck disable=SC2005,SC2006,SC2046,SC2116  # the backtick form is the subject
echo `echo \`echo inner\``
echo "$(echo "$(echo inner)")"

inner
inner

Both printed the same, and only one of them was readable. The style guide says to prefer $(command), and ShellCheck reports backtick substitution as SC2006. The only reason to know it is that it is everywhere in old scripts.

4.5 Arithmetic Expansion Evaluates Names Recursively

$((expr)) evaluates an integer expression. The property that surprises people — and that has security consequences — is that a bare name inside it is looked up and its value is then evaluated as an expression too.

a=b; b=5
echo "a=$a b=$b  and \$((a)) = $((a))"
c=2+3
echo "c=$c        and \$((c)) = $((c))"

a=b b=5  and $((a)) = 5
c=2+3        and $((c)) = 5

$((a)) printed 5. The shell looked up a, got the string b, found that b is not a number, looked it up, got 5, and stopped. And $((c)) printed 5 because the string 2+3 was evaluated as arithmetic rather than rejected as non-numeric.

This is why $(( )) must never contain data you did not produce. A value of a[$(id -u)] or x=$(rm -rf /tmp/x) inside an arithmetic context is not a string, it is code — §18.4 shows the concrete injection. When you must do arithmetic on input, validate it as digits first (§13.10).

It is also why names need no $ inside $(( )):

# shellcheck disable=SC2004  # the two forms are being contrasted on purpose
count=7
echo "$((count * 2))  — no dollar needed"
echo "$(($count * 2))  — a dollar works too, and is expanded first"

14  — no dollar needed
14  — a dollar works too, and is expanded first

Both give 14, and they get there differently: the first hands the name count to the arithmetic evaluator, the second substitutes 7 before the evaluator sees anything. With trusted integers they agree. With untrusted data the second is strictly worse, because whatever the variable holds is spliced in as source text.

$((...)): the arithmetic expansion

$((...)) replaces itself with the value of the arithmetic expression inside it, written in decimal:

x=$((2+3))
echo "$x"

5

The form $((...)) is arithmetic expansion. Names inside it are evaluated recursively, as this section's title says, and §7.8 treats the contexts in which arithmetic happens; $((...)) is the one that produces a value to use in a word.

4.6 Process Substitution Is a Filename

<(cmd) runs cmd and expands to the path of a file that reads its output. That is the whole idea, and seeing the path makes it obvious:

# shellcheck disable=SC2116  # the inner echo is what turns the fd path into text
echo "what <(...) expands to: $(echo <(true))"

what <(...) expands to: /dev/fd/63

It is a filename, so it goes wherever a filename goes — which solves the problem of a program that insists on files rather than standard input. The /dev/fd directory it names is the kernel's view of the current process's open file descriptors, so /dev/fd/63 is not a file on disk at all; opening it hands you descriptor 63, which the shell has already connected to the running command. That is why the path is meaningless to any other process and why it disappears the moment the command finishes:

diff <(printf 'a\nb\n') <(printf 'a\nc\n') && echo same || echo "differ (status $?)"

2c2
< b
---
> c
differ (status 1)

diff takes two files and cannot read two standard inputs; process substitution manufactures both without a temporary file to clean up. The output form >(cmd) is the mirror image — a filename that, when written to, feeds the command's standard input.

The other classic use is avoiding the pipeline subshell. cmd | while read ... puts the loop in a subshell so its variables are lost; while read ...; do ...; done < <(cmd) runs the loop in the current shell. §16.9 measures that difference, and it is the standard fix.

Process substitution is not POSIX — it is a bash and ksh extension, and §19.14 lists it among the constructs that fail under dash.

>(...): output process substitution

>(...) is the output form of process substitution: the shell starts the command inside and expands to a file name that, when written to, feeds that command's standard input. The input form <(...) is the one used to read; >(...) is used to write:

echo hi > >(tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]')
wait

HI

The echo wrote to the file name >(...) expanded to, and tr received hi and printed HI. The command in >(...) runs asynchronously to the rest of the script, so anything that must happen after its output is finished needs to wait for it (§16.9).

4.7 Pathname Expansion, and the Four Switches

A word containing an unquoted *, ? or [ is matched against the filesystem. If it matches, it becomes the matching names, sorted; if it does not, the default is to leave it alone.

Four shopt options change that behaviour, and each solves a real problem:

mkdir -p g && cd g && touch a.txt b.log .hidden
echo "default, no match:  $(echo nomatch*)"
shopt -s nullglob;  echo "nullglob:           [$(echo nomatch*)]"
shopt -u nullglob
shopt -s dotglob;   echo "dotglob:            $(echo *)"
shopt -u dotglob
echo "without dotglob:    $(echo *)"
shopt -s globstar
mkdir -p x/y && touch x/y/deep.txt
echo "globstar:           $(echo **/*.txt)"

default, no match:  nomatch*
nullglob:           []
dotglob:            .hidden a.txt b.log
without dotglob:    a.txt b.log
globstar:           a.txt x/y/deep.txt
Option
Effect, and when to use it
nullglob
An unmatched pattern becomes nothing instead of itself. The fix for a loop that runs once with a literal * when the directory is empty. Turn it on for the loop and off again — it also makes echo *.txt print an empty line, which surprises anything downstream.
failglob
An unmatched pattern is an error and the command does not run. Stricter than nullglob and better when a missing match means the script's assumptions are wrong.
dotglob
* matches names beginning with a dot. Without it, cp -r src/* dst/ silently leaves .env and .git behind — a genuinely common deployment bug.
globstar
** crosses directory boundaries, so **/*.txt is a recursive search. Convenient, and slower than find on a large tree because it builds the whole list first.

nullglob and failglob are worth contrasting directly, because choosing between them is a statement about what an empty match means. Under nullglob an empty match is normal and the loop simply does not run; under failglob it is a bug, the command is refused, and the script stops before doing anything with a wrong list. Use failglob when the pattern names something the script requires — a config directory, a set of migrations — and nullglob when zero matches is an ordinary Tuesday.

The safest general pattern, which needs none of them, is the explicit existence guard:

mkdir -p empty && cd empty
for f in ./*.txt; do
  [[ -e $f ]] || continue        # the unmatched pattern is not a file
  echo "processing $f"
done
echo "loop finished cleanly on an empty directory"

loop finished cleanly on an empty directory

Note ./*.txt rather than *.txt. Prefixing the pattern with ./ guarantees every result begins with ./, so a file named -rf or --help arrives as ./-rf and cannot be mistaken for an option by whatever you pass it to. ShellCheck's SC2035 asks for exactly this, and §18.6 shows the attack it prevents.

4.8 One Pass, and Only One

The rule that ties the section together: the shell expands a command once and does not re-examine what it produced. A $ that appears as the result of an expansion is data.

# shellcheck disable=SC2016,SC2034  # a literal $inner that is never expanded is the point
inner='world'
outer='$inner'
echo "one pass:  $outer"
echo "with eval: $(eval echo "$outer")"
v='a;b'
echo "a semicolon from a variable is data: $v"

one pass:  $inner
with eval: world
a semicolon from a variable is data: a;b

The first line proves the rule: $outer expanded to the four characters $inner, and the shell did not then treat them as a variable reference. The third proves the safety property that follows from it — a ; that arrives from a variable is a semicolon character, not a command separator, because the grammar was settled long before the expansion happened.

That safety property is the reason shell injection is not as easy as it looks, and it is also exactly what eval throws away. eval re-runs the whole pipeline over text you have already expanded once, so a ; in that text becomes a separator on the second pass. §18.9 develops this into the rule for when eval is defensible.

There is one important exception to "the result is data", and it is the command name:

cmd='echo hi'
$cmd

hi

The value was split into words by step 4, and the first word became the command name. So an unquoted variable in command position can choose the program that runs — not because the text was re-expanded, but because word splitting happens after substitution and the shell then looks up whatever the first word turned out to be. Building commands this way is fragile with quoting and is why §6.14 recommends an array instead.

Expansion happens once, and there is no recursive expansion

The section's rule has two halves. Expansion happens once: each word on a command line is expanded in the fixed order of §4.1, one time. And there is no recursive expansion: the result of an expansion is not expanded again, so a value that looks like an expansion stays text:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the single quotes keep the text literal
a='$HOME'
echo "$a"

$HOME

Expanding $a produced the characters $HOME, and no second pass turned them into a directory. Expansion happens once, and no recursive expansion follows it. The one command that adds a second pass on purpose is eval (§18.9), which is exactly why it is dangerous; the recursive evaluation of names inside $(( )) (§4.5) is arithmetic and not expansion.

Exercises

1. Predict the expansion. For each, say what echo actually receives. Assume n=3 and the current directory holds a.txt only.

# shellcheck disable=SC2051,SC2086  # each form is the question
echo {1..$n}
echo {1..3}
echo "*.txt"
echo *.txt
echo $((1+1)).txt
Solution 
# shellcheck disable=SC2051,SC2086,SC2116  # each form is the question
mkdir -p q && cd q && touch a.txt
n=3
echo "{1..\$n}   -> $(echo {1..$n})"
echo "{1..3}    -> $(echo {1..3})"
echo "\"*.txt\"   -> $(echo "*.txt")"
echo "*.txt     -> $(echo *.txt)"
echo "\$((1+1)).txt -> $(echo $((1+1)).txt)"

{1..$n}   -> {1..3}
{1..3}    -> 1 2 3
"*.txt"   -> *.txt
*.txt     -> a.txt
$((1+1)).txt -> 2.txt

Line 1 is §4.1's headline: brace expansion runs before parameter expansion, sees {1..$n}, decides it is not a range, and leaves it; $n is then substituted, producing the literal text {1..3} that nothing will expand.

Line 5 shows the steps composing correctly. Arithmetic expansion is a step-3 substitution, so $((1+1)) becomes 2, and the result is concatenated with the adjacent literal .txt into one word — adjacent fragments always join. Nothing globs it because it contains no pattern character.

2. Why does the count differ? Explain both results.

# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # the unquoted expansion is the question
files=$(ls)
echo "$files" | wc -l
echo $files | wc -l
Solution 
# shellcheck disable=SC2086,SC2116  # the unquoted expansion is the question
mkdir -p r && cd r && touch one two three
files=$(ls)
echo "quoted:   $(echo "$files" | wc -l | tr -d ' ') line(s)"
echo "unquoted: $(echo $files | wc -l | tr -d ' ') line(s)"

quoted:   3 line(s)
unquoted: 1 line(s)

$files holds three names separated by newlines. Quoted, echo receives one argument containing those newlines and prints them as three lines. Unquoted, word splitting cuts the value on IFS — which includes newline — into three separate arguments, and echo joins its arguments with single spaces, so wc -l sees one line.

The lesson is that an unquoted expansion does not just risk splitting a filename; it destroys the line structure of any multi-line value. That is why echo "$var" is the only correct way to print a captured value, and why counting lines through echo at all is worse than wc -l < file.

It is also a reminder that this whole example is built on parsing ls, which §3's exercise 3 and linux §4.9 both rule out: a filename may itself contain a newline, in which case even the quoted form counts wrongly.

3. Make the range work. for i in {1..$count} does not loop. Give two correct alternatives and say which you would use.

Solution 
# shellcheck disable=SC2051  # ShellCheck is right, and that is the exercise
count=4
printf 'broken:   '; for i in {1..$count}; do printf '[%s]' "$i"; done; echo
printf 'C-style:  '; for ((i = 1; i <= count; i++)); do printf '[%s]' "$i"; done; echo
printf 'seq:      '; for i in $(seq 1 "$count"); do printf '[%s]' "$i"; done; echo

broken:   [{1..4}]
C-style:  [1][2][3][4]
seq:      [1][2][3][4]

The broken form loops exactly once, with i set to the literal string {1..4} — which is worse than failing, because a script that appends $i to a filename creates a file called {1..4} and reports success.

Use the C-style loop. It is a bash builtin construct with no subprocess, it needs no quoting decisions, and count inside (( )) needs no $. seq is an external command — one fork per loop, which §21.4 measures — and it is not POSIX, so it buys nothing in portability either. seq is worth reaching for only when you need a non-integer step, which (( )) cannot do at all because bash has no floating point (§7.9).

4. The dotfile that did not deploy. A release script runs cp -r build/* /var/www/ and the site breaks because .htaccess is missing. Explain, and give two fixes with their trade-offs.

Solution

* does not match names beginning with a dot. This is not cp's behaviour — cp never sees the pattern. The shell expands build/* into a list that excludes dotfiles and hands cp the result, so cp copies exactly what it was given and reports success. Nothing anywhere reports an error, which is what makes this bug expensive.

mkdir -p build dst && touch build/index.html build/.htaccess
present() { [[ -e $1 ]] && echo present || echo MISSING; }

cp -r build/* dst/ 2>/dev/null
echo "with a bare glob:   .htaccess is $(present dst/.htaccess)"

rm -rf dst && mkdir dst
shopt -s dotglob
cp -r build/* dst/
shopt -u dotglob
echo "with dotglob:       .htaccess is $(present dst/.htaccess)"

rm -rf dst && cp -r build dst
echo "copying the dir:    .htaccess is $(present dst/.htaccess)"

with a bare glob:   .htaccess is MISSING
with dotglob:       .htaccess is present
copying the dir:    .htaccess is present

Fix one: shopt -s dotglob. It works, and it is a global switch on a global behaviour — every other glob in the script changes meaning too, including any rm, which is a genuinely dangerous side effect. Set it and unset it around the one command, as above.

Fix two, and the better one: do not glob at all. cp -r build dst copies the directory itself, dotfiles included, because no pattern is involved and the shell has nothing to expand. Where the destination must be populated rather than nested, tar -c -C build . | tar -x -C dst or rsync -a build/ dst/ do the same job — note rsync's trailing slash on the source, which means "the contents of" and is the same distinction in a different notation.

The general rule this illustrates: when a glob's job is "everything in this directory", the tool almost always has a way to say that directly, and saying it directly removes both the dotfile bug and the argument-length limit that a large directory eventually hits.

SECTION 5

Parameter Expansion in Full

Parameter expansion is the largest single feature in the shell language and the one that most separates a script that reads like a program from a script that reads like a pile of sed calls. §4 placed it in the pipeline — step three, alongside the other substitutions, before word splitting and globbing. This section is the operator set itself: eleven families of them, every one of which turns a variable into a different string without starting a process.

That last clause is the reason the section is this long. ${path##*/} and $(basename "$path") look interchangeable, and in a script that runs once a day the difference is invisible. In a loop over ten thousand lines it is the difference between a twentieth of a second and eleven seconds — §21.4 measures that — and, less obviously but more importantly, the two do not always agree. §5.9 puts them side by side on six inputs and they differ on three.

linux §2 introduced $var and ${var} as things you type at a prompt. This section treats them as what they are inside a program: a small string-manipulation language with its own pattern syntax, its own notion of "unset", and its own failure modes, all of which the reader will meet again in every remaining section of this course.

5.1 The Shape of an Expansion, and When Braces Are Required

Every form in this section has the same skeleton: ${ , a parameter, an optional operator, and }. The parameter is a variable name, a positional parameter (1, 2, …), or one of the special parameters — $@, $*, $#, $?, $-, $$, $!, $0 and $_. The operator is what the rest of the section is about.

Braces are optional when the expansion is the whole word or is followed by a character that cannot be part of a name. They become mandatory the moment the next character could continue the name, because the shell reads the longest valid name it can and does not guess what you meant.

# shellcheck disable=SC1037,SC2209  # $10 without braces is the lesson; 'file' is a value
rel=1.4
echo "without braces: $rel_final"
echo "with braces:    ${rel}_final"
set -- a b c d e f g h i j k
echo "\$10 is:        $10"
echo "\${10} is:      ${10}"
n=file
echo "concatenation:  ${n}.txt and $n.txt"

without braces: 
with braces:    1.4_final
$10 is:        a0
${10} is:      j
concatenation:  file.txt and file.txt

Two failures here, and both are silent. $rel_final is not $rel followed by _final; it is the variable rel_final, which does not exist, so the line prints nothing and the script carries on. And $10 is not the tenth positional parameter — it is $1 followed by a literal 0, giving a0. A positional parameter above nine always needs braces, which is one of the better arguments for getopts (§13) or an array (§6) over reaching directly into $11.

Underscore and digits continue a name; nothing else does. So these are all unambiguous without braces:

v=hello
echo "$v.txt $v/dir $v-1 $v,x $v:y"

hello.txt hello/dir hello-1 hello,x hello:y

Style guides split on whether to brace everything anyway. The Google Shell Style Guide asks you to "prefer brace-delimiting all other variables" while not bracing the single-character specials and positional parameters — "$1", $?, $# — and ShellCheck ships an optional check, require-variable-braces, that enforces the first half (§20.5 turns the optional checks on). The same guide attaches a warning worth repeating here, because it is the single most common misreading of this syntax: braces are not a form of quoting. ${var} is still split and still globbed; "${var}" is what you meant. Braces settle where the name ends, quotes settle what happens to the value, and the two decisions are independent. The argument for is that a consistent rule cannot be misapplied; the argument against is that "${v}" is noisier than "$v" and noise hides the cases that matter. Pick one and let the tool enforce it — this course braces when the operator requires it and when a name is followed by text, and not otherwise.

What braces are not. ${...} does not create a nested expression context. You cannot write ${#!name} to get the length of an indirect reference, and you cannot apply two operators to one parameter in one expansion. §5.9 measures both limits; the fix is always a temporary variable, and a temporary variable costs nothing.

5.2 Defaults, Assignment, Errors, and the Meaning of the Colon

Four operators handle the "this may not be set" case, and they come in pairs that differ by one colon. Without the colon the test is unset; with it the test is unset or null. That unset versus null distinction is real — an empty string is a value, and a configuration system that lets you deliberately set HTTP_PROXY= to mean "no proxy" depends on the difference.

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the single-quoted operators are labels, not expansions
unset -v u
n=
s=value
show() { printf '%-10s unset=[%s] null=[%s] set=[%s]\n' "$1" "$2" "$3" "$4"; }
show '${v-w}'  "${u-w}"  "${n-w}"  "${s-w}"
show '${v:-w}' "${u:-w}" "${n:-w}" "${s:-w}"
show '${v+w}'  "${u+w}"  "${n+w}"  "${s+w}"
show '${v:+w}' "${u:+w}" "${n:+w}" "${s:+w}"

${v-w}     unset=[w] null=[] set=[value]
${v:-w}    unset=[w] null=[w] set=[value]
${v+w}     unset=[] null=[w] set=[w]
${v:+w}    unset=[] null=[] set=[w]

Read the third and fourth rows together: + is the inverse of -. ${var:+alternate} means "if var has a usable value, use alternate instead", which is how you build an option that only appears when a variable is set. Note that the unset versus null pairing is what the third row costs you: ${var+alternate} fires for a variable that is set but empty, and ${var:+alternate} does not.

${var:-default} — use a default. Substitutes default, and leaves var alone. The overwhelmingly common one.
${var:=default} — use a default and remember it. Substitutes default and assigns it, so the next reference gets the same answer. Illegal on positional and special parameters, because you cannot assign to $1.
${var:?message} — refuse to continue. Prints message to stderr and exits a non-interactive shell. The cheapest possible precondition check.
${var:+alternate} — use an alternate. Substitutes alternate only when var has a value, and the empty string otherwise.

The difference between ${var:-default} and ${var:=default} is worth proving rather than asserting, because the two are read as synonyms far more often than they are:

unset -v a b
echo "a via :-  -> ${a:-fallback}"
echo "a is now  -> [${a-UNSET}]"
echo "b via :=  -> ${b:=fallback}"
echo "b is now  -> [${b-UNSET}]"

a via :-  -> fallback
a is now  -> [UNSET]
b via :=  -> fallback
b is now  -> [fallback]

${var:=default} inside a : command is the idiom for "default this variable once, at the top of the script": : "${LOG_LEVEL:=info}". The : builtin does nothing and ignores its arguments, so the line exists purely for the assignment's side effect. Quote the expansion — without quotes the default is subject to word splitting and globbing like any other expansion, which §4.7 covered.

${var:?message} is the one most scripts should use more. A missing argument produces a named error at the point the value is needed, instead of an empty string that propagates until something further away fails confusingly:

deploy() {
  local host=${1:?deploy: needs a hostname}
  echo "deploying to $host"
}
deploy prod-1
deploy
echo "not reached"

deploying to prod-1
example.sh: line 2: 1: deploy: needs a hostname

Three details in that output. The message is prefixed by the shell's own location and by the parameter's name — here 1, because the parameter is $1 — so you get line 2: 1: and then your text. The script exits with status 1 and not reached never prints, which is :?'s whole value: it is a die that needs no if. And it fires from inside a function, terminating the script, not just the function — so it is a precondition, not a recoverable error. §11.6 covers the recoverable kind.

The word is evaluated lazily. Whatever you put on the right of :-, := or :+ is only expanded when the expansion actually needs it, which means a command substitution there costs nothing in the common case:

expensive() { echo 'expensive ran' >&2; echo 'computed'; }
set_value=present
printf 'set var:   %s\n' "${set_value:-$(expensive)}"
unset -v missing
printf 'unset var: %s\n' "${missing:-$(expensive)}"

set var:   present
expensive ran
unset var: computed

expensive ran appears once, not twice. So ${cache:-$(recompute)} is a genuine memoisation idiom rather than a way to run the expensive thing every time and throw the answer away — and note the diagnostic appearing before the line that triggered it, which is stderr and stdout interleaving exactly as they were written (§10.3).

Finally, these operators interact with set -u (§11.2) in the way you want: ${v:-default} and ${v-default} do not trip nounset, because supplying a default is handling the unset case. That is why ${1-} is the standard way to read a possibly-absent argument under strict mode.

5.3 Length, Substrings, and the Negative-Offset Trap

${#var} is the length of the value in characters.

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the single-quoted operators are labels, not expansions
s='hello world'
empty=
unset -v gone
printf 'len of %-14s = %s\n' "'$s'" "${#s}"
printf 'len of %-14s = %s\n' "''" "${#empty}"
printf 'len of %-14s = %s\n' "unset" "${#gone}"
set -- one two three
printf 'len of %-14s = %s\n' '$#' "$#"
printf 'len of %-14s = %s\n' '${#1}' "${#1}"

len of 'hello world'  = 11
len of ''             = 0
len of unset          = 0
len of $#             = 3
len of ${#1}          = 3

An unset variable has length 0, indistinguishable from an empty one — ${#var} is not a test for existence, ${var+set} is. And $# is not ${#} of anything; it is the count of positional parameters, a special parameter that merely looks like the length operator. ${#1} is the length of $1.

"Characters" means characters in the shell's current locale, which is a claim worth measuring, because it is the kind of thing that works on the author's machine and breaks in production:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # ${#u} inside the format string is a label, not an expansion
u=$'caf\xc3\xa9 au lait'
bytes() { printf '%s' "$1" | wc -c | tr -d ' '; }
export LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8
printf 'UTF-8 locale: ${#u}=%-3s  ${u:0:4} is %s byte(s)\n' "${#u}" "$(bytes "${u:0:4}")"
export LC_ALL=C
printf 'C locale:     ${#u}=%-3s  ${u:0:4} is %s byte(s)\n' "${#u}" "$(bytes "${u:0:4}")"

UTF-8 locale: ${#u}=12   ${u:0:4} is 5 byte(s)
C locale:     ${#u}=13   ${u:0:4} is 4 byte(s)

Thirteen bytes, twelve characters. Under LC_ALL=C the shell counts bytes, and ${u:0:4} takes four bytes — cutting the two-byte é in half and producing a string that is not valid UTF-8 at all. Nothing reports an error; the mangled bytes go wherever the script sends them. Scripts that slice text containing anything outside ASCII must either pin the locale (§19.8) or not slice by index.

Note also that export is doing real work in that example. Setting the locale as a prefix — LC_ALL=C printf ... "${#u}" — does not change the answer, because the expansion is performed by the shell before printf is even started, and a prefix assignment only affects the command's environment. That is the expansion order of §4 showing up somewhere unexpected — an assignment prefix and an expansion are two different steps, and the expansion order puts the expansion first.

Substrings use ${var:offset} and ${var:offset:length}, both zero-based. This is substring expansion, and it is the only place in the language where an expansion takes two numeric arguments:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the single-quoted operators are labels, not expansions
s=abcdefghij
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${s:3}'     "${s:3}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${s:3:4}'   "${s:3:4}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${s:0:3}'   "${s:0:3}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${s: -3}'   "${s: -3}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${s:(-3)}'  "${s:(-3)}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${s: -5:2}' "${s: -5:2}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${s:3:-2}'  "${s:3:-2}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${s:-3}'    "${s:-3}"

${s:3}       defghij
${s:3:4}     defg
${s:0:3}     abc
${s: -3}     hij
${s:(-3)}    hij
${s: -5:2}   fg
${s:3:-2}    defgh
${s:-3}      abcdefghij

The last line is the trap, and it is one of the sharpest in the language. ${s:-3} is not "three characters from the end" — it is the default-value operator from §5.2, and since s is set it expands to the whole of s. A negative offset in ${var:offset} must be separated from the colon, either by a space (${s: -3}) or by parentheses (${s:(-3)}). Both are in the table above producing hij; ${s:-3} produces abcdefghij, and nothing warns you.

A negative offset is therefore the one piece of this syntax that a reader cannot skim, and the difference matters most where it is least visible: ${s:-3} in a script that usually has s set behaves like a working "last three characters" expression right up until the day s is empty, at which point it silently becomes the literal 3. Prefer the parenthesised form — a space is easy to delete and hard to see in review, and ShellCheck has no check for this.

A negative length in ${var:offset:length} means "stop this many characters before the end", which is how you drop a fixed-size suffix without a pattern. It is the one part of substring expansion with no negative-offset ambiguity, because a length is already separated from the offset by its own colon. Out-of-range values mostly degrade quietly, with one exception:

s=abc
printf 'offset past the end:   [%s]\n' "${s:10}"
printf 'length past the end:   [%s]\n' "${s:1:99}"
printf 'a negative length larger than the string:\n'
echo "[${s:0:-99}]"

offset past the end:   []
length past the end:   [bc]
a negative length larger than the string:
example.sh: line 5: -99: substring expression < 0

An offset past the end gives the empty string and a length past the end is clamped — neither is an error. But a negative length that would imply an end before the start is a fatal expansion error, which kills the shell with status 1. So the one out-of-range case that fails loudly is the one arising from arithmetic on a string shorter than you assumed.

Substring expansion also applies to the positional parameters as a group, where the offset counts from $1 and a slice is the standard way to say "everything after the first argument":

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the single-quoted operators are labels, not expansions
set -- alpha beta gamma delta
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${@:2}'   "${*:2}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${@:2:2}' "${*:2:2}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${@: -1}' "${*: -1}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${@:0:1}' "${*:0:1}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${#@}'    "${#@}"

${@:2}       beta gamma delta
${@:2:2}     beta gamma
${@: -1}     delta
${@:0:1}     example.sh
${#@}        4

"${@:2}" is the "shift without shifting" idiom — a subcommand dispatcher (§13.7) passes "${@:2}" to the handler for $1. Offset 0 is $0, the script's own name, which is why counting starts at 1 for every other purpose and 0 here; this is the only place where the positional parameters look like a zero-based array, and §6.10 explains why they are not one.

5.4 Trimming with Patterns: #, ##, %, %%

Four operators — ${var#pattern}, ${var##pattern}, ${var%pattern} and ${var%%pattern} — remove a matching piece from one end. # cuts from the front, % cuts from the back — a mnemonic that survives because # is left of % on a keyboard, and because # starts a comment (front) while % is the printf conversion prefix at the end of nothing in particular. Doubling the character makes the match greedy.

The pattern is a glob, not a regular expression: * is any string, ? is any character, [...] is a bracket expression, and with extglob on (§7.11) the extended forms apply too. It is anchored to the end it cuts from, and unanchored at the other.

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the single-quoted operators are labels, not expansions
p=/var/log/nginx/access.log.1
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${p#*/}'  "${p#*/}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${p##*/}' "${p##*/}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${p%/*}'  "${p%/*}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${p%%.*}' "${p%%.*}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${p%.*}'  "${p%.*}"
echo
f=archive.tar.gz
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${f%.*}'  "${f%.*}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${f%%.*}' "${f%%.*}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${f#*.}'  "${f#*.}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${f##*.}' "${f##*.}"

${p#*/}      var/log/nginx/access.log.1
${p##*/}     access.log.1
${p%/*}      /var/log/nginx
${p%%.*}     /var/log/nginx/access
${p%.*}      /var/log/nginx/access.log

${f%.*}      archive.tar
${f%%.*}     archive
${f#*.}      tar.gz
${f##*.}     gz
Idiom
Reads as
${p##*/}
The filename. ${var##pattern} greedily cuts everything up to and including the last /; ${var#pattern} would stop at the first.
${p%/*}
The directory. ${var%pattern} cuts the shortest trailing /…, which is the last one; ${var%%pattern} would cut back to the first slash in the whole path.
${f##*.}
The extension, without the dot. Everything after the last ..
${f%.*}
The name without its last extension. archive.tar.gz → archive.tar.
${f%%.*}
The name before the first dot. Different from the row above whenever a name has two.

The archive.tar.gz block is there to make the greedy/non-greedy choice concrete, because "strip the extension" is ambiguous English and the two readings give different answers. Decide which you mean. For a file that may have a compound extension, %.* twice is usually what a build script wants, and %%.* is what a script wants when the name is an identifier that happens to contain dots.

A pattern that does not match is not an error — the value comes through untouched:

s=plain
printf 'no match leaves it alone: [%s]\n' "${s#*/}"
printf 'empty pattern:            [%s]\n' "${s#}"
n=item42
printf 'one trailing digit:       [%s]\n' "${n%[0-9]}"
printf 'all trailing digits:      [%s]\n' "${n%%[0-9]*}"
v=v1.2.3
printf 'strip a literal prefix:   [%s]\n' "${v#v}"
printf 'a prefix that is absent:  [%s]\n' "${v#x}"

no match leaves it alone: [plain]
empty pattern:            [plain]
one trailing digit:       [item4]
all trailing digits:      [item]
strip a literal prefix:   [1.2.3]
a prefix that is absent:  [v1.2.3]

The silence is the hazard. ${tag#v} to turn v1.2.3 into 1.2.3 produces 1.2.3 when the tag has the prefix and the unchanged tag when it does not, and a release script that then compares versions numerically will compare v1.2.3 against 1.2.4 and get an answer it was never designed to produce. When the prefix must be there, test for it — [[ $tag == v* ]] || die (§7.5) — rather than trusting the expansion to tell you.

Note the difference between %[0-9] and %%[0-9]* on item42. The first removes exactly one character matching the class; the second removes the longest trailing run of digits, because [0-9]* means "a digit followed by anything". Greediness applies to the pattern's match, not to a repetition count, so a pattern removing "all the trailing digits" must be written to reach the end.

The pattern is expanded before it is matched, which means a pattern held in a variable must be quoted with care. ${p##"$prefix"} treats $prefix as literal text; ${p##$prefix} treats its contents as a glob. §5.5's whitespace-trimming idiom depends on exactly this, and it is the only place in the language where quoting inside an expansion is routine.

5.5 Substitution: /, //, /#, /%

Where # and % cut from an end, / replaces anywhere. ${var/pattern/string} replaces the first match, ${var//pattern/string} replaces every match, and prefixing the pattern with # or % gives ${var/#pattern/string} and ${var/%pattern/string}, which anchor it to the start or the end.

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the single-quoted operators are labels, not expansions
s=a/b/a/b
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${s/a/X}'   "${s/a/X}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${s//a/X}'  "${s//a/X}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${s/#a/X}'  "${s/#a/X}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${s/%b/X}'  "${s/%b/X}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${s/#b/X}'  "${s/#b/X}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${s//\//-}' "${s//\//-}"
printf '%-12s %s\n' '${s//a}'    "${s//a}"

${s/a/X}     X/b/a/b
${s//a/X}    X/b/X/b
${s/#a/X}    X/b/a/b
${s/%b/X}    a/b/a/X
${s/#b/X}    a/b/a/b
${s//\//-}   a-b-a-b
${s//a}      /b//b

Four things that are easy to get wrong and are all in that output. The anchored forms are ${var/#pattern} and ${var/%pattern}, not #/ — the slash comes first because it is the substitution operator and the anchor modifies the pattern. An anchored pattern that does not match changes nothing, as ${s/#b/X} shows; it is not an error and there is no signal — ${var/#pattern} and ${var/%pattern} share that silence with the trim operators of §5.4. The replacement may be omitted entirely, in which case matches are deleted — ${var//pattern/string} written as ${s//a} gives /b//b, which is the shortest way to strip a character class, and ${var/pattern/string} shortens the same way to delete just the first. And a literal / in the pattern must be escaped, because the operator has already claimed it.

Since the pattern is a glob, substitution covers most of what a script reaches for sed to do:

line='  padded  '
printf 'trim leading:  [%s]\n' "${line#"${line%%[![:space:]]*}"}"
t='2026-09-15T10:04:00Z'
printf 'date only:     [%s]\n' "${t%%T*}"
printf 'dashes to /:   [%s]\n' "${t//-//}"
csv='a,b,,c'
printf 'commas to sp:  [%s]\n' "${csv//,/ }"

trim leading:  [padded  ]
date only:     [2026-09-15]
dashes to /:   [2026/09/15T10:04:00Z]
commas to sp:  [a b  c]

The first line deserves unpacking, because it is the canonical whitespace trim and it looks like line noise. Read it inside out. ${line%%[![:space:]]*} removes the longest trailing run beginning with a non-space character — leaving only the leading whitespace, here two spaces. That result is then used, quoted, as the pattern in ${line#...}, which removes exactly that prefix. The quoting is what makes it work: without it, the two spaces would be re-read as a glob. The mirror image trims the right-hand side, and exercise 3 builds the pair into a function.

Two hazards worth naming. The csv line turns a,b,,c into a b c — an empty field becomes two adjacent spaces, and if that result is then split on whitespace the empty field vanishes entirely. Substitution has no notion of fields; §15.4 covers splitting properly. And a substitution whose replacement comes from data is a place where the data can smuggle in structure — §18.5 returns to this.

& in the replacement means "the text that matched", and in bash 5.x this is on by default. The & in replacement behaviour is controlled by a shell option, which is the only reason it is safe to rely on at all:

s='error: disk full'
shopt -u patsub_replacement
printf 'patsub_replacement off: [%s]\n' "${s/error/[&]}"
shopt -s patsub_replacement
printf 'patsub_replacement on:  [%s]\n' "${s/error/[&]}"
printf 'escaped ampersand:      [%s]\n' "${s/error/[\&]}"
shopt -p patsub_replacement

patsub_replacement off: [[&]: disk full]
patsub_replacement on:  [[error]: disk full]
escaped ampersand:      [[&]: disk full]
shopt -s patsub_replacement

The & in replacement rule is a genuine incompatibility, not a new feature you can ignore. patsub_replacement arrived in bash 5.2 and is on by default, so a script written for bash 4 that substitutes a literal & — a URL query string, an HTML entity, a sed-style command built as text — produces different output on a modern shell. The fix is to escape it, \&, which is correct under both because older bash never treated it specially. shopt -u patsub_replacement at the top of a script is the blunt alternative, and it is the wrong one: it changes a global for code you did not write, including anything you source.

5.6 Case Conversion

^ uppercases and , lowercases; one character converts the first character, doubled converts all of them. So ${var^} and ${var^^} uppercase, ${var,} is the lowercase-first parameter expansion and ${var,,} the lowercasing parameter expansion. An optional pattern — ${var^pattern} — restricts the conversion to characters the pattern matches — and because a pattern matches one character here, the useful patterns are bracket expressions.

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the single-quoted operators are labels, not expansions
s='hello world'
printf '%-16s %s\n' '${s^}'         "${s^}"
printf '%-16s %s\n' '${s^^}'        "${s^^}"
printf '%-16s %s\n' '${s^^[aeiou]}' "${s^^[aeiou]}"
u='HELLO WORLD'
printf '%-16s %s\n' '${u,}'         "${u,}"
printf '%-16s %s\n' '${u,,}'        "${u,,}"
printf '%-16s %s\n' '${u,,[AEIOU]}' "${u,,[AEIOU]}"
m='MiXeD'
printf '%-16s %s\n' '${m~}'         "${m~}"
printf '%-16s %s\n' '${m~~}'        "${m~~}"

${s^}            Hello world
${s^^}           HELLO WORLD
${s^^[aeiou]}    hEllO wOrld
${u,}            hELLO WORLD
${u,,}           hello world
${u,,[AEIOU]}    HeLLo WoRLD
${m~}            miXeD
${m~~}           mIxEd

The ${var^pattern} form is the one with a pattern; ${var^^} without one converts everything, and the lowercasing parameter expansion ${var,,} mirrors it exactly, as does the lowercase-first parameter expansion ${var,}. ~ and ~~ invert case rather than setting it, and they are worth knowing mainly so that a ~ inside ${ } is not misread as tilde expansion — that is a different step of the pipeline (§4.3) and it never happens here.

The pattern form is less useful than it looks: ${s^^[aeiou]} uppercases the vowels, which is a party trick. What earns its place is the unconditional pair, and specifically normalising input before comparing it:

reply=YES
case ${reply,,} in
  y|yes) echo 'accepted' ;;
  *)     echo 'declined' ;;
esac
name=deploy_target
printf 'env var name: %s\n' "${name^^}"
declare -u shouty
declare -l quiet
shouty='Mixed Case'
quiet='Mixed Case'
printf 'declare -u:   %s\n' "$shouty"
printf 'declare -l:   %s\n' "$quiet"

accepted
env var name: DEPLOY_TARGET
declare -u:   MIXED CASE
declare -l:   mixed case

case ${reply,,} is the right way to accept Y, y, YES and Yes in one branch. The alternative, shopt -s nocasematch, makes every case and [[ == ]] in the script case-insensitive until it is turned off, which is a global answer to a local question; §7.12 covers it and recommends against it for the same reason as nocaseglob.

declare -u and declare -l attach the conversion to the variable, so every subsequent assignment is converted. That is occasionally exactly right — a variable that must hold a canonical uppercase key — and usually a surprise to the next reader, who sees x='Mixed Case' and a later echo "$x" printing something else. Use it where the invariant is the point, and ${x^^} at the point of use otherwise.

These operators are bash 4.0 and later. sh, dash and bash 3.2 have none of them, which is why §19.4 shows the tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' fallback and why portable scripts still pay a process for a lowercase.

5.7 Indirection: ${!name}, ${!prefix@}, and Namerefs

${!name} expands the variable named by the value of name. One level, no more.

name=greeting
greeting='hello there'
printf 'direct:       %s\n' "$greeting"
printf 'indirect:     %s\n' "${!name}"
unset -v missing_target
ref=missing_target
printf 'unset target: [%s]\n' "${!ref}"
set -u
echo "${!ref}"

direct:       hello there
indirect:     hello there
unset target: []
example.sh: line 9: !ref: unbound variable

Indirection through a name that is not set gives the empty string, and under set -u it is an error naming !ref rather than the variable that is actually missing — a diagnostic you have to know how to read. That is the first argument for keeping indirection rare.

The ${!prefix@} and ${!prefix*} forms are a different operator that happens to share the !: they list the names of set variables beginning with a prefix. ${!prefix*} is the single-word form and ${!prefix@} the one-word-each form, and the difference is "$*" against "$@" all over again (§3.6). This is the shell's only reflection facility, and it is how a script discovers its own configuration:

# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # every APP_* name is read back through ${!v}
APP_NAME=checkout
APP_PORT=8080
APP_LOG_LEVEL=debug
OTHER=ignored
for v in "${!APP_@}"; do
  printf '%-14s = %s\n' "$v" "${!v}"
done
printf 'as one word: [%s]\n' "${!APP_*}"

APP_LOG_LEVEL  = debug
APP_NAME       = checkout
APP_PORT       = 8080
as one word: [APP_LOG_LEVEL APP_NAME APP_PORT]

"${!APP_@}" expands to one word per name and is the form to loop over, exactly as "$@" is (§3.6); ${!APP_*} joins them into a single word and is for display. The two-line loop above is a complete "print every setting this script honours" implementation — useful for a --dump-config flag, and useful in reverse for validating that nothing unexpected is set. Note that the names come back sorted, and that OTHER is absent because the prefix is matched literally, not as a glob.

Namerefs are the supported alternative to indirection. declare -n ref=target makes ref an alias: reading it reads target, and writing it writes target, which ${!name} cannot do at all.

declare -n ref=target
target='first value'
printf 'read through ref: %s\n' "$ref"
ref='written through ref'
printf 'target is now:    %s\n' "$target"
printf 'name of referent: %s\n' "${!ref}"
declare -p ref target

read through ref: first value
target is now:    written through ref
name of referent: target
declare -n ref="target"
declare -- target="written through ref"

Note the last two operators colliding usefully: applied to a nameref, ${!ref} gives the name it refers to rather than a doubly-indirect value. And declare -p prints the -n attribute, so a nameref is visible in a dump rather than looking like an ordinary variable holding a name.

The reason namerefs matter is that shell functions cannot return anything but an exit status (§9.5). A function that must produce a value either prints it — costing a command substitution, a subshell, and the loss of trailing newlines (§4.4) — or writes into a variable the caller names:

# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # host_out and port_out are namerefs; the caller reads them
split_host() {
  local spec=$1
  local -n host_out=$2 port_out=$3
  host_out=${spec%%:*}
  port_out=${spec##*:}
}
split_host 'db.internal:5432' h p
printf 'host=%s port=%s\n' "$h" "$p"

host=db.internal port=5432

That returns two values with no subprocess and no delimiter to parse. The nameref is an output parameter in the sense C and Go programmers mean: the caller owns the storage and names it, the callee fills it. §9.6 makes the output parameter a convention for this course.

And now the trap, which is severe enough that it governs how output parameters are named. Bash's local variables are dynamically scoped (§9.4), so a nameref inside a function resolves against the function's own scope first:

# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # 'out' is a nameref; the assignment lands in the caller
fill() {
  local -n out=$1
  local value='computed'
  out=$value
}
fill value
printf 'after "fill value":  [%s]\n' "${value-UNSET}"
fill result
printf 'after "fill result": [%s]\n' "${result-UNSET}"

after "fill value":  [UNSET]
after "fill result": [computed]

fill result works. fill value silently does nothing, because inside fill the name value is the function's own local, so the assignment lands there and dies when the function returns. No error, no warning, exit status 0 — the caller's variable is simply never set. The defence is a naming convention that cannot collide: prefix every local in a function that takes a nameref, _fill_value, and give the nameref itself a name no caller would choose.

A name that refers to itself is at least detected, though not fatally:

# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # 'out' is a nameref, and the circular case is the lesson
fill() { local -n out=$1; out=x; }
fill out
echo "exit status $?"

example.sh: line 2: local: warning: out: circular name reference
example.sh: line 2: warning: out: circular name reference
example.sh: line 2: warning: out: maximum nameref depth (8) exceeded
exit status 0

Three warnings on stderr, and then the function succeeds. A caller checking $? learns nothing. Treat that output as a fatal error even though bash does not, which in practice means running the script's test suite (§20.8) with stderr captured and asserting it is empty.

5.8 Parameter Transformation: the Ten ${var@OP} Forms

Bash 4.4 added a family of operators that ask a question about a parameter rather than editing its value. All ten exist in the 5.3 this course is written against; they were confirmed by running them, because the set grew across 4.4, 5.1 and 5.2 and the documentation for a version you are not running is no evidence about the shell you have.

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the single-quoted operators are labels, not expansions
v='a b'"'"'c'
printf '%-10s %s\n' '${v@U}' "${v@U}"
printf '%-10s %s\n' '${v@u}' "${v@u}"
printf '%-10s %s\n' '${v@L}' "${v@L}"
printf '%-10s %s\n' '${v@Q}' "${v@Q}"
e='tab\there and a \\ backslash'
printf '%-10s %s\n' '${e@E}' "${e@E}"
ps='\s-\v\$ '
printf '%-10s [%s]\n' '${ps@P}' "${ps@P}"
declare -i n=7
printf '%-10s %s\n' '${n@A}' "${n@A}"
printf '%-10s %s\n' '${n@a}' "${n@a}"

${v@U}     A B'C
${v@u}     A b'c
${v@L}     a b'c
${v@Q}     'a b'\''c'
${e@E}     tab	here and a \ backslash
${ps@P}    [bash-5.3$ ]
${n@A}     declare -i n='7'
${n@a}     i
Op
What it produces
@U
The value uppercased. Same as ${v^^}.
@u
The value with its first character uppercased. Same as ${v^}.
${var@L}
${var@L} — the value lowercased. Same as ${var,,}.
${var@Q}
The value quoted so that re-reading it as shell input gives the value back. The one that earns the whole family.
${var@E}
${var@E} — the value with backslash escapes expanded, as $'…' would (§3.3).
${var@P}
${var@P} — the value expanded as a PS1 prompt string.
@A
A declare command that would recreate the parameter, attributes included.
@a
The attribute flags themselves, as letters — here i for declare -i.
@K
Like @Q, but an array becomes a sequence of quoted key/value pairs.
@k
Like @K, but each key and value becomes a separate word.

${var@Q} is the important one, and the reason is §18's subject. Any time shell text must be reconstructed later — a command logged so it can be re-run, a value passed through ssh, a trap handler assembled from data, an argument forwarded to bash -c — the text has to survive a second round of parsing, and @Q is the only correct way to prepare it:

evil='; rm -rf /tmp/nothing #'
printf 'raw:    %s\n' "$evil"
printf 'quoted: %s\n' "${evil@Q}"
eval "victim=${evil@Q}"
printf 'survived eval, victim = %s\n' "$victim"

raw:    ; rm -rf /tmp/nothing #
quoted: '; rm -rf /tmp/nothing #'
survived eval, victim = ; rm -rf /tmp/nothing #

The value contains a command separator, a destructive command and a comment marker, and it passes through eval as inert text. §18.10 is clear that the best eval is the one you did not write; where one is unavoidable, every interpolated value goes through ${var@Q}.

The array forms need their subscript, which is the subtlety that makes them look broken:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016,SC2068  # the labels are literal; the unquoted @k split is the lesson
declare -A m=([host]=db [port]=5432)
declare -a a=(one 'two three')
row() { printf '%-12s %s\n' "$1" "$2"; }
row '${m@K}'    "${m@K}"
row '${m[@]@K}' "${m[@]@K}"
row '${m[*]@A}' "${m[*]@A}"
row '${a[@]@K}' "${a[@]@K}"
row '${a[*]@A}' "${a[*]@A}"
row '${a[*]@Q}' "${a[*]@Q}"
set -- ${m[@]@k}
row '${m[@]@k}' "$# words: $*"

${m@K}       
${m[@]@K}    port "5432" host "db" 
${m[*]@A}    declare -A m=([port]="5432" [host]="db" )
${a[@]@K}    0 "one" 1 "two three"
${a[*]@A}    declare -a a=([0]="one" [1]="two three")
${a[*]@Q}    'one' 'two three'
${m[@]@k}    4 words: port 5432 host db

The first row is empty and that is correct, not a bug: ${m@K} without a subscript refers to ${m[0]}, and this map has no key 0. Any transformation of a whole array needs [@] or [*] (§6.4 explains why an unsubscripted array name means element zero, which is one of the language's genuinely bad decisions).

The difference between @K and @k is word count. @K produces one word containing quoted pairs — feed it to eval and you get the array back. @k produces one word per key and per value — feed it to a for loop and you iterate over both. And ${m[@]@k} being four words there is the measurement that shows it.

Which makes @K a serialiser:

# shellcheck disable=SC2124  # ${conf[@]@K} is a single serialised word by design
declare -A conf=([retries]=3 [url]='https://example.test/a b')
snapshot=${conf[@]@K}
printf 'snapshot: %s\n' "$snapshot"
eval "declare -A restored=($snapshot)"
printf 'restored[url]     = %s\n' "${restored[url]}"
printf 'restored[retries] = %s\n' "${restored[retries]}"

snapshot: url "https://example.test/a b" retries "3" 
restored[url]     = https://example.test/a b
restored[retries] = 3

A value containing a space survives the round trip, which nothing built by hand from for k in "${!conf[@]}" and a = separator does. That is how an associative array crosses a boundary the shell otherwise cannot get it across — into a file, through an environment variable, or into a subshell (arrays are not exported; §16.6).

One caution on that output. The pairs come back in bash's internal hash order — url before retries, though retries was written first — and that order is not specified, not sorted, and not stable across bash versions. A snapshot is for restoring, not for comparing: two identical maps can serialise to two different strings. Sort the keys yourself (§6.7) if you need a comparable form.

5.9 Choosing Between an Expansion and a Process

The case for parameter expansion is usually made on speed, and speed is real — §21.4 measures a loop that calls basename against one that uses ${p##*/}. But speed is the weaker half of the argument, because it only matters in a loop. The stronger half is that the two are not the same function, and the difference shows up on inputs that a script meets by accident.

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the single-quoted operator is a column heading
printf '%-18s %-12s %-12s\n' 'input' '${p##*/}' 'basename'
for p in /var/log/app.log /var/log/ / app.log '' '/a b/c d'; do
  printf '%-18s %-12s %-12s\n' "[$p]" "[${p##*/}]" "[$(basename -- "$p")]"
done

input              ${p##*/}     basename    
[/var/log/app.log] [app.log]    [app.log]   
[/var/log/]        []           [log]       
[/]                []           [/]         
[app.log]          [app.log]    [app.log]   
[]                 []           []          
[/a b/c d]         [c d]        [c d]

They agree on the common case and disagree on two of the six: a path with a trailing slash, and the root directory. basename implements a specification that strips trailing slashes first; ${p##*/} implements "cut to the last slash" and nothing else. Neither is wrong — but a script that computes a log filename from a directory path the user typed with a trailing slash gets the empty string from one and log from the other, and the empty string usually turns into a file called .log or a mv with a missing argument.

dirname is worse, disagreeing on three of four:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the single-quoted operator is a column heading
printf '%-18s %-12s %-12s\n' 'input' '${p%/*}' 'dirname'
for p in /var/log/app.log /var/log/ / app.log; do
  printf '%-18s %-12s %-12s\n' "[$p]" "[${p%/*}]" "[$(dirname -- "$p")]"
done

input              ${p%/*}      dirname     
[/var/log/app.log] [/var/log]   [/var/log]  
[/var/log/]        [/var/log]   [/var]      
[/]                []           [/]         
[app.log]          [app.log]    [.]

The last row is the dangerous one. For a bare filename, dirname says . — the current directory, which is what every caller means — and ${p%/*} returns the filename itself, because there is no slash to cut. A script that then writes to "$dir/out.txt" creates app.log/out.txt and fails with "Not a directory", or worse, succeeds somewhere unintended. Guard it, as exercise 2 does: [[ $dir == "$path" ]] && dir=..

Use the expansion when the input's shape is known. Splitting a string your own script built, stripping a suffix you just added, defaulting a variable — the edge cases cannot arise, and the expansion is faster, needs no quoting of the result, and cannot be affected by PATH.
Use the external command when the input comes from outside and you want its specified behaviour on the awkward cases — a user argument, a path from find, a line from a file. basename and dirname are POSIX and their edge cases are documented; your ## is neither.
Stop when the expansion stops being readable. The nested-quote trim in §5.5 is at the limit. Anything needing three chained expansions, or one you have to run to understand, is a sed or awk call with a comment (§15.8) — or a sign that the script has outgrown shell entirely (§1.7).

The readability limit is also a hard limit, because the syntax does not nest. There is no expression context inside ${ }:

# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # 'greeting' is reached indirectly, through $name
name=greeting
greeting='hello'
tmp=${!name}
printf 'via a temporary: %s\n' "${#tmp}"
echo "${#!name}"

via a temporary: 5
example.sh: line 6: ${#!name}: bad substitution

bad substitution is a runtime error from the expansion, not a parse error, so it does not fire until that line runs — which in a branch taken once a month means it ships. One expansion per step, into a named temporary. The temporary also gives the intermediate value a name, which is the thing a reader most wants and ${#!name} would never have provided.

5.10 The Operator Table

Everything above, in one place, spelled the way the bash manual spells it — var for the parameter, pattern for a glob, string for replacement text. Read this as the section's index: each row names the operator, says what it produces, and points at the subsection that explains it.

Form
Produces
${var:-default}
§5.2 — default when var is unset or null; the value otherwise. Drop the colon (${var-default}) to test only for unset — the unset versus null distinction.
${var:=default}
§5.2 — as above, and assigns default to var. Illegal on a positional parameter.
${var:?message}
§5.2 — the value, or message on stderr and an exit. A precondition with no if.
${var:+alternate}
§5.2 — alternate when var has a value, and nothing when it does not. The inverse of :-.
${#var}
§5.3 — the length in characters of the current locale, which is bytes under LC_ALL=C.
${var:offset}
§5.3 — from offset to the end, zero-based.
${var:offset:length}
§5.3 — length characters from offset. A negative offset counts from the end and must be written ${var: -3} or ${var:(-3)} — without the separator it is the :- default operator instead. A negative length stops that far before the end.
${var#pattern}
§5.4 — the value with the shortest matching prefix removed.
${var##pattern}
§5.4 — the longest matching prefix removed. ${var##*/} is the filename.
${var%pattern}
§5.4 — the shortest matching suffix removed. ${var%.*} drops the last extension.
${var%%pattern}
§5.4 — the longest matching suffix removed.
${var/pattern/string}
§5.5 — the first match replaced by string. Omit /string to delete the match.
${var//pattern/string}
§5.5 — every match replaced.
${var/#pattern/string}
§5.5 — replaced only when pattern matches at the start. The anchor is /#, written ${var/#pattern} when the replacement is empty.
${var/%pattern/string}
§5.5 — replaced only at the end; ${var/%pattern} deletes a suffix.
${var^pattern}
§5.6 — the first character uppercased, if it matches pattern; ${var^} when the pattern is omitted.
${var^^}
§5.6 — every character uppercased. ${var^^pattern} restricts it.
${var,}
§5.6 — the lowercase-first parameter expansion, the mirror of ${var^}.
${var,,}
§5.6 — the lowercasing parameter expansion, the mirror of ${var^^}. ${var~} and ${var~~} invert rather than set.
${!name}
§5.7 — indirect expansion: the value of the variable whose name is the value of name. Read-only, one level.
${!prefix*}
§5.7 — the names of set variables beginning with prefix, as one word. ${!prefix@} gives one word each, and is the form to loop over.
declare -n
§5.7 — a nameref: an alias you can write through, which indirect expansion cannot do. The output-parameter mechanism.
${var@U} ${var@u} ${var@L}
§5.8 — uppercased, first-character uppercased, lowercased. The same three conversions as ^^ ^ ,,, in the transformation syntax.
${var@Q}
§5.8 — quoted so that re-reading it as shell input gives the value back. The one to reach for before any eval, ssh or bash -c.
${var@E}
§5.8 — backslash escapes expanded, as $'…' would.
${var@P}
§5.8 — expanded as a prompt string.
${var@A} ${var@a}
§5.8 — a declare command that recreates the parameter, and its attribute letters alone.
${var@K} ${var@k}
§5.8 — an array as quoted key/value pairs: one word for @K, one word per key and value for @k. Needs a subscript — ${var[@]@K}.

Three cross-cutting rules are worth restating beside the table, because each one applies to most of the rows and each has already cost somebody a bug.

Patterns are globs, and they are expanded first. pattern in any of the trim and substitute rows is matched as a glob, not a regular expression, and it goes through the expansion pipeline before matching — so a pattern in a variable is re-read as a glob unless you quote it, ${var#"$prefix"}. §5.5's whitespace trim relies on that quoting and breaks silently without it. The & in replacement text is the same class of hazard from the other direction: under bash 5.2 and later it means "the matched text" unless escaped.

A pattern that does not match is not an error. Every trim and every substitution returns the value unchanged when nothing matches, with no signal of any kind. When the presence of the prefix is a precondition rather than a possibility, test for it separately; the expansion will never tell you.

Nothing here nests. There is no expression context inside ${ }: no applying two operators in one expansion, no ${#!name}. The failure is a bad substitution at run time, so it survives until the branch containing it executes. One operator per step, into a named temporary — which also gives the intermediate value a name, and the name is usually the clearer half of the fix.

Exercises

1. Four defaults, one function. Write render host [port] [scheme] that prints scheme://host:port. The host is mandatory and its absence must abort with a named message; the port defaults to 443; the scheme defaults to https but must be settable. Then explain what render api.example.test '' http should do and why.

Solution 
render() {
  local host=${1:?render: needs a host} port=${2:-443} scheme
  scheme=${3:+$3}
  : "${scheme:=https}"
  printf '%s://%s:%s\n' "$scheme" "$host" "$port"
}
render api.example.test
render api.example.test 8080
render api.example.test 8080 http
render api.example.test '' http
render

https://api.example.test:443
https://api.example.test:8080
http://api.example.test:8080
http://api.example.test:443
example.sh: line 2: 1: render: needs a host

${1:?…} on the first parameter of the first local declaration is the whole precondition: no if, no return, and the message names the function. The final call prints it and the script exits 1 — render never runs its body.

render api.example.test '' http prints port 443, because ${2:-443} tests unset or null and an explicitly empty argument is null. That is the right behaviour here: a caller passing '' for a port means "I have nothing to say about the port", and a positional interface gives them no other way to reach the third argument. Had the requirement been "an empty port is an error", the operator to use is ${2-443} — which accepts the empty string as a value — followed by an explicit test.

The scheme line is deliberately the long way round to show :+ and := together; local scheme=${3:-https} does the same job in one operator and is what you should actually write. Keep the chained form only when the two steps really are separate decisions.

2. Change a file's extension. Write retarget path extension printing the path with its last extension replaced. It must handle a path with no directory and a path with no extension, and it must not produce app.log/out style nonsense.

Solution 
retarget() {
  local path=$1 want=$2 dir base stem
  dir=${path%/*}; [[ $dir == "$path" ]] && dir=.
  base=${path##*/}
  stem=${base%.*}
  [[ $stem == "$base" ]] && stem=$base
  printf '%s/%s.%s\n' "$dir" "$stem" "$want"
}
retarget /src/report.md html
retarget report.md html
retarget /src/archive.tar.gz html
retarget /src/README html

/src/report.html
./report.html
/src/archive.tar.html
/src/README.html

Both guards exist because §5.4's "a pattern that does not match changes nothing" rule bites twice. ${path%/*} on report.md returns report.md rather than a directory, so the comparison [[ $dir == "$path" ]] detects "there was no slash" and substitutes . — the second line of output would otherwise read report.md/report.html. The stem guard is the same test for a name with no dot; it happens to be a no-op here because ${base%.*} already returns base unchanged, and it is written out so that the intent survives a later edit.

archive.tar.gz becomes archive.tar.html, which is %.* being non-greedy: only the last extension is replaced. That is the correct reading of "its last extension" and it is the reading a build system wants. Replacing every extension would be ${base%%.*}, and you would then have to decide what .bashrc means.

Splitting dir and base before touching either is the part to keep. Doing it in one expansion means matching a . that might be in a directory name — /src/v1.2/README would lose its directory's dot to a naive ${path%.*}.

3. Trim whitespace from both ends. Write trim using only parameter expansion — no sed, no tr, no subshell beyond the one that captures the result. Show it working on strings padded on one side, both sides, and neither, and on a string that is entirely whitespace.

Solution 
trim() {
  local s=$1
  s=${s#"${s%%[![:space:]]*}"}
  s=${s%"${s##*[![:space:]]}"}
  printf '%s' "$s"
}
for raw in '  both  ' 'left only   ' '   right only' 'none' '   ' ''; do
  printf '[%s] -> [%s]\n' "$raw" "$(trim "$raw")"
done

[  both  ] -> [both]
[left only   ] -> [left only]
[   right only] -> [right only]
[none] -> [none]
[   ] -> []
[] -> []

Each line computes the whitespace to remove and then removes exactly that. ${s%%[![:space:]]*} strips the longest trailing part starting at the first non-space, leaving only the leading whitespace; ${s#"…"} then deletes that prefix. The second line mirrors it: ${s##*[![:space:]]} leaves only the trailing whitespace, and ${s%"…"} removes it.

The inner quotes are load-bearing.
