Remove them and the computed whitespace is re-interpreted as a glob pattern — where a space matches only a space the result looks the same, so the bug hides until the input contains a * or a ?, at which point the expansion removes a prefix that was never there. §5.4's rule, that the pattern is expanded before it is matched, is the reason.

The all-whitespace case works without a special branch: the first line removes everything, leaving "", and the second finds nothing to do. And printf '%s' rather than echo keeps the function from adding a newline the caller did not ask for — which matters because $(trim …) would strip it anyway (§4.4) and a caller not using command substitution would be surprised.

A note on scope: this is the readability limit §5.9 names. It is worth writing once, in a function, with these comments — and worth never writing inline.

4. Snapshot a map. You need to write an associative array to a file and read it back. Show why building key=value pairs by hand is wrong, and give the correct form.

Solution 
# shellcheck disable=SC2016,SC2145,SC2294  # @K is built for eval, and the label is literal
declare -A conf=([region]='eu-west-1' [note]="it's fine")
plain=""
for k in "${!conf[@]}"; do plain+="$k=${conf[$k]} "; done
printf 'naive:  %s\n' "$plain"
printf 'via @K: %s\n' "${conf[@]@K}"
eval "declare -A restored=(${conf[@]@K})"
printf 'restored note: %s\n' "${restored[note]}"

naive:  note=it's fine region=eu-west-1 
via @K: note "it's fine" region "eu-west-1" 
restored note: it's fine

The naive string is unparseable and the output shows both reasons. The value it's fine contains a space, so splitting the snapshot on whitespace gives note=it's and fine as separate items; and it contains an apostrophe, so anything that re-reads the text as shell input hits an unterminated quote. Choosing a different separator does not fix this — it moves the problem to whichever character you chose, and the data decides, not you.

@K emits each key and value quoted for re-reading, which is exactly the property needed, and declare -A restored=(…) consumes that form directly. Note that this is one of the rare legitimate uses of eval (§18.10): the text being evaluated was produced by the shell's own quoting operator rather than assembled from data, so there is nothing in it the shell can misread.

Two caveats to carry away. The order is bash's hash order and is not specified, so a snapshot is for restoring and never for comparing — diffing two of these is a bug. And @K is bash 5.1 and later; on an older shell the portable route is a loop emitting declare -p-style output, or admitting that a map is data and belongs in a file format that has a parser (§15.10).

SECTION 6

Arrays and Associative Arrays

Every value in the previous five sections was a string. That is not a limitation the shell apologises for — a pipeline is a stream of bytes, a filename is a string, an exit status is a number that fits in a byte — but it collides with one requirement that every non-trivial script eventually has: a list of things, where one of the things contains a space.

Arrays are the shell's answer, and they are the single feature that most reliably separates a script that survives contact with real data from one that works until someone names a directory My Documents. §3 established that word splitting is the mechanism that destroys a list stored in a string; this section is the data structure that never puts the list in a string to begin with.

bash has two kinds. An indexed array maps non-negative integers to strings and is what arr=(a b c) builds. An associative array maps arbitrary strings to strings and needs declare -A before its first assignment. They share almost all of their syntax, differ in three places that matter, and the differences are where the bugs live — §6.7 measures them side by side.

One boundary before we start. linux §2 showed $IFS and word splitting at an interactive prompt, where a list in a string is usually fine because you can see the result and retype the command. This section is about the case where nobody is watching: the script runs at 03:00, the list came from find, and one file has a newline in its name. Arrays are not a style preference there. They are the only construct that gets the right answer.

6.1 What Arrays Are For, and What a Delimited String Costs

Start with the thing an array replaces, so the cost is concrete rather than asserted. Here is a list of two filenames kept in an ordinary variable, iterated the way it is written in thousands of scripts:

files='report one.txt report two.txt'
echo "--- as a delimited string ---"
for f in $files; do echo "[$f]"; done
echo "--- as an array ---"
files=('report one.txt' 'report two.txt')
for f in "${files[@]}"; do echo "[$f]"; done

--- as a delimited string ---
[report]
[one.txt]
[report]
[two.txt]
--- as an array ---
[report one.txt]
[report two.txt]

Two files went in and four names came out. Nothing failed, nothing was reported, and a script that deletes $f would have deleted report, one.txt, report and two.txt — none of which exist, so rm would have printed four errors and exited non-zero, which is the good case. The bad case is a script that creates $f, which happily creates four wrong files.

The reflex fix is to change the delimiter, and it is worth watching that fail, because the failure is instructive rather than merely unlucky:

mkdir demo && cd demo
touch cXd.txt
files='report one.txt:report two.txt'
IFS=:
echo "--- IFS=: with a colon in a name ---"
for f in $files; do echo "[$f]"; done
files='a:b.txt:c*d.txt'
echo "--- and it still globs ---"
for f in $files; do echo "[$f]"; done

--- IFS=: with a colon in a name ---
[report one.txt]
[report two.txt]
--- and it still globs ---
[a]
[b.txt]
[cXd.txt]

The first half works, and that is the trap: it works on the data you tested with. A colon is legal in a filename on every filesystem this course cares about, so the correctness of the script now depends on an assumption about data it does not control. And the second half shows that changing IFS addressed only one of the two things that happen to an unquoted expansion. Word splitting is now on your terms; globbing is still on the filesystem's. c*d.txt was never a filename here — it was a pattern, and step 5 of §4's pipeline replaced it with the file that happened to match. Fixing that needs set -f as well, and now two global settings have to be correct for one loop to be right.

An array removes the question. There is no delimiter, so no character is special, so no data can be mistaken for structure:

A string list needs a character that cannot appear in the data. On a filesystem the only such byte is NUL, and a shell variable cannot hold one — which is why find -print0 exists and why it cannot be read into a variable, only piped (§14.9).
An array stores the boundaries separately from the bytes. Element three is element three regardless of what is in elements one and two, so no value can change how the list is read.
The cost is that arrays are a bashism. They are not in POSIX sh (§19.5), they cannot be exported to a child process (§6.15), and they cannot nest (§6.9). Those three limits define everything this section can and cannot promise.

Keep that third row in view. This section is going to spend fifteen subsections on a data structure with no nesting, no export, and a syntax that overloads [ — and it is still worth every line, because the alternative is a delimiter and the data always wins against a delimiter.

6.2 Creating an Indexed Array

There are four spellings and they produce genuinely different things, which is worth seeing in one run rather than four paragraphs:

# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # a, b, c and d are read through the nameref below
a=(one two three)
declare -a b
b[0]=zero
b[1]=one
declare -a c=([2]=two [0]=zero)
d=()
d+=(first)
d+=(second third)
for name in a b c d; do
  declare -n ref=$name
  printf '%-3s count=%s  elements: %s\n' "$name" "${#ref[@]}" "${ref[*]}"
  unset -n ref
done

a   count=3  elements: one two three
b   count=2  elements: zero one
c   count=2  elements: zero two
d   count=3  elements: first second third

a=(one two three) is the compound assignment — an array literal — and it is the one to reach for. The parentheses are shell syntax, not characters in the data, so the words inside are subject to all the usual expansions and all the usual quoting — a=(*.txt "$var" $(cmd)) all work and all mean what §4 says they mean.

b[0]=zero creates the array implicitly. You do not need declare -a for an indexed array; assigning to a subscript is enough. (declare -A for an associative array is not optional, which §6.7 proves the hard way.) declare -a b on its own declares the name without giving it any elements, which matters under set -u — see §6.15.

c=([2]=two [0]=zero) shows two things at once: an array literal may give its subscripts explicitly, and they need not be in order or contiguous. c has two elements at indices 0 and 2, which makes it sparse, the subject of §6.6.

d+=(second third) is appending to an array, and arr+=(x) is the form to use for it every time. Note d=() first: an empty compound assignment creates an array with zero elements, which is a different state from "does not exist" and different again from "exists with one empty element".

The loop is a preview of §6.13 — declare -n ref=$name makes ref an alias for whichever array $name names, which is how you write one loop body over four different arrays. unset -n removes the alias rather than the array it points at, and forgetting the -n there destroys the target instead.

declare -p is how you find out what you actually have. Guessing from echo is unreliable, because echo prints a string either way:

a=(one two three)
declare -A m=([x]=1 [y]=2)
declare -p a m
plain=hello
declare -p plain

declare -a a=([0]="one" [1]="two" [2]="three")
declare -A m=([y]="2" [x]="1" )
declare -- plain="hello"

The attribute letter is the answer: -a indexed, -A associative, -- an ordinary string. The output is also valid shell input, which is what makes declare -p the serialisation format of choice when a value has to cross a boundary (§6.15 and §16.7). Note in passing that m's two keys come back in the order y x rather than the order they were written — §6.7.

One assignment rule catches everyone once. += means something different depending on whether the right-hand side is parenthesised. With parentheses, += on an array appends new elements; without them it appends text to a single element. Appending to an array is the common case, so it is the one to get into your fingers:

# shellcheck disable=SC2179  # b+=three without parens is the lesson
a=(one two)
echo "count: ${#a[@]}"
a=(three)
echo "after a=(three), count: ${#a[@]}  -> ${a[*]}"
a+=(four)
echo "after a+=(four),  count: ${#a[@]}  -> ${a[*]}"
b=(one two)
b+=three
echo "after b+=three,   count: ${#b[@]}  -> ${b[*]}"

count: 2
after a=(three), count: 1  -> three
after a+=(four),  count: 2  -> three four
after b+=three,   count: 2  -> onethree two

Three distinct behaviours. a=(three) replaces the whole array — it does not assign to element 0 and leave the rest. a+=(four) appends a new element. And b+=three, with no parentheses, appends to element zero as if it were a plain string, turning one into onethree and leaving element 1 alone. That last line is not an error, produces no warning, and is almost never what was meant. §6.4 explains why element zero is the one that gets it.

6.3 Subscripts Are Arithmetic Expressions

A subscript on an indexed array is not a number. It is an arithmetic expression, evaluated by the same engine as $(( )) (§7.8), and that has consequences both convenient and dangerous.

a=(zero one two three four five)
i=2
echo "a[2]    = ${a[2]}"
echo "a[i]    = ${a[i]}"
echo "a[\$i]   = ${a[$i]}"
echo "a[1+1]  = ${a[1+1]}"
echo "a[i*2]  = ${a[i*2]}"
echo "a[-1]   = ${a[-1]}"
echo "a[-2]   = ${a[-2]}"

a[2]    = two
a[i]    = two
a[$i]   = two
a[1+1]  = two
a[i*2]  = four
a[-1]   = five
a[-2]   = four

The convenient half: ${a[i]} needs no $, because an arithmetic context resolves bare names itself; ${a[1+1]} and ${a[i*2]} do real arithmetic; and a negative subscript counts from the end, so ${a[-1]} is the last element. Reading through a negative subscript is bash 4.2 and later, and assigning or unsetting through one is 4.3; both are well below anything this course targets. It is worth using, because the alternative is not merely uglier but wrong the moment the array is sparse:

a=(zero one two three four)
unset 'a[4]'
unset 'a[1]'
echo "indices        = ${!a[*]}"
echo "count          = ${#a[@]}"
echo "a[-1]          = ${a[-1]}"
echo "a[\${#a[@]}-1] = ${a[${#a[@]}-1]}"

indices        = 0 2 3
count          = 3
a[-1]          = three
a[${#a[@]}-1] = two

${a[-1]} counts back from the highest assigned index and finds three. ${a[${#a[@]}-1]} computes 3 - 1 = 2 from the count and reads index 2, giving two — an element that is neither last nor an error. §6.6 develops why the count and the highest index are unrelated numbers.

The dangerous half is what happens to a name that is not a number:

a=(zero one two three)
echo "a[nosuchvar] = ${a[nosuchvar]}"
key=2
echo "a[key]       = ${a[key]}"
name=key
echo "a[name]      = ${a[name]}"

a[nosuchvar] = zero
a[key]       = two
a[name]      = two

${a[nosuchvar]} is ${a[0]}. In an arithmetic context an unset name is zero, so a typo in a subscript does not raise an error — it silently reads the first element. This is the same rule §7.8 will state for $(( )), and it is the single most common way an indexed array is misread. Worse, the third line shows the recursive resolution §4's probe bank recorded: name holds key, key holds 2, and the subscript evaluates to 2. Convenient once, baffling when unintentional.

Two guards are worth knowing. set -u does not help here, because nosuchvar is being evaluated arithmetically rather than expanded — but it does catch the resulting read when the index is out of range:

set -u
a=(zero one)
echo "start"
echo "a[99] = [${a[99]}]"
echo "done"

start
example.sh: line 4: a[99]: unbound variable

Without set -u that line prints a[99] = [] and the script carries on, which is why §11.2 argues for set -u in every script that indexes an array by a computed value.

A negative subscript that runs past the start is a different error and, notably, a non-fatal one:

# shellcheck disable=SC2320  # $? of that echo IS the claim being tested
a=(x y)
echo "a[-5] = [${a[-5]}]"
echo "status: $?"
empty=()
echo "empty[-1] = [${empty[-1]}]"
echo "still running"

example.sh: line 3: a: bad array subscript
a[-5] = []
status: 0
example.sh: line 6: empty: bad array subscript
empty[-1] = []
still running

Read the status: 0 line carefully, because it is the point. bash printed a diagnostic, expanded the subscript to the empty string, and reported success. ${a[-1]} on an array that might be empty is therefore a silent producer of empty strings, and $? will not tell you. Check ${#a[@]} first, or accept a default with ${a[-1]:-none}.

6.4 [@], [*], and Why a Bare Array Name Is Element Zero

This is the subsection §5 pointed at twice, and the rule it teaches is the one piece of array syntax with no defence.

# shellcheck disable=SC2128  # expanding without an index is the subject here
a=(alpha beta gamma)
echo "\$a          = $a"
echo "\${a}        = ${a}"
echo "\${a[0]}     = ${a[0]}"
echo "\${#a}       = ${#a}"
echo "\${#a[@]}    = ${#a[@]}"
echo "\${a^^}      = ${a^^}"

$a          = alpha
${a}        = alpha
${a[0]}     = alpha
${#a}       = 5
${#a[@]}    = 3
${a^^}      = ALPHA

An array name used without a subscript means element zero. Not the whole array, not an error, not the count — element zero. So $a is alpha, ${#a} is the length of the string alpha (5) rather than the number of elements (3), and every §5 operator applied to a bare name silently operates on the first element only. That is why ${m@K} in §5.8 came back empty for a map with no key 0, and why b+=three in §6.2 appended to element zero.

The rule exists for backward compatibility: arrays arrived in bash 2.0, and $a had to keep meaning what it meant in scripts written before they existed. Knowing the reason does not make it safe. Treat a bare array name as a bug — if you meant the whole array write [@], and if you meant the first element write [0] so the next reader can tell you meant it.

That leaves the choice between [@] and [*], which is exactly the "$@" versus "$*" distinction from §3.6, applied to a named array:

# shellcheck disable=SC2068,SC2048,SC2086  # the unquoted rows are the comparison
a=('one two' three)
printf 'quoted   [@]: '; printf '<%s> ' "${a[@]}"; echo
printf 'quoted   [*]: '; printf '<%s> ' "${a[*]}"; echo
printf 'unquoted [@]: '; printf '<%s> ' ${a[@]}; echo
printf 'unquoted [*]: '; printf '<%s> ' ${a[*]}; echo

quoted   [@]: <one two> <three> 
quoted   [*]: <one two three> 
unquoted [@]: <one> <two> <three> 
unquoted [*]: <one> <two> <three>

Four combinations, and only the first preserves the array. "${a[@]}" expands to one word per element, with element boundaries intact. "${a[*]}" expands to a single word, elements joined. And unquoted, the two are indistinguishable — both produce the joined string and then hand it to word splitting, which is how one two becomes two words and the array's structure is lost.

The joining character is not a space by definition; it is the first character of IFS:

a=(one two three)
IFS=,
echo "IFS=,      \"\${a[*]}\" = ${a[*]}"
IFS=':-'
echo "IFS=':-'   \"\${a[*]}\" = ${a[*]}"
IFS=
echo "IFS empty  \"\${a[*]}\" = ${a[*]}"
unset IFS
echo "IFS unset  \"\${a[*]}\" = ${a[*]}"

IFS=,      "${a[*]}" = one,two,three
IFS=':-'   "${a[*]}" = one:two:three
IFS empty  "${a[*]}" = onetwothree
IFS unset  "${a[*]}" = one two three

The second row is the one to read twice. IFS holds two characters, : and -, and the join used only the first. That is the rule: "${a[*]}" inserts ${IFS:0:1} between elements, not the whole of IFS and not one of its characters chosen per boundary. The last two rows complete it — IFS= (set but empty) joins with nothing, and an unset IFS falls back to the default, whose first character is a space. IFS= and unset IFS differing is §3.4's distinction, and this is the second place in the language where it is visible.

That makes [*] the shell's string-join, and the idiom is worth writing deliberately:

a=(a b c)
old=$IFS; IFS=,
csv="${a[*]}"
IFS=$old
echo "$csv"

a,b,c

Save and restore IFS around it. A global left modified is §3.4's warning, and a function that leaks IFS breaks every loop its caller runs afterwards.

6.5 Quoting Array Expansions: the One Rule

There is exactly one rule for quoting array expansions, and it has no exceptions worth teaching: "${arr[@]}", with the quotes and with @. Everything else is either a deliberate join or a bug. Here is what the alternatives cost, measured in a directory that contains a file called bq.txt:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016,SC2068  # the labels are literal; the unquoted call is the point
mkdir demo && cd demo
touch bq.txt
a=('a file.txt' '' 'b*.txt')
echo "elements stored: ${#a[@]}"
count() { echo "  received $# argument(s): $*"; }
echo 'count "${a[@]}"'; count "${a[@]}"
echo 'count ${a[@]}';   count ${a[@]}
echo 'count "${a[*]}"'; count "${a[*]}"

elements stored: 3
count "${a[@]}"
  received 3 argument(s): a file.txt  b*.txt
count ${a[@]}
  received 3 argument(s): a file.txt bq.txt
count "${a[*]}"
  received 1 argument(s): a file.txt  b*.txt

Three elements went in each time; look at what arrived. The quoted [@] delivered three arguments and the middle one is empty — that is the double space in the joined printout, and it is correct: an empty element is a value, and the function received it.

The unquoted [@] also says three, and it is three different things. a file.txt split into a and file.txt, the empty element vanished entirely because word splitting produces no word from an empty expansion, and b*.txt was globbed into the real file bq.txt. Two elements became two words, one became zero, and one became a filename that was never in the array. The count matching by coincidence is the worst part — a test that checks $# would pass.

And "${a[*]}" delivered one argument, which is at least honest about what it does.

for x in "${a[@]}" — iterate elements. The only correct loop over an array.
cmd "${a[@]}" — pass elements as arguments. §6.14 builds a whole command this way.
b=("${a[@]}") — copy an array. Note the parentheses and the quotes; without the quotes you copy a re-split, re-globbed approximation of the original.
"${a[*]}" — join into one string. Correct only when you actually want a string, and only with IFS set deliberately.

ShellCheck catches the unquoted case as SC2068 ("Double quote array expansions to avoid re-splitting elements") at the error level in ShellCheck 0.11, so a gate at --severity=error already stops it; §20.4 shows how to gate on it, or on any single check, whatever its level. It cannot catch "${a[*]}" used where "${a[@]}" was meant, because both are valid; that one is on the reader.

6.6 Length, Indices, and Sparse Arrays

Four questions come up constantly, and the shell answers them with four similar-looking expansions that must not be confused:

# shellcheck disable=SC2145  # the labels name the operator being shown
a=(zero one two three)
echo "count  \${#a[@]}  = ${#a[@]}"
echo "indices \${!a[@]} = ${!a[@]}"
echo "len of element 0  = ${#a[0]}"
echo "len of element 3  = ${#a[3]}"

count  ${#a[@]}  = 4
indices ${!a[@]} = 0 1 2 3
len of element 0  = 4
len of element 3  = 5

${#arr[@]} is the number of elements. ${!arr[@]} is the list of indices — the array indices — the ! is the same indirection sigil as §5.7's ${!name}, here meaning "the subscripts rather than the values". ${#a[0]} is the length of one element's string. And ${#a}, from §6.4, is the length of element zero, which is the one that reads like a count and is not.

On a dense array built by a=(…) the array indices are 0 1 2 … and ${#arr[@]} doubles as "one past the last index". That equivalence is not a property of arrays. It is a property of that one array, and the moment anything is removed it stops being true:

a=(zero one two three four)
unset 'a[1]'
unset 'a[3]'
echo "count      = ${#a[@]}"
echo "indices    = ${!a[*]}"
echo "values     = ${a[*]}"
idx=("${!a[@]}")
echo "highest    = ${idx[-1]}"
a[9]=nine
echo "after a[9]=nine: count=${#a[@]} indices=${!a[*]}"
echo "--- a C-style loop over count is WRONG here ---"
for (( i = 0; i < ${#a[@]}; i++ )); do printf '[%s]=%s ' "$i" "${a[$i]}"; done; echo
echo "--- iterate the real indices ---"
for i in "${!a[@]}"; do printf '[%s]=%s ' "$i" "${a[$i]}"; done; echo

count      = 3
indices    = 0 2 4
values     = zero two four
highest    = 4
after a[9]=nine: count=4 indices=0 2 4 9
--- a C-style loop over count is WRONG here ---
[0]=zero [1]= [2]=two [3]= 
--- iterate the real indices ---
[0]=zero [2]=two [4]=four [9]=nine

bash arrays are sparse: to unset an array element is to remove that index rather than shift the ones above it, and assigning to a[9] on a four-element array does not create elements 5 through 8. The count and the highest index are now unrelated numbers.

The two loops show what that costs. The C-style loop runs i from 0 to 2, reads elements 0, 1 and 2, misses four and nine entirely, and prints two empty strings for indices that do not exist — all without a single error. for i in "${!a[@]}" is the loop that is always right, and for x in "${a[@]}" is always right when you want values and do not care about position. The C-style loop over ${#a[@]} is correct only on an array you can prove is dense, which usually means one you built three lines earlier.

Note idx=("${!a[@]}") as the way to get the highest index. ${!a[@]: -1} looks like it should work and does not — ${!a[@]} is not a value that can be sliced, and bash reports invalid variable name. Copy the indices into an array first.

One more trap, and it is a quoting trap rather than an array one:

# shellcheck disable=SC2184  # an unquoted unset argument is the trap being shown
mkdir demo && cd demo
a=(zero one two)
unset a[1]
echo "unquoted, no file matches:  ${!a[*]}"
touch a1
a=(zero one two)
unset a[1]
echo "unquoted, a file named a1:  ${!a[*]}"
a=(zero one two)
unset 'a[1]'
echo "quoted, same directory:     ${!a[*]}"

unquoted, no file matches:  0 2
unquoted, a file named a1:  0 1 2
quoted, same directory:     0 2

a[1] is a glob pattern — a bracket expression matching the single character 1. When nothing in the directory matches it, the word survives unchanged and unset does what you meant, which is why the first line works and why this bug hides. Create a file called a1 and the same line silently unsets a variable named a1 instead, leaving the array untouched and reporting success.

Always quote the argument when you unset an array element, and note that the bug is data-dependent on the contents of the current directory, which makes it one of the least reproducible failures in the language. ShellCheck flags it as SC2184.

6.7 Associative Arrays, and the Key Order Nobody Promised

An associative array maps arbitrary strings to strings. It arrived in bash 4.0, and it is the reason a script that needs a lookup table no longer has to build variable names with eval (§18.10).

declare -A colour=([apple]=red [banana]=yellow)
colour[grape]=purple
colour[apple]=green
echo "apple  = ${colour[apple]}"
echo "count  = ${#colour[@]}"
echo "keys   = ${!colour[*]}"
echo "values = ${colour[*]}"
declare -p colour

apple  = green
count  = 3
keys   = grape apple banana
values = purple green yellow
declare -A colour=([grape]="purple" [apple]="green" [banana]="yellow" )

The syntax is deliberately the same as an indexed array: ${m[key]} to read, m[key]=v to write, ${#m[@]} to count, ${!m[@]} for the keys, "${m[@]}" for the values. Everything §6.5 said about quoting applies unchanged.

declare -A is not optional, and the failure when it is missing is silent and total:

m=([apple]=red [banana]=yellow)
echo "without declare -A:"
declare -p m
echo "m[apple] = [${m[apple]}]"

without declare -A:
declare -a m=([0]="yellow")
m[apple] = [yellow]

Without the declaration bash builds an indexed array, evaluates apple and banana as arithmetic expressions, gets 0 for both (§6.3), and assigns them both to index 0 — where the second overwrites the first. One element survives, every lookup returns it regardless of the key, and nothing is reported. This is the single most destructive typo available in this section, and the reason to run declare -A as its own statement where a reviewer can see it.

Now the property that must be designed around rather than worked around:

declare -A m=([one]=1 [two]=2 [three]=3 [four]=4 [five]=5)
echo "insertion order: one two three four five"
echo "iteration order: ${!m[*]}"
echo "--- sorted, which is the only order you may rely on ---"
mapfile -t keys < <(printf '%s\n' "${!m[@]}" | sort)
for k in "${keys[@]}"; do printf '%s=%s ' "$k" "${m[$k]}"; done; echo

insertion order: one two three four five
iteration order: four two three one five
--- sorted, which is the only order you may rely on ---
five=5 four=4 one=1 three=3 two=2

The iteration order of an associative array is unspecified. It is bash's internal hash order — not insertion order, not sorted, and not guaranteed stable across bash versions or across different key sets. It is deterministic for a given bash and a given sequence of insertions, which is exactly what makes it dangerous: a script that iterates a map and writes a report will produce identical output every time you test it, and different output on the machine that has a different bash.

So: iterate a map only when order does not matter, and sort the keys explicitly when it does. The mapfile -t keys < <(… | sort) line above is the idiom; §6.12 explains why it is process substitution rather than a pipe. For numeric keys use sort -n, and for reproducible output under any locale use LC_ALL=C sort, because collation order is locale-dependent and that is a second source of the same surprise.

Two more differences from indexed arrays are worth measuring, because the syntax being identical implies a similarity that is not there:

declare -A m=([1+1]=arith [two]=word)
declare -a a=([1+1]=arith)
echo "assoc keys   : ${!m[*]}"
echo "m[1+1]=${m[1+1]}   m[2]=[${m[2]}]"
echo "indexed index: ${!a[*]}   a[2]=${a[2]}"
i=two
echo "m[i]=[${m[i]}]   m[\$i]=[${m[$i]}]"

assoc keys   : two 1+1
m[1+1]=arith   m[2]=[]
indexed index: 2   a[2]=arith
m[i]=[]   m[$i]=[word]

An associative subscript is a literal string; an indexed subscript is arithmetic. The same text [1+1] is the three-character key 1+1 in m and the number 2 in a. The consequence on the last line is the one that bites: ${m[i]} looks up the key i, which does not exist, while ${a[i]} would have used the value of i. In an associative array the $ is mandatory, and omitting it produces an empty string rather than an error — so set -u will not save you either, because the key i is simply absent.

The other difference is what happens to keys that collide with the syntax:

# shellcheck disable=SC2145  # m[@] inside a string IS the point of this block
declare -A m=([@]=at ['*']=star [x]=ex)
echo "count      = ${#m[@]}"
echo "keys       = ${!m[@]}"
echo "m[x]       = ${m[x]}"
echo "m[@] means every value, not the key '@': ${m[@]}"
echo "the key itself needs quoting or a variable:"
k='@'
echo "m[\$k]      = ${m[$k]}"

count      = 3
keys       = * @ x
m[x]       = ex
m[@] means every value, not the key '@': star at ex
the key itself needs quoting or a variable:
m[$k]      = at

@ and * are perfectly legal keys and are stored and counted like any other — but ${m[@]} and ${m[*]} keep their meaning of "all values", so the literal keys become unreachable by the obvious spelling and need a variable to get at. If keys come from data you do not control, this is a real hazard rather than a curiosity, and the defence is to never write a bare subscript on untrusted input.

6.8 Maps in Practice: Sets, Counters, and Lookup Tables

Three patterns account for most of what associative arrays are actually used for, and each has a detail that is not obvious.

A set is a map whose values are ignored. The membership test is [[ -v m[key] ]], not a comparison against the empty string:

declare -A seen=()
for w in apple banana apple cherry banana apple; do
  if [[ -v seen[$w] ]]; then
    echo "duplicate: $w"
  else
    seen[$w]=1
    echo "new:       $w"
  fi
done
echo "distinct: ${#seen[@]}"

new:       apple
new:       banana
duplicate: apple
new:       cherry
duplicate: banana
duplicate: apple
distinct: 3

-v asks whether the key exists, which is the right question: a key whose value is the empty string is present, and [[ -n ${seen[$w]} ]] would call it absent. (-v on an array element is bash 4.3 and later; §7.6 covers the operator in full.) Note also that seen[$w] inside [[ ]] is written without ${ } and without quotes, and is safe there because [[ ]] does not word-split — one of the few places in the language where that is true.

A counter is a map whose values are integers, and it leans on arithmetic evaluation:

declare -A count=()
for w in the cat sat on the mat the end; do
  (( count[$w]++ ))
done
for k in $(printf '%s\n' "${!count[@]}" | sort); do
  printf '%-4s %s\n' "$k" "${count[$k]}"
done

cat  1
end  1
mat  1
on   1
sat  1
the  3

(( count[$w]++ )) works on a key that does not exist yet because an unset name is zero in an arithmetic context (§6.3, §7.8) — the same rule that makes a typo'd subscript read element zero is, here, exactly what you want. It survives set -u too, which surprises people:

set -u
declare -A count=()
w=hello
echo "about to increment an absent key"
(( count[$w]++ ))
echo "count[hello] = ${count[$w]}"
declare -A plain
plain[x]=$(( ${plain[x]:-0} + 1 ))
echo "explicit default form: ${plain[x]}"

about to increment an absent key
count[hello] = 1
explicit default form: 1

Both forms work. The second is worth knowing anyway, because ${plain[x]:-0} is explicit about the default and reads correctly to someone who does not know the arithmetic rule.

One caution on (( )) as a statement: it returns exit status 1 when the expression evaluates to zero, so (( count[$w]++ )) on the first increment returns non-zero — the post-increment yields 0 — and under set -e that terminates the script (§11.5). Write (( count[$w]++ )) || true, or use the pre-increment (( ++count[$w] )), which yields 1. This is the most common set -e surprise in the language and §11.5 returns to it.

A lookup table replaces a case statement when the branches are data rather than code:

declare -A action=(
  [start]='systemd unit up'
  [stop]='systemd unit down'
  [status]='report state'
)
run() {
  local verb=$1 known
  if [[ ! -v action[$verb] ]]; then
    known=$(printf '%s\n' "${!action[@]}" | LC_ALL=C sort | tr '\n' ' ')
    echo "unknown verb: $verb (try: ${known% })" >&2
    return 2
  fi
  echo "$verb -> ${action[$verb]}"
}
run start
run status
run frobnicate || echo "exit status $?"

start -> systemd unit up
status -> report state
unknown verb: frobnicate (try: start status stop)
exit status 2

The win over case is that the set of valid verbs is a value rather than syntax, so the error message can enumerate it — and stays correct when a verb is added, which a hand-written usage string does not. §13.7 builds a full subcommand dispatcher on this shape, with the handlers as function names in the map.

6.9 One String Per Key: What a Map Cannot Hold

The limit that shapes every design decision above: an array element is a string, and a string is all it can be. There is no array of arrays, and the attempt is a hard error rather than a silent coercion:

declare -A m
m[list]=(a b c)
echo "assignment status: $?"
echo "m[list] = [${m[list]}]"

example.sh: line 2: m[list]: cannot assign list to array member
assignment status: 1
m[list] = []

That is the clearest diagnostic in this section, and it closes the door on the obvious data structure — a map from a name to a list. §1.3's worked example rejected a shell implementation partly on this basis, and the reasoning is worth making explicit here.

The workaround is to encode the list into a string and split it back out, and the workaround is a decision about your data, not a technique:

declare -A by_dc
by_dc[eu-west]='web-1 web-2'
by_dc['us east']='db-1'
for dc in "${!by_dc[@]}"; do
  read -ra hosts <<< "${by_dc[$dc]}"
  printf '%-10s %s host(s): %s\n' "$dc" "${#hosts[@]}" "${hosts[*]}"
done
echo "--- a host name with a space breaks it ---"
by_dc[broken]='web-1 "web 2"'
read -ra hosts <<< "${by_dc[broken]}"
printf 'got %s host(s): ' "${#hosts[@]}"; printf '<%s> ' "${hosts[@]}"; echo

us east    1 host(s): db-1
eu-west    2 host(s): web-1 web-2
--- a host name with a space breaks it ---
got 3 host(s): <web-1> <"web> <2">

Notice which half worked. The keys are safe — us east contains a space and is stored and retrieved intact, because a key is a string and the map keeps its boundaries. The values are not, because the list inside them is delimited, and §6.1's entire argument applies again one level down. Quoting the inner value does not rescue it: "web 2" came back as two words carrying literal quote characters, because read -ra splits on IFS and does not process quotes.

So the honest options, in order of preference:

Invert the map. Instead of datacentre → list of hosts, keep host → datacentre. The values become single strings, the structure fits, and grouping is a loop rather than a nested container. This is the right answer more often than it looks.
Use a composite key. members[eu-west/web-1]=1 turns a map-of-sets into a flat set, and a prefix match enumerates a group. Choose the separator against the data, and know that you are choosing.
Use a newline delimiter and mapfile. A newline is legal in a filename but rare elsewhere, and mapfile -t splits on it without the quote-processing problem. Acceptable for hostnames; not acceptable for paths.
Stop. When the answer is "encode a list into a string and hope", the data has outgrown the language. §1.6's hundred-line rule and §21.7's rewrite criteria both point here, and a map of lists is one of the clearest signals either gives.

6.10 The Positional Parameters Are Not an Array

"$@" behaves so much like an array that it is routinely described as one, and the description holds right up to the point where it costs a debugging session. Here is the part that is true:

set -- alpha beta gamma
echo "what works, exactly as it would on an array:"
printf '  element <%s>\n' "$@"
echo "  count  ${#@}     joined  ${*}     slice  ${*:2:1}"
echo "what does not:"
echo "  \${!@} is indirection, not a list of indices:"
echo "${!@}"

what works, exactly as it would on an array:
  element <alpha>
  element <beta>
  element <gamma>
  count  3     joined  alpha beta gamma     slice  beta
what does not:
  ${!@} is indirection, not a list of indices:
example.sh: line 7: alpha beta gamma: invalid variable name

"$@" versus "$*", ${#@}, and the ${@:offset:length} slice from §5.3 all work exactly as their array equivalents do. ${!@} does not give you indices — ! still means indirection, so bash took the value alpha beta gamma and tried to use it as a variable name. The positional parameters have no index list, which is a clue about what they really are.

What they are is a separate, fixed, non-sparse sequence maintained by the shell, with three restrictions an array does not have:

# shellcheck disable=SC2209,SC1007,SC2270  # 1=new is the lesson: it is not an assignment
set -- alpha beta gamma
1=new
echo "status after 1=new: $?   \$1 is still $1"
set -- "${@:1:0}" new "${@:2}"
echo "rebuilt instead:    $*"

example.sh: line 3: 1=new: command not found
status after 1=new: 127   $1 is still alpha
rebuilt instead:    new beta gamma

You cannot assign to a positional parameter. 1=new is not a rejected assignment; it is not an assignment at all. 1 is not a valid variable name, so bash parses the whole word as a command name and reports 127. The script does not stop, $1 is unchanged, and the only signal is an exit status nobody checked. The replacement is set --, rebuilding the whole list, which is why the "${@:1:0}" slice appears above — it expands to nothing and exists purely to make the intent ("elements before index 1") readable.

The second restriction is that the only structural mutation is shift:

set -- alpha beta gamma delta
echo "before: $# -> $*"
shift
echo "shift:  $# -> $*"
shift 2
echo "shift 2:$# -> $*"
set -- "${@}" epsilon
echo "append: $# -> $*"
args=("$@")
args[0]=CHANGED
echo "copy edited: ${args[*]}"
echo "originals:   $*"

before: 4 -> alpha beta gamma delta
shift:  3 -> beta gamma delta
shift 2:1 -> delta
append: 2 -> delta epsilon
copy edited: CHANGED epsilon
originals:   delta epsilon

The third is that there is only one set of them per shell and per function, so you cannot have two lists in play at once. All three restrictions have the same fix, and it is the most useful line in this subsection:

set -- one two three
args=("$@")
echo "${#args[@]} elements, and now they are an array: ${args[*]}"
args[0]=CHANGED
args+=(four)
echo "indices ${!args[*]} -> ${args[*]}"

3 elements, and now they are an array: one two three
indices 0 1 2 3 -> CHANGED two three four

args=("$@") at the top of a script or function. It costs one line, and from then on you have indices, slicing that you can assign back, +=, unset, and as many lists as you need. getopts (§13.3) consumes the positional parameters, so the copy also preserves the original argument list for error messages, which is worth having.

6.11 Slicing, Appending, and Removing

An array slice is §5.3's substring expansion applied to an array — ${arr[@]:offset:length} — and the difference is what the offset counts:

a=(zero one two three four five)
echo "\${a[@]:2}     = ${a[*]:2}"
echo "\${a[@]:2:3}   = ${a[*]:2:3}"
echo "\${a[@]: -2}   = ${a[*]: -2}"
echo "\${a[@]: -3:2} = ${a[*]: -3:2}"
echo "\${a[@]:0:0}   = [${a[*]:0:0}]"
b=("${a[@]:1:3}")
echo "copy count     = ${#b[@]}  first index = ${!b[*]}"

${a[@]:2}     = two three four five
${a[@]:2:3}   = two three four
${a[@]: -2}   = four five
${a[@]: -3:2} = three four
${a[@]:0:0}   = []
copy count     = 3  first index = 0 1 2

On a string, ${s:2:3} counts characters; in an array slice ${arr[@]:offset:length} the offset and length count elements. The space in ${a[@]: -2} is mandatory for the same reason as in §5.3 — without it :- is the default-value operator — and it is the most common typo in this syntax.

Two details in the last line. A slice of [@] re-indexes from zero: b has indices 0, 1, 2 regardless of where the slice came from. And the slice must be assigned with b=("${a[@]:1:3}") — parentheses and quotes — or you get the joined-and-re-split approximation §6.5 measured.

On a sparse array the offset counts positions in the element list, not subscripts, which is easy to get backwards:

a=(zero one two three four)
unset 'a[1]'
echo "indices        = ${!a[*]}"
echo "\${a[@]:1:2}    = ${a[*]:1:2}"
echo "\${a[1]}        = [${a[1]}]"

indices        = 0 2 3 4
${a[@]:1:2}    = two three
${a[1]}        = []

${a[@]:1:2} skipped one existing element and took the next two — two and three — while ${a[1]} is empty because subscript 1 was removed. The slice and the subscript disagree, and both are behaving as documented.

Removal has three shapes and they do different things:

a=(keep drop keep2)
unset 'a[1]'
echo "after unset:   indices=${!a[*]} values=${a[*]}"
a=("${a[@]}")
echo "after reindex: indices=${!a[*]} values=${a[*]}"
b=(a b c d e)
filtered=()
for x in "${b[@]}"; do [[ $x == c ]] || filtered+=("$x"); done
echo "filtered:      ${filtered[*]}"
unset 'b[@]'
echo "unset b[@]:    count=${#b[@]}"
declare -p b

after unset:   indices=0 2 values=keep keep2
after reindex: indices=0 1 values=keep keep2
filtered:      a b d e
unset b[@]:    count=0
declare -a b=()

unset 'a[1]' leaves a hole. a=("${a[@]}") is the re-index idiom — it expands the surviving elements and rebuilds the array dense, and it is worth doing immediately after any unset if later code will use a C-style loop or a slice.

The filter loop is the general form, and it is better than unset whenever the condition is on values rather than positions: it builds a new dense array, needs no re-index step, and reads as what it does. Note filtered=() before the loop — without it, a leftover filtered from earlier in the script would be appended to.

unset 'b[@]' removes every element but leaves the array declared, which declare -p b confirms by printing declare -a b=() rather than reporting it as not found. That distinction matters under set -u (§6.15). To remove the variable entirely, unset b with no subscript.

+= on an array

+= on an array, with a parenthesised list, appends elements; with a plain value it appends to the string in element 0, and the two look alike:

# shellcheck disable=SC2145,SC2179,SC2324  # the string append is the subject
a=(1 2); a+=(3); echo "${a[@]} (${#a[@]} elements)"
b=(1 2); b+=3; echo "${b[@]} (${#b[@]} elements)"

1 2 3 (3 elements)
13 2 (2 elements)

a+=(3) added a third element. b+=3 did not: it appended the text 3 to element 0, turning 1 into 13, and left two elements. To append one element to an array, always use the parentheses, and += on an array is then the idiom that replaces a[${#a[@]}]=x (§6.6) and does not depend on the array having no gaps.

6.12 Filling an Array from a File or a String

Almost every array in a real script is built from something else: lines of a file, fields of a record, or the output of a command. bash has a purpose-built builtin for the first case — mapfile into an array — and it should be the default.

printf '%s\n' web-1 'web 2' db-1 > hosts.txt
mapfile -t lines < hosts.txt
echo "count = ${#lines[@]}"
printf '<%s>\n' "${lines[@]}"
echo "--- without -t the newline is kept ---"
mapfile raw < hosts.txt
printf '<%s>' "${raw[0]}"; echo

count = 3
<web-1>
<web 2>
<db-1>
--- without -t the newline is kept ---
<web-1
>

To mapfile into an array is to read its lines in one call (readarray is the same builtin under another name), with no loop and no subshell. -t strips the trailing newline and you want it essentially always; the second half shows what you get without it, and a trailing newline inside an element breaks comparisons in ways that take a while to see.

Note that web 2 came back as one element. Lines are split on newlines only, so spaces in the data are safe — which makes mapfile -t the correct way to read a list of filenames from a file, subject to the caveat that a filename may itself contain a newline (-d '' with find -print0 is the airtight version; §14.9).

Four options are worth knowing:

printf '%s\n' web-1 'web 2' db-1 > hosts.txt
printf 'a,b,c' > csv.txt
mapfile -t -n 2 first < hosts.txt
echo "-n 2      : ${first[*]}"
mapfile -t -s 1 rest < hosts.txt
echo "-s 1      : ${rest[*]}"
mapfile -t -O 5 padded < hosts.txt
echo "-O 5      : indices ${!padded[*]}"
mapfile -t -d , parts < csv.txt
printf -- '-d ,      : '; printf '<%s> ' "${parts[@]}"; echo

-n 2      : web-1 web 2
-s 1      : web 2 db-1
-O 5      : indices 5 6 7
-d ,      : <a> <b> <c>

-n limits the count, -s skips leading lines (a header row), -O sets the starting index, and -d changes the delimiter — -d , splits on commas, and -d '' splits on NUL, which is the pairing for find -print0. -d is bash 4.4 and later.

For splitting a string into an array rather than reading a file, read -a is the tool:

read -ra words <<< 'one two three'
printf 'read -ra : '; printf '<%s> ' "${words[@]}"; echo
IFS=, read -ra fields <<< 'a,b,,c'
printf 'IFS=,    : %s fields: ' "${#fields[@]}"; printf '<%s> ' "${fields[@]}"; echo
PATH_LIKE=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
IFS=: read -ra path <<< "$PATH_LIKE"
printf 'a PATH   : '; printf '<%s> ' "${path[@]}"; echo

read -ra : <one> <two> <three> 
IFS=,    : 4 fields: <a> <b> <> <c> 
a PATH   : </usr/local/bin> </usr/bin> </bin>

Three things to take from this. -r is not optional — without it read treats backslash as an escape and silently eats it, which §14.4 covers in full. IFS=, read is a prefix assignment (§2.3), so splitting a string into an array on a chosen delimiter changes IFS only for that one command and no save-and-restore is needed. And the empty field between the two commas survived as an empty element, because a non-whitespace IFS character delimits rather than separates — §3.4's table, and the reason IFS=, is correct for CSV-shaped data in a way that IFS=' ' is not.

The pitfall that costs the most time is structural rather than syntactic:

# shellcheck disable=SC2030,SC2031  # the lost assignment is the point of this block
printf '%s\n' a b c | mapfile -t wrong
echo "after a pipeline: count=${#wrong[@]}"
mapfile -t right < <(printf '%s\n' a b c)
echo "process substitution: count=${#right[@]} -> ${right[*]}"

after a pipeline: count=0
process substitution: count=3 -> a b c

Every component of a pipeline runs in a subshell, so mapfile on the right of a | fills an array in a child process that exits immediately afterwards (§16.6). The array in the parent is untouched, the exit status is 0, and nothing is reported. < <(cmd) — process substitution feeding a redirect — keeps mapfile in the current shell and is the correct form. The same trap applies to while read loops, and shopt -s lastpipe is the other fix; §16.8 weighs them.

Finally, a glob fills an array directly, and this is the right way to iterate files:

mkdir demo && cd demo
touch a.log b.log
shopt -s nullglob
logs=(*.log)
echo "matched ${#logs[@]}: ${logs[*]}"
none=(*.nosuch)
echo "no match with nullglob: ${#none[@]}"
shopt -u nullglob
none=(*.nosuch)
echo "no match without:       ${#none[@]} -> ${none[*]}"

matched 2: a.log b.log
no match with nullglob: 0
no match without:       1 -> *.nosuch

logs=(*.log) is safe with any filename, because the glob's results become elements directly and never pass through word splitting. shopt -s nullglob is what makes the empty case sane: without it an unmatched pattern expands to itself, so logs gets one element containing a literal *.log and a loop body runs once on a file that does not exist. §4.8 introduced the option; this is where it earns its place.

6.13 Passing an Array to a Function, and Getting One Back

A shell function takes strings, so an array is passed as an array of arguments and the call site is where the correctness lives:

join_with() {
  local sep=$1; shift
  local out=""
  local item
  for item in "$@"; do out+="${out:+$sep}$item"; done
  printf '%s' "$out"
}
a=('one two' three 'four')
echo "joined: $(join_with ' | ' "${a[@]}")"
echo "count seen by the function: $(count_them() { echo $#; }; count_them "${a[@]}")"

joined: one two | three | four
count seen by the function: 3

f "${a[@]}" is the whole technique: the array of arguments arrives as "$@" with boundaries intact. ${out:+$sep} from §5.2 is the separator-only-between-items idiom, avoiding the leading-delimiter bug that a naive out+="$item$sep" produces.

The limits are real, though. The function cannot tell where one array ended and another began, so you can pass exactly one array, and it must be last. Two arrays means a count argument or a sentinel, both of which are worse than the alternative below.

That alternative is a nameref, and it handles input and output symmetrically:

# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # `out` is a nameref; the caller is what reads it
push() {
  local -n arr=$1; shift
  arr+=("$@")
}
split_into() {
  local -n out=$1
  local sep=$2 str=$3
  local old=$IFS
  IFS=$sep read -ra out <<< "$str"
  IFS=$old
}
stack=(a)
push stack b c
echo "stack: ${stack[*]}  (${#stack[@]})"
split_into parts : 'x:y:z'
echo "parts: ${parts[*]}"

stack: a b c  (3)
parts: x y z

local -n arr=$1 makes arr an alias for the array named by the first argument, so the function reads and writes the caller's variable directly. This is the shell's output-parameter convention — §9.6 makes the general case — and returning an array is exactly what it is for, since a function's only real return value is an integer status.

Namerefs have one sharp edge, and it is worth measuring rather than warning about:

bad() {
  local -n ref=$1
  ref+=(added-by-bad)
  echo "  inside bad: ${ref[*]}"
}
good() {
  local -n _out_ref=$1
  _out_ref+=(added-by-good)
  echo "  inside good: ${_out_ref[*]}"
}
ref=(a b)
bad ref
echo "caller sees: ${ref[*]}"
ref=(a b)
good ref
echo "caller sees: ${ref[*]}"

example.sh: line 2: local: warning: ref: circular name reference
example.sh: line 2: warning: ref: circular name reference
example.sh: line 3: warning: ref: circular name reference
example.sh: line 4: warning: ref: circular name reference
example.sh: line 4: warning: ref: circular name reference
  inside bad: a b added-by-bad
caller sees: a b added-by-bad
  inside good: a b added-by-good
caller sees: a b added-by-good

When the nameref's own name equals the name it points at, bash warns and resolves to the global anyway. Read that carefully: the result here is correct, which is exactly why this is dangerous. Five warnings went to stderr, the script exited 0, and a caller that redirects stderr sees a working function. Change the caller to use a local variable with the same name and the resolution changes.

The convention is therefore mechanical: give a nameref a name no caller would choose, such as the _out_ref above. Some style guides use a __ prefix. Either way it is a naming discipline rather than a language guarantee, which is the honest description of dynamic scoping in general — §9.4 explains why bash's local makes this unavoidable.

The last option for returning an array is through stdout, which works for a list of lines and loses everything else:

# shellcheck disable=SC2207  # bad=($(emit)) is the counter-example
emit() { printf '%s\n' 'one two' three; }
mapfile -t good < <(emit)
printf 'mapfile:  %s element(s): ' "${#good[@]}"; printf '<%s> ' "${good[@]}"; echo
bad=($(emit))
printf 'unquoted: %s element(s): ' "${#bad[@]}"; printf '<%s> ' "${bad[@]}"; echo

mapfile:  2 element(s): <one two> <three> 
unquoted: 3 element(s): <one> <two> <three>

bad=($(emit)) is the form to recognise and avoid. The unquoted command substitution goes through word splitting and globbing exactly as §6.5 measured, so one two becomes two elements and any element containing * becomes a filename. mapfile -t good < <(emit) gets it right, at the cost of a newline being the only delimiter the function may use — which is a constraint you can state in the function's contract, unlike the other one.

6.14 Building a Command as an Array

This is the pattern that justifies arrays to someone who is unconvinced, because the alternative is the single most common serious bug in shell scripting: building a command in a string.

# shellcheck disable=SC2089,SC2090  # a command held in a string is the counter-example
printf '%s\n' one 'two words' three > data.txt
cmd="grep -n -e 'two words' -- data.txt"
echo "--- as a string ---"
$cmd
echo "exit: $?"
echo "--- as an array ---"
cmd=(grep -n -e 'two words' -- data.txt)
"${cmd[@]}"
echo "exit: $?"

--- as a string ---
grep: words': No such file or directory
exit: 2
--- as an array ---
2:two words
exit: 0

The string version fails and the error message shows exactly why. $cmd is expanded and then word-split, and word splitting does not know about quotes — the single quotes in the string are ordinary characters by that point, so 'two, words' and -- become three separate arguments. §4.8 made this point about the expansion order; here is its most expensive consequence. The usual "fix" is eval "$cmd", which re-parses the string and does handle the quotes — and also handles any ;, $(…) or backtick that arrived with the data, which is §18.10's subject and an injection vulnerability rather than a fix.

The array version has no such step. Each element is one argument, whatever it contains.

Conditional flags are where the pattern pays off daily:

printf '%s\n' one 'two words' three > data.txt
cmd=(grep -n)
[[ -n ${VERBOSE:-} ]] && cmd+=(--color=never)
cmd+=(-e 'two words' -- data.txt)
printf 'running:'; printf ' %q' "${cmd[@]}"; echo
"${cmd[@]}"
echo "exit: $?"

running: grep -n -e two\ words -- data.txt
2:two words
exit: 0

printf ' %q' "${cmd[@]}" before running is worth building into any script that constructs a command. %q quotes each element so the log line is re-runnable shell — note two\ words, which shows the argument boundary that a plain %s would hide. §20.14 uses the same trick for a dry-run mode.

The array also composes into a function that builds it, which is where namerefs and command arrays meet:

build_args() {
  local -n out=$1
  out=(sort)
  [[ ${NUMERIC:-0} == 1 ]] && out+=(-n)
  [[ -n ${FIELD:-} ]] && out+=(-k "$FIELD")
  return 0
}
build_args args
printf 'default : %s\n' "${args[*]}"
printf '%s\n' '2 30' '1 100' | "${args[@]}"
NUMERIC=1 FIELD=2
build_args args
printf 'tuned   : %s\n' "${args[*]}"
printf '%s\n' '2 30' '1 100' | "${args[@]}"

default : sort
1 100
2 30
tuned   : sort -n -k 2
2 30
1 100

The two runs sort differently because the second built a different command, and no string was concatenated anywhere. Note return 0 at the end: the last [[ ]] is the function's exit status, so without it build_args returns 1 whenever FIELD is unset, and under set -e (§11.5) that ends the script. A builder function that ends in a conditional needs an explicit status — a small thing that has broken a lot of scripts.

Three more places this shape is the right one: ssh "$host" "${cmd[@]}" keeps remote arguments intact; find . "${predicates[@]}" composes a query; and a run() wrapper that logs, honours --dry-run and then executes "$@" is the backbone of the deployment scripts §22.6 builds.

6.15 Arrays Are Not Exported, and Other Boundaries

Three limits close the section, and each has caused a confident bug report.

An array cannot cross into a child process. Not "is awkward to" — cannot:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # single-quoted on purpose: the child shell expands these
a=(one two three)
export a
echo "in this shell: ${a[*]} (${#a[@]})"
"$BASH" -c 'echo "in a child:    [${a[*]}] (${#a[@]})"; declare -p a 2>&1 | tail -1'
echo "--- what does get through ---"
"$BASH" -c 'echo "as a scalar:   [$a]"'

in this shell: one two three (3)
in a child:    [] (0)
/opt/homebrew/bin/bash: line 1: declare: a: not found
--- what does get through ---
as a scalar:   []

export a is accepted without complaint and does nothing useful — the child sees no variable a at all, not even element zero. The reason is that the environment is a list of name=value strings (§16.4) with no representation for a list, so there is nothing to put there. Note the diagnostic names the interpreter's path; that is the real $BASH and it will differ on your machine.

The consequences: a script cannot pass an array to another script, a sudo'd command, or an ssh session as a variable. The routes that do work are to pass the elements as arguments (child "${a[@]}", then args=("$@") on the far side), or to serialise with declare -p and re-read it — eval "$(declare -p a)" in the child, which is one of §18.10's few defensible eval uses because the text came from bash's own quoting.

An empty array under nounset is fine; an unset name is not — and the two array spellings disagree:

set -u
empty=()
echo "count: ${#empty[@]}"
printf 'expansion of an empty array: '; printf '<%s> ' "${empty[@]}"; echo
echo "bash version: ${BASH_VERSINFO[0]}.${BASH_VERSINFO[1]}"
echo "--- but a bare element reference still fails ---"
echo "[${empty[0]}]"
echo "not reached"

count: 0
expansion of an empty array: <> 
bash version: 5.3
--- but a bare element reference still fails ---
example.sh: line 7: empty[0]: unbound variable

An empty array under nounset expands to nothing — "${empty[@]}" gives zero words, not one empty word — and is not an error. This was fixed in bash 4.4; on 4.3 and earlier "${empty[@]}" under set -u aborts the script, which is why older code is full of ${empty[@]+"${empty[@]}"}. That workaround is no longer needed on any bash this course targets, and the version number is printed above so the claim is checkable rather than asserted.

The printf '<%s> ' line deserves a second look: it printed <> once, not zero times. That is printf re-using its format string for zero arguments, not the array producing an element — a printf behaviour (§14.12), and a good reminder that printf with no arguments still runs its format once.

Now the asymmetry that catches people, because it makes set -u less protective than it looks:

# shellcheck disable=SC2145,SC2016  # the three spellings are what the block compares
set -u
echo 'probing ${nothing[@]} -- no message, and the echo runs:'
echo "  [${nothing[@]}]"
echo 'probing ${#nothing[@]} -- a message, this echo is abandoned, the script continues:'
echo "  [${#nothing[@]}]"
echo 'probing $nothing -- this one stops the script:'
echo "  [$nothing]"
echo "not reached"

probing ${nothing[@]} -- no message, and the echo runs:
  []
probing ${#nothing[@]} -- a message, this echo is abandoned, the script continues:
example.sh: line 6: nothing: unbound variable
probing $nothing -- this one stops the script:
example.sh: line 8: nothing: unbound variable

Three references to the same never-declared name, three different outcomes. ${nothing[@]} is silent and yields nothing. ${#nothing[@]} prints a diagnostic and abandons that command — the echo never ran, which is why its label line is missing from the output — but the shell continues to the next one. Only the plain scalar $nothing does what set -u is advertised to do and exits.

So set -u does not guarantee that a misspelled array name is caught. The defence is declare -a or declare -A at the point a script's arrays are introduced, which turns "never declared" into "declared and empty" and makes the first two cases deliberate rather than accidental.

Finally, local on an array shadows completely, and a bare assignment does not declare:

outer=(global)
touch_it() {
  outer+=(added)
}
shadow_it() {
  local outer=(local-only)
  outer+=(more)
  echo "  inside: ${outer[*]}"
}
touch_it
echo "after touch_it:  ${outer[*]}"
shadow_it
echo "after shadow_it: ${outer[*]}"

after touch_it:  global added
  inside: local-only more
after shadow_it: global added

A function that assigns to an array without local modifies the caller's — bash's variables are dynamically scoped (§9.4), so outer+=(added) inside touch_it reaches the global. local outer=(…) creates a fresh array visible to this function and everything it calls, and the global is restored on return. Declare every array a function owns, for the same reason as every scalar, and note that local -a name with no value is the way to declare an empty one.

6.16 The Array Operator Table

Everything above in one place, spelled the way the bash manual spells it — arr for the array, key for an associative subscript, n for an index. Read it as the section's index: each row names the form, says what it produces, and points at the subsection that explains it.

Form
Produces
arr=(a b c)
§6.2 — an array literal, the compound assignment that builds an indexed array. The words inside are expanded and quoted as anywhere else, so arr=(*.txt "$v") works. Assigning it again replaces the whole array.
arr=([2]=c [0]=a)
§6.2 — a literal with explicit subscripts, which need be neither ordered nor contiguous.
declare -a arr
§6.2 — declare an indexed array. Optional before a subscript assignment, and worth writing anyway (§6.15).
declare -A arr
§6.7 — declare an associative array. Not optional: without it bash builds an indexed array and every key evaluates to 0.
arr[n]=v · arr[key]=v
§6.3, §6.7 — the array subscript assignment. An indexed subscript is an arithmetic expression; an associative one is a literal string.
arr+=(d e)
§6.2 — += on an array, appending to an array. Without the parentheses arr+=d appends to element zero instead.
${arr[n]}
§6.3 — one element. ${arr[-1]} is the last; an out-of-range negative index prints bad array subscript and still reports success.
${arr[@]}
§6.4 — every element, one word each when quoted. "${arr[@]}" is the only correct way to iterate or pass an array.
${arr[*]}
§6.4 — every element joined into a single word, separated by the first character of IFS. The shell's string-join; correct only when you want a string.
$arr
§6.4 — element zero, never the whole array. Treat a bare array name as a bug.
${#arr[@]}
§6.6 — the number of elements. Not one past the last index unless the array is dense.
${#arr[n]}
§6.6 — the length of one element's string. ${#arr} is the length of element zero, which reads like a count and is not.
${!arr[@]}
§6.6, §6.7 — the array indices, or the keys of a map. for i in "${!arr[@]}" is the loop that is correct on a sparse array.
${arr[@]:offset:length}
§6.11 — an array slice: length elements from offset, counting positions rather than subscripts. A negative offset needs a space: ${arr[@]: -2}. The result re-indexes from zero.
unset 'arr[n]'
§6.6 — unset an array element, leaving a hole rather than shifting. Quote it: arr[n] is a glob, and a matching file silently redirects the command.
unset 'arr[@]'
§6.11 — remove every element and keep the array declared. unset arr removes the variable itself.
arr=("${arr[@]}")
§6.11 — the re-index idiom: rebuild a sparse array dense.
[[ -v arr[key] ]]
§6.8 — whether a key exists, which is the right question for a set; a key whose value is empty is still present.
(( arr[key]++ ))
§6.8 — increment a counter, creating the key if absent. Returns 1 on the first bump, so pair it with || true under set -e.
mapfile -t arr < f
§6.12 — mapfile into an array (spelled readarray too): the file's lines, newlines stripped. -d changes the delimiter, -n limits, -s skips, -O sets the first index.
mapfile -t arr < <(cmd)
§6.12 — the same from a command. Not cmd | mapfile, which fills an array in a subshell that then exits.
IFS=, read -ra arr
§6.12 — splitting a string into an array on a chosen delimiter, with IFS changed for that one command only.
arr=(*.log)
§6.12 — a glob straight into an array, safe with any filename. Pair with shopt -s nullglob so no match gives zero elements rather than one literal pattern.
f "${arr[@]}"
§6.13 — passing an array to a function, and the array of arguments generally. Exactly one array can go this way, and it must be last.
local -n ref=$1
§6.13 — a nameref, which is how a function reads and writes a caller's array: returning an array. Give it a name no caller would pick, or bash resolves the collision to the global with only a warning.
args=("$@")
§6.10 — copy the positional parameters into a real array, which is what makes them indexable, sliceable and assignable.
cmd=(prog -f x); "${cmd[@]}"
§6.14 — building a command as an array, the alternative to a command in a string and to eval. printf ' %q' "${cmd[@]}" logs it re-runnably.
"${arr[@]}" when empty
§6.15 — an empty array under nounset expands to no words and is not an error on bash 4.4 and later, so the old ${arr[@]+"${arr[@]}"} guard is no longer needed.
export arr
§6.15 — accepted and useless: arrays are not exported. Pass the elements as arguments, or serialise with declare -p.
declare -p arr
§6.2 — what the variable actually is, as re-readable shell. The attribute letter (-a, -A, --) is the answer.

Three rules cut across most of those rows, and each has already cost somebody a bug.

Quoting array expansions is not optional. "${arr[@]}" — quotes and @ — is the only spelling that preserves elements. Unquoted, ${arr[@]} and ${arr[*]} are indistinguishable: both join and re-split, so an element containing a space becomes two, an empty element disappears, and an element containing * becomes whatever the filesystem offers. §6.5 measured all three happening at once, and ShellCheck's SC2068 catches the unquoted case.

An absent element and an empty one are the same string. Reading ${arr[missing]} gives the empty string, not an error, on both kinds of array — so a misspelled key produces blank output rather than a diagnostic, and set -u catches only some of those cases (§6.15). [[ -v arr[key] ]] is the test that distinguishes them.

A subscript means different things on the two kinds of array. arr[1+1] is index 2 on an indexed array and the three-character key 1+1 on a map; arr[i] reads the variable i on the first and looks up the key i on the second. The two declarations look almost identical and the same expression silently means two things, which is why declare -A belongs on its own line where a reviewer can see it.

Exercises

1. Prove the delimiter always loses. Write a function list_files that returns the names of the files in a directory, first via a space-delimited string and then via an array, and construct a directory that makes the first version wrong in two distinct ways at once.

Solution 
mkdir demo && cd demo
touch 'report one.txt' 'star*.txt' 'starXYZ.txt' 'plain.txt'
shopt -s nullglob
via_string() { local out=""; for f in *.txt; do out+="$f "; done; printf '%s' "$out"; }
via_array()  { local -a out=(*.txt); printf '%s\n' "${out[@]}"; }
echo "--- consumed as a string ---"
for f in $(via_string); do echo "[$f]"; done
echo "--- consumed as an array ---"
via_array | while IFS= read -r f; do echo "[$f]"; done

--- consumed as a string ---
[plain.txt]
[report]
[one.txt]
[star*.txt]
[starXYZ.txt]
[starXYZ.txt]
--- consumed as an array ---
[plain.txt]
[report one.txt]
[star*.txt]
[starXYZ.txt]

Four files went in and the string route produced six names. Both failures are visible, and they are different mechanisms.

report one.txt split on its space into report and one.txt — that is word splitting, step 4 of §4's pipeline, and neither of the halves is a file that exists.

Then star*.txt was re-globbed by the consumer. The producer emitted it as a literal filename, but $(via_string) is unquoted, so step 5 ran on it again and the pattern matched two files: star*.txt itself and starXYZ.txt. That is why starXYZ.txt appears twice — once from its own turn in the list and once as collateral from the other name's re-expansion. A loop that moved each file would move that one twice and, on the second pass, fail.

The second failure is the one worth dwelling on. The producer was careful and the glob it ran was correct; the damage happened at the call site, to data that was a valid filename when it left the function. A string list is unsafe at every point it is expanded, not only where it is built, which is why the fix cannot be local — and why the choice of a directory matters when demonstrating this. With no starXYZ.txt present, star*.txt re-globs to exactly itself, the output looks almost right, and the bug is invisible.

The array version is correct because the elements never pass through splitting or globbing. Note local -a out=(*.txt) — the -a is not required here, since the compound assignment implies it, but it documents the type and it is what §6.15 recommends. The while IFS= read -r consumer is the newline-safe counterpart on the reading side (§14.4); within one shell you would just use "${out[@]}" and skip the serialisation entirely.

2. Find the bug in a plausible function. This is meant to count how many times each extension appears. It runs without error and gives the wrong answer. Explain every reason, then fix it.

# shellcheck disable=SC2048,SC2034,SC2068  # this function is the question
count_extensions() {
  declare -A counts
  for f in $*; do
    ext=${f##*.}
    counts[ext]=$(( counts[ext] + 1 ))
  done
  for k in ${!counts[@]}; do
    echo "$k: ${counts[k]}"
  done
}
Solution

Four defects, and the first two are the ones that make it silently wrong rather than merely fragile.

# shellcheck disable=SC2124,SC2206,SC2048,SC2034,SC2068  # the broken version is the lesson
broken() {
  declare -A counts
  for f in $*; do
    ext=${f##*.}
    counts[ext]=$(( counts[ext] + 1 ))
  done
  for k in ${!counts[@]}; do echo "  $k: ${counts[k]}"; done
}
inspect() {
  declare -A counts
  for f in $*; do ext=${f##*.}; counts[ext]=$(( counts[ext] + 1 )); done
  printf '  '; declare -p counts
}
fixed() {
  local -A counts=()
  local f ext k
  for f in "$@"; do
    ext=${f##*.}
    (( counts[$ext]++ )) || true
  done
  for k in $(printf '%s\n' "${!counts[@]}" | LC_ALL=C sort); do
    echo "  $k: ${counts[$k]}"
  done
}
files=('a.txt' 'b log.txt' 'c.md')
echo "broken:";  broken  "${files[@]}"
echo "what broken really accumulated:"; inspect "${files[@]}"
echo "fixed:";   fixed   "${files[@]}"

broken:
  ext: 
what broken really accumulated:
  declare -A counts=([ext]="4" )
fixed:
  md: 1
  txt: 2

counts[ext] uses the literal key ext. An associative subscript is a string, not an arithmetic expression (§6.7), so every file lands under the same key. The $ is mandatory: counts[$ext].

${counts[k]} in the reporting loop has the same bug, one level worse. k is a real variable holding a real key, but the subscript is the literal string k, which is not a key in the map — so the value prints as the empty string and the broken output is ext: with nothing after it. That is why inspect is there: it runs the identical accumulation and dumps the map with declare -p, showing the count really did reach 4. A map read with the wrong key returns an empty string, not an error (§6.7), so this class of bug produces blank output rather than a diagnostic.

for f in $* joins the arguments into one string and re-splits it (§6.4), so b log.txt became two items — which is where that 4 comes from, on three files. "$@" is the fix, and it is the same bug §6.5 measured.

declare inside a function is not local in the sense people assume. It does create a function-local variable here, but local states the intent and is what the style guide asks for; more importantly counts is never reset, so a second call would accumulate. local -A counts=() fixes both.

${!counts[@]} unquoted in a for happens to work for extension names and breaks the moment a key contains a space or a glob character — and keys come from filenames, which the caller controls. Sorting through printf | sort both fixes the order (§6.7) and forces the question of what the delimiter is.

Two smaller things in the fixed version. || true after (( counts[$ext]++ )) is there because the post-increment returns 1 on the first bump and the script may run under set -e (§11.5). And local f ext k declares the loop variables, which otherwise leak to the caller by dynamic scoping (§9.4).

3. Group without nesting. You have a list of host:datacentre pairs and need to print each datacentre with its hosts. An associative array cannot hold a list (§6.9). Solve it two different ways and say when each is right.

Solution 
pairs=('web-1:eu-west' 'db-1:us-east' 'web-2:eu-west' 'cache-1:us-east')

echo "--- A: invert the map, group with a second pass ---"
declare -A dc_of=()
for p in "${pairs[@]}"; do dc_of[${p%%:*}]=${p#*:}; done
for dc in $(printf '%s\n' "${dc_of[@]}" | LC_ALL=C sort -u); do
  group=()
  for h in $(printf '%s\n' "${!dc_of[@]}" | LC_ALL=C sort); do
    [[ ${dc_of[$h]} == "$dc" ]] && group+=("$h")
  done
  printf '%-8s %s\n' "$dc" "${group[*]}"
done

echo "--- B: composite key, prefix match ---"
declare -A member=()
for p in "${pairs[@]}"; do member[${p#*:}/${p%%:*}]=1; done
for dc in eu-west us-east; do
  group=()
  for k in $(printf '%s\n' "${!member[@]}" | LC_ALL=C sort); do
    [[ $k == "$dc"/* ]] && group+=("${k#*/}")
  done
  printf '%-8s %s\n' "$dc" "${group[*]}"
done

--- A: invert the map, group with a second pass ---
eu-west  web-1 web-2
us-east  cache-1 db-1
--- B: composite key, prefix match ---
eu-west  web-1 web-2
us-east  cache-1 db-1

A inverts the relation. Each host maps to one datacentre, which fits the one-string-per-key limit exactly, and grouping becomes a filter over the keys. It is right whenever the relation really is many-to-one — and it makes "which datacentre is this host in?" an O(1) lookup, which is usually the question actually being asked. The cost is that grouping is a scan per group.

B encodes the pair into the key. member[eu-west/web-1]=1 makes a set of edges, and a prefix pattern enumerates a group. It is right when the relation is many-to-many, where A cannot be applied at all. Its cost is the separator: / is legal in neither hostname nor datacentre name here, but that is a fact about this data that must be checked, and §6.9's warning applies — you are choosing a delimiter, and the data decides whether you chose well.

Three details that are not incidental. ${p%%:*} and ${p#*:} split the pair with §5.4's trimming operators rather than a subprocess. LC_ALL=C sort makes the output reproducible regardless of the machine's locale (§6.7). And [[ $k == "$dc"/* ]] quotes $dc but not the /*, which is §7.9's rule: the right-hand side of == inside [[ ]] is a pattern, and quoting is what chooses literal or glob — getting it backwards here would either never match or match too much.

Neither version needs eval and neither builds a variable name from data, which is the whole point. If the third requirement arrives — hosts carrying their own list of tags, say — that is the signal in §6.9's fourth row, and the answer is a file format with a parser rather than a third encoding.

4. Build a command safely. Write a run() wrapper that logs a re-runnable form of a command, supports a DRY_RUN mode, and passes arguments through unharmed. Prove it survives an argument containing a space, a quote and a glob character.

Solution 
run() {
  printf '+' >&2
  printf ' %q' "$@" >&2
  printf '\n' >&2
  [[ ${DRY_RUN:-0} == 1 ]] && return 0
  "$@"
}
mkdir demo && cd demo
printf 'alpha\nbeta gamma\n' > 'my data.txt'
nasty=("my data.txt")
run grep -c . "${nasty[@]}"
DRY_RUN=1 run rm -f "it's *.txt"
run printf '%s|' 'a b' "c'd" 'e*f'
echo

+ grep -c . my\ data.txt
2
+ rm -f it\'s\ \*.txt
+ printf %s\| a\ b c\'d e\*f
a b|c'd|e*f|

The log lines are the deliverable. %q quoted the space, the apostrophe and the asterisk, so each line can be pasted back into a shell and will run the identical command — which is what makes a log useful during an incident. A plain %s would print rm -f it's *.txt, which is three arguments' worth of text on a line that looks like one argument, and is the kind of log that sends someone down the wrong path.

"$@" on the last line is the entire safety property. The arguments are never joined, so nothing is re-split and nothing is re-globbed: e*f was passed to printf as three characters even though a file matching it could have existed. Compare with a string-building wrapper, which would have had to choose between eval (§18.10) and being wrong.

Three design notes. Everything logged goes to stderr, so the wrapper does not contaminate a command's stdout — out=$(run some-cmd) still captures only what some-cmd printed. DRY_RUN returns 0, so the caller's control flow proceeds as if the command succeeded, which is what a dry run should simulate; returning the real status would need the command to run. And printf is called three times rather than once because printf ' %q' re-uses its format for every argument (§14.12) — the same behaviour §6.15 noted for an empty array — so the prefix and the newline cannot be part of that format string.

The obvious extension is [[ ${VERBOSE:-0} == 1 ]] around the logging, and the less obvious one is to have run capture and return the exit status explicitly so a trap ERR handler (§12.6) can report which command failed rather than which line.

SECTION 7

Conditionals and Arithmetic

Six sections in, the course has assembled everything a script needs to hold data: words, quoting, the expansion pipeline, every parameter expansion operator, and arrays. None of it makes a decision. This section is where a script starts choosing, and it covers the two engines bash uses to produce a truth value — the conditional expression (test, [, [[) and the arithmetic evaluator ((( )), $(( )), let).

They are separate languages with separate parsers, and the single most common class of shell bug in this area comes from not knowing which one you are in. [[ 10 > 9 ]] is false and [[ 10 -gt 9 ]] is true, and neither is a typo. 08 is a perfectly ordinary number until it reaches the arithmetic evaluator, where it is a malformed octal literal that aborts the loop containing it. A value compared with == is inert data; the same value compared with -eq is code, evaluated by an expression engine that can invoke command substitution. Every one of those is measured in the pages below.

linux §4 showed exit status at an interactive prompt, where a wrong test produces a visibly wrong answer that you retype. This section is about the case where the test is inside a deployment script that nobody is watching, the variable is empty because an upstream command failed, and the difference between [ -n $x ] and [ -n "$x" ] decides whether the script proceeds to delete something.

The branching constructs — if, while, case, for — are §8. This section is about the thing they branch on. The split is deliberate: the conditions are where the subtleties live, and they read far better once you know that if is not a keyword that takes a boolean but a keyword that takes a command.

7.1 A Condition Is a Command's Exit Status

Bash has no boolean type. It has exit status, and it has the inverted convention that goes with it: zero means success, and success is what a condition calls true.

true;   echo "true   -> $?"
false;  echo "false  -> $?"
:;      echo ":      -> $?"
! true; echo "! true -> $?"
if ! false; then echo "! false takes the then-branch"; fi

true   -> 0
false  -> 1
:      -> 0
! true -> 1
! false takes the then-branch

The inversion is not arbitrary.
