A process has one byte to report with, and there is exactly one way to succeed and a great many ways to fail — so zero is reserved for success and the other 255 values carry information about which failure. §11 spends a section on that vocabulary. Here the only consequence that matters is that every comparison you write returns 0 for true, so $? reads backwards from every other language you know.

true, false and : are real builtins whose entire job is their exit status. : is the older spelling of true and is still worth knowing, because it is also the idiomatic no-op in a branch you have not written yet, and because ${var:=default} (§5.2) is almost always written as : "${var:=default}" — the expansion does the work and : is there to consume it.

! inverts the status of a whole pipeline. It is a reserved word, recognised only in command position (§2.2), which is why ! -f file is meaningless and ! [[ -f file ]] is fine.

The thing if actually takes

printf 'alpha\nbeta\n' > names.txt
if grep -q beta names.txt; then echo "grep succeeded, so this branch ran"; fi
if [[ -s names.txt ]];    then echo "[[ ]] is a command too"; fi
if [ -s names.txt ];      then echo "[ ] is a command as well"; fi
if (( 2 + 2 == 4 ));      then echo "(( )) is a third one"; fi

grep succeeded, so this branch ran
[[ ]] is a command too
[ ] is a command as well
(( )) is a third one

Four conditions, four different commands, one mechanism. grep -q is an external program; the [ command is a builtin, and the test builtin is that same command under a second name — test -s names.txt is the identical condition, so [ -s names.txt ] and the test builtin differ only in punctuation; [[ and (( are reserved words that the parser handles itself. if treats them identically, because all it does is run a list and look at the status. There is no expression syntax in if at all. The difference between [ and [[ does not live here either: if cannot tell them apart, and every consequence of the difference between [ and [[ is about how each one's own contents are parsed.

That is why brackets are not punctuation in shell, and it is worth being blunt about it, because the habit of reading if [ ... ] as if (...) in C is the source of a whole family of confusions:

type -a test
type -a [
type -a [[
echo "--- and the external one exists too ---"
ls -l /bin/[ 2>/dev/null | tr -s ' ' | cut -d' ' -f1,9

test is a shell builtin
test is /bin/test
[ is a shell builtin
[ is /bin/[
[[ is a shell keyword
--- and the external one exists too ---
-rwxr-xr-x /bin/[

There is a program on disk called /bin/[, and a /bin/test beside it — the test builtin shadows both, and they exist for shells that have no builtin at all. It predates the builtin, it still ships, and it is the reason [ needs a closing ] as its last argument: a command receives a list of words, and something has to mark the end of the list. [[, by contrast, is a keyword — type says so — and the shell parses it rather than expanding words and handing them over. The difference between [ and [[ is entirely a consequence of that one fact, and §7.2 works through it.

A false test and a broken test are both non-zero

# shellcheck disable=SC1019,SC1072,SC1073  # [ -q ] is unparseable to shellcheck, which is the point
[[ -f /nonexistent ]]; echo "[[ -f missing ]] -> $?"
[ -f /nonexistent ];   echo "[ -f missing ]  -> $?"
[[ -o nosuchoption ]]; echo "[[ -o bogus ]]  -> $?"
[ -q ];                echo "[ -q ]          -> $?"

[[ -f missing ]] -> 1
[ -f missing ]  -> 1
[[ -o bogus ]]  -> 1
[ -q ]          -> 0

The first three are unremarkable. The fourth is a trap that has cost people real time: [ -q ] is true. -q is not a test operator, so [ sees a single argument and falls back to its one-argument rule — is this string non-empty? — and -q is a two-character non-empty string. Any misremembered operator behaves this way. [ -Z "$x" ] with a capital Z is two arguments, so [ looks for a unary operator, does not find one, and reports -Z: unary operator expected with status 2 — which is the good case. [ -q ] alone silently returns success forever.

By convention a test that could not be performed returns 2 rather than 1, and §7.2 shows several. if cannot tell 1 from 2 — both are "not zero" — which is one more reason to prefer the form that makes malformed input impossible rather than the one that reports it.

7.2 test, [, and [[: One Job, Two Parsers

The test builtin and [ are the same command; [ merely requires ] as its final argument, and test is the same builtin under its readable name. [[ is a reserved word introducing the [[ compound command. Everything below follows mechanically from that one fact, and it is the reason this course recommends the [[ compound command in bash scripts without hedging. Every entry in the difference between [ and [[ is one of these consequences, not a separate rule to memorise.

A command's arguments go through the full expansion pipeline of §4 before the command runs. A reserved word's contents do not: the shell parses [[ ... ]] itself, and inside it no word splitting and no pathname expansion happen at all.

An empty variable changes the number of arguments

# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # the unquoted expansion is the bug being shown
x=
echo "--- [ ] sees the words AFTER expansion ---"
[ $x = y ] && echo unreachable
echo "status: $?"
echo "--- [[ ]] is parsed by the shell, so it does not ---"
[[ $x == y ]] && echo unreachable
echo "status: $?"

--- [ ] sees the words AFTER expansion ---
example.sh: line 4: [: =: unary operator expected
status: 2
--- [[ ]] is parsed by the shell, so it does not ---
status: 1

[ $x = y ] with an empty x is not [ '' = y ]. The unquoted expansion produces no word at all, so the builtin receives = and y — two arguments — and applies its two-argument rule, which expects a unary operator first. It gets =. The result is a diagnostic and status 2, and §3.6 traced the same mechanism through rm -rf $dir/.

[[ $x == y ]] is parsed before anything expands. The parser has already decided that the thing left of == is an operand, so an empty value is an empty operand, and the answer is an ordinary false.

A value with a space changes which test is performed

# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # the unquoted expansion is the bug being shown
files='a.txt b.txt'
[ -f $files ] && echo unreachable
echo "status after [ -f \$files ]: $?"
[[ -f $files ]] && echo unreachable
echo "status after [[ -f \$files ]]: $?"

example.sh: line 3: [: a.txt: binary operator expected
status after [ -f $files ]: 2
status after [[ -f $files ]]: 1

[ -f $files ] split into [ -f a.txt b.txt ], three arguments, which [ reads as a binary expression whose operator is a.txt. [[ -f $files ]] tested one operand — the string a.txt b.txt — and correctly reported that no such file exists. This is §3.8's rule paying off: inside [[ ]] the quotes are genuinely optional, and this is one of the very few places in the language where that is true.

Quote anyway. [ -f "$files" ] is the direct repair for the single-bracket form, and writing [[ -f "$files" ]] costs nothing and keeps one habit rather than two. The exception is the right-hand side of a pattern operator, where quoting means something — §7.5.

The right-hand side is a filename in one and a pattern in the other

# shellcheck disable=SC2081  # the glob inside [ ] is exactly what is being measured
mkdir demo && cd demo
touch config.yaml
name=config.yaml
echo "--- inside [ ], the word is globbed before the command runs ---"
[ $name = con*  ] && echo "[ ]  matched"  || echo "[ ]  did not match"
echo "--- inside [[ ]], the right-hand side is a PATTERN, not a filename ---"
[[ $name == con* ]] && echo "[[ ]] matched" || echo "[[ ]] did not match"

--- inside [ ], the word is globbed before the command runs ---
[ ]  matched
--- inside [[ ]], the right-hand side is a PATTERN, not a filename ---
[[ ]] matched

Both printed "matched" and for entirely different reasons, which is exactly why the example is here. Inside [ ], con* was pathname-expanded against the current directory into the literal word config.yaml, and the test then compared two identical strings. Delete the file and the same line compares config.yaml against the unmatched pattern con* and says no. The test's answer depends on the contents of the directory it runs in.

Inside [[ ]] nothing was globbed. con* stayed a pattern and was matched against the value, which is what the line looks like it says. The answer does not change when the directory does.

&& and || are operators in one and command separators in the other

# shellcheck disable=SC2107  # [ a && b ] is the counter-example
a=1 b=2
echo "--- [[ ]] has its own && and || ---"
[[ $a == 1 && $b == 2 ]] && echo "[[ a && b ]] works"
echo "--- [ ] does not: && ends the command ---"
[ $a == 1 && $b == 2 ] && echo unreachable
echo "status: $?"

--- [[ ]] has its own && and || ---
[[ a && b ]] works
--- [ ] does not: && ends the command ---
example.sh: line 6: [: missing `]'
status: 2

&& is a control operator (§2.1), so in [ $a == 1 && $b == 2 ] the shell ends the [ command at the && — and that [ command never got its ]. The message names the real problem precisely. §7.7 covers what to write instead when [ ] is the only option available.

The same is true of a missing ] on its own:

# shellcheck disable=SC1072,SC1073,SC1080  # the missing ] is the demonstration
[ -n hello
echo "continuing, status $?"

example.sh: line 2: [: missing `]'
continuing, status 2

Note that the script continued. A malformed test is an ordinary command failure, not a syntax error, because [ is a command and its arguments were fine as far as the parser was concerned. Under set -e it would stop (§11), and without it a script can run to completion having silently taken the wrong branch at every such test.

[[ is bash, not POSIX

cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
[[ 1 == 1 ]] && echo "double bracket worked"
EOF
echo "--- bash ---"
bash t.sh
echo "--- bash --posix (still bash, so [[ is still there) ---"
bash --posix t.sh
echo "--- a real POSIX shell ---"
dash t.sh
echo "status: $?"

--- bash ---
double bracket worked
--- bash --posix (still bash, so [[ is still there) ---
double bracket worked
--- a real POSIX shell ---
t.sh: 1: [[: not found
status: 127

[[ arrived in bash 2.02 as a ksh compatibility feature and is in ksh and zsh as well, but it is not in POSIX and dash does not have it. Note the exit status: 127, not a syntax error, because dash looked for a command named [[ and did not find one. §19 covers what changes when a script must run under /bin/sh, and the short version is that [[ is the single largest thing you give up.

bash --posix does not help you find out. POSIX mode turns off some bash extensions and leaves others — [[ among them — so it is not a portability test. ShellCheck's -s sh mode is, and §20 sets it up as a gate.

[ ... ] / test
[[ ... ]]
An ordinary builtin. Its arguments are expanded, split and globbed first.
A reserved word. The shell parses the contents; no splitting, no globbing.
An unquoted empty or multi-word value changes the number of arguments, and therefore which test runs.
An operand is an operand whatever it expands to.
&& and || end the command. Use -a/-o (don't) or chain two tests.
&&, ||, ! and ( ) are real operators inside it.
< and > must be escaped or they redirect.
< and > are string comparison operators.
No pattern matching, no regex.
==, != take a glob pattern; =~ takes an ERE.
POSIX. Works in dash, in /bin/sh, everywhere.
bash 2.02+, ksh, zsh. Not POSIX.

Use [[ ]] when the script says #!/usr/bin/env bash. It is safer under every input, it has operators the other one cannot express, and the portability it costs you is portability you already gave up in the shebang. Use [ ] when the script is genuinely #!/bin/sh, and then quote everything without exception.

7.3 String Tests, and the Difference Between Unset and Empty

Four ways to ask about a string, and they do not all answer the same question:

# shellcheck disable=SC2034,SC2319  # the variables are read through a nameref; $? after a test is the measurement
empty=''
set=hello
unset -v missing
for probe in empty set missing; do
  declare -n v=$probe
  printf '%-8s -z:%d  -n:%d  bare:%d  -v:%d\n' "$probe" \
    "$([[ -z ${v-} ]]; echo $?)" "$([[ -n ${v-} ]]; echo $?)" \
    "$([[ ${v-} ]]; echo $?)"   "$([[ -v $probe ]]; echo $?)"
  unset -n v
done
echo "(0 = the test succeeded)"

empty    -z:0  -n:1  bare:1  -v:0
set      -z:1  -n:0  bare:0  -v:0
missing  -z:0  -n:1  bare:1  -v:1
(0 = the test succeeded)

Read the empty and missing rows against each other. -z, -n and the bare form give identical answers for a variable that is set to the empty string and one that was never set at all. They are string tests, and both cases produce the same string: nothing.

-v is the one that distinguishes them, because it takes a variable name rather than a value and asks whether that name is bound. §6.8 used it on an associative-array key for exactly this reason — a key whose value is empty is present — and §7.6 covers it with the rest of the operators that take something other than a string.

The distinction matters whenever "not configured" and "configured to nothing" are different states. ${TZ-} unset means use the system default; TZ= means UTC. A script that tests -z "$TZ" cannot tell them apart; one that tests -v TZ can.

[[ $x ]] — the bare form, no operator — is -n with fewer characters, and it is the idiom this course uses for "is there anything here". It is also the one-argument rule that made [ -q ] true in §7.1, so it is worth being aware that it is doing something slightly magical rather than being a special syntax.

The unquoted -n bug

# shellcheck disable=SC2070,SC2086  # the unquoted -n test is the bug being demonstrated
x=
[ -n $x ] && echo "[ -n \$x ] says non-empty, which is WRONG"
[ -n "$x" ] || echo "[ -n \"\$x\" ] correctly says empty"
[ -z $x ] && echo "[ -z \$x ] happens to be right here"
y='a b'
[ -z $y ] && echo unreachable
echo "[ -z \$y ] with two words: status $?"

[ -n $x ] says non-empty, which is WRONG
[ -n "$x" ] correctly says empty
[ -z $x ] happens to be right here
example.sh: line 7: [: a: binary operator expected
[ -z $y ] with two words: status 2

[ -n $x ] with an empty x becomes [ -n ]: one argument, the non-empty-string rule, and -n is a non-empty string. The test that asks "is this non-empty" returns true precisely when its argument is empty. It is silent, it is the exact inverse of the intent, and ShellCheck reports the unquoted expansion that causes it as SC2086.

[ -z $x ] gives the right answer by luck — [ -z ] is also the one-argument rule, -z is non-empty, true, which is what -z on an empty value should say. Change the value to two words and the luck runs out, as the last line shows.

Both are unconditionally fixed by quoting, and neither can happen inside [[ ]].

= and ==

x=hello
[ "$x" = hello ]  && echo "[  = ]  ok"
[ "$x" == hello ] && echo "[  == ] ok in bash (not POSIX)"
[[ $x = hello ]]  && echo "[[ = ]]  ok"
[[ $x == hello ]] && echo "[[ == ]] ok"
[[ $x != world ]] && echo "[[ != ]] ok"
echo "--- but in a POSIX sh, == is not portable ---"
sh -c '[ hello == hello ] && echo "this sh accepted ==" || echo "this sh rejected =="' 2>&1

[  = ]  ok
[  == ] ok in bash (not POSIX)
[[ = ]]  ok
[[ == ]] ok
[[ != ]] ok
--- but in a POSIX sh, == is not portable ---
this sh accepted ==

All five work in bash, and = versus == is a portability question rather than a semantic one: they are synonyms in both bracket forms. The rule that is worth carrying about = versus ==: = in [ ], == in [[ ]]. == inside single brackets is a bashism that ShellCheck flags as SC3014 under -s sh, and = inside double brackets works but reads like an assignment.

The last line is a warning about how you test portability. sh on this machine accepted == — because /bin/sh here is bash 3.2 in POSIX mode (§1.2), not a POSIX shell. A bashism will pass a /bin/sh test on macOS and fail on a Debian container where /bin/sh is dash. Test portability with the tool, not with the local sh.

7.4 Comparison: Which Operators Are Numeric, and Which Only Look It

This is the subsection §1.6 and §2.2 both pointed at, and it is the highest-value page in the section, because the wrong answer here is silent and plausible.

show() { if eval "[[ $1 ]]"; then r=true; else r=false; fi; printf '%-18s %s\n' "[[ $1 ]]" "$r"; }
printf '%-18s %s\n' 'expression' 'result'
show '10 -gt 9'
show '10 > 9'
show '9 -gt 10'
show '9 > 10'
show '010 -eq 10'
show '010 == 10'

expression         result
[[ 10 -gt 9 ]]     true
[[ 10 > 9 ]]       false
[[ 9 -gt 10 ]]     false
[[ 9 > 10 ]]       true
[[ 010 -eq 10 ]]   false
[[ 010 == 10 ]]    false

Six lines, three surprises.

< and > in [[ are string comparisons. 10 > 9 is false because the string 10 sorts before the string 9: comparison proceeds character by character, 1 comes before 9, and it stops there. It has nothing to do with magnitude. The mirror image 9 > 10 is true for the same reason. Nothing about < and > in [[ changes that; there is no numeric mode for them.

The numeric operators are the six that spell themselves out. Written against two variables they are $a -eq $b, $a -ne $b, $a -lt $b, $a -le $b, $a -gt $b and $a -ge $b, and they are the only numeric comparisons the conditional expression has, in either bracket form. Everywhere else — <, >, =, == — you are comparing text. Read them as the manual does: $a -eq $b and $a -ne $b for equality, $a -lt $b and $a -le $b for less, $a -gt $b and $a -ge $b for greater.

$a -eq $b with a=010 and b=10 is false. -eq evaluates its operands as arithmetic, and in arithmetic a leading zero means octal, so 010 is eight. §7.10 covers that rule in full; it is listed here because this is where it first produces a wrong answer, and because zero-padded numbers come out of date, out of sorted filenames and out of every CSV that has a month column in it.

Operator
What it compares
-eq -ne
-lt -le
-gt -ge
Numbers. Both sides are evaluated as arithmetic expressions, so $(( ))'s rules apply in full: octal, hexadecimal, variables without $, and operators. Available in [ ] and [[ ]] alike.
= == !=
Strings. In [[ ]] the right-hand side is a glob pattern unless quoted (§7.5). In [ ] it is a plain string, already expanded.
< >
Strings, in collation order. Operators inside [[ ]]; inside [ ] they must be written \< and \>, and they are not POSIX there at all.

Inside [ ], an unescaped > is a redirection

# shellcheck disable=SC2050,SC2071  # constant operands and \> are what this block is about
mkdir demo && cd demo
[ 10 \> 9 ] && echo "escaped: true" || echo "escaped:   [ 10 \\> 9 ] is FALSE (string order)"
[ 10 -gt 9 ] && echo "numeric:   [ 10 -gt 9 ] is true"
echo "--- unescaped, > is a redirection and the test never sees it ---"
[ 10 > 9 ] && echo "the test 'succeeded' — it tested the one word 10"
echo "and the directory now contains: $(ls)"

escaped:   [ 10 \> 9 ] is FALSE (string order)
numeric:   [ 10 -gt 9 ] is true
--- unescaped, > is a redirection and the test never sees it ---
the test 'succeeded' — it tested the one word 10
and the directory now contains: 9

This is the worst failure mode in the section, because it has no diagnostic at all. [ 10 > 9 ] is parsed as the command [ 10 ] with its output redirected into a file named 9. [ 10 ] is the one-argument rule, 10 is non-empty, the test returns true, and an empty file appears in the working directory. Every run creates it, every run says true, and the condition is meaningless.

\> escapes it into an argument and gets you a string comparison, which is almost never what someone reaching for > wanted. The operator you wanted is -gt, as in [ $have -gt $need ] — and the same applies to $a -lt $b, $a -le $b and $a -ge $b.

String order is the locale's order, not the alphabet's

# shellcheck disable=SC2072  # comparing version strings with > is the mistake being shown
for v in 5.3 10.0; do
  if [[ $v > 4.4 ]]; then echo "[[ $v > 4.4 ]] is true"; else echo "[[ $v > 4.4 ]] is FALSE"; fi
done
echo "--- and which strings sort first depends on the locale ---"
LC_ALL=C           bash -c '[[ a < B ]] && echo "C:     a sorts before B" || echo "C:     B sorts before a"'
LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 bash -c '[[ a < B ]] && echo "en_US: a sorts before B" || echo "en_US: B sorts before a"'

[[ 5.3 > 4.4 ]] is true
[[ 10.0 > 4.4 ]] is FALSE
--- and which strings sort first depends on the locale ---
C:     B sorts before a
en_US: a sorts before B

The version check works for 5.3 and fails for 10.0, which is the shape every version comparison bug has: correct for the versions that existed when it was written, wrong the first time a major number reaches two digits. §1.2 flagged [[ $BASH_VERSION > 4.4 ]] as wrong for this reason and deferred the explanation to here.

The second half is the one that bites in CI. Since bash 4.1, < and > inside [[ ]] compare according to the current locale's collation order. Under LC_ALL=C that is byte order, so every uppercase letter precedes every lowercase one. Under en_US.UTF-8 it is dictionary order, where case is a tiebreaker. A script that sorts or compares strings gives different answers on a developer's laptop and on a build agent whose locale is unset — and sort has the same property, which is why §6.7 pinned LC_ALL=C sort.

Comparing versions, properly

have=5.3.15
need=5.10.0
if [[ $have > $need ]]; then echo "string compare says $have is newer — WRONG"; fi
newest=$(printf '%s\n%s\n' "$have" "$need" | sort -V | tail -1)
echo "sort -V says the newer of the two is $newest"
IFS=. read -r maj min _ <<< "$have"
if (( maj > 5 || (maj == 5 && min >= 4) )); then
  echo "field compare: $have is at least 5.4"
else
  echo "field compare: $have is older than 5.4"
fi

string compare says 5.3.15 is newer — WRONG
sort -V says the newer of the two is 5.10.0
field compare: 5.3.15 is older than 5.4

Two working approaches. sort -V understands version strings and is a single pipeline, but it is a GNU extension — present in coreutils and in busybox, absent from some BSDs — so §19 lists it as a portability decision rather than a free one. Splitting on . and comparing fields numerically uses nothing but bash, needs no subprocess, and is what the exercise at the end of this section builds into a reusable function.

What does not work is any amount of cleverness with >. There is no string comparison that orders 5.3.15, 5.10.0 and 5.3.15-rc1 correctly, because the ordering is not lexicographic.

An arithmetic operand is an expression, not a number

# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # z is read by the arithmetic evaluator, not by name
x='1 + 1'
[[ $x -eq 2 ]] && echo "-eq evaluated '1 + 1' as arithmetic and got 2"
y=z; z=7
[[ $y -eq 7 ]] && echo "-eq followed y -> z -> 7: the operand is an EXPRESSION"
echo "--- a non-numeric operand is an error in \$(( )) but not always here ---"
n=abc
[[ $n -eq 0 ]] && echo "abc compared equal to 0 (unset name -> 0)"

-eq evaluated '1 + 1' as arithmetic and got 2
-eq followed y -> z -> 7: the operand is an EXPRESSION
--- a non-numeric operand is an error in $(( )) but not always here ---
abc compared equal to 0 (unset name -> 0)

Three things happened that a reader expecting "compare two numbers" would not predict. The string 1 + 1 was parsed and evaluated. The name z was resolved recursively — §4.5 measured the same rule for $(( )), and it applies identically here. And abc, which is not a number at all, evaluated to zero, because an unset name in an arithmetic context is zero (§7.8) and abc is an unset name.

That last one means [[ $n -eq 0 ]] is true for every value of n that happens to be a valid identifier: abc, foo, PATH_TO_NOTHING. If n came from a config file or a command's output, the test that was meant to catch "is the count zero" answers yes to typos, to empty strings, and to words.

The consequences go further than a wrong answer, because an arithmetic expression can contain command substitution. §7.13 shows the injection that follows, and the rule that prevents it: validate the shape of an untrusted value with a pattern or a regex before it ever reaches an arithmetic context.

7.5 Pattern Matching with ==, and What the Quotes Decide

Pattern matching in [[ works like this: the right-hand side of == and != is a glob pattern — the same pattern language as pathname expansion and ${var#pattern} (§5.4), matched against the value rather than against the filesystem. Quoting is the switch that turns it off.

# shellcheck disable=SC2016,SC2053  # the unquoted pattern variable is the subject
tag=v1.2.3
[[ $tag == v* ]]   && echo 'unquoted  v*  is a PATTERN  -> matched'
[[ $tag == "v*" ]] || echo 'quoted   "v*" is LITERAL    -> did not match'
pat='v*'
[[ $tag == $pat ]]   && echo 'unquoted $pat   is a pattern  -> matched'
[[ $tag == "$pat" ]] || echo 'quoted  "$pat"  is literal   -> did not match'

unquoted  v*  is a PATTERN  -> matched
quoted   "v*" is LITERAL    -> did not match
unquoted $pat   is a pattern  -> matched
quoted  "$pat"  is literal   -> did not match

This is the one place in [[ ]] where quoting changes the meaning rather than merely being redundant. Pattern matching in [[ is switched on by the absence of quotes and off by their presence, and nothing else selects between them. Everywhere else inside double brackets the quotes are optional because no splitting happens; here they decide whether * is a wildcard or an asterisk.

The rule reads in both directions and both are useful. A pattern written out in the source — v*, *.log, [0-9]* — is left unquoted deliberately. A pattern that arrives in a variable is still a pattern when the variable is unquoted, which is how you pass a caller-supplied glob into a function; quoting it turns it into a literal search for those characters. §6.14's last line, [[ $k == "$dc"/* ]], is the mixed case: the variable is quoted so a slash or a star inside it cannot alter the pattern, and the /* outside the quotes stays a wildcard.

Getting it backwards fails in whichever direction is quieter. Quote a pattern that should be live, and the test never matches. Leave a value unquoted that should be literal, and a stray * in it matches far too much.

The guard this is usually written for

check() {
  local tag=$1
  if [[ $tag != v* ]]; then
    echo "refusing $tag: tags must start with v" >&2
    return 1
  fi
  echo "version is ${tag#v}"
}
check v1.2.3
check 1.2.3 || echo "(exit $?)"

version is 1.2.3
refusing 1.2.3: tags must start with v
(exit 1)

§5.4 made the case for this: ${tag#v} removes the prefix if it is there and silently returns the string unchanged if it is not, so a release script that trusts it will compare 1.2.3 against v1.2.4 and get an answer it was never designed to produce. Test for the shape, then strip. The test costs one line and converts a silent wrong answer into a loud refusal.

!= is the same matching machinery with the result negated — it is not a different, literal comparison:

for f in notes.txt notes.md README; do
  if [[ $f != *.txt ]]; then echo "$f is not a .txt"; else echo "$f is a .txt"; fi
done

notes.txt is a .txt
notes.md is not a .txt
README is not a .txt

The right-hand side gets extended patterns even when extglob is off

mkdir demo && cd demo
touch report.tar.gz
shopt -u extglob
echo "extglob is $(shopt -q extglob && echo on || echo off)"
f=report.tar.gz
[[ $f == *.@(gz|bz2|xz) ]] && echo '[[ == ]] accepted an extglob pattern anyway'
echo "--- a pathname expansion does not even parse ---"
echo 'echo *.@(gz|bz2)' > glob.sh
bash glob.sh
echo "status: $?"

extglob is off
[[ == ]] accepted an extglob pattern anyway
--- a pathname expansion does not even parse ---
glob.sh: line 1: syntax error near unexpected token `('
glob.sh: line 1: `echo *.@(gz|bz2)'
status: 2

Since bash 4.1 the shell forces extglob on while it parses the pattern argument of == and !=, so @(gz|bz2|xz) works there with no shopt at all. The same characters in an ordinary glob are a syntax error when the option is off — and a syntax error, not a failed match, so it takes the whole file with it. §7.11 covers the extended forms and the parse-time hazard that makes this asymmetry worth remembering.

7.6 The File Test Operators

Every file test is a unary operator taking a path. There are eighteen of them that matter, they are the same in [ ] and [[ ]], and the fastest way to learn them is to see all of them against the same set of files at once.

mkdir demo && cd demo
printf 'hello\n' > regular.txt
: > empty.txt
mkdir subdir
ln -s regular.txt link.txt
ln -s nowhere    broken.txt
mkfifo pipe
printf '#!/bin/sh\necho hi\n' > script.sh && chmod u+sx script.sh
printf 'secret\n' > private.txt && chmod 000 private.txt
mkdir shared && chmod g+s shared
mkdir spool  && chmod +t spool
names=(regular.txt empty.txt subdir link.txt broken.txt pipe script.sh private.txt shared spool /dev/null)
row() { local line=$1; shift; while (( $# > 1 )); do line+=$(printf '%-8s' "$1"); shift; done; echo "$line$1"; }
row '    ' regular empty subdir link broken pipe script private shared spool /dev/null
for op in e f d s r w x h L p c b u g k O G S; do
  answers=()
  for f in "${names[@]}"; do
    if test -"$op" "$f" 2>/dev/null; then answers+=(yes); else answers+=(.); fi
  done
  row "$(printf '%-4s' "-$op")" "${answers[@]}"
done

    regular empty   subdir  link    broken  pipe    script  private shared  spool   /dev/null
-e  yes     yes     yes     yes     .       yes     yes     yes     yes     yes     yes
-f  yes     yes     .       yes     .       .       yes     yes     .       .       .
-d  .       .       yes     .       .       .       .       .       yes     yes     .
-s  yes     .       yes     yes     .       .       yes     yes     yes     yes     .
-r  yes     yes     yes     yes     .       yes     yes     .       yes     yes     yes
-w  yes     yes     yes     yes     .       yes     yes     .       yes     yes     yes
-x  .       .       yes     .       .       .       yes     .       yes     yes     .
-h  .       .       .       yes     yes     .       .       .       .       .       .
-L  .       .       .       yes     yes     .       .       .       .       .       .
-p  .       .       .       .       .       yes     .       .       .       .       .
-c  .       .       .       .       .       .       .       .       .       .       yes
-b  .       .       .       .       .       .       .       .       .       .       .
-u  .       .       .       .       .       .       yes     .       .       .       .
-g  .       .       .       .       .       .       .       .       yes     .       .
-k  .       .       .       .       .       .       .       .       .       yes     .
-O  yes     yes     yes     yes     .       yes     yes     yes     yes     yes     .
-G  yes     yes     yes     yes     .       yes     yes     yes     yes     yes     .
-S  .       .       .       .       .       .       .       .       .       .       .

Six columns of that table are worth reading carefully.

-e is "exists", -f is "is a regular file", -d file is "is a directory". They differ on subdir, on pipe and on the two symlinks, and -d file is the only one of the three that says yes to subdir alone. -f is the one you usually want when you are about to cat something; -e is the one you want when you are asking whether a name is free.

-s is "exists and has non-zero size", not "is not empty". It is yes for subdir, because a directory occupies blocks. Use -s on a file you know is a regular file, and read it as is this file worth opening.

-x file on a directory means searchable, not executable. subdir, shared and spool are all yes for -x file, and none of them is a program. A directory you can -r but not -x can be listed but not entered; the reverse can be entered but not listed. The two bits are independent and the operators report them independently.

-r file and -w file answer for you, right now. private.txt is mode 000 and reports . for both. Run the same script as root and every one of those becomes yes, because root bypasses the permission check — a script that gates on -r behaves differently under sudo in a way that has nothing to do with its logic. -w file has a second limitation worth stating: it reports the file's permissions, not the directory's, so creating or replacing a file can still fail on a read-only parent.

-c file is yes for /dev/null and -b is .. They are different tests: -c file is a character device, -b file a block device. -p file is the third of the same family and is yes only for the FIFO, so -p file is the test for "someone is on the other end of this". -b is empty in this table because there is no block device in the fixture; on Linux [[ -b /dev/sda ]] is true and on macOS [[ -b /dev/disk0 ]] is, and the names are the reason the table does not hard-code one. -S is the same story for a Unix-domain socket.

-O and -G are "owned by the effective UID" and "owned by the effective GID". They are . for /dev/null, which belongs to root. They are the right test before writing to a file you found by searching, and they are what -u file, -g file and -k file — setuid, setgid, sticky — are usually checked alongside in a hardening script (§18.16). -k file on a shared directory is the one that says deletions are restricted to owners, which is what /tmp relies on. A sweep for -u file combined with -x is the classic first pass over a filesystem you have just been handed.

Symlinks: -e follows, -h does not

mkdir demo && cd demo
printf 'x\n' > target.txt
ln -s target.txt good
ln -s nowhere    dangling
for l in good dangling; do
  printf '%-9s -e:%-3s -f:%-3s -h:%-3s\n' "$l" \
    "$( [[ -e $l ]] && echo yes || echo no )" \
    "$( [[ -f $l ]] && echo yes || echo no )" \
    "$( [[ -h $l ]] && echo yes || echo no )"
done
echo "the right test for 'this name is taken': -e || -h"
for l in good dangling missing; do
  if [[ -e $l || -h $l ]]; then echo "  $l: something is there"; else echo "  $l: free"; fi
done

good      -e:yes -f:yes -h:yes
dangling  -e:no  -f:no  -h:yes
the right test for 'this name is taken': -e || -h
  good: something is there
  dangling: something is there
  missing: free

Every operator in the table except -h file and -L file follows symlinks and reports on the target. A dangling symlink is therefore -e:no — the name exists in the directory and the thing it points at does not.

That gap is a real bug generator. [[ -e $path ]] || ln -s "$target" "$path" looks like "create it if it is not there" and fails with File exists the moment $path is a dangling link, because the test says no and ln says yes. -e || -h is the test that asks the question the code meant: is this name taken by anything at all?

-h file and -L file are the same operator under two spellings, and both are standard: POSIX.1-2024 defines them with identical wording, and so does bash's own help test. Pick one and use it consistently; -L is the one most readers recognise.

Comparing two files: -nt, -ot, -ef

mkdir demo && cd demo
printf 'old\n' > old.txt
sleep 1
printf 'new\n' > new.txt
ln old.txt hard.txt
ln -s old.txt soft.txt
[[ new.txt -nt old.txt ]] && echo "new.txt -nt old.txt"
[[ old.txt -ot new.txt ]] && echo "old.txt -ot new.txt"
[[ old.txt -ef hard.txt ]] && echo "old.txt -ef hard.txt   (the same inode)"
[[ old.txt -ef soft.txt ]] && echo "old.txt -ef soft.txt   (-ef follows the symlink)"
[[ old.txt -ef new.txt ]] || echo "old.txt is not -ef new.txt"
echo "--- a missing operand is not an error, it is an answer ---"
[[ missing.txt -nt old.txt ]] && echo "true" || echo "  missing -nt old.txt  -> false"
[[ old.txt -nt missing.txt ]] && echo "  old.txt -nt missing  -> true"

new.txt -nt old.txt
old.txt -ot new.txt
old.txt -ef hard.txt   (the same inode)
old.txt -ef soft.txt   (-ef follows the symlink)
old.txt is not -ef new.txt
--- a missing operand is not an error, it is an answer ---
  missing -nt old.txt  -> false
  old.txt -nt missing  -> true

These are the three binary file operators — the only place a binary operator in a conditional expression takes two paths rather than two strings — and they read as $a -nt $b, $a -ot $b and $a -ef $b. -nt and -ot compare modification times; -ef asks whether two paths reach the same inode, which is how you detect a hard link or a symlink to the same file — and the reason cp "$a" "$b" should be guarded when the two names might coincide.

The last two lines are the behaviour to memorise: $a -nt $b treats a missing $b as infinitely old, so existing -nt missing is true and missing -nt existing is false. That is what you want for a "rebuild the output if the source is newer" check, and it is not what you would get from a naive implementation that errored on a missing operand. $a -ot $b mirrors it, and $a -ef $b is false whenever either path is missing, because a binary operator that cannot stat both sides has nothing to compare.

One caveat that make exists to handle and a shell one-liner does not: modification-time comparison has the resolution of the filesystem, and two files written in the same fraction of a second can compare equal. The sleep 1 in the example is there for that reason and is not decoration.

-t: is this a terminal?

for fd in 0 1 2; do
  if [ -t "$fd" ]; then echo "fd $fd is a terminal"; else echo "fd $fd is not a terminal"; fi
done
echo "this is why a script must not decide to emit colour unconditionally"

fd 0 is not a terminal
fd 1 is not a terminal
fd 2 is not a terminal
this is why a script must not decide to emit colour unconditionally

-t takes a file descriptor number, not a path. All three are false here because the probe captures the script's output into a pipe, which is precisely the situation the operator exists to detect: [[ -t 1 ]] is how a program decides whether to emit ANSI colour, and [[ -t 0 ]] is how it decides whether prompting for input can possibly work. Getting it wrong is how escape sequences end up in a log file.

if [[ -t 1 ]]; then red=$'\e[31m'; reset=$'\e[0m'; else red=; reset=; fi is the whole idiom, and §14 builds it into a logging function.

-v and -o: the two that do not take a path

declare -A conf=([host]=example.com [port]='')
set -o pipefail
for k in host port missing; do
  printf 'conf[%-7s] -v:%-4s -n:%s\n' "$k" \
    "$( [[ -v conf[$k] ]] && echo yes || echo no )" \
    "$( [[ -n ${conf[$k]-} ]] && echo yes || echo no )"
done
for opt in pipefail nounset errexit; do
  printf 'set -o %-10s -> %s\n' "$opt" "$( [[ -o $opt ]] && echo on || echo off )"
done

conf[host   ] -v:yes  -n:yes
conf[port   ] -v:yes  -n:no
conf[missing] -v:no   -n:no
set -o pipefail   -> on
set -o nounset    -> off
set -o errexit    -> off

-v takes a variable name, not its value, and it is the operator §7.3 and §6.8 both pointed at. Written on an array element — -v conf[$k] — it asks whether that key exists, which is a question no string test can answer: port is present with an empty value, and -n calls it absent. -v on a variable is bash 4.2; -v on an array element is bash 4.3.

Note the subscript is written without ${ } and without quotes. Inside [[ ]] that is safe, because nothing is word-split; and it must be written that way, because -v wants the name.

-o takes a shell option name — the set -o kind, not the shopt kind — and returns whether it is on. It is how a function politely restores state: read [[ -o errexit ]], change the setting, put it back. shopt -q optname is the equivalent for the shopt family, and §16.7 covers both tables.

Every file test is out of date the moment it returns

mkdir demo && cd demo
printf 'data\n' > report.txt
if [[ -r report.txt ]]; then
  rm report.txt          # something else deletes it here
  if content=$(cat report.txt 2>&1); then
    echo "read: $content"
  else
    echo "the test passed and the read still failed: $content"
  fi
fi
echo "--- so do the thing, and check whether it worked ---"
if content=$(cat report.txt 2>/dev/null); then
  echo "read: $content"
else
  echo "could not read report.txt; carrying on"
fi

the test passed and the read still failed: cat: report.txt: No such file or directory
--- so do the thing, and check whether it worked ---
could not read report.txt; carrying on

The rm in the middle stands in for the other process, the other thread of your own pipeline, or the log rotation that fires at midnight. This is time-of-check to time-of-use, and it is not a shell flaw — the same race exists in every language that offers an exists() call.

The consequence is a rule about what file tests are for. They are good for producing a clear error message early ([[ -r $config ]] || die "cannot read $config"), for deciding between two paths that both exist, and for skipping work. They are not a substitute for handling the failure of the operation itself, because the operation can fail anyway. Attempt the read and check the status; use the test to explain, not to guarantee.

When the gap is a security boundary rather than an inconvenience — checking that a file is not a symlink before writing to it, say — the race is exploitable, and §18.17 covers the patterns that close it.

7.7 Combining Tests: &&, ||, !, and the Two Operators to Avoid

Inside [[ ]] the logical operators are part of the language:

# shellcheck disable=SC2050  # constant operands make the precedence visible
a=1 b=2
[[ $a == 1 && $b == 2 ]] && echo "&& inside [[ ]]"
[[ $a == 9 || $b == 2 ]] && echo "|| inside [[ ]]"
[[ ! $a == 9 ]] && echo "! inside [[ ]]"
[[ ( $a == 9 || $a == 1 ) && $b == 2 ]] && echo "( ) groups inside [[ ]]"
echo "--- && binds tighter than ||, as everywhere else ---"
[[ 1 == 2 && 1 == 2 || 1 == 1 ]] && echo "1 == 2 && 1 == 2 || 1 == 1  is  (a && b) || c  -> true"

&& inside [[ ]]
|| inside [[ ]]
! inside [[ ]]
( ) groups inside [[ ]]
--- && binds tighter than ||, as everywhere else ---
1 == 2 && 1 == 2 || 1 == 1  is  (a && b) || c  -> true

Four operators, conventional precedence, short-circuit evaluation, and — the detail that makes them pleasant — the parentheses need no backslashes, because [[ is parsed by the shell and ( inside it is not a subshell. Group anything with mixed && and ||, not because the precedence is surprising but because the reader should not have to know it.

-a and -o are not well defined, and that is not a style opinion

[ ] has no operators, so POSIX gave test two extra operands, -a and -o, which it reads as conjunction and disjunction. The problem is that test decides what an expression means by counting its arguments, and a value can look like an operator:

# shellcheck disable=SC2166  # -a is the counter-example; shellcheck flagging it is the next block
a='=' b=x
echo "intent: both a and b are non-empty"
[[ -n $a && -n $b ]] && echo "  [[ -n \$a && -n \$b ]]      -> true"
[ -n "$a" -a -n "$b" ]  && echo "  [ -n \$a -a -n \$b ]        -> true" \
                        || echo "  [ -n \"\$a\" -a -n \"\$b\" ]    -> FALSE, with a='='"
{ [ -n "$a" ] && [ -n "$b" ]; } && echo "  [ ... ] && [ ... ]          -> true"
echo "the five words are  -n  =  -a  -n  x , and 'test' reads the second as an operator"

intent: both a and b are non-empty
  [[ -n $a && -n $b ]]      -> true
example.sh: line 5: [: syntax error: `-n' unexpected
  [ -n "$a" -a -n "$b" ]    -> FALSE, with a='='
  [ ... ] && [ ... ]          -> true
the five words are  -n  =  -a  -n  x , and 'test' reads the second as an operator

Both operands are non-empty, so the honest answer is true. The -a form says false, and says it with a syntax error rather than silently — this time. The quoting is correct; the arguments are exactly the five words intended. What went wrong is that test saw = in the second position, took the expression to be a binary string comparison, and then found -n where it wanted the rest of the expression.

This is not a bash quirk to be worked around. POSIX says the results are unspecified for any test expression with more than four arguments, and the current edition, POSIX.1-2024, goes further: the -a and -o binary primaries and the ( ) operators have been removed from test altogether. bash still accepts them, for compatibility, which is the only reason the example above ran at all. ShellCheck agrees:

cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
f=notes.txt
if [ -f "$f" -a -r "$f" ]; then echo readable; fi
EOF
shellcheck t.sh
echo "exit: $?"

In t.sh line 3:
if [ -f "$f" -a -r "$f" ]; then echo readable; fi
             ^-- SC2166 (warning): Prefer [ p ] && [ q ] as [ p -a q ] is not well defined.

For more information:
  https://www.shellcheck.net/wiki/SC2166 -- Prefer [ p ] && [ q ] as [ p -a q...
exit: 1

In a bash script, write [[ p && q ]]. In a #!/bin/sh script, write [ p ] && [ q ]. Never -a or -o. The escaped-parenthesis forms \( and \) went out of POSIX with them and have the same argument-counting problem, so the same advice applies: group with real shell grouping, not with operands.

&& and || between commands, as a statement

The operators that combine commands are the ones from §2.5, and they are how conditions are usually written when there is no branch to take:

mkdir demo && cd demo
printf 'x\n' > config.yml
[[ -r config.yml ]] || { echo "config.yml is unreadable" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "config is readable"
command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1 || echo "jq is not installed; falling back"
echo "--- the classic a && b || c trap: c also runs when b fails ---"
true && false || echo "the || branch ran even though the condition was TRUE"

config is readable
--- the classic a && b || c trap: c also runs when b fails ---
the || branch ran even though the condition was TRUE

test || { handle; exit 1; } is the guard-clause idiom, and it reads well precisely because the failure case is the short one. Note the braces and the semicolon before the closing brace — §2.6's rules, and the reason { ... ; } rather than ( ... ) is that an exit inside a subshell exits the subshell.

command -v jq >/dev/null is the correct way to ask whether a program is available. Not which (an external program, absent on some systems, with inconsistent exit status), and not type (which finds aliases and functions too).

The last two lines are §2.5's precedence trap restated, because it appears most often in exactly this shape. a && b || c is not an if/else: || runs c whenever the thing to its left failed, and the thing to its left is a && b. If a succeeds and b fails, c runs anyway. It is a correct idiom only when b cannot fail — [[ -d $d ]] && echo yes || echo no is fine because echo does not fail — and an if statement otherwise. §8.1 writes it out.

7.8 Arithmetic Evaluation, and the Contexts It Happens In

The second engine. $(( expr )) expands to the value of an expression; (( expr )) is a command that evaluates one and reports success or failure; the let builtin is the older spelling of the same thing. All three share one evaluator, whose rules differ from the rest of the shell in ways that are convenient once learned and dangerous until then.

# shellcheck disable=SC2004,SC2034  # the two forms are contrasted on purpose; a is read through b
n=5
echo "n * 2      -> $(( n * 2 ))"
echo "\$n * 2     -> $(( $n * 2 ))"
unset -v nothing
echo "nothing+1  -> $(( nothing + 1 ))"
b=a; a=7
echo "b, where b=a and a=7 -> $(( b ))"

n * 2      -> 10
$n * 2     -> 10
nothing+1  -> 1
b, where b=a and a=7 -> 7

Variables need no $ in arithmetic. Inside an arithmetic context a bare word is looked up as a variable, so n * 2 and $n * 2 mean the same thing — that variables need no $ in arithmetic is the first thing to internalise about this evaluator, because it is what makes (( i < n )) read the way it does. Prefer the bare form: it is shorter, and it is immune to the class of bug where $n expands to something that changes the expression's structure.

An unset name is zero, not an error. This is the rule §6.3 relied on — (( count[$w]++ )) works on a key that does not exist — and the rule that made [[ $n -eq 0 ]] true for n=abc in §7.4. It is convenient exactly half the time and silent the other half, and set -u does not change it.

Names are resolved recursively. $(( b )) with b=a and a=7 yields 7: the evaluator looked up b, got the string a, and evaluated that as an expression. §4.5 measured the same behaviour and §18.4 shows what it costs when the value is untrusted.

Arithmetic and exit status: (( )) returns 1 on zero

(( 1 ));      echo "(( 1 ))       -> $?"
(( 0 ));      echo "(( 0 ))       -> $?"
(( 5 - 5 ));  echo "(( 5 - 5 ))   -> $?"
(( 2 + 2 == 5 )); echo "(( 2+2 == 5 )) -> $?"
count=0
(( count++ )); echo "(( count++ )) with count=0 -> status $?, count is now $count"
(( ++count )); echo "(( ++count )) -> status $?, count is now $count"

(( 1 ))       -> 0
(( 0 ))       -> 1
(( 5 - 5 ))   -> 1
(( 2+2 == 5 )) -> 1
(( count++ )) with count=0 -> status 1, count is now 1
(( ++count )) -> status 0, count is now 2

Arithmetic and exit status meet here, and the mapping inverts twice. (( )) maps the C convention onto the shell one: a non-zero value is success (status 0), while (( )) returns 1 on zero. That is what makes (( a > b )) read naturally as a condition — a true comparison evaluates to 1, which is non-zero, which is status 0.

It also means an arithmetic command that happens to produce zero is a "failed" command — that (( )) returns 1 on zero is a rule about the value, not about whether the evaluation worked. The last two lines are where that turns into a bug. count++ is post-increment: it yields the old value, 0, so the command's status is 1 even though the increment happened. ++count yields the new value, 1, and the status is 0.

Which is why set -e kills a counter

set -e
count=0
echo "about to run (( count++ )) under set -e, with count at 0"
(( count++ ))
echo "NOT REACHED"

about to run (( count++ )) under set -e, with count at 0

The script stopped. set -e exits on any command that returns non-zero and is not in a tested position, and (( count++ )) returned 1 on the increment from zero — exactly once, the first time, which is what makes it so effective at surviving testing and failing in production. §11.5 covers the full set of set -e surprises; this is the one that belongs here because it is a property of (( )) rather than of set -e.

Three repairs, all fine:

set -e
count=0; (( count++ )) || true;      echo "(( count++ )) || true  -> $count"
count=0; (( ++count ));              echo "(( ++count ))          -> $count"
count=0; count=$(( count + 1 ));     echo "count=\$(( count + 1 )) -> $count"

(( count++ )) || true  -> 1
(( ++count ))          -> 1
count=$(( count + 1 )) -> 1

|| true puts the command in a tested position, which is the general escape. ++count avoids the zero because pre-increment yields the new value — it works, and it works for a reason a reader has to know, so comment it. count=$(( count + 1 )) is an assignment, whose status is the assignment's, not the expression's; it is the form this course prefers, because its correctness does not depend on the value.

The let builtin, and declare -i

# shellcheck disable=SC2219,SC2324  # let and a string += are both being taught here
let 'a = 3 * 4'
echo "let 'a = 3 * 4'      -> $a"
let b=1+1 c=b*3
echo "let b=1+1 c=b*3      -> b=$b c=$c"
declare -i i
i='2+3';  echo "declare -i i='2+3'   -> $i"
i=abc;    echo "declare -i i=abc     -> $i"
j='2+3';  echo "plain    j='2+3'     -> $j"
i+=1;     echo "declare -i i+=1      -> $i  (numeric, not string append)"
j+=1;     echo "plain    j+=1        -> $j  (string append)"

let 'a = 3 * 4'      -> 12
let b=1+1 c=b*3      -> b=2 c=6
declare -i i='2+3'   -> 5
declare -i i=abc     -> 0
plain    j='2+3'     -> 2+3
declare -i i+=1      -> 1  (numeric, not string append)
plain    j+=1        -> 2+31  (string append)

The let builtin takes each argument as a separate expression and evaluates them left to right, so c=b*3 can use the b assigned by the previous argument. It is older than (( )), it needs quoting around anything with a space or a *, and its exit status follows the last expression. There is no reason to prefer it in new code; know it because you will read it.

declare -i marks a variable integer, which makes every later assignment to it an arithmetic evaluation. It has two genuine uses and one trap. The uses: an accumulator that should never hold a string, and a variable where += should add rather than concatenate — compare the last two lines, where i+=1 gave 1 and j+=1 gave 2+31. The trap: i=abc silently became 0, because the arithmetic evaluator resolved abc as an unset name. An integer variable does not validate its input; it converts it, and unconvertible input converts to zero.

Every arithmetic context in one place

arr=(zero one two three)
k=1
echo "\$(( ))          : $(( k + 1 ))"
(( k + 1 == 2 )) && echo "(( ))            : the condition held"
echo "array subscript : ${arr[k+1]}"
echo "slice            : ${arr[*]:k:2}"
echo "substring        : ${BASH_VERSION:0:k+2}"
[[ 4 -eq 2+2 ]] && echo "[[ -eq ]]        : 4 -eq 2+2"
printf 'c-style for      :'; for (( m = 0; m < 3; m++ )); do printf ' %s' "$m"; done; printf '\n'
declare -i n=1+1; echo "declare -i       : $n"

$(( ))          : 2
(( ))            : the condition held
array subscript : two
slice            : one two
substring        : 5.3
[[ -eq ]]        : 4 -eq 2+2
c-style for      : 0 1 2
declare -i       : 2

Eight places where the arithmetic evaluator runs, and the list is worth committing to memory because everything in this section applies in all of them: variables need no $ in arithmetic in every one, and arithmetic and exit status are linked in the two that are commands. An unset name is zero in an array subscript (§6.3 measured the consequence). A leading zero is octal in a substring offset. A value containing $(...) is command substitution in any of them, which is why §7.13's validation rule is not optional.

The three that surprise people are the subscripts and offsets. ${arr[k+1]} needs no $ on k and evaluates an expression; ${var:offset:length} does the same with both of its arguments; and ${arr[@]:k:2} slices using arithmetic. §5.3 and §6.11 covered the expansions themselves.

7.9 Integers Only: Truncation, Overflow, and the Absence of Floating Point

Bash offers integer arithmetic and nothing else — signed 64-bit integer arithmetic, to be exact. §1.6 listed this as one of the four reasons to write something in another language, and this subsection is the evidence.

echo " 7 / 2  = $(( 7 / 2 ))"
echo "-7 / 2  = $(( -7 / 2 ))"
echo " 7 % 3  = $(( 7 % 3 ))"
echo "-7 % 3  = $(( -7 % 3 ))"
echo " 7 % -3 = $(( 7 % -3 ))"
echo "--- so an average computed the obvious way is wrong ---"
total=7 n=2
echo "naive:   $(( total / n ))"
echo "rounded: $(( (total + n/2) / n ))"
echo "tenths:  $(( total * 10 / n )) tenths"

 7 / 2  = 3
-7 / 2  = -3
 7 % 3  = 1
-7 % 3  = -1
 7 % -3 = 1
--- so an average computed the obvious way is wrong ---
naive:   3
rounded: 4
tenths:  35 tenths

Division truncates toward zero, so -7 / 2 is -3 rather than -4. That is C's rule, not Python's floor division, and the difference shows up the moment a value can be negative. The % remainder operator takes the sign of the dividend: -7 % 3 is -1 and 7 % -3 is 1. That makes % remainder in bash C's operator rather than a mathematical modulo. A modulo used to index into an array — ${arr[i % n]} — is therefore not safe for negative i, and $(( (i % n + n) % n )) is the standard repair.

The three lines at the bottom are the whole technique for getting a useful answer out of an integer-only evaluator: scale before you divide. Multiply by 10, or 100, or 1000, do the division, and then place the decimal point yourself when you print. Adding half the divisor before dividing rounds instead of truncating.

Sixty-four bits, and nothing beyond them

echo "largest : $(( 2**63 - 1 ))"
echo "plus one: $(( 2**63 ))"
echo "smallest: $(( -2**63 ))"
echo "no overflow is reported; the value simply wraps"

largest : 9223372036854775807
plus one: -9223372036854775808
smallest: -9223372036854775808
no overflow is reported; the value simply wraps

There is no overflow diagnostic. Add one to the largest representable value and you get the smallest, silently, with exit status 0. Nine quintillion is a lot of headroom for a counter and not much at all for nanoseconds since 1970 multiplied by anything, or for a product of two file sizes, or for a naive factorial. If a computation can approach that magnitude, do it somewhere else.

No floating point at all

# shellcheck disable=SC2079,SC2320  # the decimal is the error being shown; $? is the failed expansion
echo "before"
echo "$(( 1.5 ))"
echo "status: $?"
echo "--- percentages, done by scaling before dividing ---"
used=91 total=128
echo "truncated whole percent: $(( used * 100 / total ))%"
tenths=$(( (used * 1000 + total / 2) / total ))
echo "rounded to one decimal:  $(( tenths / 10 )).$(( tenths % 10 ))%"
echo "--- and when you really need a float, leave the shell ---"
awk -v u=91 -v t=128 'BEGIN { printf "awk: %.4f%%\n", u / t * 100 }'

before
example.sh: line 3: 1.5 : arithmetic syntax error: invalid arithmetic operator (error token is ".5 ")
status: 1
--- percentages, done by scaling before dividing ---
truncated whole percent: 71%
rounded to one decimal:  71.1%
--- and when you really need a float, leave the shell ---
awk: 71.0938%

A decimal point is a syntax error, not a rounding. The message is worth reading closely: bash parsed 1 as a number and then found .5 where it wanted an operator. Any value that might carry a decimal point — a version string, a temperature, a price, anything from bc — must be kept away from $(( )) entirely.

awk is the right escape hatch for one calculation, because it is POSIX, it is everywhere, and -v passes values in without building a command string. bc -l is the other, and it is the one to use when you need arbitrary precision rather than doubles. Both cost a fork per call (§21.4), so do the arithmetic once over a whole dataset rather than once per loop iteration.

The exception, and why it is not really one

enable -f fltexpr fltexpr 2>/dev/null || { echo "fltexpr is not installed here"; exit 0; }
fltexpr 'ratio = 91 / 128'
echo "fltexpr: $ratio"
fltexpr -p '1.5 * 2'
enable -d fltexpr
type -t fltexpr || echo "and after enable -d it is gone again"

fltexpr: 0.7109375
3
and after enable -d it is gone again

bash 5.3 ships a loadable builtin called fltexpr that does floating-point arithmetic. It is real, it works, and it is not a reason to change the advice above. Loadable builtins are compiled shared objects that must be present on the machine and found via BASH_LOADABLES_PATH; a script that depends on one is a script that fails on any host where the bash-devel package was not installed, and it needs bash 5.3 besides. Know it exists — it is genuinely useful in an interactive shell — and keep awk in scripts.

7.10 The Arithmetic Operator Set, Its Bases, and Its Precedence

The evaluator implements essentially all of C's expression syntax, and the arithmetic operator precedence is C's too. The places it differs are where the bugs are.

echo "2 ** 3 ** 2   = $(( 2 ** 3 ** 2 ))   (right-associative: 2**(3**2))"
echo "(2 ** 3) ** 2 = $(( (2 ** 3) ** 2 ))"
echo "-2 ** 2       = $(( -2 ** 2 ))   <- unary minus binds TIGHTER than ** here"
echo "0 - 2 ** 2    = $(( 0 - 2 ** 2 ))"

2 ** 3 ** 2   = 512   (right-associative: 2**(3**2))
(2 ** 3) ** 2 = 64
-2 ** 2       = 4   <- unary minus binds TIGHTER than ** here
0 - 2 ** 2    = -4

** is the exponent operator — a bash extension, not in POSIX — and the ** exponent has been right-associative since bash 3.1, so 2 ** 3 ** 2 is 512 rather than 64. That matches C's absent operator as implemented by every language that has one.

-2 ** 2 is where bash parts company with the languages it resembles. It is 4, meaning the shell parsed (-2) ** 2. Python and Ruby both give -4, applying the exponent first. The last line shows the workaround and the general principle: when a unary minus meets the ** exponent, parenthesise, because half your readers will guess the other way.

n=5; echo "n++ yields $(( n++ )), n is now $n"
n=5; echo "++n yields $(( ++n )), n is now $n"
size=1500
echo "ternary: $(( size > 1024 ? 1 : 0 ))"
echo "comma:   $(( x = 1, y = 2, x + y ))"
c=0
echo "0 && c++ -> $(( 0 && c++ )), c is still $c"
echo "1 || c++ -> $(( 1 || c++ )), c is still $c"

n++ yields 5, n is now 6
++n yields 6, n is now 6
ternary: 1
comma:   3
0 && c++ -> 0, c is still 0
1 || c++ -> 1, c is still 0

The ++ increment and -- decrement operators come in two flavours each: post-increment yields the old value, pre-increment the new — the distinction that §7.8 turned into a set -e bug. -- decrement behaves identically in the other direction, and both require a variable rather than an expression — $(( 5++ )) is an error, because ++ increment has nothing to store into. The ternary in arithmetic is the only conditional expression the shell has that produces a value rather than a status, and a ternary in arithmetic is the idiomatic way to clamp or default a number: $(( n > max ? max : n )). The comma operator evaluates every sub-expression and yields the last, which is how a C-style for header initialises two variables at once; outside that header the comma operator is rarely worth the density. And &&/|| short-circuit: c++ never ran in either line, which is worth knowing before putting a side effect on the right of one.

Bases, and the leading zero

printf '%-10s %s\n' '16#ff'  "$(( 16#ff ))"
printf '%-10s %s\n' '0xff'   "$(( 0xff ))"
printf '%-10s %s\n' '2#1011' "$(( 2#1011 ))"
printf '%-10s %s\n' '8#17'   "$(( 8#17 ))"
printf '%-10s %s\n' '017'    "$(( 017 ))"
printf '%-10s %s\n' '36#zz'  "$(( 36#zz ))"
printf '%-10s %s\n' '64#_'   "$(( 64#_ ))"

16#ff      255
0xff       255
2#1011     11
8#17       15
017        15
36#zz      1295
64#_       63

The base#number form accepts any base from 2 to 64, and the digit alphabet of base#number changes shape at 37:

# shellcheck disable=SC2320  # $? is the failed arithmetic expansion, not echo
echo "36#ZZ = $(( 36#ZZ ))   36#zz = $(( 36#zz ))   (below base 37, case is ignored)"
echo "37#z  = $(( 37#z ))    (in base 37 and above, lowercase is 10-35 and uppercase is 36-61)"
echo "before 37#Z"
echo "$(( 37#Z ))"
echo "status: $?"
echo "-7 >> 1 = $(( -7 >> 1 ))   floor, unlike  -7 / 2 = $(( -7 / 2 ))   which truncates"

36#ZZ = 1295   36#zz = 1295   (below base 37, case is ignored)
37#z  = 35    (in base 37 and above, lowercase is 10-35 and uppercase is 36-61)
before 37#Z
example.sh: line 5: 37#Z: value too great for base (error token is "37#Z")
status: 1
-7 >> 1 = -4   floor, unlike  -7 / 2 = -3   which truncates

Digits above 9 are a-z (10-35); for a base above 36 the uppercase letters continue as 36-61, then @ is 62 and _ is 63 — which is why 37#Z is out of range while 37#z is 35. The last line is the one worth carrying out of this table: >> floors and / truncates, so they disagree on every negative odd number.

A hexadecimal literal is written 0x or 0X — or as 16#ff, which is the same value by the general rule — and a leading zero alone is octal, which is the one that causes trouble. Note that a hexadecimal literal needs no quoting anywhere arithmetic is evaluated:

# shellcheck disable=SC2320  # $? is the failed arithmetic expansion, not echo
echo "a zero-padded field is octal, and 08 is not an octal number:"
day=08
echo "$(( day + 0 ))"
echo "status: $?"
echo "--- 10# forces base ten ---"
echo "10#08 -> $(( 10#$day ))"
echo "--- or strip the padding first ---"
echo "\${day#0} -> $(( ${day#0} ))"

a zero-padded field is octal, and 08 is not an octal number:
example.sh: line 4: 08: value too great for base (error token is "08")
status: 1
--- 10# forces base ten ---
10#08 -> 8
--- or strip the padding first ---
${day#0} -> 8

That a leading zero is octal is the rule doing the damage, and zero-padded numbers are everywhere: date +%m gives 08, date +%d gives 09, sorted log files are named part-007, and every one of them is a valid octal literal until the digit reaches 8. Nothing announces the base, which is what makes "a leading zero is octal" worth memorising rather than looking up. 08 and 09 are the only two values in a two-digit padded field that fail, which means a script can run correctly for seven months of the year.

10#$var is the fix, and it is worth applying to every value that arrives from outside as a possibly-padded number. ${var#0} also works and is worse: it strips one zero, so 007 becomes 07, still octal. ${var##+(0)} with extglob strips them all and turns 000 into the empty string, which evaluates to zero — correct, but by accident.

The failure is loud, which is the one mercy here, and §7.4's [[ 010 -eq 10 ]] is the quiet version of the same rule: 010 is a valid octal literal, so nothing is reported and the comparison is simply wrong.

Bitwise, assignment, and the precedence table

printf '12 & 10 = %-4d 12 | 10 = %-4d 12 ^ 10 = %-4d ~12 = %d\n' \
  "$(( 12 & 10 ))" "$(( 12 | 10 ))" "$(( 12 ^ 10 ))" "$(( ~12 ))"
printf '1 << 10 = %-4d 1024 >> 3 = %d\n' "$(( 1 << 10 ))" "$(( 1024 >> 3 ))"
v=10
for op in '+= 5' '*= 2' '%= 7' '<<= 4' '|= 1'; do
  eval "(( v $op ))"
  printf 'v %-5s -> %s\n' "$op" "$v"
done
echo "--- precedence, with no parentheses ---"
printf '%-14s %s\n' '2 + 3 * 4'  "$(( 2 + 3 * 4 ))"
printf '%-14s %s\n' '1 << 2 + 3' "$(( 1 << 2 + 3 ))"
printf '%-14s %s\n' '1 | 2 & 3'  "$(( 1 | 2 & 3 ))"
printf '%-14s %s\n' '0 == 0 < 1' "$(( 0 == 0 < 1 ))"

12 & 10 = 8    12 | 10 = 14   12 ^ 10 = 6    ~12 = -13
1 << 10 = 1024 1024 >> 3 = 128
v += 5  -> 15
v *= 2  -> 30
v %= 7  -> 2
v <<= 4 -> 32
v |= 1  -> 33
--- precedence, with no parentheses ---
2 + 3 * 4      14
1 << 2 + 3     32
1 | 2 & 3      3
0 == 0 < 1     0

Every bitwise operator C has is here: &, |, ^, ~, and the << shift and its mirror >>, with C's semantics on a signed 64-bit value. A bitwise operator in bash works on the full signed 64 bits, so ~12 is -13 rather than a small positive number. 1 << 10 is the idiomatic way to write 1024 in a script that deals with sizes, and >> is an integer divide by a power of two — flooring, as the block above measured, not truncating.

Every compound assignment operator in arithmetic exists: += -= *= /= %= <<= >>= &= ^= |=. An assignment operator in arithmetic is usable anywhere arithmetic is, including inside $(( )), where it assigns as a side effect and yields the new value — which is what makes $(( total += n )) both a statement and an expression. The << shift has its own compound form, <<=, used above.

The last four lines are the precedence check. 1 << 2 + 3 is 32, meaning + binds tighter than <<; 1 | 2 & 3 is 3, meaning & binds tighter than |; 0 == 0 < 1 is 0, meaning < binds tighter than == and the expression is 0 == (0 < 1). These are C's rules exactly, so the arithmetic operator precedence table below can be read as C's, and they are also C's famous traps. Parenthesise anything that mixes shifts, bitwise operators and comparisons, for the same reason C programmers do — the arithmetic operator precedence is correct and it is not what a reader skimming the line will assume.

Tightest first
Operators
1
var++ var-- — post-increment, post-decrement
2
++var --var — pre-increment, pre-decrement
3
- + unary, ! ~ logical and bitwise negation
4
** — exponentiation, right-associative
5
* / %
6
+ - binary
7
<< >>
8
<= >= < >
9
== !=
10
& then ^ then |, in that order
11
&& then ||
12
expr ? expr : expr — the ternary
13
= *= /= %= += -= <<= >>= &= ^= |=
14
, — evaluate left to right, yield the last

7.11 Bracket Expressions, Character Classes, and extglob

The pattern language behind ==, case and every glob has three layers. *, ? and [...] are the basic ones §4.7 introduced; bracket expressions and POSIX character classes are the second; the five extglob forms are the third.

for w in abc a1c 'a c' A1C; do
  hits=()
  [[ $w == [[:alpha:]][[:alpha:]][[:alpha:]] ]] && hits+=(alpha)
  [[ $w == [[:alnum:]]* ]]                     && hits+=(alnum)
  [[ $w == *[[:space:]]* ]]                    && hits+=(space)
  [[ $w == [[:upper:]]* ]]                     && hits+=(upper)
  printf '%-7s %s\n' "[$w]" "${hits[*]}"
done
echo "--- a negated bracket takes ! or ^ ---"
[[ x == [!0-9] ]] && echo "[!0-9] matched x"
[[ x == [^0-9] ]] && echo "[^0-9] matched x"
echo "--- a range is not a promise about the alphabet ---"
shopt -p globasciiranges

[abc]   alpha alnum
[a1c]   alnum
[a c]   alnum space
[A1C]   alnum upper
--- a negated bracket takes ! or ^ ---
[!0-9] matched x
[^0-9] matched x
--- a range is not a promise about the alphabet ---
shopt -s globasciiranges

A bracket expression matches exactly one character from the set inside it. [abc], [0-9] and [a-z] are the familiar forms; [!...] and [^...] are both negation, and ! is the POSIX spelling while ^ is the one borrowed from regex. Two characters lose their meaning inside brackets and gain it back by position: a ] must come first ([]abc]), and a - must come first or last ([-abc] or [abc-]).

A POSIX character class — [[:alpha:]], [[:digit:]], [[:space:]], [[:upper:]], [[:lower:]], [[:alnum:]], [[:punct:]], [[:xdigit:]], [[:blank:]], [[:cntrl:]], [[:graph:]], [[:print:]] — is locale-aware and is the form to prefer. Every POSIX character class is spelled with the doubled brackets, which confuses everyone once: the outer pair is the bracket expression, the inner [: :] is the class, and [[:alpha:][:digit:]] puts two classes in one expression.

The last line matters more than it looks. A range like [a-z] is defined by the locale's collation order, not by the alphabet. In a locale that interleaves cases, [a-z] can match B. globasciiranges — a shopt added in bash 4.3 and on by default since 5.0, as the output confirms — forces ranges to be compared as if in the C locale, which is what nearly everyone means. Character classes are immune to the problem and are the better habit: [[:lower:]] says what [a-z] was trying to say.

The five extended forms

mkdir demo && cd demo
touch a.txt b.log c.tar.gz d.tar.bz2 report1.csv report22.csv Report.TXT
shopt -s extglob
printf '%-24s %s\n' '?(1)   zero or one'   "$(echo report?(1).csv)"
printf '%-24s %s\n' '*(2)   zero or more'  "$(echo report*(2).csv)"
printf '%-24s %s\n' '+([0-9]) one or more' "$(echo report+([0-9]).csv)"
printf '%-24s %s\n' '@(log|txt) exactly one' "$(echo *.@(log|txt))"
printf '%-24s %s\n' '!(...)  anything but' "$(echo !(*.csv|*.gz|*.bz2))"

?(1)   zero or one       report1.csv
*(2)   zero or more      report22.csv
+([0-9]) one or more     report1.csv report22.csv
@(log|txt) exactly one   a.txt b.log
!(...)  anything but     Report.TXT a.txt b.log

extglob — bash 2.02, off by default, shopt -s extglob to enable — adds five constructs, each taking a |-separated list of patterns. Spelled generically they are ?(pattern), *(pattern), +(pattern), @(pattern) and !(pattern), and the quantifier character in front is the same one the basic glob language already uses:

Form
Matches
?(pattern)
Zero or one occurrence of any pattern in the list — an optional part.
*(pattern)
Zero or more occurrences.
+(pattern)
One or more occurrences. +([0-9]) is the glob spelling of "a number".
@(pattern)
Exactly one of the alternatives. The one you reach for most: *.@(jpg|png|gif).
!(pattern)
Anything except the alternatives. The only negation the glob language has.

!(pattern) is the one with no equivalent elsewhere and the one worth internalising, because @(pattern) merely spells out an alternation you could write by hand while !(pattern) cannot be written any other way. rm !(*.keep) and cp !(node_modules|.git) dst/ are the shapes it exists for — and note that !(*.csv) above matched a.txt and b.log but also Report.TXT, because matching is case-sensitive unless §7.12's switch says otherwise.

They work in every pattern context

shopt -s extglob
f=c.tar.gz
[[ $f == *.@(gz|bz2|xz) ]] && echo "[[ == ]]      matched"
case $f in *.@(gz|bz2)) echo "case          matched";; esac
echo "\${f%%.@(tar.gz|tar.bz2)} -> ${f%%.@(tar.gz|tar.bz2)}"
echo "\${f//+([aeiou])/_}       -> ${f//+([aeiou])/_}"

[[ == ]]      matched
case          matched
${f%%.@(tar.gz|tar.bz2)} -> c
${f//+([aeiou])/_}       -> c.t_r.gz

One pattern language, four contexts: the conditional operator, case (§8.5), the trimming expansions (§5.4) and the substitution expansions (§5.5). ${f%%.@(tar.gz|tar.bz2)} is the clean way to strip a double extension, which §5.4 could only do with two nested expansions.

extglob is consulted at parse time, not at match time

mkdir demo && cd demo
touch a.gz b.txt
cat > inner.sh <<'EOF'
f() {
  shopt -s extglob
  echo "matched: $(echo *.@(gz|bz2))"
}
f
EOF
cat > outer.sh <<'EOF'
shopt -s extglob
f() {
  echo "matched: $(echo *.@(gz|bz2))"
}
f
EOF
echo "--- shopt inside the function body ---"
bash inner.sh
echo "status: $?"
echo "--- shopt before the function is parsed ---"
bash outer.sh
echo "status: $?"

--- shopt inside the function body ---
inner.sh: line 3: syntax error near unexpected token `(' while looking for matching `)'
inner.sh: line 3: `  echo "matched: $(echo *.@(gz|bz2))"'
status: 2
--- shopt before the function is parsed ---
matched: a.gz
status: 0

This is the hazard that makes extglob different from every other shopt. The option changes how the shell parses a word, and a function definition is parsed in one piece before any of it runs — so shopt -s extglob on the first line of a function body is too late for a pattern on the third. The same applies to anything inside a { } group, a loop body, or a case that the parser consumes as a unit.

Two consequences for real scripts. Set extglob near the top of the file, beside the shebang and the set -euo pipefail line, not at the point of use. And do not turn it off and on around a section, which is the habit that works for nullglob and breaks here — turning it off before a later function is parsed will break that function.

[[ ]]'s == operator is exempt, as §7.5 measured, because bash forces the option on while it parses that one argument. That exemption is the reason a script can use @(a|b) in a conditional without any shopt at all and still fall over the first time someone copies the pattern into a glob.

7.12 The Matching Switches: nocasematch, nocaseglob, GLOBIGNORE, GLOBSORT

Four settings change what patterns match. They are global, they are easy to leave on by accident, and knowing exactly which constructs each one reaches is the difference between a useful tool and an intermittent bug.

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the literal ${f%%.MD} is a column label, not an expansion
f=README.md
for state in off on; do
  if [[ $state == on ]]; then shopt -s nocasematch; else shopt -u nocasematch; fi
  printf 'nocasematch %-3s  [[ == *.MD ]]:%-4s case:%-4s ${f%%.MD}:%-12s ${f/MD/x}:%s\n' \
    "$state" \
    "$( [[ $f == *.MD ]] && echo yes || echo no )" \
    "$(case $f in *.MD) echo yes;; *) echo no;; esac)" \
    "${f%.MD}" "${f/MD/x}"
done
shopt -u nocasematch

nocasematch off  [[ == *.MD ]]:no   case:no   ${f%.MD}:README.md    ${f/MD/x}:README.md
nocasematch on   [[ == *.MD ]]:yes  case:yes  ${f%.MD}:README.md    ${f/MD/x}:README.x

nocasematch (bash 3.1) reaches [[ == ]], [[ =~ ]], case, and the substitution expansions ${var/pat/rep} and ${var//pat/rep} — the last since bash 4.4. It does not reach the trimming expansions ${var#pat} and ${var%pat}, which stayed case-sensitive in both rows, and it does not reach globbing at all. That split is not guessable; it is the kind of thing this course exists to have measured.

mkdir demo && cd demo
touch README.md readme.txt Makefile
shopt -s nocasematch
echo "nocasematch on, glob:  $(echo readme.*)"
shopt -u nocasematch
shopt -s nocaseglob
echo "nocaseglob  on, glob:  $(echo readme.*)"
shopt -u nocaseglob

nocasematch on, glob:  readme.txt
nocaseglob  on, glob:  README.md readme.txt

nocaseglob is the one for pathname expansion, and it is separate because the questions are separate: you might reasonably want case-insensitive string comparison without wanting *.jpg to also collect .JPG files, or the reverse.

Both are global and both stay on until turned off, which is the argument against them. §5.6 made the case already: case ${reply,,} in y|yes) lowercases the one value you are testing and leaves the rest of the script alone, while shopt -s nocasematch changes the behaviour of every case and [[ == ]] that runs afterwards — including ones inside functions you did not write, sourced from a library, three files away. Prefer converting the value. Reach for the switch only when you are matching a large set of patterns case-insensitively and the alternative is unreadable, and then turn it off in the same function.

mkdir demo && cd demo
touch .hidden a.txt b.txt c.log
printf '1234567890' > big.txt
printf 'x' > small.txt
echo "plain *:             $(echo *)"
GLOBIGNORE='*.log'
echo "GLOBIGNORE='*.log':  $(echo *)"
unset GLOBIGNORE
echo "GLOBSORT is new in bash 5.3:"
echo "  default (name):    $(echo *.txt)"
GLOBSORT=size  ; echo "  GLOBSORT=size:     $(echo *.txt)"
GLOBSORT=-size ; echo "  GLOBSORT=-size:    $(echo *.txt)"
unset GLOBSORT

plain *:             a.txt b.txt big.txt c.log small.txt
GLOBIGNORE='*.log':  .hidden a.txt b.txt big.txt small.txt
GLOBSORT is new in bash 5.3:
  default (name):    a.txt b.txt big.txt small.txt
  GLOBSORT=size:     a.txt b.txt small.txt big.txt
  GLOBSORT=-size:    big.txt small.txt b.txt a.txt

GLOBIGNORE is a colon-separated list of patterns removed from every glob result. It has a documented side effect that the output shows plainly: setting it to a non-empty value enables dotglob, so .hidden appeared. That is deliberate — GLOBIGNORE='.:..' was the original way to say "include dotfiles but not the two directory entries" — and it is a genuine surprise if you set the variable for an unrelated reason. bash has excluded . and .. from the results itself since 5.1.

GLOBSORT is new in bash 5.3 and sets the order a glob returns its matches in: name (the default), size, blocks, mtime, atime, ctime, numeric or none, each optionally prefixed with - for descending. for f in * sorted by mtime without piping through ls -t is a real convenience, and GLOBSORT=none skips the sort entirely, which is measurable on a directory with tens of thousands of entries. Being 5.3-only makes it unusable in anything portable — §19 — and it is worth knowing about because it removes one of the standing reasons to parse ls.

All four are global state, which is the theme. A function that sets one and does not restore it has changed the behaviour of its caller. §16.7 covers saving and restoring shell options properly; the short version is [[ -o ... ]] and shopt -p (§7.6) read the current setting so it can be put back.

7.13 Regular Expressions: =~ and BASH_REMATCH

The =~ regex operator (bash 3.0) matches its left operand against a POSIX extended regular expression and puts the captured groups in the array BASH_REMATCH. The =~ regex operator is the only regex engine in the shell itself, and it removes the most common reason to shell out to grep or sed inside a loop.

line='2026-09-16 ERROR  disk 91% full'
if [[ $line =~ ^([0-9]{4})-([0-9]{2})-([0-9]{2})[[:space:]]+([A-Z]+) ]]; then
  echo "whole match: ${BASH_REMATCH[0]}"
  echo "year=${BASH_REMATCH[1]} month=${BASH_REMATCH[2]} day=${BASH_REMATCH[3]}"
  echo "level=${BASH_REMATCH[4]}"
  echo "elements in BASH_REMATCH: ${#BASH_REMATCH[@]}"
fi

whole match: 2026-09-16 ERROR
year=2026 month=09 day=16
level=ERROR
elements in BASH_REMATCH: 5

BASH_REMATCH[0] is the whole matched text and [1] onward are the parenthesised groups, left to right by opening parenthesis — the same convention as every other regex API. It is an ordinary indexed array (§6), so ${#BASH_REMATCH[@]} counts it and "${BASH_REMATCH[@]:1}" is all the groups without the whole match, which the exercise at the end of this section uses.
