It is overwritten by the next [[ =~ ]], including one inside a function you call, so copy what you need out of it immediately.

Quoting turns the regex off

# shellcheck disable=SC2016,SC2050,SC2076  # the quoted regex is the behaviour being measured
[[ abc =~ ^a.c$ ]]   && echo 'unquoted  ^a.c$   matched'
[[ abc =~ "^a.c$" ]] || echo 'quoted   "^a.c$"  did not match — it was looked for literally'
[[ 'a.c' =~ "a.c" ]] && echo 'quoted   "a.c"    matched the literal three characters'
re='^([0-9]+)\.([0-9]+)$'
[[ 5.3 =~ $re ]]   && echo "unquoted \$re     matched: ${BASH_REMATCH[1]}.${BASH_REMATCH[2]}"
[[ 5.3 =~ "$re" ]] || echo 'quoted   "$re"    did not match'

unquoted  ^a.c$   matched
quoted   "^a.c$"  did not match — it was looked for literally
quoted   "a.c"    matched the literal three characters
unquoted $re     matched: 5.3
quoted   "$re"    did not match

The regex must be unquoted. A quoted right-hand side is matched literally instead. This changed in bash 3.2 — in 3.0 and 3.1 the quotes were stripped and the regex still applied — and it is why so much old advice on the subject is wrong. The rule today is the same one §7.5 stated for ==: quoting chooses literal or pattern, which for the =~ regex operator means the regex must be unquoted or it is not a regex at all.

The practical consequence is the idiom every bash regex should use. Put the pattern in a variable and reference it unquoted. It keeps the regex out of the shell's way — no worrying about which of ( ) | { } \ the parser might take an interest in — it can be reused, and it can be built up in pieces. ShellCheck's SC2076 flags the quoted form directly.

Escaping inside the variable is ordinary regex escaping: \. is a literal dot, and because the variable is single-quoted at assignment, the backslash reaches the regex engine intact.

It is unanchored, it is greedy, and it is POSIX ERE

# shellcheck disable=SC2050  # constant subjects keep the regex the only variable
[[ hello =~ ell ]] && echo "ell is found inside hello — =~ is not anchored"
[[ aaa =~ a+ ]] && echo "a+ against aaa matched [${BASH_REMATCH[0]}] — greedy"
[[ 'key = value' =~ ^([^=]+)=(.*)$ ]] && printf 'key=[%s] value=[%s]\n' "${BASH_REMATCH[1]}" "${BASH_REMATCH[2]}"
echo "--- POSIX ERE has no \\d and no lazy quantifier ---"
[[ 42 =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] && echo '^[0-9]+$ is how you spell it'
[[ 42 =~ ^\d+$ ]] && echo 'matched' || echo '^\d+$ does not match 42'

ell is found inside hello — =~ is not anchored
a+ against aaa matched [aaa] — greedy
key=[key ] value=[ value]
--- POSIX ERE has no \d and no lazy quantifier ---
^[0-9]+$ is how you spell it
^\d+$ does not match 42

Three differences from == that trip people who switch between them. =~ searches, it does not match the whole string, so [[ $x =~ abc ]] is true for xxabcxx — add ^ and $ when you mean the whole value. It is greedy, and the captured key above includes the trailing space because [^=]+ took as much as it could; the repair is to trim afterwards with ${k%% } (§5.4) or to write the whitespace into the regex.

And it is POSIX ERE, not PCRE. There is no \d, no \w, no \s, no \b, no lazy +?, no lookahead. Use [[:digit:]], [[:alnum:]_] and [[:space:]], which are also locale-correct. When you genuinely need PCRE, grep -P has it on GNU systems and §15 covers the choice.

A broken regex, and what BASH_REMATCH holds after a failure

# shellcheck disable=SC2050  # the broken regex and the constant subject are the demonstration
[[ abc =~ [ ]]
echo "status: $?"
echo "--- a failed match clears BASH_REMATCH ---"
[[ abc =~ (b) ]] && echo "after success: [${BASH_REMATCH[0]}]"
[[ zzz =~ (q) ]]
echo "after failure: [${BASH_REMATCH[0]}]"

example.sh: line 2: [[: invalid regular expression `[': brackets ([ ]) not balanced
status: 2
--- a failed match clears BASH_REMATCH ---
after success: [b]
after failure: []

An uncompilable regex returns 2, distinct from the 1 that means "did not match" — and bash 5.3 prints a diagnostic, which earlier versions did not. That is a real improvement: before 5.3 a typo in a regex was indistinguishable from a non-match, so a validation function could silently reject everything. On bash 5.2 and earlier, test the status against 2 explicitly if the regex is built at runtime.

A failed match clears BASH_REMATCH rather than leaving the previous result in place, so reading it after an untested [[ =~ ]] gives an empty string rather than stale data. Still test the match; an empty capture and a failed match are not the same event.

The rule this section has been building toward

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the literal $(date) is untrusted input, not an expansion
is_int() { [[ $1 =~ ^-?[0-9]+$ ]]; }
for v in 42 -7 '3.5' '1 + 1' 'x[$(date)]' ''; do
  if is_int "$v"; then echo "accept  ${v@Q}"; else echo "reject  ${v@Q}"; fi
done

accept  '42'
accept  '-7'
reject  '3.5'
reject  '1 + 1'
reject  'x[$(date)]'
reject  ''

is_int is six characters of regex and it is the guard that belongs in front of every arithmetic context that touches input from outside the script. §7.4 showed why: an arithmetic operand is an expression, not a number. Here is what that means when the value is hostile:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the literal $(date)-style payload must not expand here
input='x[$(echo INJECTED >&2)]'
echo "compared with -eq, the operand is evaluated as an expression:"
[[ $input -eq 0 ]] && echo "  (and the comparison returned true)"
echo "compared with ==, it is just a string:"
[[ $input == 0 ]] || echo "  no match, and nothing ran"

compared with -eq, the operand is evaluated as an expression:
INJECTED
  (and the comparison returned true)
compared with ==, it is just a string:
  no match, and nothing ran

The echo ran. x[...] is an array subscript, a subscript is an arithmetic expression, an arithmetic expression may contain $( ), and command substitution runs commands. Nothing was eval'd; the whole path is ordinary bash semantics. The same vector works through $(( )), through ${arr[$untrusted]} and through declare -i, and §18.4 treats it in full.

The mitigation is the one word this section keeps returning to: validate. Match the shape first with =~ or ==, then let the value into an arithmetic context. Comparing an untrusted string with == instead of -eq is inert; comparing it with -eq is executing it.

7.14 The Operator Table

Everything in this section, in the spelling the manual uses.

Conditional
True when
-z string
The string has length zero.
-n string
The string has non-zero length. [[ $x ]] is the same test.
$a = $b
$a == $b
Equal. = versus == is a portability question, not a semantic one (§7.3). Inside [[ ]] the right side is a glob pattern unless quoted (§7.5).
$a != $b
Not equal, with the same pattern rule.
$a < $b
$a > $b
Sorts before / after, in the current locale's collation order. < and > in [[ are string operators; escape them as \< \> inside [ ].
$s =~ ere
The =~ regex operator: a POSIX extended regex, matched anywhere in the string, with groups in BASH_REMATCH. bash 3.0+. The regex must be unquoted (§7.13).
$a -eq $b
$a -ne $b
$a -lt $b
$a -le $b
$a -gt $b
$a -ge $b
Arithmetic comparison. Both operands are evaluated as arithmetic expressions, with everything that implies (§7.4).
-e file
It exists. Follows symlinks.
-f file
It exists and is a regular file.
-d file
It exists and is a directory.
-s file
It exists and has size greater than zero.
-r file
Readable by the effective user, now.
-w file
Writable by the effective user. -w file says nothing about the directory, so a write can still fail.
-x file
Executable by the effective user. On a directory it means searchable.
-h file -L file
It is a symbolic link. The only operators that do not follow one. Both spellings are POSIX.
-p file
It is a named pipe (FIFO).
-S file
It is a socket.
-b file -c file
It is a block / character special file.
-u file
Its setuid bit is set. -u file is the one to pair with -x in a hardening sweep.
-g file -k file
Its setgid / sticky bit is set.
-O file -G file
It is owned by the effective UID / GID.
-N file
It has been modified since it was last read.
-t fd
The file descriptor number is open and refers to a terminal.
$a -nt $b
$a -ot $b
Newer / older by modification time. A missing file is infinitely old.
$a -ef $b
Both names refer to the same device and inode.
-v name
The variable is set, empty or not. -v arr[key] tests one element (bash 4.3+).
-o optname
The set -o shell option is enabled.
! expr
Negation.
e1 && e2
e1 || e2
Conjunction and disjunction, inside [[ ]] only. In [ ], chain two commands instead — never -a or -o (§7.7).
( expr )
Grouping inside [[ ]]. No backslashes needed; it is not a subshell.
Arithmetic
Meaning
$(( expr ))
Expands to the value. An expansion, so it goes where a word goes.
(( expr ))
A command. Status 0 when the value is non-zero, 1 when it is zero (§7.8).
let expr ...
The let builtin, the older form. Each argument is a separate expression; status follows the last.
declare -i name
Every later assignment to name is evaluated as arithmetic. Unconvertible input becomes 0.
n, not $n
Variables need no $ in arithmetic, and an unset name is zero (§7.8).
+ - * /
Integer only. / truncates toward zero.
%
The % remainder operator. It takes the sign of the dividend, so -7 % 3 is -1.
**
Exponentiation, right-associative (bash 3.1+). Not POSIX.
++ --
The ++ increment and -- decrement operators, prefix or postfix, on a variable.
& | ^ ~
Bitwise and, or, xor, not, on a signed 64-bit value.
<< >>
The << shift operators, left and right. >> floors rather than truncating.
<= >= < > == !=
Comparisons, yielding 1 or 0.
&& || !
Logical, short-circuiting, yielding 1 or 0.
c ? a : b
The ternary in arithmetic — the shell's only value-producing conditional.
,
Evaluate each in turn; the value is the last.
= += -= *= /=
%= <<= >>= &= ^= |=
The assignment operator in arithmetic, plain and compound. Usable inside $(( )) as a side effect.
precedence
The arithmetic operator precedence table is §7.10's, and it is C's.
base#n
Base 2 to 64. Case-insensitive below base 37 (§7.10).
0x… 0…
A hexadecimal literal is 0x… or 16#…; a leading zero alone is octal. Use 10#$var on anything zero-padded.
(( expr )) status
Arithmetic and exit status: (( )) returns 1 on zero and 0 otherwise (§7.8).

Exercises

1. The argument that disappears. The function below is meant to check whether its first argument is --force. Run it with --force, then with an empty string, and explain the diagnostic. Then fix it twice — once keeping [ ], once with [[ ]] — and say which you would ship and why.

# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # the unquoted $1 is the bug the exercise asks about
check() {
  if [ $1 = "--force" ]; then echo "forcing"; else echo "not forcing"; fi
}
Solution 
# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # the unquoted $1 is the bug the exercise asks about
check() {
  if [ $1 = "--force" ]; then echo "forcing"; else echo "not forcing"; fi
}
check --force
check ""
echo "status: $?"

forcing
example.sh: line 3: [: =: unary operator expected
not forcing
status: 0

The first call works. The second produces a diagnostic and then takes the else branch, and the combination is what makes this dangerous: the function printed a plausible answer and returned 0, so a caller checking the status learns nothing.

$1 is empty, so the unquoted expansion contributes no word at all. [ receives two arguments, = and --force, and applies its two-argument rule, which wants a unary operator in the first position. = is not one. The test fails with status 2, if reads 2 as false, and echo "not forcing" runs — which happens to be the right answer here, and would not be if the test were [ $1 = "--quiet" ] in a function whose else-branch deleted something.

Both repairs:

posix_check() {
  if [ "$1" = "--force" ]; then echo "forcing"; else echo "not forcing"; fi
}
bash_check() {
  if [[ $1 == "--force" ]]; then echo "forcing"; else echo "not forcing"; fi
}
for f in posix_check bash_check; do
  printf '%-13s' "$f:"; "$f" --force
  printf '%-13s' "$f:"; "$f" ""
done

posix_check: forcing
posix_check: not forcing
bash_check:  forcing
bash_check:  not forcing

Quoting "$1" is the direct fix and is the only fix available in a #!/bin/sh script: the quoted empty expansion produces an empty word, [ gets three arguments, and the binary rule applies correctly.

[[ ]] fixes it without the quotes because nothing is word-split inside it — but ship [[ $1 == "--force" ]] with the right-hand side quoted anyway. Not for splitting, which cannot happen, but because --force contains no pattern metacharacters today; quoting it says "this is a literal" and survives someone later changing it to a value that does.

The one to ship is [[ ]] if the shebang says bash, for the reason §7.2 gave: it is correct under inputs that the other form is not, and the portability you trade away was already spent.

2. Seven months of the year. This loop increments a zero-padded month. Predict what it prints, run it, and explain both the message and the lines that are missing. Then repair it.

for month in 07 08 09 10; do
  next=$(( month + 1 ))
  echo "$month -> $next"
done
Solution 
echo "--- as written ---"
for month in 07 08 09 10; do
  next=$(( month + 1 ))
  echo "$month -> $next"
done
echo "the loop is over; the script did not stop"
echo "--- repaired ---"
for month in 07 08 09 10; do
  echo "$month -> $(( 10#$month + 1 ))"
done

--- as written ---
07 -> 8
example.sh: line 3: 08: value too great for base (error token is "08")
the loop is over; the script did not stop
--- repaired ---
07 -> 8
08 -> 9
09 -> 10
10 -> 11

07 worked because 7 is a valid octal digit. 08 is not, so the arithmetic evaluation failed — and the failure did more than skip one iteration. The error abandoned the entire for loop: 09 and 10 never ran, and execution resumed at the line after done. An expansion error in a non-interactive shell aborts the command it occurs in, and the command here is the whole loop.

That is the detail worth taking away. A reader who expects one bad value to produce one bad line will look at the output, see three lines where they expected four, and start debugging the wrong thing. Under set -e the script would have exited outright instead, which is at least unambiguous.

10#$month forces base ten and is the general repair, correct for 007 and 000 as well as 08. Note it is written 10#$month and not 10#month: the 10# prefix is part of the literal, so the variable has to be expanded into it rather than resolved by the evaluator.

A second repair worth knowing is to strip the padding with a pattern — ${month##+(0)} with extglob on — but it turns 00 into the empty string, which then evaluates to zero by the unset-name rule. That is the right answer reached by an accident, and 10# states the intent.

3. A pattern in a variable. Given a list of filenames and a pattern held in a variable, show that quoting the right-hand side of == changes the result, and state the rule for when each form is what you want.

Solution 
# shellcheck disable=SC2053  # the unquoted pattern variable is the subject of the exercise
files=(app.log app.log.1 app.log.gz notes.txt)
pat='*.log'
echo "--- unquoted right-hand side ---"
for f in "${files[@]}"; do [[ $f == $pat ]] && echo "  match: $f"; done
echo "--- quoted right-hand side ---"
for f in "${files[@]}"; do [[ $f == "$pat" ]] && echo "  match: $f"; done
echo "(the quoted run matched nothing, because no file is literally named *.log)"

--- unquoted right-hand side ---
  match: app.log
--- quoted right-hand side ---
(the quoted run matched nothing, because no file is literally named *.log)

Unquoted, $pat expands and the result is then read as a pattern, so *.log matches app.log and nothing else — note that it does not match app.log.1 or app.log.gz, because the pattern is anchored at both ends against the whole value. Quoted, the expansion is a literal string, and the test asks whether any file is named with an actual asterisk.

The rule is about where the pattern came from and what you intend:

Leave it unquoted when the variable is holding a pattern on purpose — a caller-supplied filter, a table of rules, a config value documented as a glob. This is the only way to pass a pattern into a function, since the function receives it as a string.

Quote it when the variable holds data — a filename, a user's input, a value read from a file. An unquoted $user_input on the right of == means a value containing * matches things it should not, which in a permission check is a vulnerability rather than a bug.

Quote the data part and leave the pattern part bare when both appear, as §6.14's [[ $k == "$dc"/* ]] does. That expression tests whether a key starts with the value of $dc followed by a slash and anything — and it is correct precisely because the quotes fall between the two halves.

4. A version comparison that is actually right. Write newer_or_equal have need returning 0 when have is at least need, for three-part versions. It must handle a two-digit component, reject a malformed version with a distinct status, and use no external commands. Test it against 5.3.15 / 4.4.0, 10.0.0 / 9.9.9, 1.2.3 / 1.2.3, 1.2.3 / 1.10.0 and 1.09.0 / 1.9.0.

Solution 
# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # splitting a literal pair on purpose
newer_or_equal() {
  local have=$1 need=$2
  [[ $have =~ ^([0-9]+)\.([0-9]+)\.([0-9]+)$ ]] || { echo "bad version: $have" >&2; return 2; }
  local -a h=("${BASH_REMATCH[@]:1:3}")
  [[ $need =~ ^([0-9]+)\.([0-9]+)\.([0-9]+)$ ]] || { echo "bad version: $need" >&2; return 2; }
  local -a n=("${BASH_REMATCH[@]:1:3}")
  local i
  for i in 0 1 2; do
    (( 10#${h[i]} > 10#${n[i]} )) && return 0
    (( 10#${h[i]} < 10#${n[i]} )) && return 1
  done
  return 0
}
for pair in '5.3.15 4.4.0' '10.0.0 9.9.9' '1.2.3 1.2.3' '1.2.3 1.10.0' '1.09.0 1.9.0'; do
  set -- $pair
  if newer_or_equal "$1" "$2"; then echo "$1 >= $2"; else echo "$1 <  $2"; fi
done
newer_or_equal 5.3 4.4 || echo "(exit $?)"

5.3.15 >= 4.4.0
10.0.0 >= 9.9.9
1.2.3 >= 1.2.3
1.2.3 <  1.10.0
1.09.0 >= 1.9.0
bad version: 5.3
(exit 2)

Every line of the function is doing something this section measured.

The regex both validates and parses, in one operation. ^...$ anchors it, because §7.13 showed =~ searches rather than matching the whole string — without the anchors, 1.2.3-rc1 would pass. The failure branch returns 2, keeping "malformed input" distinct from "older", so a caller can tell the two apart; returning 1 for both would make a typo look like an out-of-date version and trigger an upgrade path.

BASH_REMATCH is copied immediately. local -a h=("${BASH_REMATCH[@]:1:3}") takes the three groups, skipping element 0, using §6.11's slice syntax. It has to happen before the second [[ =~ ]], which overwrites the array — writing both matches first and then reading both copies would silently compare need against itself.

10# on every component. 1.09.0 versus 1.9.0 is the case that requires it: without the prefix, 09 is a malformed octal literal and the comparison aborts. With it, both are 9 and the versions compare equal, which is the right answer.

(( )) rather than [[ -gt ]]. Either works; (( )) reads as arithmetic, which is what the comparison is, and it needs no $ on the array elements.

Early return on the first difference. Comparing major, then minor, then patch and stopping at the first inequality is what makes 10.0.0 >= 9.9.9 come out right where any string comparison fails. Falling off the loop means all three were equal, which satisfies "or equal".

Two extensions worth knowing. Pre-release suffixes (1.2.3-rc1 sorts before 1.2.3) need the regex to capture a fourth optional group and a rule that an absent suffix outranks a present one — semver's rule, and the reason this function rejects rather than guesses. And if a fixed three-part shape is too strict, IFS=. read -ra parts <<< "$v" (§6.12) splits an arbitrary number of components into an array, at the cost of doing the validation separately.

SECTION 8

Control Flow

§7 built the two engines that produce a truth value: the conditional expression and the arithmetic evaluator. This section is the machinery that acts on one. if, while, until, for, case and select are the whole of bash's control flow — there is no switch beyond case, no do … while, no for … else, no labelled break — and every one of them is a compound command whose behaviour is defined by exit status, exactly as §7.1 defined a condition.

That definition has consequences that surprise people arriving from any other language, and most of this section is about them rather than about syntax. A loop has an exit status of its own, and it is not the status of its condition. A for loop's word list goes through the whole expansion pipeline of §4, so an unquoted variable in it is split and globbed. A glob that matches nothing is not an empty list — it is one iteration with the pattern itself as the value. A while read loop at the end of a pipeline runs in a subshell, and every variable it sets is gone when it finishes. A command in the body of a line-reading loop can silently eat the rest of the input. break inside a function does not leave the loop that called the function. Every one of those is measured below under bash 5.3.

linux §4 used for and while at an interactive prompt to repeat a command a few times. This section treats them as the structure of a program: loops that must terminate, handle malformed input, survive a name containing spaces or starting with a dash, and report failure through their status rather than printing and carrying on. Functions, which is what most loop bodies should call, are §9; the options of read itself are §14.6, and this section uses only the two that every line-reading loop needs.

8.1 if, elif and else

The if statement runs a list of commands and branches on the exit status of the last one. That is the whole of its semantics: the condition is not an expression but a list of commands (§2.5), and everything in §7 was about which commands to put in it.

if CONDITION-LIST; then
  COMMANDS
elif CONDITION-LIST; then
  COMMANDS
else
  COMMANDS
fi

then, elif, else and fi are reserved words, recognised only where a command could start (§2.2). That is why the ; before then is required when then shares the line: without it, then is just another argument to the last command in the condition. The Google Shell Style Guide puts ; then and ; do on the same line as the if, for or while, with else and the closing fi or done on lines of their own, aligned with the opening keyword — the layout used throughout this course.

An elif chain

elif [ is the form you will read most often in existing scripts, because a chain of [ ] tests is exactly what #!/bin/sh allows. This function resolves a configuration file by precedence — an environment variable first, then a local override, then the default:

mkdir demo && cd demo
pick_config() {
  if [ -n "$APP_CONFIG" ]; then
    echo "using \$APP_CONFIG: $APP_CONFIG"
  elif [ -f app.local.conf ]; then
    echo "using app.local.conf"
  elif [ -f app.conf ]; then
    echo "using app.conf"
  else
    echo "no configuration found" >&2
    return 1
  fi
}
pick_config;                          echo "  status $?"
touch app.conf;          pick_config; echo "  status $?"
touch app.local.conf;    pick_config; echo "  status $?"
APP_CONFIG=/etc/app.conf pick_config; echo "  status $?"

no configuration found
  status 1
using app.conf
  status 0
using app.local.conf
  status 0
using $APP_CONFIG: /etc/app.conf
  status 0

Three things in it are worth noticing. The branches are tried in order and the first true one wins, so precedence is expressed by position: moving the elif [ -f app.conf ] test above the elif [ -f app.local.conf ] test would silently make the override useless. The first call fails because nothing exists yet, and the else branch both reports on standard error and returns 1 — a function that cannot do its job should say so through its status, not only in prose. And APP_CONFIG=/etc/app.conf pick_config sets the variable for that one call only (§2.3), which is why the fourth line wins without the earlier calls seeing it.

Each elif [ … ] here quotes "$APP_CONFIG". In a bash script [[ -n $APP_CONFIG ]] would need no quotes, for the reasons §7.2 measured; in a chain that must also run under /bin/sh, the quotes are not optional.

The status of an if statement, and what $? means inside it

if false; then echo never; fi
echo "no branch ran:              status $?"
if true; then false; fi
echo "the branch's last command:  status $?"
if grep -q x /nonexistent 2>/dev/null; then :; else echo "inside else, \$? is still the condition's: $?"; fi
if ! grep -q x /nonexistent 2>/dev/null; then echo "inside a negated if, \$? is: $?"; fi

no branch ran:              status 0
the branch's last command:  status 1
inside else, $? is still the condition's: 2
inside a negated if, $? is: 0

POSIX defines the exit status of if precisely: it is the status of the then or else list that ran, or zero if no branch ran. So if false; then echo never; fi succeeds. That matters as the last command of a function, where it becomes the function's return status — a function ending in an if with no else returns 0 when the condition was false, which is almost never an accident you want.

The last two lines are the more practical trap. Inside else, $? still holds the condition's status, so the else branch can report exactly why the test failed — here grep's 2, meaning "could not read the file", as distinct from 1, "no match". Inside a negated if !, it cannot: ! inverted the status to 0 in order to take the branch, and that 0 is all $? has left. If a failure branch needs the real status, write the positive test with the work in else, or capture it first:

grep -q x /nonexistent 2>/dev/null
status=$?
if (( status != 0 )); then
  echo "grep failed with status $status"
fi

A branch cannot be empty

bash -c 'if true; then fi' 2>&1
echo "status: $?"
bash -c 'if true; then :; fi' && echo "a lone : is a valid branch"

bash: -c: line 1: syntax error near unexpected token `fi'
bash: -c: line 1: `if true; then fi'
status: 2
a lone : is a valid branch

The grammar requires at least one command between then and fi, so a branch you have not written yet is a syntax error that ends the script at that point — after every command before it has already run, as §2.7 measured. : — the builtin that does nothing and succeeds, from §7.1 — is the placeholder. A comment is not enough, because comments are removed before parsing.

a && b || c is not an if statement

§7.7 promised this written out. a && b || c looks like "if a then b else c", and behaves like it only while b cannot fail:

# shellcheck disable=SC2015  # the && || chain is the bug being shown
deploy() { echo "  deploying..."; return 1; }
ready=yes
echo "--- [[ ]] && deploy || echo ---"
[[ $ready == yes ]] && deploy || echo "  not ready, skipping"
echo "--- the if statement it was meant to be ---"
if [[ $ready == yes ]]; then
  deploy || echo "  deploy failed with status $?"
else
  echo "  not ready, skipping"
fi

--- [[ ]] && deploy || echo ---
  deploying...
  not ready, skipping
--- the if statement it was meant to be ---
  deploying...
  deploy failed with status 1

The first form printed both "deploying..." and "not ready, skipping", which is a lie: the environment was ready and the deploy was attempted. || runs its right-hand side whenever the whole of [[ … ]] && deploy failed, and deploy failing is enough. The if statement keeps the two questions separate — was the environment ready, and did the deploy work — and can report the deploy's own status. ShellCheck flags the chain as SC2015 for exactly this reason.

The short form is still correct when the middle command cannot fail: [[ -d $dir ]] && echo yes || echo no is fine, because echo to a working terminal does not fail. The rule is simple enough to apply without thinking: if the middle command does real work, write an if statement.

8.2 The while Loop and the until Loop

A while loop runs its condition list, and if the last command succeeded, runs the body and goes round again. An until loop is the same with the test inverted: it runs the body while the condition fails. Neither has a special syntax for the condition; like if, they take a list of commands.

n=3
while (( n > 0 )); do
  echo "n=$n"
  (( n-- ))
done
echo "after the loop: n=$n"

n=3
n=2
n=1
after the loop: n=0

The condition is an arithmetic command (§7.8), so n needs no $, and (( n-- )) does the decrement. The last line shows that the loop variable is an ordinary variable of the enclosing scope: it still holds 0 afterwards, which is the value that made the condition false.

until for retrying

The until loop exists because some conditions read better positively. "Keep trying until it works" is the canonical one, and a retry helper is the most useful until loop you will write:

attempts=0
flaky() { (( ++attempts >= 3 )); }        # fails twice, then succeeds

retry() {
  local max=$1 n=1
  shift
  until "$@"; do
    if (( n >= max )); then
      echo "giving up after $n attempts" >&2
      return 1
    fi
    echo "attempt $n failed; retrying" >&2
    (( n++ ))
  done
  echo "succeeded on attempt $n"
}
retry 5 flaky;  echo "status $?"
attempts=0
retry 2 flaky;  echo "status $?"

attempt 1 failed; retrying
attempt 2 failed; retrying
succeeded on attempt 3
status 0
attempt 1 failed; retrying
giving up after 2 attempts
status 1

until "$@" runs the function's remaining arguments as a command — the "$@" form from §3.5, which keeps every argument intact — so retry 5 flaky retries any command without eval. The body has one decision to make on each failure: give up, or go round again. A retry loop without a maximum is an infinite loop that happens to terminate on the good days; this one returns 1 after max attempts, and the caller learns about it through the status.

The messages go to standard error, because they are diagnostics and the command's real output may be piped somewhere. A production version would also wait between attempts — typically sleep with a delay that doubles each time — which is left out here so the example runs instantly.

The condition is a list, and only its last status counts

printf 'alpha\nbeta\nEND\ngamma\n' > input.txt
while IFS= read -r line; [[ $line != END ]]; do
  echo "got $line"
done < input.txt

got alpha
got beta

while IFS= read -r line; [[ $line != END ]]; do runs two commands per iteration and tests the second. That makes a clean sentinel loop, but it has a sharp edge worth stating plainly: the status of read is discarded. On a file with no END line, read fails at end of input, line is left empty, [[ '' != END ]] is true, and the loop spins forever. Put the test that must stop the loop last, or combine them with &&: while IFS= read -r line && [[ $line != END ]]; do.

A loop has an exit status, and it is not the condition's

while false; do :; done
echo "body never ran:          status $?"
i=0
while (( i < 2 )); do (( i++ )); false; done
echo "body's last command:     status $?"
until true; do :; done
echo "until, body never ran:   status $?"

body never ran:          status 0
body's last command:     status 1
until, body never ran:   status 0

The exit status of a while loop or an until loop is the status of the last command executed in the body, or 0 if the body never ran. The condition's final, loop-ending status is never the loop's status — if it were, every while loop would return non-zero, since a false condition is how it ends. The second line is the surprise: the body's last command was false, so the loop as a whole returns 1. A loop that ends a function becomes the function's return status, and §8.10 measures what set -e makes of that.

8.3 The for Loop over a Word List

The for loop that shell had first takes a list of words and binds a name to each in turn. POSIX calls it for name [ in [word ... ]]; it is the for in list form, and it is the one to reach for whenever you already have the items.

for env in dev staging prod; do
  echo "deploying to $env"
done
echo "after the loop, env is still: $env"

deploying to dev
deploying to staging
deploying to prod
after the loop, env is still: prod

Two properties are visible already. The name is an ordinary variable that is not scoped to the loop — env still holds prod afterwards — so inside a function, declare it local first, as the style guide's own example does, or it leaks into the caller's scope (§9.4). And the list is written out literally, which is the only case in which a for in list loop is trivially safe.

The list goes through the expansion pipeline

Everything after in is expanded exactly like the arguments of a command: brace expansion, parameter expansion, word splitting, pathname expansion, quote removal, in §4's order.

# shellcheck disable=SC2086,SC2066  # both loops are what is being measured
mkdir demo && cd demo
touch a.txt b.txt
list='one two *.txt'
for w in $list;   do echo "unquoted: [$w]"; done
for w in "$list"; do echo "quoted:   [$w]"; done

unquoted: [one]
unquoted: [two]
unquoted: [a.txt]
unquoted: [b.txt]
quoted:   [one two *.txt]

The unquoted $list was split on spaces into three words, and the third, *.txt, was then globbed against the directory into two filenames. The quoted "$list" produced one word and one iteration. Neither is a loop over "the items in a string", because a string has no items; there are only words after expansion. A for in list loop over a variable is a loop over what splitting and globbing make of it. If the items are data, they belong in an array.

for name with no in list

show_args() {
  local arg
  for arg; do echo "  <$arg>"; done
}
show_args 'two words' '' '*'

  <two words>
  <>
  <*>

Omitting in is defined to mean in "$@", so the loop walks the positional parameters with every argument intact — including the empty one and the literal *. It is shorter, and it is exactly equivalent, but the Google Shell Style Guide recommends writing in "$@" out anyway for clarity. Follow that; the implicit form surprises readers more often than it saves typing.

Loop over array elements

§6 established that "${arr[@]}" expands to exactly one word per element. A loop over array elements is simply that expansion in a for list:

# shellcheck disable=SC2048,SC2016  # the unquoted ${files[*]} is the bug; the headings print code
files=('annual report.csv' 'notes.txt' '')
echo '--- "${files[@]}": one iteration per element ---'
for f in "${files[@]}"; do echo "  [$f]"; done
echo '--- ${files[*]} unquoted: split again, empty element gone ---'
for f in ${files[*]}; do echo "  [$f]"; done
echo '--- "${!files[@]}": the indices ---'
for i in "${!files[@]}"; do echo "  $i -> [${files[i]}]"; done

--- "${files[@]}": one iteration per element ---
  [annual report.csv]
  [notes.txt]
  []
--- ${files[*]} unquoted: split again, empty element gone ---
  [annual]
  [report.csv]
  [notes.txt]
--- "${!files[@]}": the indices ---
  0 -> [annual report.csv]
  1 -> [notes.txt]
  2 -> []

The quoted "${files[@]}" gives three iterations, including one for the empty element. The unquoted ${files[*]} gives three different ones: the element containing a space was split in two, and the empty element vanished. When you need the position as well as the value, loop over the indices with "${!files[@]}" — which is also the only correct way to walk a sparse array (§6.6), because the indices need not be 0 … n-1.

8.4 How to Loop over a Glob

A glob in a for list is the right way to loop over files, and a loop over a glob is the most common for loop in real scripts. It is expanded by the shell itself into one word per matching name, so a filename containing spaces, newlines or quote characters arrives in the loop variable exactly as it is on disk. Two details decide whether a loop over a glob is correct: what happens when nothing matches, and what the body does with a name that looks like an option.

A glob that matches nothing

mkdir demo && cd demo
echo "--- no .log files, no guard ---"
for f in *.log; do echo "  processing $f"; done
echo "--- guarded with [[ -e ]] ---"
for f in *.log; do
  [[ -e $f ]] || continue
  echo "  processing $f"
done
echo "--- with nullglob ---"
shopt -s nullglob
for f in *.log; do echo "  processing $f"; done
echo "  (the body never ran)"

--- no .log files, no guard ---
  processing *.log
--- guarded with [[ -e ]] ---
--- with nullglob ---
  (the body never ran)

With no .log files present, the first loop ran once, with f set to the literal string *.log. §4.7 explained why: an unmatched pattern is left in place rather than removed. In a loop that means the body is handed a filename that does not exist, and a processing step that, say, compresses it, fails with a confusing message about a file named *.log.

There are two repairs. [[ -e $f ]] || continue guards each iteration, works in every bash version and under #!/bin/sh as [ -e "$f" ] || continue, and correctly skips the pattern. shopt -s nullglob removes the unmatched pattern instead, so the list is genuinely empty and the body never runs; that is cleaner but it is a global switch, and §4.7 showed that it also turns an unrelated echo *.txt later in the script into an empty line. The guard, which §4.7 introduced, is the local fix; nullglob set and unset around the loop is the structural one.

Never loop over $(ls)

# shellcheck disable=SC2045,SC2016  # iterating over ls is the bug; the headings print code
mkdir demo && cd demo
touch -- 'annual report.txt' b.txt -n
echo '--- for f in $(ls) ---'
for f in $(ls); do echo "  [$f]"; done
echo '--- for f in * ---'
for f in *; do echo "  [$f]"; done
echo '--- echo "$f" versus printf on the file named -n ---'
for f in *; do echo "$f"; done
for f in *; do printf '%s\n' "$f"; done

--- for f in $(ls) ---
  [-n]
  [annual]
  [report.txt]
  [b.txt]
--- for f in * ---
  [-n]
  [annual report.txt]
  [b.txt]
--- echo "$f" versus printf on the file named -n ---
annual report.txt
b.txt
-n
annual report.txt
b.txt

$(ls) produces text, and an unquoted command substitution in a for list is split on whitespace, so annual report.txt became two iterations naming two files that do not exist. The glob gave one iteration per file, because the shell produced the names directly and never turned them into text. ShellCheck reports the ls form as SC2045.

The last part of the probe is the other half of correctness. A file named -n is legal, and * delivered it faithfully — but echo "$f" then read it as echo -n, printed nothing and suppressed its own newline. The quoting was correct and the output was still wrong, because the problem is not splitting but option parsing. printf '%s\n' "$f" is immune, because its first argument is the format. For commands that take a filename, -- ends option parsing (rm -- "$f"), or a glob written as ./* makes every name start with ./, which no command reads as an option.

*/ restricts a glob to directories, and **/*.sh with shopt -s globstar recurses (§4.7). For more than a few thousand files, or for anything that must filter by size, age or type, find … -print0 read with while IFS= read -r -d '' is the scalable form, and §14 builds that loop.

8.5 The case Statement

The case statement compares one word against a sequence of patterns and runs the commands attached to the first that matches. It is bash's only multi-way branch, and it matches patterns, not values — the same glob language as [[ == ]] (§7.5), which makes it far more expressive than a switch on integers. Each clause is a pattern list, a ), some commands, and a ;; terminator.

case WORD in
  PATTERN|PATTERN) COMMANDS ;;
  PATTERN)         COMMANDS ;;
esac

describe() {
  case $1 in
    start|begin)    echo "$1: starting" ;;
    stop)           echo "$1: stopping" ;;
    *.tar.gz|*.tgz) echo "$1: a gzipped tarball" ;;
    [0-9]*)         echo "$1: begins with a digit" ;;
    '')             echo "(empty): nothing to do" ;;
    *)              echo "$1: unknown" ;;
  esac
}
for word in start begin stop 'site backup.tgz' 42abc '' '*' restart; do
  describe "$word"
done

start: starting
begin: starting
stop: stopping
site backup.tgz: a gzipped tarball
42abc: begins with a digit
(empty): nothing to do
*: unknown
restart: unknown

Every line of that output teaches something about case patterns:

  • start|begin) — | separates alternative patterns for one clause. It is not a pipe here.
  • *.tar.gz|*.tgz) matched the word site backup.tgz, which contains a space. The word after case is not split and not globbed; it undergoes tilde, parameter, command and arithmetic expansion, process substitution and quote removal — nothing that splits or globs. case $1 in is safe unquoted, which is one of the very few places that is true.
  • [0-9]*) is a bracket expression (§7.11): a word beginning with a digit.
  • '') matches the empty string, and it must be quoted to do so — an empty pattern cannot be written any other way.
  • *) matched the word *, and the catch-all matched restart. A final *) clause is the default of other languages and belongs in every case statement that handles input, even when all it does is report an error.

The ;; terminator ends a clause, and every clause but the last needs one: after its commands run, the case statement is finished. Formatting follows the style guide — alternatives indented two spaces, a one-line clause with a space after the ) and before the ;;, and a clause whose commands do not fit on one line written as the pattern on its own line, then the commands, then ;; on its own line.

The first matching case pattern wins

# shellcheck disable=SC2221,SC2222,SC2320  # overlapping patterns and case's own $? are the point
for f in report.tar.gz notes.gz; do
  case $f in
    *.gz)     echo "$f: *.gz matched first" ;;
    *.tar.gz) echo "$f: never reached" ;;
  esac
done
name=README
case $name in
  *.md) echo "markdown" ;;
esac
echo "no pattern matched: status $?"

report.tar.gz: *.gz matched first
notes.gz: *.gz matched first
no pattern matched: status 0

*.gz is a strictly more general case pattern than *.tar.gz, so the second clause is unreachable and ShellCheck says so (SC2222). Order clauses from most specific to least, exactly as §8.1 ordered an elif chain. The last lines show the status rule: when no pattern matches, case returns 0, so a case with no catch-all silently does nothing and succeeds.

Quoting inside a case pattern

# shellcheck disable=SC2254  # the unquoted $pat is deliberately a pattern
pat='*.txt'
for f in notes.txt '*.txt'; do
  case $f in
    "$pat") echo "$f: equals the literal string *.txt" ;;
    $pat)   echo "$f: matches the pattern *.txt" ;;
  esac
done

notes.txt: matches the pattern *.txt
*.txt: equals the literal string *.txt

Patterns follow §7.5's rule: a quoted pattern is literal, an unquoted expansion is a pattern. "$pat" matched only the word that literally is *.txt; bare $pat matched notes.txt because * in the expanded value was active. When a pattern comes from a variable, decide which you mean and quote accordingly — ShellCheck's SC2254 assumes you meant the literal.

;& fallthrough and ;;& continue matching

Bash 4.0 added two more terminators. ;& fallthrough runs the next clause's commands without testing its pattern; ;;& continue matching goes on to test the remaining patterns and runs every further clause that matches.

enable_from() {
  echo "level $1:"
  case $1 in
    debug) echo "  debug output on" ;&
    info)  echo "  info output on" ;&
    warn)  echo "  warnings on" ;&
    error) echo "  errors on" ;;
    *)     echo "  unknown level" ;;
  esac
}
enable_from warn
enable_from debug
enable_from verbose

level warn:
  warnings on
  errors on
level debug:
  debug output on
  info output on
  warnings on
  errors on
level verbose:
  unknown level

;& fallthrough suits a cumulative setting: each level enables itself and then falls through to everything above it, so warn enables warnings and errors, and debug enables all four. The ;; on error stops the fall before *), which is why unknown level is printed only for verbose.

tag() {
  local tags=()
  case $1 in
    *.gz|*.bz2|*.xz) tags+=(compressed) ;;&
    *.tar|*.tar.*)   tags+=(archive) ;;&
    .*)              tags+=(hidden) ;;&
    *)               echo "$1: ${tags[*]:-plain}" ;;
  esac
}
for f in data.tar.gz .cache.xz notes.txt backup.tar; do tag "$f"; done

data.tar.gz: compressed archive
.cache.xz: compressed hidden
notes.txt: plain
backup.tar: archive

;;& continue matching turns case into a sequence of independent tests. data.tar.gz matched both the compression pattern and the archive pattern, and the final *) always runs, so it reports whatever the earlier clauses collected. Without ;;& you would need three separate case statements or three [[ == ]] tests.

Use both sparingly. The Google Shell Style Guide says to avoid ;& and ;;& outright, and the reason is visible in the first probe: the order of the clauses has become behaviour, and a later edit that inserts a clause between info and warn silently changes what info enables. POSIX.1-2024 standardised ;& fallthrough but not ;;& continue matching, and neither exists before bash 4.0:

cat > levels.sh <<'EOF'
case warn in
  warn)  echo "warnings on" ;&
  error) echo "errors on" ;;
esac
EOF
/bin/sh levels.sh; echo "/bin/sh (bash 3.2): status $?"
bash levels.sh;    echo "bash 5.3:          status $?"

levels.sh: line 2: syntax error near unexpected token `&'
levels.sh: line 2: `  warn)  echo "warnings on" ;&'
/bin/sh (bash 3.2): status 2
warnings on
errors on
bash 5.3:          status 0

macOS's /bin/sh is bash 3.2 (§1.2), so a script using ;& fails to parse there — the whole file, not just the clause.

extglob in case patterns

With shopt -s extglob, case patterns accept the extended operators of §7.11, which makes a single pattern expressive enough to validate a format:

shopt -s extglob
for v in 1.2.3 v10.0.1 1.2 latest ''; do
  case $v in
    ?(v)+([0-9]).+([0-9]).+([0-9])) echo "[$v] a version" ;;
    latest|stable)                  echo "[$v] a channel" ;;
    *)                              echo "[$v] not recognised" ;;
  esac
done

[1.2.3] a version
[v10.0.1] a version
[1.2] not recognised
[latest] a channel
[] not recognised

?(v)+([0-9]).+([0-9]).+([0-9]) reads "an optional v, then three runs of digits separated by dots", and anchors the whole word the way every glob does. 1.2 has only two components and falls to the catch-all. The same parse-time rule §7.11 measured applies here: shopt -s extglob must run on an earlier line than the case that uses it, and must not be inside the same function.

8.6 The C-Style for Loop

The C-style for loop is ksh-93's arithmetic for, added to bash in 2.04:

for (( INIT; CONDITION; STEP )); do
  COMMANDS
done

All three parts are arithmetic expressions (§7.8): INIT runs once, the body runs while CONDITION evaluates to non-zero, and STEP runs after each iteration. Names need no $, and assignment operators work as in C.

# shellcheck disable=SC2051,SC2016  # {1..$n} is the mistake being shown
for (( i = 0; i < 3; i++ )); do echo "i=$i"; done
n=4
echo '--- {1..$n} does not expand ---'
for i in {1..$n}; do echo "  [$i]"; done
echo "--- the arithmetic loop takes variables ---"
for (( i = 1; i <= n; i++ )); do printf ' %d' "$i"; done; echo
echo "--- and so does seq, at the cost of a process ---"
for i in $(seq "$n"); do printf ' %d' "$i"; done; echo

i=0
i=1
i=2
--- {1..$n} does not expand ---
  [{1..4}]
--- the arithmetic loop takes variables ---
 1 2 3 4
--- and so does seq, at the cost of a process ---
 1 2 3 4

The second part is the reason to know this loop. {1..$n} did not produce a range — it produced the single word {1..4}, for the reason §4.2 measured: brace expansion runs before parameter expansion, so when braces are expanded $n is not yet a number. A range whose bounds are variables needs the C-style for loop, or seq, which works but costs a process and is not in POSIX. {1..10} with literal bounds is fine.

Commas, empty parts, and walking backwards

for (( i = 0, j = 10; i < j; i += 3, j -= 3 )); do
  echo "i=$i j=$j"
done
tries=0
for (( ;; )); do
  (( ++tries > 2 )) && break
  echo "try $tries"
done
echo "--- walking an array backwards ---"
steps=(build test package deploy)
for (( i = ${#steps[@]} - 1; i >= 0; i-- )); do
  echo "  undo ${steps[i]}"
done

i=0 j=10
i=3 j=7
try 1
try 2
--- walking an array backwards ---
  undo deploy
  undo package
  undo test
  undo build

The comma operator (§7.10) lets INIT and STEP update two variables, so i and j close in from both ends. Any of the three parts may be empty — an empty condition counts as true — so for (( ;; )) is an infinite loop that must be left with break. The last loop walks an array backwards by index — the natural shape for undoing steps in the reverse of the order they were done, which is exactly the order §12 tears down what a script built.

Reach for the C-style for loop when you are counting; reach for for … in "${arr[@]}" when you are visiting items. Indexing an array with a counter is slower to read, fails on sparse arrays, and is only worth it when you need the neighbour of the current element or are going backwards.

8.7 break, continue, and break n

The break builtin leaves the innermost enclosing loop and continues after its done. The continue builtin abandons the current iteration and starts the next one — for while and until by re-running the condition, for for by binding the next word. Both are special builtins in POSIX terms, which is meant to make them impossible to replace — but bash enforces that only in POSIX mode, so the break builtin and the continue builtin can be shadowed by a function in an ordinary script:

cat > shadow.sh <<'EOF'
break() { echo "  a function named break ran"; }
for i in 1 2; do echo "  i=$i"; break; done
EOF
echo "--- bash ---"
bash shadow.sh
echo "--- bash --posix ---"
bash --posix shadow.sh; echo "  status $?"

--- bash ---
  i=1
  a function named break ran
  i=2
  a function named break ran
--- bash --posix ---
shadow.sh: line 1: `break': is a special builtin
  status 2

The loop never ended early: break called the function. bash --posix refuses the definition outright, as POSIX requires. Nobody writes this on purpose, but a sourced library that defines a function named break, continue or return changes what that word means in every script that sources it, and nothing reports why.

for f in a.txt skip.me b.txt stop.here c.txt; do
  [[ $f == skip.* ]] && continue
  [[ $f == stop.* ]] && break
  echo "processing $f"
done
echo "after the loop: f=$f"

processing a.txt
processing b.txt
after the loop: f=stop.here

continue skipped skip.me without processing it; break left the loop at stop.here, so c.txt was never reached. The loop variable keeps the value it had when break ran, which is how a search loop reports what it found. Bash has no for … else to tell "broke out" from "ran to the end" — test the variable afterwards, or set a flag before the break.

break n and continue n

Both builtins take a count. break n leaves n levels of enclosing loop; continue n starts the next iteration of the nth enclosing loop. This probe runs the same nested scan four ways, with the builtin in $how:

# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # $row is split into its cells on purpose
scan() {
  local how=$1 row cell
  for row in '1 2 3' '4 X 6' '7 8 9'; do
    for cell in $row; do
      [[ $cell == X ]] && $how
      printf '%s' "$cell"
    done
    printf '|'
  done
  echo
}
for how in 'continue' 'break' 'continue 2' 'break 2'; do
  printf '%-11s %s\n' "$how:" "$(scan "$how")"
done

continue:   123|46|789|
break:      123|4|789|
continue 2: 123|4789|
break 2:    123|4

Read the four lines against the grid 1 2 3 / 4 X 6 / 7 8 9:

  • continue skipped only the cell X; the row finished with 6 and printed its |.
  • break left the inner loop at X: the row was cut short after 4, but its | still printed and row three ran.
  • continue 2 abandoned the rest of row two including its |, and went straight on to row three.
  • break 2 left both loops, so nothing after 4 ran at all.

break 2 is the idiomatic way out of a nested search, and the only one that does not need a flag variable.

What break n does when n is wrong

# shellcheck disable=SC2043,SC2105  # misused break is what is being measured
for i in 1 2; do
  for j in a b; do
    echo "$i$j"
    break 5
  done
done
echo "--- break 5 inside two loops left both ---"
for i in 1; do break 0; done
echo "break 0: status $?"
break
echo "break outside any loop: status $?"

1a
--- break 5 inside two loops left both ---
example.sh: line 9: break: 0: loop count out of range
break 0: status 1
example.sh: line 11: break: only meaningful in a `for', `while', or `until' loop
break outside any loop: status 0

break 5 inside two loops left both, silently: POSIX specifies that a count larger than the number of enclosing loops exits the outermost one. break 0 is an error with status 1, and the loop ran to completion. A break with no enclosing loop at all prints a diagnostic but returns 0, so a script with a misplaced break carries on and nothing checking status notices.

A function cannot break its caller's loop

# shellcheck disable=SC2104,SC2106  # both breaks are the mistakes being measured
stop_here() { break; }
for i in 1 2 3; do
  echo "i=$i"
  [[ $i == 2 ]] && stop_here
done
echo "--- the function's break did not reach the caller's loop ---"
for i in 1 2 3; do
  echo "i=$i"
  [[ $i == 2 ]] && ( break )
done
echo "--- nor did a break in a subshell ---"

i=1
i=2
example.sh: line 2: break: only meaningful in a `for', `while', or `until' loop
i=3
--- the function's break did not reach the caller's loop ---
i=1
i=2
example.sh: line 10: break: only meaningful in a `for', `while', or `until' loop
i=3
--- nor did a break in a subshell ---

Both loops ran all three iterations. A break inside a function called from a loop reports that it is not in a loop, because POSIX defines "enclosing" lexically — a loop encloses a break only if the break is written inside it, not merely executed while it runs. Bash has enforced that since 4.4; before it, the function's break did leave the caller's loop. A break inside a subshell ( … ) cannot reach the parent's loop either — since bash 5.0 it does not even end the subshell early. When a helper function needs to stop its caller's loop, it should return a status and let the loop decide: stop_here || break.

8.8 Reading a File Line by Line

Reading a file line by line is the most common loop in shell scripts and the one most often written slightly wrong. The correct while read loop has four parts, and each exists because leaving it out breaks a specific kind of input:

while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n $line ]]; do
  printf '%s\n' "$line"
done < input.txt
  • IFS= for the read command only, so leading and trailing whitespace is kept (§3.4).
  • -r, so a backslash is data rather than an escape character.
  • || [[ -n $line ]], so a final line with no trailing newline is still processed.
  • done < input.txt, a redirect on the loop rather than a pipe into it.

§14 covers the rest of read — -d, -n and -t in §14.6, -a in §14.2, -p in §14.8. This subsection is about the loop.

What each part protects

printf '  indented\nback\\slash\nno newline at the end' > input.txt
echo "--- while IFS= read -r line ---"
while IFS= read -r line; do echo "[$line]"; done < input.txt
echo "--- ... || [[ -n \$line ]] keeps the last line ---"
while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n $line ]]; do echo "[$line]"; done < input.txt
echo "--- plain read line mangles it ---"
# shellcheck disable=SC2162  # read without -r is the bug being shown
while read line || [[ -n $line ]]; do echo "[$line]"; done < input.txt

--- while IFS= read -r line ---
[  indented]
[back\slash]
--- ... || [[ -n $line ]] keeps the last line ---
[  indented]
[back\slash]
[no newline at the end]
--- plain read line mangles it ---
[indented]
[backslash]
[no newline at the end]

The first loop lost the last line. read returns non-zero when it reaches end of input before a newline, even though it has already stored the partial line in line — so a file whose last line has no terminator, which is common for files written by editors and other programs, has that line silently dropped. || [[ -n $line ]] runs the body one more time when that partial line is non-empty.

The third loop is read line without IFS= and -r: the leading spaces were trimmed and back\slash lost its backslash. ShellCheck reports the missing -r as SC2162, and there is no case where you want it.

A while read loop in a pipeline runs in a subshell

# shellcheck disable=SC2002,SC2030,SC2031,SC2034  # the lost count is what is being shown
printf 'a\nb\nc\n' > input.txt
count=0
cat input.txt | while IFS= read -r line; do (( count++ )); done
echo "after a pipeline:             count=$count"
count=0
while IFS= read -r line; do (( count++ )); done < input.txt
echo "after a redirect:             count=$count"
count=0
while IFS= read -r line; do (( count++ )); done < <(grep -v b input.txt)
echo "after process substitution:   count=$count"

after a pipeline:             count=0
after a redirect:             count=3
after process substitution:   count=2

cat input.txt | while … counted three lines and then threw the count away: every part of a pipeline runs in a subshell (§6.12, §16.6), so count was incremented in a child process that exited at done. The redirect done < input.txt runs the loop in the current shell, and process substitution done < <(command) does the same when the input is a command's output rather than a file — grep -v b removed one line, so the count is 2. The style guide recommends exactly this: process substitution or readarray (§6.12) rather than piping into while. §16.8 covers the third option, shopt -s lastpipe.

Splitting each line into fields

cat > users.txt <<'EOF'
# name:shell:uid
alice:/bin/bash:1001

bob:/bin/zsh:1002:extra:fields
EOF
while IFS=: read -r name shell uid rest; do
  [[ -z $name || $name == '#'* ]] && continue
  echo "$name uses ${shell##*/} (uid $uid)${rest:+, ignoring: $rest}"
done < users.txt

alice uses bash (uid 1001)
bob uses zsh (uid 1002), ignoring: extra:fields

IFS=: splits each line on colons into the named variables, and the last variable receives the rest of the line, unsplit — that is how bob's extra fields ended up in rest rather than being lost. The continue skips blank lines and comments, with '#'* quoted so that the # is not read as starting a comment. A space is not IFS whitespace when IFS=:, so it is not trimmed: a line carol : /bin/sh:1003 gives name the value carol with both spaces. §3.4's rule is that only whitespace characters in IFS are stripped from field edges, so data padded for readability needs an explicit trim (§5.4).

A command in the body can steal the loop's input

printf 'web1\nweb2\nweb3\n' > hosts.txt
check_host() {
  local greeting
  IFS= read -r greeting             # anything in the body that reads standard input
  echo "  checked $1${greeting:+, and swallowed $greeting}"
}
echo "--- the body inherits the loop's standard input ---"
while IFS= read -r host; do check_host "$host"; done < hosts.txt
echo "--- give the body its own standard input ---"
while IFS= read -r host; do check_host "$host" < /dev/null; done < hosts.txt
echo "--- or read the list from descriptor 3 ---"
while IFS= read -r -u 3 host; do check_host "$host"; done 3< hosts.txt < /dev/null

--- the body inherits the loop's standard input ---
  checked web1, and swallowed web2
  checked web3
--- give the body its own standard input ---
  checked web1
  checked web2
  checked web3
--- or read the list from descriptor 3 ---
  checked web1
  checked web2
  checked web3

The first loop checked two hosts out of three. check_host reads a line from standard input, and a loop body inherits the loop's standard input — which is hosts.txt. So the first call consumed web2, and the loop's next read got web3. Any command that reads standard input does this, and several do it by default when you would not expect it: ssh forwards standard input to the remote command, ffmpeg reads it for interactive keys, and a read buried in a function does it as shown here. The symptom is always the same — a loop that processes the first item and silently skips some or all of the rest.

There are two fixes. < /dev/null on the body command gives it an empty input of its own. The structural fix is to put the list on a different descriptor: 3< hosts.txt opens the file on descriptor 3 for the loop, and read -u 3 reads from it, so the body's standard input is left alone. The trailing < /dev/null in the probe is only there so the example does not wait on your terminal; in a real script the body would see the script's own standard input. read -u has existed since bash 2.05b; in #!/bin/sh, write read -r host <&3. §10 covers descriptors in full.

8.9 The select Loop and the PS3 Prompt

The select loop, from ksh, prints a numbered menu, reads a choice, and runs its body with the chosen word — then shows the prompt again, until something in the body runs break. It is the fastest way to give an interactive script a menu.

PS3='Deploy which environment? '
select env in dev staging prod quit; do
  case $env in
    quit) echo "bye"; break ;;
    '')   echo "'$REPLY' is not on the menu" ;;
    *)    echo "deploying to $env (you typed $REPLY)" ;;
  esac
done <<'EOF'
2
9
prod

4
EOF
echo "select finished: status $?"

1) dev
2) staging
3) prod
4) quit
Deploy which environment? deploying to staging (you typed 2)
Deploy which environment? '9' is not on the menu
Deploy which environment? 'prod' is not on the menu
Deploy which environment? 1) dev
2) staging
3) prod
4) quit
Deploy which environment? bye
select finished: status 0

The menu went to standard error and the PS3 prompt text was printed before each read. For each line of input, select sets two variables: REPLY to exactly what was typed, and the loop variable to the menu word if the reply was a valid number, or to the empty string otherwise. That is why the case tests env for '' and reports REPLY — typing prod instead of 3 is not a selection. An empty line re-displays the whole menu, which is the probe's fourth input. 4 selected quit, whose clause ran break, and the status of the select loop was the status of the last command in its body.

When PS3 is unset, select prompts with #?, which tells a user nothing, so set the PS3 prompt before every select loop. The list after in is expanded like a for list, so select f in *.conf offers the matching files, and omitting in offers the positional parameters.

PS3='pick one>'
select choice in alpha beta; do
  echo "chose $choice"
done <<< '1'
status=$?
echo
echo "input ran out, so select returned: status $status"

1) alpha
2) beta
pick one>chose alpha
pick one>

input ran out, so select returned: status 1

At end of input, select stops and returns 1 — the manual's rule, measured here with no break in the body. So a select loop fed from a closed pipe or run from cron exits quietly with a failure status, which is correct but easy to overlook. select is interactive by nature: a script that must also run unattended should take its choice as an argument (§13) and fall back to a menu only when standard input is a terminal, [[ -t 0 ]].

8.10 Infinite Loops, Deadlines, and a Loop's Input and Output

An infinite loop in a script is legitimate — polling for a condition, a worker processing a queue, a supervisor restarting a child — provided that something inside it is guaranteed to end it. while true, while : and for (( ;; )) are the three spellings, and they are equivalent; while true reads most clearly. What matters is the exit: an infinite loop in a script that nobody is watching must end on its own, and a polling loop needs two exits — success, and giving up.

wait_for_file() {
  local path=$1 timeout=$2
  local deadline=$(( SECONDS + timeout ))
  while :; do
    if [[ -e $path ]]; then
      echo "$path appeared"
      return 0
    fi
    if (( SECONDS >= deadline )); then
      echo "timed out waiting for $path" >&2
      return 1
    fi
    sleep 0.2
  done
}
( sleep 1; touch ready.flag ) &
wait_for_file ready.flag 10;  echo "status $?"
wait_for_file never.flag 1;   echo "status $?"

ready.flag appeared
status 0
timed out waiting for never.flag
status 1

SECONDS is a bash variable that counts whole seconds since the shell started, so deadline=$(( SECONDS + timeout )) is a deadline that costs no process to check. The loop exits through return 0 when the file appears — created here by a background subshell after a second — or through return 1 when the deadline passes. The sleep is what keeps the loop from burning a CPU core: an infinite loop without a wait in it polls as fast as the machine can go. Note that SECONDS counts whole seconds, so a one-second deadline can fire anywhere from just after zero to one second of real time; for sub-second precision, compare EPOCHREALTIME (bash 5.0) instead, and bash 5.3's BASH_MONOSECONDS reads the system's monotonic clock, which a wall-clock adjustment cannot move.

Redirecting and piping a whole loop

done can carry a redirect or start a pipeline, and when it does, the redirect applies to the entire loop and the file is opened once:

for n in 3 1 2; do echo "item $n"; done | sort
for n in 1 2 3; do echo "line $n"; done > out.txt
echo "out.txt has $(grep -c '' out.txt) lines"
while IFS= read -r line; do
  echo "${line^^}"
done < out.txt > upper.txt 2> errors.txt
cat upper.txt

item 1
item 2
item 3
out.txt has 3 lines
LINE 1
LINE 2
LINE 3

done | sort sorts all of the loop's output together. done > out.txt writes every iteration's output to the file through one open descriptor — cheaper than >> out.txt inside the body, which reopens the file on every iteration, and correct where that is not: > out.txt inside the body would truncate it every time. The last loop has an input redirect, an output redirect and a standard error redirect all on its done, which is the complete shape of a filter written in shell. ${line^^} upper-cases each line (§5.6).

Loops and set -e

A while condition that becomes false is not a failure under set -e — the shell exempts every command whose status is being tested, and a loop condition always is. What set -e does see is a failing command in the body, and, less obviously, the loop's own status from §8.2:

set -e
print_a() {
  local f
  for f in a b; do
    [[ $f == a ]] && echo "found a"
  done
}
print_a
echo "not reached: the loop's status became the function's, and set -e saw a failed command"

found a

The loop printed found a and finished normally — [[ $f == a ]] && echo failing on b is exempt from set -e, because it is the left side of &&. But that failed test was the body's last command, so the loop returned 1; the loop was the function's last command, so print_a returned 1; and print_a as a simple command returning 1 is exactly what set -e exits on. The script died on a line with nothing wrong with it. End such a function with return 0, or write the test as an if. §11.5 works through this trap and the others set -e sets.

8.11 The Control-Flow Table

Every construct in this section in one place, with the rule that is easiest to get wrong.

Construct
Behaviour and status
if …; then …; elif …; then …; else …; fi
First true branch wins. Status is that of the branch that ran, or 0 if none ran. A branch must contain a command; use :. Inside else, $? is the condition's status (§8.1).
a && b || c
Not an if statement: c also runs when b fails (§8.1).
while list; do …; done
until list; do …; done
The condition is a list; only its last status counts. The loop's status is the body's last command, or 0 if the body never ran (§8.2).
for name in words; do …; done
The words are fully expanded: split and globbed unless quoted. The name is not local to the loop. for name alone means in "$@" (§8.3).
for f in *.ext
An unmatched glob gives one iteration with the pattern itself: guard with [[ -e $f ]] || continue or use nullglob. Never $(ls) (§8.4).
case word in pat|pat) …;; esac
The word is not split or globbed. First matching pattern wins. Quoted pattern text is literal. No match returns 0 (§8.5).
;; · ;& · ;;&
End the case · run the next clause's commands without testing it · test the remaining patterns. The last two are bash 4.0; POSIX.1-2024 has ;& only (§8.5).
for (( init; cond; step ))
Arithmetic throughout. The only built-in loop over a range with variable bounds; {1..$n} does not expand. Empty cond is true (§8.6).
break [n] · continue [n]
Leave, or restart, the nth enclosing loop. n too large means the outermost. Lexical only: no effect from inside a function (4.4+) or subshell (5.0+) (§8.7).
while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n $line ]]; do … done < file
The complete line-reading loop. A pipe into it runs it in a subshell; a body command reading stdin steals lines — use < /dev/null or read -u 3 with 3< file (§8.8).
select name in words; do …; done
Menu on stderr, prompt from PS3, input in REPLY; name is empty for an invalid choice. Ends on break, or at end of input with status 1 (§8.9).
while : · while true · for (( ;; ))
Infinite loops. Give each one a success exit, a deadline and a sleep (§8.10).
done > file · done | cmd
Redirects the whole loop, opening the file once (§8.10).

Exercises

1. The notification that lies. This backup loop is meant to send "done" when a backup succeeds and "FAILED" when it does not. Explain what it does for an empty $src, then rewrite the chain as an if statement that handles all three cases — empty name, success and failure — and reports the failing status.

# shellcheck disable=SC2015  # the chain is the bug the exercise asks about
backup() { echo "  copying $1"; [[ $1 != *busy* ]]; }
notify() { echo "  notified: $1"; }
for src in data.db busy.db ''; do
  echo "--- [$src] ---"
  [[ -n $src ]] && backup "$src" && notify "backup of $src done" || notify "backup of $src FAILED"
done
Solution 
# shellcheck disable=SC2015  # the chain is the bug the exercise asks about
backup() { echo "  copying $1"; [[ $1 != *busy* ]]; }
notify() { echo "  notified: $1"; }
for src in data.db busy.db ''; do
  echo "--- [$src] ---"
  [[ -n $src ]] && backup "$src" && notify "backup of $src done" || notify "backup of $src FAILED"
done

--- [data.db] ---
  copying data.db
  notified: backup of data.db done
--- [busy.db] ---
  copying busy.db
  notified: backup of busy.db FAILED
--- [] ---
  notified: backup of  FAILED

The first two results are right, which is what makes the chain dangerous. The third is not: with an empty $src, [[ -n $src ]] failed, || ran, and the chain reported "backup of FAILED" — with a double space where the name should be — for a backup that was never attempted. a && b && c || d runs d when any of a, b or c fails, and the three reasons are indistinguishable afterwards. It would also report failure if notify itself failed after a successful backup.

The rewrite:

backup() { echo "  copying $1"; [[ $1 != *busy* ]]; }
notify() { echo "  notified: $1"; }
for src in data.db busy.db ''; do
  echo "--- [${src}], rewritten ---"
  if [[ -z $src ]]; then
    notify "nothing to back up"
  elif backup "$src"; then
    notify "backup of $src done"
  else
    notify "backup of $src FAILED (status $?)"
  fi
done

--- [data.db], rewritten ---
  copying data.db
  notified: backup of data.db done
--- [busy.db], rewritten ---
  copying busy.db
  notified: backup of busy.db FAILED (status 1)
--- [], rewritten ---
  notified: nothing to back up

The rewrite has one branch per outcome. The elif backup "$src" form runs the backup as the condition itself, so the else branch can read the backup's own status from $? (§8.1) and put it in the message. The empty case gets its own message rather than being reported as a failure.

2. The next free filename. Write next_free BASE EXT [MAX], which prints BASE.EXT if no file by that name exists, and otherwise the first of BASE.1.EXT, BASE.2.EXT, … up to MAX (default 99) that does not exist. If every name is taken it must print a message on standard error and return 1. Test it in a directory holding backup.tar, backup.1.tar and backup.2.tar.

Solution 
mkdir demo && cd demo
touch backup.tar backup.1.tar backup.2.tar
next_free() {
  local base=$1 ext=$2 max=${3:-99} n candidate
  if [[ ! -e $base.$ext ]]; then
    echo "$base.$ext"
    return 0
  fi
  for (( n = 1; n <= max; n++ )); do
    candidate=$base.$n.$ext
    [[ -e $candidate ]] || { echo "$candidate"; return 0; }
  done
  echo "no free name among $base.1.$ext .. $base.$max.$ext" >&2
  return 1
}
next_free report tar;    echo "  status $?"
next_free backup tar;    echo "  status $?"
next_free backup tar 2;  echo "  status $?"

report.tar
  status 0
backup.3.tar
  status 0
no free name among backup.1.tar .. backup.2.tar
  status 1

The counting loop is a C-style for loop because the bound is a variable — {1..$max} would not expand (§8.6). The return 0 inside the loop is the "found it" exit, and falling out of the loop is the "not found" case, so no flag variable is needed: code after the loop runs only if no iteration returned. That is the idiom that replaces a for … else in shell.

A caveat worth knowing before you use this for real: between next_free deciding a name is free and the caller creating the file, another process can create it. For a lock-free guarantee, create the file atomically with set -o noclobber and > "$candidate" inside the loop and treat failure as "taken" — §17 covers exactly that race.

3. A log summary. A log file has lines of the form TIMESTAMP LEVEL MESSAGE, plus blank lines and comment lines starting with #, and its last line has no trailing newline. Write a loop that counts the lines at each level and prints the first ERROR line's timestamp and message. Build the file with printf so the missing final newline is really there, and make sure the final line is counted.

Solution 
printf '%s\n' \
  '2026-09-17T10:00:01 INFO  service started' \
  '# rotated at midnight' \
  '2026-09-17T10:00:05 WARN  disk at 81%' \
  '' \
  '2026-09-17T10:01:17 ERROR upload failed: timeout' \
  '2026-09-17T10:01:18 INFO  retrying upload' > app.log
printf '2026-09-17T10:01:19 ERROR upload failed: timeout' >> app.log

declare -A count=()
first_error=
while IFS=' ' read -r stamp level message || [[ -n $stamp ]]; do
  case $stamp in
    ''|'#'*) continue ;;
  esac
  count[$level]=$(( ${count[$level]:-0} + 1 ))
  if [[ $level == ERROR && -z $first_error ]]; then
    first_error="$stamp $message"
  fi
done < app.log
for level in INFO WARN ERROR; do
  printf '%-5s %d\n' "$level" "${count[$level]:-0}"
done
echo "first error: ${first_error:-none}"

INFO  2
WARN  1
ERROR 2
first error: 2026-09-17T10:01:17 upload failed: timeout

ERROR 2 is the check that the last line was read: without || [[ -n $stamp ]] the count is 1. The test uses $stamp rather than a whole-line variable because the fields are split by read itself, and stamp is the one that is non-empty on any real line.

Three choices are deliberate. The case with ''|'#'*) skips blank and comment lines in one clause, with # quoted. IFS=' ' splits on spaces — and because a space is IFS whitespace, the two spaces after INFO count as one separator (§3.4), so message does not start with a space. And the count is kept with count[$level]=$(( ${count[$level]:-0} + 1 )) rather than (( count[$level]++ )): the level is text read from a file, and putting file contents inside an arithmetic subscript is the injection pattern §18.4 dissects. The form used here only ever does arithmetic on a number the script itself stored.

4. A service dispatcher. Write svc ACTION [-v|--verbose] [--] NAME..., where ACTION is one of start, stop, restart or status. It should print what it would do for each name (restart is a stop followed by a start), print a line per name with -v, accept -- so a name may begin with a dash, and return 2 with a usage message for an unknown action, an unknown option, or no names. Use case for the action and for option parsing.

Solution 
usage() { echo "usage: svc {start|stop|restart|status} [-v] NAME..." >&2; }
svc() {
  local action=${1-} verbose=0 name
  shift || { usage; return 2; }
  case $action in
    start|stop|restart|status) ;;
    *) usage; return 2 ;;
  esac
  while (( $# > 0 )); do
    case $1 in
      -v|--verbose) verbose=1 ;;
      --)           shift; break ;;
      -*)           echo "svc: unknown option: $1" >&2; return 2 ;;
      *)            break ;;
    esac
    shift
  done
  (( $# > 0 )) || { usage; return 2; }
  for name in "$@"; do
    case $action in
      restart) echo "stop $name"; echo "start $name" ;;
      start)   echo "start $name" ;;
      stop)    echo "stop $name" ;;
      status)  echo "$name: running" ;;
    esac
    (( verbose )) && echo "  ($action done for $name)"
  done
  return 0
}
svc restart -v web worker; echo "status $?"
svc status -- -odd-name;   echo "status $?"
svc reload web;            echo "status $?"
svc start -x web;          echo "status $?"
svc start;                 echo "status $?"

stop web
start web
  (restart done for web)
stop worker
start worker
  (restart done for worker)
status 0
-odd-name: running
status 0
usage: svc {start|stop|restart|status} [-v] NAME...
status 2
svc: unknown option: -x
status 2
usage: svc {start|stop|restart|status} [-v] NAME...
status 2

The shape is the standard hand-written option loop: while (( $# > 0 )) with a case on $1, shift at the bottom, and break for the first argument that is not an option. -- shifts itself away and breaks, so -odd-name is left as a name; -*) catches unknown options only after -- has had its chance, which is why clause order matters. §13.3 replaces this loop with getopts, which handles bundled short options like -vq that this one does not.

restart is written as two commands in one clause rather than with ;& fallthrough into start. That would work, but it would make the order of the case clauses part of the program's behaviour — the reason the style guide says to avoid it (§8.5). (( verbose )) && echo … is safe as the body's last command only because the function ends with an explicit return 0; without it, a non-verbose call would return the (( )) status 1, the trap §8.2 measured for loops.

SECTION 9

Functions and Scope

A shell function is the only unit of abstraction bash has. There are no modules, no classes, no closures and no first-class values; there is a name bound to a compound command, which runs in the current shell when the name is used as a command. Everything a larger script needs — a library, an interface, a testable piece, a stack trace — is built out of that one mechanism, and this section is about how far it can be pushed and where it gives way.

The mechanism looks familiar and is not. A function is called like a command, not like a function: its arguments are words, it has no parameter list, and it replaces the positional parameters for its duration. It returns a status, not a value — return 300 returns 44. Its variables are global unless declared local, and a local variable is visible to every function it calls, because bash scopes names dynamically rather than lexically. Capturing a function's output with $(…) runs it in a subshell, so a counter it increments never moves. A script's library loaded with a relative path works from one directory and not from another. Every one of those is measured below under bash 5.3, and each has a standard answer.

linux §2 defined a function at the prompt as a shorter alias. This section treats functions as the interface of a program: what each one takes, what it prints, what it returns, what it may touch, how a file of them is loaded, and how a script tells a reader where it failed. §6.13 already passed arrays in and out of functions; §12 covers the RETURN and ERR traps that fire around them; §20 tests them with bats, which depends on the main guard of §9.14.

9.1 Grouping: the Compound Command a Function Is Made Of
