§2.6 introduced the two grouping constructs, and a function body is nothing more than one of them with a name attached, so their difference is worth restating in the terms a function needs. Grouping with braces, { list; }, runs the list in the current shell: assignments, cd and exit all take effect in the shell that is running the script. Subshell grouping, ( list ), forks a copy of the shell, runs the list in the copy, and discards the copy with everything it changed.

( echo "in ( ): exiting"; exit 3 )
echo "after ( ): the script is still running, status $?"
{ echo "in { }: exiting"; exit 4; }
echo "after { }: never printed"

in ( ): exiting
after ( ): the script is still running, status 3
in { }: exiting

The difference is measured in the one command that cannot be undone. exit 3 inside parentheses ended only the subshell, so the script carried on and saw status 3 in $?. exit 4 inside braces ended the script, and the last line never ran. That is the whole reason { } is not a subshell and ( ) is a subshell matters for functions: a function body written with braces that calls exit ends the script, which is usually the point of a die function, and one written with parentheses ends only itself.

So the choice of brackets for a body is a choice about state. Grouping with braces shares everything with the caller, because { } is not a subshell; subshell grouping shares nothing that could leak back, because ( ) is a subshell, at the price of a process. The rest of this subsection shows one reason to want each.

A group has one set of redirections

Grouping with braces is also how several commands share one redirection, without a process and without opening the file more than once:

mkdir demo && cd demo
{
  echo "report generated"
  printf '%s\n' alpha beta
} > report.txt
cat report.txt

report generated
alpha
beta

Three commands wrote to report.txt through a single >. Writing >> report.txt after each line instead reopens the file three times and silently depends on the first line truncating it. §10 treats redirections on compound commands in full; here it is enough that a group is one command as far as a redirection is concerned — and so, as §9.2 shows, is a function.

A function whose body is a subshell

Since a function body can be any compound command, it can be ( … ) instead of { … }, and that is occasionally exactly right:

# shellcheck disable=SC2030,SC2031  # the assignment lost with the subshell is the demonstration
mkdir -p demo/build && cd demo
in_build() (
  cd build || exit
  echo "  inside: $(basename "$PWD")"
  status=done
)
in_build
echo "after: $(basename "$PWD"), status=${status-unset}"

  inside: build
after: demo, status=unset

in_build() ( … ) changed directory and set status, and neither survived the call: the caller is still in demo and status is unset. A subshell body is the cheapest way to write a function that must not leak a cd, an IFS change, a set -o option or a trap into its caller, and the one case where subshell grouping is preferable to a careful restore. It costs a fork per call, which matters inside a loop that runs thousands of times (§21), and it cannot return data through a variable for the same reason — only its output and its status come back.

9.2 Defining a Shell Function

A shell function is a name bound to a compound command. The function definition is itself a command: executing it stores the body under the name and does nothing else, and the body runs later, each time the name is used as a command.

The three forms, and the function keyword

greet() { echo "posix form: hello, $1"; }
function greet_ksh { echo "ksh form: hello, $1"; }
function greet_both() { echo "both at once: hello, $1"; }
greet world
greet_ksh world
greet_both world

posix form: hello, world
ksh form: hello, world
both at once: hello, world

All three produce the same function. name() compound-command is the POSIX form, and the only one /bin/sh accepts. function name compound-command is the Korn shell form, which bash also accepts; the function keyword makes the parentheses optional. function name() … combines the two. ShellCheck accepts all three in a bash script and reports the function keyword as SC2112 in a #!/bin/sh script, where neither function form exists. The Google Shell Style Guide requires the parentheses and says the function keyword "is optional, but must be used consistently throughout a project"; this course uses name() {, which is the portable form and the one every shell reader recognises.

In ksh93 the function keyword changes the semantics — a function name defined function gets its own lexical scope for typeset variables and its own traps. In bash it changes nothing, which is worth knowing so that nobody reaches for it expecting ksh's behaviour.

A function exists from the moment its definition runs

# shellcheck disable=SC2218  # calling before the definition is the demonstration
say_hi
say_hi() { echo "hi"; }
say_hi

example.sh: line 2: say_hi: command not found
hi

A function definition is executed like any other command, in order. The first call ran before the definition and failed with 127, exactly as a command that does not exist would; the script then carried on, defined the function and called it successfully. This is why the style guide says to "put all functions together in the file just below constants" and to call them from a main at the bottom (§9.12): a script that interleaves definitions and calls works only in the order it happens to be written.

The body can be any compound command

cat > bodies.sh <<'EOF'
is_number() [[ $1 =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]
count_to() for (( i = 1; i <= $1; i++ )); do printf '%d ' "$i"; done
is_number 42 && echo "42 is a number"
is_number 4x || echo "4x is not"
count_to 3; echo
EOF
bash bodies.sh

42 is a number
4x is not
1 2 3

The grammar says name() compound-command, and braces are merely the most common compound command. is_number() [[ … ]] is a complete function definition whose body is a conditional expression and whose status is the test's; count_to() for (( … )) is a loop. Both are legal bash, and the example writes them to a file and runs it for a reason: ShellCheck cannot parse them. ShellCheck 0.11.0 stops at each with SC1064, "Expected a { to open the function definition", and a parse error means nothing else in the file is checked. Bash accepts any compound command as a body; ShellCheck parses { } and ( ) bodies and, measured here, stops at [[ ]], for, if and case ones. Write function bodies with { } or ( ) only.

What a function name may contain

log::info() { echo "[info] $*"; }
backup-db()  { echo "backing up"; }
log::info "names may contain :: and -"
backup-db
echo "--- the same definitions under bash --posix ---"
"$BASH" --posix -c 'log::info() { :; }; backup-db() { :; }; echo "posix mode accepted both"'
echo "--- and under dash ---"
dash -c 'backup-db() { :; }'
echo "status $?"

[info] names may contain :: and -
backing up
--- the same definitions under bash --posix ---
posix mode accepted both
--- and under dash ---
dash: 1: Syntax error: Bad function name
status 2

In bash's default mode a function name is far looser than a variable name: log::info and backup-db are both accepted, and the :: form is the style guide's own convention for separating a library's functions from everyone else's (§9.12). Posix mode rejected non-identifier function names until bash 5.3, whose NEWS records that "Posix mode no longer requires function names to be valid shell identifiers" — which is why bash --posix accepted both here. dash, the /bin/sh of Debian and Ubuntu, did not: a #!/bin/sh script must stick to letters, digits and underscores.

Two names are unavailable in any mode. A function may not share a name with a reserved word — if() { :; } is a syntax error — and in posix mode, since bash 4.3, it may not share a name with a POSIX special builtin such as break, export or set (§8.7 measured what happens with break in default mode, where the definition is allowed and silently wins).

Redirections attached to the definition

warn() {
  printf 'warning: %s\n' "$*"
} >&2
warn "disk nearly full" 2>/dev/null
echo "the message went to stderr, so it was discarded"
warn "visible this time" 2>&1

the message went to stderr, so it was discarded
warning: visible this time

A redirection written after the closing brace belongs to the function definition, and bash applies it every time the function runs, not once when it is defined. warn therefore always writes to standard error without a >&2 on each printf inside it. The caller's own redirections still apply on top — 2>/dev/null discarded the first warning and 2>&1 showed the second on standard output — because they are applied around the call, outside the function's own.

9.3 Calling a Function, and What the Call Replaces

Calling a function uses exactly the syntax of running a command: the name, then words. There is no parameter list in a function definition, and nothing checks how many arguments a call passes. Inside the body the arguments are the positional parameters — $1, $2, $#, "$@" — for the duration of the call.

show() {
  echo "  \$0=$0  \$#=$#  \$1=[$1]  \$2=[$2]"
  echo "  FUNCNAME=${FUNCNAME[0]}"
  set -- replaced
  echo "  after set --, \$1=[$1]"
}
set -- script-arg-1 script-arg-2
show 'two words' ''
echo "caller's \$1 is untouched: [$1], \$#=$#"

  $0=example.sh  $#=2  $1=[two words]  $2=[]
  FUNCNAME=show
  after set --, $1=[replaced]
caller's $1 is untouched: [script-arg-1], $#=2

Four facts are visible. The function's $1 and $2 are its own arguments, and the empty second argument still counts in $# because it was quoted at the call. $0 is not the function name — it is still the script's name — and the function name is in FUNCNAME[0] instead (§9.10). set -- replaced inside the function changed only the function's positional parameters. And when calling a function returns, the caller's positional parameters are restored exactly: $1 is script-arg-1 again. A function cannot read the script's arguments except by being passed them, which is why a script's top level ends with main "$@" rather than main.

Because nothing declares a function's arguments, the first lines of a function should name them, and the rest of the body should use the names:

copy_with_backup() {
  local src=$1 dest=$2
  (( $# == 2 )) || { echo "usage: copy_with_backup SRC DEST" >&2; return 2; }
  cp -- "$src" "$dest"
}

That is the whole of bash's parameter declaration — a convention, enforced by the author. §13 builds full option parsing on the same positional parameters.

A function is found before a builtin or a program

When the shell looks up a command name that contains no slash, it checks aliases, then reserved words, then functions, then builtins, then the directories in PATH. A function therefore shadows both a builtin and an external program of the same name:

mkdir demo && cd demo
touch notes.txt
mkdir src
# shellcheck disable=SC2119,SC2120  # the wrapper is called with no arguments on purpose
# a function takes precedence over the external ls
ls() { command ls -F "$@"; }
ls
echo "type says: $(type -t ls)"
echo "--- and over a builtin ---"
cd() { echo "  cd was called with: $*"; builtin cd "$@"; }
cd src && echo "  now in $(basename "$PWD")"

notes.txt
src/
type says: function
--- and over a builtin ---
  cd was called with: src
  now in src

ls now appends / to directories, and cd announces itself, for the rest of the script. The two escape hatches inside the wrappers are what make this safe. command ls runs ls while skipping functions, and builtin cd runs the builtin while skipping functions; without them, the wrapper calls itself.

# shellcheck disable=SC2264  # the accidental self-call is the bug being shown
FUNCNEST=20
ls() { ls -F "$@"; }        # meant to call the real ls
ls
echo "status $?"

example.sh: line 3: ls: maximum function nesting level exceeded (20)
status 1

This ls was meant to add a flag to the real ls, and instead called itself until it reached the nesting limit that FUNCNEST=20 set (§9.7). Without FUNCNEST the recursion continues until bash exhausts its stack and crashes. Shadowing a command is legitimate in an interactive startup file and occasionally in a test that stubs out a slow program, but in a script it changes what a familiar name means for every line that follows. Give a wrapper its own name, ls_marked, rather than stealing an existing one.

9.4 local, and Why Bash's Scoping Is Dynamic

Every variable a function assigns is global unless the function declares it otherwise. That default is the source of most function bugs in shell, and §8.3 already met the commonest one: a loop variable is not local.

print_all() {
  for item in "$@"; do echo "  $item"; done
}
item=precious
print_all a b
echo "the caller's item is now: $item"

  a
  b
the caller's item is now: b

print_all has no visible variables, and it still overwrote the caller's item, because for item assigns to the global item. The fix is the local builtin:

print_all() {
  local item
  for item in "$@"; do echo "  $item"; done
}
item=precious
print_all a b
echo "the caller's item is still: $item"

  a
  b
the caller's item is still: precious

The local builtin, local item, creates a new variable named item for the duration of the call. Assignments inside the function change that variable, and when the function returns it is destroyed and the caller's item is visible again, untouched. The rule this course follows, and the style guide states, is declare every variable a function uses with local, including loop variables, including ones that happen not to collide today. The local builtin accepts the same attribute options as declare — local -a, local -A, local -i, local -r, local -n — and several names in one command, local src=$1 dest=$2 i.

Local variables are dynamically scoped

What local does not do is make the variable private to the function's text. In a language with lexical scoping — C, Python, JavaScript — a local variable is visible only in the code written inside the function. In bash, local variables are dynamically scoped: a local is visible to the function that declared it and to every function that function calls, for as long as the call is running.

show_level() { echo "  show_level sees level=$level"; }
outer() {
  local level=outer
  show_level
  inner
}
inner() {
  local level=inner
  show_level
}
level=global
outer
show_level

  show_level sees level=outer
  show_level sees level=inner
  show_level sees level=global

show_level declares nothing and prints level. Which level it sees depends not on where show_level is written but on who called it: called from outer, it sees outer's local; called from inner — itself called from outer — it sees inner's local, which hides outer's; called from the top level, it sees the global. Name lookup walks the call stack from the innermost call outwards and takes the first variable of that name it finds. That is dynamic scoping; every POSIX shell that has local variables at all scopes them this way, and Perl's local works the same way.

It works in the other direction too, and that is the half that bites:

set_status() { status=written-by-callee; }
run_job() {
  local status=initial
  set_status
  echo "  inside run_job: status=$status"
}
status=global
run_job
echo "global status: $status"

  inside run_job: status=written-by-callee
global status: global

set_status assigns to status without declaring it. It does not reach the global: it reaches the nearest status on the call stack, which is run_job's local. The global status is untouched, and run_job's own variable was overwritten by a function it merely called. A function without local modifies whatever variable of that name is visible where it is called from, which depends on its callers, not on its own code. Two helpers that both use i as a counter, one calling the other, are the classic result; exercise 1 measures it.

Dynamic scoping is also why §5.7 found that a nameref resolves against the function's own locals first, and why every nameref in this course has a name no caller would choose (§9.6).

declare and typeset inside a function are local too

setup() {
  declare config=from-declare
  declare -g mode=from-declare-g
  typeset other=from-typeset
}
setup
echo "config=[${config-unset}] mode=[${mode-unset}] other=[${other-unset}]"

config=[unset] mode=[from-declare-g] other=[unset]

Inside a function, declare and its synonym typeset create local variables exactly as local does, so declare -A map in a function makes a local associative array, which is what §6 relied on. The one way to create a global from inside a function is declare -g, which exists precisely for a function that initialises global state.

local outside a function is an error, not a silent global assignment:

# shellcheck disable=SC2168  # local at the top level is the error being shown
local x=1
echo "status $?"

example.sh: line 2: local: can only be used in a function
status 1

The status of local x=$(cmd) is local's

# shellcheck disable=SC2155  # masking the status is what is being measured
fetch() { echo "partial"; return 7; }
one_line() {
  local data=$(fetch)
  echo "  one line:  status $?, data=$data"
}
two_lines() {
  local data
  data=$(fetch)
  echo "  two lines: status $?, data=$data"
}
one_line
two_lines

  one line:  status 0, data=partial
  two lines: status 7, data=partial

local data=$(fetch) ran fetch, which returned 7, and then ran the local builtin, which succeeded — and the status of the whole line is the builtin's 0. The failure is gone. Splitting the declaration from the assignment gives the command substitution's status back to $?, because a plain assignment's status is that of the last command substitution in it. The style guide requires this form whenever the value comes from a command substitution, and ShellCheck reports the one-line form as SC2155. The same masking applies to export, readonly and declare, and §11.5 shows that it also defeats set -e.

local IFS is restored for you

§3.7 gave three safe ways to change IFS and one unsafe one; inside a function a fourth is better than all of them, and §3's exercise 2 promised it here — make it local:

join_colon() {
  local IFS=:
  echo "$*"
}
join_colon usr local bin
printf 'IFS after the call: %q\n' "$IFS"

usr:local:bin
IFS after the call: $' \t\n'

local IFS=: changed the separator that "$*" joins with for the duration of the call, and restored the original space-tab-newline when the function returned, with no saved copy and no chance of forgetting to put it back on an early return. Any special variable works the same way. Shell options do not live in variables, so they need local - or a subshell body (§9.1); §16.7 compares the two.

9.5 The return Builtin: a Status, Not a Value

A function has one channel for a result that is not output: its exit status, an integer from 0 to 255. The return builtin ends the function and sets that status. In most languages a return statement is how a function hands back a value, so the most important sentence about bash's return is the negative one: the return status is not a value. It is a success-or-failure code, with room for a few distinct failures, and a function return value in the sense other languages mean does not exist.

# shellcheck disable=SC2152  # out-of-range and non-numeric returns are what is measured
count_files() { return 300; }
count_files; echo "return 300 -> \$? is $?"
neg() { return -1; }
neg;         echo "return -1  -> \$? is $?"
word() { return abc; }
word;        echo "return abc -> \$? is $?"

return 300 -> $? is 44
return -1  -> $? is 255
example.sh: line 6: return: abc: numeric argument required
return abc -> $? is 2

Nothing complained about return 300. The status was reduced modulo 256 to 44, so a function that "returns a count" returns a wrong number as soon as the count passes 255, silently. return -1 became 255, also modulo 256 — negative arguments have been accepted since bash 4.3. Only a non-numeric argument is an error, reported with status 2. Because the return status is not a value, data of any kind — a count, a string, a path — must come back another way (§9.6), and a function return value in bash is best kept to the small set of codes a caller branches on.

What a function returns without a number

check() {
  grep -q needle /nonexistent 2>/dev/null
  return
}
check; echo "bare return: status $?"
fall_off() { [[ -e /nonexistent ]]; }
fall_off; echo "no return at all: status $?"
ends_in_if() { if [[ -e /nonexistent ]]; then echo found; fi; }
ends_in_if; echo "ends in an if with no else: status $?"

bare return: status 2
no return at all: status 1
ends in an if with no else: status 0

A bare return returns the status of the last command executed, here grep's 2 for an unreadable file, so a function can end early and pass on the failure that caused it. A function that ends without return does the same with its last command, so fall_off returns the test's 1. The third line is §8.1's trap in function form: an if whose condition was false and which has no else has status 0, so a function ending in one reports success when nothing happened. When a function's status matters, end it with an explicit return.

return leaves the function; exit leaves the script

stop_function() { echo "  return leaves the function"; return 1; echo "  not reached"; }
stop_script()   { echo "  exit leaves the script";     exit 1;   echo "  not reached"; }
stop_function; echo "after stop_function, status $?"
stop_script;   echo "after stop_script: never printed"

  return leaves the function
after stop_function, status 1
  exit leaves the script

exit inside a function ends the whole script, not the function — a function runs in the current shell, and exit ends the current shell. That is exactly what a die helper wants and exactly what a library function must never do, since its caller may be an interactive shell that sourced the library (§1.5). The return builtin also works at the top level of a sourced file, where it stops reading the file (§9.13); anywhere else it is an error:

return 0
echo "status $?, and the script carried on"

example.sh: line 1: return: can only `return' from a function or sourced script
status 2, and the script carried on

The script carried on after the error, with status 2 in $?.

Designing with status

Because the status is the only non-output result, a well-designed bash function uses it the way a well-designed command does: 0 for success, and distinct small numbers for distinct failures the caller might want to tell apart — 1 for "no" or "not found", 2 for a usage error, following the convention of grep and test. A function whose job is to answer a question should be the condition, printing nothing:

is_port() {
  [[ $1 =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] && (( $1 >= 1 && $1 <= 65535 ))
}
for p in 22 0 65536 http 8080; do
  if is_port "$p"; then echo "$p: valid port"; else echo "$p: not a port"; fi
done

22: valid port
0: not a port
65536: not a port
http: not a port
8080: valid port

is_port returns the status of its last list, so if is_port "$p" reads as English and composes with &&, ||, while and until like any command. (( $1 >= 1 && $1 <= 65535 )) runs only after the regular expression has confirmed $1 is digits, which matters: §7.13 showed a string like x[$(cmd)] running a command when it reaches an arithmetic context unvalidated, and validating with =~ first is the fix it measured; §18.4 treats the injection in full. A predicate function never echoes true or false for the caller to compare; its status already is the answer.

9.6 Returning Data: Standard Output, and Output Parameters

A function that computes a string, a list or a number has two ways to hand it back: print it, or write it into a variable its caller names. Each has a cost, and the choice is a design decision rather than a style preference.

Returning data via stdout

basename_no_ext() {
  local name=${1##*/}
  printf '%s\n' "${name%.*}"
}
stem=$(basename_no_ext /var/log/app/server.log)
echo "stem=$stem"

stem=server

Returning data via stdout makes a function behave exactly like a command: the caller captures it with $(…), pipes it, or lets it print. It is the most readable convention and the right default for a function whose output is text a human or a pipeline would want. It has three costs, all measured here:

counter=0
next_id() {
  (( counter++ ))
  printf 'id-%d\n' "$counter"
}
a=$(next_id)
b=$(next_id)
echo "a=$a b=$b counter=$counter"
lines() { printf 'one\ntwo\n\n\n'; }
out=$(lines)
printf 'captured %q\n' "$out"

a=id-1 b=id-1 counter=0
captured $'one\ntwo'

next_id incremented counter and printed the new value — and both calls printed id-1, and counter is still 0 afterwards. A command substitution runs its command in a subshell (§4.4, §16), so the increment happened in a copy that was thrown away. Any side effect a function has — setting a variable, cd, reading a line from shared input — is lost when the caller captures its output. The second cost is on the last line: trailing newlines are stripped by every command substitution, so text that must end in a newline cannot be returned this way intact. The third is speed: each $(f) forks a process, which is invisible for one call and dominant inside a loop over thousands of lines (§21).

A function that returns data via stdout must also keep standard output clean: every diagnostic goes to standard error, or the caller captures it as data.

Output parameters

The alternative is an output parameter: the caller passes the name of a variable, and the function assigns to that name. Bash's own builtins already use this convention — read name, mapfile name, and printf -v:

printf -v padded '%05d' 42
echo "padded=$padded"

padded=00042

printf -v padded formatted into the variable padded instead of printing, with no subshell and no newline stripping. A function gets the same ability from a nameref, which §5.7 introduced and §6.13 used to return arrays. A nameref output parameter is local -n bound to the name the caller passed:

# Globals:   none
# Arguments: $1 - name of the variable to receive the stem
#            $2 - a path
# Returns:   0, or 2 if the path has no file name
path_stem() {
  local -n _path_stem_out=$1
  local _path_stem_name=${2##*/}
  [[ -n $_path_stem_name ]] || return 2
  _path_stem_out=${_path_stem_name%.*}
}
path_stem stem /var/log/app/server.log && echo "stem=$stem"
path_stem stem /var/log/app/ || echo "no file name: status $?"

stem=server
no file name: status 2

path_stem stem … assigned through _path_stem_out straight into the caller's stem, and the function's status stayed free to report failure: the second call returned 2 and left stem alone. That combination — data in a named variable, success or failure in the status — is the closest bash comes to a function that returns a value and an error, and it composes with if and && without a subshell.

§5.7 measured the trap that governs how a nameref output parameter is written: dynamic scoping means the nameref resolves the caller's name against the function's own locals first, so a caller who happens to name the output variable the same as one of the function's locals gets nothing. The convention this course uses for every output parameter is therefore mechanical: prefix every local in the function, including the nameref itself, with the function's name — _path_stem_out, _path_stem_name. It is verbose, and it cannot collide with anything a caller writes. The header comment names the output parameter as an argument, so a reader knows $1 is a variable name rather than a value.

The REPLY convention

# REPLY is bash's own convention: read and select put their result there
to_upper() { REPLY=${1^^}; }
to_upper 'make me loud'
echo "$REPLY"

MAKE ME LOUD

The simplest output parameter is a fixed global. read with no name stores into REPLY, and select does too (§8.9), so a small helper that stores its result in REPLY follows bash's own precedent and needs no nameref. It is only safe when the caller copies the value immediately, before calling anything else that might overwrite it. For a helper called in one place, that is fine; for a library function, a nameref output parameter is the robust form.

The choice, then: return data via stdout when the result is text someone might pipe and the function has no side effects to lose; use an output parameter when the function runs in a loop, must set more than one value, must return an array (§6.13), must preserve trailing newlines, or has side effects the caller needs to keep.

9.7 Recursion, and FUNCNEST

Functions may call themselves. Recursion in a function works as in any language, with one prerequisite that is easy to miss: every variable the function uses must be local, because each call's variables must survive the calls it makes.

factorial() {
  local n=$1
  if (( n <= 1 )); then
    echo 1
  else
    echo $(( n * $(factorial $(( n - 1 ))) ))
  fi
}
factorial 10

3628800

This recursion in a function returns its result via stdout, so each level captures the next with $(…) — ten nested subshells for factorial 10. That is acceptable for a demonstration and a poor pattern for real work; a C-style loop (§8.6) computes the same product in one process. Recursion earns its place in shell where the data itself is recursive, and the canonical example is a directory tree:

mkdir -p demo/a/b demo/c && cd demo
touch a/one a/b/two c/three top
walk() {
  local dir=$1 depth=$2 entry
  for entry in "$dir"/*; do
    [[ -e $entry ]] || continue
    printf '%*s%s\n' $(( depth * 2 )) '' "${entry##*/}"
    [[ -d $entry ]] && walk "$entry" $(( depth + 1 ))
  done
  return 0
}
walk . 0

a
  b
    two
  one
c
  three
top

Each call lists one directory, indents by its depth, and recurses into subdirectories. local dir=$1 depth=$2 entry is not decoration, as the same function without it shows:

# the same walk with 'local' removed
walk() {
  dir=$1 depth=$2
  for entry in "$dir"/*; do
    [[ -e $entry ]] || continue
    printf '%*s%s\n' $(( depth * 2 )) '' "${entry##*/}"
    [[ -d $entry ]] && walk "$entry" $(( depth + 1 ))
  done
  return 0
}
mkdir -p demo/a/b demo/c && cd demo
touch a/one a/b/two c/three top
walk . 0

a
  b
    two
    one
    c
      three
      top

Without local, the recursive call for a overwrote the global dir and depth, so when it returned, the outer loop carried on printing one, c, three and top at the wrong depths — and one is shown under b rather than under a. Nothing failed; the output is simply wrong. The for loop's list had already been expanded, which is why the loop still visited every entry. In a function that recurses, a missing local does not crash — it corrupts. (For a real tree walk, find does this in one process and handles names this loop does not; §14 builds the null-delimited find loop. The recursive walk is here because it shows what recursion requires of scope.)

Limiting the depth with FUNCNEST

Bash has no recursion limit by default. A function that recurses without a base case keeps going until the process runs out of stack and is killed by a segmentation fault: down() { down; }; down run that way here exited with status 139 — 128 plus signal 11, SIGSEGV — after printing nothing at all. In a script that means no error message and no cleanup. The FUNCNEST variable, added in bash 4.2, sets a maximum nesting depth:

# shellcheck disable=SC2264  # the unbounded recursion is the point
down() { down; }
FUNCNEST=100
down
echo "status $?, and the script carried on"

example.sh: line 2: down: maximum function nesting level exceeded (100)
status 1, and the script carried on

At depth 100 the call failed with "maximum function nesting level exceeded (100)" and status 1, the whole chain of calls unwound, and the script carried on. Inside bash the limit is held in a C variable named funcnest_max, declared in the execute_cmd.h header the bash package installs; the manual documents only the variable's side of it — a FUNCNEST greater than 0 sets funcnest_max, and any other value means no limit.

echo "FUNCNEST is ${FUNCNEST-unset} by default"
depth() { (( $1 == 0 )) && return; depth $(( $1 - 1 )); }
depth 5000 && echo "5000 levels deep: fine"

FUNCNEST is unset by default
5000 levels deep: fine

FUNCNEST is unset by default, and 5,000 levels ran without trouble here — how deep a script can go before the stack runs out depends on the operating system's stack limit (ulimit -s), not on bash. A script that recurses over untrusted input, such as a directory tree someone else controls, should set FUNCNEST to a generous number near the top, so that runaway recursion becomes an error with a message instead of a crash.

9.8 Inspecting, Wrapping and Removing Functions

A function is stored in the shell as text and can be listed, printed, tested for and removed at runtime. declare -f is the tool for all but the last.

greet() {
  local who=${1:-world}
  echo "hello, $who"
}
helper() { :; }
declare -F
echo "---"
declare -f greet
echo "---"
declare -F greet && echo "greet is defined"
declare -F nosuch || echo "nosuch is not: status $?"

declare -f greet
declare -f helper
---
greet () 
{ 
    local who=${1:-world};
    echo "hello, $who"
}
---
greet
greet is defined
nosuch is not: status 1

declare -F with no name lists every defined function name, one declare -f name line each. declare -f greet prints the definition — not the text you wrote, but bash's own re-serialisation of the parsed body, which is why the layout changed and semicolons appeared. That regenerated text is reusable as input, which is what export -f and the copy below depend on. declare -F greet with a name prints the name and succeeds if the function exists, fails with status 1 if it does not, and is the correct way to test for a function:

if declare -F on_exit_hook > /dev/null; then
  on_exit_hook
fi

type -t answers a broader question — what kind of thing a name resolves to:

# shellcheck disable=SC2033  # no function is passed to another process here
greet() { :; }
for name in greet if cd ls nosuch; do
  printf '%-7s %s\n' "$name" "$(type -t "$name" || echo 'not found')"
done

greet   function
if      keyword
cd      builtin
ls      file
nosuch  not found

It prints function, keyword, builtin, file or alias, and nothing with status 1 for a name that does not resolve. Use declare -F to ask "is there a function called this" and type -t to ask "what will run if I type this".

unset -f, and what bare unset removes

# shellcheck disable=SC2034,SC2329  # 'name' is both a variable and a function on purpose
name() { echo "  the function ran"; }
name=value
unset name
echo "after 'unset name':  variable=[${name-unset}], function: $(type -t name)"
name
unset -f name
echo "after 'unset -f name': $(type -t name || echo gone)"

after 'unset name':  variable=[unset], function: function
  the function ran
after 'unset -f name': gone

A name can be both a variable and a function at once, because they live in separate tables. Bare unset name removes the variable if there is one, and only removes a function of that name if no variable exists — so here the variable went and the function survived and still ran. unset -f name names the function table explicitly, and unset -v name the variable table. In a script, always write which one you mean; ShellCheck cannot tell from the text which a bare unset will hit.

readonly -f protects a function from both redefinition and unset -f:

# shellcheck disable=SC2329  # neither die is called; redefining one is the test
die() { echo "fatal: $*" >&2; exit 1; }
readonly -f die
die() { echo "redefined"; }
echo "redefinition status $?"
unset -f die
echo "unset status $?"

example.sh: line 4: die: readonly function
redefinition status 1
example.sh: line 6: unset: die: cannot unset: readonly function
unset status 1

Both attempts failed with status 1 and a message, and the original die is still defined. That is useful for the handful of functions a library's correctness depends on — a die that someone's later definition silently replaces is a script that no longer stops on errors.

Wrapping a function under a new name

# shellcheck disable=SC2119,SC2120,SC2329  # the copy is called only through eval's definition
greet() { echo "hello from ${FUNCNAME[0]}"; }
# copy a function under a new name, then wrap the original
eval "original_$(declare -f greet)"
greet() { echo "[wrapped]"; original_greet "$@"; }
greet

[wrapped]
hello from original_greet

declare -f greet prints greet () { … }; prefixing the text with original_ turns it into the definition of original_greet, and eval runs that definition. The new greet then wraps the copy. FUNCNAME[0] inside the copy says original_greet, because it is now genuinely a different function. This is the one eval in this section, and it is safe only because the text being evaluated came from declare -f rather than from input; §18.10 is about every other eval. It is how test frameworks and debugging hooks intercept a function without editing its source — the same effect as command and builtin give for commands (§9.3).

9.9 export -f: Functions in Child Processes

A function lives in the shell that defined it. A child process — a script run with bash script.sh, a bash -c string, anything started by find -exec or xargs — starts a new bash that has never seen it. export -f marks a function for export, so child bash processes receive it through the environment:

mkdir demo && cd demo
printf 'Q3 figures\n' > 'annual report.txt'
touch notes.md
describe() { printf '%s: %s bytes\n' "$1" "$(wc -c < "$1" | tr -d ' ')"; }
echo "--- without export -f ---"
find . -name '*.txt' -exec bash -c 'describe "$1"' _ {} \;
echo "--- with export -f ---"
export -f describe
find . -name '*.txt' -exec bash -c 'describe "$1"' _ {} \;

--- without export -f ---
_: line 1: describe: command not found
--- with export -f ---
./annual report.txt: 11 bytes

Without export -f, the bash -c that find started reported describe: command not found (the _ at the start of the message is the $0 the example passed, the conventional placeholder). With it, the child ran the function against the file whose name contains a space, passed safely as "$1". This is the main legitimate use of export -f: making a function usable as the command run by find -exec, xargs or parallel, which cannot call a function directly because a function is not a program.

How an exported function travels

describe() { echo "described"; }
export -f describe
env | grep -A1 '^BASH_FUNC_'

BASH_FUNC_describe%%=() {  echo "described"
}

An exported function is an environment variable named BASH_FUNC_describe%% whose value is the function's text starting with () {. The prefix and the %% suffix — which no ordinary variable name can contain — were adopted after the 2014 Shellshock vulnerability (CVE-2014-6271), in which bash executed commands that followed a function definition in any environment variable whose value began with () {. Since bash 4.4, function names containing / or = cannot be exported at all.

Two consequences follow from that encoding. The function arrives only in bash:

describe() { echo "described"; }
export -f describe
bash -c 'describe'
dash -c 'describe'

described
dash: 1: describe: not found

dash sees an environment variable with an odd name and no function. A #!/bin/sh script, sh -c, system() from another language on Debian, and any other shell will not have the function. And the child receives a copy of the text, not of the state: any global variables the function reads must be exported separately, and arrays cannot be exported at all (§6.15). A function that needs more than its arguments is a poor candidate for export -f; pass it everything as arguments, as describe "$1" does.

9.10 The Call Stack: FUNCNAME, BASH_SOURCE, BASH_LINENO, and caller

Bash keeps a call stack while functions run and exposes it through three arrays, all added in bash 3.0 for the bash debugger and all useful in ordinary scripts for error messages that say where they came from:

  • FUNCNAME — the names of the functions currently executing. ${FUNCNAME[0]} is the current function, ${FUNCNAME[1]} the one that called it, and the last element is main, bash's name for the top level of the script.
  • BASH_SOURCE — the source file each of those functions was defined in, element for element.
  • BASH_LINENO — the line number, in the file one frame further out, from which each function was called.
cat > lib.sh <<'EOF'
where() {
  local i
  for (( i = 0; i < ${#FUNCNAME[@]}; i++ )); do
    printf '  FUNCNAME[%d]=%-10s BASH_SOURCE[%d]=%-10s BASH_LINENO[%d]=%s\n' \
      "$i" "${FUNCNAME[i]}" "$i" "${BASH_SOURCE[i]}" "$i" "${BASH_LINENO[i]}"
  done
}
EOF
cat > app.sh <<'EOF'
source ./lib.sh
load_config() {
  where
}
deploy() {
  load_config
}
deploy
EOF
bash app.sh

  FUNCNAME[0]=where      BASH_SOURCE[0]=./lib.sh   BASH_LINENO[0]=3
  FUNCNAME[1]=load_config BASH_SOURCE[1]=app.sh     BASH_LINENO[1]=6
  FUNCNAME[2]=deploy     BASH_SOURCE[2]=app.sh     BASH_LINENO[2]=8
  FUNCNAME[3]=main       BASH_SOURCE[3]=app.sh     BASH_LINENO[3]=0

Read one row at a time and the offset in BASH_LINENO becomes clear. FUNCNAME[0] is where, and BASH_SOURCE[0] is ./lib.sh, because where was defined in the library. BASH_LINENO[0] is 3 — not a line of lib.sh but of app.sh, the file in BASH_SOURCE[1], where load_config called where. In general, frame i was called from line BASH_LINENO[i] of file BASH_SOURCE[i+1]. The last frame is the pseudo-function main with line 0: the top level of app.sh, which nothing called. Note that a script with its own function called main therefore shows main twice, as the next example does.

FUNCNAME has no elements outside any function, and assigning to it has no effect. BASH_SOURCE[0] at the top level of a file is that file's path as bash opened it — which is what §9.13 uses to find a library and §9.14 uses to tell executing from sourcing.

The caller builtin

The caller builtin reads the same stack one frame at a time, already formatted:

cat > app.sh <<'EOF'
report() {
  echo "  caller 0: $(caller 0)"
  echo "  caller 1: $(caller 1)"
  caller 2 || echo "  caller 2: status $? (no such frame)"
  echo "  caller:   $(caller)"
}
middle() {
  report
}
middle
EOF
bash app.sh

  caller 0: 8 middle app.sh
  caller 1: 10 main app.sh
  caller 2: status 1 (no such frame)
  caller:   8 app.sh

caller 0 prints the line, function and file of the current function's call site: report was called from line 8, inside middle, in app.sh. caller 1 goes one frame further out. When the frame does not exist, caller prints nothing and returns 1, which makes it a natural loop condition. Without an argument it prints only the line and file of the current call. The manual says of the numbered form that it "may be used, for example, to print a stack trace", which is the next example.

A die that prints a stack trace

Those two facts — one frame per call, status 1 past the end — give a complete stack trace in a few lines:

cat > app.sh <<'EOF'
die() {
  local frame=0 line func file
  echo "fatal: $*" >&2
  while read -r line func file < <(caller "$frame"); do
    echo "  at $func ($file:$line)" >&2
    (( frame++ ))
  done
  exit 1
}
parse_port() {
  [[ $1 =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || die "not a port: $1"
  echo "$1"
}
load_config() {
  parse_port "$1"
}
main() {
  load_config 8080
  load_config http
}
main "$@"
EOF
bash app.sh

8080
fatal: not a port: http
  at parse_port (app.sh:11)
  at load_config (app.sh:15)
  at main (app.sh:19)
  at main (app.sh:21)

The first call succeeded and printed 8080. The second failed in parse_port, and die printed the message followed by every frame from the innermost out, in the same shape as a Java or Python traceback: the failure was at line 11 inside parse_port, which was called at line 15 inside load_config, which was called at line 19 inside the script's own main, which was called at line 21 from the top level — bash's main. The loop reads each frame with read -r line func file < <(caller "$frame"), process substitution (§4.6) rather than a pipe so that the loop runs in the current shell (§8.8), and stops at the first frame caller cannot produce. §12.6 connects the same function to the ERR trap so that a trace is printed for failures nobody anticipated.

9.11 Aliases Are Not Functions

An alias is a text substitution applied to the first word of a command before parsing, and it is the interactive shell's tool for abbreviations. People reach for it in scripts because it looks shorter than a function, and it does not work there:

# shellcheck disable=SC2262,SC2263  # the alias failing in a script is the demonstration
alias ll='ls -l'
ll 2>&1
echo "status $?"

example.sh: line 3: ll: command not found
status 127

Aliases are expanded only when the expand_aliases shell option is on, and it is off in a non-interactive shell, so ll was looked up as a command and not found. Turning the option on is not enough either:

# shellcheck disable=SC2262,SC2263  # the alias failing on its own line is the demonstration
shopt -s expand_aliases
alias greet='echo hello'; greet 2>&1
greet

example.sh: line 3: greet: command not found
hello

Alias expansion happens when a line is read, before any command on it runs. alias greet=…; greet is one line, read in full before the alias builtin executed, so greet was not yet an alias. On the next line it was. The same rule means an alias defined inside a function body or an if block is not active anywhere else inside that compound command, which is read as a unit.

And an alias has no arguments:

shopt -s expand_aliases
alias backup='echo cp -v'
backup_fn() { echo cp -v "$1" "$1.bak"; }
backup notes.txt
backup_fn notes.txt

cp -v notes.txt
cp -v notes.txt notes.txt.bak

The alias can only prepend text, so backup notes.txt became echo cp -v notes.txt with no destination. The function could use its argument twice, which is the whole difference. The style guide's rule is unambiguous — "for almost every purpose, shell functions are preferred over aliases" — and in a script the purpose is never an exception: write a function.

9.12 Naming and Organising Functions

Nothing in bash enforces a structure, so every script larger than a screen needs one imposed by convention. The Google Shell Style Guide supplies a complete set, and this course follows it:

  • Function names are lower case, with underscores between words: load_config, not loadConfig or LoadConfig. Environment variables and constants are upper case; functions and local variables never are, so a name's case says which it is.
  • A library's functions carry a package prefix separated by ::: logs::stale, semver::compare. The prefix is the only namespace bash has, and since §9.3 showed a function shadows anything of the same name, it is also the only defence against two libraries both defining log or trim.
  • Put all functions together, just below the constants. "Don't hide executable code between functions." A function exists only from the line its definition runs (§9.2), so a script whose top-level code sits between definitions works or fails depending on its layout.
  • A function called main is required once a script has any other function, and "the last non-comment line in the file should be a call to main": main "$@". That keeps all top-level work in one place, lets every variable main uses be local, and makes the main guard of §9.14 a one-line change.
  • Every function that is not both short and obvious gets a header comment describing its API: a description, then Globals: (the globals it reads or modifies), Arguments:, Outputs: (what goes to stdout or stderr), and Returns: (statuses other than the default).

A complete, short script in that layout:

cat > rotate-logs <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# Compress log files older than the newest KEEP in a directory.

set -o nounset

readonly DEFAULT_KEEP=3

#######################################
# Print a message to stderr, prefixed with the script name.
# Arguments:
#   Message words.
# Outputs:
#   Writes the message to stderr.
#######################################
err() {
  echo "${0##*/}: $*" >&2
}

#######################################
# List the files in a directory that fall outside the newest KEEP.
# Arguments:
#   Directory, number of files to keep.
# Outputs:
#   One file name per line, oldest first.
# Returns:
#   0, or 1 if the directory does not exist.
#######################################
logs::stale() {
  local dir=$1 keep=$2
  local -a files
  [[ -d $dir ]] || { err "no such directory: $dir"; return 1; }
  files=("$dir"/*.log)
  [[ -e ${files[0]} ]] || return 0
  (( ${#files[@]} > keep )) || return 0
  printf '%s\n' "${files[@]:0:${#files[@]}-keep}"
}

main() {
  local dir=${1:?usage: rotate-logs DIR [KEEP]} keep=${2:-$DEFAULT_KEEP}
  local f
  logs::stale "$dir" "$keep" | while IFS= read -r f; do
    echo "would compress: $f"
  done
}

main "$@"
EOF
mkdir logs
touch logs/app-{01..05}.log
bash rotate-logs logs
bash rotate-logs missing

would compress: logs/app-01.log
would compress: logs/app-02.log
rotate-logs: no such directory: missing

Reading it top to bottom gives the shape every script in this course has from here on: shebang and file comment, options, constants, functions each with a header, main, and main "$@" as the last line. The Globals: field is left out where a function uses none. err prefixes messages with the script's name taken from $0, so they identify their source when the script runs inside a larger pipeline. logs::stale returns data via stdout because its output is a list its caller pipes, and returns 1 through its status for a missing directory — which, because main pipes it, the script does not notice. That is a real limitation of piping a function, and §11's pipefail is its cure.

A function's header is also the documentation §13 turns into --help, and the thing a reviewer reads first. Writing it forces the one question bash never asks on your behalf: what does this function touch that it was not passed?

9.13 A Function Library and the source Builtin

A function library is a file of function definitions meant to be loaded into another script rather than run. Loading it is sourcing a library: the current shell reads the file and executes its commands as if they were written at that point — which, for a file of definitions, defines the functions and does nothing else. §1.5 established that sourcing runs in the current process; this subsection is about doing it reliably.

Three things can go wrong when sourcing a library, and each has a measured example below: the file is looked for in the wrong directory, a file of the same name elsewhere is found first, or the file is loaded twice. A fourth is a matter of discipline rather than mechanics — the library doing something at load time that its caller did not ask for — and the subsection ends with the rules that prevent it.

source and the . builtin

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # single-quoted text is for the file and the child shells
echo 'loaded_by=${1:-no arguments}' > settings.sh
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
. ./settings.sh
echo ". ./settings.sh         -> $loaded_by"
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source ./settings.sh staging
echo "source ./settings.sh staging -> $loaded_by"
"$BASH" --posix -c 'source ./settings.sh; echo "bash --posix accepts source too: $loaded_by"'
dash -c '. ./settings.sh; echo "dash accepts .: $loaded_by"'
dash -c 'source ./settings.sh'
echo "dash and source: status $?"

. ./settings.sh         -> no arguments
source ./settings.sh staging -> staging
bash --posix accepts source too: no arguments
dash accepts .: no arguments
dash: 1: source: not found
dash and source: status 127

The . builtin is the POSIX name, and the source builtin is bash's synonym for it with identical behaviour. Both accept extra arguments, which become the positional parameters while the file is read — source ./settings.sh staging gave the file $1=staging, and with no arguments the file sees none. bash --posix accepts source too, but dash does not: source is a bashism, and . is the spelling to use in anything that might run under /bin/sh. In a bash script either is correct; this course writes source because it is searchable and cannot be mistaken for a stray period.

Finding the library: relative paths are relative to the caller

A relative path given to source is resolved against the current directory, not against the script that contains the source line:

mkdir -p tool/lib && cd tool
echo 'log::info() { echo "[info] $*"; }' > lib/log.sh
cat > deploy <<'EOF'
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source lib/log.sh
log::info "deploying"
EOF
bash deploy
cd .. && bash tool/deploy

[info] deploying
tool/deploy: line 2: lib/log.sh: No such file or directory
tool/deploy: line 3: log::info: command not found

source lib/log.sh worked when run from inside tool, and failed from its parent, because the second run looked for ./lib/log.sh relative to where it was started. Then log::info was not defined, the call returned 127, and a script without set -e carried on regardless. A script that works only from its own directory will be broken by the first cron job or CI step that runs it from somewhere else.

The usual repair is to build the path from BASH_SOURCE[0], the path of the file being read, and the usual first attempt has a bug of its own:

mkdir -p tool/lib
echo 'log::info() { echo "[info] $*"; }' > tool/lib/log.sh
cat > tool/deploy <<'EOF'
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source "${BASH_SOURCE[0]%/*}/lib/log.sh"
log::info "deploying $1"
EOF
bash tool/deploy web
cd tool && bash deploy api

[info] deploying web
deploy: line 2: deploy/lib/log.sh: Not a directory
deploy: line 3: log::info: command not found

${BASH_SOURCE[0]%/*} removes the last / and everything after it (§5.4), which gives tool for tool/deploy. But run as bash deploy, the path contains no / at all, %/* removes nothing, and the library path becomes deploy/lib/log.sh. The trimming idiom is correct only when a slash is guaranteed. The robust version resolves the directory once and absolutely:

mkdir -p tool/lib && cd tool
cat > lib/log.sh <<'EOF'
# shellcheck shell=bash
# log.sh - logging helpers. Source this file; do not execute it.

log::info()  { printf '[info] %s\n'  "$*"; }
log::error() { printf '[error] %s\n' "$*" >&2; }
EOF
cat > deploy <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
SCRIPT_DIR=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd) || exit
readonly SCRIPT_DIR
# shellcheck source=lib/log.sh
source "$SCRIPT_DIR/lib/log.sh"
log::info "deploying $1 from $(basename "$SCRIPT_DIR")/"
log::error "this line went to stderr"
EOF
bash deploy api
cd .. && bash tool/deploy web

[info] deploying api from tool/
[error] this line went to stderr
[info] deploying web from tool/
[error] this line went to stderr

dirname returns . for a bare name, and cd … && pwd turns whatever it returned into an absolute path, so SCRIPT_DIR is right from any working directory. It is computed once, made readonly, and every library is sourced from it. Two limits remain, stated rather than hidden. If the script is reached through a symbolic link, BASH_SOURCE[0] is the link's path, so the libraries must sit beside the link; resolving links portably needs readlink -f or realpath, and older macOS has neither. And bash 5.3 added source -p PATH to search a given path for the file, which is cleaner and does not exist in any older bash — a script that uses it has made 5.3 its minimum version.

The # shellcheck source=lib/log.sh directive tells ShellCheck where the file is, since it cannot evaluate $SCRIPT_DIR. With it, ShellCheck checks the library's functions against their uses; without it, it reports SC1091 and skips the file. A source whose target is genuinely unknowable is marked source=/dev/null.

A bare filename searches PATH

mkdir bin
echo 'echo "  found in PATH: bin/helpers.sh"' > bin/helpers.sh
PATH="$PWD/bin:$PATH"
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source helpers.sh
touch helpers.sh
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source helpers.sh && echo "  a PATH match is preferred over ./helpers.sh"
shopt -u sourcepath
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source helpers.sh && echo "  with sourcepath off, ./helpers.sh (empty) was read"

  found in PATH: bin/helpers.sh
  found in PATH: bin/helpers.sh
  a PATH match is preferred over ./helpers.sh
  with sourcepath off, ./helpers.sh (empty) was read

source helpers.sh, with no slash, searched the directories in PATH before the current directory, because the sourcepath option is on by default — so a file in bin won over ./helpers.sh, and the current directory was used only after the option was turned off. A library loaded by a bare name can be replaced by anything earlier in PATH. Always source with a path that contains a slash: ./lib.sh or "$SCRIPT_DIR/lib.sh".

An include guard, and the status of source

Libraries load other libraries, and a file sourced twice re-runs its top level: a readonly assignment then fails with "readonly variable" and resets nothing useful. An include guard makes a second load a no-op:

cat > log.sh <<'EOF'
# shellcheck shell=bash
[[ -n ${_LOG_SH_LOADED-} ]] && return 0
readonly _LOG_SH_LOADED=1
readonly LOG_PREFIX='[app]'
echo "  log.sh loaded"
EOF
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source ./log.sh
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source ./log.sh && echo "  second source returned early, status $?"
echo "LOG_PREFIX=$LOG_PREFIX"

  log.sh loaded
  second source returned early, status 0
LOG_PREFIX=[app]

The first source defined _LOG_SH_LOADED and ran the file. The second found it set and executed return 0 at the top level of the sourced file, which stops reading the file and makes source itself return 0. The guard variable is named after the file with a leading underscore so it collides with nothing a user writes.

printf 'echo "  loading"\nreturn 5\necho "  never"\n' > partial.sh
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source ./partial.sh
echo "source's status is the file's return: $?"
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source ./missing.sh
echo "a missing file: status $?"

  loading
source's status is the file's return: 5
example.sh: line 6: ./missing.sh: No such file or directory
a missing file: status 1

The status of source is the status of the last command the file ran, or the argument of a top-level return — here 5, and the line after the return never ran. A file that cannot be found gives status 1 and a message. So a script can, and should, check that its libraries loaded: source "$SCRIPT_DIR/lib/log.sh" || exit 1. §11 makes that the default by turning on set -e before the first source.

What a library must not contain follows from all of this. It must not call exit, which ends the shell that sourced it (§1's exercise 3). It must not do work at load time beyond defining functions and constants, because the loader cannot choose not to run it. It must not set -e, cd or change IFS globally, because every such change lands in the caller. And it should not have an executable bit or a shebang, unless it is also meant to be run — which is §9.14.

9.14 The Main Guard: a File That Is Both a Library and a Command

A script's functions are only testable if a test can load them without running the script. §1's exercise 3 introduced the main guard that makes that possible — the shell counterpart of Python's if __name__ == "__main__": — and this subsection develops it into the layout of a file that is both a function library and a command.

The main guard compares BASH_SOURCE[0], the file being read, with $0, the name the shell was started with. When the file is executed they are the same path; when it is sourced, $0 is the sourcing script or shell, and they differ:

cat > semver.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# semver.sh - compare two versions. Executable, and sourceable for its functions.

#######################################
# Compare two MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH versions.
# Arguments:
#   Two versions.
# Outputs:
#   -1, 0 or 1 on stdout.
# Returns:
#   0, or 2 if either argument is not a version.
#######################################
semver::compare() {
  local -a a b
  local i
  [[ $1 =~ ^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$ && $2 =~ ^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$ ]] || return 2
  IFS=. read -ra a <<< "$1"
  IFS=. read -ra b <<< "$2"
  for i in 0 1 2; do
    if (( 10#${a[i]} < 10#${b[i]} )); then echo -1; return 0; fi
    if (( 10#${a[i]} > 10#${b[i]} )); then echo 1; return 0; fi
  done
  echo 0
}

main() {
  if (( $# != 2 )); then
    echo "usage: ${0##*/} VERSION VERSION" >&2
    return 2
  fi
  semver::compare "$@" || { echo "${0##*/}: not a version" >&2; return 2; }
}

if [[ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} == "$0" ]]; then
  main "$@"
fi
EOF
echo "--- executed ---"
bash semver.sh 1.10.0 1.9.3
bash semver.sh 1.2; echo "status $?"
echo "--- sourced, as a test would ---"
source ./semver.sh
[[ $(semver::compare 2.0.0 2.0.0) == 0 ]] && echo "equal versions compare 0"
semver::compare 1.x 1.0.0; echo "a bad version: status $?"

--- executed ---
1
usage: semver.sh VERSION VERSION
status 2
--- sourced, as a test would ---
equal versions compare 0
a bad version: status 2

The comparison is §7's exercise 4 repackaged. Executed, semver.sh compares its arguments and prints 1, because 10 is greater than 9 numerically even though "10" < "9" as strings — the 10# prefix also stops a leading zero being read as octal (§7.10). With one argument it prints usage and returns 2. Sourced, it defines semver::compare and main and runs neither, so a test can call semver::compare directly and assert on both its output and its status. That is exactly what §20's bats tests do: source the script, call the functions, check the results, never touch main.

Three details make the layout work. main uses return, not exit, so it behaves correctly if a test does call it after sourcing; the guard's main "$@" is the script's last command, so its status becomes the script's exit status anyway. All work lives in functions, so sourcing has no side effects to guard against. And the functions carry a semver:: prefix, so a test that sources several scripts does not get one script's compare silently replaced by another's (§9.3).

Where the guard is wrong, and a stricter test

The comparison has a gap worth knowing before relying on it:

cat > lib.sh <<'EOF'
if [[ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} == "$0" ]]; then
  echo "  guard says: executed"
else
  echo "  guard says: sourced  (BASH_SOURCE[0]=[${BASH_SOURCE[0]}], \$0=[$0])"
fi
EOF
echo "bash lib.sh:";   bash lib.sh
echo "bash < lib.sh:"; bash < lib.sh

bash lib.sh:
  guard says: executed
bash < lib.sh:
  guard says: sourced  (BASH_SOURCE[0]=[], $0=[bash])

When bash reads a script from standard input — bash < lib.sh, or the curl … | bash installer pattern — there is no source file, BASH_SOURCE[0] is empty, $0 is bash, and the guard concludes the file was sourced. main never runs, and nothing reports an error. A test that does not depend on either variable asks bash directly whether return is legal here, which is true exactly when a file is being sourced (or a function is running):

cat > both.sh <<'EOF'
greet() { echo "  hello"; }
if (return 0 2>/dev/null); then
  echo "  sourced: defining functions only"
else
  echo "  executed: running"
  greet
fi
EOF
echo "bash both.sh:";   bash both.sh
echo "source both.sh:"
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source ./both.sh
echo "bash < both.sh:"; bash < both.sh

bash both.sh:
  executed: running
  hello
source both.sh:
  sourced: defining functions only
bash < both.sh:
  executed: running
  hello

(return 0 2>/dev/null) tries the return builtin in a subshell, so the attempt cannot actually return from anything, and discards the error message it produces at a script's top level. It succeeded only when the file was sourced, and got bash < both.sh right where the BASH_SOURCE comparison did not. Use the BASH_SOURCE form for a file that is only ever run by path, which it documents more clearly, and the return form for a file that might be piped into bash. Either way the guard wraps a single line — main "$@" — and the rest of the file is the same library.

9.15 The Function Table

Every rule in this section in one place.

Construct
Behaviour, and the rule that is easiest to get wrong
{ list; } · ( list )
Current shell · forked subshell. exit, cd and assignments in ( ) do not reach the caller (§9.1).
name() { …; }
The portable function definition. Exists only once the definition has run. The body may be any compound command, including ( … ) (§9.1, §9.2).
function name { …; }
The ksh form. In bash it changes nothing; not accepted by /bin/sh (§9.2).
name() { …; } >&2
A redirection on the definition applies on every call (§9.2).
name arg…
Arguments become $1… $#, "$@" for the call; $0 is unchanged. A function shadows a builtin or program; bypass with command or builtin (§9.3).
local name[=value]
Dynamically scoped: visible to every function called while it exists. Without it every assignment is global. local x=$(cmd) hides cmd's status (§9.4).
declare · declare -g
Local inside a function · global from inside a function (§9.4).
return [n]
A status 0–255, reduced modulo 256: return 300 is 44. Bare return passes on the last command's status (§9.5).
$(func)
Returns data via stdout. Runs in a subshell: side effects are lost, trailing newlines stripped (§9.6).
local -n _func_out=$1
Nameref output parameter. Prefix every local with the function's name to avoid capturing the caller's name (§9.6).
FUNCNEST=n
Maximum nesting depth (bash 4.2); unset means unlimited, which ends in a crash (§9.7).
declare -f · declare -F · type -t
Print definitions · list names or test for a function · what kind of name (§9.8).
unset -f · readonly -f
Remove a function (bare unset prefers the variable) · forbid redefining or removing it (§9.8).
export -f name
Passes the function to child bash processes as BASH_FUNC_name%%; no other shell sees it (§9.9).
FUNCNAME · BASH_SOURCE · BASH_LINENO · caller n
The call stack. Frame i was called from line BASH_LINENO[i] of BASH_SOURCE[i+1]; the outermost frame is main (§9.10).
alias
Not expanded in scripts; takes no arguments. Use a function (§9.11).
source file · . file
Same builtin; . is POSIX. Relative paths resolve against the current directory, bare names search PATH. Status is the file's last command or top-level return (§9.13).
[[ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} == "$0" ]] · (return 0 2>/dev/null)
Main guard: executed or sourced. The first is fooled by a script read from stdin (§9.14).

Exercises

1. The grid with one row. This script is meant to print a 3-by-5 grid and a 3-by-2 grid. Run it, explain exactly why each prints what it does, and fix it.

# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # the leaked loop counter is the bug
print_row() {
  for (( i = 0; i < $1; i++ )); do printf '#'; done
  echo
}
print_grid() {
  for (( i = 0; i < $1; i++ )); do print_row "$2"; done
}
echo "3 rows of 5:"; print_grid 3 5
echo "3 rows of 2:"; print_grid 3 2
Solution 
# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # the leaked loop counter is the bug
print_row() {
  for (( i = 0; i < $1; i++ )); do printf '#'; done
  echo
}
print_grid() {
  for (( i = 0; i < $1; i++ )); do print_row "$2"; done
}
echo "3 rows of 5:"; print_grid 3 5
echo "3 rows of 2:"; print_grid 3 2

3 rows of 5:
#####
3 rows of 2:
##

Neither function declares i, so both loops use the same global variable (§9.4). print_grid sets i=0 and calls print_row 5, whose loop runs i up to 5 and leaves it there. Back in print_grid, i++ makes it 6, 6 < 3 is false, and the outer loop ends after one row. With 2 columns the inner loop leaves i at 2, the increment makes it 3, and the outer loop ends after one row again. With 1 column the inner loop would leave i at 1 every time and the outer loop would never end.

The fix is one local i in each function:

print_row() {
  local i
  for (( i = 0; i < $1; i++ )); do printf '#'; done
  echo
}
print_grid() {
  local i
  for (( i = 0; i < $1; i++ )); do print_row "$2"; done
}
echo "3 rows of 5:"; print_grid 3 5
echo "3 rows of 2:"; print_grid 3 2

3 rows of 5:
#####
#####
#####
3 rows of 2:
##
##
##

The declaration in print_row is the one that repairs this bug: it gives the inner loop its own i, which hides the outer one and disappears on return. The declaration in print_grid is what stops the next bug, where the caller of print_grid has an i of its own. Dynamic scoping means the two are not redundant — each function protects its callers, and neither can protect itself from a callee that forgets.

2. An output parameter that returns two values. Write split_kv KEYVAR VALUEVAR STRING, which splits KEY=VALUE at the first = into the two named variables. It must return 1, and leave both variables alone, for a string with no = or an empty key. A value may contain further = characters and may be empty. Test it against host=db.internal, url=https://x.test/?a=1, empty=, =nokey and junk.

Solution 
# Globals:   none
# Arguments: $1 - name of the variable to receive the key
#            $2 - name of the variable to receive the value
#            $3 - a KEY=VALUE string
# Returns:   0, or 1 if $3 contains no '=' or has an empty key
split_kv() {
  local -n _split_kv_key=$1 _split_kv_value=$2
  local _split_kv_input=$3
  [[ $_split_kv_input == ?*=* ]] || return 1
  _split_kv_key=${_split_kv_input%%=*}
  _split_kv_value=${_split_kv_input#*=}
}
for line in 'host=db.internal' 'url=https://x.test/?a=1' 'empty=' '=nokey' 'junk'; do
  if split_kv k v "$line"; then
    printf '%-26s key=[%s] value=[%s]\n' "$line" "$k" "$v"
  else
    printf '%-26s rejected (status %d)\n' "$line" "$?"
  fi
done

host=db.internal           key=[host] value=[db.internal]
url=https://x.test/?a=1    key=[url] value=[https://x.test/?a=1]
empty=                     key=[empty] value=[]
=nokey                     rejected (status 1)
junk                       rejected (status 1)

Two namerefs make the function return two values without a subshell, and the status is free to report rejection (§9.6). [[ $_split_kv_input == ?*=* ]] checks both conditions at once: ? requires at least one character before an =, so =nokey fails, and a string without = cannot match at all. %%=* removes the longest suffix starting at an =, which leaves everything before the first one; #*= removes the shortest prefix ending at an =, which leaves everything after it, = characters included (§5.4).

Every local carries the _split_kv_ prefix, including the namerefs. Without it, a caller writing split_kv key value "$line" would collide with locals named key and value, and §5.7 measured what happens then: the assignment lands in the function's own variable and the caller's stays empty, with status 0. The header comment says which arguments are variable names, which a reader cannot tell from the call.

3. A die with a status. Write a build.sh with a die that prints the script's name and a message, then a stack trace, then exits with the status in DIE_STATUS or 1 if it is unset. Use it in a require function that checks a command exists and dies with 127, the shell's own "command not found" status, if it does not. Call require from main for one command that exists and one that does not.

Solution 
cat > build.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#######################################
# Print a message and a stack trace to stderr, then exit.
# Arguments:
#   Message words.
#######################################
die() {
  local frame=0 line func file
  printf '%s: %s\n' "${0##*/}" "$*" >&2
  while read -r line func file < <(caller "$frame"); do
    printf '  at %s (%s:%s)\n' "$func" "$file" "$line" >&2
    (( ++frame ))
  done
  exit "${DIE_STATUS:-1}"
}
require() {
  command -v "$1" > /dev/null || DIE_STATUS=127 die "required command not found: $1"
}
main() {
  require printf
  require no-such-compiler
}
main "$@"
EOF
bash build.sh
echo "exit status $?"

build.sh: required command not found: no-such-compiler
  at require (build.sh:17)
  at main (build.sh:21)
  at main (build.sh:23)
exit status 127

The trace reads outwards from the failure: die was called at line 17 in require, which was called at line 21 in the script's main, which was called at line 23 from bash's top-level frame, also named main (§9.10). The loop uses caller's status as its end condition, and reads each frame through process substitution so the loop body runs in the current shell.

DIE_STATUS=127 die … passes the status as an assignment prefix (§2.3). For a function call in bash's default mode that assignment is visible inside the function and restored afterwards, so die reads it without it leaking into later calls. exit is correct in die and nowhere else in this script: die exists to end the program. And the header says what it does, because a reader of require needs to know that die does not return.

4. A library and a command in one layout. Build a small project: lib/strings.sh, a library with an include guard and a strings::trim function that trims leading and trailing whitespace into an output parameter; and trim, a command that sources the library from its own directory and prints each argument trimmed inside brackets. trim must work from any directory, and sourcing trim must define its functions without running it.

Solution 
mkdir -p proj/lib && cd proj
cat > lib/strings.sh <<'EOF'
# shellcheck shell=bash
# strings.sh - string helpers. Source it; it has no side effects.
[[ -n ${_STRINGS_SH_LOADED-} ]] && return 0
_STRINGS_SH_LOADED=1

#######################################
# Trim leading and trailing whitespace into a variable.
# Arguments:
#   Name of the output variable, then the string.
#######################################
strings::trim() {
  local -n _strings_trim_out=$1
  local _strings_trim_s=$2
  _strings_trim_s=${_strings_trim_s#"${_strings_trim_s%%[![:space:]]*}"}
  _strings_trim_s=${_strings_trim_s%"${_strings_trim_s##*[![:space:]]}"}
  _strings_trim_out=$_strings_trim_s
}
EOF
cat > trim <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# trim - print each argument with surrounding whitespace removed.
SCRIPT_DIR=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd) || exit
# shellcheck source=lib/strings.sh
source "$SCRIPT_DIR/lib/strings.sh"

main() {
  local arg trimmed
  for arg in "$@"; do
    strings::trim trimmed "$arg"
    printf '[%s]\n' "$trimmed"
  done
}

if [[ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} == "$0" ]]; then
  main "$@"
fi
EOF
chmod +x trim
cd .. && proj/trim '  padded  ' $'\ttabs and newline\n' 'none'
source proj/trim
strings::trim value '   sourced   '
echo "sourced: [$value]; main is defined but did not run: $(type -t main)"

[padded]
[tabs and newline]
[none]
sourced: [sourced]; main is defined but did not run: function

The command was run from the parent directory as proj/trim, which is the case §9.13 showed breaking a relative source; SCRIPT_DIR makes it work from anywhere. The tab and the newline were trimmed along with spaces because [:space:] includes both.

The trim itself is two parameter expansions (§5.4). ${s%%[![:space:]]*} is the run of leading whitespace — the longest suffix starting at the first non-space character, removed — and ${s#"…"} strips exactly that run from the front, quoted so it is matched literally rather than as a pattern. The second line does the same from the end. No sed, no subshell, and the result goes through a nameref output parameter with prefixed locals.

The last line shows the main guard working: after source proj/trim, strings::trim is callable and main is defined but did not run — nothing was printed when the file was sourced. A bats test for this project would do exactly that and call main only when it means to.

SECTION 10

Redirection and File Descriptors

Every command a script runs starts life holding three open files, and most of what makes a script usable by other programs is deciding what those three are. A redirection is the shell opening, copying, moving or closing one of them before a command runs. The syntax is small — a digit, an arrow, a word — but it is a language of its own, with an order of evaluation, a failure mode, a scope and a handful of operators that look alike and do very different things. 2>&1 >file and >file 2>&1 differ by the order of two tokens and send error messages to different places. > /dev/stdout keeps a script's output on one operating system and throws half of it away on another. A > inside a loop leaves one line in a file that should hold a thousand.

The model that makes all of it predictable is the one the kernel uses: a process has a table of numbered file descriptors, each pointing at an open file, and a redirection is an edit to that table. Once the table is in view, the ordering rule, the difference between duplicating and reopening a file, and the reason a function's diagnostics belong on standard error are all consequences rather than rules to memorise. Every claim below was measured under bash 5.3, and the two that differ between Linux and macOS say so.

linux §4 taught redirection at the prompt: the three streams, >, 2>, pipes, a here document, /dev/null. This section treats it as part of a program's design — descriptors a script opens and owns, redirections on whole loops and functions, the exec builtin changing the shell's own descriptors, and the discipline that keeps data and diagnostics apart so that a script composes with others. §8.8 already used a second descriptor to stop a loop body stealing the loop's input; §14 covers read and printf, which do the reading and writing; §16 covers the pipelines and process substitutions that connect descriptors between processes; §17 uses a descriptor as a lock.

10.1 File Descriptors: the Table a Redirection Edits

A file descriptor is a small non-negative integer that a process uses to refer to an open file. The kernel keeps a table per process; open() returns the lowest free number, read() and write() take the number, and close() frees it. "File" is meant broadly — a descriptor can refer to a regular file, a terminal, a pipe, a socket or a device, and the process reading from it does not need to know which.

Three numbers have fixed meanings by convention, and every program on a Unix system follows it:

Descriptor
Name and purpose
fd 0
Standard input. Where a program reads its input when it is given no file name. < redirects it.
fd 1
Standard output. Where a program writes its results. > redirects it, and | connects it to the next command's standard input.
fd 2
Standard error. Where a program writes diagnostics — errors, warnings, progress. 2> redirects it, and a pipe does not carry it.

When you run a script from a terminal, fd 0, fd 1 and fd 2 all refer to that terminal, which is why input, output and errors all appear in the same window and why the distinction between standard output and standard error is invisible until something redirects one of them. Descriptors 3 to 9 are free for a script to use; §10.7 and §10.8 show how and why.

A redirection edits that table for one command. Here is a function that lists which of the descriptors 0 to 12 are open, called three times:

open_fds() {
  local fd list=
  for fd in {0..12}; do
    [[ -e /dev/fd/$fd ]] && list+=" $fd"
  done
  echo "open:$list"
}
open_fds
open_fds 3> notes.txt 7< /dev/null
open_fds

open: 0 1 2
open: 0 1 2 3 7
open: 0 1 2

The first call saw the three standard descriptors. The second, with 3> notes.txt 7< /dev/null attached, saw 3 and 7 as well, because the shell opened notes.txt for writing on fd 3 and /dev/null for reading on fd 7 before running the function. The third call saw only 0, 1 and 2 again: the redirection lasted exactly as long as the command it was attached to, and the shell restored its own table afterwards.

For an external program the mechanism is simple. The shell forks, edits the child's table, and then executes the program, which inherits whatever the table holds. For a builtin or a function there is no child, so bash saves the descriptors it is about to replace, runs the command in its own process, and puts them back. Both look the same from outside, and §10.8 shows one place where the saving leaks through.

Descriptors are inherited
