A child process starts with a copy of its parent's descriptor table. That is how a redirection reaches a program at all, and it applies to every descriptor, not only the standard three:

exec 3> log.txt
echo "from the shell" >&3
bash -c 'echo "from a child bash" >&3'
sh -c 'echo "from sh" >&3'
exec 3>&-
cat log.txt

from the shell
from a child bash
from sh

Fd 3 was opened once, by the script, and two separate programs wrote to it without being told a file name. Neither bash -c nor sh -c opened anything: they inherited fd 3 already open and wrote to it. That is the mechanism behind every idiom in this section — a script decides what a descriptor refers to, and everything it runs uses the descriptor by number.

A descriptor has a position, and copies share it

The kernel does not store the position within a file in the descriptor; it stores it in the open file description that the descriptor points to, the record created by one call to open(). Every read or write through any descriptor pointing at that record moves the same position. Two separate opens create two records with two positions:

printf '%s\n' one two three four > lines.txt
{ read -r a; read -r b; } < lines.txt
echo "one open, two reads: $a, $b"
read -r a < lines.txt
read -r b < lines.txt
echo "two opens, two reads: $a, $b"

one open, two reads: one, two
two opens, two reads: one, one

With one redirection on a group, the file was opened once, and the second read carried on from where the first stopped. With a redirection on each read, the file was opened twice, and each open started at the beginning. The difference between opening a file and copying a descriptor that already refers to one comes back in §10.6, where it decides whether two writers overwrite each other, and in §10.12, where it is the entire difference between >&1 and > /dev/stdout on Linux.

10.2 >, >> and <: Opening a File on a Descriptor

The three basic operators each open a file on a descriptor. [n]>word opens word for writing on descriptor n, or on fd 1 if no number is given. [n]>>word does the same but appends. [n]<word opens word for reading on n, or on fd 0. The number, when there is one, must touch the operator: 2>file redirects fd 2, while 2 >file passes 2 as an argument and redirects fd 1.

A > redirection truncates before the command runs

A > redirection creates the file if it does not exist and truncates it to zero length if it does, and it does that while setting up the command — before the command has read anything:

# shellcheck disable=SC2094  # reading and writing the same file is the demonstration
printf '%s\n' cherry apple banana > fruit.txt
sort fruit.txt > fruit.txt
[[ -s fruit.txt ]] || echo "fruit.txt is now empty"
nosuchcommand > created.txt
[[ -e created.txt ]] && echo "created.txt exists anyway"

fruit.txt is now empty
example.sh: line 5: nosuchcommand: command not found
created.txt exists anyway

sort fruit.txt > fruit.txt emptied the file. The shell opened fruit.txt for writing and truncated it, then started sort, which opened the same file, found it empty and sorted nothing. No command that reads a file can write its result to the same file through >; write to a temporary file and rename it, which §17 does properly with mktemp. ShellCheck reports this pattern as SC2094, and the directive above the example is there because the damage is the demonstration.

The second half is the same order seen from the other side. nosuchcommand does not exist and the shell reported command not found — and created.txt exists anyway, because the file was created before the shell went looking for the command. A > redirection is performed as part of starting a command, whether or not the command then runs.

>> append

>> append mode opens the file for writing at its end, creating it if needed:

echo "run 1" > history.txt
echo "run 2" >> history.txt
echo "run 3" >> history.txt
cat history.txt
echo "run 4" > history.txt
cat history.txt

run 1
run 2
run 3
run 4

Each >> added a line; the final > truncated the file and left one. The kernel's append mode has a property the shell relies on: every write through an appending descriptor goes to the current end of the file, even if another process has written there in the meantime. Two scripts writing whole lines to the same log with >> do not overwrite each other, which is not true of two scripts that each opened it with > (§10.6 measures the difference). That is why a log file is opened with >> append rather than >, even by a script that is sure it is the only writer.

< input redirection, and what happens when a redirection fails

A < input redirection makes a file the command's standard input. The command never learns the file's name — it sees a descriptor — and the shell, not the command, is the one that opens the file:

# shellcheck disable=SC2320  # $? is the status of the echo whose redirection failed
printf '%s\n' cherry apple > fruit.txt
report() { echo "report ran"; sort; }
report < fruit.txt
report < missing.txt
echo "status $?"
echo "never written" > no/such/dir/out.txt
echo "status $?"

report ran
apple
cherry
example.sh: line 5: missing.txt: No such file or directory
status 1
example.sh: line 7: no/such/dir/out.txt: No such file or directory
status 1

report sorted the lines it received on standard input. Given a file that does not exist, the redirection failed, the error came from bash (it is prefixed with the script's name and line, not with sort:), and report did not run: "report ran" is printed once, not twice. A failed redirection skips the command and sets the status to 1. The output case is identical — echo did not run, because the directory no/such/dir does not exist and the file could not be created.

That is a real difference from passing the file name as an argument. sort missing.txt runs sort, which prints its own message in its own format and exits with its own status (2, for both GNU and BSD sort). sort < missing.txt never starts sort. A script that checks for status 2 after sort misses the redirection failure entirely, and one that sets set -e (§11) stops on it either way.

A redirection may appear anywhere in a simple command

The shell collects redirections from wherever they appear in a simple command and removes them before building the argument list:

> out.txt echo "redirection first"
cat out.txt
echo "in the" > out.txt "middle"
cat out.txt

redirection first
in the middle

> out.txt echo … and echo "in the" > out.txt "middle" are both legal and both mean what echo … > out.txt means. Nobody should write the second form, but the rule behind it is worth knowing: redirections are not arguments, and they are not positional. The convention — redirections at the end, in the order they are meant to be performed — is what makes §10.4's ordering rule readable.

The target is expanded, and must be one word

The word after the operator goes through the ordinary expansions (§4): parameters, command substitution, tilde, arithmetic. It must come out as exactly one word, and an unquoted variable holding a space does not:

# shellcheck disable=SC2086,SC2320  # the unquoted target is the demonstration
file="monthly report.txt"
echo "unquoted" > $file
echo "status $?"
echo "quoted" > "$file"
cat "monthly report.txt"

example.sh: line 3: $file: ambiguous redirect
status 1
quoted

> $file split into two words, and bash refused with ambiguous redirect and status 1 rather than guess which file was meant. The command did not run. Quoting the target fixes it, exactly as §3 says it fixes every other expansion. A glob in a target is expanded too, and is an ambiguous redirect unless it matches exactly one file — one more reason never to leave a redirection target unquoted.

10.3 Standard Output and Standard Error Are Separate on Purpose

Standard output is for a program's result — the data another program might consume. Standard error is for everything a person needs to see and a consuming program must not: errors, warnings, progress, prompts. The two are separate descriptors so that they can be sent to different places, and a well-behaved command writes each kind of message to the right one:

lookup() {
  echo "looking up $1" >&2
  echo "$1=42"
}
lookup answer > result.txt
echo "result.txt holds: $(cat result.txt)"
lookup answer 2> errors.txt
echo "errors.txt holds: $(cat errors.txt)"

looking up answer
result.txt holds: answer=42
answer=42
errors.txt holds: looking up answer

> result.txt captured the result and let the diagnostic through to the terminal; 2> errors.txt captured the diagnostic and let the result through. The function did not need to know where either was going. If it had written "looking up answer" to standard output, the first redirection would have put it inside result.txt, and every program reading that file would have had to know to skip it.

When both go to the same place, the order is the order of the writes

When standard output and standard error both reach the same destination, what you see is the order in which the bytes were written. With bash's own builtins that is exactly the order of the commands, because bash writes a builtin's output before the builtin returns. Programs written in C, Python or most other languages do not behave that way:

echo "--- bash builtins, both streams into one pipe:"
{ echo "out 1"; echo "err" >&2; echo "out 2"; } 2>&1 | cat
echo "--- awk, the same three writes:"
awk 'BEGIN { print "out 1"; print "err" > "/dev/stderr"; print "out 2" }' 2>&1 | cat

--- bash builtins, both streams into one pipe:
out 1
err
out 2
--- awk, the same three writes:
err
out 1
out 2

The same three writes produced two different orders. awk, like most C programs, uses the C library's standard I/O, which buffers standard output when it is not a terminal — collecting it in memory and writing it in large blocks, at exit at the latest — but writes standard error immediately. So "err" reached the pipe first, and both "out" lines arrived together when awk finished. At a terminal the same program would have printed them in order, because standard output to a terminal is line-buffered.

That is why a log file capturing both streams from a program can show an error before the output that led to it. §5.2's example showed a diagnostic ahead of the line that triggered it for the simpler reason: the diagnostic really was written first, while that line was still being expanded. A buffering program adds a second reason, and nothing in the log says which one applies. Nothing in the shell reorders anything: it passes descriptors, and each program decides when to write. §21 covers the buffering itself and stdbuf, which changes it for programs that use C's standard I/O.

A redirection applies to one command, not to a pipeline

Each command in a pipeline has its own redirections. A 2>/dev/null at the end of a pipeline silences the last command only:

talk() { echo "to stdout"; echo "to stderr" >&2; }
{ talk | sed 's/^/piped: /' 2>/dev/null; } 2> stray.txt
echo "reached stderr anyway: $(cat stray.txt)"
{ talk 2>/dev/null | sed 's/^/piped: /'; } 2> stray.txt
echo "reached stderr this time: [$(cat stray.txt)]"

piped: to stdout
reached stderr anyway: to stderr
piped: to stdout
reached stderr this time: []

In the first pipeline, 2>/dev/null belonged to sed, and talk's error message escaped to the group's standard error, captured here in stray.txt so it can be shown. Moved onto talk, the same redirection silenced it. To silence a whole pipeline, group it and redirect the group — { a | b; } 2>/dev/null — which §10.11 treats in general.

10.4 Merging Streams: 2>&1 and the Ordering of Redirections

2>&1 makes fd 2 a copy of fd 1: "standard error goes wherever standard output is going right now". It does not link the two descriptors permanently. It copies what fd 1 refers to at the moment the redirection is performed, and redirections are performed from left to right. The ordering of 2>&1 relative to a > is therefore not a style question, and it is the most common redirection bug there is. The ordering of 2>&1 is also the first thing to check when a log file is mysteriously missing its error messages:

# shellcheck disable=SC2069  # the wrong order is half of the demonstration
talk() { echo "to stdout"; echo "to stderr" >&2; }
talk > a.txt 2>&1
talk 2>&1 > b.txt
echo "--- a.txt"; cat a.txt
echo "--- b.txt"; cat b.txt

to stderr
--- a.txt
to stdout
to stderr
--- b.txt
to stdout

> a.txt 2>&1 captured both lines. 2>&1 > b.txt captured only standard output, and "to stderr" appeared on the terminal. The table makes it obvious. In each column, the redirections are applied one at a time to a table that starts with both descriptors on the terminal:

talk >a.txt 2>&1
fd 1
fd 2
start
terminal
terminal
>a.txt
a.txt
terminal
2>&1
a.txt
a.txt
talk 2>&1 >b.txt
fd 1
fd 2
start
terminal
terminal
2>&1
terminal
terminal
>b.txt
b.txt
terminal

On the right, 2>&1 copied fd 1 while fd 1 was still the terminal, which changed nothing, and the later > b.txt moved fd 1 alone. So >file 2>&1 versus 2>&1 >file comes down to one question: was fd 1 already pointing at the file when fd 2 copied it? Read a redirection list left to right, one table edit at a time, and the answer is never in doubt. The form to write is >file 2>&1 — redirect, then copy. Every later case of >file 2>&1 versus 2>&1 >file in this section is the same two edits in one order or the other.

&> redirection and &>>

Bash has a shorthand for the common case. An &> redirection sends both standard output and standard error to one file, and &>> appends both:

talk() { echo "to stdout"; echo "to stderr" >&2; }
talk &> run.log
talk &>> run.log
wc -l < run.log | tr -d ' '
talk >& old-style.log
cat old-style.log

4
to stdout
to stderr

talk &> run.log is exactly talk > run.log 2>&1, and talk &>> run.log is exactly talk >> run.log 2>&1, so after the pair the log has four lines. The manual prefers &> to the older >& form, which also works but means something else entirely when the word after it is a number or - (>&2 duplicates, >&- closes — §10.6). &>> arrived in bash 4.0.

Neither is POSIX, and in a POSIX shell &> is not an error — which is the problem:

cat > both.sh <<'EOF'
echo hi &> out.txt
wait
echo "out.txt holds: [$(cat out.txt)]"
EOF
echo "bash:"; bash both.sh
echo "dash:"; dash both.sh

bash:
out.txt holds: [hi]
dash:
hi
out.txt holds: []

dash, Debian's /bin/sh, read echo hi &> out.txt as two commands: echo hi &, which runs echo in the background with its output still on the terminal, and > out.txt, an empty command whose only effect is to truncate out.txt. The file ended up empty, "hi" went to the terminal, and nothing reported an error. A #!/bin/sh script must spell it > out.txt 2>&1; §19 collects the other bash-only redirections, and ShellCheck flags &> in a sh script as SC3020.

Sending standard error through a pipe

A pipe connects fd 1 of one command to fd 0 of the next and leaves fd 2 alone. To send both streams through, copy fd 2 onto fd 1 on the left-hand command; bash 4.0 added |& as shorthand for 2>&1 |. To send only standard error through a pipe, use the ordering rule deliberately:

talk() { echo "to stdout"; echo "to stderr" >&2; }
talk 2>&1 | sed 's/^/both: /'
talk |& sed 's/^/both again: /'
talk 2>&1 >/dev/null | sed 's/^/only stderr: /'

both: to stdout
both: to stderr
both again: to stdout
both again: to stderr
only stderr: to stderr

2>&1 >/dev/null reads left to right: fd 2 becomes a copy of fd 1, which at that moment is the pipe; then fd 1 is moved to /dev/null. Only standard error reaches sed. This is the one place the "wrong" order is exactly right, and it is how a script filters or counts another command's error messages while discarding its output.

Swapping standard output and standard error

The same reasoning, with a spare descriptor to hold one side, swaps the two streams:

talk() { echo "to stdout"; echo "to stderr" >&2; }
{ talk 3>&1 1>&2 2>&3 3>&- | sed 's/^/piped: /'; } 2> other.txt
echo "the other stream: $(cat other.txt)"

piped: to stderr
the other stream: to stdout

3>&1 saves the pipe on fd 3; 1>&2 points fd 1 at standard error; 2>&3 points fd 2 at the saved pipe; 3>&- closes the spare so talk does not inherit it (§10.6). The error message went through the pipe and the ordinary output went to standard error. It is rarely needed, but when it is — piping a tool's diagnostics into a filter while its data goes elsewhere — this is the whole idiom, and it is four table edits read left to right.

10.5 noclobber, and Forcing a Clobber

set -o noclobber, or its short form set -C, makes > refuse to overwrite an existing regular file. It is the shell's guard against the accident §10.2 measured, where a redirection destroyed a file before anything else happened:

# shellcheck disable=SC2320  # $? is the status of the echo whose redirection failed
echo "first" > out.txt
set -o noclobber
echo "second" > out.txt
echo "status $?"
echo "third" >| out.txt
echo "fourth" >> out.txt
cat out.txt
echo "discard" > /dev/null && echo "/dev/null is not a regular file, so it is allowed"
echo "flags: $-"

example.sh: line 4: out.txt: cannot overwrite existing file
status 1
third
fourth
/dev/null is not a regular file, so it is allowed
flags: hBC

With noclobber set, > out.txt failed with cannot overwrite existing file, status 1, and the command did not run — the ordinary failed-redirection rule. >| is forcing a clobber: it overwrites even with noclobber set, so a script that means to replace a file says so in the operator. >> is unaffected because appending destroys nothing, and /dev/null is exempt because noclobber only protects regular files. $- gained a C, which is how a script tests whether the option is on.

In an interactive shell, noclobber in a startup file is a reasonable safety net. In a script it is a design decision: every > that is meant to replace a file must become >|, which documents intent at the cost of noise. Most scripts do not set it globally; forcing a clobber with >| is still worth knowing because a script you source, or a user's environment, might have set it.

Creating a file only if it does not exist

noclobber has a second use that has nothing to do with safety. The kernel implements it with O_EXCL, which makes "create this file, but only if it does not already exist" a single atomic operation:

set -C
if echo "$$" > run.lock 2>/dev/null; then echo "took the lock"; fi
if echo "$$" > run.lock 2>/dev/null; then echo "took it twice"; else echo "second attempt refused"; fi

took the lock
example.sh: line 3: run.lock: cannot overwrite existing file
second attempt refused

The first redirection created run.lock; the second found it existing and failed. Its error message appeared despite the 2>/dev/null on the same command — §10.4's rule again: redirections are performed left to right, > run.lock failed first, and the command was abandoned before 2>/dev/null was reached. Put the 2> first, or wrap the attempt in a group, { echo "$$" > run.lock; } 2>/dev/null, to silence it. No other process can slip in between the check and the creation, because there is no gap — which is exactly the property a lock file needs, and exactly what [[ -e run.lock ]] || echo "$$" > run.lock does not have. §17 builds a lock on this, and shows why flock is usually better.

10.6 Duplicating, Closing and Moving a File Descriptor

2>&1 is one instance of a general operator. n>&m makes descriptor n a copy of output descriptor m; n<&m does the same for input. A copy is not a new open: both numbers now point at the same open file description, so they share its position (§10.1). Duplicating a file descriptor is how a script gives a second name to a file it already has open, and it is the operator every idiom in §10.4 was built from.

n<&m: an input descriptor handed on

printf '%s\n' "name,role" "alice,admin" "bob,viewer" > table.csv
exec 3< table.csv
read -r header <&3
echo "header: $header"
echo "the rest, read by sort from the same descriptor:"
sort -r <&3
exec 3<&-

header: name,role
the rest, read by sort from the same descriptor:
bob,viewer
alice,admin

The script opened table.csv once, on fd 3, and read the header line through it. sort -r <&3 made sort's standard input a copy of fd 3 — and sort received only the two data rows, because the copy shares the position the read had advanced past the header. Opening the file again with sort -r < table.csv would have sorted the header in with the data. Duplicating a file descriptor, not reopening the file, is how a script consumes part of a file itself and hands the rest to a program — and duplicating a file descriptor is cheap, since no file is opened at all.

Copies share a position; two opens overwrite each other

The same distinction on the output side decides whether two writers cooperate or collide:

exec 3> one.txt 4>&3
echo "first, via 3" >&3
echo "second, via 4" >&4
exec 3>&- 4>&-
echo "--- one open, duplicated:"; cat one.txt
exec 3> two.txt 4> two.txt
echo "first, via 3" >&3
echo "second, via 4" >&4
exec 3>&- 4>&-
echo "--- the same file opened twice:"; cat two.txt

--- one open, duplicated:
first, via 3
second, via 4
--- the same file opened twice:
second, via 4

With 4>&3, both descriptors shared one position: the second write landed after the first, and the file has both lines. With 3> two.txt 4> two.txt, the file was opened twice, each open had its own position starting at 0, and the second write overwrote the first. That is the whole reason >file 2>&1 is correct and >file 2>file is not — the second form opens the file twice, and a program writing to both descriptors produces a file in which one stream overwrites the other.

n>&-: closing a descriptor

n>&- and n<&- close descriptor n — closing a descriptor is written as a duplication from the word -. A command that then writes to it gets an error from the kernel, EBADF:

# shellcheck disable=SC2320  # $? is the status of the echo whose redirection failed
echo "hello" >&-
echo "status $?"
echo "to fd 5" >&5
echo "status $?"

example.sh: line 2: echo: write error: Bad file descriptor
status 1
example.sh: line 4: 5: Bad file descriptor
status 1

echo "hello" >&- closed fd 1 for echo, which reported write error: Bad file descriptor and returned 1. Redirecting to a descriptor that was never opened fails earlier, in the redirection itself, with bash reporting the number. Closing a descriptor with n>&- is not common in day-to-day scripts, but it has two real uses. It releases a descriptor a script opened with exec once it has finished with it (§10.7), and it keeps a spare descriptor from being inherited by a program that has no business holding it — which is why §10.4's swap ended with 3>&-. A long-running child that inherits a pipe's write end keeps the pipe open, and the reader on the other end never sees end-of-file.

Moving a file descriptor: n>&m-

n>&m- is a duplication and a close in one step: descriptor m is copied to n and then closed. Moving a file descriptor is useful when a descriptor needs a different number and the old one must not linger:

# shellcheck disable=SC2320  # $? is the status of the echo whose redirection failed
exec 3> log.txt
echo "via 3" >&3
exec 4>&3-
echo "via 4" >&4
echo "via 3 again" >&3
echo "status $?"
exec 4>&-
cat log.txt

example.sh: line 6: 3: Bad file descriptor
status 1
via 3
via 4

After exec 4>&3-, writing through fd 4 worked and writing through fd 3 failed with Bad file descriptor, because moving a file descriptor left nothing on fd 3. n<&m- is the input form. Both came from ksh93 and have been in bash since 2.05b; neither is POSIX, where the same effect is n>&m m>&-.

10.7 exec Redirection: Changing the Shell's Own Descriptors

A redirection attached to a command lasts for that command. The exec builtin with redirections and no command applies them to the shell itself, where they last until changed again. That is exec redirection, and it is how a script opens a file once and uses it for many commands:

exec 3> audit.log
echo "step 1 done" >&3
echo "step 2 done" >&3
printf 'step %d done\n' 3 >&3
exec 3>&-
cat audit.log

step 1 done
step 2 done
step 3 done

exec 3> audit.log opened the file on fd 3, a custom file descriptor, for the rest of the script. Three separate commands wrote through it without reopening it, and exec 3>&- closed it. Compare >> audit.log on each line: three opens, three closes, and a file that is only as consistent as the last writer to open it. For a loop writing thousands of lines, one exec 3> is also cheaper: it saves an open and a close per line. A custom file descriptor is conventionally numbered 3 to 9; numbers from 10 up are where bash keeps its own saved descriptors, which is §10.8's subject.

Redirecting the rest of the script, and restoring it

exec can redirect standard output and standard error themselves, and a copy made first lets the script restore them:

cat > job.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
exec 4>&1 5>&2 > job.log 2>&1
echo "starting"
ls no-such-dir
echo "finished"
exec 1>&4 2>&5 4>&- 5>&-
echo "job done; the log has $(wc -l < job.log | tr -d ' ') lines"
EOF
bash job.sh
sed 's/^ls: .*/ls: (its error message)/' job.log

job done; the log has 3 lines
starting
ls: (its error message)
finished

exec 4>&1 5>&2 > job.log 2>&1 reads left to right like any other list: save the current standard output on fd 4 and standard error on fd 5, then point fd 1 at the log and fd 2 at wherever fd 1 now points. From there every command's output and errors went to the log without a redirection on any of them. exec 1>&4 2>&5 4>&- 5>&- put both back and closed the spares, so the final message reached the terminal. The copy is essential: without saving fd 1 first there is nothing to restore it to. Hard-coding exec > /dev/tty is wrong in a script that might run under cron or CI, where there is no terminal. The sed only replaces ls's message, which differs between GNU and BSD ls.

This is the standard way to give a script a log without threading >> "$LOG" 2>&1 through every line. §12 pairs it with a trap so the descriptors are restored even when the script is interrupted, and §16 extends it with process substitution to send output to the log and the terminal at once.

When an exec redirection fails

A failed redirection on an ordinary command skips that command. On exec the rules depend on the shell:

cat > open.sh <<'EOF'
exec 3< missing.txt
echo "still running, status $?"
EOF
echo "bash:";         bash open.sh;         echo "exit $?"
echo "bash --posix:"; bash --posix open.sh; echo "exit $?"
echo "dash:";         dash open.sh;         echo "exit $?"

bash:
open.sh: line 1: missing.txt: No such file or directory
still running, status 1
exit 0
bash --posix:
open.sh: line 1: missing.txt: No such file or directory
exit 1
dash:
open.sh: 1: cannot open missing.txt: No such file
exit 2

In its default mode bash reported the error, set the status to 1 and carried on. With --posix, and in dash, the script ended at the failed exec: POSIX treats a redirection error on a special builtin, exec among them, as fatal to a non-interactive shell. A script that carries on regardless of which shell runs it is relying on bash's leniency, so a script that opens a file with exec should test the result itself — exec 3< "$config" || die "cannot read $config" — and not assume it either stops or continues.

Opening for reading and writing: <>

[n]<>word opens a file for reading and writing on descriptor n, or on fd 0. Unlike >, it does not truncate, and it creates the file if it does not exist:

printf '%s\n' alpha beta gamma > data.txt
exec 3<> data.txt
read -r first <&3
echo "read: $first"
echo "BETA" >&3
exec 3>&-
cat data.txt

read: alpha
alpha
BETA
gamma

After reading "alpha", fd 3's position was at the start of the second line, and writing "BETA" overwrote "beta" in place, byte for byte. Opening for reading and writing is the only redirection that can modify the middle of a file, which is rarely what a script wants — sed -i or a rewrite through a temporary file is almost always clearer. Its real uses are elsewhere:

exec 3<> fresh.txt
[[ -e fresh.txt ]] && echo "<> created fresh.txt"
exec 3>&-
printf '%s\n' keep me > kept.txt
: <> kept.txt
cat kept.txt

<> created fresh.txt
keep
me

<> created fresh.txt without truncating anything, and : <> kept.txt opened an existing file and left its contents intact — a way to ensure a file exists without the risk > carries. The other real uses are descriptors that are inherently two-way: a network socket (§10.12), and a named pipe, where opening for reading and writing keeps an open from blocking until the other end appears (§17.11). A script opening for reading and writing a regular file should have a reason it can state.

10.8 The {fd}> Automatic Descriptor, and varredir_close

Numbering descriptors by hand has the problem numbering anything by hand has: two pieces of code that both pick 3 collide. Since bash 4.1, any redirection that takes a descriptor number can take {varname} instead, and bash picks a free descriptor of 10 or above and stores its number in the variable:

exec {log}> app.log
echo "the shell chose fd $log"
echo "started" >&"$log"
echo "stopped" >&"$log"
exec {log}>&-
cat app.log

the shell chose fd 10
started
stopped

exec {log}> app.log chose fd 10 and stored 10 in log; the writes used >&"$log", and exec {log}>&- closed the descriptor whose number log holds. The {fd}> automatic descriptor form is the right choice for any descriptor opened inside a function or a library, because the function cannot know which numbers its caller is using:

count_lines() {
  local fd n=0 line
  exec {fd}< "$1" || return
  while read -r -u "$fd" line; do
    n=$((n + 1))
  done
  exec {fd}<&-
  echo "$1: $n lines"
}
printf '%s\n' a b c > three.txt
exec 3< three.txt
count_lines three.txt
read -r line <&3
echo "the caller's fd 3 is untouched, and reads: $line"

three.txt: 3 lines
the caller's fd 3 is untouched, and reads: a

count_lines opened its file on whatever descriptor bash chose, read it with read -u "$fd", and closed it. The caller had its own file open on fd 3 throughout, and it was not disturbed. A function that hard-coded exec 3< "$1" would have replaced the caller's fd 3, and the caller's next read <&3 would have read from the wrong file. The variable is local, like any other the function uses (§9.4).

An automatic descriptor outlives its command

There is one important difference from a numbered redirection, and bash documents it as intended: with {varname}, the redirection outlives the command it is written on, so the script can manage the descriptor's lifetime itself. A {fd}> automatic descriptor attached to an ordinary command stays open after the command finishes, as if it had been opened with exec:

is_open() { [[ -e /dev/fd/$1 ]]; }
for n in 1 2 3; do
  echo "$n" {fd}>> nums.txt >&"$fd"
done
for f in 10 11 12; do is_open "$f" && echo "fd $f is still open"; done

fd 10 is still open
fd 11 is still open
fd 12 is still open

Each pass of the loop opened nums.txt again on a new descriptor, and none was ever closed — three descriptors leaked in three iterations. The order inside the loop matters too: {fd}>> nums.txt must come before >&"$fd", because $fd is expanded when its own redirection is performed, left to right, and before that it holds nothing.

A leaked descriptor is harmless in a three-line example and a real failure in a long-running loop: a process has a limit on open descriptors, which ulimit -n prints and which ranges from a few hundred to over a million depending on the system and its configuration, and a script that leaks one per item fails partway through a large enough batch with Too many open files — on the machine with the low limit, not the one it was tested on.

varredir_close closes them for you

Bash 5.2 added a shell option for scripts that use {fd} on ordinary commands:

is_open() { [[ -e /dev/fd/$1 ]]; }
shopt -s varredir_close
for n in 1 2 3; do
  echo "$n" {fd}>> nums.txt >&"$fd"
done
echo "fd was $fd each time"
is_open "$fd" || echo "and it is closed now"
exec {keep}> kept.log
is_open "$keep" && echo "an exec redirection still stays open: fd $keep"
cat nums.txt

fd was 10 each time
and it is closed now
an exec redirection still stays open: fd 10
1
2
3

With shopt -s varredir_close set, each automatic descriptor opened on an ordinary command was closed when the command finished, so the loop reused fd 10 every time and nothing was left open afterwards. An exec {keep}> redirection is deliberately exempt — it exists to open a descriptor for later — and stayed open. Before relying on varredir_close, remember that it is 5.2 and later; a script that must run under an older bash closes its descriptors explicitly, with {fd}>&-, which is clearer in any case.

Descriptors from 10 up belong to bash

The manual warns that descriptors above 9 "may conflict with file descriptors the shell uses internally". §10.1 said that bash saves a descriptor before replacing it for a builtin or function, and those saved copies are where it puts them. The saving is visible:

{ true >&10; } 2>/dev/null && echo "a write to fd 10 succeeded"
[[ -e /dev/fd/10 ]] || echo "yet fd 10 is not open"

a write to fd 10 succeeded
yet fd 10 is not open

A write to fd 10 succeeded, although nothing in the script had opened fd 10. The 2>/dev/null on the group made bash save the script's real fd 2 before replacing it, and it saved it on fd 10 — so true >&10 wrote to a copy of the saved standard error. [[ -e /dev/fd/10 ]] checks the descriptor directly and correctly finds it closed. Hard-coding a descriptor of 10 or more can therefore collide with bash's own bookkeeping; {fd} is safe because bash chooses a number it is not using, and a hand-picked number should stay in 3 to 9.

10.9 Here Documents

A here document supplies a command's standard input from the lines of the script itself:

command <<DELIMITER
lines of input
DELIMITER

The shell reads the lines after the command, up to a line consisting of exactly the delimiter, and gives them to the command as its standard input (or as descriptor n, written n<<DELIMITER). <<EOF is the traditional spelling, and nothing about the word EOF is special — any word works, and a descriptive one (<<SQL, <<USAGE) makes a long script easier to read.

An unquoted delimiter: the body is expanded

With an unquoted delimiter such as <<EOF, the body is treated much like a double-quoted string that spans lines:

name=world
cat <<EOF
hello, $name; a command's output: $(tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]' <<< loud); 2+2=$((2 + 2))
a literal \$name, a backslash \\, "double" and 'single' quotes kept
joined \
onto one line
EOF

hello, world; a command's output: LOUD; 2+2=4
a literal $name, a backslash \, "double" and 'single' quotes kept
joined onto one line

Parameter expansion, command substitution and arithmetic expansion all ran. A backslash quotes $, ` and \, and nothing else, so \$name and \\ produced a literal $name and a single backslash. Double and single quotes are ordinary characters in the body, and were printed as typed. A backslash at the end of a line joined it to the next. Word splitting and pathname expansion do not happen in a here document — a * in the body is a *.

The quoted heredoc delimiter: the body is literal

§2.8 used a heredoc as a block comment and promised the rule in full here. If any part of the delimiter word is quoted, the body is not expanded at all:

# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # name is set to show that it is NOT expanded
name=world
cat <<'EOF'
hello, $name; $(echo not run); $((2 + 2)); \$ and \\ exactly as typed
EOF

hello, $name; $(echo not run); $((2 + 2)); \$ and \\ exactly as typed

Nothing was expanded and no backslash was removed: the body arrived exactly as typed. The quoting can take any form:

v=expanded
cat <<"EOF"
double-quoted delimiter: $v
EOF
cat <<\EOF
backslash delimiter: $v
EOF
cat <<EOF
unquoted delimiter: $v
EOF
cat > partial.sh <<'OUTER'
v=expanded
cat <<E"O"F
partly quoted delimiter: $v
EOF
OUTER
bash partial.sh

double-quoted delimiter: $v
backslash delimiter: $v
unquoted delimiter: expanded
partly quoted delimiter: $v

<<"EOF", <<\EOF and even <<E"O"F all quote the delimiter, and in every case the delimiter line itself is still the plain word EOF, because the shell performs quote removal on the delimiter word. The partly quoted form runs from a generated file here because ShellCheck 0.11 cannot parse it — it reports SC1044, "Couldn't find end token", and checks nothing after it — which is reason enough to write <<'EOF' and nothing cleverer. A quoted heredoc delimiter is the rule to reach for first, because it is the safe default. §2's exercise 4 showed a heredoc used as a comment that deleted a file because its delimiter was unquoted, and the same hazard applies to every heredoc whose body is code for another program.

Generating a file for another program

The choice matters most when the body is a configuration file or a script in another language that uses $ itself. A systemd unit, an awk program, a Makefile and a Dockerfile all have their own $ syntax. An unquoted delimiter lets the shell interpolate its own variables and requires every $ meant for the target program to be escaped:

app=shop port=8080
cat <<EOF > shop.service
[Service]
User=$app
ExecStart=/usr/bin/$app --port $port --home \${HOME}
EOF
cat shop.service

[Service]
User=shop
ExecStart=/usr/bin/shop --port 8080 --home ${HOME}

$app and $port are the shell's, expanded while generating the file; \${HOME} is systemd's, escaped so that it reaches the file intact — systemd substitutes ${HOME} in ExecStart= with the home directory of the User= it runs the service as. With a quoted delimiter every $ would have been literal, including the two the script meant to fill in. So the rule is: quote the delimiter when the body contains no shell variables, and when it contains both kinds, leave it unquoted and escape every $ that belongs to the target. Write the escaped ones deliberately and check the generated file, because a missed escape produces no error — it silently substitutes the shell's value, often an empty string.

<<- tab stripping

A heredoc's body and delimiter begin at column one, which fights with indentation inside a function or an if. <<- removes leading tab characters from every body line and from the delimiter line:

cat > indented.sh <<'EOF'
print_help() {
	cat <<-END
		usage: tool [-v] FILE
	    four spaces after one tab survive
	END
}
print_help
EOF
bash indented.sh

usage: tool [-v] FILE
    four spaces after one tab survive

The heredoc and its terminator were indented with tabs inside the function, and <<- tab stripping removed all of them. The line with a tab followed by four spaces kept its spaces: only tabs are stripped, and only leading ones. That makes <<- fragile in practice. An editor set to expand tabs to spaces silently turns the terminator into four spaces followed by END, the heredoc never ends, and the rest of the script becomes its body. The Google Shell Style Guide, which otherwise says "Whatever you do, don't use tabs", makes exactly one exception: "the body of <<- tab-indented here-document." Use <<- tab stripping where the files are known to keep tabs — with an .editorconfig rule, for example — and otherwise leave heredocs unindented.

The delimiter must match exactly

The terminator is a line consisting of exactly the delimiter — no leading blanks (except tabs under <<-) and no trailing ones. cat -e marks the end of each line with $, which makes the trailing space visible:

printf '%s\n' 'cat <<EOF' 'body' 'EOF ' '  EOF' 'echo "still inside"' 'EOF' 'echo "after"' > near.sh
cat -e near.sh
echo "--- running it:"
bash near.sh

cat <<EOF$
body$
EOF $
  EOF$
echo "still inside"$
EOF$
echo "after"$
--- running it:
body
EOF 
  EOF
echo "still inside"
after

EOF with a trailing space and EOF with two leading ones were both body text, and so was echo "still inside"; the document ended at the bare EOF. The failure is silent when a real terminator follows later, as here. When none does, bash reads to the end of the file:

cat > unfinished.sh <<'OUTER'
echo "start"
cat <<EOF
line one
line two
OUTER
bash unfinished.sh
echo "status $?"

start
unfinished.sh: line 4: warning: here-document at line 2 delimited by end-of-file (wanted `EOF')
line one
line two
status 0

Bash printed a warning, treated the end of the file as the end of the document, and exited 0 — cat succeeded. The warning goes to standard error and is easy to lose in a log, so ShellCheck is the better defence: it reports a terminator with trailing whitespace (SC1118) and one that is never found (SC1044), both statically.

Where the heredoc goes on the line

The << is a redirection like any other, so the command can carry more redirections and be part of a pipeline, and the body starts on the line after the command however long that line is:

cat <<EOF > greeting.txt
written to a file
EOF
cat greeting.txt
tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]' <<EOF | sed 's/^/> /'
piped onward
EOF

written to a file
> PIPED ONWARD

cat <<EOF > greeting.txt wrote the document to a file — the usual way to generate one. tr … <<EOF | sed … piped the transformed document onward. The body always begins on the next line, and a pipeline, a && or a ; belongs on the first line, before the body, not after the terminator.

A heredoc is expanded each time it runs

A heredoc inside a function or a loop is expanded when the command runs, not when the function is defined:

runs=0
banner() {
  runs=$((runs + 1))
  cat <<EOF
== $1 (call $runs) ==
EOF
}
banner build
banner test

== build (call 1) ==
== test (call 2) ==

Each call saw the current values of $1 and runs. A heredoc is not a template stored once; it is text the shell expands at the moment it passes it to the command, like any double-quoted string.

How the document reaches the command

Bash has to put the body somewhere the command can read from. Since bash 5.1, a document smaller than the pipe buffer arrives through a pipe; a larger one is written to a temporary file:

[[ -p /dev/stdin ]] <<EOF && echo "a small document arrives through a pipe"
x
EOF
big=$(printf '%070000d' 0)
[[ -f /dev/stdin ]] <<EOF && echo "a 70,000-byte document arrives as a file"
$big
EOF

a small document arrives through a pipe
a 70,000-byte document arrives as a file

Two consequences are worth knowing. A program that needs to seek on its standard input, or to read it twice, can fail on a small heredoc that worked under older versions, where every document was a file. And a large heredoc needs a writable temporary directory — bash tries TMPDIR first, then the system's usual ones — so a script run in a locked-down container with a read-only /tmp can fail on its biggest heredoc and nowhere else.

10.10 Here Strings

A here string, <<<word, is a heredoc written as a single word: the word is expanded and passed to the command's standard input, followed by a newline:

read -r first rest <<< "alpha beta gamma"
echo "first=$first rest=$rest"
IFS= read -r -d '' s <<< "abc"
printf 'what the command received: %q\n' "$s"
pattern='*  two  spaces'
# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # the unquoted word is the demonstration
cat <<< $pattern

first=alpha rest=beta gamma
what the command received: $'abc\n'
*  two  spaces

read split the string exactly as it would split a line from a file. The command receives the expanded word plus a newline — %q shows it as $'abc\n' — so a here string always ends with a newline even when the word does not. The word goes through parameter expansion, command substitution, arithmetic expansion and quote removal, but not word splitting or pathname expansion: <<< $pattern passed * two spaces unchanged, runs of spaces intact, without quotes. Quote it anyway; it costs nothing and reads as intended.

Why <<< beats echo … | for read

A here string is not just shorter than echo "$line" |. It changes where the reading command runs:

# shellcheck disable=SC2030,SC2031,SC2034  # the lost assignment is the demonstration
line="a b c"
echo "$line" | read -r x y z
echo "after a pipe: x=${x-unset}"
read -r x y z <<< "$line"
echo "after a here string: x=$x"

after a pipe: x=unset
after a here string: x=a

echo "$line" | read -r x y z ran read in a subshell, as every part of a pipeline runs (§16), so x was set in the subshell and lost when it exited. A here string is a redirection, not a pipeline, and read ran in the current shell. That is the main reason here strings exist in scripts, and read -r a b <<< "$line" is the idiom to split a variable into fields. It also avoids a process, which matters in a loop (§21).

Here strings are not POSIX

<<< has been in bash since 2.05b. It is not in POSIX, and a POSIX shell rejects it outright:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the $x is meant for the generated script
printf '%s\n' 'read -r x <<< "hi"' 'echo "$x"' > hs.sh
echo "bash:"; bash hs.sh
echo "dash:"; dash hs.sh

bash:
hi
dash:
hs.sh: 1: Syntax error: redirection unexpected

dash refused the whole script with a syntax error before running anything, and ShellCheck reports a here string in a sh script as SC3011. In #!/bin/sh, use a heredoc — read -r x <<EOF / $line / EOF — or printf '%s\n' "$line" | when running in a subshell does not matter. §19 lists the portable replacement for every bash-only redirection in one place.

10.11 A Redirection Applies to a Compound Command

A redirection applies to a compound command as a whole: an if, a case, a loop, a { } group or a ( ) subshell can carry redirections after its closing keyword, and every command inside runs with them. §9.1 used this on a group and §9.2 on a function definition; it is most important on loops.

Redirecting a whole loop

for n in 1 2 3; do
  echo "line $n" > inside.txt
done
for n in 1 2 3; do
  echo "line $n"
done > outside.txt
echo "--- inside.txt:";  cat inside.txt
echo "--- outside.txt:"; cat outside.txt

--- inside.txt:
line 3
--- outside.txt:
line 1
line 2
line 3

With > inside the loop, the file was truncated and rewritten on every iteration, and only the last line survived. Redirecting a whole loop, with done > outside.txt, opened the file once before the loop started, and every echo wrote through the same descriptor. This is the redirection bug that most often reaches production, because it works — it produces a file, containing a valid line — and fails only in the count. The fix is also faster: one open instead of one per iteration.

Input works the same way. done < file redirects the loop's standard input, which is how while read loops read a file (§8.8), and a loop can carry input and output redirections together:

printf '%s\n' web1 web2 web3 > hosts.txt
count=0
while read -r host; do
  count=$((count + 1))
  echo "checked $host"
done < hosts.txt > checked.txt 2> failures.txt
echo "count=$count, checked.txt has:"
cat checked.txt

count=3, checked.txt has:
checked web1
checked web2
checked web3

The loop read hosts.txt, wrote its results to checked.txt and would have written any errors to failures.txt, all with three redirections on done. Because the redirection is on the loop and not in a pipeline, the loop runs in the current shell and count survived it — the pipeline version, cat hosts.txt | while …, would have lost it (§16). The same shape gives a loop more than one input: each file on its own descriptor, each read choosing one with <&n:

while read -r name <&3 && read -r role <&4; do
  echo "$name: $role"
done 3<<NAMES 4<<ROLES
alice
bob
NAMES
admin
viewer
ROLES

alice: admin
bob: viewer

Two heredocs on descriptors 3 and 4 fed the loop in lockstep, and it stopped when the shorter input ran out. The same pattern reads two files — done 3< names.txt 4< roles.txt — and it is §8.8's fix for the stdin thief generalised: when a loop needs its input and its body needs standard input too, give the loop's input a descriptor of its own.

if, groups, and other compound commands

if grep -q needle haystack.txt; then
  echo "found"
else
  echo "not found, status $?"
fi 2>/dev/null
{ echo "one"; echo "two" >&2; } > both.txt 2>&1
cat both.txt

not found, status 2
one
two

fi 2>/dev/null silenced grep's complaint about the missing file for the whole if, including its condition; the else branch still printed to standard output, which was not redirected. The group sent both of its commands' output to one file, in order, because > both.txt 2>&1 applied to the group as a whole.

The target is expanded once, before the body runs

A redirection on a compound command is performed once, when the compound command starts. Its target is expanded then and not again:

out=first.txt
{
  echo "a"
  out=second.txt
  echo "b"
} > "$out"
echo "first.txt: $(tr '\n' ' ' < first.txt)"
[[ -e second.txt ]] || echo "second.txt was never created"

first.txt: a b 
second.txt was never created

The group changed out halfway through, but the file had already been opened as first.txt, and both lines went there. A loop that needs a different file per iteration must put the redirection inside the loop, on the command that writes, with >> or with a target that changes per iteration — accepting the open per iteration that costs.

10.12 The Special Files: /dev/null, /dev/stdin, /dev/fd and /dev/tcp

A handful of paths behave specially in redirections. Some are real files provided by the operating system; others bash implements itself when the system does not provide them. The distinction matters in exactly one place, and that place has cost people data.

/dev/null

/dev/null is a character device that discards everything written to it and reads as empty:

# shellcheck disable=SC2320  # $? is the status of the echo whose redirection failed
echo "discarded" > /dev/null
echo "write status $?"
read -r line < /dev/null
echo "read status $?, line=[${line-}]"
[[ -c /dev/null ]] && echo "/dev/null is a character device"

write status 0
read status 1, line=[]
/dev/null is a character device

A write to it succeeds and goes nowhere; a read from it gets end-of-file immediately, so read returns 1 with nothing read. That second property is the useful one for §8.8's stdin thief: < /dev/null gives a command an input it cannot block on and cannot steal from. >/dev/null 2>&1 (or &>/dev/null) discards all of a command's output, which is correct when only its status matters — if grep -q … makes it unnecessary for grep, but not for most commands. Discarding standard error hides the reason something failed, so do it only for a command whose failure you handle.

/dev/stdin, /dev/stdout, /dev/stderr and /dev/fd/N

These name a process's own descriptors: /dev/stdin is fd 0, /dev/stdout fd 1, /dev/stderr fd 2, and /dev/fd/N is descriptor N. They exist for programs that insist on a file name:

printf 'from the pipe\n' | cat /dev/stdin
echo "to stderr, by name" > /dev/stderr

from the pipe
to stderr, by name

cat /dev/stdin read the pipe, the way cat - would; a program without a - convention can still be given its standard input by that name. The man page says bash uses these files when the operating system provides them and emulates them — as a duplication of the descriptor — when it does not. Linux and macOS both provide them, and they do not behave the same:

{ echo "one"; echo "two" >&1; } > out1.txt
{ echo "one"; echo "two" >> /dev/stdout; } > out2.txt
echo "--- >&1:";          cat out1.txt
echo "--- >> /dev/stdout:"; cat out2.txt

--- >&1:
one
two
--- >> /dev/stdout:
one
two

That output — both lines in both files — is what macOS prints, and what Linux prints for these two forms. The dangerous form is the one not shown. { echo one; echo two > /dev/stdout; } > out.txt keeps both lines on macOS, where opening /dev/stdout duplicates fd 1. On Linux /dev/stdout is a symbolic link through /proc/self/fd/1 to out.txt itself, so opening it is a new open of the file, with >, which truncates it: measured under Debian with bash 5.2, out.txt held only two, and echo "second" > /dev/fd/3 after a first write through fd 3 likewise left only the second line. Section 10.1's distinction between copying a descriptor and opening a file is the whole explanation. The portable rule is to use >&1, >&2 and >&3 in scripts and never > /dev/stdout, > /dev/stderr or > /dev/fd/N; >> is safe on both, but there is no reason to prefer it to the operator that says what it means.

/dev/tcp and /dev/udp

/dev/tcp/host/port does not exist on any file system. Bash recognises the path in a redirection and opens a TCP connection to host on port, putting the socket on the descriptor. A connection needs both reading and writing, so it is opened with <>. Here a small Python program stands in for a server on the loopback interface, reached through process substitution (§4.6) so the script can read the port it chose:

cat > server.py <<'EOF'
import socket
server = socket.create_server(("127.0.0.1", 0))
print(server.getsockname()[1], flush=True)
conn, _ = server.accept()
line = conn.makefile().readline()
conn.sendall(f"server heard: {line}".encode())
conn.close()
EOF
exec {srv}< <(python3 server.py)
read -r port <&"$srv"
exec {sock}<> "/dev/tcp/127.0.0.1/$port"
echo "hello over tcp" >&"$sock"
read -r reply <&"$sock"
exec {sock}>&- {srv}<&-
echo "$reply"

server heard: hello over tcp

exec {sock}<> "/dev/tcp/127.0.0.1/$port" connected; >&"$sock" sent a line; read <&"$sock" read the reply; {sock}>&- closed the connection. /dev/udp/host/port does the same for UDP. A connection that fails is an ordinary failed redirection, and so it makes a cheap port check:

port_open() { { : <> "/dev/tcp/$1/$2"; } 2>/dev/null; }
if port_open 127.0.0.1 9; then echo "port 9 is open"; else echo "port 9 is closed"; fi
# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # the failed open is the demonstration; sock is never used
exec {sock}<> /dev/tcp/127.0.0.1/9
echo "status $?"

port 9 is closed
example.sh: connect: Connection refused
example.sh: line 4: /dev/tcp/127.0.0.1/9: Connection refused
status 1

port_open tries to open the socket, discards the error, and returns the status — : <> does nothing with the descriptor except open and close it. Without the 2>/dev/null bash prints the failure twice, once from connect and once for the redirection. The /dev/tcp feature is a compile-time option: it was enabled in both builds this course was measured on, Homebrew's and Debian's, but a minimal or embedded build can leave it out, and no POSIX shell has it. It speaks raw TCP only — no TLS, no HTTP — so it is a tool for a health check in an image that has no curl or nc, not a way to talk to real web services. §18 returns to it, because a variable reaching a /dev/tcp path is an outbound connection an attacker chooses.

10.13 Stdout versus Stderr Discipline

§10.3 said what the two streams are for. Stdout versus stderr discipline is that rule applied to a whole script, and it is what decides whether the script can be used as a part of something larger. Standard output carries the result and nothing else. Everything else — progress, warnings, errors, prompts — goes to standard error.

The rule, measured

cat > users.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# users.sh - print one user name per line; progress goes to stderr.
log() { printf '%s: %s\n' "${0##*/}" "$*" >&2; }
log "reading 3 records"
printf '%s\n' carol alice bob
log "done"
EOF
chmod +x users.sh
names=$(./users.sh)
echo "captured: ${names//$'\n'/,}"
./users.sh 2>/dev/null | sort

users.sh: reading 3 records
users.sh: done
captured: carol,alice,bob
alice
bob
carol

users.sh writes its three names to standard output and its progress to standard error through a log function. $(./users.sh) captured exactly the names, while the progress still reached the person running it, and ./users.sh 2>/dev/null | sort sorted the data with the messages removed. Now the same script with its progress on standard output:

cat > noisy.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "reading 3 records"
printf '%s\n' carol alice bob
EOF
chmod +x noisy.sh
./noisy.sh | sort
count=$(./noisy.sh | wc -l | tr -d ' ')
echo "count=$count"

alice
bob
carol
reading 3 records
count=4

The progress line was sorted in among the names, and a line count reported 4 users where there are 3. Nothing failed; the script simply cannot be composed with anything. This applies to functions exactly as it does to scripts: §9.6 returned data from a function through standard output, which works only if nothing else the function prints goes there.

A set of logging functions

The usual shape is a small set of functions that log to stderr, each adding the program's name so a message is attributable when several scripts share a terminal or a log:

cat > deploy.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
readonly PROG=${0##*/}
VERBOSE=${VERBOSE:-0}

info()  { (( VERBOSE )) && printf '%s: %s\n' "$PROG" "$*" >&2; return 0; }
warn()  { printf '%s: warning: %s\n' "$PROG" "$*" >&2; }
die()   { printf '%s: error: %s\n' "$PROG" "$*" >&2; exit 1; }

info "checking the release directory"
[[ -d release ]] || die "no release directory here"
warn "release/ is empty"
echo "release-1.4.2"
EOF
chmod +x deploy.sh
mkdir work && cd work || exit
../deploy.sh
echo "status $?"
mkdir release
VERBOSE=1 ../deploy.sh > version.txt
echo "version.txt: $(cat version.txt)"

deploy.sh: error: no release directory here
status 1
deploy.sh: checking the release directory
deploy.sh: warning: release/ is empty
version.txt: release-1.4.2

The three functions all log to stderr; they differ in when they speak and what happens after. info speaks only when VERBOSE is set, warn always, and die prints and exits with status 1 — §9.10 extended it with a stack trace, and §11 connects it to the exit status conventions. The first run died in the script's first check, with a message naming the script, and status 1. The second ran with VERBOSE=1 and its standard output redirected: the version went to version.txt, while the verbose message and the warning still reached the terminal. That is the property the discipline buys — a caller can redirect the data without silencing the diagnostics, and silence the diagnostics without losing the data.

Three details are easy to get wrong. info ends with return 0, because a function whose last command is a false (( VERBOSE )) would return 1, and under set -e a quiet info call would end the script (§11.5). The messages use printf '%s\n' rather than echo, so a message beginning with -n is printed rather than taken as an option (§14). And messages go to >&2, not > /dev/stderr, for §10.12's reason.

Speaking past a capture

A function whose output is captured by $(…) has its standard output going into a variable, and sometimes it needs to say something to the person as well. Standard error is the usual answer. When standard error is itself redirected — to a log, say — and a message must still reach the original destination, save that destination on a spare descriptor first:

pick_colour() {
  echo "choosing a colour..." >&3
  echo "blue"
}
exec 3>&2
colour=$(pick_colour)
echo "colour=$colour"
exec 3>&-

choosing a colour...
colour=blue

exec 3>&2 gave the script a handle on its original standard error before anything else changed. Inside $(pick_colour) standard output was the capture, but fd 3 was inherited and still pointed at the terminal, so the message reached the person and only blue reached colour. This is the same save-a-copy move as §10.7's restore, used for the opposite reason, and an interactive prompt inside a captured function (§14) relies on it.

Status is not output

The last part of the discipline is that the exit status carries success or failure, and neither stream substitutes for it. A script that prints "ERROR" on standard output and exits 0 has told every caller it succeeded. Report the failure on standard error and exit non-zero; a caller can then test the status without parsing any text, which is the subject of §11.

10.14 The Redirection Table

Every operator in this section in one place. n is a descriptor number and defaults to the one shown; every operator accepts {var} in place of n (§10.8).

Operator
Effect, and the rule that is easiest to get wrong
[n]>file
Open for writing on fd 1; create, or truncate before the command runs. A failed redirection skips the command, status 1 (§10.2).
[n]>>file
Open for appending on fd 1; every write goes to the current end (§10.2).
[n]<file
Open for reading on fd 0. The shell opens it, so the command never runs if it is missing (§10.2).
[n]>|file
Like >, but overwrites even under set -o noclobber / set -C (§10.5).
[n]<>file
Open for reading and writing on fd 0; creates, never truncates (§10.7).
>file 2>&1
Both streams to file. 2>&1 >file sends only fd 1 there: redirections run left to right (§10.4).
&>file · &>>file
Bash shorthand for >file 2>&1 · >>file 2>&1. In /bin/sh &> backgrounds the command and truncates the file (§10.4).
cmd |& cmd2
Bash shorthand for cmd 2>&1 | cmd2 (§10.4).
n>&m · n<&m
Make n a copy of m. Copies share a position; opening the same file twice does not (§10.6).
n>&- · n<&-
Close n. Writing to it fails with Bad file descriptor (§10.6).
n>&m- · n<&m-
Move m to n: copy, then close m (§10.6).
exec 3>file
No command: the redirection applies to the shell for the rest of the script. Save a copy first to restore it (§10.7).
exec {fd}>file
Bash picks a free fd ≥ 10 and stores it in fd. On an ordinary command it stays open unless varredir_close is set (§10.8).
<<EOF · <<'EOF'
Here document; unquoted delimiter expands $, ` and \; any quoting makes the body literal (§10.9).
<<-EOF
Strips leading tabs (not spaces) from the body and the terminator (§10.9).
<<< word
Here string: one word plus a newline; no splitting or globbing; read runs in the current shell. Not POSIX (§10.10).
done > file
A redirection on a compound command is performed once, for all of it (§10.11).
/dev/null · /dev/fd/N · /dev/tcp/h/p
Discard · descriptor N by name, which reopens the file on Linux, so use >&N · a TCP socket, opened with <> (§10.12).
>&2
Where every message that is not the result belongs (§10.13).

Exercises

1. The nightly script with one line of summary. This script is meant to record every step in summary.txt and both streams of build in build.log. Run it, explain each wrong result, and fix both bugs.

cat > nightly.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
build() { echo "compiling"; echo "warning: unused variable" >&2; }
for step in fetch build test; do
  echo "== $step" > summary.txt
done
build 2>&1 > build.log
echo "summary: $(cat summary.txt)"
echo "build.log: $(cat build.log)"
EOF
bash nightly.sh
Solution 
cat > nightly.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
build() { echo "compiling"; echo "warning: unused variable" >&2; }
for step in fetch build test; do
  echo "== $step" > summary.txt
done
build 2>&1 > build.log
echo "summary: $(cat summary.txt)"
echo "build.log: $(cat build.log)"
EOF
bash nightly.sh

warning: unused variable
summary: == test
build.log: compiling

Two bugs, one from §10.11 and one from §10.4. The > inside the loop truncated summary.txt on every iteration, so only the last step survived. And build 2>&1 > build.log copied fd 2 while fd 1 was still the terminal, then moved fd 1 alone: the warning went to the terminal (it is the first line of the output) and the log holds only "compiling".

cat > nightly.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
build() { echo "compiling"; echo "warning: unused variable" >&2; }
for step in fetch build test; do
  echo "== $step"
done > summary.txt
build > build.log 2>&1
echo "summary: $(tr '\n' ' ' < summary.txt)"
echo "build.log: $(tr '\n' ' ' < build.log)"
EOF
bash nightly.sh

summary: == fetch == build == test 
build.log: compiling warning: unused variable

done > summary.txt opens the file once for the whole loop, and > build.log 2>&1 points fd 1 at the log before fd 2 copies it. Written as &> build.log, the second fix is the same in bash; the explicit form also works in /bin/sh.

2. quietly. Write quietly CMD [ARG...], which runs a command and prints nothing if it succeeds. If it fails, it prints everything the command wrote to either stream, followed by a line naming the command and its status, all on standard error, and returns the command's status. Test it with a command that succeeds and one that fails with status 3.

Solution 
# quietly CMD [ARG...] - run CMD, showing its output only if it fails.
# Returns CMD's exit status.
quietly() {
  local output status
  output=$("$@" 2>&1)
  status=$?
  if (( status != 0 )); then
    printf '%s\n' "$output" >&2
    printf 'quietly: %s exited with status %d\n' "$1" "$status" >&2
  fi
  return "$status"
}
chatty() { echo "step 1"; echo "step 2" >&2; return "${1:-0}"; }
quietly chatty 0 && echo "first call: silent, status 0"
quietly chatty 3
echo "second call: status $?"

first call: silent, status 0
step 1
step 2
quietly: chatty exited with status 3
second call: status 3

output=$("$@" 2>&1) captures both streams: inside the command substitution fd 1 is the capture, and 2>&1 copies it to fd 2 (§10.4). The status is saved on the next line, before anything else can overwrite $?. On failure both the captured output and the summary go to >&2, so a caller that redirects quietly's standard output still sees the diagnostics (§10.13), and return "$status" passes the command's own status on (§9.5).

Two limits are worth stating. Capturing into a variable holds the whole output in memory and loses its trailing newlines (§4.4), which is fine for a build step and wrong for a command that prints gigabytes; that version captures to a mktemp file instead (§17.10). And the two streams are merged in the order the command wrote them, which is the buffering order §10.3 measured, not necessarily the order the events happened.

3. A unit file from a function. Write render_unit NAME PORT, which prints a systemd unit file whose Description, StateDirectory and ExecStart use the two arguments. ExecStart must also pass --data ${STATE_DIRECTORY} and an ExecReload line must contain $MAINPID, both literally, because systemd substitutes them itself when the service starts. The heredoc must be indented inside the function.

Solution 
render_unit() {
  local name=$1 port=$2
  cat <<-EOF
	[Unit]
	Description=$name on port $port

	[Service]
	StateDirectory=$name
	ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/$name --port $port --data \${STATE_DIRECTORY}
	ExecReload=/bin/kill -HUP \$MAINPID
	EOF
}
render_unit shop 8080 > shop.service
cat shop.service

[Unit]
Description=shop on port 8080

[Service]
StateDirectory=shop
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/shop --port 8080 --data ${STATE_DIRECTORY}
ExecReload=/bin/kill -HUP $MAINPID

The delimiter is unquoted, because $name and $port must expand, and the two $ characters that belong to systemd are escaped as \$ so they reach the file intact (§10.9). The body and the terminator are indented with tabs and the heredoc is opened with <<-, which strips them; the blank line between the sections is empty, so it survives as an empty line. If your editor converted those tabs to spaces, the heredoc never ends and bash warns that it was delimited by end-of-file — the reason §10.9 calls <<- fragile. Check the output with systemd-analyze verify shop.service on a system that has systemd.

4. Two files in lockstep. Write zip_lines FILE1 FILE2, which prints line1 | line2 for each pair of lines until either file ends. It must not disturb any descriptor its caller has open, must return 1 if either file cannot be opened, and must leave no descriptor open when it returns, whether it succeeds or fails.

Solution 
# zip_lines FILE1 FILE2 - print "line1 | line2" pairs until either file ends.
zip_lines() {
  local left right a b
  exec {left}< "$1" || return
  exec {right}< "$2" || { exec {left}<&-; return 1; }
  while IFS= read -r -u "$left" a && IFS= read -r -u "$right" b; do
    printf '%s | %s\n' "$a" "$b"
  done
  exec {left}<&- {right}<&-
}
printf '%s\n' alice bob carol > names.txt
printf '%s\n' admin viewer > roles.txt
zip_lines names.txt roles.txt
zip_lines names.txt missing.txt
echo "status $?"
[[ -e /dev/fd/10 || -e /dev/fd/11 ]] || echo "no descriptor leaked"

alice | admin
bob | viewer
example.sh: line 5: missing.txt: No such file or directory
status 1
no descriptor leaked

Each file is opened on an automatic descriptor (§10.8), so the function cannot collide with a caller's fd 3 or 4, and each read -u names the descriptor it reads. IFS= and -r keep each line exactly as written (§8.8). The loop condition is two reads joined by &&, so it ends as soon as either file runs out.

The error paths are where descriptors leak. If the second open fails, the first is already open, so the failure branch closes left before returning 1; without that, every failed call would leak one descriptor. The success path closes both. The last line of the test checks for descriptors 10 and 11 — the ones the function would have used — and finds none. In bash 5.2 and later varredir_close does not help here, because these descriptors were opened with exec, which it deliberately leaves alone.

SECTION 11

Exit Status, errexit and Error Handling

A shell script's default response to a failed command is to carry on. The failed command prints a message, sets a status that nothing is obliged to read, and the next line runs as if nothing had happened — so a script whose first step failed goes on to publish, delete or overwrite on the strength of a result it never got. Every other language in this collection stops on an unhandled error. Bash stops only when you ask it to, and asking is less simple than it looks.

This section is about the one byte a command reports when it finishes, and everything a script can do with it. It starts with the byte itself and the conventions that give its values meaning, then covers the three options people turn on to make bash stricter — set -u, set -e and pipefail — and spends most of its length on set -e, because set -e is the option whose actual behaviour differs most from what its users believe. §1.6 called error handling in bash "bolted on"; this is where the bolts are. The section ends with the ERR trap, which turns a silent exit into a report.

linux §4 introduced $?, && and || at the prompt. This section treats failure as a design problem: which statuses a script should return, where set -e does and does not stop, why a function's behaviour depends on how it was called, and how to write code that is correct whether or not strict mode is on. §12 builds on it with traps and cleanup; §13 builds a command-line interface on its usage conventions; §20 checks all of it with ShellCheck and tests it with bats. Every claim below was measured under bash 5.3 on macOS and bash 5.2 on Debian, which agreed on every one.

11.1 Exit Status: One Byte Reported to the Parent

Every command finishes with an exit status, a number from 0 to 255 that its parent receives through the wait system call. By convention 0 means success and every other value means some kind of failure. That inversion — zero is true — is what §7.1 built the whole of if on. A non-zero exit status is not an exception, a message or a crash: it is a number, and a script that does not look at it has thrown it away.

The special parameter $? holds the status of the most recent command, and "most recent" is meant literally:

true;  echo "true: $?"
false; echo "false: $?"
printf '%s\n' apple banana > fruit.txt
grep -q apple fruit.txt;  echo "grep, a match: $?"
grep -q cherry fruit.txt; echo "grep, no match: $?"
grep -q apple nosuch.txt 2>/dev/null; echo "grep, an error: $?"
false
echo "the echo above reported success, so now \$? is $?"

true: 0
false: 1
grep, a match: 0
grep, no match: 1
grep, an error: 2
the echo above reported success, so now $? is 1

false is the simplest command with a non-zero exit status. grep shows why a status is a number rather than a boolean: 0 for a match, 1 for no match, and 2 for trouble — here a missing file. A script that tests only "zero or not" cannot tell "the log has no errors" from "the log does not exist", and §11.6 shows how to keep them apart. The last line shows the property that causes more bugs than any other in this section: $? is replaced by every command, including the echo that was supposed to report it. Anything that needs a status must read it on the very next command, or copy it into a variable there.

Compound commands and functions have a status too

Every compound command reports a status, and the rule for each is worth knowing precisely, because set -e (§11.3) acts on it:

if false; then echo "not printed"; fi
echo "an if with no branch taken: $?"
# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # the loop has nothing to iterate over
for f in; do :; done
echo "a for loop with nothing to do: $?"
last_fails() { echo "working"; false; }
last_fails
echo "a function whose last command failed: $?"

an if with no branch taken: 0
a for loop with nothing to do: 0
working
a function whose last command failed: 1

An if whose condition was false and that has no else returns 0: nothing in it failed, because a condition is a question rather than a failure. A for loop with nothing to iterate over returns 0. A loop that ran returns the status of the last command its body executed, and a function returns the status of the last command it ran unless it says otherwise with return (§9.5). That last rule, applied without thinking, is behind three of §11.5's traps.

The exit builtin

The exit builtin ends the shell with a status. exit 3 exits with 3; a bare exit exits with the status of the last command run, which is almost never what the reader of the script expects it to mean:

cat > check.sh <<'EOF'
echo "checking"
exit 3
echo "never printed"
EOF
bash check.sh
echo "check.sh exited $?"
bash -c 'false; exit'
echo "a bare exit passes on the last status: $?"
bash -c 'exit 300'; echo "exit 300 -> $?"
bash -c 'exit -1';  echo "exit -1 -> $?"
( exit 4 ); echo "exit in a subshell leaves only the subshell: $?"

checking
check.sh exited 3
a bare exit passes on the last status: 1
exit 300 -> 44
exit -1 -> 255
exit in a subshell leaves only the subshell: 4

Nothing after exit runs. The argument is taken modulo 256, so exit 300 is 44 and exit -1 is 255 — the same arithmetic §9.5 measured for return, because the kernel keeps only the low eight bits. Inside a subshell, exit leaves the subshell, which is how ( exit 4 ) produces a status of 4 without ending anything else, and which every probe in this section uses to make a command that fails with a chosen status.

Use exit 0 explicitly when a script has succeeded, and a named non-zero status when it has not. Leaving the status to "whatever ran last" produces this:

cat > report.sh <<'EOF'
echo "report written"
[[ -n ${DEBUG-} ]] && echo "debug: 12 rows"
EOF
bash report.sh
echo "report.sh exited $?"
DEBUG=1 bash report.sh
echo "with DEBUG set it exited $?"

report written
report.sh exited 1
report written
debug: 12 rows
with DEBUG set it exited 0

report.sh did its work and exited 1, because its last line was a test that is false whenever DEBUG is unset. Every caller — a CI job, a cron wrapper, make, another script under set -e — sees a failure. The script is correct only when debugging is on, which is exactly the situation in which nobody would notice. Ending the script with exit 0, or writing the debug line as an if, fixes it; §11.5 meets the same shape inside functions.

11.2 set -u: Unset Variables Are Errors

By default, expanding a variable that was never set produces an empty string, silently. The set -u option, also spelled set -o nounset, makes it an error:

cat > greet.sh <<'EOF'
first_name=Ada
echo "Hello, $firstname"
echo "greeting sent"
EOF
bash greet.sh
echo "without set -u: status $?"
bash -u greet.sh
echo "with set -u: status $?"

Hello, 
greeting sent
without set -u: status 0
greet.sh: line 2: firstname: unbound variable
with set -u: status 1

Without the option, a misspelled name expanded to nothing and the script reported success after greeting nobody. With it, bash printed firstname: unbound variable, naming the variable and the line, and exited with status 1 before the next command. An unbound variable is bash's term for a name with no value at all, which is different from one set to the empty string: name= is set, and set -u accepts it.

The option applies to parameter expansion, which includes the positional parameters and array elements, and it applies everywhere — in a function, in a condition, in an arithmetic expression. A script that is not interactive exits on the spot.

Asking for a default: ${var:-} under nounset

The fix for a variable that may legitimately be unset is not to turn the option off, but to say so at the point of use with one of §5's default operators, which never trigger it:

set -u
echo "[${colour:-}] [${colour-}] [${colour:-blue}] [${colour:+set}]"
# shellcheck disable=SC2120  # called with no arguments on purpose
show_args() { echo "$# argument(s): [$*]"; for a in "$@"; do echo "  $a"; done; }
# shellcheck disable=SC2119
show_args
empty=()
echo "an empty array: [${empty[*]}] (${#empty[@]} elements)"
[[ -v colour ]] || echo "colour is not set, and [[ -v ]] said so without expanding it"
echo "the length of an unset variable: ${#colour}"
echo "not reached"

[] [] [blue] []
0 argument(s): []
an empty array: [] (0 elements)
colour is not set, and [[ -v ]] said so without expanding it
example.sh: line 10: colour: unbound variable

${colour:-} is the idiom to learn: "the value, or empty if unset or empty". It reads as a deliberate statement that an unset value is expected here, and it is the standard way of writing ${var:-} under nounset for anything that comes from the environment or an optional argument. ${colour-} differs only for a variable set to the empty string (§5.2). [[ -v colour ]] tests whether a variable is set without expanding it, so it is also safe.

The special parameters $@ and $* are exempt: calling a function with no arguments and expanding "$@" is not an error, and $# is 0. Bash 4.1 settled that rule to follow a POSIX interpretation. An array with no elements expands to nothing without error, too, since bash 4.4; older versions reported it as an unbound variable, which is why scripts written for them contain the workaround ${arr[@]+"${arr[@]}"}. The last line shows one expansion that is not exempt: the length of an unset variable, ${#colour}, stopped the script.

Positional parameters in functions

A function's $1 is a positional parameter like any other, so a missing argument is an unbound variable:

set -u
greet() {
  local name=${1-}
  [[ -n $name ]] || { echo "greet: missing name" >&2; return 2; }
  echo "hello, $name"
}
greet Ada
greet
echo "status $?"
# shellcheck disable=SC2120  # called with no argument on purpose
bad_greet() { echo "hello, $1"; }
# shellcheck disable=SC2119
bad_greet
echo "not reached"

hello, Ada
greet: missing name
status 2
example.sh: line 11: $1: unbound variable

greet reads its argument as ${1-} and reports a missing one itself, with a message and a status of 2 — the usage-error convention of §11.4 — which its caller can test. bad_greet expanded $1 directly and took the whole script down with $1: unbound variable, a message that tells the person running the script nothing about what they did wrong. set -u is a net for mistakes in the script; it is not an argument checker, and a function that can be called without an argument should check for one itself.

Arrays and set -u

An array element that does not exist is unset, so reading one is an error — which is exactly the check §6.3 wanted when it indexed an array with a computed value:

set -u
declare -A port=([http]=80 [https]=443)
echo "https -> ${port[https]}"
echo "ftp -> ${port[ftp]-none}"
[[ -v 'port[ftp]' ]] || echo "no ftp entry"
echo "ftp -> ${port[ftp]}"
echo "not reached"

https -> 443
ftp -> none
no ftp entry
example.sh: line 6: port[ftp]: unbound variable

The existing key read normally; the missing one could be given a default with ${port[ftp]-none} or tested with [[ -v 'port[ftp]' ]] (quoted, so the brackets are not taken as a glob); and reading it bare ended the script.
