Without set -u, a lookup against a misspelled key returns an empty string and the script goes on to connect to port nothing.

set -u is not suspended in a condition

set -e, below, is switched off inside conditions. set -u is not:

set -u
if [[ $mode == fast ]]; then
  echo "fast"
fi
echo "not reached"

example.sh: line 2: mode: unbound variable

The script exited on the if line. A test like [[ $mode == fast ]] against an optional variable must be written [[ ${mode-} == fast ]]. This is the property that makes set -u cheap to adopt: it has no exceptions to learn, and every failure it produces names the variable responsible.

Code you did not write

The one real cost of set -u is other people's code. A file that is sourced runs in the current shell with the current options, and a file written without set -u in mind will stop a script that uses it. Turn the option off around the source, and on again immediately:

cat > legacy.env <<'EOF'
# A file this script does not own: it reads a variable that may be unset.
APP_HOME=${APP_ROOT}/app
EOF
set -u
set +u
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source ./legacy.env
set -u
echo "APP_HOME is [$APP_HOME]"
( source ./legacy.env ) 2>&1
echo "the same file under set -u: status $?"

APP_HOME is [/app]
./legacy.env: line 2: APP_ROOT: unbound variable
the same file under set -u: status 1

Sourced with the option off, legacy.env expanded the unset APP_ROOT to nothing and set APP_HOME=/app. Sourced with the option on — here in a subshell, so that the failure could be shown without ending the example — it stopped with APP_ROOT: unbound variable. Python virtual environments' activate scripts used to need this treatment and no longer do; a vendor's environment file or an old in-house library still may.

11.3 set -e: Exit When a Command Fails

The set -e option, also spelled set -o errexit, tells the shell to exit as soon as a command fails:

cat > nightly.sh <<'EOF'
echo "step 1: fetch"
( exit 3 )
echo "step 2: publish, as if step 1 had worked"
EOF
bash nightly.sh
echo "without set -e: status $?"
bash -e nightly.sh
echo "with set -e: status $?"

step 1: fetch
step 2: publish, as if step 1 had worked
without set -e: status 0
step 1: fetch
with set -e: status 3

Without the option, nightly.sh ran step 2 after step 1 failed and reported success. With it, the script stopped at the failing command and exited with that command's status, 3. Note what it did not do: print anything. set -e exits silently. The failed command may have printed its own message, and ( exit 3 ) did not, so the only evidence is the status and the missing output. §11.10's ERR trap is how a strict script reports where it stopped.

What counts as failing

The manual's rule is that the shell exits when "a pipeline (which may consist of a single simple command), a list, or a compound command" returns non-zero, subject to exceptions below. In practice, that covers more than external commands:

try() { bash -ec "$1" 2>&1; echo "  -> $1  exits $?"; }
try 'echo hi > no/such/dir/out.txt; echo continued'
try '[[ 2 -gt 3 ]]; echo continued'
try 'n=0; (( n > 5 )); echo continued'
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # each argument is a script for bash -c
try 'config=$(false); echo continued'
# shellcheck disable=SC2016
try 'echo "value: $(false)"; echo continued'
try '{ false; echo "in the group"; }; echo continued'

bash: line 1: no/such/dir/out.txt: No such file or directory
  -> echo hi > no/such/dir/out.txt; echo continued  exits 1
  -> [[ 2 -gt 3 ]]; echo continued  exits 1
  -> n=0; (( n > 5 )); echo continued  exits 1
  -> config=$(false); echo continued  exits 1
value: 
continued
  -> echo "value: $(false)"; echo continued  exits 0
  -> { false; echo "in the group"; }; echo continued  exits 1

A failed redirection stops the script, before the command it was attached to runs (§10.2). A false [[ ]] or (( )) stops it — both have been subject to set -e since bash 4.1, which is why (( n > 5 )) as a statement is a bug under set -e and (( n > 5 )) && … is not. An assignment whose value is a command substitution has the status of that substitution, so config=$(false) stops the script. But echo "value: $(false)" did not stop it, because the status of that line is echo's, and echo succeeded; §11.6 calls this a masked exit code. A brace group returns the status of its last command, and the script stopped on the false inside it.

Where errexit does not apply

The exceptions are the part that matters, and the manual lists them exactly. The shell does not exit if the failing command is:

Position
Why it is exempt
the test after if or elif
A condition is expected to be false sometimes; that is what it is for.
the list after while or until
The same: the loop ends when it is false.
any command in an && or || list except the last
Its status is being tested by the operator that follows it.
any command in a pipeline except the last
A pipeline's status is its last command's, unless pipefail is set (§11.7).
a command preceded by !
Its status is being inverted, which means it is being tested.

The common thread is that a command whose status is being tested is not treated as a failure, because testing is how a script handles one. Every failure in the next example is in one of those five positions, and the script finished:

set -e
if grep -q key /dev/null; then echo "found"; fi
while grep -q key /dev/null; do :; done
grep -q key /dev/null && echo "found"
grep -q key /dev/null || echo "|| ran its right-hand side"
# shellcheck disable=SC2251  # a bare ! is one of the exempt positions being listed
! grep -q key /dev/null
grep -q key /dev/null | cat
echo "every failure above was exempt, and the script is still running"

|| ran its right-hand side
every failure above was exempt, and the script is still running

That is the design, and it is sound: the whole point of if grep -q … is that grep may fail. The trouble in §11.5 comes from how far the exemption reaches — not just to the command in the tested position, but to everything that command runs.

Errexit and &&

The && rule deserves its own example, because test && action is such a common line. Errexit and && interact like this: the left-hand side is exempt, the last command is not.

set -e
[[ -f settings.conf ]] && echo "loading settings.conf"
echo "a false left-hand side of && is exempt"
touch settings.conf
[[ -f settings.conf ]] && grep -q debug settings.conf
echo "not reached: the last command of the list failed"

a false left-hand side of && is exempt

At the top level [[ -f settings.conf ]] && echo … is safe: when the file is missing, the test fails in an exempt position, the echo does not run, and the script carries on even though the line's status is 1. When the file exists and the last command fails, the script stops. The first case is the manual's rule applied exactly: the command that failed, [[, was not the last in its list, so it was exempt, and a list that returns non-zero only because an exempt command failed does not stop the script. The same && line placed as the last command of a function is a different matter again, because then its status becomes the function's return value; §11.5 shows how that ends a script.

! exempts the whole command

! inverts a pipeline's status and exempts it from set -e, even when the inverted status is non-zero:

set -e
# shellcheck disable=SC2251  # the bare ! is the demonstration
! true
echo "! true is exempt, although its status is $?"
# shellcheck disable=SC2251  # the bare ! is the demonstration
true && ! true
echo "still running: ! makes the whole command exempt, even at the end of a list"

! true is exempt, although its status is 1
still running: ! makes the whole command exempt, even at the end of a list

! true has status 1 and did not stop the script — and neither did true && ! true, whose last command failed. POSIX specifies this, and it means ! cmd on a line of its own is never a way to assert that a command fails: a line meant to stop the script when cmd succeeds must be written if cmd; then exit 1; fi, or cmd && exit 1. ShellCheck reports the bare form as SC2251.

Turn it on inside the script

set -e belongs on a line of the script, not in the shebang:

cat > backup.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash -e
( exit 3 )
echo "backup.sh kept going"
EOF
chmod +x backup.sh
./backup.sh; echo "run as ./backup.sh: status $?"
bash backup.sh; echo "run as bash backup.sh: status $?"

run as ./backup.sh: status 3
backup.sh kept going
run as bash backup.sh: status 0

The shebang #!/bin/bash -e worked when the script was run as ./backup.sh, because the kernel read the shebang and passed -e. Run as bash backup.sh — how CI systems, sudo bash, and most people debugging a script run it — the shebang is an ordinary comment, and the script ran with no errexit at all. §1.3 showed the other reason: Linux passes everything after the interpreter path as a single argument, so #!/usr/bin/env bash -e does not work there at all. Write set -e (or the whole of §11.9's header) as the script's first command.

11.4 Exit Code Conventions

A status of zero means success; beyond that, the values mean what the program says they mean. There is no single standard, but there are exit code conventions that nearly every tool follows, and a script that follows them can be used by other scripts without anyone reading its source.

What the common tools return

printf '%s\n' a b > one.txt
printf '%s\n' a c > two.txt
diff -q one.txt one.txt > /dev/null; echo "diff, identical: $?"
diff -q one.txt two.txt > /dev/null; echo "diff, different: $?"
diff -q one.txt nosuch.txt > /dev/null 2>&1; echo "diff, trouble: $?"
# shellcheck disable=SC2050,SC2170  # a malformed test on purpose
[ 1 -eq one ] 2>/dev/null; echo "test, malformed: $?"
# shellcheck disable=SC2034,SC2162  # an invalid option on purpose
read -Z line 2>/dev/null; echo "read, a bad option: $?"

diff, identical: 0
diff, different: 1
diff, trouble: 2
test, malformed: 2
read, a bad option: 2

diff follows the same three-way pattern as grep: 0 for "no differences", 1 for "different", 2 for "something went wrong". test returns 2 for a malformed expression, and every bash builtin returns 2 when it is used wrongly — an invalid option, a missing argument. The pattern generalises into the rule most programs follow:

Status
Meaning by convention
0
Success. For a predicate like grep or diff, "yes".
1
General failure. For a predicate, "no" — which is not an error.
2
Usage error (bash builtins, GNU tools), or "trouble" for a predicate that uses 1 for "no".
3–125
Specific failures a program documents for itself. curl, rsync and ssh each have a table.
126
The shell found the command but could not execute it.
127
The shell could not find the command.
128+n
The command was killed by signal n.
255
What exit -1 becomes; ssh uses it for its own errors, to keep them apart from the remote command's.

126 and 127: statuses that come from the shell

Two values are produced by the shell itself when it cannot run a command, rather than by the command:

printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/sh' 'echo hi' > tool.sh
./tool.sh 2>&1; echo "status $?"
nosuchtool 2>&1; echo "status $?"
mkdir bin
./bin 2>&1; echo "status $?"

example.sh: line 2: ./tool.sh: Permission denied
status 126
example.sh: line 3: nosuchtool: command not found
status 127
example.sh: line 5: ./bin: Is a directory
status 126

A file without execute permission and a directory both give 126: the shell found something by that name and could not execute it. A name that is not on PATH gives 127. §1.3 showed the case that surprises people: a script whose shebang names a missing interpreter gives 126, not 127, with a message about the script, because the kernel reports the failure against the file you asked to run. A script that returns 126 or 127 for its own reasons makes those cases impossible to tell apart, which is why the range from 126 up is reserved.

128+n signal exit statuses

A process killed by a signal does not exit at all, so it has no status of its own. The shell reports it as 128 plus the signal number:

for sig in INT TERM; do
  { bash -c 'kill -s "$1" "$$"' _ "$sig"; } 2>/dev/null
  status=$?
  echo "killed by SIG$sig: status $status, and kill -l $status says $(kill -l "$status")"
done

killed by SIGINT: status 130, and kill -l 130 says INT
killed by SIGTERM: status 143, and kill -l 143 says TERM

Each bash -c sends a signal to itself; the braces and 2>/dev/null around it silence a report the parent shell prints about the death, whose wording differs between systems (§12.1). SIGINT is signal 2 and SIGTERM is 15, so the statuses are 130 and 143. kill -l converts a status back to a signal name. The values that turn up most are 130 (someone pressed Ctrl-C), 143 (a service manager or timeout asked the process to stop), 137 (SIGKILL: 9, often the kernel's out-of-memory killer), and 141 (SIGPIPE: 13, which §11.7 shows is usually harmless). These 128+n signal exit statuses are why a script's own statuses stay below 126: a caller seeing 130 can conclude "interrupted" only if nothing ever returns 130 for another reason. §12.5 covers what a script should do when it receives a signal.

sysexits.h: a vocabulary for the specific failures

For the range 3–125 there is one published vocabulary. BSD's sysexits.h, shipped on macOS and in glibc, defines names from 64 up: EX_USAGE 64 (command line usage error), EX_DATAERR 65, EX_NOINPUT 66 (cannot open input), EX_UNAVAILABLE 69, EX_SOFTWARE 70, EX_CANTCREAT 73, EX_TEMPFAIL 75 (a temporary failure; the caller is invited to retry), EX_NOPERM 77 and EX_CONFIG 78. Mail software uses them, and so do some command-line tools, but neither POSIX nor GNU requires them, and plenty of well-known programs use 2 for a usage error instead.

The practical conventions for a script are these. Return 0 on success and 1 for a general failure. Return 2 (or 64) for a usage error. If callers need to tell failures apart — "retry later" from "give up", for example — pick specific values below 126, preferably the sysexits.h ones, and document them in the usage text. And never return a status the shell or the kernel uses for something else.

A usage function

A usage function prints how to call the script. The convention is that it prints to standard output when the user asked for it, with -h, and exits 0; and to standard error when the user got it wrong, and exits 2:

cat > rotate <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
readonly PROG=${0##*/}

usage() {
  cat <<USAGE
Usage: $PROG [-h] [-n KEEP] DIR
Compress all but the newest KEEP log files in DIR (default 5).
USAGE
}

keep=5
while getopts ':hn:' opt; do
  case $opt in
    h) usage; exit 0 ;;
    n) keep=$OPTARG ;;
    *) usage >&2; exit 2 ;;
  esac
done
shift $((OPTIND-1))
(( $# == 1 )) || { usage >&2; exit 2; }
echo "would keep $keep in $1"
EOF
chmod +x rotate
./rotate -n 3 logs
./rotate -h > help.txt
echo "-h: status $?, and $(grep -c '' help.txt) lines went to standard output"
./rotate -x 2> err.txt
echo "-x: status $?, and $(grep -c '' err.txt) lines went to standard error"

would keep 3 in logs
-h: status 0, and 2 lines went to standard output
-x: status 2, and 2 lines went to standard error

./rotate -h > help.txt captured two lines of help and a status of 0, because asking for help is a successful run whose output is the help. ./rotate -x printed the same text to standard error and exited 2, because that run failed. The same function serves both cases; the caller of usage decides where it goes with a redirection (§10.13), and the heredoc keeps the text readable. getopts itself is §13's subject; what matters here is that a script with a usage function answers a wrong invocation with text and a status a caller can both use.

A die function with a status

§10.13's die printed a message and exited with status 1. A die function that accepts an optional status lets a script use the conventions above without an exit on every line:

cat > import.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
readonly PROG=${0##*/}
readonly EX_USAGE=64 EX_NOINPUT=66

# die [STATUS] MESSAGE... - print MESSAGE to stderr and exit with STATUS (default 1).
die() {
  local status=1
  if [[ $1 =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; then status=$1; shift; fi
  printf '%s: error: %s\n' "$PROG" "$*" >&2
  exit "$status"
}

(( $# == 1 )) || die "$EX_USAGE" "usage: $PROG FILE"
[[ -r $1 ]] || die "$EX_NOINPUT" "cannot read $1"
grep -q '^id,' "$1" || die "$1 has no header row"
echo "importing $1"
EOF
chmod +x import.sh
./import.sh;            echo "status $?"
./import.sh rows.csv;   echo "status $?"
echo "name" > rows.csv
./import.sh rows.csv;   echo "status $?"
echo "id,name" > rows.csv
./import.sh rows.csv;   echo "status $?"

import.sh: error: usage: import.sh FILE
status 64
import.sh: error: cannot read rows.csv
status 66
import.sh: error: rows.csv has no header row
status 1
importing rows.csv
status 0

Each failure named the program and said what was wrong, on standard error, and each exited with its own status: 64 for a usage error, 66 for input that could not be opened, and the default 1 for a file that was readable but wrong. The status is optional and recognised only when the first argument is entirely digits, so die "3 files missing" is a message, not a status. The named constants cost one line and keep the numbers out of the call sites, where they would otherwise have to be looked up.

11.5 The set -e Traps

set -e is described as "exit when a command fails". The manual's full description is longer, and the gap between the two is a set of situations in which a script under set -e exits when nothing is wrong, or carries on when something is. Each of them has cost somebody an outage, and several have already appeared in this course, where they were promised to this subsection.

An arithmetic command that evaluates to zero

(( expr )) returns 1 when the expression evaluates to 0 (§7.8), and a post-increment evaluates to the old value:

set -e
count=0
(( ++count ));             echo "pre-increment from 0: count=$count"
count=$(( count + 1 ));    echo "an assignment: count=$count"
errors=0
(( errors++ )) || true;    echo "post-increment with || true: errors=$errors"
warnings=0
(( warnings++ ))
echo "not reached"

pre-increment from 0: count=1
an assignment: count=2
post-increment with || true: errors=1

(( warnings++ )) evaluated to 0 on the first increment, returned 1, and ended the script — once, the first time, which is what lets it survive testing and fail in production (§6.8 and §7.8 each met it). let behaves identically. The fixes shown are the pre-increment, which evaluates to the new value; an arithmetic assignment, whose status is always 0; and || true, which puts the command in a tested position. The assignment form is the one that cannot be broken by a later edit.

A function whose last command is a false test

A function returns the status of its last command. If that command is a test that is false in the ordinary course of things, the function "fails", and under set -e a call to it on its own line ends the script:

set -e
VERBOSE=0
info() { (( VERBOSE )) && echo "info: $*" >&2; }
echo "starting"
info "checking the release directory"
echo "not reached"

starting

info stays quiet when VERBOSE is 0, which is correct; but its last command was (( VERBOSE )) && echo …, whose status was 1, so info returned 1 and the script died on a line with nothing wrong with it. This is §10.13's info without its return 0, and it is the same trap as §2's [[ … ]] && cmd guard used as a function's last line, and §11.1's report.sh at the scale of a whole script. Two fixes:

set -e
VERBOSE=0
info() { (( VERBOSE )) && echo "info: $*" >&2; return 0; }
note() { if (( VERBOSE )); then echo "note: $*" >&2; fi; }
echo "starting"
info "checking the release directory"
note "checking again"
echo "reached: both functions return 0 when they stay quiet"

starting
reached: both functions return 0 when they stay quiet

End the function with return 0, or write the test as an if, whose status is 0 when no branch runs (§11.1). The if form is the more robust of the two, because it stays correct when someone adds a line after it.

A loop that ends a function

A loop returns the status of the last command its body ran, so a loop whose last iteration took the "false" branch of a test hands that status to the function around it — §8.10's version of the same trap:

set -e
show_admins() {
  local user
  for user in "$@"; do
    [[ $user == *:admin ]] && echo "${user%:*}"
  done
}
show_admins ada:admin bob:viewer carol:admin
echo "reached: the loop's last iteration found an admin"
show_admins ada:admin bob:viewer
echo "not reached: this time the last test was false"

ada
carol
reached: the loop's last iteration found an admin
ada

The first call ended on an admin, so its last test was true and the function returned 0. The second call's last user was a viewer, so the function returned 1 and the script stopped. Whether the script survives depends on the order of the data. The fix is the same as before: return 0 after the loop, or an if inside it.

local masks the exit status

§9.4 showed that local x=$(cmd) returns local's status, not the command's. Under set -e that means the failure is invisible — local masks the exit status and the script carries on with an empty value:

set -e
load_config() {
  # shellcheck disable=SC2155  # the masking is the demonstration
  local config=$(cat settings.conf 2>/dev/null)
  echo "load_config carried on with config=[$config]"
}
load_config
load_config_fixed() {
  local config
  config=$(cat settings.conf 2>/dev/null)
  echo "not reached"
}
load_config_fixed

load_config carried on with config=[]

settings.conf does not exist, cat failed, and load_config carried on with an empty configuration, because the status set -e saw was the status of local, which succeeded. Splitting the declaration from the assignment — local config on one line, config=$(…) on the next — makes the substitution's status the assignment's, and the script stopped where it should. ShellCheck reports the one-line form as SC2155, and that directive has to be written out in the example because the bug is the point.

declare masks the exit status in the same way, and so do export and readonly, which are also builtins that take assignments as arguments:

set -e
# shellcheck disable=SC2155,SC2034  # every line is the masking this demonstrates
declare version=$(exit 3); echo "declare:  status $?"
# shellcheck disable=SC2155
export token=$(exit 3);    echo "export:   status $?"
# shellcheck disable=SC2155,SC2034
readonly limit=$(exit 3);  echo "readonly: status $?"
# shellcheck disable=SC2034
plain=$(exit 3) || echo "a plain assignment: status $?"

declare:  status 0
export:   status 0
readonly: status 0
a plain assignment: status 3

All three returned 0 around a substitution that failed with 3. Only the plain assignment kept the 3. Because declare masks the exit status whatever its options, declare -r name=$(cmd) hides a failure just as local does. So wherever a value comes from a command, declare the name first and assign it on its own line: declare -r name=$(cmd) becomes an assignment followed by readonly name, and export name=$(cmd) becomes an assignment followed by export name.

Errexit in a condition: a function called from if, || or !

This is the trap that most undermines set -e, and the manual states it in one sentence: "If a compound command or shell function executes in a context where -e is being ignored, none of the commands executed within the compound command or function body will be affected by the -e setting." In other words, errexit in a condition is off for everything the condition runs:

set -e
deploy() {
  echo "deploy: stopping the old version"
  ( exit 1 )
  echo "deploy: starting the new version, although the stop failed"
}
if deploy; then echo "deploy reported success"; fi
deploy || echo "not printed: deploy returned 0 again"
echo "---"
deploy
echo "not reached"

deploy: stopping the old version
deploy: starting the new version, although the stop failed
deploy reported success
deploy: stopping the old version
deploy: starting the new version, although the stop failed
---
deploy: stopping the old version

Called as if deploy, the function ran with set -e switched off for its entire body. The stop step failed, the start step ran anyway, the last command succeeded, and deploy returned 0: "deploy reported success". Called as deploy || …, exactly the same happened, and the || branch never ran because the function did not fail. Only when it was called on its own line did set -e apply to its body, and the script stopped at the failed stop step.

The consequence is that a function's behaviour depends on how it is called. A function written to rely on set -e for its error handling has none whenever its caller checks it — which is precisely when the caller is trying to handle an error. Turning set -e on inside the function does not help:

set -e
careful() {
  set -e
  ( exit 1 )
  echo "careful: carried on anyway"
}
careful && echo "careful reported success"

careful: carried on anyway
careful reported success

The set -e inside careful ran, and was ignored, because "if a compound command or shell function sets -e while executing in a context where -e is ignored, that setting will not have any effect until the compound command or the command containing the function call completes". There is no option to change this. A function that must stop at its first failure has to say so itself:

set -e
deploy() {
  echo "deploy: stopping the old version"
  ( exit 1 ) || return
  echo "not reached"
}
deploy || echo "deploy failed with status $?"

deploy: stopping the old version
deploy failed with status 1

( exit 1 ) || return returns the failed command's status (a bare return uses $?, §9.5), and that works in every calling context, with set -e on or off. This is the strongest argument for writing explicit checks at the points that matter, which §11.6 turns into a habit and §11.9 into a policy.

Checking $? after the fact

A pattern that reads correctly and never runs under set -e:

set -e
touch app.log
echo "checking app.log"
grep -q ERROR app.log
# shellcheck disable=SC2181  # the $? test after the fact is the demonstration
if (( $? != 0 )); then
  echo "no errors today"
fi
echo "not reached"

checking app.log

grep found nothing, returned 1 on its own line, and set -e ended the script before the if could look at $?: "checking app.log" is the last thing it printed. The if is dead code. Write the command in the condition — if ! grep -q ERROR app.log; then — which is also what ShellCheck's SC2181 recommends for other reasons.

Other traps in the family belong to later subsections: a failure inside a command substitution that is ignored (§11.8), a pipeline whose earlier stages fail unnoticed (§11.7), and a background job whose failure is noticed only by wait (§11.8).

11.6 Checking Return Values by Hand

set -e is a net, and §11.5 showed its holes. Checking return values by hand is what closes them. The Google Shell Style Guide's rule is short: "Always check return values and give informative return values." In practice that means four idioms, and one pitfall in the most natural-looking of them.

if ! cmd and the status it throws away

if ! cmd; then is the idiomatic way to act on a failure. It has one flaw: inside the branch, $? is the status of ! cmd, which is 0:

if ! grep -q x nosuch.txt 2>/dev/null; then
  echo "if !: \$? in the branch is $?"
fi
grep -q x nosuch.txt 2>/dev/null || echo "||: \$? on the right-hand side is $?"
if grep -q x nosuch.txt 2>/dev/null; then
  :
else
  echo "else: \$? is $?"
fi

if !: $? in the branch is 0
||: $? on the right-hand side is 2
else: $? is 2

if ! cmd reported 0, which is the status of the negation. The || form and the else branch of a positive if both saw grep's real 2. So use if ! cmd when only the fact of failure matters, and one of the other two forms when the status is needed — to report it, to return it, or to tell grep's "no" from grep's "trouble".

Branching on the status

A predicate's status carries three answers, and a script that collapses them to two treats "cannot read the file" as "no". Capture the status without tripping set -e, then branch on it:

count_errors() {
  local status
  grep -q ERROR "$1" 2>/dev/null && status=0 || status=$?
  case $status in
    0) echo "$1: has errors" ;;
    1) echo "$1: clean" ;;
    *) echo "$1: could not be read (grep status $status)" >&2; return 2 ;;
  esac
}
echo "ERROR disk full" > bad.log
echo "ok" > good.log
count_errors bad.log
count_errors good.log
count_errors gone.log
echo "status $?"

bad.log: has errors
good.log: clean
gone.log: could not be read (grep status 2)
status 2

cmd && status=0 || status=$? runs cmd in a tested position, so it is safe under set -e, and leaves its real status in status either way. That is one of the few correct uses of a && b || c (§8.1), because status=0 cannot fail. The case then gives each value a meaning, and the "could not be read" branch prints to standard error and returns 2, so this function is itself a well-behaved predicate.

cmd || die: die on failure

The shortest check is cmd || die "message", for a command whose failure means the script cannot continue. The textbook case is cd:

mkdir -p project/build && touch project/{main.c,notes.txt}
cd project
# shellcheck disable=SC2164  # the unchecked cd is the demonstration
cd buid
echo "cleaning in ${PWD##*/}:" *
cd buid || { echo "cd failed; nothing cleaned" >&2; }

example.sh: line 4: cd: buid: No such file or directory
cleaning in project: build main.c notes.txt
example.sh: line 6: cd: buid: No such file or directory
cd failed; nothing cleaned

The directory is build, the script said buid, and cd failed — and the next command ran in the directory the script was already in. It listed the project's source files as the files it was about to clean. Had the line been a delete rather than an echo, it would have deleted them. ShellCheck reports an unchecked cd as SC2164. With cd buid || die … the script stops there; with set -e it would too, but only if the cd is not inside a function called from a condition (§11.5), which is why the explicit check stays even in strict scripts. Die on failure is the right response whenever continuing would act on the wrong thing.

Writing a useful error message to stderr

An error message to stderr should let the reader fix the problem without opening the script. Four rules cover it, all visible in §11.4's die:

  • Name the program. import.sh: error: … tells someone reading a CI log which of twelve scripts failed. ${0##*/} gives the name without its directory.
  • Say what was being attempted and on what. "cannot read rows.csv" rather than "read failed". Quote a value that may contain spaces.
  • Do not repeat what the failed command already said. grep: gone.log: No such file or directory is already on standard error; a second line saying "file not found" adds nothing. Add context the command could not know: which step, which file list, what to do next.
  • Put it on standard error, and exit non-zero. §10.13's rule, which is what lets a caller capture the output and test the status.

A masked exit code

A masked exit code is a status that was lost because another command's status replaced it. §11.5 showed local. There are several more ways, and none of them produces a message:

# shellcheck disable=SC2320  # each $? is read deliberately
echo "result: $(exit 3)"; echo "an argument substitution: $?"
# shellcheck disable=SC2034
out=$(exit 3); echo "an assignment keeps it: $?"
( exit 3 ) | tee copy.txt; echo "piped through tee: $?"
f() { ( exit 3 ); echo "done"; }; f; echo "a function that echoes last: $?"

result: 
an argument substitution: 0
an assignment keeps it: 3
piped through tee: 0
done
a function that echoes last: 0

A command substitution inside an argument is masked by the command it is an argument to. An assignment keeps the status. A pipeline reports its last command's status, so piping through tee to keep a log hides the failure of the command being logged — §11.7's pipefail is the remedy. And a function that does something after the failing command returns that something's status. Each of these reads as correct, which is what makes a masked exit code dangerous.

Keeping a status and passing it on

When a failure must be reported rather than acted on at once, save the status on the line that produced it, do the reporting, and return it:

run_quiet() {
  local output status
  output=$("$@" 2>&1) && status=0 || status=$?
  if (( status != 0 )); then
    printf '%s\n' "$output" >&2
    echo "$1 failed with status $status" >&2
  fi
  return "$status"
}
set -e
run_quiet bash -c 'echo "compiling"; echo "error: missing header" >&2; exit 4' || echo "caller saw $?"
run_quiet true && echo "quiet on success"

compiling
error: missing header
bash failed with status 4
caller saw 4
quiet on success

run_quiet captures both streams (§10.4), saves the status without tripping set -e, prints the captured output and a summary only on failure, and returns the command's own status, so the caller saw 4 and decided what to do. $1 in the summary is the command's name — here bash, which is why the message says bash failed. This is §10's exercise 2, quietly, made safe to call from a strict script.

11.7 Pipelines: PIPESTATUS and pipefail

The exit status of a pipeline is the exit status of its last command. §2.4 showed the consequence in one line; here it is in a script, where the exit status of a pipeline is all that set -e and $? can see:

printf '%s\n' "b 2" "a 1" > scores.txt
grep '[0-9]' nosuch.txt | sort > sorted.txt
echo "the pipeline: $?"
grep '[0-9]' nosuch.txt 2>/dev/null | sort > sorted.txt
echo "every stage: ${PIPESTATUS[*]}"
echo "PIPESTATUS again, after that echo: ${PIPESTATUS[*]}"

grep: nosuch.txt: No such file or directory
the pipeline: 0
every stage: 2 0
PIPESTATUS again, after that echo: 0

grep failed with 2, sort sorted nothing successfully, and the pipeline reported 0. Under set -e the script would have carried on with an empty sorted.txt. The other stages' statuses are not lost, though — they are in an array.

PIPESTATUS

PIPESTATUS holds the status of every command in the most recent foreground pipeline, in order. A simple command counts as a pipeline of one, so the next command overwrites the array, exactly as it overwrites $?: the second echo above printed the status of the first echo. Copy the whole array on the line after the pipeline, before anything else runs:

grep '[0-9]' nosuch.txt 2>/dev/null | sort | head -n 5
statuses=("${PIPESTATUS[@]}")
for i in "${!statuses[@]}"; do
  echo "stage $i exited ${statuses[i]}"
done
(( statuses[0] <= 1 )) || echo "grep failed outright, not merely found nothing" >&2

stage 0 exited 2
stage 1 exited 0
stage 2 exited 0
grep failed outright, not merely found nothing

statuses=("${PIPESTATUS[@]}") takes the copy; after that the values can be inspected at leisure. The final check distinguishes grep's "no match", which is fine, from its "error", which is not. This is the form the Google style guide recommends when a script must treat each stage's failure differently.

set -o pipefail

Most scripts want something simpler: a pipeline that fails if any of its stages failed. set -o pipefail gives exactly that. The pipeline's status becomes that of the rightmost command that failed, or 0 if all of them succeeded:

set -o pipefail
grep '[0-9]' nosuch.txt 2>/dev/null | sort > sorted.txt
echo "with pipefail: $?"
( exit 2 ) | ( exit 3 ) | true
echo "rightmost failure wins: $?"
true | true | true
echo "all succeed: $?"

with pipefail: 2
rightmost failure wins: 3
all succeed: 0

The same pipeline now reported grep's 2. With two failing stages the rightmost wins, 3 rather than 2. pipefail has been in bash since 3.0, and POSIX added it in the 2024 edition, but /bin/sh implementations are still catching up: Debian's dash 0.5.12 accepts it, and the dash that ships with macOS rejects it with Illegal option -o pipefail. §19 covers what that means for a portable script.

§9.12 ended with a function piped into a loop whose failure the script did not notice, and promised pipefail as the cure. Here it is on the same shape:

cat > rotate.sh <<'EOF'
set -e
stale_logs() {
  [[ -d $1 ]] || { echo "no such directory: $1" >&2; return 1; }
  printf '%s\n' "$1"/*.log
}
stale_logs "$1" | while IFS= read -r f; do echo "would compress $f"; done
echo "rotate finished"
EOF
bash rotate.sh missing
echo "set -e alone: status $?"
bash -o pipefail rotate.sh missing
echo "with pipefail: status $?"

no such directory: missing
rotate finished
set -e alone: status 0
no such directory: missing
with pipefail: status 1

set -e alone could not see the function's return 1, because it was not the last stage of the pipeline; the script printed "rotate finished" and exited 0. With pipefail the pipeline's status was 1, and set -e stopped the script there.

When pipefail makes things worse: SIGPIPE

A reader that exits before its writer has finished closes the pipe. The writer's next write gets SIGPIPE and the writer is killed, which is how head -n 1 can stop an infinite producer. Without pipefail that is invisible. With it, the writer's 141 becomes the pipeline's status:

set -o pipefail
seq 1 100000 | grep -q '^1$'
echo "grep -q stopped reading early: $?, stages ${PIPESTATUS[*]}"
seq 1 100000 | grep '^1$' > /dev/null
echo "grep read everything: $?"
seq 1 100000 | head -n 1 > /dev/null
echo "head -n 1: $?, and kill -l says $(kill -l 141)"

grep -q stopped reading early: 141, stages 141 0
grep read everything: 0
head -n 1: 141, and kill -l says PIPE

grep -q exits as soon as it finds a match, and seq, still writing, was killed with SIGPIPE: status 141, and kill -l 141 names the signal. Removing -q fixed it, because grep without -q reads its whole input. head -n 1 failed the same way. This is the case BashFAQ/105 calls a race: whether the writer is still writing when the reader leaves depends on how much it writes, so a pipeline that passes with ten lines of input can fail with a hundred thousand. A small input fits in the pipe's buffer, the writer finishes before the reader exits, and the failure never appears in testing.

Three responses, in order of preference. Let the reader consume everything — drop -q, or use sed -n 1p instead of head -n 1, at the cost of reading input nobody needs. Avoid the pipe — grep -q pattern file rather than cat file | grep -q pattern. Or accept 141 from a stage whose early termination is expected:

set -o pipefail
first_line() {
  "$@" | head -n 1
  local -a st=("${PIPESTATUS[@]}")
  (( st[0] == 0 || st[0] == 141 )) || return "${st[0]}"
  return "${st[1]}"
}
first_line seq 1 100000
echo "status $?"
first_line bash -c 'echo "partial"; exit 5'
echo "status $?"

1
status 0
partial
status 5

first_line treats a SIGPIPE on the producer as success and still reports a real failure, here the 5 from a command that printed one line and then failed. That is more code than most pipelines deserve, which is why the first two responses come first.

11.8 Subshells, Command Substitution and inherit_errexit

set -e applies "to the shell environment and each subshell environment separately". A subshell has its own copy of the option, and what it does with it depends on what kind of subshell it is.

Errexit in a subshell

A ( … ) subshell inherits set -e. A failure inside it ends the subshell, the subshell's status is the failed command's, and the parent then decides what to do with that status by its own rules:

set -e
( echo "first subshell"; ( exit 3 ); echo "first subshell carried on" ) || echo "not printed"
( echo "second subshell"; ( exit 3 ); echo "not reached" )
echo "not reached either: the parent saw status 3"

first subshell
first subshell carried on
second subshell

The first subshell was on the left of ||, a tested position, so — the §11.5 trap again, from the other side — errexit in a subshell there is ignored for the subshell's whole body. It ran past ( exit 3 ), printed "first subshell carried on", and returned 0, so the || branch never ran. The second subshell was on its own line, so errexit applied inside it: it stopped at the failure and returned 3, and the parent, also under set -e, exited with 3. A subshell does not stop its parent directly; its status does.

The same rule applies to a subshell used as an if condition:

set -e
if ( ( exit 3 ); echo "the subshell carried on" ); then
  echo "and reported success"
fi

the subshell carried on
and reported success

A subshell does not escape the tested-position rule by being a separate process. It inherits the fact that errexit is being ignored.

Errexit and command substitution

A command substitution runs in a subshell too, but bash treats it differently: outside POSIX mode it clears set -e inside every $( … ). The interaction of errexit and command substitution is therefore that failures inside the substitution are ignored, and only its final status reaches the parent:

set -e
version=$( ( exit 3 ); echo "1.4.2" )
echo "version=$version, and the script is still running"
shopt -s inherit_errexit
version=$( ( exit 3 ); echo "1.4.2" )
echo "not reached"

version=1.4.2, and the script is still running

The first substitution ran ( exit 3 ), carried on, printed 1.4.2, and exited 0, so version got a value and the assignment succeeded. After shopt -s inherit_errexit the substitution kept set -e, stopped at the failure, exited 3, and the assignment's status stopped the script.

inherit_errexit

The inherit_errexit option, added in bash 4.4, makes command substitutions inherit set -e as ( … ) subshells already do. POSIX mode turns it on automatically, and dash behaves the same way:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the body is expanded by the shell that runs it
body='set -e; v=$( ( exit 3 ); echo ran ); echo "v=$v"'
bash -c "$body";          echo "bash: status $?"
bash --posix -c "$body";  echo "bash --posix: status $?"
dash -c "$body";          echo "dash: status $?"

v=ran
bash: status 0
bash --posix: status 3
dash: status 3

Plain bash printed v=ran; bash --posix and dash both stopped inside the substitution and exited 3. Where it matters most is a function whose output is captured, which is how §9.6 returns a value:

set -e
shopt -s inherit_errexit
release_name() {
  local tag
  tag=$(grep -m1 '^v' tags.txt)
  echo "release-${tag#v}"
}
printf '%s\n' v1.4.2 v1.4.1 > tags.txt
name=$(release_name); echo "got $name"
: > tags.txt
name=$(release_name); echo "not reached: got $name"

got release-1.4.2

The first call found a tag and produced release-1.4.2. The second found no tags: grep failed inside release_name, and with inherit_errexit that stopped the function, the substitution returned 1, and the assignment ended the script. Without the option, release_name would have carried on and printed release- — a plausible-looking name for a release that does not exist.

Two more rules for substitutions

When a line contains only assignments, its status is that of the last command substitution in it:

# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # only the statuses matter here
a=$(exit 3) b=$(true); echo "a=\$(exit 3) b=\$(true): $?"
a=$(true) b=$(exit 3); echo "a=\$(true) b=\$(exit 3): $?"

a=$(exit 3) b=$(true): 0
a=$(true) b=$(exit 3): 3

A failure in the first of two substitutions on one line is masked by the second. Put each assignment that runs a command on its own line.

And a background job is outside set -e entirely until something waits for it:

set -e
( exit 3 ) &
echo "a failing background job does not stop the script"
wait "$!"
echo "not reached: wait returned the job's status"

a failing background job does not stop the script

( exit 3 ) & failed without affecting the script, because a background job's status is not known when the next line runs. wait "$!" returned the job's status, and set -e acted on that. §17 builds on this: a script that starts parallel work must wait for each job and check what it returns.

11.9 Strict Mode: set -euo pipefail and the Arguments Against It

Strict mode is the name for turning on set -e, set -u and pipefail together at the top of a script. set -euo pipefail is its usual spelling — three options, one line. Aaron Maxwell's article "Use Bash Strict Mode (Unless You Love Debugging)" named it the unofficial strict mode and recommended a second line with it:

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
IFS=$'\n\t'

The unofficial strict mode's set line is widely adopted and this course uses it. Its IFS line is not recommended here. Its purpose is to stop an unquoted expansion splitting on spaces, which §3 fixed at the source by quoting; and it breaks every read that splits on spaces:

line="ada 36"
read -r name age <<< "$line"
echo "default IFS: name=[$name] age=[$age]"
IFS=$'\n\t'
read -r name age <<< "$line"
echo "strict-mode IFS: name=[$name] age=[$age]"

default IFS: name=[ada] age=[36]
strict-mode IFS: name=[ada 36] age=[]

With the default IFS, read split "ada 36" into two fields. With the strict-mode IFS, the space is not a separator, so name got the whole line and age got nothing. A script that quotes its expansions gets nothing from the second line and loses a working read.

The arguments against strict mode

The arguments against strict mode are serious, and most of them are §11.5. Greg Wooledge's BashFAQ/105, "Why doesn't set -e (or set -o errexit, or trap ERR) do what I expected?", catalogues the surprises — the arithmetic increment, the && at the end of a function, the ignored failures in a function called from a condition, expr returning 1 for a zero result, the SIGPIPE race under pipefail — and ends with its author's recommendation: "don't use set -e. Add your own error checking instead." The points behind that recommendation:

  • Its rules are not the rules people believe. "Exits on any failure" is wrong in both directions, as §11.5 showed.
  • It is action at a distance. Whether a line in a function stops the script depends on how the caller called the function, which the function cannot see.
  • It changed between versions. [[ and (( were brought under it in bash 4.1, command substitutions have their own option since 4.4, and different shells disagree on the details.
  • It creates false confidence. A script with set -e at the top looks as if it handles errors, and the reviewer reads no further.

The counter-argument is that a script without set -e fails open: every unchecked command, including the ones nobody thought could fail, is ignored. With set -e, most of those stop the script, and the exceptions are a finite list that this section has now measured.

This course takes a position between the two: use strict mode as a net, and never rely on it for correctness. Every command whose failure matters is checked explicitly (§11.6) — especially inside functions, which may be called from a condition — and set -e catches the ones nobody thought of. set -u and pipefail have no comparable downside and are always worth having.

Ignoring a failure on purpose

Under strict mode, a command that is allowed to fail must say so. || true does it, and so does || : — the null command from §2.8, used here to mean "this failure is expected":

set -euo pipefail
printf '%s\n' "INFO start" "INFO done" > app.log
errors=$(grep -c ERROR app.log || true)
echo "errors: $errors"
# The lock may not exist yet; any failure to remove it is fine.
rmdir run.lock 2>/dev/null || :
echo "still running"
errors=$(grep -c ERROR app.log)
echo "not reached"

errors: 0
still running

grep -c prints a count and exits 1 when the count is 0, so errors=$(grep -c ERROR app.log) ends a strict script whenever the log is clean. || true inside the substitution keeps the printed 0 and discards the status. rmdir run.lock 2>/dev/null || : removes a lock that may not exist. Both lines are an assertion that the failure is harmless, so write a comment saying why when it is not obvious — a bare || true also hides the failures that are not harmless.

When a failure must be observed rather than ignored, and the command is not easily put in a condition, switch set -e off around it:

set -euo pipefail
set +e
output=$(bash -c 'echo "partial"; exit 5' 2>&1)
status=$?
set -e
echo "captured [$output] and status $status"

captured [partial] and status 5

The status is saved on the line after the command, before set -e comes back on. §11.6's cmd && status=0 || status=$? does the same in one line; the set +e form is clearer when several lines need the exemption.

A header for every script

The header this course uses from here on:

mkdir -p tool/lib
printf '%s\n' 'log() { printf "%s\n" "$*" >&2; }' > tool/lib/log.sh
cat > tool/deploy <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -Eeuo pipefail
shopt -s inherit_errexit

SCRIPT_DIR=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)
readonly SCRIPT_DIR
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source "$SCRIPT_DIR/lib/log.sh"
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source "$SCRIPT_DIR/lib/config.sh"
log "deploying"
EOF
bash tool/deploy 2>/dev/null
echo "status $?"
echo 'DEPLOY_TARGET=staging' > tool/lib/config.sh
bash tool/deploy
echo "status $?"

status 1
deploying
status 0

set -Eeuo pipefail is strict mode plus -E, which §11.10 explains. shopt -s inherit_errexit closes §11.8's gap. Both come before the first source, so a library that cannot be found stops the script instead of letting it run without its functions: the first run exited 1 at the source of the missing config.sh and never reached log. (Its No such file or directory message is discarded in the example only because it names the absolute path of the directory the example ran in.) That is what §9.13 meant by making a library's failure to load fatal by default. With the file present, the script ran.

11.10 The ERR Trap and errtrace

set -e exits without saying where. The ERR trap is the mechanism for saying it: trap 'command' ERR runs command whenever a command fails, under exactly the conditions in which set -e would exit. §12 covers traps in general; this is the one that belongs to error handling.

When the ERR trap fires

trap 'echo "ERR: \"$BASH_COMMAND\" exited $? on line $LINENO" >&2' ERR
grep -q needle /dev/null
if grep -q needle /dev/null; then :; fi
grep -q needle /dev/null || true
echo "the script carried on: an ERR trap reports, it does not stop anything"

ERR: "grep -q needle /dev/null" exited 1 on line 2
the script carried on: an ERR trap reports, it does not stop anything

A trap ERR handler ran for the failed grep on its own line, and not for the one in the if or the one followed by || true, because those are the same exempt positions as §11.3's table. Inside the trap, $? is the failed command's status, $LINENO is the line it was on, and $BASH_COMMAND is the command itself. Note that the trap ERR fires and the script continues: on its own the trap only reports.

Combined with set -e, it reports and then the script exits with the failed command's status:

cat > build.sh <<'EOF'
set -e
trap 'echo "${0##*/}: line $LINENO: \"$BASH_COMMAND\" exited $?" >&2' ERR
echo "compiling"
grep -q main src.txt
echo "not reached"
EOF
touch src.txt
bash build.sh
echo "status $?"

compiling
build.sh: line 4: "grep -q main src.txt" exited 1
status 1

The script stopped at the failed grep, and the trap said which line and which command. The status is still 1: the trap runs before the shell exits, and does not change the status unless it calls exit itself.

errtrace: the trap inside functions

An ERR trap is not inherited by functions, command substitutions or subshells, unless the errtrace option — set -E, or set -o errtrace — is on. Without it, a failure inside a function is invisible to the trap:

cat > build.sh <<'EOF'
set -e
trap 'echo "ERR: \"$BASH_COMMAND\" exited $? on line $LINENO" >&2' ERR
compile() {
  echo "compiling"
  grep -q main src.txt
}
compile
EOF
touch src.txt
bash build.sh;    echo "without errtrace: status $?"
bash -E build.sh; echo "with errtrace: status $?"

compiling
without errtrace: status 1
compiling
ERR: "grep -q main src.txt" exited 1 on line 5
with errtrace: status 1

Without errtrace the script exited with status 1 and no report at all: set -e stopped the script inside compile, where the ERR trap did not apply. With -E the trap ran inside the function and reported the grep and its line. Since most of a well-structured script's work happens inside functions, an ERR trap without -E misses most failures, which is why the header in §11.9 includes it. errtrace has been in bash since 3.0.

Keep the status, and read it first

A trap that calls a function must capture $? before doing anything else, because the first command in the handler replaces it — §11.1's rule, in the place it is easiest to forget:

cat > job.sh <<'EOF'
set -Ee
on_err() {
  local status=$?
  echo "job.sh: line $1: \"$2\" exited $status" >&2
}
trap 'on_err "$LINENO" "$BASH_COMMAND"' ERR
( exit 7 )
EOF
bash job.sh
echo "status $?"

job.sh: line 7: "( exit 7 )" exited 7
status 7

on_err reads $? in its first line, into a local, declared on its own line of the function (§11.5), and receives $LINENO and $BASH_COMMAND as arguments, expanded when the trap fires. The script exited with 7, the failed command's status, so a caller sees the real reason. §12.6 extends this handler with the call stack from §9.10's FUNCNAME and BASH_LINENO, so a failure deep in a library reports the whole chain of calls that led to it.

11.11 The Error-Handling Table

Where set -e and the ERR trap apply, where they do not, and the options that change them.

Construct
Under set -e, and the rule that is easiest to get wrong
cmd on its own line
Exits with cmd's status, silently (§11.3).
if cmd · while cmd · ! cmd
Exempt — and so is everything a function or group called there runs (§11.5).
a && b · a || b
a is exempt; b is not. As a function's last line, the list's status is the function's (§11.3, §11.5).
a | b
Only b counts, unless set -o pipefail; then the rightmost failure. SIGPIPE is 141 (§11.7).
(( n++ )) · let
Fails when the value is 0. Use n=$(( n + 1 )) (§11.5).
local x=$(cmd)
local, declare, export and readonly mask the status. Declare, then assign (§11.5).
x=$(cmd)
Exits if cmd's status is non-zero; with several substitutions, the last one counts (§11.8).
echo "$(cmd)"
Never exits: the status is echo's (§11.6).
inside $( … )
set -e is off unless shopt -s inherit_errexit or POSIX mode (§11.8).
( … )
Inherits set -e, stops at a failure, and the parent sees the status (§11.8).
cmd &
Ignored until wait, which returns its status (§11.8).
$undefined under set -u
Always an error, even in a condition; "$@" and empty arrays are exempt (§11.2).
trap … ERR
Fires where set -e would exit; inherited by functions and subshells only with set -E (§11.10).
cmd || true · cmd || :
Declares a failure harmless. Say why (§11.9).
#!/bin/bash -e
Lost when the script is run as bash script. Use set -Eeuo pipefail in the file (§11.3, §11.9).

And the statuses a script should return: 0 for success, 1 for failure, 2 (or EX_USAGE, 64) for a usage error, specific documented values below 126 when callers need to tell failures apart, and never 126, 127 or 128 and up, which belong to the shell and the kernel (§11.4).

Exercises

1. The deploy that reported success. This script builds and publishes a release. Run from an empty directory, it prints "deployed" and exits 0, although there is no HEAD.txt and no dist directory. Find every reason it did not stop, and rewrite it so that each missing piece stops it with a useful message.

cat > deploy.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e
build() {
  # shellcheck disable=SC2155
  local commit=$(git_head)
  echo "building $commit"
}
git_head() { grep -m1 '^commit ' HEAD.txt | cut -d' ' -f2; }
publish() {
  cd dist
  echo "publishing $(ls | wc -l | tr -d ' ') file(s)"
}
if build && publish; then
  echo "deployed"
fi
EOF
mkdir release && cd release
bash ../deploy.sh
echo "status $?"
Solution 
cat > deploy.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e
build() {
  # shellcheck disable=SC2155
  local commit=$(git_head)
  echo "building $commit"
}
git_head() { grep -m1 '^commit ' HEAD.txt | cut -d' ' -f2; }
publish() {
  cd dist
  echo "publishing $(ls | wc -l | tr -d ' ') file(s)"
}
if build && publish; then
  echo "deployed"
fi
EOF
mkdir release && cd release
bash ../deploy.sh
echo "status $?"

grep: HEAD.txt: No such file or directory
building 
../deploy.sh: line 10: cd: dist: No such file or directory
publishing 0 file(s)
deployed
status 0

Four problems, each from this section. The functions are called as if build && publish, so set -e is off inside both of them for their whole bodies (§11.5). Inside build, local commit=$(git_head) masks the substitution's status (§11.5) — and even without local, git_head's pipeline would report cut's success rather than grep's failure without pipefail (§11.7). cd dist is unchecked, so publish counted the files in the current directory, which happened to be none (§11.6).

cat > deploy.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -Eeuo pipefail
shopt -s inherit_errexit
die() { printf 'deploy: error: %s\n' "$*" >&2; exit 1; }
build() {
  local commit
  commit=$(git_head)
  [[ -n $commit ]] || die "HEAD.txt names no commit"
  echo "building $commit"
}
git_head() { grep -m1 '^commit ' HEAD.txt | cut -d' ' -f2; }
publish() {
  cd dist || die "no dist directory"
  echo "publishing $(find . -type f | wc -l | tr -d ' ') file(s)"
}
build
publish
echo "deployed"
EOF
bash deploy.sh
echo "status $?"
echo "commit 4f2a9c1" > HEAD.txt
bash deploy.sh
echo "status $?"
mkdir dist && touch dist/app.js
bash deploy.sh
echo "status $?"

grep: HEAD.txt: No such file or directory
status 2
building 4f2a9c1
deploy.sh: line 13: cd: dist: No such file or directory
deploy: error: no dist directory
status 1
building 4f2a9c1
publishing 1 file(s)
deployed
status 0

The functions are called on their own lines, so set -e applies inside them; commit is declared and assigned separately; pipefail and inherit_errexit make grep's failure inside $(git_head) stop the script — the first run exited 2, grep's status, with grep's own message; an empty commit is caught by an explicit check; and cd dist || die names the problem. find . -type f replaces ls, which ShellCheck advises against parsing (SC2012) and which would also have counted directories. Each missing piece now stops the script at the right place, and the last run shows it still succeeds when everything is there.

2. A tally that dies on a clean log. tally.sh counts ERROR lines across log files under strict mode. Run on b.log a.log or a.log b.log, it prints nothing and exits 1. Find both bugs, and make a missing file exit with status 2.

cat > tally.sh <<'EOF'
set -euo pipefail
total=0
for f in "$@"; do
  n=$(grep -c ERROR "$f")
  (( total += n ))
done
echo "total: $total"
EOF
printf '%s\n' "INFO ok" > a.log
printf '%s\n' "ERROR x" "ERROR y" > b.log
bash tally.sh b.log a.log; echo "status $?"
bash tally.sh a.log b.log; echo "status $?"
Solution 
cat > tally.sh <<'EOF'
set -euo pipefail
total=0
for f in "$@"; do
  n=$(grep -c ERROR "$f")
  (( total += n ))
done
echo "total: $total"
EOF
printf '%s\n' "INFO ok" > a.log
printf '%s\n' "ERROR x" "ERROR y" > b.log
bash tally.sh b.log a.log; echo "status $?"
bash tally.sh a.log b.log; echo "status $?"

status 1
status 1

The first bug is grep -c: it prints 0 and exits 1 when there are no matches, so the assignment fails on a.log in either order. || true inside the substitution is the obvious fix, and it reveals the second bug:

cat > tally.sh <<'EOF'
set -euo pipefail
total=0
for f in "$@"; do
  n=$(grep -c ERROR "$f" || true)
  (( total += n ))
done
echo "total: $total"
EOF
printf '%s\n' "INFO ok" > a.log
printf '%s\n' "ERROR x" "ERROR y" > b.log
bash tally.sh b.log a.log; echo "status $?"
bash tally.sh a.log b.log; echo "status $?"

total: 2
status 0
status 1

In the order b.log a.log, total was already 2 when a.log added 0, and (( total += 0 )) evaluated to 2: true. In the order a.log b.log, it evaluated to 0 + 0, and an arithmetic command that evaluates to 0 returns 1 (§11.5). Whether the script works depends on the order of its arguments. The fix is an arithmetic assignment, whose status is always 0:

cat > tally.sh <<'EOF'
set -euo pipefail
total=0
for f in "$@"; do
  n=$(grep -c ERROR "$f") || (( $? == 1 )) || exit 2
  total=$(( total + n ))
done
echo "total: $total"
EOF
printf '%s\n' "INFO ok" > a.log
printf '%s\n' "ERROR x" "ERROR y" > b.log
bash tally.sh a.log b.log; echo "status $?"
bash tally.sh a.log gone.log; echo "status $?"

total: 2
status 0
grep: gone.log: No such file or directory
status 2

|| (( $? == 1 )) || exit 2 accepts grep's "no match" and turns anything else into status 2, which || true would have hidden: a missing file now stops the script with grep's own message instead of counting as zero errors.

3. A step runner. Write step NAME COMMAND [ARG...], which runs a command, prints NAME ok on standard output or NAME FAILED (status N) on standard error, and returns the command's status. It must work in a script under set -euo pipefail, and a caller must be able to decide whether a failed step stops the script.

Solution 
set -euo pipefail
# step NAME COMMAND [ARG...] - run COMMAND, report NAME's outcome, return its status.
step() {
  local name=$1 status=0
  shift
  "$@" || status=$?
  if (( status == 0 )); then
    printf '%-10s ok\n' "$name"
  else
    printf '%-10s FAILED (status %d)\n' "$name" "$status" >&2
  fi
  return "$status"
}
step lint true
step test bash -c 'exit 3' || echo "the caller decides: carrying on after test"
step package true
step deploy bash -c 'exit 5'
echo "not reached"

lint       ok
test       FAILED (status 3)
the caller decides: carrying on after test
package    ok
deploy     FAILED (status 5)

"$@" || status=$? runs the command in a tested position, so a failure is recorded rather than fatal, and status starts at 0 so the success case needs no branch. The function returns the command's status, and the caller chooses: step test … || echo … carried on after a failure, while step deploy … on its own line stopped the script with the command's status, 5. The printf '%-10s' pads the name so the results line up (§14).

One limit follows from §11.5: if COMMAND is a shell function, it runs in a tested position, so set -e is off inside it. A function passed to step must check its own failures, as §11.6 recommends for every function anyway.

4. A one-line failure report. Write an ERR handler for a strict script that prints SCRIPT: line N: \COMMAND` exited S` on standard error and exits with the failed command's status. Test it with a failure inside a function.

Solution 
cat > job.sh <<'EOF'
set -Eeuo pipefail
on_err() {
  local status=$? line=$1 cmd=$2
  printf '%s: line %s: `%s` exited %d\n' "${0##*/}" "$line" "$cmd" "$status" >&2
  exit "$status"
}
trap 'on_err "$LINENO" "$BASH_COMMAND"' ERR
fetch() {
  echo "fetching"
  grep -q '^ok$' response.txt
}
fetch
echo "not reached"
EOF
echo "error" > response.txt
bash job.sh
echo "status $?"

fetching
job.sh: line 10: `grep -q '^ok$' response.txt` exited 1
status 1

set -E makes the trap reach inside fetch, which is where the failure happened, and the reported line is the grep's line within the file (§11.10). on_err saves $? before anything else, receives $LINENO and $BASH_COMMAND as arguments expanded when the trap fired, and calls exit with the saved status. The exit is not strictly needed under set -e, which would exit with the same status once the handler finished, but it makes the handler correct in a script that uses the trap without set -e. §12.6 adds the call stack.

SECTION 12

Traps, Signals and Cleanup

A script that is interrupted halfway through leaves its half-finished work behind. The temporary file it was building stays in /tmp, the lock directory it created stays in place and blocks the next run, the background job it started keeps running with nobody to collect it, and the caller that pressed Ctrl-C may not even find out the script was interrupted. §1.1 called half-completed work the default failure mode of a shell script, and promised that cleanup has to be arranged explicitly. This section is that arrangement.

The mechanism is the trap builtin, which runs a piece of code when the shell receives a signal or reaches one of four events bash defines itself: EXIT, ERR, DEBUG and RETURN. §11.10 covered the ERR trap, because it belongs to error handling. This section covers everything else: what a signal is and which ones a script meets, how trap works, the EXIT trap as the one place cleanup belongs, how to exit after a signal so that the caller knows what happened, why a signal can sit unhandled for as long as a foreground command runs, how traps behave in subshells and child processes, how to send signals with kill, and the two debugging traps. It ends with a long-running script that reloads its configuration on SIGHUP, reports progress on SIGUSR1, and stops cleanly on SIGTERM.

linux §7.4–§7.7 covered signals as a system administrator meets them: kill, killall, zombies, job control at the prompt. This section is about the other side — a bash script as the process receiving the signal, and as the parent responsible for the processes it started. §16 builds on it with processes, subshells and the environment, and §17 with concurrency and locking, which leans on everything here about wait and process groups. Every claim below was measured under bash 5.3 on macOS and bash 5.2 on Debian. They agreed on every example except two, which show behaviour new in 5.3 — trap -P with BASH_TRAPSIG, and a bare exit inside a trap — and are labelled where they appear.

12.1 Signal Handling in a Script: What a Signal Is

A signal is a small, numbered notification that the kernel delivers to a process. It carries no data beyond its number. Some come from the kernel itself (a write to a pipe nobody reads produces SIGPIPE), some from the terminal (Ctrl-C produces SIGINT), and most of the ones a script cares about from another process calling kill: a service manager stopping a service, a container runtime stopping a container, a user in another terminal, or the script itself.

Every signal has a default action, which is what happens to a process that has made no arrangement for it. For most signals the default is to terminate the process. A process can change that for any signal except two: it can catch the signal, running a handler of its own instead, or it can ignore it. Signal handling in a script means doing that from bash, and the tool is trap. Everything else in this section follows from those three possible dispositions: default, caught, ignored.

Signal name versus number

Each signal has a name, like SIGTERM, and a number. The names are standard; most of the numbers are not. POSIX fixes the numbers of only seven signals (as an XSI extension, for kill and trap to accept): 1 SIGHUP, 2 SIGINT, 3 SIGQUIT, 6 SIGABRT, 9 SIGKILL, 14 SIGALRM and 15 SIGTERM. Every other number varies between systems. The kill -l builtin converts in both directions:

for sig in HUP INT QUIT KILL TERM; do
  n=$(kill -l "$sig")
  printf 'SIG%-4s is signal %2d; a process it kills reports status %d\n' "$sig" "$n" $(( 128 + n ))
done
kill -l 143
kill -l 137

SIGHUP  is signal  1; a process it kills reports status 129
SIGINT  is signal  2; a process it kills reports status 130
SIGQUIT is signal  3; a process it kills reports status 131
SIGKILL is signal  9; a process it kills reports status 137
SIGTERM is signal 15; a process it kills reports status 143
TERM
KILL

Given a name, kill -l prints the number; given a number, the name. Given an exit status above 128, it subtracts 128 first — which is why kill -l 143 says TERM. §11.4 introduced that encoding: a process killed by signal n has no exit status of its own, and the shell reports it as 128 + n. The same numbers are why a script's own exit statuses should stay below 126.

The case that bites is SIGUSR1. It is signal 30 on macOS and signal 10 on Linux, and SIGUSR2 is 31 and 12. A script that writes kill -10 "$pid" sends SIGUSR1 on Linux and SIGBUS on macOS. The rule is short: write signal names, never numbers, except for those seven, and when you need to print a status caused by a signal, print its name with kill -l "$status", which is what every example in this section does. kill -l with no argument lists every signal the system has, in a layout that differs between systems — 31 signals here on macOS, 64 including the real-time signals on Debian — and trap -l prints the same list.

What the default actions do to a script

Each of the common signals ends a script that has no trap for it, and the status says which one did it:

for sig in HUP INT TERM KILL; do
  { bash -c 'echo "  working"; kill -s "$1" "$$"; echo "  never printed"' _ "$sig"; } 2>/dev/null
  status=$?
  echo "SIG$sig: status $status ($(kill -l "$status"))"
done
bash -c 'kill -s QUIT "$$"; echo "  SIGQUIT: bash ignored it and carried on"'

  working
SIGHUP: status 129 (HUP)
  working
SIGINT: status 130 (INT)
  working
SIGTERM: status 143 (TERM)
  working
SIGKILL: status 137 (KILL)
  SIGQUIT: bash ignored it and carried on

SIGHUP, SIGINT, SIGTERM and SIGKILL each ended the script before its last echo, with status 129, 130, 143 and 137. The last line is the exception: bash ignores SIGQUIT in all cases, so a script survives kill -s QUIT. That comes from bash itself, not from the default action — SIGQUIT's default is to terminate with a core dump, and the programs a script runs still get that default, so Ctrl-\ at a terminal still stops a foreground command. SIGQUIT is the terminal's "quit, and leave a core file for debugging" key, and it is almost never something a script should handle.

The example used kill -s NAME to send the signal and { …; } 2>/dev/null around the child. The braces matter: when a child dies of a signal, the parent shell prints a report about it, and the wording differs between systems — Terminated: 15 followed by the command on macOS, Terminated alone on Debian. The report is written by the parent, so a redirection on the child command does not silence it; one on a group around the command does, because the report is printed while the group's redirection is in force. Examples that kill a child do this so that their output is the same everywhere.

SIGKILL cannot be trapped

Two signals cannot be caught, blocked or ignored: SIGKILL and SIGSTOP. That is their purpose: they are the operating system's guarantee that any process can be stopped or frozen whatever its code does.

bash -c 'trap "echo \"  caught TERM, finishing up\"; exit 0" TERM; kill -s TERM "$$"'
echo "a TERM trap: status $?"
{ bash -c 'trap "echo \"  caught KILL\"" KILL; echo "  trap on KILL returned $?"; kill -s KILL "$$"'; } 2>/dev/null
echo "a KILL trap: status $? ($(kill -l $?))"

  caught TERM, finishing up
a TERM trap: status 0
  trap on KILL returned 0
a KILL trap: status 137 (KILL)

The TERM trap ran and the script decided how to end — with status 0, because the trap said exit 0. The KILL trap was accepted without complaint (trap returned 0, and POSIX says setting one "produces undefined results") and did nothing at all: the process ended with 137, and nothing it asked to run ran. SIGKILL cannot be trapped, and so no cleanup can run on SIGKILL. That is why every service manager sends SIGTERM first and SIGKILL only later, and why a script that ignores SIGTERM does not avoid being stopped — it only guarantees that it will be stopped without cleaning up. It is also why kill -9 is the wrong first reach: it gives the target no chance to remove its lock files.

The signals a script meets

Signal
Default action
Where it comes from, and what a script should do
SIGHUP (1)
terminate
The controlling terminal went away — an SSH session dropped, a terminal window closed. By convention, a long-running program that has no terminal treats it as "reload your configuration" (§12.11).
SIGINT (2)
terminate
Ctrl-C, sent to every process in the terminal's foreground process group. Clean up and exit by re-raising it (§12.5).
SIGQUIT (3)
terminate + core
Ctrl-\. Bash itself ignores it; the commands it runs do not.
SIGKILL (9)
terminate
Cannot be caught or ignored. Nothing runs afterwards.
SIGUSR1, SIGUSR2
terminate
No meaning of their own; each program defines one. A common use is "report your progress" (§12.11). Numbers differ by system.
SIGPIPE (13 on both)
terminate
A write to a pipe whose reader has gone. Status 141, usually harmless (§11.7).
SIGALRM (14)
terminate
A timer expired. Scripts rarely meet it.
SIGTERM (15)
terminate
"Please stop." The default signal of kill, and what systemd, Docker and Kubernetes send first. Clean up and exit.
SIGCHLD
ignore
A child process stopped or ended. Bash handles it internally for wait.
SIGSTOP, SIGTSTP
stop
SIGSTOP cannot be caught; SIGTSTP is Ctrl-Z. Job control, linux §7.7.
SIGCONT
continue
Resumes a stopped process.
SIGWINCH
ignore
The terminal window was resized. Interactive programs only.

The default actions are POSIX's, from <signal.h>. SIGPIPE is 13 on macOS and Linux alike, although POSIX does not fix it.

Three stop sequences account for most of the SIGTERMs a script will ever receive, and all three follow it with SIGKILL if the process has not exited in time. systemd sends SIGTERM to every process in the service's control group (KillMode=control-group, the default), waits TimeoutStopSec= (90 seconds unless configured), then sends SIGKILL to whatever is left. docker stop sends SIGTERM to the container's main process only, waits 10 seconds for a Linux container, then sends SIGKILL. Kubernetes does the same to the container through its runtime, after 30 seconds by default. A script that is someone's main process in any of those places must exit promptly on SIGTERM, and §12.7 shows why that is harder than it looks.

12.2 The trap Builtin

The trap builtin takes an action — a string of shell code — and one or more conditions: signal names, or EXIT, ERR, DEBUG or RETURN. When a condition arises, bash runs the action as though by eval, in the current shell, and then carries on from where it was:

trap 'echo "  INT trap ran"' INT
for i in 1 2 3; do
  if (( i == 2 )); then kill -s INT "$$"; fi
  echo "iteration $i"
done
echo "the loop finished"

iteration 1
  INT trap ran
iteration 2
iteration 3
the loop finished

The INT trap ran when the signal arrived, during the second iteration, and the loop then continued. A trapped signal does not end the script unless the action says exit. This is the first thing to know about trap: it replaces the default action. Once a script traps SIGINT, Ctrl-C no longer stops it unless the handler stops it, and a handler that prints "interrupted" and returns leaves a script that cannot be interrupted.

Single quotes: the action is expanded when it runs

The action is a string, so the quotes around it decide when its expansions happen. With double quotes they happen once, when trap is called; with single quotes they happen each time the trap runs:

msg=early
# shellcheck disable=SC2064  # expanded now, deliberately, to show the difference
trap "echo \"double quotes: $msg\"" USR1
msg=late
kill -s USR1 "$$"
trap 'echo "single quotes: $msg"' USR1
kill -s USR1 "$$"
msg=later
kill -s USR1 "$$"

double quotes: early
single quotes: late
single quotes: later

The double-quoted action captured early, the value when trap ran, and kept it. The single-quoted action read $msg each time it ran, and saw late and then later. Almost every action should be single-quoted, because the variables it refers to — a temporary file's name, a list of background PIDs — are usually set after the trap is installed. ShellCheck reports a double-quoted trap as SC2064 for exactly this reason; the disable directive above marks it as deliberate. The one common case where double quotes are right comes below, in "One handler, several signals".

Listing traps: trap and trap -p

trap with no arguments prints every trap that is set, and trap -p with signal names prints just those, both in a form that can be read back into the shell:

tmp=work.tmp
trap 'rm -f -- "$tmp"; echo "it'\''s tidy"' EXIT
trap 'echo interrupted' INT TERM
trap '' HUP
echo "--- trap"
trap
echo "--- trap -p INT"
trap -p INT
echo "--- trap -p USR1 (never set)"
trap -p USR1
echo "--- after trap - INT"
trap - INT
trap

--- trap
trap -- 'rm -f -- "$tmp"; echo "it'\''s tidy"' EXIT
trap -- '' SIGHUP
trap -- 'echo interrupted' SIGINT
trap -- 'echo interrupted' SIGTERM
--- trap -p INT
trap -- 'echo interrupted' SIGINT
--- trap -p USR1 (never set)
--- after trap - INT
trap -- 'rm -f -- "$tmp"; echo "it'\''s tidy"' EXIT
trap -- '' SIGHUP
trap -- 'echo interrupted' SIGTERM
it's tidy

Each line is a complete trap command, with the action re-quoted — note it'\''s for the apostrophe — and the signal given its full name. trap -p USR1 printed nothing, because no USR1 trap was set. POSIX specifies this output format so that a script can save its traps with saved=$(trap -p) and restore them later with eval "$saved". That works because trap -p inside a command substitution, which is a subshell, still reports the parent's traps (§12.8 measures it). The last listing shows the traps after trap - INT, and the final line of output is the EXIT trap running as the script ended.

Ignoring a signal: trap '' SIGINT, and trap - to reset

Two special actions change a signal's disposition instead of setting a handler. An empty action, trap '' SIGINT, ignores the signal. A single hyphen, trap - SIGINT, restores the default. Use trap - to reset a trap you set, never trap '' …, which does something else:

trap 'echo "caught INT"' INT
kill -s INT "$$"
trap '' TERM
kill -s TERM "$$"
echo "TERM is ignored"
trap - TERM
echo "TERM is back to its default; the next line ends the script"
kill -s TERM "$$"
echo "never printed"

caught INT
TERM is ignored
TERM is back to its default; the next line ends the script

The INT trap caught the first signal. trap '' TERM made the script ignore SIGTERM entirely, so the first kill -s TERM did nothing. trap - TERM put back the default, and the second SIGTERM ended the script at once, killed by the signal: the last echo never ran. Ignoring a signal with trap '' is different from catching it with a handler that does nothing, such as trap : INT, in a way that matters later: an ignored signal stays ignored in every command the script runs, and a caught one does not (§12.8). That is why ignoring a signal, trap '' SIGINT for example, should be done around the smallest possible stretch of code and undone with trap - SIGINT straight after — around a critical section, say, that must not be abandoned half-written. Use trap - to reset whenever a handler is no longer wanted.

Names, numbers and mistakes

trap accepts a signal with or without SIG, in any case, or as a number:

trap 'echo caught' sigterm
trap -p TERM
# shellcheck disable=SC2172  # the number form, shown in order to discourage it
trap 'echo caught' 15
trap -p TERM
trap 'echo caught' SIGFOO
echo "status $?"
# shellcheck disable=SC2172  # an invalid number, on purpose
trap 'echo caught' 99
echo "status $?"

trap -- 'echo caught' SIGTERM
trap -- 'echo caught' SIGTERM
example.sh: line 6: trap: SIGFOO: invalid signal specification
status 1
example.sh: line 9: trap: 99: invalid signal specification
status 1

sigterm and 15 both set the SIGTERM trap, and trap -p always prints the canonical name. An invalid name or number is not fatal, but it prints a diagnostic and returns 1 — and the trap you meant to set is not set, which ShellCheck cannot know. Use the name without SIG (POSIX's spelling; SIGTERM is a bash extension that dash rejects) and never a number other than the seven fixed ones.

One handler, several signals
