A trap can list several signals, as trap 'echo interrupted' INT TERM did above, but then the handler cannot tell which one arrived. To pass the signal name in, set each trap separately, with the name expanded when the trap is set — the one place where double quotes are right:

on_signal() { echo "caught SIG$1"; }
for sig in HUP INT TERM; do
  # shellcheck disable=SC2064  # $sig must be expanded now, once per signal
  trap "on_signal $sig" "$sig"
done
kill -s TERM "$$"
kill -s HUP "$$"
trap -p TERM

caught SIGTERM
caught SIGHUP
trap -- 'on_signal TERM' SIGTERM

Each trap's action is a fixed string, on_signal TERM or on_signal HUP, and trap -p confirms it. §12.5 uses this shape to re-raise the signal that arrived.

$? inside a trap, and after it

The action runs between two commands of the script. What $? holds inside it, and what it holds afterwards, is specified:

trap 'echo "  in the handler, \$? is $?"; false' USR1
( exit 3 )
echo "before kill, \$? is $?"
kill -s USR1 "$$"
echo "after the handler, \$? is $? - the handler's false did not leak out"

before kill, $? is 3
  in the handler, $? is 0
after the handler, $? is 0 - the handler's false did not leak out

Inside the handler, $? was the status of the last command before the trap ran — here kill, which succeeded, not the ( exit 3 ) two commands earlier. After the handler, $? was put back to the value it had before the trap ran: the handler's own false did not leak into the script. POSIX requires both: "The value of $? after the trap action completes shall be the value it had before the trap action was executed." A handler can therefore run any commands it likes without disturbing a status the interrupted code was about to test. The exception is exit, which ends the script with whatever status the handler chooses (§12.3).

BASH_TRAPSIG and trap -P (bash 5.3)

Bash 5.3 added two conveniences. The variable BASH_TRAPSIG holds the number of the signal whose trap is running, so one handler set on several signals can tell them apart, and trap -P SIGNAL prints just the action, without the trap -- '…' SIG wrapper:

trap 'echo "SIG$(kill -l "$BASH_TRAPSIG") (BASH_TRAPSIG=$BASH_TRAPSIG)"' INT TERM
trap 'echo "EXIT (BASH_TRAPSIG=$BASH_TRAPSIG)"' EXIT
trap -P INT
kill -s INT "$$"
kill -s TERM "$$"
echo "outside a trap: ${BASH_TRAPSIG-unset}"

echo "SIG$(kill -l "$BASH_TRAPSIG") (BASH_TRAPSIG=$BASH_TRAPSIG)"
SIGINT (BASH_TRAPSIG=2)
SIGTERM (BASH_TRAPSIG=15)
outside a trap: unset
EXIT (BASH_TRAPSIG=0)

trap -P INT printed the action unquoted and bare. BASH_TRAPSIG was 2 in the INT trap and 15 in the TERM trap, kill -l turned each into a name, and it was 0 in the EXIT trap. Outside any trap it is unset. Both are new in bash 5.3: on 5.2, trap -P is an invalid option and BASH_TRAPSIG is simply unset, so the handler above prints SIG and an error. One trap per signal, as above, works everywhere and is what this course uses; BASH_TRAPSIG is the shorter form for a script that can require 5.3. Its value inside an ERR trap is an internal number that differs between systems, not a signal; do not use it there.

12.3 trap EXIT: Cleanup That Always Runs

The trap EXIT condition fires when the shell exits, and in bash that covers almost every way a script can end. That makes trap EXIT the one place cleanup belongs:

for how in 'echo "  end of script"' 'exit 3' 'set -e; false' \
           'kill -s TERM $$' 'kill -s INT $$' 'kill -s HUP $$' 'kill -s KILL $$'; do
  { bash -c "trap 'echo \"  EXIT trap ran\"' EXIT; $how"; } 2>/dev/null
  echo "$how -> status $?"
done

  end of script
  EXIT trap ran
echo "  end of script" -> status 0
  EXIT trap ran
exit 3 -> status 3
  EXIT trap ran
set -e; false -> status 1
  EXIT trap ran
kill -s TERM $$ -> status 143
  EXIT trap ran
kill -s INT $$ -> status 130
  EXIT trap ran
kill -s HUP $$ -> status 129
kill -s KILL $$ -> status 137

The EXIT trap ran at the end of the script, on an explicit exit 3, when set -e stopped the script, and when the script was killed by SIGTERM, SIGINT or SIGHUP. In each case the script's status was still the one that would have been reported without the trap. The one exception is SIGKILL, after which nothing runs.

The signal cases need a caveat. POSIX says the EXIT condition "may occur" when a shell is killed by a signal whose trap action is the default, and shells differ. Bash 5.3 and 5.2 run it; dash does not, and neither does the bash 3.2 that macOS ships as /bin/bash and /bin/sh — all three measured. A portable script, or one that might be run by an old bash, must trap the signals too, and §12.5 shows how to do that without cleaning up twice.

Temporary file cleanup

The canonical use is temporary file cleanup. mktemp creates a file with an unpredictable name in $TMPDIR (or /tmp) and prints the name; the script records it and arranges for its removal before doing anything that could fail:

cat > convert.sh <<'EOF'
set -euo pipefail
tmp=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f -- "$tmp"' EXIT
echo "$tmp" > last-tmp            # recorded only so the caller can check
sort data.txt > "$tmp"
grep -q zebra "$tmp"              # fails: there is no zebra
mv -- "$tmp" sorted.txt
EOF
grep -v '^trap' convert.sh > convert-notrap.sh
printf '%s\n' pear apple > data.txt
for script in convert-notrap.sh convert.sh; do
  bash "$script"
  echo "$script exited $?"
  if [[ -e $(<last-tmp) ]]; then echo "  its temp file was left behind"; else echo "  its temp file is gone"; fi
done

convert-notrap.sh exited 1
  its temp file was left behind
convert.sh exited 1
  its temp file is gone

Both scripts failed at the same line, because there is no zebra in the sorted data. The one without the trap left its temporary file behind, and a script like it that runs every few minutes fills /tmp with them. The one with the trap removed it on the way out, even though set -e ended the script. Three details make the trap line right. It is single-quoted, so $tmp is read when the trap runs. It uses rm -f, which does not fail when the file is already gone — here the file might have been renamed by mv on the success path — so the cleanup is safe to run in any state. And it uses --, so a name that begins with a hyphen cannot be read as an option. The trap is set immediately after mktemp, before anything that can fail: every line between creating a resource and registering its cleanup is a line that can leak it.

A temporary directory works the same way, with mktemp -d and rm -rf:

cat > build.sh <<'EOF'
set -euo pipefail
workdir=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/build.XXXXXX")
trap 'rm -rf -- "${workdir:?}"' EXIT
echo "$workdir" > last-workdir
mkdir -- "$workdir/out"
printf 'hello\n' > "$workdir/out/index.html"
echo "built ${workdir##*/}" | sed 's/\.[^.]*$/.XXXXXX/'
EOF
bash build.sh
[[ -d $(<last-workdir) ]] && echo "left behind" || echo "the directory and everything in it are gone"

built build.XXXXXX
the directory and everything in it are gone

${workdir:?} is §5.2's error expansion. If workdir were ever empty, the expansion fails with a message instead of running rm -rf -- with an empty argument, and a guard like this costs nothing on a line that deletes a directory tree. The template form mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/build.XXXXXX" gives the directory a recognisable name and is the portable spelling: GNU and BSD mktemp both accept a template, but they disagree about what -t means. §17.10 returns to temporary files, because a predictable name in a shared directory is a security hole, and mktemp's random name is what closes it.

exit inside a trap, and why trap EXIT runs once

The EXIT trap sees the script's exit status in $?, and can change it by calling exit itself:

bash -c 'trap "echo \"  EXIT trap sees \$?\"" EXIT; exit 3'
echo "script status $?"
bash -c 'trap "echo \"  EXIT trap runs once, and calls exit 7\"; exit 7" EXIT; exit 3'
echo "script status $?"

  EXIT trap sees 3
script status 3
  EXIT trap runs once, and calls exit 7
script status 7

The first trap read $? and saw 3, the status the script was exiting with, and the script still exited 3. The second called exit 7, and the script's status became 7. It also printed its message once: an exit inside a trap on EXIT does not start the EXIT trap again, because the shell is already exiting. So trap EXIT runs once, however it is reached. That makes exit inside a trap the way a handler overrides the status, and the reason every handler that is not trying to change the status must preserve it: read $? on the handler's first line, and end with exit "$status" or let the handler fall off the end.

A bare exit in a trap — no argument — is where bash versions differ:

bash -c 'trap "echo \"  TERM trap: false, then a bare exit\"; false; exit" TERM; kill -s TERM "$$"'
echo "status $?"

  TERM trap: false, then a bare exit
status 0

The handler's last command before exit was false. Bash 5.3 exited 0, the value of $? from before the trap ran — here kill's status — following POSIX interpretation 1602. Bash 5.2 exits 1, the status of false. Always give exit an explicit status inside a trap.

A cleanup handler must not fail

An EXIT trap runs with the script's options still in force, including set -e. A cleanup handler that runs a failing command under set -e stops at that command:

cat > build.sh <<'EOF'
set -e
cleanup() {
  echo "cleanup: stopping the test server"
  false                                   # a cleanup step that fails
  echo "cleanup: removing the build directory"
}
trap cleanup EXIT
echo "build succeeded"
EOF
bash build.sh
echo "build.sh exited $?"

build succeeded
cleanup: stopping the test server
build.sh exited 1

The build succeeded. Then the cleanup handler's second step failed, set -e ended the handler on the spot, the build directory was never removed, and the script exited 1 — so a successful build was reported as a failure by the code that was supposed to tidy up after it. Cleanup code is the worst place to fail, because it runs when things have already gone wrong and because nothing runs after it. The fix is to make the handler immune to its own failures:

cat > build.sh <<'EOF'
set -e
cleanup() {
  local status=$?
  set +e
  echo "cleanup: stopping the test server"
  false
  echo "cleanup: removing the build directory"
  exit "$status"
}
trap cleanup EXIT
echo "build succeeded"
EOF
bash build.sh
echo "build.sh exited $?"

build succeeded
cleanup: stopping the test server
cleanup: removing the build directory
build.sh exited 0

The handler saves the status on its first line, turns set -e off for itself with set +e, runs every step whether or not the previous one succeeded, and exits with the saved status. The set +e does not leak anywhere, because the script is exiting. Each step should also be written so that it cannot fail for a reason that does not matter: rm -f rather than rm, and kill … 2>/dev/null for a process that may already be gone. The next subsection builds a cleanup handler for a script that holds several resources.

12.4 Cleanup Handlers for Real Scripts

A script that holds one temporary file needs one line of trap. A real script holds several things — a temporary directory, a lock, a background process, a redirected output — acquires them at different points, and must release exactly the ones it acquired, in reverse order, even if some of the releases fail. Three facts shape the design.

There is one EXIT trap

Setting a trap replaces whatever was set before for that condition. There is one EXIT trap per shell, and the last trap … EXIT wins:

cat > lib.sh <<'EOF'
lib_tmp=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f -- "$lib_tmp"; echo "lib: removed its temp file"' EXIT
EOF
cat > main.sh <<'EOF'
source ./lib.sh
trap 'echo "main: finished"' EXIT
echo "main: working"
EOF
bash main.sh

main: working
main: finished

lib.sh created a temporary file and set an EXIT trap to remove it. main.sh then set its own EXIT trap, which silently replaced the library's, so the library's file was never removed and nothing reported it. A library must therefore never call trap on EXIT itself. The script that owns the process owns its traps, and a library that needs cleanup should offer a function for the script to call, or register its cleanup through the mechanism below. Exercise 3 writes a helper that appends to the existing trap instead of replacing it.

A cleanup registry

The pattern that scales is a list of cleanup commands, added to as each resource is acquired and run in reverse order by the single EXIT trap. Reverse order matters: a file inside a directory must be removed before the directory, a server started after a lock must be stopped before the lock is released. §8.6 walked an array backwards by index for this reason:

cat > release.sh <<'EOF'
set -Eeuo pipefail
cleanups=()
add_cleanup() { cleanups+=("$1"); }
run_cleanups() {
  local status=$? i
  set +e
  for (( i = ${#cleanups[@]} - 1; i >= 0; i-- )); do
    eval "${cleanups[i]}" || echo "cleanup failed: ${cleanups[i]}" >&2
  done
  exit "$status"
}
trap run_cleanups EXIT

mkdir staging;             add_cleanup 'rmdir staging && echo "removed staging"'
: > staging/manifest;      add_cleanup 'rm staging/manifest && echo "removed the manifest"'
echo "server started";     add_cleanup 'echo "stopped the server"; false'
echo "releasing"
grep -q version staging/manifest
EOF
bash release.sh
echo "release.sh exited $?"
[[ -e staging ]] || echo "staging is gone"

server started
releasing
stopped the server
cleanup failed: echo "stopped the server"; false
removed the manifest
removed staging
release.sh exited 1
staging is gone

Each add_cleanup comes right after the step that makes it necessary, so the registry holds exactly what was acquired. When grep failed, run_cleanups ran the three commands last to first. The first of them failed — its false stands for a stop command that errors — and the handler reported it on standard error and carried on, so the manifest and the staging directory were still removed. The script exited 1, the status of the grep, not of the failed cleanup. eval runs a string as code, and §18 warns against it with good reason; here the strings are constants written into the script itself, never data, which is the case where it is safe.

Restoring state: descriptors and the terminal

Some cleanups do not remove anything but put something back. §10.7 saved standard output on a spare descriptor with exec and redirected the script's output to a log, and promised that a trap would restore it even when the script was interrupted:

cat > nightly.sh <<'EOF'
exec 3>&1 1>nightly.log
trap 'exec 1>&3 3>&-; echo "nightly: done, $(grep -c "" nightly.log) lines in nightly.log"' EXIT
echo "step 1"
echo "step 2"
EOF
bash nightly.sh
cat nightly.log

nightly: done, 2 lines in nightly.log
step 1
step 2

exec 3>&1 1>nightly.log saves the original standard output on fd 3 and sends everything after it to the log. The EXIT trap puts fd 1 back and closes fd 3, so the final message reaches the terminal however the script ends. Without the trap, a script that set -e stops halfway ends with its last message in a log nobody is looking at.

The terminal is the other common case. A script that turns off echo to read a password must turn it back on, or an interrupt leaves the user's terminal not showing what they type:

if [[ -t 0 ]]; then
  trap 'stty echo' EXIT
  stty -echo
fi
IFS= read -r -p 'Password: ' password
echo
printf 'read a password of %d characters\n' "${#password}"

[[ -t 0 ]] checks that standard input is a terminal first, since stty fails otherwise. The trap is set before stty -echo, so there is no window in which echo is off and nothing will turn it back on. §14 covers read -s, which does the same job for a single read.

Child processes

A background job does not end when the script that started it ends. A script that starts workers and then fails leaves them running, and the fix is a trap that signals them:

cat > fetch.sh <<'EOF'
# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # $pids is a list of PIDs, split on purpose
trap 'pids=$(jobs -p); [[ -z $pids ]] || kill $pids' EXIT
for n in 1 2 3; do sleep 30 & echo "$!" >> children; done
echo "started 3 workers, then failed"
exit 1
EOF
grep -v '^trap' fetch.sh > fetch-notrap.sh
for script in fetch-notrap.sh fetch.sh; do
  : > children
  bash "$script"; echo "$script exited $?"
  sleep 0.2
  alive=0
  while read -r pid; do
    if kill -0 "$pid" 2>/dev/null; then alive=$(( alive + 1 )); kill "$pid"; fi
  done < children
  echo "  $alive of its workers were still running"
done

started 3 workers, then failed
fetch-notrap.sh exited 1
  3 of its workers were still running
started 3 workers, then failed
fetch.sh exited 1
  0 of its workers were still running

Both scripts started three sleep 30 workers in the background and exited 1. After the one without the trap, all three were still running, orphaned: reparented to init (or to a service manager acting as a subreaper), with nobody waiting for them. The trap in fetch.sh read jobs -p, the PIDs of the script's background jobs, and sent them SIGTERM. The test for an empty list matters: kill with no PID is a usage error. The unquoted $pids is deliberate word splitting, one argument per PID, and the shellcheck disable=SC2086 directive says so. jobs -p works inside the trap because the trap runs in the script's own shell, which still knows its jobs. §12.9 covers a stronger version, signalling the whole process group, which also reaches the children's children.

12.5 Exiting Correctly After a Signal

The EXIT trap handles cleanup. It does not decide how the script ends when a signal arrives, and there are two tempting ways of deciding that are both wrong. The first is to trap each signal with a handler that cleans up and exits — which runs the cleanup twice. The second is to exit with a status of 128 plus the signal number, which reports the right number and still misleads the caller.

Idempotent cleanup

A script with an EXIT trap and a signal trap that calls the same cleanup runs it twice when a signal arrives, because the signal handler's exit triggers the EXIT trap:

cat > job.sh <<'EOF'
cleanup() {
  echo "cleanup: removing job.lock"
  rmdir job.lock 2>/dev/null || echo "cleanup: rmdir failed, job.lock was already gone"
}
trap cleanup EXIT
trap 'cleanup; exit 130' INT
mkdir job.lock
kill -s INT "$$"
EOF
bash job.sh
echo "job.sh exited $?"

cleanup: removing job.lock
cleanup: removing job.lock
cleanup: rmdir failed, job.lock was already gone
job.sh exited 130

The INT handler removed job.lock and called exit 130, and the EXIT trap then ran the same cleanup a second time and found the directory gone. Here the damage is a spurious error. With rm -rf of a directory that another run has since created, or a "decrement the counter" step, it is worse. There are two defences, and a robust script uses both. Idempotent cleanup means writing each step so that running it twice is harmless — rm -f rather than rm, a kill whose failure is ignored, a flag checked before a step that must happen once. And structure: cleanup goes in the EXIT trap alone, and the signal handlers do nothing but end the script, so the EXIT trap is the only path to it. Idempotent cleanup is still worth having under that structure, because an EXIT trap can be reached from a state the author did not think about.

Why exit 130 is not good enough

When a script is interrupted, the process that ran it needs to know that it was interrupted, not merely that it failed. This matters most for Ctrl-C. When the user presses it at a terminal, the terminal sends SIGINT to every process in the foreground process group — the script, and any caller that ran it, such as a loop in another script. Bash's rule for that case is described in its manual, and is known as wait and cooperative exit from the write-up cited below: a bash that receives SIGINT while waiting for a foreground command waits for the command to finish, and then acts on the SIGINT itself — exiting, if it has no trap — only if the command was killed by SIGINT. If the command handled the signal and exited normally, bash assumes the command meant it as part of its normal operation (as an editor uses Ctrl-C to cancel a command) and carries on.

The next example is a batch script that runs three jobs in a loop. The job traps SIGINT to clean up, then ends one of two ways. The example makes batch.sh the leader of its own process group with set -m and sends SIGINT to the whole group, which is exactly what Ctrl-C at a terminal does:

for ending in 'exit 130' 'trap - INT; kill -s INT "$$"'; do
  cat > job.sh <<EOF
trap 'echo "  job \$1: interrupted, cleaning up"; $ending' INT
: > "ready.\$1"
sleep 1
echo "  job \$1: finished"
EOF
  cat > batch.sh <<'EOF'
for n in 1 2 3; do bash job.sh "$n"; done
echo "  batch: all jobs done"
EOF
  echo "job.sh's INT trap ends with: $ending"
  set -m; bash batch.sh & leader=$!; set +m      # batch.sh leads its own process group
  until [[ -e ready.1 ]]; do sleep 0.05; done
  kill -s INT -- "-$leader"                      # what Ctrl-C at a terminal does
  wait "$leader"
  echo "batch.sh exited $?"
  rm -f ready.?
done

job.sh's INT trap ends with: exit 130
  job 1: interrupted, cleaning up
  job 2: finished
  job 3: finished
  batch: all jobs done
batch.sh exited 0
job.sh's INT trap ends with: trap - INT; kill -s INT "$$"
  job 1: interrupted, cleaning up
batch.sh exited 130

With exit 130, the job cleaned up and exited normally with status 130. batch.sh also received the SIGINT, but its foreground command had not died of it, so bash concluded that the job had dealt with the interrupt and carried on — jobs 2 and 3 ran, and the batch reported success. The user pressed Ctrl-C and the batch ran to completion. With the second ending, the handler reset SIGINT to its default with trap - INT and sent the signal to its own process with kill -s INT "$$". The job died of SIGINT, the batch saw it, and stopped at once with 130.

The distinction lives below the shell. When a process exits, its parent's wait system call receives either an exit status or the number of the signal that killed it, and a C program tells them apart with WIFSIGNALED. The shell's $? folds both into one number, which is why 130 looks the same either way, but the parent's kernel-level view is different, and programs act on it: bash, as shown; xargs, which POSIX requires to stop processing its input when a command is terminated by a signal; and Python's subprocess, which reports a negative returncode. The standard account of all this is Martin Cracauer's "Proper handling of SIGINT/SIGQUIT", which compares the ways a shell can respond to an interrupted child, identifies bash's as wait and cooperative exit, and puts the lesson plainly: you cannot fake the proper exit status with a special numeric value. The only way to report "I was killed by SIGINT" is to be killed by it.

Re-raising the signal

So a signal handler that has done its work should restore the default disposition and send the same signal to its own process. Combined with the structure above — cleanup in the EXIT trap, the signal traps only re-raising — the pattern looks like this:

cat > job.sh <<'EOF'
cleanup() { echo "cleanup: ran once"; }
trap cleanup EXIT
on_signal() {
  echo "caught SIG$1"
  trap - "$1"
  kill -s "$1" "$$"
}
trap 'on_signal INT' INT
trap 'on_signal TERM' TERM
trap 'on_signal HUP' HUP
kill -s TERM "$$"
echo "never printed"
EOF
{ bash job.sh; } 2>/dev/null
status=$?
echo "job.sh exited $status ($(kill -l "$status"))"

caught SIGTERM
cleanup: ran once
job.sh exited 143 (TERM)

on_signal receives the name of the signal, from one trap per signal as §12.2 arranged them. It resets that signal with trap - "$1", so that the second delivery is not caught again, and sends it with kill -s "$1" "$$". The script died of SIGTERM, bash ran the EXIT trap on the way out, cleanup ran exactly once, and the caller saw 143, with the signal recorded where only a real death by signal can record it. $$ is the script's own PID; §12.9 explains why that is right even when the handler runs in a subshell.

This is the pattern for bash 5, which runs the EXIT trap on a death by signal. In dash, or bash 3.2, the EXIT trap would not run after the re-raise, so a script meant to be portable must run the cleanup in the signal handler, then trap - EXIT so it cannot run again, then re-raise; §19 collects that.

What the EXIT trap sees after a signal

One consequence of re-raising surprises people. The EXIT trap that runs after a death by signal sees in $? the status of the last command that ran, not 128 plus the signal:

cat > job.sh <<'EOF'
caught=
cleanup() {
  local status=$?
  echo "cleanup: \$? is $status, caught is '${caught:-nothing}'"
}
trap cleanup EXIT
trap 'caught=TERM; trap - TERM; kill -s TERM "$$"' TERM
kill -s TERM "$$"
EOF
{ bash job.sh; } 2>/dev/null
echo "job.sh exited $?"

cleanup: $? is 0, caught is 'TERM'
job.sh exited 143

$? was 0 in the cleanup, the status of the kill that re-raised the signal, although the script went on to die with 143. A cleanup that needs to know why the script is ending — to write "interrupted" rather than "failed" to a log, say — must record it itself, as caught=TERM does here, in the signal handler before it re-raises.

12.6 The Stack-Trace Handler

§11.10 installed an ERR trap that reported the failed command and its line, and §9.10 walked the call stack with caller to print a stack trace from a die function. This subsection connects the two, so that an unexpected failure anywhere in a strict script reports the whole chain of calls that led to it. It is also a demonstration that code which works in an ordinary function can break when it runs as a trap under strict mode.

Here is §9.10's loop, moved into an ERR handler, in a script whose failure is three calls deep and in a sourced library. The configuration file is missing, so grep fails with status 2:

cat > lib.sh <<'EOF'
load_config() {
  local file=$1
  grep -q '^port=' "$file"
}
EOF
cat > deploy.sh <<'EOF'
set -Eeuo pipefail
source ./lib.sh
on_err() {
  local status=$? frame=0 line func file
  echo "error: '$BASH_COMMAND' exited $status" >&2
  while read -r line func file < <(caller "$frame"); do
    echo "  at $func ($file:$line)" >&2
    (( frame++ ))
  done
  exit "$status"
}
trap on_err ERR
prepare() {
  load_config app.conf
}
main() {
  prepare
  echo "deployed"
}
main "$@"
EOF
bash deploy.sh
echo "deploy.sh exited $?"

grep: app.conf: No such file or directory
error: 'grep -q '^port=' "$file"' exited 2
  at load_config (./lib.sh:3)
deploy.sh exited 1

The handler printed one frame and the script exited 1 — a stack trace missing three of its four frames, and an exit status that is no longer grep's 2. The cause is §11.5's first trap. (( frame++ )) evaluates to the old value of frame, which is 0 on the first pass, and an arithmetic command that evaluates to 0 has status 1. Under set -e that ends the shell, from inside the handler, with status 1. The same loop worked in §9.10 because that script did not use set -e. A handler inherits the script's options, and every line in it must be correct under them:

cat > lib.sh <<'EOF'
load_config() {
  local file=$1
  grep -q '^port=' "$file"
}
EOF
cat > deploy.sh <<'EOF'
set -Eeuo pipefail
source ./lib.sh
on_err() {
  local status=$? frame=0 line func file
  echo "error: '$BASH_COMMAND' exited $status" >&2
  while read -r line func file < <(caller "$frame"); do
    echo "  at $func ($file:$line)" >&2
    frame=$(( frame + 1 ))
  done
  exit "$status"
}
trap on_err ERR
prepare() {
  load_config app.conf
}
main() {
  prepare
  echo "deployed"
}
main "$@"
EOF
bash deploy.sh
echo "deploy.sh exited $?"
echo 'host=example' > app.conf
bash deploy.sh
echo "deploy.sh exited $?"

grep: app.conf: No such file or directory
error: 'grep -q '^port=' "$file"' exited 2
  at load_config (./lib.sh:3)
  at prepare (deploy.sh:14)
  at main (deploy.sh:17)
  at main (deploy.sh:20)
deploy.sh exited 2
error: 'grep -q '^port=' "$file"' exited 1
  at load_config (./lib.sh:3)
  at prepare (deploy.sh:14)
  at main (deploy.sh:17)
  at main (deploy.sh:20)
deploy.sh exited 1

With frame=$(( frame + 1 )), an assignment whose status is always 0, the handler walks the whole stack. caller 0 inside the handler describes the place the handler was called from, which for an ERR trap is the failed command itself: line 3 of lib.sh, in load_config. Each further frame is one call further out, ending with bash's main for the top level of the script, which is why main appears twice — once for the script's own function of that name and once for the top level, as §9.10 explained. The script exited 2, grep's status, because the handler saved $? on its first line and passed it to exit. The second run, with a configuration file that has no port= line, shows the same trace for the ordinary "no match" status 1. set -E is essential to all of this: without errtrace, the ERR trap does not run inside functions at all (§11.10).

The while read … < <(caller "$frame") loop ends when caller finds no frame and returns 1. That failure is in a loop condition, one of the positions §11.3 exempts, so it neither triggers the ERR trap nor ends the script.

Failures inside command substitutions

A command substitution is a subshell, and with errtrace and inherit_errexit (§11.8) a failure inside one is reported twice:

cat > report.sh <<'EOF'
set -Eeuo pipefail
shopt -s inherit_errexit
on_err() {
  local status=$? frame=0 line func file
  echo "error: '$BASH_COMMAND' exited $status (subshell level $BASH_SUBSHELL)" >&2
  while read -r line func file < <(caller "$frame"); do
    echo "  at $func (line $line)" >&2
    frame=$(( frame + 1 ))
  done
  exit "$status"
}
trap on_err ERR
count_errors() { grep -c ERROR "$1"; }
summary() {
  local n
  n=$(count_errors app.log)
  echo "$n errors"
}
summary
EOF
echo 'INFO ok' > app.log
bash report.sh
echo "report.sh exited $?"

error: 'grep -c ERROR "$1"' exited 1 (subshell level 1)
  at count_errors (line 13)
  at summary (line 16)
  at main (line 19)
error: 'n=$(count_errors app.log)' exited 1 (subshell level 0)
  at summary (line 16)
  at main (line 19)
report.sh exited 1

The first report came from inside the substitution, at subshell level 1, where grep -c found no match: its trace includes count_errors. The handler's exit ended only that subshell, with status 1. The assignment n=$(count_errors app.log) then had status 1 in the parent, which triggered the trap a second time, at level 0, with a shorter stack. Both reports are true: the first says where the failure happened, the second where the script noticed it. BASH_SUBSHELL distinguishes them, so a handler that wants only the innermost report can print when BASH_SUBSHELL is greater than 0 and exit quietly otherwise, at the cost of saying nothing about failures at the top level that did not start in a subshell.

12.7 Signals Are Delayed Until the Foreground Command Finishes

The rule that surprises almost everyone who writes a long-running script is in the manual's section on signals: "If bash is waiting for a command to complete and receives a signal for which a trap has been set, it will not execute the trap until the command completes." Signals are delayed until the foreground command finishes. A script that runs sleep 300 and receives SIGTERM handles it five minutes later.

cat > service.sh <<'EOF'
trap 'echo "service: TERM trap ran"' TERM
: > ready
sleep 1
echo "service: sleep finished with status $?"
EOF
bash service.sh & pid=$!
until [[ -e ready ]]; do sleep 0.05; done
kill -s TERM "$pid"
wait "$pid"; echo "service.sh exited $?"

service: TERM trap ran
service: sleep finished with status 0
service.sh exited 0

The SIGTERM was sent to the script while its sleep 1 was running. The trap ran only after the sleep finished — and the sleep finished normally, with status 0, because the signal went to the script and not to it. The script then carried on to the end. With sleep 300, or a curl downloading a large file, or a psql running a long query, the script would sit on the SIGTERM for as long as that command took. Under systemd that is mitigated, because systemd sends SIGTERM to every process in the service, including the sleep. Under docker stop, it is not, because Docker signals only the container's main process.

wait and signal delivery

The way out is to run the long command in the background and wait for it. The wait builtin is interruptible: when a trapped signal arrives, wait returns at once with a status greater than 128, and the trap runs straight after:

cat > service.sh <<'EOF'
trap 'echo "service: TERM trap ran"; stop=1' TERM
stop=0
: > ready
sleep 1 & child=$!
wait "$child"
status=$?
echo "service: wait returned $status ($(kill -l "$status"))"
if (( stop )); then
  kill -s TERM "$child"
  echo "service: stopped its sleep and is exiting"
fi
EOF
bash service.sh & pid=$!
until [[ -e ready ]]; do sleep 0.05; done
kill -s TERM "$pid"
wait "$pid"; echo "service.sh exited $?"

service: TERM trap ran
service: wait returned 143 (TERM)
service: stopped its sleep and is exiting
service.sh exited 0

This time the trap ran immediately and wait returned 143, SIGTERM's status, without waiting for the sleep. That is the whole trick, and the manual states it directly: when bash is in wait and a trapped signal arrives, wait returns "with an exit status greater than 128, immediately after which the shell executes the trap." What wait does not do is stop the background command, which is still running; the script must signal it, as this one does with kill -s TERM "$child", or it will leave an orphan behind.

This interaction between wait and signal delivery matters most where a script is the main process of a container. Measured on Linux with docker stop -t 3 against three versions of a bash script run as the container's command:

The script
Status
What happened
sleep 60; echo done
137
Ignored SIGTERM; killed after the timeout.
trap '…; exit 0' TERM; sleep 60
137
The trap was delayed behind sleep; killed after the timeout, the trap never ran.
trap '…; exit 0' TERM; sleep 60 & wait $!
0
The trap ran at once and the container stopped cleanly.

The first row is a Linux rule about the first process in a PID namespace, not about bash: the kernel delivers to PID 1 only the signals for which it has installed a handler, so a script running as PID 1 with no TERM trap does not die of SIGTERM — measured in a python:3.14 container, where bash -c 'kill -s TERM $$; echo survived' prints survived. The second row is the delay. Only the third stops when asked, so any script that is a container's entry point, or a service's main process, needs both the trap and the & wait shape around anything that can take a while.

Waiting again after a handled signal

wait returning early is exactly right for a signal that should stop the script. For one that should not — a request for a progress report, say — the script must wait again, because the command it was waiting for is still running:

cat > copy.sh <<'EOF'
trap 'echo "copy: still working"' USR1
: > ready
{ sleep 0.5; echo "the copy's output"; } > out.txt & child=$!
until wait "$child"; do
  status=$?
  (( status > 128 )) && kill -0 "$child" 2>/dev/null || break
done
echo "copy: done, wrote: $(<out.txt)"
EOF
bash copy.sh & pid=$!
until [[ -e ready ]]; do sleep 0.05; done
kill -s USR1 "$pid"
wait "$pid"; echo "copy.sh exited $?"

copy: still working
copy: done, wrote: the copy's output
copy.sh exited 0

The USR1 trap printed its report and wait returned early, with a status above 128. The loop condition then checked whether the child was still running with kill -0 (§12.9) and, since it was, waited again; when the child finished, wait returned its real status and the loop ended. A status above 128 on its own does not prove that the wait was interrupted, since the child may itself have died of a signal, which is why the loop also checks that the child is still alive. §12.11 uses the other approach: a loop that waits a short time over and over, and checks flags set by the handlers after each wait.

12.8 Traps in Subshells and Child Processes

A trap belongs to one shell. What happens to it in a subshell, and in a program the script starts, follows from one rule in the manual: "Trapped signals that are not being ignored are reset to their original values in a subshell or subshell environment when one is created." Caught signals revert to their defaults; ignored signals stay ignored.

Subshells

trap 'echo "parent: EXIT trap"' EXIT
trap 'echo "parent: INT trap"' INT
trap '' HUP
saved=$(trap -p)
echo "--- \$(trap -p) saw the parent's traps:"
echo "$saved"
( kill -s INT "$BASHPID"; echo "subshell survived" )
echo "a subshell sent itself INT: status $?"
( kill -s HUP "$BASHPID"; echo "a subshell ignores HUP, as the parent does" )
( trap 'echo "subshell: its own EXIT trap"' EXIT; echo "subshell: working" )
echo "parent: carrying on"

--- $(trap -p) saw the parent's traps:
trap -- 'echo "parent: EXIT trap"' EXIT
trap -- '' SIGHUP
trap -- 'echo "parent: INT trap"' SIGINT
a subshell sent itself INT: status 130
a subshell ignores HUP, as the parent does
subshell: working
subshell: its own EXIT trap
parent: carrying on
parent: EXIT trap

saved=$(trap -p) captured the parent's traps. That is a deliberate exception: since bash 4.2, a subshell keeps the parent's trap strings for display until it sets a trap of its own, so that saved=$(trap -p) works (§12.2). But the traps are not active there. A subshell that sent itself SIGINT died of it with 130, despite the parent's INT trap; the parent's HUP was ignored, and the subshell ignored it too. A subshell can set traps of its own, and its EXIT trap runs when the subshell ends — before the parent's, which ran only when the script itself exited. The same applies to every kind of subshell: ( … ), command substitutions, the elements of a pipeline and background jobs. A cleanup trap set in the script does not run when a subshell exits, and a subshell that creates a resource must clean it up itself.

Ignored signals are inherited

When a script ignores a signal, every program it starts inherits that. And a non-interactive shell that starts with a signal already ignored cannot trap it:

cat > child.sh <<'EOF'
trap 'echo "child: caught INT"' INT
trap -p INT
kill -s INT "$$"
echo "child: still running"
EOF
bash child.sh
echo "--- the same child, started with INT ignored:"
trap '' INT
bash child.sh

trap -- 'echo "child: caught INT"' SIGINT
child: caught INT
child: still running
--- the same child, started with INT ignored:
trap -- '' SIGINT
child: still running

Started normally, child.sh trapped and handled its SIGINT. Started from a script that ran trap '' INT first, the same child found the signal already ignored: its trap was silently ineffective, trap -p showed the inherited empty action, and the SIGINT it sent itself did nothing. POSIX requires this — "Signals that were ignored on entry to a non-interactive shell cannot be trapped or reset" — and bash's manual repeats it. It is how nohup works: it sets SIGHUP to ignored and then runs the command, and a shell script run that way cannot undo it. (A compiled program can; the rule is the shell's.) It is also why ignoring a signal in a script is not a local decision — every command started while it is ignored inherits it — and why a trap with an empty action should be undone as soon as possible.

Background jobs ignore SIGINT

There is one more inherited ignore, and bash sets it itself. The manual: "When job control is not in effect, asynchronous commands ignore SIGINT and SIGQUIT." Job control is off in a script by default, so every & job a script starts ignores Ctrl-C:

cat > worker.sh <<'EOF'
trap 'echo "worker: caught INT"' INT
trap -p INT
: > ready
sleep 1
echo "worker: finished"
EOF
bash worker.sh & pid=$!
until [[ -e ready ]]; do sleep 0.05; done
kill -s INT "$pid"
wait "$pid"; echo "background worker exited $?"
rm ready
set -m; bash worker.sh & pid=$!; set +m
until [[ -e ready ]]; do sleep 0.05; done
kill -s INT "$pid"
wait "$pid"; echo "with job control, worker exited $?"

trap -- '' SIGINT
worker: finished
background worker exited 0
trap -- 'echo "worker: caught INT"' SIGINT
worker: caught INT
worker: finished
with job control, worker exited 0

The background worker could not trap SIGINT, because it was ignored when the worker started, and the signal did nothing: the worker finished its sleep and exited 0. With set -m, which turns job control on, the same worker ran in its own process group without the inherited ignore, and its trap caught the signal. The reason for the rule is Ctrl-C: without it, pressing Ctrl-C to stop a foreground command would also kill every background job the script had started. The consequence is that a script that starts background workers owns stopping them — Ctrl-C will not do it. Exercise 4 is a supervisor built on that.

The ignore is set up in the child just after it is forked, so a SIGINT sent the moment after & can arrive before it is in place and kill the job. A signal sent half a second later is ignored. A result that depends on a race like that is not a result, and the examples in this section always wait for the process they signal to say it is ready.

12.9 The kill Builtin, Process Groups, and $$ versus BASHPID

Bash has a kill builtin, which takes priority over /bin/kill and accepts job specifications like %1, which only the shell can resolve, as well as PIDs. Its forms:

{
  sleep 30 & kill "$!";          wait "$!"; echo "kill PID          -> $(kill -l $?)"
  sleep 30 & kill -s USR1 "$!";  wait "$!"; echo "kill -s USR1 PID  -> $(kill -l $?)"
  sleep 30 & kill -HUP "$!";     wait "$!"; echo "kill -HUP PID     -> $(kill -l $?)"
  sleep 30 & kill -n 9 "$!";     wait "$!"; echo "kill -n 9 PID     -> $(kill -l $?)"
  sleep 30 & kill -s TERM %%;    wait "$!"; echo "kill -s TERM %%   -> $(kill -l $?)"
} 2>/dev/null

kill PID          -> TERM
kill -s USR1 PID  -> USR1
kill -HUP PID     -> HUP
kill -n 9 PID     -> KILL
kill -s TERM %%   -> TERM

kill PID sends SIGTERM, the default. kill -s NAME PID is the POSIX form and the one to prefer, because it reads unambiguously; kill -NAME PID is the traditional short form (the example sends USR1 where INT might be expected, because §12.8 shows a background job ignores INT); kill -n NUMBER takes a number; and %% is the current job in bash's job table, even with job control off. Each child was killed by the signal named, and wait returned 128 plus its number, which kill -l turned back into a name. kill -l itself was covered in §12.1. kill returns 0 if at least one signal was sent, and 1 otherwise.

kill -0: is it still running?

Signal 0 is not a signal. kill -0 PID performs every check of sending one — that the process exists, and that the script is allowed to signal it — and sends nothing:

sleep 30 & pid=$!
kill -0 "$pid" && echo "kill -0: the sleep is running"
kill "$pid"; wait "$pid" 2>/dev/null
kill -0 "$pid" 2>/dev/null || echo "kill -0: after wait, it is gone (status $?)"

kill -0: the sleep is running
kill -0: after wait, it is gone (status 1)

kill -0 succeeded while the sleep ran and failed after wait had collected it. That makes it the standard test for "is my child still running", as §12.7 used it, with two limits. It succeeds for a process that has ended but not yet been collected by its parent — a zombie (linux §7.5) — which the Linux verification of this section met: in a container whose PID 1 never collects orphaned processes, kill -0 kept succeeding for workers that had been dead for some time, until the container was given an init (docker run --init). And it cannot distinguish the script's child from an unrelated process that has since been given the same PID, which is why it is reliable only for the script's own children, which the kernel does not reuse until wait has collected them.

$$ versus BASHPID

Two variables hold a process ID, and they differ exactly where it matters:

top=$$
( [[ $$ == "$top" ]] && echo "subshell:            \$\$ is still the script's PID" )
( [[ $BASHPID != "$top" ]] && echo "subshell:            BASHPID is its own" )
v=$(printf '%s' "$BASHPID"); [[ $v != "$top" ]] && echo "command substitution: BASHPID is its own"
echo | { [[ $BASHPID != "$top" ]] && echo "pipeline element:    BASHPID is its own"; }
[[ $BASHPID == "$top" ]] && echo "top level:           BASHPID and \$\$ agree"

subshell:            $$ is still the script's PID
subshell:            BASHPID is its own
command substitution: BASHPID is its own
pipeline element:    BASHPID is its own
top level:           BASHPID and $$ agree

$$ is the PID of the script — the top-level shell — and it keeps that value in every subshell, command substitution and pipeline element. BASHPID, added in bash 4.0, is the PID of the process actually running the code. At the top level they are equal; everywhere else they differ. The choice between $$ versus BASHPID follows from what the code wants to signal:

trap 'echo "script:   got TERM"' TERM
( trap 'echo "subshell: got TERM"' TERM; kill -s TERM "$BASHPID" )
( trap 'echo "subshell: got TERM"' TERM; kill -s TERM "$$" )

subshell: got TERM
script:   got TERM

A subshell that sends SIGTERM to $BASHPID signals itself, and its own trap caught it. A subshell that sends it to $$ signals the whole script, whose trap caught it. That second behaviour is what §12.5's re-raise wants: kill -s "$1" "$$" must end the script, even if the handler happens to run in a subshell. Use BASHPID for "this process", and $$ for "the script".

Sending a signal to a process group

Every process belongs to a process group, identified by the PID of its leader. A negative PID in kill means "every process in this group". Sending a signal to a process group is how a whole tree of processes is stopped at once — it is what the terminal does for Ctrl-C, and what systemd's control group does for a service:

cat > svc.sh <<'EOF'
sleep 30 &
echo "$!" > child.pid
wait
EOF
for target in 'the PID' 'the process group'; do
  : > child.pid
  set -m; bash svc.sh & leader=$!; set +m        # svc.sh leads a new process group
  until [[ -s child.pid ]]; do sleep 0.05; done
  child=$(<child.pid)
  if [[ $target == 'the PID' ]]; then kill -s TERM "$leader"; else kill -s TERM -- "-$leader"; fi
  wait "$leader"
  echo "TERM to $target: svc.sh exited $?"
  sleep 0.2
  if kill -0 "$child" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "  its sleep is still running, now an orphan"
    kill "$child"
  else
    echo "  its sleep got the signal too"
  fi
done

TERM to the PID: svc.sh exited 143
  its sleep is still running, now an orphan
TERM to the process group: svc.sh exited 143
  its sleep got the signal too

svc.sh started a background sleep and waited for it. SIGTERM to the script's PID killed the script and left the sleep running, reparented, with nobody waiting for it. SIGTERM to the process group, kill -s TERM -- "-$leader", reached both. The -- ends kill's options, so that the negative number is read as a PID rather than as a signal. set -m is what gave svc.sh a group of its own: with job control on, each job is started as the leader of a new process group. Without it, a script's background jobs share the script's group.

Never write kill 0 or kill -- -$$ in a script without thinking through what group it is in. 0 means "my own process group". A script started from an interactive shell leads a group of its own, because the interactive shell has job control on; but a script started by another script is in its caller's group, since a shell without job control creates no new groups. kill 0 then signals the caller and every sibling as well. Create a group deliberately with set -m, as these examples do, and signal only a group whose leader you started.

12.10 trap DEBUG and trap RETURN

Bash has two more trap conditions, neither a signal, both added for the bash debugger and both usable in ordinary scripts.

trap DEBUG: before every command

A trap DEBUG action runs before every simple command, for, case, select, ((, [[ and arithmetic for, and before the first command of a function. BASH_COMMAND holds the command about to run, and LINENO its line:

trap 'echo "  [debug] line $LINENO: $BASH_COMMAND"' DEBUG
total=0
add() { total=$(( total + $1 )); }
add 5
set -T
add 7
trap - DEBUG
echo "total is $total"

  [debug] line 2: total=0
  [debug] line 4: add 5
  [debug] line 5: set -T
  [debug] line 6: add 7
  [debug] line 3: add 7
  [debug] line 3: total=$(( total + $1 ))
  [debug] line 7: trap - DEBUG
total is 12

The trap reported every top-level command, but not the commands inside add the first time it was called: the DEBUG trap is not inherited by functions unless the functrace option is on, set -T, or the function has the trace attribute (below). After set -T, the second call was traced inside the function: first a line for the function itself, reporting the line on which add was defined, then its assignment. set -x (§20) prints similar information, but a DEBUG trap is code, so it can decide what to print, send it to a separate file, or count commands. Because it runs before every command, it is slow, and belongs in debugging sessions rather than in production.

With the extdebug shell option on, a DEBUG trap can also skip the command: if the action returns a non-zero status, the command is not run. That makes a dry-run guard possible, and gets the status wrong very easily:

shopt -s extdebug
deploy() { echo "DEPLOYING to $1"; }
trap '[[ $BASH_COMMAND == deploy* ]] && { echo "dry run, skipped: $BASH_COMMAND"; false; }' DEBUG
echo "building"
deploy prod
echo "done"

dry run, skipped: deploy prod

The trap was meant to skip only deploy. But [[ … ]] && { … } has status 1 whenever the test is false, which was the case for every other command, so extdebug skipped them all: "building" and "done" never ran. A DEBUG trap under extdebug must return 0 for every command it means to allow:

shopt -s extdebug
deploy() { echo "DEPLOYING to $1"; }
dry_run() {
  if [[ $BASH_COMMAND == deploy* ]]; then
    echo "dry run, skipped: $BASH_COMMAND"
    return 1
  fi
}
trap dry_run DEBUG
echo "building"
deploy prod
echo "done"

building
dry run, skipped: deploy prod
done

The if form returns 0 when its condition is false, and return 1 skips only the command that matched. extdebug has other effects too — it changes what declare -F prints and enables extra debugger behaviour — so it is a tool for debugging sessions, not a switch to leave on.

trap RETURN: when a function or sourced file returns

A trap RETURN action runs when a function or a file run with source finishes. Its inheritance rules are the same as DEBUG's:

f() { trap 'echo "  RETURN trap: leaving ${FUNCNAME[0]:-a sourced file}"' RETURN; echo "in f"; }
g() { echo "in g"; }
f
g
trap -p RETURN
printf 'echo "in lib.sh"\n' > lib.sh
source ./lib.sh
set -T
g

in f
  RETURN trap: leaving f
in g
trap -- 'echo "  RETURN trap: leaving ${FUNCNAME[0]:-a sourced file}"' RETURN
in lib.sh
  RETURN trap: leaving a sourced file
in g
  RETURN trap: leaving g

f set a RETURN trap inside itself, and it ran when f returned. g, called next, did not trigger it, even though trap -p shows the trap is still set: a function does not inherit the RETURN trap unless set -T is on or the function has the trace attribute. The trap did fire when lib.sh finished being sourced, because source is not a function call. After set -T, g triggered it too. A trap set inside a function is global, not local to the function — which is a surprise in its own right, and is why a function that sets one should also remove it.

That makes RETURN a function-scoped cleanup, with one gap:

work() {
  local tmp=scratch.$1
  : > "$tmp"
  trap 'rm -f -- "$tmp"; echo "  RETURN: removed $tmp"; trap - RETURN' RETURN
  [[ $1 == b ]] && exit 3
  echo "work $1: done"
}
work a
work c
( work b )
echo "work b exited the whole (sub)shell with $?, and left:" scratch.*

work a: done
  RETURN: removed scratch.a
work c: done
  RETURN: removed scratch.c
work b exited the whole (sub)shell with 3, and left: scratch.b

The function sets a RETURN trap that removes its scratch file and then removes itself with trap - RETURN, so it does not fire for the next function to return. It cleaned up after work a and work c. work b called exit, and the RETURN trap did not run: a function that ends by exit — or by set -e, or a signal — does not return, and its scratch file was left behind. A RETURN trap is fine for tidying up after the normal path; a resource that must be released on every path belongs in the EXIT trap's registry (§12.4).

Tracing one function: declare -ft

The trace attribute makes one function inherit the DEBUG and RETURN traps without turning set -T on for everything. declare -ft NAME sets it:

deploy() {
  local target=$1
  echo "deploying to $target"
}
build() { echo "building"; }
trap '[[ ${FUNCNAME[0]-} == deploy ]] && echo "  [trace] $BASH_COMMAND"' DEBUG
declare -ft deploy
build
deploy prod
trap - DEBUG

building
  [trace] deploy prod
  [trace] local target=$1
  [trace] echo "deploying to $target"
deploying to prod

Only deploy was traced: build ran untraced, and the trap's own test on FUNCNAME[0] kept the top-level commands out of the output. Setting the attribute on the function that is misbehaving, and leaving the rest alone, is often the quickest way to see what a large script is doing — faster to read than set -x over the whole run.

12.11 A Long-Running Script: Reload, Report, Stop

A script that runs for hours — a queue worker, a watcher, a poller — needs all of this at once. The convention it should follow comes from daemons: SIGHUP re-reads the configuration, SIGUSR1 reports status, and SIGTERM or SIGINT stops it cleanly, finishing the item in hand rather than abandoning it halfway. The shape that makes this reliable is to do nothing in the handlers except set a flag, and to act on the flags at one safe point in the main loop:

cat > worker.sh <<'EOF'
set -u
reload=0 report=0 stop=0 processed=0
trap 'reload=1' HUP
trap 'report=1' USR1
trap 'stop=1' TERM INT
load_config() { prefix=$(<worker.conf); echo "config loaded: prefix is $prefix"; }
load_config
while (( ! stop )); do
  for item in queue/*; do
    [[ -e $item ]] || break
    echo "$prefix ${item#queue/}"
    mv -- "$item" done/
    processed=$(( processed + 1 ))
  done
  if (( reload )); then reload=0; load_config; fi
  if (( report )); then report=0; echo "status: $processed processed"; fi
  sleep 0.1 & wait "$!"
done
echo "stopping cleanly after $processed items"
EOF
mkdir queue done
echo 'job' > worker.conf
bash worker.sh > worker.log & worker=$!
wait_for() { until grep -q "$1" worker.log; do sleep 0.05; done; }
wait_for 'config loaded'
touch queue/a queue/b;              wait_for 'job b'
kill -s USR1 "$worker";             wait_for 'status: 2'
echo 'task' > worker.conf
kill -s HUP "$worker";              wait_for 'prefix is task'
touch queue/c;                      wait_for 'task c'
kill -s TERM "$worker"
wait "$worker"; echo "worker.sh exited $?"
cat worker.log

worker.sh exited 0
config loaded: prefix is job
job a
job b
status: 2 processed
config loaded: prefix is task
task c
stopping cleanly after 3 items

The handlers are one assignment each. The main loop processes whatever is in the queue, then checks the flags: a pending reload reads worker.conf again, a pending report prints the count, and a pending stop ends the loop after the current round. It waits between rounds with sleep 0.1 & wait "$!", so a signal cuts the wait short instead of waiting behind the sleep (§12.7). The driver sent USR1 after two items and got status: 2 processed; changed the configuration and sent HUP, and the next item used the new prefix; and sent TERM, and the worker finished the round, printed its summary and exited 0.

Setting a flag and acting on it later is the rule for any handler that does more than clean up and exit, for two reasons. A signal can arrive at any point, in the middle of a multi-line update of the script's state; a handler that modifies the same state can see it half-changed. And a handler that acts immediately cannot choose where to act, whereas the main loop can choose the point where the work is between items. The worker above is never interrupted mid-item by its own reload.

12.12 The Signals-and-Traps Table

The conditions trap accepts, what each means, and the rule for each that is easiest to get wrong.

Construct
What it does, and the rule that is easiest to get wrong
trap 'action' SIG…
Runs action when a signal arrives, then carries on. Single-quote it (SC2064). Replaces any earlier trap for that condition (§12.2, §12.4).
trap '' SIG
Ignores the signal — and every command started meanwhile inherits the ignore and cannot trap it (§12.8).
trap - SIG
Restores the default. The way to undo a trap (§12.2).
trap -p [SIG] · trap -P SIG
Lists traps as re-readable commands; works inside $( ). -P prints the bare action, bash 5.3 only (§12.2).
trap … EXIT
Runs once when the shell exits, including on set -e, and on a fatal signal in bash 5 (not in dash or bash 3.2); never on SIGKILL (§12.3).
trap … ERR
Runs where set -e would exit; reaches into functions only with set -E (§11.10, §12.6).
trap … DEBUG
Before every command; into functions only with set -T or declare -ft. Skips a command under extdebug if it returns non-zero (§12.10).
trap … RETURN
When a function or sourced file returns; not when a function ends by exit (§12.10).
exit in a trap
Sets the script's status; does not re-run the EXIT trap. Give it an explicit status (§12.3).
trap - SIG; kill -s SIG "$$"
The way to end after a signal, so the caller sees a death by signal, not exit 130 (§12.5).
cmd in the foreground
A trapped signal waits until it finishes. Use cmd & wait $! (§12.7).
( … ) · $( … ) · &
Caught signals revert to the default; ignored ones stay ignored. Background jobs ignore SIGINT and SIGQUIT (§12.8).
kill -s SIG PID
Names, not numbers (USR1 is 30 on macOS, 10 on Linux). -0 tests existence (§12.1, §12.9).
kill -s SIG -- -PGID
Signals a whole process group. Never kill 0 in a script (§12.9).
$$ · BASHPID
The script's PID everywhere, versus the current process's (§12.9).

And the rule behind all of them: cleanup goes in one EXIT trap, registered as each resource is acquired, written so that it can neither fail nor do harm if it runs twice; signal handlers set a flag or re-raise, and do nothing else.

Exercises

1. A nightly job that cleans up the wrong things. nightly.sh takes a lock, makes a temporary file, and does its work. It is run from a loop, and its author says it "cleans up after itself". Find three ways its cleanup is wrong — one of them removes something that is not its own — and fix them.

cat > nightly.sh <<'EOF'
lock=nightly.lock
tmp=$(mktemp)
cleanup() {
  rm -f -- "$tmp"
  rmdir -- "$lock" 2>/dev/null || echo "rmdir: $lock was already gone"
  echo "cleaned up"
}
trap 'cleanup; exit 0' INT TERM
trap cleanup EXIT
mkdir -- "$lock" 2>/dev/null || { echo "another run holds the lock" >&2; exit 1; }
: > "ready.$1"
echo "run $1: working"
sleep 1
echo "run $1: finished"
EOF
Solution

Two experiments show the problems. The first starts a second run while the first holds the lock; the second presses Ctrl-C (by signalling the loop's process group) during the first of three runs:

cat > nightly.sh <<'EOF'
lock=nightly.lock
tmp=$(mktemp)
cleanup() {
  rm -f -- "$tmp"
  rmdir -- "$lock" 2>/dev/null || echo "rmdir: $lock was already gone"
  echo "cleaned up"
}
trap 'cleanup; exit 0' INT TERM
trap cleanup EXIT
mkdir -- "$lock" 2>/dev/null || { echo "another run holds the lock" >&2; exit 1; }
: > "ready.$1"
echo "run $1: working"
sleep 1
echo "run $1: finished"
EOF
echo "--- a second run while the first holds the lock:"
bash nightly.sh 1 & first=$!
until [[ -e ready.1 ]]; do sleep 0.05; done
bash nightly.sh 2; echo "run 2 exited $?"
[[ -d nightly.lock ]] && echo "the lock is still held" || echo "the lock is GONE while run 1 is still working"
wait "$first"
echo "--- Ctrl-C during a run, from a loop of three:"
cat > loop.sh <<'EOF'
for n in 1 2 3; do bash nightly.sh "$n"; done
EOF
rm -f ready.?
set -m; bash loop.sh & leader=$!; set +m
until [[ -e ready.1 ]]; do sleep 0.05; done
kill -s INT -- "-$leader"
wait "$leader"; echo "loop.sh exited $?"

--- a second run while the first holds the lock:
run 1: working
another run holds the lock
cleaned up
run 2 exited 1
the lock is GONE while run 1 is still working
run 1: finished
rmdir: nightly.lock was already gone
cleaned up
--- Ctrl-C during a run, from a loop of three:
run 1: working
cleaned up
rmdir: nightly.lock was already gone
cleaned up
run 2: working
run 2: finished
cleaned up
run 3: working
run 3: finished
cleaned up
loop.sh exited 0

The traps are set before the lock is taken. The second run failed to get the lock and exited 1, as it should — and its EXIT trap then ran rmdir on the lock the first run was holding. The lock was gone while run 1 was still working, so a third run could have started alongside it. A cleanup must release only what its own script acquired: set the traps after the lock is taken, or record what was acquired as §12.4's registry does. The cleanup runs twice. cleanup; exit 0 in the signal trap is followed by the EXIT trap, so each interrupted run cleaned up twice and found the lock already gone (§12.5). exit 0 swallows the interrupt. Run 1 was interrupted, reported success, and the loop went on to runs 2 and 3; the whole loop then exited 0 (§12.5).

cat > nightly.sh <<'EOF'
set -Eeuo pipefail
lock=nightly.lock
if ! mkdir -- "$lock" 2>/dev/null; then
  echo "another run holds the lock" >&2
  exit 1
fi
tmp=
cleanup() {
  local status=$?
  set +e
  [[ -n $tmp ]] && rm -f -- "$tmp"
  rmdir -- "$lock"
  echo "cleaned up"
  return "$status"
}
trap cleanup EXIT
for sig in INT TERM HUP; do
  # shellcheck disable=SC2064  # $sig is expanded now, once per signal
  trap "trap - $sig; kill -s $sig \$\$" "$sig"
done
tmp=$(mktemp)
: > "ready.$1"
echo "run $1: working"
sleep 1
echo "run $1: finished"
EOF
echo "--- a second run while the first holds the lock:"
bash nightly.sh 1 & first=$!
until [[ -e ready.1 ]]; do sleep 0.05; done
bash nightly.sh 2; echo "run 2 exited $?"
[[ -d nightly.lock ]] && echo "the lock is still held" || echo "the lock is GONE while run 1 is still working"
wait "$first"
echo "--- Ctrl-C during a run, from a loop of three:"
cat > loop.sh <<'EOF'
for n in 1 2 3; do bash nightly.sh "$n"; done
EOF
rm -f ready.?
set -m; bash loop.sh & leader=$!; set +m
until [[ -e ready.1 ]]; do sleep 0.05; done
kill -s INT -- "-$leader"
wait "$leader"; echo "loop.sh exited $? ($(kill -l $?))"
[[ -d nightly.lock ]] && echo "the lock was left behind" || echo "no lock left behind"

--- a second run while the first holds the lock:
run 1: working
another run holds the lock
run 2 exited 1
the lock is still held
run 1: finished
cleaned up
--- Ctrl-C during a run, from a loop of three:
run 1: working
cleaned up
loop.sh exited 130 (INT)
no lock left behind

The lock is taken first, and only a run that holds it installs the trap that releases it. Cleanup lives in the EXIT trap alone, saves the status, cannot fail under set -e, and removes the temporary file only if it was created. The signal traps reset the signal and re-raise it, so the interrupted run died of SIGINT and the loop stopped with it, leaving no lock behind. A losing run no longer touches the winner's lock.

2. A timeout in pure bash. macOS does not ship a timeout command (Homebrew's coreutils adds one). Write with_timeout SECONDS COMMAND [ARG...], which runs a command, kills it with SIGTERM if it is still running after SECONDS, and returns 124 in that case (as GNU timeout does) or the command's own status otherwise. It must not leave any process running after it returns.

Solution 
with_timeout() {
  local secs=$1 cmd watcher status=0
  shift
  "$@" & cmd=$!
  (
    trap 'kill "$sleeper" 2>/dev/null; exit 0' TERM
    sleep "$secs" & sleeper=$!
    wait "$sleeper"
    kill -s TERM "$cmd" 2>/dev/null
  ) & watcher=$!
  wait "$cmd" || status=$?
  kill -s TERM "$watcher" 2>/dev/null
  wait "$watcher"
  if (( status == 128 + $(kill -l TERM) )); then return 124; fi
  return "$status"
}
with_timeout 1 sleep 5;              echo "sleep 5 with a 1s limit:     $?"
with_timeout 5 sleep 0.2;            echo "sleep 0.2 with a 5s limit:   $?"
with_timeout 5 bash -c 'exit 3';     echo "a command that fails with 3: $?"

sleep 5 with a 1s limit:     124
sleep 0.2 with a 5s limit:   0
a command that fails with 3: 3

The command runs in the background and a watcher subshell sleeps and then signals it. wait "$cmd" returns the command's status, or 143 if the watcher killed it, which is translated to 124. After the wait, the watcher is no longer needed and is sent SIGTERM.

The part that is easy to get wrong is the watcher. The obvious version is ( sleep "$secs"; kill -s TERM "$cmd" ) &, and killing it leaves its sleep running. The limit here is an unusual 31.5 seconds so that ps can count exactly this sleep and no other:

naive_timeout() {
  local secs=$1 cmd watcher status=0
  shift
  "$@" & cmd=$!
  ( sleep "$secs"; kill -s TERM "$cmd" 2>/dev/null ) & watcher=$!
  wait "$cmd" || status=$?
  kill -s TERM "$watcher" 2>/dev/null
  return "$status"
}
naive_timeout 31.5 sleep 0.3
sleep 0.2
ps -A -o command= | awk '$1 == "sleep" && $2 == "31.5" { n++ } END { print n + 0, "orphaned sleep 31.5 left running" }'
pkill -x -f 'sleep 31.5'
exit 0

1 orphaned sleep 31.5 left running

SIGTERM to the watcher killed the subshell, and its sleep 30 — a separate process in the foreground of that subshell — was left behind, orphaned, for the rest of its run. That is §12.7's delay again, seen from the other side. The solution's watcher runs its sleep in the background and waits for it, so its TERM trap runs immediately and kills the sleep before exiting. Every process with_timeout starts is gone when it returns.

One limit remains: a command that exits 143 by itself is reported as a timeout. GNU timeout avoids that by recording whether it sent the signal, and a flag file or the watcher's exit status would do the same here.

3. A trap you can add to. Write add_exit_trap ACTION, which adds ACTION to the EXIT trap instead of replacing it, so a library can register its cleanup without destroying the script's. It must work on bash 5.2, so trap -P is not available, and must handle actions containing quotes.

Solution 
add_exit_trap() {
  local -a words=()
  eval "words=( $(trap -p EXIT) )"          # trap -- 'ACTION' EXIT, quoted by bash itself
  local existing=${words[2]-}
  # shellcheck disable=SC2064  # both actions are complete strings; expanding them now is the point
  trap "${existing:+$existing; }$1" EXIT
}
add_exit_trap 'echo "first: remove the temp file"'
add_exit_trap "echo 'second: it'\''s the lock'"
add_exit_trap 'echo "third: stop the server"'
trap -p EXIT
echo "exiting"

trap -- 'echo "first: remove the temp file"; echo '\''second: it'\''\'\'''\''s the lock'\''; echo "third: stop the server"' EXIT
exiting
first: remove the temp file
second: it's the lock
third: stop the server

trap -p EXIT prints trap -- 'ACTION' EXIT with the action quoted by bash itself, so eval can split it into words safely: the output is shell syntax that bash generated, not data from outside. The third word is the existing action, or nothing when no trap is set. The new trap is the old action, a semicolon, and the new one, and ${existing:+…; } leaves out the separator when there was nothing before. The trap -p output shows the three actions joined, with the apostrophe in the second quoted correctly through two rounds, and the actions ran in the order they were added. On bash 5.3, existing=$(trap -P EXIT) replaces the eval line; §12.4's array registry is still the better design for a script that controls its own code, because it runs the cleanups in reverse order and survives a failure in any one of them.

4. A supervisor that stops its workers. supervise.sh starts three workers in the background and waits for them. Press Ctrl-C, and the supervisor exits — but the workers keep running. Explain why, and fix it so that Ctrl-C or SIGTERM stops every worker, and the supervisor still exits in a way its caller recognises as an interrupt.

cat > worker.sh <<'EOF'
: > "ready.$1"
while :; do sleep 0.1; done
EOF
cat > supervise.sh <<'EOF'
pids=()
for n in 1 2 3; do
  bash worker.sh "$n" & pids+=("$!")
done
printf '%s\n' "${pids[@]}" > workers.pid
wait
EOF
Solution 
cat > worker.sh <<'EOF'
: > "ready.$1"
while :; do sleep 0.1; done
EOF
cat > supervise.sh <<'EOF'
pids=()
for n in 1 2 3; do
  bash worker.sh "$n" & pids+=("$!")
done
printf '%s\n' "${pids[@]}" > workers.pid
wait
EOF
set -m; bash supervise.sh & leader=$!; set +m
until [[ -e ready.1 && -e ready.2 && -e ready.3 ]]; do sleep 0.05; done
kill -s INT -- "-$leader"
wait "$leader"
echo "supervise.sh exited $? ($(kill -l $?))"
sleep 0.3
alive=0
while read -r pid; do
  if kill -0 "$pid" 2>/dev/null; then alive=$(( alive + 1 )); kill "$pid"; fi
done < workers.pid
echo "$alive of its 3 workers are still running"

supervise.sh exited 130 (INT)
3 of its 3 workers are still running

The supervisor was killed by SIGINT with 130, as it should be. The workers were not, although the signal went to the whole process group, because they are background jobs: bash starts every & job with SIGINT ignored when job control is off (§12.8). All three were still running after their supervisor had gone.

cat > worker.sh <<'EOF'
: > "ready.$1"
while :; do sleep 0.1; done
EOF
cat > supervise.sh <<'EOF'
pids=()
stop() {
  local sig=$1
  echo "supervisor: SIG$sig, stopping ${#pids[@]} workers"
  kill -s TERM "${pids[@]}" 2>/dev/null
  wait "${pids[@]}"
  echo "supervisor: all workers stopped"
  trap - "$sig"
  kill -s "$sig" "$$"
}
for sig in INT TERM HUP; do
  # shellcheck disable=SC2064  # $sig is expanded now, once per signal
  trap "stop $sig" "$sig"
done
for n in 1 2 3; do
  bash worker.sh "$n" & pids+=("$!")
done
printf '%s\n' "${pids[@]}" > workers.pid
wait
EOF
set -m; bash supervise.sh & leader=$!; set +m
until [[ -e ready.1 && -e ready.2 && -e ready.3 ]]; do sleep 0.05; done
kill -s INT -- "-$leader"
wait "$leader"
status=$?
sleep 0.3
alive=0
while read -r pid; do
  if kill -0 "$pid" 2>/dev/null; then alive=$(( alive + 1 )); kill "$pid"; fi
done < workers.pid
echo "supervise.sh exited $status ($(kill -l "$status")), and $alive of its 3 workers are still running"

supervisor: SIGINT, stopping 3 workers
supervisor: all workers stopped
supervise.sh exited 130 (INT), and 0 of its 3 workers are still running

The supervisor now traps INT, TERM and HUP, and its handler forwards SIGTERM to every worker, waits for them to exit, and then re-raises the signal it received (§12.5). It sends SIGTERM rather than forwarding SIGINT because the workers cannot receive SIGINT at all. The wait inside the handler matters: without it, the supervisor would exit while the workers were still shutting down, and whatever started the supervisor would believe everything had stopped. The wait at the end of the script is interrupted by the signal (§12.7), so the supervisor handles Ctrl-C at once, not when its workers happen to finish.

SECTION 13

Building a CLI: getopts and Completion

A script that only its author runs can take its arguments in any order the author remembers. A script that other people run — a colleague, a CI job, a cron entry written two years later by someone who never read the source — is a command-line program, and it is judged the way every command-line program is judged. Does -h say how to use it? Does -vn3 mean what it means to ls and grep? Does a mistyped option produce a message that says what was wrong, on standard error, with a status a caller can test? Does a file named -x.txt get treated as a file? Does pressing Tab after the command name offer anything useful? None of this is difficult, but none of it happens by accident, and a script that gets it wrong is one that people have to read before they can use.

This section builds that interface. It starts with the conventions a command line is expected to follow, then parses options with the getopts builtin — the option string, OPTARG, OPTIND, the two ways it reports errors, where it stops and why — and then handles what getopts does not: long options, subcommands like git commit and kv set, help text, --version, and validating what the user passed before the script acts on it. The second half is programmable completion: the complete and compgen builtins, writing a completion function that knows a script's subcommands, options and data, testing that function without a terminal, and installing it so that the bash-completion project loads it on demand.

§11.4 set the conventions this section builds on: a usage function that prints to standard output with status 0 when asked for help and to standard error with status 2 when the invocation is wrong, and die [STATUS] MESSAGE. §8's fourth exercise wrote an option loop by hand with while and case, and §6.8 built a lookup table that §13.7 turns into a subcommand dispatcher. Every example below was measured under bash 5.3 on macOS and bash 5.2 on Debian, which agreed on all of them except compgen -V, new in 5.3 and labelled where it appears. Two examples need tools macOS does not ship — util-linux's getopt and the bash-completion package — and were run on Debian, which the text says where they appear. What readline does when Tab is really pressed — how it splits the line, whether it adds a space — was checked by pressing Tab in an interactive bash on a pseudo-terminal, since no script can observe it otherwise.

13.1 Command Line Interface Design: What a Script Promises

Command line interface design is mostly a matter of not surprising anyone. The people who run a script have spent years with ls, grep, tar and git, and they bring those programs' rules with them. A script that follows the same rules can be used without reading it; one that invents its own gets misused, and the misuse is the script's fault. The rules come from two places. POSIX's Utility Syntax Guidelines (XBD chapter 12) describe how options and operands are written; they are the rules getopts implements. The GNU coding standards add long options, --help and --version, which nearly every tool on a Linux system follows and which POSIX does not cover.

Where those rules differ, this section says which to follow — most visibly on whether positional arguments after options may be followed by more options, which POSIX forbids and GNU allows.

The vocabulary first. In grep -c -i -e error app.log, grep is the utility name, -c, -i and -e are options, error is an option-argument (it belongs to -e), and app.log is an operand — the thing the command acts on. Options change how a command behaves; operands are what it works on. A good interface keeps that distinction clean: a script that deletes old backups takes the directory as an operand and the number to keep as an option (prune -k 5 /backups), because the directory is the subject and the count is a setting with a sensible default.

The guidelines that matter most for a script:

Guideline
What it says, and what it means for a script
3, 4 — one letter
Each option is a single alphanumeric character after a -. -W is reserved for vendor options. Long names (--verbose) are a GNU addition (§13.6).
5 — grouping
Options without arguments may be grouped behind one -, and the last of the group may take an argument: -vn3 means -v -n 3. A hand-written parser almost never allows this (§13.2); getopts does (§13.3).
6, 7 — arguments
An option-argument should be a separate word (-n 3), though -n3 must be accepted too. Option-arguments should not be optional: -n either always takes one or never does.
9 — order
All options come before operands. POSIX tools stop looking for options at the first operand; GNU tools accept positional arguments after options and options after them (§13.5).
10 — --
The first -- ends the options, and everything after it is an operand even if it starts with -. This is how a file named -v is passed safely.
11 — repetition
The order of different options should not matter; a repeated option is applied in order, so -n 3 -n 5 means 5.
13 — -
An operand of - means standard input (or standard output, when the operand is an output file).

Two of these are worth seeing, because they are the ones scripts break. The -- end of options marker exists because an operand can look like an option:

printf '%s\n' 'keep this line' '-v marks a verbose run' > notes.txt
grep -c -v notes.txt < /dev/null
echo "grep -c -v notes.txt: status $?"
grep -c -- -v notes.txt
echo "grep -c -- -v notes.txt: status $?"

0
grep -c -v notes.txt: status 1
1
grep -c -- -v notes.txt: status 0

grep -c -v notes.txt did not search notes.txt for -v. It read -v as grep's own "invert the match" option, took notes.txt as the pattern, found no file operand, and read standard input — here empty, so it counted 0 lines and exited 1. Interactively it would simply have hung waiting for input. grep -c -- -v notes.txt searched for the text -v and found it once. The same trap applies to every operand that comes from a variable, a glob or a user: rm $file with file=-rf is the classic, and for f in *; do cmd "$f"; done in a directory containing a file named -n is the common version. A script whose options are parsed by getopts honours the -- end of options marker automatically (§13.5); a script that passes operands on to other commands should put -- in front of them, as this course's examples that hand a variable to mv or rm do.

Guideline 13 is what lets a command sit in a pipeline:

printf 'from a file\n' > part2.txt
printf 'from a pipe\n' | cat - part2.txt

from a pipe
from a file

cat - part2.txt read standard input where the - was, then the file. A script that takes a file operand should accept - the same way, which usually costs one line: [[ $file == - ]] && file=/dev/stdin.

The rest of the contract

The syntax is half of what a user expects. The rest comes from the GNU standards and from the conventions §11 established, and together they are the checklist this section works through:

  • -h and --help print usage to standard output and exit 0. Nothing else happens: --help never starts the work (§13.9).
  • --version prints the program name and version on one line and exits 0 (§13.9).
  • A usage error — an unknown option, a missing argument, a bad value — prints a short message naming the program and the problem to standard error, usually with a pointer to --help, and exits with status 2 (or EX_USAGE, 64). The exit code for usage errors is distinct from the exit code for a failure of the work itself, so that a caller can tell "you called me wrong" from "I tried and it failed" (§11.4, §13.10). Choose one exit code for usage errors and use it everywhere in the script.
  • Output that is data goes to standard output; everything else goes to standard error — progress, warnings, diagnostics — so that script | next-command receives only the data (§10.13).
  • Defaults are sensible and documented, and every default can be overridden, by an option or, for settings that belong to the environment, by an environment variable (§13.10).
  • Nothing destructive happens by default. A script that deletes or overwrites should offer -n (dry run) or ask, and should never interpret a missing operand as "everything".
  • Silence on success is the Unix default: a script that did what it was asked prints nothing unless its output is the point. -v adds detail; -q removes even the warnings.

A last design choice comes before any code: options or subcommands. A script that does one thing with variations — compress these logs, keeping five — takes options. A script that does several different things to the same data — set, get, delete and list keys in a store — takes a subcommand as its first operand, as git, docker and systemctl do, and each subcommand takes its own options (§13.7).
