Forcing the second shape into the first produces --set, --get and --delete options that are mutually exclusive, which is a subcommand interface with worse error messages.

13.2 Parsing by Hand, and Where It Breaks

§8's fourth exercise parsed options with a loop over "$@" and a case on $1. The shape is worth seeing once more, because it is what most scripts do, and because its failures are exactly the ones getopts exists to fix:

cat > count <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
verbose=0 limit=10
while (( $# > 0 )); do
  case $1 in
    -v) verbose=1 ;;
    -n) limit=$2; shift ;;
    --) shift; break ;;
    -*) echo "count: unknown option: $1" >&2; exit 2 ;;
    *)  break ;;
  esac
  shift
done
echo "verbose=$verbose limit=$limit operands=[$*]"
EOF
bash count -v -n 3 file.txt
bash count -vn3 file.txt
bash count -n3 file.txt
bash count -n
echo "status $?"

verbose=1 limit=3 operands=[file.txt]
count: unknown option: -vn3
count: unknown option: -n3
verbose=0 limit= operands=[]
status 0

The first call worked: separate options, separate argument. The next two are ordinary invocations that every standard tool accepts — -vn3 is Guideline 5's grouping and -n3 is Guideline 6's attached argument — and the loop rejected both as unknown options, because its case compares whole words and neither word is -v or -n. Adding clauses for them is possible (§13.6 does it, for the long-option parser that needs it anyway), but every combination of bundled flags is a new case, and the loop grows faster than the option list.

The last call is worse, because it did not fail. count -n with no argument set limit to the empty string from the missing $2, and the shift at the bottom of the loop, which had nothing left to shift, returned 1 — which nobody checked. The script printed limit= and exited 0. With set -u the $2 would at least have stopped it with an unbound variable message; without it, a missing argument became an empty value that the rest of the script would have used. A hand-written loop has to check $# > 1 before every option that takes an argument, and most do not.

None of this is exotic. A parser that handles grouping, attached arguments, missing arguments, unknown options and -- correctly is about as much code as the loop above — but it is the same code in every script, and it has been written already.

13.3 The getopts Builtin: Option String, OPTARG and OPTIND

The getopts builtin is POSIX's option parser, built into every shell. It parses one option each time it is called, so it is always used as the condition of a while loop, with a case inside to act on each option:

cat > count <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
verbose=0 limit=10
while getopts 'vn:' opt; do
  case $opt in
    v) verbose=1 ;;
    n) limit=$OPTARG ;;
    *) exit 2 ;;
  esac
done
shift $((OPTIND - 1))
echo "verbose=$verbose limit=$limit operands=[$*]"
EOF
bash count -v -n 3 file.txt
bash count -vn3 file.txt
bash count -n3 -v file.txt other.txt
bash count file.txt

verbose=1 limit=3 operands=[file.txt]
verbose=1 limit=3 operands=[file.txt]
verbose=1 limit=3 operands=[file.txt other.txt]
verbose=0 limit=10 operands=[file.txt]

The same count now accepts all four forms. getopts 'vn:' opt has three parts. The option string vn: lists the options the script accepts, one character each: v alone, and n with the colon for an argument. A letter followed by a colon takes an argument: n: means -n must be given a value, which getopts delivers in the variable OPTARG. That is the colon for an argument rule, and it is the only syntax the option string has, apart from a leading colon (§13.4). opt is the name of the variable getopts sets to the option it found, without the dash, so the case compares against v and n. The *) clause catches anything else; §13.4 covers what that is.

After the loop comes the line every getopts script has: shift $((OPTIND-1)). getopts never modifies the positional parameters. It walks over them, keeping its place in OPTIND, the index of the next argument to examine, which starts at 1 when the shell starts. When the loop ends, OPTIND points at the first operand, so shifting away OPTIND - 1 arguments leaves exactly the operands in "$@". That is why file.txt other.txt came out as the operands after -n3 -v.

Watching OPTIND and OPTARG change makes the mechanism concrete. This loop parses a fixed argument list, set with set --, and prints both variables after each call, along with the argument OPTIND now points at:

set -- -vn3 -q file.txt
while getopts 'qvn:' opt; do
  printf 'opt=%s  OPTARG=%-7s OPTIND=%s  (next: %s)\n' \
    "$opt" "${OPTARG-unset}" "$OPTIND" "${!OPTIND-none}"
done
echo "loop ended: opt=$opt OPTIND=$OPTIND"
shift $((OPTIND - 1))
echo "after the shift: $# operand(s): $*"

opt=v  OPTARG=unset   OPTIND=1  (next: -vn3)
opt=n  OPTARG=3       OPTIND=2  (next: -q)
opt=q  OPTARG=unset   OPTIND=3  (next: file.txt)
loop ended: opt=? OPTIND=3
after the shift: 1 operand(s): file.txt

Four things happen here that a hand-written loop gets wrong.

Grouping. -vn3 produced two options, v and n with OPTARG=3. After v, OPTIND was still 1: getopts was still inside the first word, and remembers the position within it internally. Only after taking n and its attached argument did it move on to word 2.

OPTARG is unset for an option without an argument. POSIX requires this, so a stale OPTARG from an earlier option can never be mistaken for a value. A script reads OPTARG only in the case clauses for options that take one.

The end. When getopts reaches something that is not an option — here file.txt — it returns a non-zero status, which ends the while loop, and sets opt to ?. OPTIND is left pointing at file.txt, index 3.

The shift. shift $((OPTIND-1)) removed two words, -vn3 and -q, and left one operand. The shift uses OPTIND, not a count of options found, because three options were found in two words.

An option-argument is taken whatever it looks like

A letter followed by a colon takes the next word as its argument, even if that word looks like an option:

cat > count <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
verbose=0 limit=10
while getopts 'vn:' opt; do
  case $opt in
    v) verbose=1 ;;
    n) limit=$OPTARG ;;
    *) exit 2 ;;
  esac
done
shift $((OPTIND - 1))
echo "verbose=$verbose limit=$limit operands=[$*]"
EOF
bash count -n -v file.txt
bash count -n '' file.txt

verbose=0 limit=-v operands=[file.txt]
verbose=0 limit= operands=[file.txt]

count -n -v file.txt set limit to -v, and verbose mode stayed off. That is what POSIX specifies, and it is correct: the option string says -n takes an argument, and -v is the next word, so -v is the argument. It is also how a negative number or a pattern that starts with a dash gets passed. The consequence is that a mistake like forgetting the number after -n is not always detected by getopts — it is only detected when -n is the last word — and the script has to validate limit itself (§13.10). An empty string is also a valid argument: -n '' set limit to empty, and getopts had no complaint.

What getopts returns

getopts returns 0 when it found an option — including an option it does not know — and 1 when there are no more:

set -- -v
getopts 'v' opt; echo "found -v: status $?, opt=$opt"
getopts 'v' opt; echo "no more options: status $?, opt=$opt"
set -- -x
OPTIND=1
getopts 'v' opt 2>/dev/null; echo "unknown -x: status $?, opt=$opt"

found -v: status 0, opt=v
no more options: status 1, opt=?
unknown -x: status 0, opt=?

The second call found nothing left and returned 1, with opt set to ?. The third found -x, which is not in the option string, and returned 0 with opt set to ?. An unknown option does not end the loop; it arrives in the case as ?, and the script decides what to do. The OPTIND=1 before it matters: getopts had finished with the first set -- list, and starting again on a new list needs OPTIND reset by hand, as bash's manual says, since the shell resets it only when it starts. §13.5 shows what happens when that is forgotten inside a function.

13.4 Invalid Options and Missing Arguments: Two Ways to Report Them

getopts has two modes for reporting what went wrong, chosen by the first character of the option string. Without a leading colon it reports errors itself:

cat > count <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
while getopts 'vn:' opt; do
  case $opt in
    v) echo "saw -v" ;;
    n) echo "saw -n $OPTARG" ;;
    '?') echo "opt is '?', OPTARG is ${OPTARG-unset}"; exit 2 ;;
  esac
done
EOF
bash count -v -x
echo "status $?"
bash count -n
echo "status $?"

saw -v
count: illegal option -- x
opt is '?', OPTARG is unset
status 2
count: option requires an argument -- n
opt is '?', OPTARG is unset
status 2

In this default mode, an invalid option prints count: illegal option -- x to standard error — the script's $0, then bash's wording, which is fixed — sets opt to ? and unsets OPTARG, so the script cannot say which option it was. A missing argument, -n at the end of the line, prints option requires an argument -- n and produces the same ?. The script can only tell that something was wrong, and the messages are bash's rather than the script's.

The other mode starts the option string with a colon. The bash manual calls it silent error reporting:

cat > count <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
readonly PROG=${0##*/}
while getopts ':vn:' opt; do
  case $opt in
    v) echo "saw -v" ;;
    n) echo "saw -n $OPTARG" ;;
    :) echo "$PROG: -$OPTARG needs an argument" >&2; exit 2 ;;
    '?') echo "$PROG: unknown option -$OPTARG" >&2; exit 2 ;;
  esac
done
EOF
bash count -v -x
echo "status $?"
bash count -n
echo "status $?"

saw -v
count: unknown option -x
status 2
count: -n needs an argument
status 2

With :vn:, getopts prints nothing and tells the script what happened instead. An invalid option sets opt to ? and OPTARG to the offending letter, x. A missing argument sets opt to : — a different value, so the two errors can be told apart — and OPTARG to the option that needed the argument, n. The script then writes its own message in its own format and exits with its own status. Nearly every script should use silent error reporting: it is the only mode in which the script can name the bad option, send the message through the same function as its other errors, and add "Try --help" (§13.9). The two error clauses, :) and '?'), are the whole cost.

A third variable, OPTERR, turns off the default mode's messages without changing anything else. It is a bash extension; POSIX's getopts page does not mention it. Setting OPTERR=0 silences the messages but leaves the default mode's behaviour otherwise, so OPTARG is still unset and both errors are still ?:

cat > count <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
OPTERR=0
while getopts 'vn:' opt; do
  echo "opt=$opt OPTARG=${OPTARG-unset}"
done
EOF
bash count -x -n

opt=? OPTARG=unset
opt=? OPTARG=unset

Both errors arrived as ? with no OPTARG, and nothing was printed at all, so the user learns nothing. OPTERR=0 is the worst of both modes, and a leading colon is the right way to take over error reporting. Bash initialises OPTERR to 1 each time a shell or a script starts, so setting it affects only the script that sets it.

Quote the ? in the case

? is a pattern character in a case clause (§8.5), matching any single character — and every option getopts returns is a single character. An unquoted ?) clause matches all of them:

cat > count <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
while getopts ':vn:' opt; do
  case $opt in
    ?) echo "unknown option -$OPTARG" >&2; exit 2 ;;
    v) echo "saw -v" ;;
    n) echo "saw -n $OPTARG" ;;
  esac
done
echo "parsed everything"
EOF
bash count -v -n 3
echo "status $?"

unknown option -
status 2

-v fell into the ?) clause, which reported unknown option - (with an empty OPTARG, since -v takes no argument) and exited 2 on a correct command line. Put first, an unquoted ?) swallows every option; put last, as POSIX's own example does, it works only because everything else matched earlier. Write it as '?') or \?) wherever it appears, so that it matches only a literal question mark, and the clause order stops mattering.

Order the error clauses

The common shortcut is a single *) clause for errors, which catches ? and : alike. In silent mode that loses the distinction the colon was added for:

cat > count <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
while getopts ':vn:' opt; do
  case $opt in
    v) echo "saw -v" ;;
    n) echo "saw -n $OPTARG" ;;
    *) echo "count: unknown option -$OPTARG" >&2; exit 2 ;;
  esac
done
EOF
bash count -n

count: unknown option -n

count -n told the user that -n is an unknown option, which it is not; it is a known option missing its argument. *) matched the : returned for a missing argument, and the clause could only print one message. With silent error reporting, give :) its own clause before the catch-all. In default mode, a single *) is fine, because both errors arrive as ? anyway and bash has already printed the right message.

Whatever the mode, a usage error exits 2, and says so on standard error. §13.9 adds the "Try --help" line and §13.10 the validation that getopts cannot do. The exit code for usage errors is the same across a script: pick 2 or EX_USAGE (64) and use it for every error that is the caller's fault (§11.4).

13.5 Operands, the -- End of Options, and Where Parsing Stops

getopts stops at the first argument that is not an option. What counts as "not an option" is precise, and each case is one a script meets:

cat > count <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
verbose=0
while getopts 'v' opt; do
  case $opt in
    v) verbose=1 ;;
    *) exit 2 ;;
  esac
done
shift $((OPTIND - 1))
echo "verbose=$verbose operands:$(printf ' [%s]' "$@")"
EOF
bash count -v a.txt b.txt
bash count a.txt -v
bash count -v -- -v.txt
bash count -v - b.txt
bash count '' -v

verbose=1 operands: [a.txt] [b.txt]
verbose=0 operands: [a.txt] [-v]
verbose=1 operands: [-v.txt]
verbose=1 operands: [-] [b.txt]
verbose=0 operands: [] [-v]

count a.txt -v did not see -v as an option. getopts stopped at a.txt, the first operand, and -v became the second operand. That is Guideline 9 — options come before operands — and it is how every POSIX utility behaves: on macOS, ls dir -l looks for a file named -l. GNU tools are different: they reorder the command line so that positional arguments after options and options after positional arguments are both accepted, which is why ls dir -l works on Linux. A script parsed with getopts behaves the POSIX way, and users who live on Linux will occasionally type an option after an operand and be surprised.

The other lines show the rest of the rule. -- was consumed and ended the options, so -v.txt after it was an operand. A lone - is an operand, not an option — it is Guideline 13's "standard input". And an empty string is an operand too: count '' -v stopped at the empty word, so -v was never parsed. That last case happens when a script passes "$unset_variable" as the first argument.

Accepting options after positional arguments

If a script should accept options anywhere, GNU-style, getopts can be run repeatedly: parse options until the first operand, take that operand, and start getopts again on what remains:

cat > count <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
verbose=0 limit=10
operands=()
while (( $# > 0 )); do
  OPTIND=1
  while getopts 'vn:' opt; do
    case $opt in
      v) verbose=1 ;;
      n) limit=$OPTARG ;;
      *) exit 2 ;;
    esac
  done
  shift $((OPTIND - 1))
  if [[ ${1-} == -- ]]; then shift; operands+=("$@"); break; fi
  if (( $# > 0 )); then operands+=("$1"); shift; fi
done
echo "verbose=$verbose limit=$limit operands:$(printf ' [%s]' "${operands[@]}")"
EOF
bash count a.txt -v b.txt -n 3
bash count a.txt -- -v

verbose=1 limit=3 operands: [a.txt] [b.txt]
verbose=0 limit=10 operands: [a.txt] [-v]

The outer loop runs getopts from OPTIND=1 on the current positional parameters, shifts off the options it found, and moves one operand into an array. a.txt -v b.txt -n 3 then parsed as two options and two operands, in any order. -- still works: after it, everything is an operand, so a.txt -- -v kept -v as a file name. This is the only case where resetting OPTIND in the middle of parsing is correct, and it is also the reason not to do it lightly — a user who is used to POSIX behaviour can no longer pass a file named -v without --. For most scripts, options first is the simpler contract to explain.

getopts in a function: local OPTIND

A function has its own positional parameters (§9.3), so it can parse its own options with getopts. But OPTIND is an ordinary shell variable, shared by the function and its caller, and it is not reset when a function is called:

greet() {
  local opt shout=0
  while getopts 's' opt; do
    [[ $opt == s ]] && shout=1
  done
  shift $((OPTIND - 1))
  if (( shout )); then echo "HELLO, ${1^^}"; else echo "hello, $1"; fi
}
greet -s ada
greet -s grace
greet bob

HELLO, ADA
hello, grace
hello,

The first call worked. It left OPTIND at 2. The second call started parsing at index 2 — the word grace — which is not an option, so getopts stopped at once and -s was never seen: hello, grace, lower case. The third call also started at 2, which was past the only argument, so the shift removed bob and printed an empty name. POSIX's page on getopts says a function and its caller sharing OPTIND produces unspecified results; in bash, the results are these.

The fix is one word:

greet() {
  local opt shout=0 OPTIND=1
  while getopts 's' opt; do
    [[ $opt == s ]] && shout=1
  done
  shift $((OPTIND - 1))
  if (( shout )); then echo "HELLO, ${1^^}"; else echo "hello, $1"; fi
}
greet -s ada
greet -s grace
greet bob
echo "the caller's OPTIND is still $OPTIND"

HELLO, ADA
HELLO, GRACE
hello, bob
the caller's OPTIND is still 1

local OPTIND=1 gives each call its own index, starting at 1, and restores the caller's when the function returns, which is why the caller's OPTIND was still 1 afterwards. Any function that calls getopts should declare local OPTIND=1 opt (and OPTARG, if the caller might be using it). The subcommand handlers in §13.7 do.

Parsing a list other than "$@"

getopts normally parses the positional parameters, but it takes an optional list of words after the variable name, and parses those instead:

args=(-v -n 5 extra)
OPTIND=1
while getopts 'vn:' opt "${args[@]}"; do
  echo "opt=$opt OPTARG=${OPTARG-unset}"
done
echo "operands start at index $((OPTIND - 1)): ${args[*]:OPTIND-1}"
echo "and \$# is still $#"

opt=v OPTARG=unset
opt=n OPTARG=5
operands start at index 3: extra
and $# is still 0

The array was parsed without touching $@, which stayed empty. There is no shift for an array, so the operands are taken with a slice starting at OPTIND - 1 — the index is still 1-based, like the positional parameters. This is useful for options that arrive from somewhere other than the command line: a configuration value such as DEFAULT_OPTS='-v -n 5' split into an array, or the arguments collected for a subcommand. Reset OPTIND=1 before each new list.

13.6 Long Options

getopts handles single-letter options only. POSIX's guidelines stop there, but users expect --verbose and --limit=3 from anything that looks like a modern tool, and long options are self-documenting in a way -n is not: a cron entry reading backup --keep 7 --compress needs no comment. There are two ways to add them in bash, and both are written by hand.

Manual long option parsing

The first is to go back to §13.2's while/case loop and fix its faults deliberately. Manual long option parsing has to handle four spellings of an option with an argument — -n 3, -n3, --limit 3 and --limit=3 — and grouped short options, and check for a missing argument before using $2:

cat > count <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
readonly PROG=${0##*/}
usage_error() { printf '%s: %s\n' "$PROG" "$1" >&2; exit 2; }

verbose=0 limit=10
while (( $# > 0 )); do
  case $1 in
    -v | --verbose) verbose=1 ;;
    -n | --limit)
      (( $# > 1 )) || usage_error "$1 needs an argument"
      limit=$2
      shift ;;
    --limit=*) limit=${1#*=} ;;
    -n?*) limit=${1#-n} ;;
    --) shift; break ;;
    -[!-]?*)
      set -- "${1:0:2}" "-${1:2}" "${@:2}"
      continue ;;
    -?*) usage_error "unknown option: $1" ;;
    *) break ;;
  esac
  shift
done
echo "verbose=$verbose limit=$limit operands:$(printf ' [%s]' "$@")"
EOF
bash count --verbose --limit 3 a.txt
bash count --limit=7 -v a.txt
bash count -vn3 a.txt
bash count -n3 -- --odd.txt
bash count --limit
echo "status $?"
bash count --colour a.txt
echo "status $?"

verbose=1 limit=3 operands: [a.txt]
verbose=1 limit=7 operands: [a.txt]
verbose=1 limit=3 operands: [a.txt]
verbose=0 limit=3 operands: [--odd.txt]
count: --limit needs an argument
status 2
count: unknown option: --colour
status 2

Each clause handles one spelling. -n | --limit checks $# > 1 before reading $2 and shifts once for the argument, and once more at the bottom of the loop. --limit=* takes everything after the first = with ${1#*=} (§5.4). -n?* is the attached form, -n3, and must come after the plain -n clause and before the grouping clause. The grouping clause, -[!-]?*, matches a single dash followed by at least two characters — -vn3 — and splits off the first letter: set -- "${1:0:2}" "-${1:2}" "${@:2}" turns -vn3 into -v -n3, and continue goes round the loop again without shifting, so the next pass handles -v and the one after it handles -n3 through the attached-argument clause. That is the only part of the loop that is not obvious, and it is what gives the hand-written parser Guideline 5's grouping.

The order of clauses is part of the parser. -- must come before -?*, or it would be reported as an unknown option. -n?* must come before -[!-]?*, or -n3 would be split into -n -3, and -3 would be reported as unknown. And -?* must come before *), so that anything starting with a dash that was not recognised is an error rather than an operand. A lone - matches none of the dash clauses (each needs at least one more character), so it falls through to *) and is an operand, as Guideline 13 wants.

This is the shape to use when a script needs long options. It is longer than a getopts loop, but every line in it is visible and testable, and it has no dependency on anything outside bash.

Long options through getopts

The second way uses a trick that bash's getopts allows: - in the option string, followed by a colon. getopts then treats --limit=7 as the option - with the argument limit=7, because it sees a dash, the "option letter" -, and the rest of the word as an attached argument. The script splits that argument itself:

cat > count <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
readonly PROG=${0##*/}
usage_error() { printf '%s: %s\n' "$PROG" "$1" >&2; exit 2; }

verbose=0 limit=10
while getopts ':vn:-:' opt; do
  if [[ $opt == - ]]; then
    opt=${OPTARG%%=*}
    if [[ $OPTARG == *=* ]]; then
      OPTARG=${OPTARG#*=}
    else
      unset OPTARG
    fi
  fi
  case $opt in
    v | verbose) verbose=1 ;;
    n | limit)
      if [[ ! -v OPTARG ]]; then
        (( OPTIND <= $# )) || usage_error "--$opt needs an argument"
        OPTARG=${!OPTIND}
        OPTIND=$(( OPTIND + 1 ))
      fi
      limit=$OPTARG ;;
    :) usage_error "-$OPTARG needs an argument" ;;
    '?') usage_error "unknown option: -$OPTARG" ;;
    *) usage_error "unknown option: --$opt" ;;
  esac
done
shift $((OPTIND - 1))
echo "verbose=$verbose limit=$limit operands:$(printf ' [%s]' "$@")"
EOF
bash count --verbose --limit 3 a.txt
bash count --limit=7 -v a.txt
bash count -vn3 a.txt
bash count --colour a.txt
echo "status $?"

verbose=1 limit=3 operands: [a.txt]
verbose=1 limit=7 operands: [a.txt]
verbose=1 limit=3 operands: [a.txt]
count: unknown option: --colour
status 2

When opt is -, the loop splits OPTARG at the first =: the part before it becomes the option name, and the part after it, if there was an =, becomes the argument. The case then handles v and verbose in one clause, and n and limit in another. --limit 3, with the value as a separate word, needs the value taken by hand: ${!OPTIND} is the word OPTIND points at (an indirect expansion, §5.7), and incrementing OPTIND consumes it. Grouping, attached short arguments and -- still come from getopts, and so does silent error reporting for the short options.

It works — it also works in dash, whose getopts accepts the same -: spelling — but it is a trick. POSIX says option characters should be alphanumeric, and nothing requires a shell to accept - in the option string. The manual loop is easier to read, and a reviewer who has not seen -: before will stop at it. Use whichever is already in the codebase; for a new script with long options, prefer the manual loop.

Neither version supports GNU's abbreviations, where --verb is accepted for --verbose because it is an unambiguous prefix. That is a feature of GNU getopt_long, and the one parser available to a script that implements it is util-linux's getopt command (§13.8).

13.7 Subcommand Dispatch

A script that does several different things takes a subcommand first: kv set colour blue, kv get colour, kv list -l. Subcommand dispatch is the part that reads the first operand and runs the right code for it. §6.8 built a lookup table for exactly this — an associative array from a verb to a description — and promised to finish it with the handlers as function names in the map. Here it is finished, as a complete small tool: a key-value store kept in a text file, one KEY=VALUE per line.

cat > kv <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# kv - a key-value store in a text file, one KEY=VALUE per line.
set -Eeuo pipefail
readonly PROG=${0##*/}

die() { printf '%s: %s\n' "$PROG" "$*" >&2; exit 1; }
usage_error() {
  printf '%s: %s\n' "$PROG" "$1" >&2
  printf "Try '%s help' for more information.\n" "$PROG" >&2
  exit 2
}

store=${KV_FILE:-kv.db}
declare -A data=()

load() {
  local line
  [[ -e $store ]] || return 0
  while IFS= read -r line; do
    data[${line%%=*}]=${line#*=}
  done < "$store"
}

save() {
  local key
  for key in "${!data[@]}"; do
    printf '%s=%s\n' "$key" "${data[$key]}"
  done | LC_ALL=C sort > "$store.tmp"
  mv -- "$store.tmp" "$store"
}

cmd_set() {
  (( $# == 2 )) || usage_error "set: expected KEY VALUE"
  [[ $1 =~ ^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$ ]] || usage_error "set: bad key: $1"
  data[$1]=$2
  save
}

cmd_get() {
  (( $# == 1 )) || usage_error "get: expected KEY"
  [[ -v data[$1] ]] || die "no such key: $1"
  printf '%s\n' "${data[$1]}"
}

cmd_del() {
  (( $# >= 1 )) || usage_error "del: expected KEY..."
  local key
  for key in "$@"; do
    [[ -v data[$key] ]] || die "no such key: $key"
    unset 'data[$key]'
  done
  save
}

cmd_list() {
  local long=0 opt key OPTIND=1
  while getopts 'l' opt; do
    case $opt in
      l) long=1 ;;
      *) usage_error "list: unknown option" ;;
    esac
  done
  shift $((OPTIND - 1))
  (( ${#data[@]} > 0 )) || return 0
  for key in "${!data[@]}"; do
    [[ $key == "${1-}"* ]] || continue
    if (( long )); then
      printf '%-10s %s\n' "$key" "${data[$key]}"
    else
      printf '%s\n' "$key"
    fi
  done | LC_ALL=C sort
}

cmd_help() {
  echo "Usage: $PROG [-f FILE] COMMAND [ARGS...]"
  echo "Commands: $(printf '%s\n' "${!commands[@]}" | LC_ALL=C sort | tr '\n' ' ')"
}

declare -A commands=(
  [set]=cmd_set [get]=cmd_get [del]=cmd_del [list]=cmd_list [help]=cmd_help
)

main() {
  local opt
  while getopts ':f:' opt; do
    case $opt in
      f) store=$OPTARG ;;
      :) usage_error "-$OPTARG needs an argument" ;;
      *) usage_error "unknown option: -$OPTARG" ;;
    esac
  done
  shift $((OPTIND - 1))
  (( $# > 0 )) || usage_error "no command given"
  local handler=${commands[$1]-}
  [[ -n $handler ]] || usage_error "unknown command: $1"
  load
  "$handler" "${@:2}"
}

main "$@"
EOF
chmod +x kv
./kv set colour blue
./kv set size 'extra large'
./kv -f other.db set colour red
./kv get size
./kv list -l
./kv -f other.db list -l
./kv del colour; ./kv list
./kv get colour; echo "status $?"
./kv frobnicate; echo "status $?"
./kv set 'bad key' x; echo "status $?"

extra large
colour     blue
size       extra large
colour     red
size
kv: no such key: colour
status 1
kv: unknown command: frobnicate
Try 'kv help' for more information.
status 2
kv: set: bad key: bad key
Try 'kv help' for more information.
status 2

The structure is the one every subcommand CLI has.

Global options first. main parses options that apply to every subcommand — here only -f FILE, which selects the store — with getopts and shifts them away. What remains starts with the subcommand's name. ./kv -f other.db set colour red wrote to other.db and left kv.db alone.

A table from name to handler. commands maps each subcommand to a function. ${commands[$1]-} looks the name up, with a - default so that an unknown name is empty rather than an error under set -u (§11.2), and an empty result is a usage error that names the bad subcommand and points at help. frobnicate was rejected that way, with status 2. The table is data, so the list of valid names is always right: cmd_help enumerates it rather than repeating it.

"${@:2}" to the handler. The handler is called with every argument after the subcommand's name, the "shift without shifting" idiom from §5.3, so each handler sees its own arguments as $1, $2 and so on, and can check their number with $#. cmd_set requires exactly two, cmd_del at least one.

Handlers parse their own options. cmd_list takes -l and parses it with its own getopts loop, which is why it declares local OPTIND=1: main already moved the global OPTIND (§13.5). kv list -l printed keys and values in two columns, and kv list keys alone.

Two kinds of failure, two statuses. kv get colour after the key was deleted failed with status 1 and no such key — the command was used correctly, and the work failed. kv set 'bad key' x failed with status 2 and a usage message, because the caller passed something that is never valid. A script that calls kv can tell the two apart (§13.10).

The store itself is kept simple so that the dispatch stays visible. load reads the file into an associative array; save writes it back sorted, to a temporary file that is then renamed over the original, so that an interrupted write never leaves a half-written store (§12.3's cleanup and §17's locking are what a production version would add). Keys are restricted to a safe alphabet by a regular expression in cmd_set, which also keeps them safe to complete (§13.12).

Listing the subcommands

An associative array has no order (§6.7), and that matters as soon as a script prints its subcommands:

declare -A commands=([set]=1 [get]=1 [del]=1 [list]=1 [help]=1)
echo "as stored:  ${!commands[*]}"
mapfile -t names < <(printf '%s\n' "${!commands[@]}" | LC_ALL=C sort)
echo "sorted:     ${names[*]}"

as stored:  del get help set list
sorted:     del get help list set

The five names came back in hash order — del get help set list — which is stable for a given bash but is not any order a reader expects. That is why cmd_help pipes the names through sort; for a help screen, the order is better chosen by hand (§13.9).

Discovering handlers by name

An alternative to the table is a naming convention: every function named cmd_something is a subcommand, and declare -F finds them:

cmd_set()  { echo "set $*"; }
cmd_get()  { echo "get $*"; }
cmd_list() { echo "list $*"; }
helper()   { :; }
mapfile -t commands < <(declare -F | sed -n 's/^declare -f cmd_//p')
echo "discovered: ${commands[*]}"
dispatch() {
  if declare -F "cmd_$1" > /dev/null; then
    "cmd_$1" "${@:2}"
  else
    echo "unknown command: $1" >&2
    return 2
  fi
}
dispatch get colour
dispatch helper; echo "status $?"

discovered: get list set
get colour
unknown command: helper
status 2

declare -F lists every function name, and the sed keeps those starting with cmd_ and strips the prefix. The dispatcher checks declare -F "cmd_$1", which succeeds only if that function exists, so helper — a real function, but not a cmd_ one — was refused. Adding a subcommand is then just defining a function. The cost is that the list is implicit: nothing stops a helper from being named cmd_something by mistake, and the command names are limited to what a function name can contain. The explicit table is easier to review, and it can map two names to one handler ([rm]=cmd_del) or hide one ([debug-dump] left out of help). Either works; what does not work is a case statement with the list of commands written out again in the help text, because the two drift apart.

Git adds one more layer: a subcommand that is not built in is looked up as an executable called git-NAME on PATH, which is how git lfs works. A script can do the same — command -v "kv-$1" — when other people need to add subcommands without editing it.

13.8 getopt versus getopts

The names are one letter apart and the tools are unrelated. getopts, with an s, is the shell builtin this section has used so far. getopt, without one, is an external program that rewrites a command line into a normalised form for a script to parse. There are two very different programs called getopt, and which one a system has decides whether it is usable.

The BSD getopt, which macOS ships as /usr/bin/getopt, is the original from the 1980s. Its manual page recommends args=`getopt abo: $*` followed by set -- $args, both unquoted, and its BUGS section says that "arguments containing white space or embedded shell metacharacters generally will not survive intact":

set -- -v -n 3 'my file.txt'
# shellcheck disable=SC2048,SC2086  # the man page's own recipe, unquoted, which is the point
args=$(getopt vn: $*)
# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # and unquoted again, as the man page says
set -- $args
printf '[%s] ' "$@"; echo
echo "$# words; the file name was split in two"

[-v] [-n] [3] [--] [my] [file.txt] 
6 words; the file name was split in two

The file name my file.txt became two operands. The unquoted $* split it before getopt saw it, and the unquoted $args would split and glob the output again even if it had not; there is no way to quote the output of this getopt, because it produces a space-separated string with no quoting of its own. It cannot be used safely on arguments that might contain spaces, which means on any file name.

util-linux's getopt, which every mainstream Linux distribution ships, is a different program with the same name. It supports long options, GNU-style abbreviations, and — the important part — it quotes its output, so that the script can pass it to eval set -- and get back exactly the words it started with. getopt -T tells the two apart: util-linux's exits with status 4, the BSD one exits 0. This example was run on Debian 13 with util-linux 2.41:

# Linux only: util-linux getopt (macOS's /usr/bin/getopt is the BSD one)
cat > count <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
readonly PROG=${0##*/}
verbose=0 limit=10
parsed=$(getopt -o vn: -l verbose,limit: -n "$PROG" -- "$@") || exit 2
eval set -- "$parsed"
while true; do
  case $1 in
    -v | --verbose) verbose=1; shift ;;
    -n | --limit) limit=$2; shift 2 ;;
    --) shift; break ;;
  esac
done
echo "verbose=$verbose limit=$limit operands:$(printf ' [%s]' "$@")"
EOF
getopt -T
echo "getopt -T: status $?"
getopt -o vn: -l verbose,limit: -- -v --limit 3 'my file.txt' -n5 --verb -- -odd
bash count -v --limit 3 'my file.txt' -n5 --verb -- -odd
bash count --colour a.txt
echo "status $?"
bash count --limit
echo "status $?"

On Debian, it prints:

getopt -T: status 4
 -v --limit '3' -n '5' --verbose -- 'my file.txt' '-odd'
verbose=1 limit=5 operands: [my file.txt] [-odd]
count: unrecognized option '--colour'
status 2
count: option '--limit' requires an argument
status 2

The second line is getopt's own output. Every option-argument is quoted, --verb has been expanded to --verbose, -n5 has been split into -n '5', and the operand my file.txt, which appeared in the middle of the options, has been moved after -- in one piece. The parsing loop that follows is simple because the input is normalised: every option is a separate word, every argument is the word after it, and -- always marks the end. The eval is safe here — the one case where §18's warnings about eval do not apply — because the string is shell syntax generated by getopt, with every piece of user input single-quoted, not user input itself. Errors are reported in GNU's wording under the script's name (-n "$PROG"), and getopt exits non-zero, which the script turns into a status of 2.

It is a good parser, and it is the only way for a bash script to get GNU's full behaviour — long options, abbreviations, and options after operands (which getopt reorders unless POSIXLY_CORRECT is set or the option string starts with +). The problem is portability. A script that uses it fails on macOS, where getopt -o … is passed to the BSD program and misparsed, and on BSDs; Homebrew's gnu-getopt provides the util-linux version on macOS, but it is keg-only — installed at $(brew --prefix gnu-getopt)/bin/getopt, not on PATH — precisely so that it does not replace the system one. The rule for choosing:

  • getopts for any script that has to run beyond Linux, or in /bin/sh (it is POSIX), or that has only short options. It is the default.
  • The manual loop of §13.6 when the script needs long options and must stay portable.
  • util-linux getopt when the script only ever runs on Linux, needs long options with abbreviations or GNU reordering, and checks getopt -T first so that it fails clearly anywhere else:
getopt -T > /dev/null
if (( $? != 4 )); then
  echo "${0##*/}: needs util-linux getopt (on macOS: brew install gnu-getopt)" >&2
  exit 1
fi

The BSD getopt is never the right choice. The comparison of getopt versus getopts is really between one builtin that is everywhere and one external program that is excellent on Linux and absent elsewhere.

13.9 Help Text, Usage Messages and --version

A usage message is the short form: one or two lines showing how to call the program, printed on a usage error. Help text is the long form printed by -h or --help: the usage lines, a sentence saying what the program does, every option, and anything else a user needs to run it without reading the source. §11.4 set the rule for where each goes: help that was asked for goes to standard output with status 0, so that kv --help | less works; a usage message caused by a mistake goes to standard error with status 2.

The usage line has a notation of its own, the one every man page's SYNOPSIS uses:

  • [-v] — an optional option; [-f FILE] an optional option with an argument, the argument in capitals.
  • -o OUTFILE without brackets — a required option. (Required options are a design smell: if it is required, it could usually be an operand. §13.10.)
  • FILE... — one or more operands; [FILE...] — zero or more.
  • -q | -v or [-q|-v] — mutually exclusive choices.
  • COMMAND [ARGS...] — a subcommand and its own arguments.

A good help text has the usage lines first, then one sentence on what the program does, then the options with their defaults, then — for a subcommand CLI — the commands, and at the end anything that affects how it is called from other scripts: environment variables and exit statuses. Keep it under 80 columns, because it is read in terminals.

Help text from the code

The help text is the documentation most likely to go stale, because it is written once and the code keeps changing. §9.12 wrote a header comment above each function and promised that it could become --help. For a subcommand CLI, a one-line marker above each handler does that job: the help is extracted from the script itself, so a handler cannot be added without its help line sitting right above it.

cat > kv <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
readonly PROG=${0##*/} VERSION=1.4.0

#@ set KEY VALUE     Store VALUE under KEY, replacing any old value.
cmd_set() { :; }
#@ get KEY           Print the value stored under KEY.
cmd_get() { :; }
#@ del KEY...        Delete one or more keys.
cmd_del() { :; }
#@ list [-l] [PREFIX]
#@                   List keys starting with PREFIX; -l shows values too.
cmd_list() { :; }

usage() {
  cat <<USAGE
Usage: $PROG [-f FILE] COMMAND [ARGS...]
       $PROG -h | --help | --version

A key-value store kept in a text file, one KEY=VALUE per line.

Options:
  -f FILE    use FILE as the store (default: \$KV_FILE, then ./kv.db)
  -h, --help print this help and exit
  --version  print the version and exit

Commands:
USAGE
  sed -n 's/^#@ /  /p' "$0"
  cat <<USAGE

Exit status: 0 on success, 1 if a key does not exist, 2 on a usage error.
USAGE
}

case ${1-} in
  -h | --help) usage; exit 0 ;;
  --version) echo "$PROG $VERSION"; exit 0 ;;
esac
EOF
bash kv --help
bash kv --version

Usage: kv [-f FILE] COMMAND [ARGS...]
       kv -h | --help | --version

A key-value store kept in a text file, one KEY=VALUE per line.

Options:
  -f FILE    use FILE as the store (default: $KV_FILE, then ./kv.db)
  -h, --help print this help and exit
  --version  print the version and exit

Commands:
  set KEY VALUE     Store VALUE under KEY, replacing any old value.
  get KEY           Print the value stored under KEY.
  del KEY...        Delete one or more keys.
  list [-l] [PREFIX]
                    List keys starting with PREFIX; -l shows values too.

Exit status: 0 on success, 1 if a key does not exist, 2 on a usage error.
kv 1.4.0

Each handler is preceded by a line starting #@, which is an ordinary comment to bash. usage prints its fixed parts from heredocs (§10.9) and the commands with sed -n 's/^#@ / /p' "$0", which prints only the marked lines, with the marker replaced by two spaces of indent. The order of commands in the help is the order of the handlers in the file, which is the author's choice, not a hash order. A description too long for one line continues on a second #@ line, as list does. The unquoted heredoc delimiter lets $PROG expand, and the \$KV_FILE is escaped so that it is printed as a name rather than the variable's current value.

Reading "$0" has one requirement: the script must be a file that can be read, which it is when it is run as a command. It fails when the script is piped into bash (curl … | bash), where there is no file; a script designed to run that way keeps its help in a heredoc. Use "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}" instead of "$0" for a file that is sourced as a library (§9.10).

--version

--version prints the program's name and version on the first line and exits 0: kv 1.4.0. That exact shape matters more than it looks, because other scripts parse it — a deploy check running kv --version | awk '{print $2}' — and the GNU standards specify it for that reason. A copyright line and licence may follow on later lines. Keep the version in one readonly constant at the top of the script, where a release process can find and change it.

-h and --help are handled before anything else can fail, which is why the example checks $1 before parsing: a user who types kv --help should get help even if their KV_FILE points at a missing file or they are not in the right directory. For the same reason, help never needs a lock, a network connection or a configuration file.

Usage errors that help

A usage error message says three things: which program, what was wrong, and where to look. The kv in §13.7 does all three in two lines:

kv: unknown command: frobnicate
Try 'kv help' for more information.

The first line names the program because the error may appear in a log alongside a hundred others. It names the bad input, quoted where it could contain spaces. The second line is the GNU convention: it points at the help without printing all of it, because a full help text in reply to a typo pushes the actual error off the screen. Both lines go to standard error, and the status is 2. For a subcommand's usage error, the message names the subcommand — kv: set: expected KEY VALUE — so that the user knows which usage to check.

13.10 Argument Validation, Defaults and Precedence

getopts checks the shape of a command line — which options exist, which take arguments — and nothing about the values. Argument validation is the script's job, and it belongs in one place, straight after parsing and before any work starts, so that a bad invocation fails before it has changed anything. A script that validates as it goes can fail halfway through, and §1.1 called half-completed work the default failure mode of a shell script.

Numbers

The most common value to validate is a number, and bash makes it easy to get wrong in three ways: accepting something that is not a number, reading a leading zero as octal (§7.10), and overflowing. A regular expression handles the first, 10# the second, and a digit count the third:

is_uint() { [[ $1 =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; }
for limit in 3 012 08 -1 '' 1e3 ' 5' 99999999999999999999; do
  if is_uint "$limit"; then
    echo "$(printf '%-24q' "$limit") accepted, as the number $(( 10#$limit ))"
  else
    echo "$(printf '%-24q' "$limit") rejected"
  fi
done

3                        accepted, as the number 3
012                      accepted, as the number 12
08                       accepted, as the number 8
-1                       rejected
''                       rejected
1e3                      rejected
\ 5                      rejected
99999999999999999999     accepted, as the number 7766279631452241919

^[0-9]+$ rejected a negative number, an empty string, 1e3 and a leading space, and $(( 10#$limit )) read 08 as 8 rather than failing as invalid octal. The last line is the trap: a string of twenty digits passes the regular expression, and bash's 64-bit arithmetic silently wraps it round to an unrelated number, 7766279631452241919. A check that only asks "is it digits?" passes an overflowing value straight through; the check must also bound the length, or compare the value against a range with the digits limited first.

Validating before arithmetic is not only about correctness. §4.5 showed that arithmetic evaluates a variable's value as an expression, recursively, and promised this subsection would say what to do about it:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # a literal $(...), which is the point
limit='x[$(echo "this ran" >&2)]'
if (( limit > 0 )); then echo "positive"; else echo "not positive"; fi
[[ $limit =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || echo "validated first: rejected, and nothing ran"

this ran
not positive
validated first: rejected, and nothing ran

(( limit > 0 )) evaluated limit, found the string x[$(echo "this ran" >&2)], evaluated that as an array subscript — and ran the command substitution inside it. A user who can set an option's value can run a command through any arithmetic context that uses it, which is why the first line printed this ran. §18 shows the concrete attack. The defence is the rule this subsection is about: validate that a value is digits with [[ =~ ]], which treats it as a string and never evaluates it, before the value reaches (( )), $(( )), an array index, or [[ -eq ]].

Everything else, in one place

A script's validation section checks every constraint that getopts cannot:

cat > export.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
readonly PROG=${0##*/}
usage_error() {
  printf '%s: %s\n' "$PROG" "$1" >&2
  printf "Try '%s -h' for more information.\n" "$PROG" >&2
  exit 2
}

format=csv limit= out= quiet=0 verbose=0
while getopts ':f:hn:o:qv' opt; do
  case $opt in
    h) echo "Usage: $PROG [-q|-v] [-f csv|json] [-n LIMIT] -o OUTFILE INPUT..."; exit 0 ;;
    f) format=$OPTARG ;;
    n) limit=$OPTARG ;;
    o) out=$OPTARG ;;
    q) quiet=1 ;;
    v) verbose=1 ;;
    :) usage_error "-$OPTARG needs an argument" ;;
    *) usage_error "unknown option: -$OPTARG" ;;
  esac
done
shift $((OPTIND - 1))

case $format in
  csv | json) ;;
  *) usage_error "-f: unknown format '$format' (expected csv or json)" ;;
esac
if [[ -n $limit ]]; then
  [[ $limit =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || usage_error "-n: '$limit' is not a whole number"
  if [[ ! $limit =~ ^0*[0-9]{1,4}$ ]] || (( 10#$limit < 1 || 10#$limit > 1000 )); then
    usage_error "-n: $limit is out of range (1-1000)"
  fi
  limit=$(( 10#$limit ))
fi
[[ -n $out ]] || usage_error "-o OUTFILE is required"
(( ! (quiet && verbose) )) || usage_error "-q and -v cannot be used together"
(( $# >= 1 )) || usage_error "expected at least one INPUT file"
for f in "$@"; do
  [[ -r $f ]] || usage_error "cannot read input file '$f'"
done
readonly format limit out quiet verbose
echo "ok: format=$format limit=${limit:-all} out=$out inputs=$*"
EOF
touch in.txt
bash export.sh -f json -n 010 -o out.json in.txt
bash export.sh -f xml -o out in.txt
bash export.sh -n 5000 -o out in.txt
bash export.sh -n 99999999999999999999 -o out in.txt
bash export.sh -n ten -o out in.txt
bash export.sh in.txt
bash export.sh -q -v -o out in.txt
bash export.sh -o out missing.txt
echo "last status $?"

ok: format=json limit=10 out=out.json inputs=in.txt
export.sh: -f: unknown format 'xml' (expected csv or json)
Try 'export.sh -h' for more information.
export.sh: -n: 5000 is out of range (1-1000)
Try 'export.sh -h' for more information.
export.sh: -n: 99999999999999999999 is out of range (1-1000)
Try 'export.sh -h' for more information.
export.sh: -n: 'ten' is not a whole number
Try 'export.sh -h' for more information.
export.sh: -o OUTFILE is required
Try 'export.sh -h' for more information.
export.sh: -q and -v cannot be used together
Try 'export.sh -h' for more information.
export.sh: cannot read input file 'missing.txt'
Try 'export.sh -h' for more information.
last status 2

Each check follows the same pattern — a condition, and a usage error that names the option and the bad value — and each one caught its case. An enumerated value, -f, is checked with a case listing the accepted words, and the message lists them too. A number with a range, -n, is checked in two steps: ^[0-9]+$ for "is it a number", and then a bounded pattern and a range comparison for "is it an acceptable one", so the two failures get different messages, and a twenty-digit value is rejected as out of range instead of wrapping. A required argument, -o, is checked by testing that the variable was set, because getopts has no notion of a required option: an option is optional by definition, and making one mandatory is the script's own rule, and a required argument that is always given is usually better as an operand. Mutually exclusive options, -q and -v, are checked together. Operands are counted, and input files are checked for readability up front, so that a typo in the third file name fails before the first file is processed.

Two details matter. The limit is converted with 10# after validation, so -n 010 became 10, and the numeric variables are then made readonly, so that no later code can change a validated setting by accident. And every failure goes through usage_error with status 2, because each of them is the caller's mistake; a failure of the work itself — the export ran out of disk — would use 1 or a specific status. Keeping the exit code for usage errors separate means a wrapper can retry a failed run but not a misconfigured one.

Default values and where settings come from

A default value is what a setting has when nobody says otherwise, and a script should be usable with none of its options given. Set the defaults once, before parsing, as the examples in this section do (verbose=0 limit=10), so that the parsing loop only ever overrides them and the defaults are visible in one line.

Settings can come from more places than the command line, and a user needs to know which wins. The convention every well-behaved tool follows, from lowest priority to highest, is: the built-in default, then a configuration file, then an environment variable, then a command-line option:

cat > kvpath <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
store=
[[ -r kv.conf ]] && store=$(sed -n 's/^store=//p' kv.conf)
store=${KV_FILE:-${store:-kv.db}}
while getopts 'f:' opt; do
  case $opt in
    f) store=$OPTARG ;;
    *) exit 2 ;;
  esac
done
echo "store: $store"
EOF
bash kvpath
echo 'store=from-config.db' > kv.conf
bash kvpath
KV_FILE=from-env.db bash kvpath
KV_FILE=from-env.db bash kvpath -f from-flag.db

store: kv.db
store: from-config.db
store: from-env.db
store: from-flag.db

Each source overrode the one before it. The built-in default kv.db applied when nothing else was set. The configuration file replaced it, KV_FILE in the environment replaced that, and -f on the command line beat everything. The rule behind the order is that the more specific and the more recent the source, the more it should win: a command-line option applies to one run and was typed just now, an environment variable to a session, a configuration file to every run. ${KV_FILE:-${store:-kv.db}} implements the bottom three levels in one nested expansion (§5.2), and the option loop, running last, implements the top one.

Environment variables for settings should be named after the program (KV_FILE, not FILE), documented in the help text, and read once at the top of the script — never a variable that happens to exist for other reasons, like DEBUG or VERBOSE, which other tools may have set. The configuration file here is read with sed, not sourced, because sourcing a configuration file runs it as code, with the same injection risk as the arithmetic above; §18 covers reading configuration safely.

13.11 How Programmable Completion Works

When Tab is pressed at a bash prompt, the line editor, readline, asks bash for the possible completions of the word under the cursor. Without any configuration, bash offers command names for the first word, and for any other word, variable names after $, user names after ~, host names after @, and file names otherwise. That default is why Tab after kv get offers the files in the current directory, which are never what kv get wants.

Programmable completion replaces the default for a named command. A compspec — a completion specification — is registered for the command with the complete builtin, and from then on, Tab on that command's arguments runs the compspec instead. A compspec can list fixed words, name a category (files, directories, users, signals, functions), or call a shell function that computes the candidates from anything it likes: a script's subcommands, the keys in its data file, the hosts in a configuration. The complete builtin is the only way to register one. A compspec is only ever active in an interactive shell with line editing — a script never completes anything — so a completion is a small piece of code that a script ships for its users' shells.

compgen: the same machinery, printed

The compgen builtin takes the same options as complete and prints the candidates it would generate, one per line, instead of registering anything. It is how completion functions generate candidates, and running the compgen builtin at a prompt is the easiest way to see what an option does:

mkdir -p proj/src proj/docs && cd proj
touch app.log error.log notes.txt src/main.sh
echo "-W:  $(compgen -W 'start stop status restart' -- st | tr '\n' ' ')"
echo "-d:  $(compgen -d | LC_ALL=C sort | tr '\n' ' ')"
echo "-f:  $(compgen -f -- e | tr '\n' ' ')"
echo "-X:  $(compgen -f -X '!*.log' | LC_ALL=C sort | tr '\n' ' ')"
echo "-A:  $(compgen -A builtin -- comp | tr '\n' ' ')"
echo "-P:  $(compgen -W 'alpha beta' -P '<' -S '>' | tr '\n' ' ')"
compgen -W 'start stop' -- x
echo "no match: status $?"

-W:  start stop status 
-d:  docs src 
-f:  error.log 
-X:  app.log error.log 
-A:  compgen complete compopt 
-P:  <alpha> <beta> 
no match: status 1

Each option names a source of candidates, and compgen keeps only those that begin with the word after --. -W takes a word list: st matched start, stop and status but not restart. -d generates directory names and -f file names, both from the current directory. -X removes candidates matching a pattern, and with a leading ! it removes those not matching, so -f -X '!*.log' kept only the log files. -A names one of two dozen categories (builtin, command, function, variable, user, hostname, signal, service and more; several have single-letter forms, like -b for builtins and -c for commands). -P and -S add a prefix and suffix to each candidate. When nothing matches, compgen returns 1.

The -- before the word matters for the same reason it did in §13.1: the word being completed is user input, and a user completing - would otherwise pass compgen an option.

Registering a compspec

complete takes the same options and one or more command names:

complete -W 'start stop status restart' -o default svc
complete -d mkproject
complete -f -X '!*.log' logview
complete -p svc mkproject logview
complete -r mkproject
complete -p mkproject
echo "status $?"

complete -o default -W 'start stop status restart' svc
complete -d mkproject
complete -f -X '!*.log' logview
example.sh: line 6: complete: mkproject: no completion specification
status 1

complete -p prints the compspecs for the named commands as complete commands that would recreate them — the form to use when checking what is registered, or to see how an existing command's completion works (complete -p git in a shell with bash-completion loaded). complete -r removes one, after which complete -p reports that there is no completion specification and returns 1. Without a name, complete -p lists every compspec in the shell.

The -o default on svc is one of the comp-options, which change how readline treats what the compspec generates rather than what it generates:

  • -o default — if the compspec produces no candidates, fall back to readline's file-name completion. Without it, a compspec that has nothing to offer offers nothing at all, and Tab does nothing, even where a file name is valid. Pressing Tab after svc no in a directory containing notes.txt completed the file name with -o default, and did nothing for the same compspec registered without it. -o bashdefault falls back to bash's own defaults (variables, users, commands) first.
  • -o nospace — do not append a space after a completed word. Readline normally adds one, because a completed word is usually finished. For a word that continues, like --env= or a directory path, the space is wrong: completing --c to --count= with a space would leave the cursor after --count=, and the value would become a separate argument. With -o nospace the line becomes --count= and the value can be typed straight after it.
  • -o filenames — tell readline that the candidates are file names, so that it appends / to directories (and no space after them), and quotes special characters, so that completing my file.txt produces my\ file.txt.
  • -o dirnames and -o plusdirs — fall back to, or add, directory names.
  • -o nosort — keep the candidates in the order the compspec produced them, instead of readline sorting them alphabetically.

The last three options of complete are special names instead of commands: -D sets the default compspec, used for every command that has none; -E for an empty line; and -I (bash 5.0) for the command word itself. §13.13 uses -D to load completions only when they are first needed.

The flow

For a command with a compspec, bash builds the candidate list in a fixed order — the one the bash manual describes under "Programmable Completion" — and the order explains how the options combine:

1. Find a compspec
By the full path of the command word, then its last component, then the -D default. None found: bash's default completion.
2. Actions
-A and its short forms (-f, -d, -c…), keeping candidates that start with the word.
3. -G glob
A pathname pattern; its matches need not start with the word.
4. -W words
The word list, split and expanded, then prefix-matched.
5. -F function
Called with COMP_WORDS and the rest set; its COMPREPLY is added unfiltered (§13.12).
6. -C command
Run like a command substitution; each line of its output is a candidate (Exercise 4).
7. -X filter
Removes candidates matching the pattern (! inverts; & stands for the word).
8. -P, -S
Prefix and suffix added to every candidate.
9. Fallbacks
No candidates: -o dirnames, -o bashdefault, then -o default. -o plusdirs adds directories either way.

A compspec with only -W or -f is enough for a command whose arguments are all of one kind. Anything that depends on position — a subcommand first, then its arguments — needs a function, which is §13.12.

-W expands its words

Step 4 says the word list is expanded, and the bash manual means it: each word goes through brace, tilde, parameter and arithmetic expansion and command substitution, and then word splitting. For a fixed list written in the script, that is harmless. For a list built from data, it is a code-execution path:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # a literal $(...) in the data, which is the point
printf '%s\n' 'draft' 'final version' '$(echo "this ran" >&2)' > titles.txt
words=$(< titles.txt)
compgen -W "$words" -- ''

this ran
draft
final
version

The third title in the file was a string containing $(…), and compgen -W ran it: this ran was printed while generating the completions. The second title, final version, came back as two candidates, because the list is split on IFS. A completion is run by the user's own shell, on the user's own data, so this is more often a correctness bug than an attack — a file name or a branch name containing $ or a space — but the fix is the same either way: when the candidates come from data, filter them in bash instead of passing them through -W:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the same literal $(...)
printf '%s\n' 'draft' 'final version' '$(echo "this ran" >&2)' 'fix-typos' > titles.txt
cur=f
matches=()
while IFS= read -r title; do
  [[ $title == "$cur"* ]] && matches+=("$title")
done < titles.txt
printf '[%s]\n' "${matches[@]}"

[final version]
[fix-typos]

A loop that compares each candidate with [[ $title == "$cur"* ]] treats the titles as strings and nothing else. final version stayed one candidate, and the $(…) title did not match f, but would not have run if it had. Keep compgen -W for word lists the script itself writes, and quote the variable holding the current word as it is quoted here, so that a * in it is matched literally (§7.5).

13.12 Completion Functions

A completion function is registered with complete -F FUNCTION COMMAND, and bash calls it every time Tab is pressed on that command's arguments. It is given the line, split into words, and it answers by filling the array COMPREPLY with candidates. What it does in between is ordinary bash, which is why a completion function can know a script's subcommands, its options and its data.

What the function receives

Bash calls the function with three arguments and a set of variables:

  • $1 is the name of the command being completed, $2 the word being completed (the part before the cursor), and $3 the word before it.
  • COMP_WORDS is an array of the words on the line, split the way readline splits them (§13.13), and COMP_CWORD is the index in COMP_WORDS of the word the cursor is in.
  • COMP_LINE is the whole line as a string, and COMP_POINT the cursor's position in it, as a character index.
  • COMP_TYPE and COMP_KEY say how completion was invoked: Tab once, Tab twice for a listing, or a menu-completion key. A function rarely needs them.

A function can be run by hand with those variables set to what bash would set, which is the key to testing it:

_show() {
  printf 'COMP_WORDS=(%s)  COMP_CWORD=%s\n' "${COMP_WORDS[*]}" "$COMP_CWORD"
  printf 'COMP_LINE=[%s]  COMP_POINT=%s\n' "$COMP_LINE" "$COMP_POINT"
  printf '1=[%s]  2=[%s]  3=[%s]\n' "$1" "$2" "$3"
}
COMP_WORDS=(kv get al) COMP_CWORD=2 COMP_LINE='kv get al' COMP_POINT=9
_show kv al get

COMP_WORDS=(kv get al)  COMP_CWORD=2
COMP_LINE=[kv get al]  COMP_POINT=9
1=[kv]  2=[al]  3=[get]

For kv get al with the cursor at the end, COMP_WORDS holds three words and COMP_CWORD is 2, the index of al. COMP_POINT is 9, the length of the line. $2 (printed as 2=) and COMP_WORDS[COMP_CWORD] are the same here, and usually are, but not always: when the cursor is in the middle of a word, $2 is only the part before it; after a =, which readline treats as a word of its own, $2 is empty while COMP_WORDS[COMP_CWORD] is =; and for a word typed inside quotes, "my fi, COMP_WORDS holds it with its opening quote while $2 holds my fi without it. All three were measured by pressing Tab in an interactive bash, and they are why completion functions written for =-separated options read COMP_WORDS rather than $2 (§13.13).

COMPREPLY is read when the function returns. Bash does not filter it: unlike -W, whatever the function puts there is offered, whether it matches the current word or not. A function that sets COMPREPLY=(set get del list) regardless of the word offers all four even after kv g. Filtering by the current word is the function's job, which is why every function here passes the word to compgen … -- "$cur", or compares against it in a loop.

A completion for kv

The kv tool of §13.7 has global options, subcommands, subcommand options, and data — the keys in its store — and its completion function handles all four. It lives in its own file, kv-completion.bash, which the user's shell sources (§13.13 says where it is installed). The rest of the example is a harness, try, that sets the variables as bash would and prints what the function offered:

cat > kv-completion.bash <<'EOF'
# bash completion for kv
_kv() {
  local cur=${COMP_WORDS[COMP_CWORD]} prev=${COMP_WORDS[COMP_CWORD-1]}
  local store=${KV_FILE:-kv.db} cmd= i word
  COMPREPLY=()

  # Find the subcommand, and a -f FILE given before it.
  for (( i = 1; i < COMP_CWORD; i++ )); do
    word=${COMP_WORDS[i]}
    if [[ $word == -f ]]; then
      (( i++ ))
      store=${COMP_WORDS[i]}
    elif [[ $word != -* ]]; then
      cmd=$word
      break
    fi
  done

  if [[ $prev == -f ]]; then
    compopt -o filenames
    mapfile -t COMPREPLY < <(compgen -f -- "$cur")
    return 0
  fi

  if [[ -z $cmd ]]; then
    if [[ $cur == -* ]]; then
      mapfile -t COMPREPLY < <(compgen -W '-f -h --help --version' -- "$cur")
    else
      mapfile -t COMPREPLY < <(compgen -W 'set get del list help' -- "$cur")
    fi
    return 0
  fi

  case $cmd in
    get | del | set)
      [[ $cmd == set ]] && (( COMP_CWORD - i > 1 )) && return 0
      [[ -r $store ]] || return 0
      local key
      while IFS= read -r word; do
        key=${word%%=*}
        [[ $key == "$cur"* ]] && COMPREPLY+=("$key")
      done < "$store"
      ;;
    list)
      [[ $cur == -* ]] && COMPREPLY=(-l)
      ;;
  esac
  return 0
}
complete -F _kv kv
EOF
source ./kv-completion.bash
printf '%s\n' colour=blue count=3 size=large > kv.db
printf '%s\n' city=Lisbon > other.db

compopt() { opts+=("$*"); }
try() {
  local opts=()
  COMP_WORDS=("$@")
  COMP_CWORD=$(( ${#COMP_WORDS[@]} - 1 ))
  COMP_LINE="$*" COMP_POINT=${#COMP_LINE}
  _kv kv "${COMP_WORDS[COMP_CWORD]}" "${COMP_WORDS[COMP_CWORD-1]}"
  printf '%-20s -> %s%s\n' "$COMP_LINE|" "${COMPREPLY[*]}" "${opts:+   (compopt ${opts[*]})}"
}
try kv ''
try kv l
try kv --
try kv get c
try kv del ''
try kv set co
try kv set colour ''
try kv -f other.db get ''
try kv -f o
try kv list -

kv |                 -> set get del list help
kv l|                -> list
kv --|               -> --help --version
kv get c|            -> colour count
kv del |             -> colour count size
kv set co|           -> colour count
kv set colour |      -> 
kv -f other.db get | -> city
kv -f o|             -> other.db   (compopt -o filenames)
kv list -|           -> -l

The function works out where on the command line the cursor is, then what is valid there.

Finding the subcommand. The loop walks COMP_WORDS from 1 up to the word being completed, skipping options, and stops at the first non-option word: that is the subcommand. -f is special, because its argument is a separate word that must not be mistaken for a subcommand, so the loop skips it and remembers it as the store to read — which is how kv -f other.db get completed the keys from other.db (city) rather than from the default store. A completion that ignored -f would offer keys from the wrong file.

Completing an option's argument. If the previous word is -f, the current word is a file name, and the function asks compgen -f for one. compopt -o filenames switches on file-name handling for this completion only — a trailing / on directories and quoting of special characters — which the compspec as a whole should not have, because subcommand names are not file names. compopt (bash 4.0) changes the comp-options of the completion that is currently running; with a command name it changes that command's compspec permanently, and with no options it prints the current ones. It is the one completion builtin macOS's /bin/bash 3.2 lacks, as §1.2 noted, so completions written for it cannot switch options per word.

Completing the subcommand. With no subcommand yet, the word is either an option (it starts with -) or a subcommand name, and compgen -W generates both from fixed lists the script wrote.

Completing the data. For get, del and the key of set, the candidates are the keys in the store. The function reads the file and filters in a loop, as §13.11 recommended for data, and stops offering keys after set KEY: the next word is a value, and nothing useful can be suggested for it, so COMPREPLY stays empty. list offers its one option, -l.

mapfile -t COMPREPLY < <(compgen …) is how the function fills the array from compgen's output. The common shortcut, COMPREPLY=($(compgen -W "…" -- "$cur")), splits the output on spaces and expands globs in it, so a candidate containing a space becomes two and one containing * becomes a list of files; ShellCheck reports it as SC2207. mapfile takes one candidate per line (§6.12).

Everything in the function is local. A completion function runs in the user's interactive shell, not in a subshell, so a variable it forgets to declare local is left behind in that shell after every Tab — and a set -e, shopt or IFS change in it would change the user's shell. It should also cope with whatever options the user's shell has, which is why ${COMPREPLY[0]-}-style defaults and return 0 are worth the characters: some users run interactive shells with set -u.

Testing a completion without a terminal

The harness is worth reusing for every completion function. try sets COMP_WORDS to its arguments, the last one being the word under the cursor, and COMP_CWORD to its index; then it calls the function with the three arguments bash would pass and prints COMPREPLY. An empty string as the last argument means the cursor is after a space, on a new, empty word. Only compopt needs special handling, because outside a completion it refuses to run:

compopt -o nospace
echo "status $?"

example.sh: line 1: compopt: not currently executing completion function
status 1

The harness therefore defines a function named compopt, which takes precedence over the builtin (§9.3) and records the options instead, so the test also shows what the function asked readline to do: (compopt -o filenames) for the -f case. What a harness cannot show is what readline does with the result, and that is the one part checked by pressing Tab: in an interactive bash, kv get s then Tab completed to kv get size with a space, kv -f su to kv -f subdir/ without one, and kv -f other.db get to city, from the other store. A completion function that passes the harness and was tried once at a real prompt is tested; one that was only tried at a prompt is not, because nobody retries every case after every change.

compgen -V: no subshell (bash 5.3)

Bash 5.3 added -V NAME to compgen, which stores the candidates in an array instead of printing them:

compgen -V found -W 'set get del list help' -- 'd'
declare -p found

declare -a found=([0]="del")

compgen -V COMPREPLY -W '…' -- "$cur" fills the array directly, without the process substitution and the subshell it costs. On bash 5.2, the version Debian ships, -V is an invalid option. Completion code that is shared with other people should keep the mapfile form until 5.3 is common.

13.13 Word Breaks, Installation, and the bash-completion Project

COMP_WORDBREAKS

Readline does not split the line into words the way the shell does. It splits at every character in COMP_WORDBREAKS:

printf '%q\n' "$COMP_WORDBREAKS"

$' \t\n"\'@><=;|&(:'

Space, tab and newline are expected. The rest are not: ", ', @, >, <, =, ;, |, &, ( and : are all word breaks too, and each of them becomes a word of its own in COMP_WORDS. That was measured by pressing Tab: kv --file=d arrived as the four words kv, --file, = and d, and kv host:80 x as kv, host, :, 80 and x. This is the source of nearly every confusing completion bug. A completion function that checks $prev == --env to decide it is completing the value of --env= never sees --env as the previous word, because the previous word is =.

A function that completes --option=value handles the three positions explicitly:

_deploy() {
  local cur=${COMP_WORDS[COMP_CWORD]} prev=${COMP_WORDS[COMP_CWORD-1]}
  COMPREPLY=()
  if [[ $cur == = ]]; then
    prev=${COMP_WORDS[COMP_CWORD-1]} cur=
  elif [[ $prev == = ]]; then
    prev=${COMP_WORDS[COMP_CWORD-2]}
  else
    prev=
  fi
  case $prev in
    --env)
      mapfile -t COMPREPLY < <(compgen -W 'dev staging prod' -- "$cur")
      return 0 ;;
  esac
  if [[ $cur == -* ]]; then
    mapfile -t COMPREPLY < <(compgen -W '--env= --dry-run --help' -- "$cur")
    [[ ${COMPREPLY[0]-} == *= ]] && compopt -o nospace
  fi
  return 0
}

compopt() { opts+=("$*"); }
try() {
  local opts=()
  COMP_WORDS=("$@")
  COMP_CWORD=$(( ${#COMP_WORDS[@]} - 1 ))
  _deploy deploy "${COMP_WORDS[COMP_CWORD]}" "${COMP_WORDS[COMP_CWORD-1]}"
  printf '%-34s -> %s%s\n' "$(printf '[%s]' "$@")" "${COMPREPLY[*]}" "${opts:+   (compopt ${opts[*]})}"
}
try deploy --e
try deploy --env =
try deploy --env = st
try deploy --dry-run --env = ''

[deploy][--e]                      -> --env=   (compopt -o nospace)
[deploy][--env][=]                 -> dev staging prod
[deploy][--env][=][st]             -> staging
[deploy][--dry-run][--env][=][]    -> dev staging prod

When the current word is = itself, the option is the word before it, and the value typed so far is empty. When the previous word is =, the option is two words back. The candidates are then the values alone — staging, not --env=staging — because readline replaces only the current word, the part after the =. When the option name itself is being completed, --env= is offered with compopt -o nospace, so that the value can be typed straight after the =. All four were checked by pressing Tab: deploy --e completed to deploy --env= with no space, and deploy --env=st to deploy --env=staging with one.

The colon causes the same problem for anything that contains one: host:port, package::module, a URL, a Windows-style path. A candidate like db:5432 offered for the word db:5, which readline sees as 5, would be inserted after the colon, producing db:db:5432. The fix is to strip everything up to the last colon from each candidate before returning it; bash-completion's _comp_ltrim_colon_completions does exactly that.

Do not change COMP_WORDBREAKS to avoid the problem. It is one variable for the whole interactive shell, so removing = or : from it changes the completion of every other command the user has, and the bash manual warns that unsetting it loses its special meaning for the rest of the session, even if it is set again.

The bash-completion project

The completions most Linux users see — git, ssh, systemctl, apt, the options of nearly every GNU tool — come from bash-completion, a separate project that is installed as a package, not part of bash. Debian 13's bash-completion 2.16 installs 1,129 completion files. It also provides a library of helper functions for writing completions, which solve the problems of this section once: reassembling COMP_WORDS around = and :, completing file names with the right quoting, stripping colons, and ignoring redirections on the line.

The central helper is _comp_initialize, which sets the local variables cur, prev, words and cword from the raw completion variables. Since 2.12 the library's public functions have been renamed with a _comp_ prefix; the older _init_completion and _get_comp_words_by_ref, which most completions found online still use, survive only as deprecated wrappers in a compatibility file. The -s option splits --opt=value for the function, so that prev is the option and cur the value. This example was run on Debian 13, with bash 5.2 and bash-completion 2.16, and is the same deploy completion written with the helpers:

# Linux only: needs the bash-completion package, at Debian's path
source /usr/share/bash-completion/bash_completion
echo "bash-completion ${BASH_COMPLETION_VERSINFO[*]}"
_deploy() {
  # shellcheck disable=SC2034  # _comp_initialize sets all six
  local cur prev words cword was_split comp_args
  _comp_initialize -s -- "$@" || return
  case $prev in
    --env)
      _comp_compgen -- -W 'dev staging prod'
      return ;;
  esac
  [[ $was_split ]] && return
  if [[ $cur == -* ]]; then
    _comp_compgen -- -W '--env= --dry-run --help'
    [[ ${COMPREPLY-} == *= ]] && compopt -o nospace
  fi
}

compopt() { opts+=("$*"); }
try() {
  local opts=()
  COMP_LINE=$1 COMP_POINT=${#1}
  read -ra COMP_WORDS <<< "$2"
  [[ $1 == *' ' ]] && COMP_WORDS+=('')
  COMP_CWORD=$(( ${#COMP_WORDS[@]} - 1 ))
  COMPREPLY=()
  _deploy deploy "${COMP_WORDS[COMP_CWORD]}" "${COMP_WORDS[COMP_CWORD-1]}"
  printf '%-20s -> %s%s\n' "$1|" "${COMPREPLY[*]}" "${opts:+   (compopt ${opts[*]})}"
}
try 'deploy --e'      'deploy --e'
try 'deploy --env='   'deploy --env ='
try 'deploy --env=st' 'deploy --env = st'
try 'deploy --env st' 'deploy --env st'

On Debian, it prints:

bash-completion 2 16 0
deploy --e|          -> --env=   (compopt -o nospace)
deploy --env=|       -> dev staging prod
deploy --env=st|     -> staging
deploy --env st|     -> staging

With -s, --env=st produced prev=--env and cur=st, so the one case $prev in --env) clause handled both --env=st and --env st, and none of the three-position logic above was needed. was_split is set when the split happened, and the function returns early in that case, because a word containing = is never an option name to complete. _comp_compgen -- -W '…' is the library's wrapper around compgen that fills COMPREPLY safely. The harness this time sets COMP_LINE and COMP_POINT as well, because _comp_initialize rebuilds the words from the line.

The trade-off is a dependency. A completion that uses the helpers works only in a shell where bash-completion is loaded, which is common on Linux desktops and servers and not the default on macOS, where Homebrew's bash-completion@2 has to be installed and sourced. For a script's own completion, the self-contained style of §13.12 works everywhere; the helpers are the better choice for a completion contributed to a system that already has them.

Installing a completion

A completion file is sourced into the user's interactive shell, which leaves four places to put it:

  • ~/.bashrc — source /path/to/kv-completion.bash. Simple, loaded on every shell start whether kv is used or not, and bash-completion is not involved.
  • The user's bash-completion directory — ${BASH_COMPLETION_USER_DIR:-${XDG_DATA_HOME:-$HOME/.local/share}/bash-completion}/completions/kv. bash-completion loads it the first time kv is completed.
  • The system directory, for a package that installs kv — pkg-config --variable=completionsdir bash-completion prints it, /usr/share/bash-completion/completions on Debian. Also loaded on demand.
  • On macOS, bash-completion is not installed at all. Homebrew's bash-completion@2 (2.18 at the time of writing) provides it, enabled by sourcing $(brew --prefix)/etc/profile.d/bash_completion.sh from the shell's start-up file — Homebrew's caveat says ~/.bash_profile, the project's README recommends ~/.bashrc sourced from it — after which the user directory above works exactly as on Linux.
