In both bash-completion directories the file must be named after the command — kv or kv.bash — because that is how it is found. Loading on demand is not magic; it is a bash feature, and bash-completion's loader is an elaborate version of the one in the bash manual:

_completion_loader() {
  local f=$HOME/.local/share/kv-completions/$1.bash
  # shellcheck source=/dev/null  # which file is known only at run time
  [[ -r $f ]] && source "$f" && return 124
}
complete -D -F _completion_loader -o bashdefault -o default

complete -D makes the loader the default compspec, called for any command without one of its own. It looks for a file named after the command ($1), sources it — which registers the command's real compspec — and returns 124, a status with a special meaning here: it tells bash to start completion again from the beginning, and this time it finds the new compspec. A completion file is therefore read only when its command is first completed, which keeps shell start-up fast however many completions are installed. That was checked by pressing Tab: with only the loader registered, Tab on lazy x sourced lazy.bash from the directory and completed with the function it defined.

A completion file should work in any user's shell, and that means: every variable local; no set, shopt or IFS changes left behind; no output on standard output or error when sourced; function names prefixed with _ and the command's name (_kv) to avoid colliding with other completions; and no work at source time beyond defining the function and calling complete. Anything slow — reading a large file, running a command — happens when Tab is pressed, and should be fast enough that Tab does not stall: a completion that makes a network request will be switched off by its users.

13.14 The CLI Table

The constructs of this section, and the rule for each that is easiest to get wrong.

Construct
What it does, and the rule that is easiest to get wrong
while getopts ':ab:' opt
Parses one option per call. b: takes an argument, in OPTARG; the leading : selects silent error reporting (§13.3, §13.4).
shift $((OPTIND - 1))
Leaves only the operands in "$@". getopts never shifts by itself (§13.3).
'?') · :)
Silent mode's unknown option and missing argument, with the letter in OPTARG. Quote the ?: bare, it matches every option (§13.4).
OPTERR=0
Silences default-mode messages but keeps OPTARG unset. Use a leading colon instead (§13.4).
local OPTIND=1
Required in any function that calls getopts, or the second call starts where the first stopped (§13.5).
--
Ends the options; getopts consumes it. Pass it before operands handed to other commands (§13.1, §13.5).
first operand
getopts stops there: cmd file -v leaves -v as an operand (POSIX; GNU tools reorder) (§13.5).
-[!-]?*) · --opt=*)
Manual long-option parsing: split groups and = forms yourself, and check $# before $2 (§13.6).
${commands[$1]-}
Subcommand dispatch through a table of handlers, called with "${@:2}" (§13.7).
getopt
util-linux's is excellent and Linux-only (check getopt -T = 4); the BSD one splits arguments and is never safe (§13.8).
-h/--help · --version
Standard output, status 0, before anything can fail. A usage error: standard error, status 2, and a "Try" line (§13.9).
[[ $n =~ ^[0-9]{1,4}$ ]]
Validate before arithmetic: digits, bounded length, then 10#. Unvalidated input in (( )) can run commands (§13.10).
default → file → env → option
Precedence of settings, lowest to highest (§13.10).
complete -W/-F/-C
Registers a compspec; complete -p shows it. -W expands its words: never pass it data (§13.11).
compgen … -- "$cur"
Candidates matching the word; fill COMPREPLY with mapfile -t, not =($(…)) (§13.11, §13.12).
COMP_WORDS · COMP_CWORD
The line split at COMP_WORDBREAKS, where = and : are words of their own (§13.12, §13.13).
COMPREPLY
Offered unfiltered: the function must match the current word itself (§13.12).
compopt -o nospace
Per-completion options, bash 4.0+; fails outside a completion, so a test harness stubs it (§13.12).
complete -D … return 124
Load a completion on first use: source it, return 124, bash retries (§13.13).

And the rule behind all of them: a script's interface is a promise to people who will not read its source, so it should behave like the tools they already know — options first and grouped, -- honoured, help on standard output, errors on standard error with status 2, every value checked before it is used — and its completion should be generated from the same lists the script itself uses, so that the two cannot disagree.

Exercises

1. Four bugs in a backup script. This script's author says -v, -k and -o "sometimes don't work". Find four bugs in its option handling, and fix them so that every option works, every usage error goes to standard error with status 2, and -h prints the usage to standard output with status 0.

cat > backup <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
verbose=0 keep=7 dest=/var/backups
while getopts 'vk:o' opt; do
  case $opt in
    ?) echo "usage: backup [-v] [-k KEEP] [-o DIR] SRC"; exit 1 ;;
    v) verbose=1 ;;
    k) keep=$OPTARG ;;
    o) dest=$OPTARG ;;
  esac
done
src=$1
echo "backing up $src to $dest, keeping $keep (verbose=$verbose)"
EOF
Solution

Running it three ways:

cat > backup <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
verbose=0 keep=7 dest=/var/backups
while getopts 'vk:o' opt; do
  case $opt in
    ?) echo "usage: backup [-v] [-k KEEP] [-o DIR] SRC"; exit 1 ;;
    v) verbose=1 ;;
    k) keep=$OPTARG ;;
    o) dest=$OPTARG ;;
  esac
done
src=$1
echo "backing up $src to $dest, keeping $keep (verbose=$verbose)"
EOF
bash backup -v photos; echo "status $?"
bash backup -o /mnt/usb photos; echo "status $?"
bash backup photos; echo "status $?"

usage: backup [-v] [-k KEEP] [-o DIR] SRC
status 1
usage: backup [-v] [-k KEEP] [-o DIR] SRC
status 1
backing up photos to /var/backups, keeping 7 (verbose=0)
status 0

Bug 1: the unquoted ?) is first. ? matches any single character in a case pattern, so every option — v, o, anything — landed in the usage clause, and only a run with no options at all worked (§13.4). Quoting it as '?') is the fix, and it reveals the next two bugs, which were hidden behind the first:

cat > backup <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
verbose=0 keep=7 dest=/var/backups
while getopts 'vk:o' opt; do
  case $opt in
    '?') echo "usage: backup [-v] [-k KEEP] [-o DIR] SRC"; exit 1 ;;
    v) verbose=1 ;;
    k) keep=$OPTARG ;;
    o) dest=$OPTARG ;;
  esac
done
src=$1
echo "backing up $src to $dest, keeping $keep (verbose=$verbose)"
EOF
bash backup -v photos; echo "status $?"
bash backup -o /mnt/usb photos; echo "status $?"
bash backup -k photos; echo "status $?"

backing up -v to /var/backups, keeping 7 (verbose=1)
status 0
backing up -o to , keeping 7 (verbose=0)
status 0
backing up -k to /var/backups, keeping photos (verbose=0)
status 0

Bug 2: there is no shift $((OPTIND - 1)). After the loop $1 is still the first option, so backup -v photos backed up -v. Bug 3: o has no colon in the option string, so -o takes no argument: getopts returned o with OPTARG unset, dest became empty, and /mnt/usb was the first operand. The third run shows that nothing validates -k: -k photos took photos as the number to keep and left no source at all. Bug 4 is the usage clause itself: it prints to standard output and exits 1, so a caller cannot tell a usage error from a failed backup, and there is no -h.

cat > backup <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
readonly PROG=${0##*/}
usage() { echo "Usage: $PROG [-v] [-k KEEP] [-o DIR] SRC"; }
usage_error() {
  echo "$PROG: $1" >&2
  usage >&2
  exit 2
}

verbose=0 keep=7 dest=/var/backups
while getopts ':hvk:o:' opt; do
  case $opt in
    h) usage; exit 0 ;;
    v) verbose=1 ;;
    k) keep=$OPTARG ;;
    o) dest=$OPTARG ;;
    :) usage_error "-$OPTARG needs an argument" ;;
    '?') usage_error "unknown option: -$OPTARG" ;;
  esac
done
shift $((OPTIND - 1))
[[ $keep =~ ^[0-9]{1,3}$ ]] || usage_error "-k: '$keep' is not a number from 0 to 999"
(( $# == 1 )) || usage_error "expected one SRC directory"
src=$1
echo "backing up $src to $dest, keeping $((10#$keep)) (verbose=$verbose)"
EOF
bash backup -v photos; echo "status $?"
bash backup -o /mnt/usb photos; echo "status $?"
bash backup -vk3 -o /mnt/usb photos; echo "status $?"
bash backup -k photos; echo "status $?"
bash backup -o; echo "status $?"
bash backup; echo "status $?"
bash backup -h; echo "status $?"

backing up photos to /var/backups, keeping 7 (verbose=1)
status 0
backing up photos to /mnt/usb, keeping 7 (verbose=0)
status 0
backing up photos to /mnt/usb, keeping 3 (verbose=1)
status 0
backup: -k: 'photos' is not a number from 0 to 999
Usage: backup [-v] [-k KEEP] [-o DIR] SRC
status 2
backup: -o needs an argument
Usage: backup [-v] [-k KEEP] [-o DIR] SRC
status 2
backup: expected one SRC directory
Usage: backup [-v] [-k KEEP] [-o DIR] SRC
status 2
Usage: backup [-v] [-k KEEP] [-o DIR] SRC
status 0

The option string is now :hvk:o: — silent error reporting, -h added, and both k and o taking arguments. :) and '?') report which option was wrong, on standard error, with the usage line and status 2. The shift leaves the operands, which are counted: exactly one source. -k is validated as up to three digits and converted with 10#, so -k photos is now an error rather than a setting. Grouping works too, -vk3, because getopts provides it.

2. A port number. Write valid_port, which succeeds if its argument is a TCP port number — an integer from 1 to 65535 — and fails otherwise, without ever evaluating its argument as arithmetic before it is known to be digits. Test it with at least 80, 0, 65536, 080, an empty string, +80, a leading space, a twenty-digit number and x[$(date)]. Should 080 be accepted?

Solution 
valid_port() {
  [[ $1 =~ ^[0-9]{1,5}$ ]] || return 1
  (( 10#$1 >= 1 && 10#$1 <= 65535 ))
}
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the last value is a literal $(...), deliberately
for p in 80 8080 65535 0 65536 080 '' -1 +80 ' 80' 1e3 99999999999999999999 'x[$(date)]'; do
  if valid_port "$p"; then r=valid; else r=invalid; fi
  printf '%-24q %s\n' "$p" "$r"
done

80                       valid
8080                     valid
65535                    valid
0                        invalid
65536                    invalid
080                      valid
''                       invalid
-1                       invalid
+80                      invalid
\ 80                     invalid
1e3                      invalid
99999999999999999999     invalid
x\[\$\(date\)\]          invalid

The regular expression runs first and admits only one to five digits, so everything that reaches the arithmetic is a short string of digits: no sign, no space, no expression, and no twenty-digit number that would wrap round (§13.10). The range check then uses 10# so that 080 is read as 80 rather than failing as an invalid octal number; without it, (( 080 >= 1 )) is an arithmetic error. The x[$(date)] case is the one that matters for safety: it never reaches (( )), so the command substitution never runs.

Whether 080 should be valid is a design decision, not a fact. Accepting it is lenient and harmless for a port; rejecting leading zeros (^[1-9][0-9]{0,4}$) is stricter and avoids any doubt about octal. Either is defensible, but the choice should be made on purpose, and the function above makes it by reading the value as decimal.

3. Completing services. deploy [--env=ENV] [--dry-run] SERVICE... deploys services, each defined by a file services/NAME.conf. Write a completion function that completes the options, completes --env= with dev, staging and prod, completes service names from the .conf files, and does not offer a service that is already on the line. Test it with the harness from §13.12.

Solution 
mkdir services
touch services/{api,web,worker,web-legacy}.conf
_deploy() {
  local cur=${COMP_WORDS[COMP_CWORD]} prev=${COMP_WORDS[COMP_CWORD-1]}
  local -A used=()
  local w f name
  COMPREPLY=()

  # --env=VALUE arrives as three words: --env, =, and the value (§13.13).
  if [[ $cur == = && $prev == --env ]]; then
    cur=
  elif [[ $prev == = && ${COMP_WORDS[COMP_CWORD-2]} == --env ]]; then
    :
  elif [[ $cur == -* ]]; then
    mapfile -t COMPREPLY < <(compgen -W '--env= --dry-run --help' -- "$cur")
    [[ ${COMPREPLY[0]-} == *= ]] && compopt -o nospace
    return 0
  else
    for w in "${COMP_WORDS[@]:1:COMP_CWORD-1}"; do used[$w]=1; done
    for f in services/*.conf; do
      [[ -e $f ]] || continue
      name=${f#services/}
      name=${name%.conf}
      [[ $name == "$cur"* && ! -v used[$name] ]] && COMPREPLY+=("$name")
    done
    return 0
  fi
  mapfile -t COMPREPLY < <(compgen -W 'dev staging prod' -- "$cur")
}

compopt() { opts+=("$*"); }
try() {
  local opts=()
  COMP_WORDS=("$@")
  COMP_CWORD=$(( ${#COMP_WORDS[@]} - 1 ))
  _deploy deploy "${COMP_WORDS[COMP_CWORD]}" "${COMP_WORDS[COMP_CWORD-1]}"
  printf '%-34s -> %s%s\n' "$(printf '[%s]' "$@")" "${COMPREPLY[*]}" "${opts:+   (compopt ${opts[*]})}"
}
try deploy ''
try deploy w
try deploy web ''
try deploy web worker w
try deploy --
try deploy --env =
try deploy --env = s
try deploy --env = prod api ''

[deploy][]                         -> api web-legacy web worker
[deploy][w]                        -> web-legacy web worker
[deploy][web][]                    -> api web-legacy worker
[deploy][web][worker][w]           -> web-legacy
[deploy][--]                       -> --env= --dry-run --help   (compopt -o nospace)
[deploy][--env][=]                 -> dev staging prod
[deploy][--env][=][s]              -> staging
[deploy][--env][=][prod][api][]    -> web-legacy web worker

The function first handles the --env= value in the two positions §13.13 described: the cursor straight after =, or in a word after =. An option being typed is completed from a fixed word list, with nospace when the only candidate ends in =. Anything else is a service name. Service names come from a glob, not from ls (§8.4), with the directory and the .conf suffix trimmed by parameter expansion, and the [[ -e $f ]] guards against the glob matching nothing. Words already on the line are recorded in an associative array used as a set (§6.8), so that deploy web worker w offered only web-legacy. The names are compared with [[ == "$cur"* ]], not passed through compgen -W, because they come from file names, which can contain anything (§13.11).

The list is in the glob's order, which depends on the locale — web-legacy sorts before web here because - comes before . in the C locale — but that does not matter at the prompt, because readline sorts what it displays unless the compspec has -o nosort.

4. A completion that cannot drift. A completion function kept in a separate file has to repeat the script's list of subcommands, and the two drift apart when a subcommand is added. Make kv complete itself: register it with complete -C, so that bash runs the script to get the candidates, and have the script recognise that it is being run for completion and print them. Test it without a terminal.

Solution 
cat > kv <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
readonly PROG=${0##*/}
store=${KV_FILE:-kv.db}
commands=(set get del list help)

# Called by bash's completion with $2 = the word, $3 = the word before it,
# and the line in COMP_LINE. Prints one candidate per line.
complete_words() {
  local cur=$1 prev=$2 line=${COMP_LINE:0:COMP_POINT} cmd= i key
  local -a words
  read -ra words <<< "$line"
  [[ $line == *' ' ]] && words+=('')
  if [[ $prev == -f ]]; then
    compgen -f -- "$cur"
    return 0
  fi
  for (( i = 1; i < ${#words[@]} - 1; i++ )); do
    case ${words[i]} in
      -f) store=${words[i+1]-}; (( i++ )) ;;
      -*) ;;
      *) cmd=${words[i]}; break ;;
    esac
  done
  case $cmd in
    '')
      compgen -W "${commands[*]}" -- "$cur" ;;
    get | del)
      [[ -r $store ]] || return 0
      while IFS= read -r key; do
        key=${key%%=*}
        [[ $key == "$cur"* ]] && printf '%s\n' "$key"
      done < "$store" ;;
  esac
  return 0
}

if [[ -v COMP_LINE ]]; then
  complete_words "$2" "$3"
  exit 0
fi
echo "$PROG: running normally with: $*"
EOF
chmod +x kv
printf '%s\n' colour=blue count=3 size=large > kv.db
printf '%s\n' city=Lisbon > other.db

try() {
  printf '%-22s -> ' "'$1'"
  COMP_LINE=$1 COMP_POINT=${#1} ./kv kv "$2" "$3" | tr '\n' ' '
  echo
}
try 'kv '                   ''  kv
try 'kv g'                  g   kv
try 'kv get c'              c   get
try 'kv -f o'               o   -f
try 'kv -f other.db get '   ''  get
./kv get colour

'kv '                  -> set get del list help 
'kv g'                 -> get 
'kv get c'             -> colour count 
'kv -f o'              -> other.db 
'kv -f other.db get '  -> city 
kv: running normally with: get colour

With complete -C kv kv registered in the user's shell (the full path of the script, if it is not on PATH), bash runs the script on every Tab, passing the command name, the current word and the previous word as $1, $2 and $3, and the line in the environment as COMP_LINE and COMP_POINT. The script checks for COMP_LINE, which is never set when it is run normally, and prints one candidate per line. The subcommand list is the same commands array the script dispatches on, and the store is the one the script would use, including -f, so the completion is always right about both. That was checked by pressing Tab: kv g completed to kv get, kv get s to the key size, and kv -f o to other.db.

Two things are different from a -F function. The script is a separate process, so COMP_WORDS is not available — bash sets it only for functions, which was also confirmed at a real prompt — and the script splits COMP_LINE itself; read -ra does not understand quotes, which is acceptable for kv's keys, since cmd_set forbids spaces in them. And the script cannot call compopt, since it is not running inside the completion; per-word options have to be set on the compspec (complete -o default -C kv kv). What it gains is that completion is part of the program: this is how many tools written in other languages provide their completions, by a hidden argument or environment variable that makes the program print candidates.

SECTION 14

Input and Output: read, mapfile and printf

A script's contact with the outside world goes through three builtins. read takes a line — or a field, a fixed number of characters, a record ending in any byte you choose — from standard input or any open file descriptor, and splits it into variables. mapfile takes a whole stream into an array in one call. printf writes, and it is the only way of writing that behaves the same everywhere, for every string, including one that begins with a dash or contains a backslash. All three look simple, and all three have defaults that quietly change the data: read without -r eats backslashes, read with the default IFS trims whitespace, read returns failure on a last line that has no newline, and printf treats its first argument as a program in a small formatting language. This section is about knowing exactly what each one does to the bytes, so that a script can be trusted with input it did not choose.

The editorial boundary is §10's. §10 owns the plumbing — file descriptors, redirection, here-documents, /dev/tty, and which stream a message belongs on. §8.8 owns the line-reading loop, while IFS= read -r line, and the three ways it goes wrong around the loop: a pipe that runs it in a subshell, a body command that steals its input, and field splitting per line. This section owns the builtins those two sections use: every option of read, the field-splitting rules it applies, mapfile, printf's conversions and why its format string must never contain data, and echo, which the collection has avoided since §3 and whose reasons are given in §14.14.

Every example was measured under bash 5.3 on macOS and bash 5.2 on Debian. They agree except where a feature is new in 5.3 (%ls, %#q, and printf's handling of an out-of-range number) and where the platform genuinely differs (what /bin/sh is, and which locales are installed); each of those is labelled where it appears. What read does on a terminal — the prompt, silent input, a single keypress, a pre-filled answer — cannot be seen in a transcript made from pipes, and was checked by typing into an interactive bash on a pseudo-terminal, against the same functions the examples define.

14.1 What the read Builtin Does

The read builtin reads one line from standard input, splits it into fields, and assigns the fields to the names it was given. It is a builtin rather than a program for a reason that explains most of its behaviour: it has to set variables in the current shell, which no child process can do, and it has to stop reading at exactly the end of the line, so that the next read — or the next command — gets the rest of the input. Everything that follows is a consequence of those two jobs.

Reading into multiple variables

Given more than one name, read splits the line on IFS and hands out the fields in order. The last name gets everything that is left, not just the next field:

read -r first second rest <<< 'deploy web-1 now please'
printf 'first=[%s] second=[%s] rest=[%s]\n' "$first" "$second" "$rest"
read -r name extra <<< 'solo'
printf 'name=[%s] extra=[%s] extra is %s\n' "$name" "$extra" "${extra+set}"
read -r <<< '  kept as typed  '
printf 'REPLY=[%s]\n' "$REPLY"
read -r line <<< '  kept as typed  '
printf 'line=[%s]\n' "$line"

first=[deploy] second=[web-1] rest=[now please]
name=[solo] extra=[] extra is set
REPLY=[  kept as typed  ]
line=[kept as typed]

Reading into multiple variables follows three rules, all visible above. The fields go to the names left to right: first got deploy, second got web-1. The last name took the rest of the line, now please, with its internal space intact — which is what makes read -r cmd args a way to separate a command from its arguments. And names left over when the fields run out are set to the empty string, not left unset: extra is empty and ${extra+set} says it is set, so a script under set -u can use every name it gave read without checking.

The REPLY variable

With no name at all, read puts the line into REPLY — and puts it there unsplit and untrimmed. The first read above stored kept as typed with both its leading and trailing spaces, while read -r line on the same input stored kept as typed. That difference is not a quirk to memorise but a consequence of the rule the next subsection explains: trimming is part of field splitting, and with no names there is nothing to split into. The REPLY variable is therefore the one form of read that keeps the whole line without IFS=, and it is occasionally useful for exactly that. In a script it is usually clearer to name the variable and write IFS= explicitly, since a reader has to know this rule to see that $REPLY holds the raw line.

The status

read succeeds when it read a complete line and fails at end of file. That is what makes it a loop condition:

printf 'one\ntwo\n' > two-lines.txt
{
  read -r a; echo "status $? a=[$a]"
  read -r b; echo "status $? b=[$b]"
  read -r c; echo "status $? c=[$c]"
} < two-lines.txt
read -r x < /dev/null; echo "empty input: status $?"
read -r 1bad <<< 'x'; echo "bad name: status $?"

status 0 a=[one]
status 0 b=[two]
status 1 c=[]
empty input: status 1
example.sh: line 8: read: `1bad': not a valid identifier
bad name: status 1

The first two reads got their lines and returned 0; the third found end of file and returned 1, with c set to empty. An empty input is simply end of file at once. The last case is the one to notice: read given an invalid variable name printed a diagnostic and also returned 1. POSIX asks for a status greater than 1 on an error, and bash returns 1, so a while read loop whose variable name is wrong ends immediately and silently, looking exactly like a loop over an empty file. The diagnostic on standard error is the only sign.

read has two POSIX options, -r (§14.4) and -d (§14.6), the second added only in POSIX.1-2024. Everything else in this section — -a, -n, -N, -p, -s, -t, -u, -e, -i — is bash, and a script run by sh must not use it (§19).

14.2 IFS with read: How a Line Becomes Fields

read splits a line with the same algorithm as word splitting (§3.4), with one change for the last variable. The same two classes of IFS character apply: whitespace characters in IFS (space, tab, newline) are trimmed from both ends and any run of them counts as one separator, while other characters each end exactly one field, so two in a row produce an empty field between them. That is why IFS with read is the tool for colon- and comma-separated data, and why the choice of IFS decides whether empty fields survive:

IFS=: read -r user _ uid _ _ home shell <<< 'www:*:70:70:World Wide Web Server:/Library/WebServer:/usr/bin/false'
printf 'user=%s uid=%s home=%s shell=%s\n' "$user" "$uid" "$home" "$shell"
IFS=: read -r user rest <<< 'www:*:70:70:World Wide Web Server:/Library/WebServer:/usr/bin/false'
printf 'rest=[%s]\n' "$rest"
IFS=, read -r a b c <<< 'x,,z'
printf 'empty middle: [%s][%s][%s]\n' "$a" "$b" "$c"
IFS=' ' read -r a b c <<< 'x    z'
printf 'spaces:       [%s][%s][%s]\n' "$a" "$b" "$c"

user=www uid=70 home=/Library/WebServer shell=/usr/bin/false
rest=[*:70:70:World Wide Web Server:/Library/WebServer:/usr/bin/false]
empty middle: [x][][z]
spaces:       [x][z][]

The first line reads a password-file entry — seven colon-separated fields — in one read, with _ as the conventional name for each field the script does not want. IFS=: is a prefix assignment (§2.3), so it applies to the read command alone, and nothing has to be saved and restored afterwards. Asked for only two names on the same line, read gave user the first field and rest everything after the first colon, with the remaining colons untouched: the last name takes the rest of the line, not the rest of the fields.

The last two lines are the two classes side by side. With IFS=,, the empty field between the two commas was kept, so z landed in the third variable where it belongs. With IFS=' ', the four spaces between x and z were a single separator, and z moved into the second variable. For data where a field may be empty, a whitespace IFS silently shifts every later field one place left. That includes tab, which counts as whitespace, so read cannot split tab-separated data that has empty fields:

line=$'web-1\t\t8080'
IFS=$'\t' read -r -a fields <<< "$line"
declare -p fields
mapfile -t -d $'\t' fields < <(printf '%s' "$line")
declare -p fields

declare -a fields=([0]="web-1" [1]="8080")
declare -a fields=([0]="web-1" [1]="" [2]="8080")

The empty middle field vanished, and the port moved into the second element. mapfile -d $'\t' (§14.7) splits on the delimiter without any whitespace rules, so it kept all three fields; printf '%s' feeds it the line without a trailing newline, which would otherwise end up in the last field. For TSV, split each line that way, or with parameter expansion (§5.4), whenever a field may be empty.

What the last variable keeps

POSIX specifies the rest-of-line rule precisely: the last variable receives the unsplit remainder with leading and trailing IFS whitespace removed. For a non-whitespace delimiter bash does one thing more, which is easiest to see across a series of inputs:

for input in 'a,b' 'a,b,' 'a,b,,' 'a,b,c' 'a,b,c,'; do
  IFS=, read -r one two <<< "$input"
  printf '%-8s one=[%s] two=[%s]\n' "$input" "$one" "$two"
done

a,b      one=[a] two=[b]
a,b,     one=[a] two=[b]
a,b,,    one=[a] two=[b,,]
a,b,c    one=[a] two=[b,c]
a,b,c,   one=[a] two=[b,c,]

a,b, and a,b gave the same result: a single trailing delimiter after the last field is removed, because it only terminates that field. a,b,, kept b,, — with two delimiters, the remainder is not a single terminated field any more, so it is kept whole. And whenever there are more fields than names, the remainder keeps its delimiters (b,c, b,c,). The practical consequence is that IFS=, read -r one two is not a way to split off exactly two fields: to know how many fields a line had, read them into an array.

read -a: the fields into an array

read -a puts every field into an indexed array, starting at 0, after clearing it:

IFS=, read -r -a fields <<< 'id,name,,email,'
declare -p fields
read -r -a words <<< '   spread   out   words   '
declare -p words
echo "IFS is still ${IFS@Q}"

declare -a fields=([0]="id" [1]="name" [2]="" [3]="email")
declare -a words=([0]="spread" [1]="out" [2]="words")
IFS is still $' \t\n'

The comma-separated line kept its empty third field and — by the same terminating-delimiter rule — produced no empty field for the trailing comma. The whitespace-separated line was trimmed at both ends and every run of spaces collapsed. And IFS itself is unchanged after both commands, because each assignment was a prefix. §6 used read -ra to split a string into an array; this is the rule behind it.

14.3 The Trailing Newline and read

read reads up to a newline, and its status says whether it found one. That definition has a consequence which catches almost every script at least once. A text file is supposed to end with a newline, and nearly every editor and tool writes one; but files produced by printf '%s', by Windows tools, by some APIs, and by a careless echo -n do not. On such a file the last line is real data that read reports as a failure:

printf 'alpha\nbeta\ngamma' > no-final-newline.txt
while IFS= read -r line; do
  echo "[$line]"
done < no-final-newline.txt
echo "after the loop, line=[$line]"

[alpha]
[beta]
after the loop, line=[gamma]

The last line without newline

The loop printed two lines, not three. read did read gamma — the value is there after the loop — but it hit end of file before a newline, so it returned 1, and while treated that as the end. POSIX states exactly this: if end of file is detected before a terminating newline, the variables are set and the exit status is 1. Nothing is lost, it is just never processed, which is worse than an error because nothing reports it.

The last line without newline is the reason §8.8's loop has a fourth part:

printf 'alpha\nbeta\ngamma' > no-final-newline.txt
printf 'alpha\nbeta\n\n' > blank-last-line.txt
for f in no-final-newline.txt blank-last-line.txt; do
  n=0
  while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n $line ]]; do
    (( ++n ))
  done < "$f"
  echo "$f: $n lines by read, $(wc -l < "$f" | tr -d ' ') newlines by wc -l"
done

no-final-newline.txt: 3 lines by read, 2 newlines by wc -l
blank-last-line.txt: 3 lines by read, 3 newlines by wc -l

|| [[ -n $line ]] runs the body once more when read failed but still delivered something. Both files now count three lines. The comparison with wc -l is worth reading: wc -l counts newline characters, not lines, so it reported 2 for the file whose last line has no newline. A script that checks its work against wc -l will be off by one on exactly the files that trigger the bug.

The second file shows why the test is -n $line and not simply "run once more": its third line is empty but properly terminated, so read returned 0 for it and the loop ended normally at the true end of file, where line was empty and the extra test was false. An empty final line is counted once, and not twice.

Where newlines come from, and where they go

The trailing newline and read interact in one more place worth knowing, because the two most common ways of feeding a string to read treat newlines oppositely:

data=$(printf 'value\n\n\n')
printf '%s' "$data" | wc -c | tr -d ' '
wc -c <<< "$data" | tr -d ' '
read -r v <<< "$data"; echo "status $? v=[$v]"
printf '%s' "$data" | { read -r v; echo "status $? v=[$v]"; }

5
6
status 0 v=[value]
status 1 v=[value]

$(…) removed all of the trailing newlines, so data holds five bytes, value. A here-string adds one, so <<< "$data" supplied six. That is why read -r v <<< "$data" returned 0 — its input was a complete line — while printf '%s' "$data" | read … returned 1 on the same value: printf '%s' wrote no newline, so read met end of file first. Both assigned value. A script that tests read's status on data from printf '%s' sees failure where nothing failed; a here-string, or printf '%s\n', gives it the complete line it expects.

14.4 read -r: Backslash Mangling Without -r

Without -r, read treats a backslash as an escape character. That was a sensible default for a terminal in 1979, where it let a user type a long line over several physical lines, and it is wrong for nearly every use a script puts read to — reading file names, paths, configuration and data, any of which can contain a backslash:

cat > paths.txt <<'EOF'
C:\Users\dev\notes.txt
a tab written as \t
line one \
line two
EOF
echo '--- read without -r'
# shellcheck disable=SC2162  # without -r, which is the point
while read line; do printf '[%s]\n' "$line"; done < paths.txt
echo '--- read -r'
while read -r line; do printf '[%s]\n' "$line"; done < paths.txt

--- read without -r
[C:Usersdevnotes.txt]
[a tab written as t]
[line one line two]
--- read -r
[C:\Users\dev\notes.txt]
[a tab written as \t]
[line one \]
[line two]

Every backslash in the input was removed or changed something. C:\Users\dev\notes.txt lost all three of its backslashes; the \t written as two characters came out as a t, because read does not interpret escape sequences — it simply removes the backslash and keeps the next character. And the backslash at the end of the third line joined two lines into one: read treated backslash-newline as a line continuation, removed both characters, and kept reading, so the loop ran three times for four lines. With read -r, every byte came through as it is in the file.

That is backslash mangling without -r, and it is silent: no warning, no failed status, just a different string. A path from a Windows share, a regular expression, a JSON string with an escaped quote, a password — each is damaged, and the damage is only visible if someone compares the output with the input.

The backslash also changes how the line is split:

# shellcheck disable=SC2162  # without -r, which is the point
read a b <<< 'first\ word second'
printf 'without -r: a=[%s] b=[%s]\n' "$a" "$b"
read -r a b <<< 'first\ word second'
printf 'with -r:    a=[%s] b=[%s]\n' "$a" "$b"

without -r: a=[first word] b=[second]
with -r:    a=[first\] b=[word second]

Without -r, \ is an escaped space, which does not split, so a got first word and the backslash vanished. With -r the backslash is data and the space splits as usual. POSIX describes the first behaviour exactly: an unescaped backslash preserves the literal value of the following byte and prevents it from being used to split fields.

There is one rule to take from this subsection, and it has no exceptions in scripts: always write read -r. ShellCheck reports every read without it (SC2162). The only code that should omit it is code that deliberately wants backslash-newline continuation from a person typing at a terminal, and even there read -e (§14.8) is the better tool. The complete safe form for reading a line exactly as it is written is IFS= read -r line — IFS= so that leading and trailing whitespace is kept, -r so that backslashes are — and while IFS= read -r line is that form as a loop, which §8.8 builds with its other two parts.

14.5 Reading From Somewhere Other Than Standard Input

read reads from standard input unless told otherwise, and there are three ways of telling it otherwise: redirect its standard input, give it a descriptor with -u, or give it a here-string or process substitution as input.

read -u, and two files in step

A redirection on a loop (done < file) makes the file the standard input of everything in the loop, which is why §8.8 had to protect the loop's input from commands in its body. read -u FD reads from another descriptor instead, which leaves standard input alone and makes it possible to read two files at once:

printf '%s\n' web-1 web-2 db-1 > hosts.txt
printf '%s\n' 10.0.0.1 10.0.0.2 10.0.0.9 > addrs.txt
while IFS= read -r host <&3 && IFS= read -r addr <&4; do
  printf '%-6s %s\n' "$host" "$addr"
done 3< hosts.txt 4< addrs.txt
echo '--- the same, with -u'
exec 3< hosts.txt 4< addrs.txt
while IFS= read -r -u 3 host && IFS= read -r -u 4 addr; do
  printf '%-6s %s\n' "$host" "$addr"
done
exec 3<&- 4<&-

web-1  10.0.0.1
web-2  10.0.0.2
db-1   10.0.0.9
--- the same, with -u
web-1  10.0.0.1
web-2  10.0.0.2
db-1   10.0.0.9

Both loops pair each host with its address, line by line, which is paste's job done in the shell — useful when each pair needs logic, not just joining. The first loop redirects each read from a descriptor (<&3); the second uses read -u 3, which says the same thing and is what bash scripts usually write. The loop ends when either file runs out, because && needs both reads to succeed.

The exec 3< hosts.txt form in the second half opens the descriptors for the rest of the script, and the exec 3<&- 4<&- at the end closes them (§10.7). The first half's done 3< hosts.txt 4< addrs.txt opens them for the loop alone, and is the better choice whenever the descriptors are only needed there. Because standard input is untouched either way, a command in the body that reads standard input — ssh, ffmpeg, a read asking the user a question — no longer steals lines from the files, which makes read -u the cleaner of §8.8's two fixes for that problem.

A command's output into variables

To read a command's output into variables, the command has to be on the other side of a redirection, not a pipe:

printf 'one two\nthree\n' > words.txt
read -r lines words bytes < <(wc < words.txt)
echo "lines=$lines words=$words bytes=$bytes"
{ read -r header; read -r first_row; } < <(printf 'name,size\nlog.txt,120\nold.txt,80\n')
echo "header=$header first_row=$first_row"

lines=2 words=3 bytes=14
header=name,size first_row=log.txt,120

wc prints its three counts padded with spaces (more padding on macOS than on Linux), and read absorbed the difference: leading whitespace is trimmed and runs of spaces are one separator. < <(…) is process substitution (§4.6), which gives read the command's output as a file, while read itself runs in the current shell. The braces in the second example group two read commands under one redirection, so they consume the stream one line after the other: the header, then the first row, with the rest left unread.

Why not a pipe

printf 'from a pipe\n' | read -r got
echo "piped: got=[${got-unset}]"
shopt -s lastpipe
printf 'from a pipe\n' | read -r got
echo "lastpipe: got=[${got-unset}]"

piped: got=[unset]
lastpipe: got=[from a pipe]

printf … | read -r got ran read in a subshell — each part of a pipeline does (§16) — so got was set there and discarded when the subshell exited, and the main script found it unset. This is the most common way to lose a read's result, and it is always silent. shopt -s lastpipe runs the last part of a pipeline in the current shell, which makes the pipe version work; it applies only when job control is off, which is the case in scripts but not at an interactive prompt, so a pipeline tested by typing it will behave differently from the same line in a script. Process substitution or a here-string needs no option and works in both, which is why this course uses them.

14.6 read's Other Options: -d, -n, -N, -t, -a and -p

§8.8 used read with -r and nothing else. The other options change what counts as the end of the input, how much is read, and how long read waits.

read -d: a different delimiter

read -d DELIM reads up to the first DELIM character instead of a newline. read -d ';' reads one statement from a SQL file; read -d '' reads up to a NUL byte, which is §14.9's subject, and when there is no NUL it reads the whole of the input:

read -r -d ';' first <<< 'SELECT 1; SELECT 2;'
echo "status $? first=[$first]"
read -r -d '' all <<< $'line 1\nline 2'
echo "status $?"
printf 'all=[%s]\n' "$all"
IFS= read -r -d '' all <<< $'  line 1\nline 2'
printf 'IFS= all=%q\n' "$all"

status 0 first=[SELECT 1]
status 1
all=[line 1
line 2]
IFS= all=$'  line 1\nline 2\n'

The first read stopped at the semicolon. The second, with -d '', read to end of file — and so returned 1, because it never found its delimiter — and delivered both lines in one variable. That makes read -r -d '' var a way of reading a whole stream into a variable without $(…), provided the status is ignored (|| true under set -e). The last line shows that trimming still applies: without IFS=, leading spaces and the trailing newline were removed; with it, the value is exactly the input, including the here-string's newline. Only the first character of the -d argument counts, and -d '' is how the empty string, a NUL, is written: read -d '' is therefore both "read up to a NUL" and, when the input has none, "read everything".

read -n and read -N: a number of characters

read -n N returns after N characters or at a newline, whichever comes first. read -N N reads exactly N characters, treating a newline as an ordinary character, and does no field splitting at all:

read -r -n 4 code <<< 'ABCD-1234'; echo "-n 4: [$code]"
read -r -n 4 code <<< 'AB';        echo "-n 4, short line: [$code] status $?"
printf 'AB\nCD' | { read -r -n 4 code; echo "-n 4 stops at a newline: [$code]"; }
printf 'AB\nCD' | { read -r -N 4 code; printf -- '-N 4 reads through it: %q\n' "$code"; }
printf '  x y' | { read -r -n 4 code; echo "-n 4 splits: [$code]"; }
printf '  x y' | { read -r -N 4 code; echo "-N 4 does not: [$code]"; }

-n 4: [ABCD]
-n 4, short line: [AB] status 0
-n 4 stops at a newline: [AB]
-N 4 reads through it: $'AB\nC'
-n 4 splits: [x]
-N 4 does not: [  x ]

-n 4 took four characters from a long line and the whole of a short one, where it returned 0 because it found a newline. From AB\nCD it stopped at the newline; -N 4 read straight through it and returned AB, a newline, and C. The last two lines are the difference that matters for data: -n still splits and trims, so four characters x became x, while -N assigned exactly the characters read.

read -N is how a shell script reads fixed-width records:

printf 'HDR1ABCD0005ENDX' > record.bin
{
  read -r -N 4 magic
  read -r -N 4 id
  read -r -N 4 len
  read -r -N 4 tail
} < record.bin
echo "magic=$magic id=$id len=$((10#$len)) tail=$tail"

magic=HDR1 id=ABCD len=5 tail=ENDX

Four read -N 4 calls took the header's four fixed-width fields in order, because each read leaves the input positioned after what it consumed. The length field is 0005, and $((10#$len)) reads it as decimal — without 10# a zero-padded number is read as octal, and 0008 would be an error (§7.10). read -n 1 is the other common use: a single keypress at a terminal, without Enter, which §14.8 uses for a yes-or-no question.

read -t: timeouts

read -t SECONDS gives up after that many seconds, which may be fractional. A timed-out read returns a status greater than 128:

{ sleep 2; echo late; } | { read -r -t 0.5 answer; echo "timed out: status $? answer=[$answer]"; }
{ printf 'par'; sleep 2; echo 'tial'; } | { read -r -t 1 answer; echo "partial: status $? answer=[$answer]"; }
read -r -t 5 answer <<< 'in time'; echo "in time: status $? answer=[$answer]"

timed out: status 142 answer=[]
partial: status 142 answer=[par]
in time: status 0 answer=[in time]

The status is 142 — 128 plus 14, the number of SIGALRM, the signal traditionally used for timeouts — so the three outcomes can be told apart: 0 for a line, 1 for end of file, more than 128 for a timeout. The second line shows that input received before the timeout is not lost: read gave up with par in the variable — bash has kept partial input on a timeout since 4.0 — so a script that uses the value after a timeout must check the status first. In a script, read -t is how a prompt gets a default when nobody answers; in a pipeline it is how a consumer notices that its producer has stalled.

read -t 0 is a special case. It reads nothing, and returns 0 if input is available and 1 if not:

read -t 0 <<< 'waiting'; echo "data waiting:  $?"
read -t 0 < /dev/null;  echo "end of file:   $?"
{ sleep 1; echo x; } | { read -t 0; echo "nothing yet:   $?"; }

data waiting:  0
end of file:   0
nothing yet:   1

Data waiting in a here-string gives 0. End of file gives 0 too, because a read would not block — it would return at once with end of file — which is what "available" means here. A pipe whose writer has not written yet gives 1. So read -t 0 answers "would a read block?", not "is there a line?", and it is only useful as a quick check before a real read.

The variable TMOUT supplies a default timeout for every read that does not give one:

{ sleep 2; echo late; } | {
  TMOUT=0.5
  read -r answer
  echo "TMOUT: status $? answer=[$answer]"
}

TMOUT: status 142 answer=[]

TMOUT=0.5 made a plain read time out with status 142. In an interactive shell TMOUT also logs out an idle prompt, which is why some administrators set it in /etc/profile, and why a script that inherits it may see read fail unexpectedly: a script that relies on read waiting should set TMOUT= itself, or pass an explicit -t.

read -a and read -p

read -a NAME was §14.2's: the fields into an array. read -p PROMPT prints a prompt before reading — on standard error, and only if the input is a terminal:

read -r -p 'Name? ' name <<< 'Ada'
echo "name=$name"

name=Ada

Name? is nowhere in the output, because the here-string is not a terminal. That is deliberate — a script fed from a file or a pipe should not print prompts that nobody will read, into a stream that may be data — and it means prompting is §14.8's subject, where the input is a person.

14.7 The mapfile Builtin and readarray

The mapfile builtin reads lines into an indexed array in a single call; readarray is the same builtin under another name. It replaces the loop that appends each read to an array, and it is faster and harder to get wrong:

printf '%s\n' web-1 web-2 'db 1' cache > hosts.txt
mapfile -t hosts < hosts.txt
declare -p hosts
mapfile hosts < hosts.txt
declare -p hosts

declare -a hosts=([0]="web-1" [1]="web-2" [2]="db 1" [3]="cache")
declare -a hosts=([0]=$'web-1\n' [1]=$'web-2\n' [2]=$'db 1\n' [3]=$'cache\n')

mapfile -t strips each line's delimiter. Without -t, every element ends in a newline, as the second result shows, and a newline hiding at the end of an element breaks every comparison it takes part in ([[ ${hosts[0]} == web-1 ]] is false). Use -t essentially always. The db 1 element kept its space: mapfile splits on lines only and does no field splitting, so it needs neither IFS= nor -r — it never interprets backslashes at all.

mapfile was added in bash 4.0, so it is absent from macOS's /bin/bash 3.2 (§1.2); the loop is the fallback there.

The options: -n, -s, -O, -d, -u

printf '%s\n' '# host list' web-1 web-2 'db 1' cache > hosts.txt
mapfile -t -s 1 -n 2 first_two < hosts.txt
declare -p first_two
old=(a b c d e f)
mapfile -t -s 1 old < hosts.txt
declare -p old
old=(a b c d e f)
mapfile -t -s 1 -O 4 old < hosts.txt
declare -p old
mapfile -t -d , cols <<< 'id,name,,email'
declare -p cols
mapfile -t -d , cols < <(printf '%s' 'id,name,,email')
declare -p cols

declare -a first_two=([0]="web-1" [1]="web-2")
declare -a old=([0]="web-1" [1]="web-2" [2]="db 1" [3]="cache")
declare -a old=([0]="a" [1]="b" [2]="c" [3]="d" [4]="web-1" [5]="web-2" [6]="db 1" [7]="cache")
declare -a cols=([0]="id" [1]="name" [2]="" [3]=$'email\n')
declare -a cols=([0]="id" [1]="name" [2]="" [3]="email")

mapfile -n COUNT stops after that many lines and -s COUNT skips that many first, so -s 1 -n 2 skipped the comment line and took the next two. mapfile -n leaves the rest of the input unread, so a group of commands sharing one redirection can take a file's header with mapfile -n 3 and then process the body with a loop. mapfile clears the array before filling it: old had six elements and came back with four. -O ORIGIN starts storing at that index and does not clear, so it appends to an existing array — a to d survived, and the file's lines were stored from index 4. mapfile -d DELIM uses a different delimiter, and the last two results show a trap in it: a here-string adds a newline (§14.3), so the last field was email plus a newline, which -t did not remove because the delimiter was a comma. Feeding the same string with printf '%s' gave clean fields. mapfile -d '' reads NUL-delimited data, which §14.9 uses. -u FD reads from a descriptor, like read -u.

mapfile -c: a callback

mapfile -c QUANTUM -C COMMAND runs a command every QUANTUM lines, which is how a long read reports progress:

seq 1 7 > numbers.txt
progress() { printf 'callback: index %s, line %q\n' "$1" "$2"; }
mapfile -t -c 3 -C progress nums < numbers.txt
echo "total ${#nums[@]}"

callback: index 2, line 3
callback: index 5, line 6
total 7

The callback was called with two arguments: the index of the element about to be assigned and the line that will be stored there. With -c 3 it ran before storing the third line (index 2) and the sixth (index 5), and never for the last, partial group. Printing progress to standard error while mapfile loads a large file is the typical use; the callback runs in the current shell, so it can also count or collect.

Where mapfile's input comes from

mapfile has the same subshell problem as read, and a few edge cases worth measuring once:

# shellcheck disable=SC2030  # lost in the pipe's subshell, which is the point
printf 'x\ny\n' | mapfile -t piped
# shellcheck disable=SC2031  # and so empty here
echo "piped: ${#piped[@]} elements"
mapfile -t subst < <(printf 'x\ny\n')
echo "process substitution: ${#subst[@]} elements"
mapfile -t empty < /dev/null
echo "empty input: ${#empty[@]} elements, status $?"
mapfile -t trailing <<< "$(printf 'x\ny\n')"
echo "here-string: ${#trailing[@]} elements"
mapfile -t blank <<< ''
echo "empty here-string: ${#blank[@]} element"

piped: 0 elements
process substitution: 2 elements
empty input: 0 elements, status 0
here-string: 2 elements
empty here-string: 1 element

A pipe ran mapfile in a subshell and the array was lost (the lastpipe fix from §14.5 applies here too). Process substitution kept it. Empty input produced an empty array, not an array with one empty element, and a status of 0 — mapfile does not fail at end of file, which is what you want, but it means its status says nothing about whether any lines arrived: check ${#array[@]}. A here-string from $(…) gave two elements, because $(…) stripped the trailing newline and <<< added exactly one back. But an empty here-string gave one element, the empty string, because <<< '' is a newline — which is one empty line. To read a command's output, use process substitution, not a here-string of its captured output.

Process substitution has one cost: the producer's exit status is not mapfile's.

mapfile -t lines < <(printf 'partial\n'; exit 3)
echo "mapfile status $?, ${#lines[@]} line"
wait "$!"; echo "producer status $?"

mapfile status 0, 1 line
producer status 3

mapfile succeeded, having read the one line the producer wrote before it failed with status 3. $! holds the process substitution's process ID, and wait "$!" retrieves its status (bash 4.4 and later can wait for the most recent process substitution). A script that must know whether the whole list was produced should check this, or capture into a variable first with out=$(cmd) || die … and read the lines from that.

Why mapfile is faster

read is required to leave the input positioned exactly after the line it read, so that the next command sees the rest. On a regular file bash reads a buffer and then moves the file offset back with lseek. On a pipe it cannot move back, so it has to read one byte at a time. That is measurable, on Linux, by counting system calls:

# Linux only: strace counts system calls, and macOS has no strace
seq 1000 > numbers.txt
reads() {
  strace -f -c -e trace=read bash -c "$1" 2>&1 | awk '$NF == "read" { print $4 }'
}
wc -c < numbers.txt
printf '%-50s %6s\n' 'COMMAND' 'READS'
for cmd in \
  'while IFS= read -r l; do :; done < numbers.txt' \
  'cat numbers.txt | while IFS= read -r l; do :; done' \
  'mapfile -t a < numbers.txt' \
  'cat numbers.txt | mapfile -t a' \
  'awk "END { print NR }" numbers.txt > /dev/null' \
  ':'
do
  printf '%-50s %6s\n' "$cmd" "$(reads "$cmd")"
done

3893
COMMAND                                             READS
while IFS= read -r l; do :; done < numbers.txt       1006
cat numbers.txt | while IFS= read -r l; do :; done   3902
mapfile -t a < numbers.txt                              7
cat numbers.txt | mapfile -t a                       3902
awk "END { print NR }" numbers.txt > /dev/null          9
:                                                       5

The file is 3,893 bytes and 1,000 lines. Read from the file, the loop made about one read(2) per line; from a pipe, one per byte — 3,902, which is the file's size plus the handful that bash and cat make anyway, as the : baseline shows. mapfile from a file made 7 in total. From a pipe it too must read byte by byte, because it stops at a count or a delimiter and must not over-read either. (This was measured with strace under bash 5.2 on Debian; macOS has no strace, but the byte-at-a-time rule is bash's, not the kernel's.)

The rule this gives: for a large input, prefer a file or process substitution over a pipe; prefer mapfile to a read loop when the lines are going into an array anyway; and when the work per line is substantial, move the whole job into a tool that reads in blocks — awk, which counted the same thousand lines, made 9 read calls in total, only four more than the empty baseline (§21).

14.8 Asking a Person: Prompts, Passwords and Confirmation

A script that asks questions has two audiences: the person at the terminal, and every automated caller — cron, CI, a pipe — that will run it with nobody there. A prompt that works for the first and hangs or misreads for the second is the usual failure, so every example here decides first which situation it is in.

read -p, read -s and read -n 1

read -p PROMPT shows its prompt only when the input is a terminal (§14.6), and writes it to standard error. The second property is what lets a prompt work inside a command substitution: in name=$(read -r -p 'Name? ' n; echo "$n"), standard output is the capture, but standard error is still the terminal, so the person sees the question and only the answer is captured — which was checked by typing into a real terminal, and is the same property §10.13's "speaking past a capture" relies on. Redirecting standard error hides the prompt, and was also checked: read -p … 2>/dev/null waits silently for an answer to a question nobody can see.

read -s turns off echo, so what is typed does not appear — the answer to §12.4's stty -echo, for a single read. The newline typed at the end is not echoed either, so the next output starts on the prompt's line unless the script prints one:

read -r -s -p 'Password: ' password
printf '\n'
check_password "$password"

On a terminal, typing hunter2 and Enter showed Password: and nothing more, and password held seven characters. Two cautions. read -s only stops the terminal from echoing; the value is still an ordinary shell variable, visible to set -x tracing (§20) and to anything the script passes it to on a command line, where ps can see it (§18). And an interrupted read -s does not leave the terminal silent: bash restores echo when read is interrupted, which was checked by pressing Ctrl-C at a real prompt and then asking stty. A script that turned echo off with stty -echo itself, interrupted the same way, left it off — also checked — which is why that script needs §12.4's trap.

read -n 1 returns after one character without waiting for Enter, which suits a yes-or-no question. read -e uses readline, so the person can edit the line with the arrow keys and the usual editing keys, and read -i TEXT, which works only with -e, puts TEXT into the line as a default the person can accept with Enter or edit — both checked on a pseudo-terminal: Enter accepted staging, and Ctrl-U followed by prod replaced it.

A confirmation function

confirm() {
  local prompt=$1 default=${2:-n} answer
  if [[ ! -t 0 ]]; then
    printf '%s [non-interactive: %s]\n' "$prompt" "$default" >&2
    answer=$default
  else
    local hint='[y/N]'
    [[ $default == y ]] && hint='[Y/n]'
    read -r -p "$prompt $hint " answer || return 1
    answer=${answer:-$default}
  fi
  [[ ${answer,,} == y || ${answer,,} == yes ]]
}
if confirm 'Delete 3 old backups?'; then echo deleting; else echo 'kept them'; fi
if confirm 'Rotate logs?' y; then echo rotating; else echo 'not rotating'; fi

Delete 3 old backups? [non-interactive: n]
kept them
Rotate logs? [non-interactive: y]
rotating

The function checks [[ -t 0 ]] before anything else (§7.6): with no terminal on standard input, there is nobody to ask, so it uses the default and says so on standard error, where the log of a non-interactive run will show which answers were assumed. Both calls above ran that way, since the example's input is not a terminal. At a terminal the same function shows Delete 3 old backups? [y/N] and reads a line; an empty answer takes the default, ${answer,,} lower-cases it (§5.6) so that Y, yes and YES are all accepted, and the status is the answer, so the function reads naturally in an if. Each path — y, Enter with each default, YES, and no terminal — was typed at a real prompt.

Two design points are easy to miss. The default is n unless the caller asks otherwise, and the capital letter in [y/N] is the conventional way of showing which one Enter chooses. And read … || return 1: at end of file — Ctrl-D, or a closed input — read fails and the function says no, rather than proceeding with whatever was in answer.

Prompting when standard input is data

A script that reads a list from standard input or from a file with done < file cannot also read answers from standard input: the answer would be the next line of the list. The person is at /dev/tty, the terminal of the process whatever its standard streams are, and a script can open it on a spare descriptor:

printf 'db-1\nweb-1\n' > targets.txt
if { exec 3< /dev/tty; } 2> /dev/null; then
  have_tty=1
else
  have_tty=0
fi
while IFS= read -r host; do
  if (( have_tty )) && read -r -u 3 -p "restart $host? [y/N] " answer; then
    [[ $answer == y ]] && echo "restarting $host"
  else
    echo "no terminal: not restarting $host" >&2
  fi
done < targets.txt

no terminal: not restarting db-1
no terminal: not restarting web-1

The exec 3< /dev/tty is tried once, inside a brace group whose standard error goes to /dev/null, so that on a machine with no terminal — a cron job, CI, the run above — the failure to open it is silent and have_tty records the answer. With a terminal, each read -u 3 -p asks on the terminal while the loop's own input keeps coming from targets.txt: at a real prompt, answering y and then n restarted db-1 and skipped web-1, and the host list was not disturbed. Without one, every host takes the safe answer. The -p prompt appears because read's input, descriptor 3, is a terminal; it does not matter that standard input is a file.

Two rules for scripts that prompt. Every question needs a non-interactive answer — a default, or an option such as -y or --yes that pre-answers it — so that the script can run unattended. And a prompt is never data: it goes to standard error (which -p does already), so that script > out.txt captures results and not questions.

14.9 Null-Delimited Data

A file name may contain any byte except / and NUL, and that includes a newline. A list of file names separated by newlines therefore cannot be read back reliably, and the failure is not hypothetical:

mkdir in && cd in || exit 1
touch plain.log 'two  spaces.log' -- '-n.log' $'line\nbreak.log' ' leading.log'
find . -name '*.log' | sort | while IFS= read -r f; do
  printf '[%s]\n' "$f"
done

[./ leading.log]
[./-n.log]
[./line]
[./plain.log]
[./two  spaces.log]
[break.log]

Five files produced six lines: line and break.log look like two files, and a script acting on this list would try to operate on two names that do not exist. (leading.log kept its leading space only because the loop set IFS=, as §14.4's safe form does.) The only byte that cannot occur in a path is NUL, so the only safe delimiter for a list of paths is NUL, and NUL-delimited data is the discipline of using it end to end. find -print0 writes it, read -d '' and mapfile -d '' read it, printf '%s\0' writes it from the shell, and xargs -0, sort -z and grep -z pass it along on both GNU and macOS systems; GNU tools add more, such as du -0, which macOS's du rejects.

The loop

mkdir in && cd in || exit 1
touch plain.log 'two  spaces.log' -- '-n.log' $'line\nbreak.log' ' leading.log'
count=0
while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do
  printf '%q\n' "$f"
  (( ++count ))
done < <(find . -name '*.log' -print0 | sort -z)
echo "count=$count"

./\ leading.log
./-n.log
$'./line\nbreak.log'
./plain.log
./two\ \ spaces.log
count=5

Five files, five iterations, and %q (§14.13) shows each name unambiguously, including the one with a newline in it. Each part of the loop is there for a reason. -d '' makes NUL the delimiter. IFS= keeps leading and trailing whitespace, which is part of a file name. -r keeps backslashes. < <(…) keeps the loop in the current shell, so that count survives it (§14.5). And sort -z sorts NUL-delimited records, so that the order is deterministic — find returns names in directory order, which differs between filesystems.

Leaving any part out loses a name:

printf ' leading.log\0' | { read -r -d '' f; printf 'without IFS=: [%s]\n' "$f"; }
printf ' leading.log\0' | { IFS= read -r -d '' f; printf 'with IFS=:    [%s]\n' "$f"; }
# shellcheck disable=SC2162  # without -r, which is the point
printf 'back\\slash\0' | { IFS= read -d '' f; printf 'without -r:   [%s]\n' "$f"; }

without IFS=: [leading.log]
with IFS=:    [ leading.log]
without -r:   [backslash]

Without IFS=, leading.log lost its leading space, and a script would then look for a file that does not exist. Without -r, back\slash lost its backslash. Neither produces an error.

mapfile -d '', xargs -0, and -exec

When the names are needed as a list rather than one at a time, mapfile -d '' reads them into an array, and the array can be expanded as arguments with no splitting at all:

mkdir in && cd in || exit 1
touch plain.log 'two  spaces.log' -- '-n.log' $'line\nbreak.log' ' leading.log'
mapfile -t -d '' logs < <(find . -name '*.log' -print0 | sort -z)
echo "${#logs[@]} files"
printf '%s\0' "${logs[@]}" | xargs -0 bash -c 'echo "xargs passed $# arguments"' _
find . -name '*.log' -exec bash -c 'echo "-exec passed $# arguments"' _ {} +

5 files
xargs passed 5 arguments
-exec passed 5 arguments

mapfile -t -d '' gave an array of five names; -t removes each NUL, just as it removes each newline when the delimiter is a newline. printf '%s\0' "${logs[@]}" writes the array back out as NUL-delimited data, and xargs -0 passed all five to a command as five separate arguments. The last line is the alternative that avoids the shell altogether: find -exec … {} + passes the names to a command directly, as arguments, and needs no delimiter because the names never become a stream. When the work is a single command per batch of files, -exec … + is the simplest correct choice; when it needs shell logic per file, the loop above is.

A variable cannot hold a NUL

Bash strings are C strings, so a NUL byte cannot be stored in a variable:

x=$(printf 'one\0two')
echo "length ${#x}: [$x]"
y=$'one\0two'
echo "length ${#y}: [$y]"

example.sh: line 1: warning: command substitution: ignored null byte in input
length 6: [onetwo]
length 3: [one]

Command substitution dropped the NUL, warned about it on standard error, and joined the two halves into onetwo. $'one\0two' stopped at the NUL and kept one. That is why NUL-delimited data is always handled as a stream — piped, redirected, or read one record at a time with read -d '' — or as an array, whose elements are separate strings, and never as a single variable to be split later. It is also why a list of NUL-separated names can be saved to a file but not to a variable:

mkdir in && cd in || exit 1
touch 'a b.txt' $'c\nd.txt'
find . -name '*.txt' -print0 | sort -z > ../list.nul
cd .. || exit 1
tr '\0' '@' < list.nul; echo
tr '\0' '\n' < list.nul | wc -l | tr -d ' '
mapfile -t -d '' back < list.nul
declare -p back

./a b.txt@./c
d.txt@
3
declare -a back=([0]="./a b.txt" [1]=$'./c\nd.txt')

tr '\0' '@' makes the NULs visible: two names, one containing a newline, each terminated by a NUL. wc -l counted 3 lines in what is two records, which is the §14.3 lesson again — a newline count is not a record count. mapfile -d '' read the file back into exactly the two names. A NUL-delimited file is the safe way to pass a list of paths between two scripts, or between two runs of one.

14.10 The printf Builtin: Format String and Conversions

The printf builtin writes its arguments according to a format. Its first argument is the printf format string: ordinary characters are copied to the output, backslash escapes such as \n and \t are interpreted, and each conversion specification, beginning with %, is replaced by the next argument, formatted. printf adds nothing on its own — no newline, no space between arguments — so what it prints is exactly what the format says.

printf 'Hello, %s. You have %d new messages.\n' 'Ada' 3
printf '%s|%d|%i|%f|%e|%g|%x|%X|%o|%c|%%\n' word 42 -7 3.14159 12345.678 0.0001 255 255 8 hello
printf '%o %c\n' 420 65

Hello, Ada. You have 3 new messages.
word|42|-7|3.141590|1.234568e+04|0.0001|ff|FF|10|h|%
644 6

The second line uses each common conversion once. The %s conversion prints a string as it is. The %d conversion (and %i, its synonym) prints an integer. The %f conversion prints a floating-point number, with six decimal places unless told otherwise; %e prints it in exponent notation and %g chooses whichever of the two is shorter. The %x conversion prints an integer in hexadecimal — %X with capital letters — and the %o conversion in octal. The %c conversion prints the first character of its argument, which is why hello became h. And %% prints a percent sign; a bare % followed by anything else is a conversion, which is §14.11's problem. The last line is two conversions that surprise people coming from C: %o of 420 is 644, the octal file mode rw-r--r--, and %c of 65 is 6, the first character of the string 65, not the character whose code is 65.

The conversions in one place, with the argument each expects and what goes wrong most often:

Conversion
Prints, and the thing to know
%s conversion
A string, byte for byte. The only safe way to print data, since nothing in the argument is interpreted.
%d conversion · %i
A signed integer. The argument is parsed like an arithmetic literal: 010 is octal, 0x10 hexadecimal, and anything not wholly a number is an error.
%f conversion · %e · %g
A floating-point number — bash's only way of formatting a fraction, since its arithmetic is integer-only (§7.9). Six decimals by default; the decimal point follows the locale.
%x conversion · %X
An integer in hexadecimal, lower or upper case. %02x is the usual form for a byte.
%o conversion
An integer in octal, as file modes are written: printf '%o' 420 prints 644.
%c conversion
The first character of the argument — not a character code, which is what C's %c takes.
%b · %q · %(fmt)T
Escapes interpreted in the argument; quoting for the shell; a formatted time (§14.13).
%%
A literal percent sign, and the only way to write one in a printf format string.

Everything in a printf format string that is not a conversion or an escape is copied literally, which is why the same format can carry a label, a separator and a unit around its values, as the table below does.

Field width, precision and left justify

Between the % and the conversion letter, a specification can carry flags, a width and a precision:

printf '[%8s]  [%-8s]  [%.3s]  [%8.3s]\n' report report report report
printf '[%6d]  [%-6d]  [%06d]  [%+d]  [% d]\n' 42 42 42 42 42
printf '[%8.2f]  [%-8.2f]  [%.0f]  [%08.3f]\n' 3.14159 3.14159 3.14159 -3.14159
printf '[%#x]  [%#o]  [%.3d]\n' 255 8 7
printf '[%*s]  [%-*s]  [%.*f]\n' 10 right 10 left 2 2.71828

[  report]  [report  ]  [rep]  [     rep]
[    42]  [42    ]  [000042]  [+42]  [ 42]
[    3.14]  [3.14    ]  [3]  [-003.142]
[0xff]  [010]  [007]
[     right]  [left      ]  [2.72]

The field width is a minimum: %8s pads report to eight characters, on the left, and a longer value is never truncated. The - flag is left justify: %-8s pads on the right, which is what a column of names needs. The printf precision, after a dot, means different things for different conversions: for %s it is a maximum number of characters, so %.3s truncated report to rep, and %8.3s truncated and then padded; for %f it is the number of decimal places; for %d it is a minimum number of digits, so %.3d gave 007. Of the three meanings, the printf precision on a string is the one to be careful with, since it cuts silently: a value longer than the precision loses its end, and nothing reports it.

The other flags: 0 pads a number with zeros instead of spaces, + always prints a sign, a space prints a space where a plus sign would go, and # selects an "alternate form" — 0x in front of hexadecimal, a leading 0 for octal. On the last line, * in place of a number takes the width or precision from the argument list, before the value: %*s with 10 right padded right to ten. That is how a width computed at run time gets into a format without building the format string from data (§14.11).

Together these make columns. The same format, reused for each row (§14.12), lines up a table:

printf '%-10s %8s %6s\n' SERVICE MEMORY UPTIME
printf '%-10s %7.1fM %5dd\n' web 512.25 14 worker 1024 3 db 8192.75 120

SERVICE      MEMORY UPTIME
web          512.2M    14d
worker      1024.0M     3d
db          8192.8M   120d

%-10s left-justifies the name, %7.1f right-justifies the number with one decimal, and the literal M and d are ordinary format characters. Note that 512.25 was printed as 512.2, not 512.3, and 8192.75 as 8192.8, which is the next subject.

Numbers: what printf accepts, and how it rounds

The numeric conversions parse their arguments as the shell's arithmetic would, with one addition:

printf '%d %d %d %d %d\n' 0x1F 010 -0 "'A" '"a'
printf '%.0f %.0f %.0f %.0f\n' 0.5 1.5 2.5 3.5
printf '%.2f %.2f\n' 2.675 2.665
printf '%d\n' 12abc; echo "status $?"
printf '%d\n' 3.5;   echo "status $?"
printf '%d\n' 99999999999999999999; echo "status $?"
printf '%d\n' 08; echo "status $?"

31 8 0 65 97
0 2 2 4
2.67 2.67
example.sh: line 4: printf: 12abc: invalid number
12
status 1
example.sh: line 5: printf: 3.5: invalid number
3
status 1
example.sh: line 6: printf: 99999999999999999999: Result too large
9223372036854775807
status 1
example.sh: line 7: printf: 08: invalid octal number
0
status 1

0x1F is hexadecimal and 010 is octal, so it printed 8 — a zero-padded number read from a file or a date is not decimal to printf any more than to $(( )). -0 is 0. And a leading quote is a rule from POSIX: an argument beginning with ' or " is the numeric value of the character after it, so "'A" gave 65 — the portable way of getting a character's code.

Rounding is not what school taught. %.0f gave 0 2 2 4 for 0.5 1.5 2.5 3.5: exact halves round to the even neighbour, which is what the C library does. And 2.675 rounded to 2.67, not 2.68, because 2.675 cannot be stored exactly in binary and the stored value is slightly less than 2.675 (2.665's is slightly more, so it rounds up). A script that needs money or percentages rounded a particular way should work in integers — cents, basis points — and format with %d and string slicing, or leave the arithmetic to awk or bc.

The error cases are the important ones. An argument that is not entirely a number — 12abc, 3.5 for %d, 08 — produces a diagnostic on standard error, prints whatever prefix it could convert, and makes printf's status 1, while carrying on with the rest of the format, exactly as POSIX requires. So printf '%d' "$input" is not validation: it prints 12 for 12abc and continues, and only its status reveals the problem. Validate first (§13.10). A number too large for 64 bits printed the largest one there is, 9223372036854775807; bash 5.3 reports this as an error (Result too large) with status 1, while 5.2 printed a warning and returned 0 — one of a set of changes to printf's overflow handling in 5.3.

The locale's decimal point

%f follows the locale's LC_NUMERIC for both what it prints and what it accepts:

LC_ALL=de_DE.UTF-8 printf '%.2f\n' 3.14159; echo "status $?"
LC_ALL=de_DE.UTF-8 printf '%.2f\n' 3,14159
LC_ALL=C printf '%.2f\n' 3.14159

example.sh: line 1: printf: 3.14159: invalid number
3,00
status 1
3,14
3.14

Under a German locale the decimal separator is a comma: 3.14159 was rejected as an invalid number and printed as 3,00, while 3,14159 was accepted and printed as 3,14. This was measured on macOS, which ships that locale; on a system without it installed, bash warns that it cannot set the locale and stays in the C locale, printing 3.14. The consequence is the same either way: a script that formats numbers for a program or a file, rather than for a person, should set LC_ALL=C for that printf — or for the whole script — so that the output does not depend on where it runs. The same applies to sort, tr and [[ a < b ]], whose results also follow the locale — §5.3 measured the same for ${#var}, and §19 pins the locale for a whole script.

14.11 The Format Is Code: Never Put Data in It

§3.2 promised this subsection: printf "$x" is a bug. The format string is a small program — its % specifications consume arguments and its backslashes are escapes — so a format built from data runs that data as a program:

msg='Disk 90% full'
# shellcheck disable=SC2059  # data in the format: the bug being shown
printf "$msg\n"
msg='Saved to C:\temp\new'
# shellcheck disable=SC2059  # the same bug
printf "$msg\n"
user='%s%s%s'
# shellcheck disable=SC2059  # and again
printf "Hello, $user!\n"
echo '--- the same data, as arguments'
for msg in 'Disk 90% full' 'Saved to C:\temp\new' '%s%s%s'; do
  printf '%s\n' "$msg"
done

Disk 90 0.000000ull
Saved to C:	emp
ew
Hello, !
--- the same data, as arguments
Disk 90% full
Saved to C:\temp\new
%s%s%s

Three ordinary messages, three different failures. Disk 90% full contains % f, which is a conversion — a space flag and f — so it printed a floating-point zero where % f was and ull after it. Saved to C:\temp\new contains \t and \n, which the format interpreted as a tab and a newline. And a user name of %s%s%s consumed three arguments that did not exist and printed nothing. The last three lines are the fix: the format is a constant, '%s\n', and the data is an argument, which %s prints byte for byte whatever it contains. ShellCheck reports the unsafe form as SC2059.

The damage is not limited to wrong output. A * width in data is taken from the next argument:

name='%*d'
# shellcheck disable=SC2059  # data in the format: the bug being shown
out=$(printf "Hello, $name" 2000000 2>&1)
echo "printed ${#out} bytes"
out=$(printf 'Hello, %s' "$name")
echo "printed ${#out} bytes: $out"

printed 2000007 bytes
printed 10 bytes: Hello, %*d

A name of %*d in the format, followed by any number-like argument, made printf pad to two million characters: 2,000,007 bytes from a ten-character format. A larger number writes gigabytes, and inside $(…) the shell holds all of it in memory. Printed as an argument with %s, the whole greeting is ten bytes. If a script's arguments come from outside — a web hook, a file name, a message — the width is theirs to choose.

And bash's printf has a conversion that writes to variables:

counter=unchanged
data='%n'
# shellcheck disable=SC2059  # data in the format: the bug being shown
printf "$data" counter
echo "counter=$counter"

counter=0

%n stores the number of characters printed so far into the variable named by the next argument, so a data-controlled format followed by arguments can overwrite a variable of the script's — here counter became 0. It is rarely useful, and it is one more reason the rule has no exceptions: the format is always a literal, and data is always an argument. When a format really must vary — a width known only at run time — the variable part goes through * (§14.10), not into the string.

14.12 printf Reuses the Format

POSIX specifies what happens when the arguments and the conversions do not match in number, and both halves are useful. When there are more arguments than conversions, the format is used again, as often as needed, until the arguments run out. When there are fewer, the missing ones are treated as an empty string for %s, %b and %c, and as zero for the numeric conversions:

# shellcheck disable=SC2183  # an odd number of arguments, on purpose
printf '%s=%s\n' host web-1 port 8080 debug
echo '--- no arguments at all'
# shellcheck disable=SC2183  # no arguments, on purpose
printf '[%s][%d]\n'
echo '--- one conversion, many arguments'
printf '<%s> ' alpha beta gamma; echo
names=()
printf '<%s> ' "${names[@]}"; echo

host=web-1
port=8080
debug=
--- no arguments at all
[][0]
--- one conversion, many arguments
<alpha> <beta> <gamma> 
<>

'%s=%s\n' with five arguments ran three times: two full pairs and debug=, with the missing value empty. That printf reuses the format is what turns one printf into a loop — the table in §14.10 printed three rows from one call. With no arguments at all the format still runs once, with every conversion empty or zero, which is why printf '<%s> ' "${names[@]}" for an empty array printed <> — the behaviour §6.15 noticed and §6's fourth exercise worked around by printing a prefix and a newline with separate calls.

Joining and repeating

The reuse rule is the shell's join:

parts=(usr local bin)
printf -v path '/%s' "${parts[@]}"
echo "$path"
printf -v csv '%s,' a b c
echo "${csv%,}"
printf -v rule '%*s' 20 ''
echo "${rule// /-}"

/usr/local/bin
a,b,c
--------------------

'/%s' applied to each element built /usr/local/bin; '%s,' built a,b,c,, and ${csv%,} removed the final comma (§5.4). The third line repeats a character: %*s with width 20 and an empty argument prints twenty spaces, and ${rule// /-} turns them into a rule line — a whole line of dashes with no loop and no seq.

printf -v: into a variable

printf -v NAME stores the output in a variable instead of printing it. It is the same as NAME=$(printf …) except that it does not create a subshell and does not strip trailing newlines:

printf -v stamp '%04d-%02d-%02d' 2026 9 7
echo "stamp=$stamp"
printf -v 'grid[3]' '%s' 'set by -v'
declare -p grid
printf -v empty ''
echo "empty is ${empty+set} and ${#empty} long"

stamp=2026-09-07
declare -a grid=([3]="set by -v")
empty is set and 0 long

printf -v is the way to build a zero-padded date, a padded label or any formatted string for later use. It can assign to an array element, as the second line does (quote the name, or [3] is a glob). And since bash 4.4, printf -v var '' sets var to the empty string, rather than leaving it unchanged, so it can be used to clear as well as set.

Widths count bytes, not characters

printf's widths and precisions come from C, where a string is bytes. In a UTF-8 locale, an accented letter is two bytes, and the arithmetic is done on the bytes:

export LC_ALL=C.UTF-8
for w in cafe café naïve; do
  printf '[%-6s] [%-6ls] %d characters\n' "$w" "$w" "${#w}"
done
printf -v bytes '%.3s' naïve
printf -v chars '%.3ls' naïve
LC_ALL=C printf '%%.3s gave %q, %%.3ls gave %q\n' "$bytes" "$chars"

[cafe  ] [cafe  ] 4 characters
[café ] [café  ] 4 characters
[naïve] [naïve ] 5 characters
%.3s gave $'na\303', %.3ls gave $'na\303\257'

%-6s padded cafe to six columns but café to only five, because é is two bytes and the six were bytes; naïve got no padding at all. ${#w} counts characters in a UTF-8 locale, which is why the character counts beside them are right.
