Precision is worse, because it can cut a character in half: %.3s of naïve produced na and the first byte of ï (\303), which is not valid UTF-8. Bash 5.3 adds %ls, which counts characters in a multibyte locale — the second column in each row is aligned, and %.3ls kept the whole ï. Under 5.2, which Debian 13 ships, %ls is the same as %s. For a script that must run on both, pad by hand, which exercise 2 does: compute the padding from ${#field} and print it with %*s.

14.13 Bash's Own Conversions: %b, %q and %(fmt)T

POSIX defines %b; bash adds %q, %Q and %(fmt)T, and they are among the most useful things in the shell.

The %b conversion and escape sequences

The %b conversion prints its argument with backslash escape sequences interpreted, the way the format string's are:

printf '%s\n' 'tab:\t| newline:\n|'
printf '%b\n' 'tab:\t| newline:\n|'
printf '%b|%b\n' 'stop here\c and never this' 'nor this'
echo '<- no newline: the rest of the format and the second argument were dropped'
printf 'format: \x41 \101 \e[0m|\n' | cat -vet
LC_ALL=C.UTF-8 printf 'Unicode: \u00e9 \U0001F600\n'

tab:\t| newline:\n|
tab:	| newline:
|
stop here<- no newline: the rest of the format and the second argument were dropped
format: A A ^[[0m|$
Unicode: é 😀

%s printed \t and \n as two characters each; %b turned them into a tab and a newline. That is the distinction: escape sequences in the format are always interpreted, escape sequences in an argument only under %b. It makes %b the right conversion for text that is meant to contain escapes — a message catalogue, a string from a configuration file written with \n in it — and the wrong one for anything else, since a file name containing \n would be printed as two lines.

%b has one escape the format does not: \c, which stops all output from that printf at once — the rest of the argument, every remaining argument, and the rest of the format, including its newline, as POSIX specifies. That is why the next echo continued on the same line. (In the format itself, \c is not special and is printed as written.) The last line shows the format's own escapes: \x41 hexadecimal and \101 octal are both A, and \e is the escape character, 033, which starts a terminal escape sequence such as \e[0m (reset colours) — cat -vet displays it as ^[. \u and \U produce Unicode characters by code point in a UTF-8 locale (bash 4.2 and later), as the last line shows.

The %q conversion: quoting for the shell

The %q conversion prints its argument quoted so that the shell would read it back as the same single word:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # a literal $HOME, which is the point
printf '%q\n' plain 'two words' "it's" '' '*.txt' $'tab\there' '$HOME'
printf '%#q\n' 'two words' "it's"
printf '[%.4Q]\n' 'two words'
args=(--name 'Ada Lovelace' --note "it's fine")
printf -v cmd '%q ' deploy "${args[@]}"
echo "${cmd% }"
eval "set -- ${cmd% }"
echo "$# words; \$3=[$3]"

plain
two\ words
it\'s
''
\*.txt
$'tab\there'
\$HOME
'two words'
'it'\''s'
[two\ ]
deploy --name Ada\ Lovelace --note it\'s\ fine
5 words; $3=[Ada Lovelace]

Each argument came out in a form that is safe to paste into a command line: a space and a quote escaped with backslashes, an empty string as '', a glob character escaped so it will not expand, $HOME escaped so it will not be substituted, and a tab — which no other quoting can show legibly — in $'…' form. %#q, new in bash 5.3, uses single quotes instead of backslashes, which is easier to read for long values; under 5.2 it is the same as %q. %Q applies a precision to the unquoted value and then quotes it, so %.4Q quoted the first four characters.

%q is the right way to show a user a command that will be run — a dry run, a log line, an error message about a file name — because it is unambiguous: every name in §14.9 printed with %q could be seen for what it was. It is also a way to build a command string that eval can safely split back into the original words, as the last lines show: the five words, including Ada Lovelace and it's fine, were quoted by %q, eval read them back, and $3 was still Ada Lovelace. Before reaching for that, though, remember that an array (§6) holds a command without any quoting at all; %q with eval is for a command that must pass through a string — a file, an ssh command line (§18), a job queue. The ${var@Q} expansion (§5.8) does the same quoting for a single variable, in single-quote style.

%(fmt)T: dates without date

%(fmt)T formats a time, given as seconds since the epoch, with a strftime pattern between the parentheses:

export TZ=UTC
printf '%(%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S)T\n' 0
printf '%(%A, %d %B %Y)T\n' 1790000000
printf '%(%s)T\n' 1790000000
TZ=Asia/Tokyo printf '%(%H:%M %Z)T\n' 1790000000
TZ=America/New_York printf '%(%Y-%m-%d %H:%M %z)T\n' 0

1970-01-01 00:00:00
Monday, 21 September 2026
1790000000
23:13 JST
1969-12-31 19:00 -0500

Epoch 0 is midnight on 1 January 1970, in UTC. %A, %d %B %Y spelled out a weekday and month; %s printed the epoch seconds back. The zone is the TZ variable — here UTC, and Asia/Tokyo for the last line, where the same instant was 23:13 on the local clock. The first line of the example sets TZ because without it %(…)T uses the machine's zone, and the last line shows what that means: in New York, five hours behind UTC in winter, epoch 0 was still 31 December 1969. A timestamp that will be compared, sorted or read on another machine should be written in UTC, or with the offset (%z) included.

Two special arguments give the current time:

printf -v now '%(%s)T' -1
printf -v start '%(%s)T' -2
(( now >= start )) && echo 'now >= shell start'
[[ $now == "$EPOCHSECONDS" ]] && echo 'now == EPOCHSECONDS'
printf -v today '%(%F)T'
[[ $today =~ ^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$ ]] && echo 'no argument means now'

now >= shell start
now == EPOCHSECONDS
no argument means now

-1 is the current time and -2 is the time the shell started, and with no argument at all %(…)T uses the current time too (bash 4.3 and later). printf '%(%s)T' -1 is the same as $EPOCHSECONDS, a variable bash 5.0 added. Since %(fmt)T is a builtin, a script that timestamps every log line no longer runs date — a new process — for each one; §14.15's logging function uses it. It formats only; to parse a date or do date arithmetic across months, date is still needed, and its options differ between GNU and BSD (§19).

14.14 Why echo Is Not Portable

This course has written printf '%s\n' where most scripts would write echo, and this subsection is why. echo has no single definition. Bash's echo treats -n, -e and -E as options; other shells' echo interprets backslashes by default; and POSIX, rather than choose, says that if the first argument is -n or any argument contains a backslash, the results are implementation-defined. So echo is not portable is not a style opinion but the standard's own position, and its application usage section says so in one line: "New applications are encouraged to use printf instead of echo."

Bash's own echo is consistent, but has three modes:

echo -n 'no newline'; echo '|'
# shellcheck disable=SC2028  # a literal backslash-t, which is the point
echo 'a\tb'
echo -e 'a\tb'
# shellcheck disable=SC2028  # and again
echo -E 'a\tb'
shopt -s xpg_echo
# shellcheck disable=SC2028  # and under xpg_echo
echo 'a\tb'
shopt -u xpg_echo

no newline|
a\tb
a	b
a\tb
a	b

echo -n suppresses the newline. By default bash's echo prints backslashes literally, so 'a\tb' came out as written; echo -e interprets escape sequences, making it a tab; -E turns interpretation off again. And the xpg_echo shell option makes plain echo interpret escapes, as the POSIX XSI extension and System V echo do — the same line printed a tab once shopt -s xpg_echo was set. A script cannot know from echo 'a\tb' alone which of these it will get: an inherited xpg_echo, or a bash built with it on by default, changes the output.

echo cannot print every string

The deeper problem is that echo cannot print some strings at all, because its first argument might be an option:

for x in -n -e -E -neE plain '-n -e' '-x'; do
  # shellcheck disable=SC2116  # the echo is what is being tested
  printf '%-6s echo printed [%s]\n' "$x" "$(echo "$x")"
done
echo -- -n

-n     echo printed []
-e     echo printed []
-E     echo printed []
-neE   echo printed []
plain  echo printed [plain]
-n -e  echo printed [-n -e]
-x     echo printed [-x]
-- -n

-n, -e, -E and -neE were taken as options and printed nothing — so a variable holding any of them produces an empty line, or none, and no error. -n -e and -x were printed, because bash only recognises an argument made entirely of the letters n, e and E. And echo has no -- to end its options: echo -- -n printed -- -n, the last line. A variable whose value is outside the script's control — a file name, a user's input, a line from a file — can therefore not be printed reliably with echo. This is what §8.4's -n file name ran into.

Across shells

for sh in /bin/dash /bin/sh "$BASH"; do
  printf '%s\n' "--- ${sh##*/}"
  "$sh" -c 'echo -n "x"; echo "|"; echo "a\tb|"; echo -e "y|"' | cat -vt
done

--- dash
x|
a^Ib|
-e y|
--- sh
-n x
|
a^Ib|
-e y|
--- bash
x|
a\tb|
y|

The same three echo commands in three shells. dash, which is Debian's and Ubuntu's /bin/sh, interprets \t by default and has no -e, so echo -e y printed -e y. macOS's /bin/sh is bash 3.2 in POSIX mode with xpg_echo on, and it goes further: it does not accept -n either, so echo -n x printed -n x and a newline. bash accepted both options and printed the backslash literally. The /bin/sh rows are the macOS measurement; on Debian /bin/sh is dash, so its row matches dash's. Three shells, three different outputs, from a line that looks too simple to get wrong.

printf instead of echo

The replacement is mechanical, and printf instead of echo is always correct:

Instead of
Write
echo "$x"
printf '%s\n' "$x" — prints any string, including -n and backslashes, exactly.
echo -n "$x"
printf '%s' "$x"
echo -e "$x"
printf '%b\n' "$x" — only when the value is meant to contain escapes (§14.13).
echo "$@"
printf '%s\n' "$*" for one line; printf '%s\n' "$@" for one argument per line.
echo "text"
echo is fine for a constant string that does not begin with - and contains no backslash; the rule is about data, not about banning a word.

This course keeps echo for fixed messages in examples, where the string is visible and harmless, and uses printf '%s\n' for every value that came from a variable. That is a reasonable policy for any script: the question to ask of each echo is whether its arguments could ever begin with a dash or contain a backslash — and "only if someone creates a strange file" counts as yes.

14.15 Output for People: Messages, Colour and Blocks of Text

§10.13 split a script's output into data on standard output and messages on standard error, and built info, warn and die. §7.6 showed the test that decides whether colour is safe. This subsection puts them together into the logging library a real script sources, using printf for every part of it.

A logging library with colour and timestamps

cat > logging.sh <<'EOF'
# shellcheck shell=bash
if [[ -t 2 && -z ${NO_COLOR-} && ${TERM-dumb} != dumb ]]; then
  _c_red=$'\e[31m' _c_yellow=$'\e[33m' _c_dim=$'\e[2m' _c_off=$'\e[0m'
else
  _c_red='' _c_yellow='' _c_dim='' _c_off=''
fi

_log() {
  local level=$1 colour=$2; shift 2
  printf '%s%(%H:%M:%S)T%s %s%-5s%s %s\n' \
    "$_c_dim" -1 "$_c_off" "$colour" "$level" "$_c_off" "$*" >&2
}
info()  { (( ${VERBOSE:-0} )) && _log INFO '' "$@"; return 0; }
warn()  { _log WARN "$_c_yellow" "$@"; }
error() { _log ERROR "$_c_red" "$@"; }
EOF
source ./logging.sh
# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # read by info() in logging.sh
VERBOSE=1
{
  info 'starting'
  warn 'disk is 91% full'
  error 'backup failed: exit 3'
} 2>&1 | sed -E 's/^[0-9]{2}:[0-9]{2}:[0-9]{2}/HH:MM:SS/'

HH:MM:SS INFO  starting
HH:MM:SS WARN  disk is 91% full
HH:MM:SS ERROR backup failed: exit 3

The library decides once, when it is loaded, whether to colour its messages, and it colours them only if three things are true. Standard error is a terminal — [[ -t 2 ]], not -t 1, because the messages go to standard error, and a script whose output is redirected to a file may still have its messages on the terminal, or the other way round (§7.6's idiom tested descriptor 1 because it coloured standard output). NO_COLOR is not set, a widely-followed convention (no-color.org) by which a user turns colour off for every program that honours it. And the terminal is not dumb, the type that editors' shells and some CI systems declare. Otherwise the colour variables are empty strings, and the same printf prints plain text — no second code path.

Each message is one printf call: %(%H:%M:%S)T with -1 stamps the time without running date, %-5s pads the level so that the messages line up whatever the level's length, and the colour codes are arguments printed with %s, not pieces of the format (§14.11). The example pipes its standard error through sed to replace the time, since a timestamp differs on every run; that is the only change. Run on a real terminal, the same library printed WARN and ERROR in yellow and red escape sequences; with NO_COLOR=1, or with the script's standard error piped, it printed none — all three checked on a pseudo-terminal. info ends with return 0 for §10.13's reason: a quiet info must not return the false status of (( VERBOSE )).

Deciding once has a consequence worth knowing: redirecting a single call later (warn … 2> file) does not turn its colour off, since the choice was made when the library was sourced. Scripts rarely do that, and a library that re-tested the descriptor on every message would pay for one test per line to support it; this one does not.

A here-document for a block of text

For a block of text — usage, a generated file, a report — one printf per line is noise. A here-document for a block of text keeps the text looking like the output (§10.9):

PROG=backup
usage() {
  cat <<EOF
Usage: $PROG [-v] [-k COUNT] SOURCE DEST

Copy SOURCE to DEST, keeping COUNT old copies (default 5).

  -k COUNT   copies to keep
  -v         say what is being done
  -h         show this help
EOF
}
usage

Usage: backup [-v] [-k COUNT] SOURCE DEST

Copy SOURCE to DEST, keeping COUNT old copies (default 5).

  -k COUNT   copies to keep
  -v         say what is being done
  -h         show this help

The unquoted EOF lets $PROG expand, so the program's name is written once; everything else is copied exactly, including the blank line and the alignment of the option list. cat <<EOF is the usual reader, and the usage function prints to standard output, as §11.4 and §13.9 required, so that script -h | less works. Use a quoted delimiter (<<'EOF') when the text contains $ or backticks that must appear literally, and <<- with tab indentation when the here-document sits inside indented code (§10.9). When the block needs formatting — aligned columns computed from data — printf with a reused format (§14.12) does it instead.

14.16 The Input and Output Table

The constructs of this section, and the rule for each that is easiest to get wrong.

Construct
What it does, and the rule that is easiest to get wrong
read -r a b rest
Splits one line on IFS; the last name takes the rest of the line, and leftover names are set to empty (§14.1).
read (no name)
The whole line, untrimmed, into REPLY (§14.1).
IFS=, read -r
A prefix assignment: non-whitespace IFS keeps empty fields, whitespace IFS collapses them (§14.2).
|| [[ -n $line ]]
Processes a last line with no newline, for which read returns 1 with the data assigned (§14.3).
read -r
Always. Without it backslashes vanish and a trailing one joins lines — silently (§14.4).
read -u 3 · < <(cmd)
Read from another descriptor, or from a command, without a pipe's subshell (§14.5).
read -d ''
Up to a NUL; with no NUL, the whole input, with status 1 (§14.6, §14.9).
read -n N · -N N
-n stops at a newline and splits; -N reads exactly N characters and does not (§14.6).
read -t SECS
Status above 128 on timeout, with partial input assigned. -t 0 asks only whether a read would block (§14.6).
mapfile -t arr
Lines into an array, delimiters stripped; clears the array first unless -O; returns 0 even for no input (§14.7).
read -p · -s · -e -i
Prompt on standard error, only on a terminal; silent input; a pre-filled, editable answer (§14.8).
exec 3< /dev/tty
Ask the person while standard input is data; always have a non-interactive answer (§14.8).
find -print0 · sort -z · xargs -0
NUL is the only safe delimiter for paths; keep it a stream or an array, never a variable (§14.9).
%-10s · %8.2f · %*s
Width is a minimum, - left-justifies, precision truncates strings; widths count bytes (§14.10, §14.12).
printf '%s\n' "$x"
The format is a constant and data is an argument, always (§14.11).
printf '%s,' "${a[@]}"
The format is reused for every argument, and runs once with none (§14.12).
printf -v var
Format into a variable with no subshell and no newline stripping (§14.12).
%b · %q · %(fmt)T
Escapes in an argument; quoting for the shell; a timestamp without date — set TZ (§14.13).
echo
Only for constant text that does not start with - or contain a backslash (§14.14).

And the rule behind all of them: input is not text until a script has decided what its delimiters, its escapes and its whitespace mean, and output is not text until the script has decided which bytes it will print — so every read says -r and chooses its IFS, every list of paths is delimited by NUL, and every value is printed by printf from a constant format.

Exercises

1. Three bugs in a CSV reader. This deliberately broken script reads a small CSV file of users and prints each one, then the count. It prints three users and says there are 0. Find the three bugs and fix them.

cat > users.csv <<'EOF'
name,home,shell
ada,C:\Users\ada,/bin/bash
grace,/home/grace,
linus,/home/linus,/bin/zsh
EOF
printf 'ken,/home/ken,/bin/sh' >> users.csv
count=0
cat users.csv | while IFS=, read name home shell; do
  [[ $name == name ]] && continue
  echo "$name: home=$home shell=${shell:-none}"
  count=$((count + 1))
done
echo "$count users"
Solution

Running the deliberately broken version:

cat > users.csv <<'EOF'
name,home,shell
ada,C:\Users\ada,/bin/bash
grace,/home/grace,
linus,/home/linus,/bin/zsh
EOF
printf 'ken,/home/ken,/bin/sh' >> users.csv
count=0
cat users.csv | while IFS=, read name home shell; do
  [[ $name == name ]] && continue
  echo "$name: home=$home shell=${shell:-none}"
  count=$((count + 1))
done
echo "$count users"

ada: home=C:Usersada shell=/bin/bash
grace: home=/home/grace shell=none
linus: home=/home/linus shell=/bin/zsh
0 users

Bug 1: read without -r. C:\Users\ada became C:Usersada (§14.4). Bug 2: the pipe. cat users.csv | while … runs the loop in a subshell, so count was incremented there and the echo after the loop saw the original 0 (§14.5, §8.8). Bug 3: the last line. The file was written without a final newline, so read returned 1 on ken and the loop ended without printing him (§14.3).

cat > users.csv <<'EOF'
name,home,shell
ada,C:\Users\ada,/bin/bash
grace,/home/grace,
linus,/home/linus,/bin/zsh
EOF
printf 'ken,/home/ken,/bin/sh' >> users.csv
count=0
{
  IFS= read -r _header
  while IFS=, read -r name home shell || [[ -n $name ]]; do
    printf '%s: home=%s shell=%s\n' "$name" "$home" "${shell:-none}"
    (( ++count ))
  done
} < users.csv
echo "$count users"

ada: home=C:\Users\ada shell=/bin/bash
grace: home=/home/grace shell=none
linus: home=/home/linus shell=/bin/zsh
ken: home=/home/ken shell=/bin/sh
4 users

The loop now reads with -r, from a redirection on a brace group rather than a pipe, and with || [[ -n $name ]] for the unterminated last line. The group also reads the header with its own read before the loop, which replaces the [[ $name == name ]] && continue test — a test that would also have skipped a real user called name. printf replaces echo, so a name that begins with - would be printed rather than taken as an option (§14.14), and (( ++count )) replaces the $((…)) assignment. The IFS=, is kept: it is right for this data, and a field containing a comma would need a real CSV parser, which is a job for another language (§21).

2. Aligned columns. Write a function columns that reads tab-separated lines on standard input and prints them as aligned columns, two spaces apart, the last column unpadded. Test it with names containing accented letters, such as José and São Paulo, in a UTF-8 locale. Does printf '%-*s' do the job?

Solution

The first version pads with printf '%-*s':

columns() {
  local -a lines widths=() f
  local line i last
  mapfile -t lines
  for line in "${lines[@]}"; do
    IFS=$'\t' read -r -a f <<< "$line"
    for i in "${!f[@]}"; do
      (( ${#f[i]} > ${widths[i]:-0} )) && widths[i]=${#f[i]}
    done
  done
  last=$(( ${#widths[@]} - 1 ))
  for line in "${lines[@]}"; do
    IFS=$'\t' read -r -a f <<< "$line"
    for (( i = 0; i < last; i++ )); do
      printf '%-*s  ' "${widths[i]}" "${f[i]-}"
    done
    printf '%s\n' "${f[last]-}"
  done
}
export LC_ALL=C.UTF-8
printf 'NAME\tCITY\tVISITS\nAda\tLondon\t12\nJos\u00e9\tS\u00e3o Paulo\t7\nLinus\tHelsinki\t130\n' | columns

NAME   CITY       VISITS
Ada    London     12
José  São Paulo  7
Linus  Helsinki   130

The ASCII rows line up, and José does not. The width of the first column is 5, from Linus, and ${#f[i]} measured José correctly as four characters; but %-5s pads to five bytes, and José is already five bytes, so it got no padding and the rest of its row moved one column left (§14.12). São Paulo happens to be the widest city, which is why that column looks right — a lucky coincidence in this data, not a property of the code.

The portable fix pads by hand, computing the padding from the character count:

columns() {
  local -a lines widths=() f
  local line i last pad
  mapfile -t lines
  for line in "${lines[@]}"; do
    IFS=$'\t' read -r -a f <<< "$line"
    for i in "${!f[@]}"; do
      (( ${#f[i]} > ${widths[i]:-0} )) && widths[i]=${#f[i]}
    done
  done
  last=$(( ${#widths[@]} - 1 ))
  for line in "${lines[@]}"; do
    IFS=$'\t' read -r -a f <<< "$line"
    for (( i = 0; i < last; i++ )); do
      pad=$(( widths[i] - ${#f[i]} + 2 ))
      printf '%s%*s' "${f[i]-}" "$pad" ''
    done
    printf '%s\n' "${f[last]-}"
  done
}
export LC_ALL=C.UTF-8
printf 'NAME\tCITY\tVISITS\nAda\tLondon\t12\nJos\u00e9\tS\u00e3o Paulo\t7\nLinus\tHelsinki\t130\n' | columns

NAME   CITY       VISITS
Ada    London     12
José   São Paulo  7
Linus  Helsinki   130

$(( widths[i] - ${#f[i]} + 2 )) is the number of spaces a field needs, counted in characters, and printf '%s%*s' "$field" "$pad" '' prints the field followed by that many spaces — %*s of an empty string is a run of spaces. The function reads its input once with mapfile -t (§14.7), computes each column's width in a first pass, and prints in a second, splitting each line with IFS=$'\t' read -r -a (§14.2) — which, as §14.2 measured, collapses an empty cell, so a table that may have blank cells should split with mapfile -d $'\t' instead. On bash 5.3, printf '%-*ls ' would do the same, since %ls counts characters; the hand-padded version also runs on 5.2, which is what Debian ships. Characters are not quite columns, either: an East Asian character is usually two columns wide, and a combining accent zero, so a truly general columns needs a tool that knows display widths. column -t -s $'\t' from util-linux 2.41 (on Debian, in the bsdextrautils package) aligned the same table correctly, José included.

3. A prompt with a default and a timeout. Write ask PROMPT DEFAULT [SECONDS], which prints the answer on standard output so it can be used as env=$(ask 'Environment?' staging 10). It should show the default in the prompt, return the default on an empty answer, on a timeout, or when there is no terminal, and leave the terminal tidy after a timeout.

Solution 
ask() {
  local prompt=$1 default=$2 timeout=${3:-10} answer
  if [[ ! -t 0 ]]; then
    printf '%s\n' "$default"
    return 0
  fi
  if read -r -t "$timeout" -p "$prompt [$default] " answer; then
    printf '%s\n' "${answer:-$default}"
  else
    (( $? > 128 )) && printf '\n' >&2
    printf '%s\n' "$default"
  fi
}
env=$(ask 'Environment?' staging 5 < /dev/null)
echo "env=$env"

env=staging

The run above has no terminal on standard input, so ask returned the default without asking — the non-interactive answer every prompt needs (§14.8). On a pseudo-terminal the same function was checked three ways: typing prod returned prod; pressing Enter returned staging; and waiting past the timeout returned staging after printing a newline, so that the next output did not continue on the prompt's line.

The function works inside $(…) because the prompt from read -p goes to standard error, which is still the terminal, while only the answer is written to standard output (§14.8). The timeout is told apart from end of file by the status: read -t returns more than 128 on a timeout (§14.6), and only then does the function print the newline, on standard error, where it cannot end up in the captured answer. Ctrl-D (end of file) takes the default too, which is the same "no answer" as the other cases. A version that must distinguish "the person chose the default" from "nobody answered" should return a different status in the second case, and let the caller decide.

4. Renaming files with spaces, safely. Write a script that plans the renaming of every .jpg file in the current directory, replacing each whitespace character in the name with _. It must print the mv commands it would run, not run them; handle every possible file name, including ones containing newlines or beginning with -; and refuse a rename that would overwrite an existing file or another planned name.

Solution 
mkdir photos && cd photos || exit 1
touch 'Beach Day.jpg' 'Beach_Day.jpg' $'odd\nname.jpg' 'Plain.jpg' -- '-rf.jpg' 'two  gaps.jpg'
plan=0 clash=0
declare -A taken=()
while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do
  name=${f#./}
  new=${name//[[:space:]]/_}
  [[ $new == -* ]] && new=_$new
  [[ $new == "$name" ]] && { taken[$new]=1; continue; }
  if [[ -e $new || -n ${taken[$new]-} ]]; then
    printf 'skip %q: %q already exists\n' "$name" "$new" >&2
    (( ++clash ))
    continue
  fi
  taken[$new]=1
  printf 'mv -- %q %q\n' "$name" "$new"
  (( ++plan ))
done < <(find . -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.jpg' -print0 | sort -z)
echo "$plan to rename, $clash clash(es)" >&2

mv -- -rf.jpg _-rf.jpg
skip Beach\ Day.jpg: Beach_Day.jpg already exists
mv -- $'odd\nname.jpg' odd_name.jpg
mv -- two\ \ gaps.jpg two__gaps.jpg
3 to rename, 1 clash(es)

The names come from find -print0 | sort -z into a read -r -d '' loop (§14.9), so a name containing a newline arrived as one name and a name beginning with - as data. ${name//[[:space:]]/_} replaces every whitespace character — including the newline — with _ (§5.5). A new name that would begin with - gets an _ prefix, since -rf.jpg is legal but hostile. The plan is printed with printf 'mv -- %q %q\n': %q makes every name unambiguous and safe to paste (§14.13), and the -- makes the mv command itself safe for names beginning with - (§13.1).

The clash check tests both the filesystem ([[ -e $new ]]) and the names already planned (the taken associative array, §6.8), because two different names — a b.jpg with a space and a b.jpg with a tab — can map to the same new name, and neither exists yet when the plan is made. Beach Day.jpg was skipped because Beach_Day.jpg already exists. The summary goes to standard error, so that the plan on standard output can be reviewed, saved, and run with bash plan.sh once it has been read.

One more trap is worth knowing, because it makes the clash test platform-dependent. macOS's default filesystem is case-insensitive:

touch Plain.jpg
if [[ -e plain.jpg ]]; then echo 'plain.jpg exists'; else echo 'plain.jpg does not exist'; fi

plain.jpg exists

That is the macOS answer; on Linux the same test prints plain.jpg does not exist. A version of this exercise that also lower-cased names reported Plain.jpg as clashing with itself on macOS and renamed it on Linux. A rename that changes only case needs to compare the two names first, and on a case-insensitive filesystem to go through a temporary name.

SECTION 15

Text Processing in the Shell

Most of what a script does to text is small: take the file name off a path, trim the spaces from a value read out of a configuration file, split host:port into two variables, check whether a line contains a word, join a list of names with commas. Every one of those jobs can be done by starting a program — basename, sed, cut, grep, paste — and every one of them can also be done inside the shell with an expansion bash already has. Text processing in the shell is the skill of knowing which is which: which jobs belong in the shell, where starting a process in a loop costs a hundred times the work it does, and which belong to a real text tool, where a shell loop is slower, longer and wrong on the inputs nobody tested.

The editorial boundary is set by three other places. §5 teaches the parameter expansion operators themselves — #, %, /, ^, :offset:length — and §5.9 compares ${p##*/} with basename on awkward paths. §14 teaches read, mapfile and printf, the builtins that move text in and out. And the Linux course's §5 teaches grep, sed and awk as tools: regular expression dialects, addresses, sed -i, awk's fields and patterns. This section owns what sits between them — the recipes: trimming, splitting, joining, searching, replacing, iterating, sorting, storing a map in a file, handling file names — each built from those operators, measured on the inputs that break the obvious version, and paired with the rule for when to hand the job to a tool instead.

Every example was measured under bash 5.3 on macOS and bash 5.2 on Debian, and the two agree byte for byte except for one feature that is new in 5.3 (${ command; }, in §15.1), labelled where it appears. Where the external tools differ between macOS and GNU — grep -P, sed -i, sort order in a locale — the example prints what holds on both, and the prose reports each platform's measured behaviour.

15.1 What a Subprocess Costs

Every external command a script runs is a new process: bash forks a copy of itself, the copy replaces itself with the program, the program starts up, does its work, and exits, and bash waits for it. For a program that processes a large file, that start-up cost is nothing. For basename applied to one short string, it is nearly all the cost there is, because the work — finding the last slash — takes less time than loading the program does. The same is true of $(echo "$x" | cut -d: -f1), $(echo "$s" | tr a-z A-Z), and $(expr length "$s"): a process started, and in the case of a pipeline two, to do what an expansion does in the shell's own memory. That per-value work is where text processing in the shell wins outright.

Avoiding a subprocess is therefore not a micro-optimisation when the command sits inside a loop. A loop over ten thousand files that calls basename and dirname for each one starts twenty thousand processes, and on any machine that is the difference between a script that finishes before you look up and one you wait for. §21.4 times exactly that loop. This subsection does something more useful for reasoning about a script: it counts the programs a piece of code runs, which does not vary between machines or between runs — and a count is what shows whether avoiding a subprocess was achieved, or only intended.

Counting the programs a script runs

The measuring instrument is a set of spies: tiny scripts with the same names as the real tools, placed first on PATH, that each write their own name to a log and then exec the real program. The script under test runs unchanged, and the log records every external program it started:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the labels passed to calls are literal text
# Spies: each logs its own name to calls.log, then runs the real tool
mkdir spy
for tool in basename cat; do
  printf '#!/bin/sh\necho %s >> "%s/calls.log"\nexec %s "$@"\n' \
    "$tool" "$PWD" "$(command -v "$tool")" > "spy/$tool"
  chmod +x "spy/$tool"
done
PATH=$PWD/spy:$PATH
: > calls.log
calls() {
  mapfile -t log < calls.log; : > calls.log
  printf '%-34s %d program(s) run\n' "$1" "${#log[@]}"
}

paths=(/var/log/app.log /srv/web/index.html /etc/hosts /home/ada/notes.txt)
printf 'port=8080\n' > settings.conf

for p in "${paths[@]}"; do name=$(basename -- "$p"); done
calls 'name=$(basename -- "$p") x4'
for p in "${paths[@]}"; do name=${p##*/}; done
calls 'name=${p##*/} x4'
conf=$(cat settings.conf)
calls 'conf=$(cat settings.conf)'
conf=$(< settings.conf)
calls 'conf=$(< settings.conf)'
echo "last name: $name, conf: $conf"

name=$(basename -- "$p") x4        4 program(s) run
name=${p##*/} x4                   0 program(s) run
conf=$(cat settings.conf)          1 program(s) run
conf=$(< settings.conf)            0 program(s) run
last name: notes.txt, conf: port=8080

The loop with $(basename -- "$p") ran basename four times, once per path. The loop with ${p##*/} ran nothing: the expansion happens inside bash. $(cat settings.conf) ran cat once, and $(< settings.conf) ran no program at all, because bash recognises that form and reads the file itself (§15.2). The results — the last name and the contents of conf — are the same in both halves of each pair; only the cost differs.

The spies count programs executed, which is the dominant cost, but it is not the only one. A command substitution $(…) forks a subshell even when everything inside it is a builtin, so $(printf '%s' "$x") starts no program and still copies the shell. That fork is cheaper than a fork followed by an exec, and it is still a process. The rule that follows from both costs is simple enough to apply by eye: in a loop, an expansion is free, a builtin in $(…) costs a fork, and an external command costs a fork and a program start — so a loop body should contain as few of the second kind and none of the third as the job allows.

${ command; }: command substitution without a subshell

Bash 5.3 added a form of command substitution that runs in the current shell, which removes the fork as well:

# Bash 5.3 and later: ${ command; } and ${| command; }
count=0
bump() { (( ++count )); printf 'call %d\n' "$count"; }

a=$(bump)
echo "\$(bump)     printed [$a]; count is now $count"
b=${ bump; }
echo "\${ bump; }  printed [$b]; count is now $count"

outer=$BASHPID
inner=$(printf '%s' "$BASHPID")
[[ $inner == "$outer" ]] || echo "command substitution ran in a child process"
inner=${ printf '%s' "$BASHPID"; }
[[ $inner == "$outer" ]] && echo "the new form ran in this process"

stamp=${| printf -v REPLY '%s-%03d' build 7; }
echo "\${| ...; } expanded to [$stamp]"

$(bump)     printed [call 1]; count is now 0
${ bump; }  printed [call 1]; count is now 1
command substitution ran in a child process
the new form ran in this process
${| ...; } expanded to [build-007]

$(bump) printed call 1, but the counter it incremented belonged to a child process that then exited, so count in the script was still 0 — the subshell trap §9.6 described for functions that return data. ${ bump; } ran the function in the current shell: it captured the same output, and count is 1 afterwards. The BASHPID comparison shows the difference directly: inside $(…) it is a different process, inside ${ …; } the same one. The syntax needs the space after ${ and the ; (or a newline) before }, exactly like a brace group (§9.1). The variant ${| command; } does not capture output at all: it runs the command and expands to whatever the command left in REPLY, which makes it a way to call a function that returns its result in a variable, with no output and no fork involved.

Both are bash 5.3 only. Bash 5.2 — what Debian 13 ships — reports ${ bump; }: bad substitution for each one when the line runs, and the variable is empty. In a script that must run on 5.2, use printf -v (§14.12) or an output parameter (§9.6) for the same effect, which work on every bash from 4.3. The new forms are worth knowing because they are where the language is going, and worth avoiding in shared scripts until the bash they target is 5.3 everywhere.

Where the boundary really is

None of this means a script should avoid external commands. A single sed over a whole file does in one process what a shell loop would do in thousands of iterations, and §15.8 counts that too. The cost that matters is per item: one process per line, per file, per field. Text processing in the shell is the right choice for work on one value at a time — a variable, a path, an argument — and a tool is the right choice for work on a stream. Most slow scripts are the second job done with the first technique — text processing in the shell applied to a stream: a while read loop around a file that calls cut, sed or grep on every line.

15.2 Reading a File into a Variable

Reading a file into a variable is how a script takes in a small configuration value, a token, a template, a list of names. The obvious way is $(cat file). The shell's way is $(<file), which bash — and ksh, and zsh — treat as a special case: when a command substitution contains nothing but an input redirection, the shell reads the file itself and runs no program. §15.1 counted it: $(cat settings.conf) ran one program, and $(< settings.conf) ran none.

$(<file) is still a command substitution, and it has every property §4.4 gave them:

printf 'first line\nsecond line\n\n\n' > notes.txt
notes=$(< notes.txt)
printf '[%s]\n' "$notes"
printf '%s bytes on disk, %s in the variable\n' "$(wc -c < notes.txt | tr -d ' ')" "${#notes}"

missing=$(< no-such-file.txt)
echo "status $?, missing=[$missing]"

printf 'key\0value\n' > with-nul.bin
data=$(< with-nul.bin)
printf '%q\n' "$data"

[first line
second line]
25 bytes on disk, 22 in the variable
example.sh: line 6: no-such-file.txt: No such file or directory
status 1, missing=[]
example.sh: line 10: warning: command substitution: ignored null byte in input
keyvalue

The file had 25 bytes, ending in three newlines; the variable holds 22 characters, because command substitution strips every trailing newline, not just the last one. For a value that is a single line, that is what you want — a token file ends in a newline, and nobody wants it in the token. For content whose exact bytes matter, it is a silent change. A missing file is an ordinary redirection error: the message names the file, the variable is set to empty, and the status of the assignment is 1, so a script under set -e (§11.3) stops there — and one without it carries on with an empty value, which is the case to guard with || die. And a file containing a NUL byte loses it, with a warning on standard error: a shell variable is a C string and cannot hold a NUL (§14.9), so $(<file) is for text only.

Keeping every byte

When the trailing newlines matter — writing the content back out, comparing it, computing a checksum — there are three ways to read a file exactly:

printf 'first line\nsecond line\n\n\n' > notes.txt

IFS= read -r -d '' exact < notes.txt
echo "read -d '': status $?, ${#exact} characters"

sentinel=$(cat notes.txt; printf x)
sentinel=${sentinel%x}
echo "sentinel:   ${#sentinel} characters"

mapfile lines < notes.txt
printf -v joined '%s' "${lines[@]}"
echo "mapfile:    ${#lines[@]} elements, ${#joined} characters"

read -d '': status 1, 25 characters
sentinel:   25 characters
mapfile:    4 elements, 25 characters

IFS= read -r -d '' exact reads up to a NUL byte; a text file has none, so it reads the whole file, with nothing stripped because IFS is empty and nothing unescaped because of -r (§14.6). It returns status 1, because it reached end of file before the delimiter it was looking for — so under set -e it must be written IFS= read -r -d '' exact < file || true, or the script stops on a read that succeeded. The sentinel form appends an x inside the substitution, so the newlines are no longer trailing and survive, then removes it; it is portable to any POSIX shell and costs a cat. mapfile without -t keeps each line's newline in its element (§14.7), so joining the elements back together reproduces the file. All three agree on 25 characters, the size on disk.

The useless use of cat

The useless use of cat — UUOC, in the name it was given on Usenet in the 1990s — is cat used to feed a single file into a command that could have opened the file itself:

printf 'GET /a 200\nGET /b 404\nPOST /c 200\n' > access.log

# shellcheck disable=SC2002  # the useless cat is the point
cat access.log | grep -c ' 200$'
grep -c ' 200$' access.log
< access.log grep -c ' 200$'

2
2
2

All three print 2. The first starts cat and a pipe to do what grep's file argument does for free; the second hands grep the file name; the third redirects standard input and has the advantage of reading left to right like the pipeline it replaces, with the input first. The disable=SC2002 comment on the first line is there because ShellCheck reports this pattern as SC2002 — and ShellCheck 0.11 no longer reports it by default (measured: the same line is clean under 0.11), which is a fair summary of how much it matters when done once.

In a script, the UUOC matters for three reasons that are not about speed. cat file | while read … runs the loop in a subshell, and every variable set in it is lost (§8.8, §16). A command given the file name knows it: grep -l, wc and error messages can name the file, and a redirection lets the shell report a missing file before the command runs, with a clearer message and without starting it. And wc -l < file prints only the count, where wc -l file prints the count followed by the name — which is why the redirection is the form to use when the number goes into a variable. (On macOS, wc also pads the count with leading spaces; $(( $(wc -l < f) )) or tr -d ' ' normalises it.)

cat is not useless when it concatenates, which is its job, or when a function should read either named files or standard input, as every Unix filter does:

printf 'b\na\n' > one.txt
printf 'c\n'    > two.txt
sorted_lines() { cat -- "$@" | sort; }

sorted_lines one.txt two.txt | paste -sd' ' -
printf 'z\ny\n' | sorted_lines | paste -sd' ' -

a b c
y z

cat -- "$@" with two arguments concatenates the two files; with no arguments, "$@" expands to nothing and cat reads standard input — so sorted_lines works both ways with one line of code, the same convention sort, grep and awk follow. The -- makes a file name beginning with - safe (§15.11). This UUOC-that-isn't is the right way to write a filter function.

$(<file) reads the whole file into memory, and so does every form above. For a configuration value or a template that is exactly right. For a log file of unknown size it is not, and the job is a stream — a while read loop (§8.8) for per-line logic that needs the shell, or a tool (§15.8) for everything else.

15.3 Trimming, Prefixes, Suffixes and Paths

§5.4 taught the four trimming operators. This subsection uses them for the jobs scripts actually do, and each job has an edge case that the one-line version gets wrong.

Trimming whitespace

Trimming whitespace from both ends of a value — a line from a configuration file, a field from a form, the output of a command that pads — has no dedicated operator, and three good ways:

shopt -s extglob
s=$'  \t hello   world \n'

t=${s##+([[:space:]])}
t=${t%%+([[:space:]])}
printf 'extglob:  [%s]\n' "$t"

t=${s#"${s%%[![:space:]]*}"}
t=${t%"${t##*[![:space:]]}"}
printf 'portable: [%s]\n' "$t"
printf 'squeezed: [%s]\n' "${t//+([[:space:]])/ }"

read -r t <<< "$s"
printf 'read:     [%s]\n' "$t"
read -r t <<< $'  first line\nsecond line  '
printf 'read, two lines: [%s]\n' "$t"

extglob:  [hello   world]
portable: [hello   world]
squeezed: [hello world]
read:     [hello   world]
read, two lines: [first line]

The first uses extglob (§7.11): +([[:space:]]) is "one or more whitespace characters", and ## and %% remove the longest such run from the front and the back. The second is the portable idiom that §5's third exercise built into a trim function and explained step by step: the inner expansion computes exactly the leading (then the trailing) whitespace, and the outer one removes that string, quoted so that it is matched literally rather than as a pattern. It needs no shell option and works in any POSIX shell, which is why it is the one to copy into a library.

The third, read -r t <<< "$s", trims because reading into a variable trims IFS whitespace (§14.2). It is short and it is correct for a single line, and the last line shows its limit: read stops at the first newline, so a value that contains one is cut there, not trimmed. All three trim tabs and newlines as well as spaces — [[:space:]] includes them, and so does the default IFS — and none of them touches the whitespace in the middle, which is hello world in all three results. Trimming whitespace in the middle is a different job, squeezing, and the squeezed line shows it: ${t//+([[:space:]])/ } with extglob replaces every run of whitespace with one space.

Stripping a prefix, and quoting the pattern

Stripping a prefix is ${s#prefix}, and the thing to know is that prefix is a pattern, not a string. When the prefix comes from a variable, its glob characters are live unless the expansion is quoted:

title='[draft] Quarterly report'
prefix='[draft] '
# shellcheck disable=SC2295  # the unquoted pattern is the bug being shown
echo "unquoted: [${title#$prefix}]"
echo "quoted:   [${title#"$prefix"}]"

for f in report.tar.gz notes.txt archive.tar; do
  if [[ $f == *.tar.gz ]]; then
    echo "$f -> ${f%.tar.gz}"
  else
    echo "$f -> left alone"
  fi
done

unquoted: [[draft] Quarterly report]
quoted:   [Quarterly report]
report.tar.gz -> report
notes.txt -> left alone
archive.tar -> left alone

[draft] unquoted is a bracket expression — "one of d, r, a, f, t" — followed by a space, and it did not match the start of the title, so stripping the prefix did nothing at all. Quoted, as ${title#"$prefix"}, it is the literal string, and it was removed. The mirror bug is worse: a prefix like * unquoted matches everything, and ${s##$prefix} then empties the variable. ShellCheck reports the unquoted form as SC2295, and the rule is the same as for [[ == ]] in §7.5: quote a variable inside a pattern unless you mean it as a pattern.

The second half shows stripping a suffix conditionally. ${f%.tar.gz} on a name that does not end in .tar.gz returns the name unchanged, which is usually wrong for the caller — notes.txt would be "extracted" into a directory called notes.txt. Testing with [[ $f == *.tar.gz ]] first turns a silent no-op into a decision. When the operator's result is used as a new name, check that the prefix or suffix was there. And stripping a suffix held in a variable follows the quoting rule above: ${f%"$ext"}, never ${f%$ext}.

basename in the shell, and dirname in the shell

§5.9 measured ${p##*/} and ${p%/*} against basename and dirname and found them disagreeing on trailing slashes, on / and on a bare file name, and recommended the commands for paths that come from outside. The alternative, when a loop is long enough that the processes matter (§15.1), is to implement basename in the shell properly — following the algorithm POSIX specifies for the commands, rather than "cut at the last slash":

# basename and dirname in the shell, following the POSIX algorithm
base() {
  local p=$1
  if [[ $p != *[!/]* ]]; then            # empty, or nothing but slashes
    [[ -n $p ]] && p=/
    printf '%s\n' "$p"; return
  fi
  p=${p%"${p##*[!/]}"}                  # drop trailing slashes
  printf '%s\n' "${p##*/}"
}
dir() {
  local p=$1
  if [[ $p != *[!/]* ]]; then
    [[ -n $p ]] && p=/ || p=.
    printf '%s\n' "$p"; return
  fi
  p=${p%"${p##*[!/]}"}                  # drop trailing slashes
  [[ $p == */* ]] || { printf '.\n'; return; }
  p=${p%/*}                             # drop the last component
  p=${p%"${p##*[!/]}"}                  # and the slashes before it
  printf '%s\n' "${p:-/}"
}

printf '%-18s %-10s %-10s %s\n' input base dir 'same as the commands?'
for p in /var/log/app.log /var/log/ app.log / // /// /a a//b/ /usr//lib// .. ''; do
  b=$(base "$p") d=$(dir "$p")
  same=yes
  [[ $b == "$(basename -- "$p")" && $d == "$(dirname -- "$p")" ]] || same=NO
  printf '%-18s %-10s %-10s %s\n' "[$p]" "[$b]" "[$d]" "$same"
done

input              base       dir        same as the commands?
[/var/log/app.log] [app.log]  [/var/log] yes
[/var/log/]        [log]      [/var]     yes
[app.log]          [app.log]  [.]        yes
[/]                [/]        [/]        yes
[//]               [/]        [/]        yes
[///]              [/]        [/]        yes
[/a]               [a]        [/]        yes
[a//b/]            [b]        [a]        yes
[/usr//lib//]      [lib]      [/usr]     yes
[..]               [..]       [.]        yes
[]                 []         [.]        yes

Every row agrees with the real commands, on macOS and on GNU coreutils, including the inputs where the one-operator versions failed: a trailing slash (/var/log/ → log and /var), the root (/ → / and /), a bare name (app.log → directory .), a run of slashes (///, a//b/, /usr//lib//), and the empty string. The steps are POSIX's, in order. If the string is empty or all slashes, the answer is fixed. Otherwise remove trailing slashes; for the base name, take what follows the last slash. For dirname in the shell, a string with no slash left has directory .; otherwise remove the last component and then the slashes before it, and an empty result means the root.

p=${p%"${p##*[!/]}"} is the trailing-slash step, and it is the trimming idiom from above with [!/] in place of [![:space:]]: ${p##*[!/]} is the run of slashes at the end, and the outer expansion removes it. Two functions of eight lines each are more than ${p##*/}, and that is the trade: they are correct on every input, they cost no process, and they are what the "basename in the shell" row of the table in §15.12 means. The one input POSIX leaves to the implementation is exactly // (some systems treat a leading // as a distinct root); the functions treat it as a run of slashes and return /, which is what both platforms measured here do too.

Parameter expansion instead of sed

Most one-line sed commands in scripts are a substitution on a single value, and parameter expansion instead of sed does the same with no process and no regular expression to escape:

f=holiday.photo.JPG
echo "sed:       $(printf '%s\n' "$f" | sed 's/\.[^.]*$/.png/')"
echo "expansion: ${f%.*}.png"

v=v2.14.1-rc3
echo "sed:       $(printf '%s\n' "$v" | sed -e 's/^v//' -e 's/-.*//')"
v=${v#v}
echo "expansion: ${v%%-*}"

sed:       holiday.photo.png
expansion: holiday.photo.png
sed:       2.14.1
expansion: 2.14.1

s/\.[^.]*$/.png/ — replace the last extension — is ${f%.*}.png. s/^v// then s/-.*// — strip a leading v and everything from the first - — is two expansions, ${v#v} and ${v%%-*}. The expansion versions are shorter, have no quoting problem when the value contains / or & (both of which a sed replacement treats as syntax, §15.8), and run in the shell. The rule for choosing parameter expansion instead of sed is the one from §15.1: one value, use the expansion; a file or a stream, use sed — and when the expansion needs three steps to do what a single regular expression says clearly, use the sed and write a comment (§15.8).

15.4 Splitting a String into Fields, Properly

§5.5 left a promise: substitution has no notion of fields, and replacing , with a space and letting word splitting do the rest loses empty fields. §14.2 showed IFS=, read -r -a keeping an empty field in the middle and dropping a single trailing delimiter. Put together, splitting a string into an array has one more trap, and it is at the end of the string:

printf '%-9s %-6s %-12s %s\n' input read read+comma 'mapfile+comma'
for s in 'a,b,c' 'a,,c' 'a,b,' ',a' 'a,b,,' ''; do
  IFS=, read -r -a plain <<< "$s"
  IFS=, read -r -a fixed <<< "$s,"
  mapfile -t -d , mapped < <(printf '%s,' "$s")
  printf '%-9s %-6s %-12s %s\n' "[$s]" "${#plain[@]}" "${#fixed[@]}" "${#mapped[@]}"
done

input     read   read+comma   mapfile+comma
[a,b,c]   3      3            3
[a,,c]    3      3            3
[a,b,]    2      3            3
[,a]      2      2            2
[a,b,,]   3      4            4
[]        0      1            1

read -a gets the count wrong in exactly one case: a,b, is three fields — the third one empty — and read reports two, because a trailing non-whitespace delimiter terminates the last field instead of starting a new one (§14.2). The same rule gives a,b,, three fields rather than four. For CSV-like data, where web-1,, means "host, no alias, no address", that drops real fields, and every line with an empty last field shifts the column count.

The fix is to append one delimiter before splitting. Every field, including the last, is then terminated by a delimiter, so the "trailing delimiter" rule removes exactly the one that was added, and nothing that belonged to the data. The read+comma column is right on every row, and mapfile -d , with the delimiter appended by printf '%s,' gives the same counts. The one row that deserves thought is the empty string: with the delimiter appended it is one empty field, not zero fields. That is the right answer for a CSV cell and the wrong one for "a list of hosts, possibly empty", so a caller that means the second should test [[ -z $s ]] first.

A split function

Wrapped as a function with a nameref (§5.7), the rule becomes something to call rather than remember:

# split NAME SEPARATOR STRING: every field, empty ones included
split() {
  local -n _out=$1
  mapfile -t -d "$2" _out < <(printf '%s%s' "$3" "$2")
}
split fields , 'web-1,,10.0.0.5,'
declare -p fields
split fields , $'multi\nline,value'
declare -p fields

declare -a fields=([0]="web-1" [1]="" [2]="10.0.0.5" [3]="")
declare -a fields=([0]=$'multi\nline' [1]="value")

mapfile -d splits on any single byte, applies no whitespace rules, and — unlike read -a — does not stop at a newline, which is why the second call kept multi and line in one field. read -a reads one line:

s=$'one,two\nthree,four'
IFS=, read -r -a f <<< "$s"
declare -p f

declare -a f=([0]="one" [1]="two")

three,four never reached the array. §14.6's read -d '' removes that limit, but it then keeps the trailing newline of a here-string in the last field; mapfile -d with printf '%s%s' sends neither a newline nor anything else extra, which is why the function uses it.

The unquoted split

The shortest way to split is to set IFS and expand unquoted, arr=($s), and it is the one to recognise in other people's scripts and not write:

mkdir globdir && cd globdir || exit
touch alpha.log beta.log
s='*.log,readme'
IFS=,
# shellcheck disable=SC2206  # the unquoted split is the bug being shown
arr=($s)
unset IFS
declare -p arr
IFS=, read -r -a arr <<< "$s"
declare -p arr

declare -a arr=([0]="alpha.log" [1]="beta.log" [2]="readme")
declare -a arr=([0]="*.log" [1]="readme")

The unquoted expansion was split on commas, and then each field went through pathname expansion (§4.7): *.log matched two files in the directory and became two elements. The data decided how many elements there were. read -a does no globbing, and got *.log as a literal field. ShellCheck reports the unquoted form as SC2206; set -f around it would fix the globbing and leave the IFS save-and-restore, the empty-field loss and the trailing-delimiter rule, which is four things to get right instead of none.

Splitting on more than one character

IFS is a set of single characters, so IFS='=>' splits on = or >, never on the two-character string. A multi-character separator needs the trimming operators in a loop:

s='name=>ada=>role=>admin'
sep='=>'
parts=()
while [[ $s == *"$sep"* ]]; do
  parts+=("${s%%"$sep"*}")
  s=${s#*"$sep"}
done
parts+=("$s")
declare -p parts

declare -a parts=([0]="name" [1]="ada" [2]="role" [3]="admin")

${s%%"$sep"*} is everything before the first separator; ${s#*"$sep"} is everything after it; the loop moves one field at a time into the array until no separator is left, and the remainder is the last field. The separator is quoted in both patterns so it is matched literally, and the loop keeps empty fields, because an empty string before a separator is appended like any other. For a separator that is one byte, the function above is simpler; for one that is several, this is the tool.

Changing IFS temporarily

§3.7 gave three safe ways of changing IFS temporarily: a prefix assignment for one command, a subshell for several, and a saved value put back afterwards. The third has a trap that §3.7's example could not show, because it only appears when IFS was unset to begin with — which is what unset IFS leaves behind, and what a library function inherits from a caller that did it:

unset IFS
saved=$IFS
IFS=,
IFS=$saved
words='a b c'
# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # splitting is the point
set -- $words
echo "after a naive restore: $# field(s), IFS is ${IFS+set but empty}"

unset IFS
# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # splitting is the point
set -- $words
echo "after unset IFS:       $# field(s)"

after a naive restore: 1 field(s), IFS is set but empty
after unset IFS:       3 field(s)

saved=$IFS stored the empty string, because an unset variable expands to nothing. Restoring it did not unset IFS; it set it to empty — and an empty IFS means no splitting at all, so a b c became one field. An unset IFS behaves as the default, and an empty one turns splitting off; the save-and-restore turned one into the other. The robust form of changing IFS temporarily is not to save it at all, but to give the change a scope:

fields_of() {
  local IFS=$1
  local -a f
  read -r -a f <<< "$2"
  echo "${#f[@]} fields: ${f[*]}"
}
fields_of : 'a:b:c'
fields_of , 'x,y'
printf 'IFS after the calls: %q\n' "$IFS"

3 fields: a:b:c
2 fields: x,y
IFS after the calls: $' \t\n'

local IFS=$1 makes the change visible to the function and everything it calls, and bash restores the caller's value — set, empty or unset, whichever it was — when the function returns. That is the fourth safe pattern, and in a script built from functions (§9) it is the best one: the scope is visible in the code and cannot be forgotten on an early return.

Parameter expansion instead of cut

cut selects fields from a line, and inside a script it is usually applied to one value at a time — which is the §15.1 pattern of a process per item. read with a chosen IFS does the same job in the shell, and so does parameter expansion instead of cut for the first and last fields:

line='www:*:70:70:World Wide Web Server:/Library/WebServer:/usr/bin/false'

echo "cut:       $(cut -d: -f1,7 <<< "$line")"
IFS=: read -r user _ _ _ _ _ shell <<< "$line"
echo "read:      $user:$shell"
echo "expansion: ${line%%:*}:${line##*:}"

echo "cut on a line with no colon:    [$(cut -d: -f2 <<< 'no delimiter here')]"
echo "cut -s on a line with no colon: [$(cut -s -d: -f2 <<< 'no delimiter here')]"

cut:       www:/usr/bin/false
read:      www:/usr/bin/false
expansion: www:/usr/bin/false
cut on a line with no colon:    [no delimiter here]
cut -s on a line with no colon: []

All three produced www:/usr/bin/false. read with _ for the unwanted fields takes any set of fields in one statement; ${line%%:*} and ${line##*:} take the first and the last. The last two lines are a cut behaviour worth knowing even where cut is the right tool: given a line with no delimiter at all, cut -f2 prints the whole line, not an empty field — so a malformed line passes straight through as if it were field 2. -s suppresses such lines. IFS=: read -r a b on the same line would set a to the whole line and b to empty, which is at least an empty field where one was asked for. Parameter expansion instead of cut is the choice for one value; cut over a whole file, once, is still the fastest way to take a column (§15.8).

15.5 Searching and Replacing Inside a String

String contains

Whether a string contains another string is a pattern match, [[ $s == *"$sub"* ]], and the quotes around $sub are the whole of the correctness:

s='error: disk full on /dev/sda'
printf '%-8s %-9s %s\n' sub unquoted quoted
for sub in disk '[xyz]' '*' 'sd?' '/dev/'; do
  u=no q=no
  # shellcheck disable=SC2053  # the unquoted pattern is the bug being shown
  [[ $s == *$sub* ]] && u=yes
  [[ $s == *"$sub"* ]] && q=yes
  printf '%-8s %-9s %s\n' "$sub" "$u" "$q"
done

sub      unquoted  quoted
disk     yes       yes
[xyz]    no        no
*        yes       no
sd?      yes       no
/dev/    yes       yes

Unquoted, the right-hand side of == is a pattern (§7.5), so * "matches" every string and sd? matches any three characters starting sd — both said yes to a line that contains neither. [xyz] said no only because the line happens to contain none of those letters; with an x anywhere in the line it would have said yes. Quoted, each is a literal substring, and the answers are right. The string contains test is the most common place a variable lands inside a pattern, and ShellCheck's SC2053 flags the unquoted form.

In a script that must also run under sh, the portable string contains test is case, which has had pattern matching since the first Unix shells:

contains() {
  case $1 in
    *"$2"*) return 0 ;;
    *)      return 1 ;;
  esac
}
contains 'error: disk full' 'disk' && echo 'has disk'
contains 'error: disk full' '*'    || echo 'has no literal *'

has disk
has no literal *

The quoting rule is the same inside case: *"$2"* matches $2 literally. =~ works too ([[ $s =~ "$sub" ]], quoted, is a literal match), but it compiles a regular expression for a job that needs none, so == is the one to reach for.

Replacing all occurrences

Replacing all occurrences of a substring is ${s//old/new} (§5.5), and both halves need thought when they come from variables:

s='a.b.c'
old='.' new='::'
echo "${s//"$old"/"$new"}"
old='*'
echo "unquoted * : [${s//$old/-}]"
echo "quoted *   : [${s//"$old"/-}]"

a::b::c
unquoted * : [-]
quoted *   : [a.b.c]

The pattern half follows the rule above: $old unquoted as * matched the whole string and replaced it with a single -, while "$old" quoted matched only a literal *, of which there was none. The replacement half has a rule of its own that is new in bash 5.2:

s='host1 host2'
new='web&db'
echo "unquoted: ${s//host/$new}"
echo "quoted:   ${s//host/"$new"}"
shopt -u patsub_replacement
echo "option off, unquoted: ${s//host/$new}"

unquoted: webhostdb1 webhostdb2
quoted:   web&db1 web&db2
option off, unquoted: web&db1 web&db2

With the replacement unquoted, & in it was replaced by the text that matched — host — so web&db became webhostdb, like & in a sed replacement. This is the patsub_replacement shell option, which bash 5.2 added and turned on by default. Quoted, "$new" is literal. Turning the option off restores the old behaviour, but a library function cannot know what its caller has set, so the robust habit is the same as for patterns: quote the replacement whenever it is a variable. Every script written before 5.2 that did ${s//x/$y} with a $y that might contain & changed meaning when the shell was upgraded; §15.9 shows one such function.

Counting occurrences

With replacing all occurrences by nothing and a length, counting needs no loop:

csv='id,name,,email,phone'
commas=${csv//[!,]/}
echo "${#commas} commas, so $(( ${#commas} + 1 )) fields"
s='the cat sat on the mat with the hat'
rest=${s//the/}
echo "'the' appears $(( (${#s} - ${#rest}) / 3 )) times"

4 commas, so 5 fields
'the' appears 3 times

${csv//[!,]/} deletes every character that is not a comma, leaving only the commas, and its length is the count. For a substring longer than one character, delete every occurrence and divide the change in length by the substring's length: 35 characters minus 26 is 9, and 9 divided by 3 is 3. (The second count would also be fooled by theme and other; counting words, as opposed to substrings, is grep -ow's job, §15.8.)

String length: characters or bytes

${#s} is the string length in characters of the current locale, which is not the number of bytes:

w='José'
LC_ALL=C.UTF-8
echo "UTF-8 locale: ${#w} characters"
LC_ALL=C
echo "C locale:     ${#w} characters"
printf '%s' "$w" | wc -c | tr -d ' '

UTF-8 locale: 4 characters
C locale:     5 characters
5

In a UTF-8 locale é is one character, and José has a string length of 4; in the C locale each byte is a character, and it has 5, which is also what wc -c counts. A script that validates a field's length against a limit must decide which one the limit means — a database column declared as VARCHAR(4) counts characters, and a protocol field of four bytes counts bytes. The locale bash uses is whatever LC_ALL, LC_CTYPE or LANG say when the expansion runs, so a script that needs one answer on every machine must set it: local LC_ALL=C inside a function for bytes, and a UTF-8 locale explicitly for characters. (C.UTF-8 exists on current macOS and on Debian; a locale such as en_US.UTF-8 is present on macOS and must be generated on a minimal Linux system.) §14.12 showed the same split in printf's widths, which count bytes regardless of the locale.

Comparing without case

a='README.md' b='readme.MD'
[[ ${a,,} == "${b,,}" ]] && echo 'same name, ignoring case'
shopt -s nocasematch
[[ $a == "$b" ]] && echo 'same with nocasematch'
shopt -u nocasematch

same name, ignoring case
same with nocasematch

${a,,} lowercases a copy for the comparison (§5.6), and leaves the variables as they were; nocasematch (§7.12) makes == and case ignore case while it is set, and must be switched back off, because it affects every later match in the script. The expansion is the local and self-contained form.

15.6 Iterating over Characters

Iterating over characters is ${s:i:1} in a C-style for loop — substring expansion (§5.3) taking one character at a time:

w='café!'
LC_ALL=C.UTF-8
for (( i = 0; i < ${#w}; i++ )); do printf '[%s]' "${w:i:1}"; done; echo
LC_ALL=C
for (( i = 0; i < ${#w}; i++ )); do printf '[%q]' "${w:i:1}"; done; echo

[c][a][f][é][!]
[c][a][f][$'\303'][$'\251'][\!]

In a UTF-8 locale the loop saw five characters, and é was one of them. In the C locale it saw six, and é arrived as two separate bytes, \303 and \251, each printed by %q as the invalid fragment it is. The loop is only as correct as the locale it runs in, and — as §15.5 found for lengths — the locale is the environment's unless the script sets it.

read can also take one character at a time, and the difference between its two options shows up on whitespace and newlines:

printf 'a b\nc' | while IFS= read -r -n 1 c; do printf '<%q>' "$c"; done; echo
printf 'a b\nc' | while IFS= read -r -N 1 c; do printf '<%q>' "$c"; done; echo

<a><\ ><b><''><c>
<a><\ ><b><$'\n'><c>

With IFS= and -r, read -n 1 delivered the space (printed by %q as \) but returned an empty string for the newline, because -n still stops at the delimiter, and the delimiter is not stored. read -N 1 reads exactly one character, whatever it is, and delivered the newline. When iterating over characters from a stream, -N 1 is the option that sees all of them (§14.6).

What character loops are for

A character loop is useful when each character needs logic — a small tokeniser, a validator for an identifier, a checksum digit:

LC_ALL=C.UTF-8
s='mississippi'
declare -A freq=()
for (( i = 0; i < ${#s}; i++ )); do
  (( ++freq[${s:i:1}] ))
done
for c in "${!freq[@]}"; do printf '%s %d\n' "$c" "${freq[$c]}"; done | sort -k2,2nr -k1,1

i 4
s 4
p 2
m 1

A frequency count, keyed by character in an associative array (§6.8), then sorted by count and character so the output does not depend on the order of the keys (§6.7). The same answer with tools:

s='mississippi'
fold -w1 <<< "$s" | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr -k2,2 | head -2 |
  while read -r n c; do echo "$c $n"; done
printf '%s' "$s" | tr -cd 's' | wc -c | tr -d ' '

i 4
s 4
4

fold -w1 puts each character on its own line, and sort | uniq -c counts them; tr -cd s deletes everything except s and wc -c counts what is left. The tool versions start four or five processes in total whatever the length of the string, while the loop starts none — and the loop's cost grows with the length, because in a multi-byte locale ${s:i:1} has to walk the string from the start to find character i, so each step costs more than the one before. For a word, loop. For a file, use the tools. GNU fold counts bytes, and splits é into its two bytes, so for multi-byte text grep -o . is the portable way to put one character per line.

15.7 Sorting in the Shell

Bash has no sort builtin, and sorting in the shell means handing the elements to sort and reading the result back into an array — one process for the whole array, which is the right cost:

hosts=(web-10 db-2 web-9 cache-1 db-10)
mapfile -t sorted < <(printf '%s\n' "${hosts[@]}" | sort)
declare -p sorted
mapfile -t sorted < <(printf '%s\n' "${hosts[@]}" | sort -t- -k1,1 -k2,2n)
declare -p sorted
mapfile -t newest < <(printf '%s\n' 3 1 3 2 1 | sort -rnu)
declare -p newest

declare -a sorted=([0]="cache-1" [1]="db-10" [2]="db-2" [3]="web-10" [4]="web-9")
declare -a sorted=([0]="cache-1" [1]="db-2" [2]="db-10" [3]="web-9" [4]="web-10")
declare -a newest=([0]="3" [1]="2" [2]="1")

printf '%s\n' "${hosts[@]}" writes one element per line, sort sorts them, and mapfile -t reads them back (§14.7). The first sort is by character, so db-10 comes before db-2 and web-10 before web-9. The second tells sort the structure: split on - (-t-), sort by the first field as text (-k1,1) and then by the second as a number (-k2,2n). Each -k names a start and an end field; -k2 without the ,2 means "from field 2 to the end of the line", which is the classic mistake when a line has more fields after the key. The third shows -r (descending), -n (numeric) and -u (one of each), all in one call.

Two edge cases need handling in code rather than options. An empty array is not an empty input:

hosts=()
mapfile -t sorted < <(printf '%s\n' "${hosts[@]}" | sort)
echo "${#sorted[@]} element(s): ${sorted[*]@Q}"
(( ${#hosts[@]} )) && mapfile -t sorted < <(printf '%s\n' "${hosts[@]}" | sort) || sorted=()
echo "${#sorted[@]} element(s)"

1 element(s): ''
0 element(s)

printf '%s\n' with no arguments still runs the format once (§14.12), so sort received one empty line and the "sorted" array has one empty element. Guarding with (( ${#hosts[@]} )) avoids calling sort at all. And an element can contain a newline, which a newline-separated sort would split in two. The NUL-delimited forms are the answer, as they are everywhere in §14.9:

names=('b b' $'a\nnewline' 'c')
mapfile -t -d '' sorted < <(printf '%s\0' "${names[@]}" | sort -z)
declare -p sorted

declare -a sorted=([0]=$'a\nnewline' [1]="b b" [2]="c")

printf '%s\0', sort -z and mapfile -d '' keep each element whole. sort -z is supported by GNU coreutils and by macOS's sort, which covers the systems this course measures; §19 deals with what a strictly POSIX system can be relied on for.

Sort order is the locale's

Sorting in the shell has one trap that no option on the command line shows. sort, and bash's own [[ < ]], order strings by the collation rules of the current locale, and those rules differ between the C locale and every other one — and between systems:

words=(banana Apple _tmp apple 10 9 Banana)
c=$(printf '%s\n' "${words[@]}" | LC_ALL=C sort | paste -sd' ' -)
echo "C: $c"
en=$(printf '%s\n' "${words[@]}" | LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 sort | paste -sd' ' -)
[[ $c == "$en" ]] && echo 'en_US.UTF-8 agrees' || echo 'en_US.UTF-8 orders them differently'
LC_ALL=C
# shellcheck disable=SC2050  # comparing two literals is the point
[[ apple < Banana ]] && echo 'C: apple < Banana' || echo 'C: Banana < apple'

C: 10 9 Apple Banana _tmp apple banana
en_US.UTF-8 orders them differently
C: Banana < apple

In the C locale, the order is by byte value: digits, then uppercase, then _, then lowercase. en_US.UTF-8 orders the same seven words differently, and not the same way on every system. Measured for this section, macOS gives _tmp 10 9 apple Apple banana Banana and Debian's glibc gives 10 9 apple Apple banana Banana _tmp: both interleave the cases, and they disagree about where the underscore goes. [[ apple < Banana ]] answers according to the same rules, so it is false in the C locale and true in en_US.UTF-8. A script whose output feeds a comparison, a comm, a join or a checked-in file must pin the locale — LC_ALL=C sort — or two machines will disagree about the "same" sorted list. A script that shows a sorted list to a person can leave the locale alone, and that person will see their own locale's order.

Sorting versions

§7.4 compared two version numbers; sorting a list of them is the same problem at scale:

versions=(1.10.0 1.9.2 1.2.10 1.2.9 10.0.0)
printf '%s\n' "${versions[@]}" | sort | paste -sd' ' -
printf '%s\n' "${versions[@]}" | sort -t. -k1,1n -k2,2n -k3,3n | paste -sd' ' -
printf '%s\n' "${versions[@]}" | sort -V | paste -sd' ' -

1.10.0 1.2.10 1.2.9 1.9.2 10.0.0
1.2.9 1.2.10 1.9.2 1.10.0 10.0.0
1.2.9 1.2.10 1.9.2 1.10.0 10.0.0

A plain sort put 1.10.0 before 1.2.10 and 10.0.0 last only by luck. Splitting on . and sorting each field numerically is portable to any POSIX sort, and correct for purely numeric versions of a fixed number of parts. sort -V understands version strings in general, suffixes included; it is in GNU coreutils and in the sort that ships with current macOS, and its absence from POSIX and from some BSDs is why §7.4 called it a portability decision rather than a free one.

15.8 When to Reach for grep, sed and awk

The rule from §15.1 decides most cases: one value, use an expansion; a stream, use a tool, once. The mistake it prevents is calling a tool once per line, which is the most common reason a shell script is slow:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the labels passed to calls are literal text
# Spies: each logs its own name to calls.log, then runs the real tool
mkdir spy
for tool in sed cut; do
  printf '#!/bin/sh\necho %s >> "%s/calls.log"\nexec %s "$@"\n' \
    "$tool" "$PWD" "$(command -v "$tool")" > "spy/$tool"
  chmod +x "spy/$tool"
done
PATH=$PWD/spy:$PATH
: > calls.log
calls() {
  mapfile -t log < calls.log; : > calls.log
  printf '%-34s %d program(s) run\n' "$1" "${#log[@]}"
}

printf '%s\n' 'ada:admin' 'linus:dev' 'grace:admin' 'ken:dev' 'barbara:ops' > users.txt

# shellcheck disable=SC2034,SC2001  # a tool per line is the bug; only its cost is measured
while IFS= read -r line; do
  name=$(cut -d: -f1 <<< "$line")
  role=$(sed 's/.*://' <<< "$line")
done < users.txt
calls 'cut and sed per line'

# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # only the cost of splitting is measured
while IFS=: read -r name role; do :; done < users.txt
calls 'read splits each line'

sed 's/:.*//' users.txt > names.txt
calls 'one sed over the file'
echo "names: $(paste -sd' ' names.txt)"

cut and sed per line               10 program(s) run
read splits each line              0 program(s) run
one sed over the file              1 program(s) run
names: ada linus grace ken barbara

The first loop called cut and sed for each of five lines — ten programs, and ten thousand for a thousand-line file. The second did the same splitting with read and ran none. The third took the first column of the whole file with one sed. When a loop's body is only text manipulation, one of the other two forms always exists.

When to reach for awk is when the job has fields and state: sums, counts, grouping, conditions that compare fields, output formatted from several of them. When to reach for sed is when the job is substitution or selection on lines — s/// and addresses — with no arithmetic. And grep is for the question "which lines match", or just "does any line match". Put shortly, when to reach for sed is a question about lines and substitutions, and when to reach for awk is a question about fields and totals. The Linux course's §5.3–§5.5 teaches the three as tools; what follows is what changes when they are called from a script, where the pattern or the data comes from a variable, the exit status is a decision, and the program is code that someone will have to read.

grep in a script: the status has three values

printf 'port=8080\n' > app.conf
for f in app.conf other.conf; do
  grep -q '^port=' "$f"
  echo "$f: status $?"
done
if grep -q '^host=' other.conf 2>/dev/null; then
  echo 'has a host'
else
  echo 'no host line (or no file, or an error - if cannot tell which)'
fi

app.conf: status 0
grep: other.conf: No such file or directory
other.conf: status 2
no host line (or no file, or an error - if cannot tell which)

grep -q is silent and its status is the answer: 0 when a line matched, 1 when none did. But it has a third value, 2, for an error — here, a file that does not exist. if grep -q treats 2 exactly like 1, so a script that checks a configuration file for a setting concludes "not set" when the file is missing, is unreadable, or the pattern is invalid. When the difference matters, capture the status and decide on all three:

printf 'port=8080\n' > app.conf
has_setting() {
  local status=0
  grep -q -e "^$1=" -- "$2" || status=$?
  case $status in
    0) return 0 ;;
    1) return 1 ;;
    *) echo "has_setting: cannot read $2" >&2; exit 2 ;;
  esac
}
has_setting port app.conf && echo 'port is set'
has_setting host app.conf || echo 'host is not set'
has_setting host missing.conf
echo 'not reached'

port is set
host is not set
grep: missing.conf: No such file or directory
has_setting: cannot read missing.conf

|| status=$? captures the status without tripping set -e (§11.6), and the case turns 2 into a hard failure — status 2 for the whole script, as the run shows — while 0 and 1 remain answers. The pattern is passed with -e and the file after --, so neither can be mistaken for an option; that matters as soon as either comes from data.

Literal patterns, words and whole lines

printf '%s\n' 'price: 3.50' 'price: 3x50' '-v flag' 'total 350' 'total 3500' > data.txt
echo "regex 3.50:  $(grep -c '3.50' data.txt) line(s)"
echo "fixed 3.50:  $(grep -cF '3.50' data.txt) line(s)"
echo "plain 350:   $(grep -c '350' data.txt) line(s)"
echo "word 350:    $(grep -cw '350' data.txt) line(s)"
echo "whole line:  $(grep -cx 'total 350' data.txt) line(s)"
echo "pattern -v:  $(grep -c -e '-v' data.txt) line(s)"

regex 3.50:  2 line(s)
fixed 3.50:  1 line(s)
plain 350:   2 line(s)
word 350:    1 line(s)
whole line:  1 line(s)
pattern -v:  1 line(s)

A pattern built from data is a regular expression unless told otherwise, and . matches any character, so 3.50 also matched 3x50. -F makes the pattern a fixed string — the grep equivalent of quoting a variable inside [[ == ]] — and should be the default whenever the pattern is a value rather than a regex. -w matches only whole words, so 350 matched total 350 and not total 3500, where a plain grep 350 finds both. -x matches only whole lines, which is how to test for an exact entry in a list file. And a pattern that starts with - must be introduced with -e, or grep parses it as an option.

grep -E, grep -P, and the choice between them

§7.13 noted that bash's =~ uses POSIX extended regular expressions, with no \d, no \w, no \b and no lookaround, and promised this section would cover the choice when those are wanted. grep -E is the same dialect, and everything it lacks has a spelling in it:

printf '%s\n' 'id=42' 'id=abc' 'code 404 at 10:32' > mixed.txt
grep -E '^id=[[:digit:]]+$' mixed.txt
grep -oE '[[:digit:]]{3}' mixed.txt
grep -E '(^|[^[:alnum:]_])at([^[:alnum:]_]|$)' mixed.txt

id=42
404
code 404 at 10:32
