[[:digit:]] for \d, [[:digit:]]{3} with -o to print only the matched part, and (^|[^[:alnum:]_])at([^[:alnum:]_]|$) for \bat\b — clumsy, but portable, and in this case -w would do it. grep -P, for Perl-compatible regular expressions, is a GNU grep feature: on Debian it matched \d as expected, and on macOS, whose grep is BSD grep 2.6.0, it is rejected with grep: invalid option -- P and status 2. The choice is therefore: -E with POSIX classes for anything that must run on more than one system, -P only in scripts that declare GNU grep as a dependency, and — when a pattern genuinely needs lookaround or lazy quantifiers — a language whose regex engine is part of it, which is one of §21's signs that the script has outgrown the shell.

sed in a script: data in the replacement

A sed substitution built from a variable is a small program assembled from data, and the replacement half has three special characters:

printf 'url=https://old.example.com/api\n' > app.conf
new='new.example.com&beta'
sed "s/old.example.com/$new/" app.conf

# shellcheck disable=SC2001  # one bracket expression; an expansion would need eight
sed_escape() { printf '%s\n' "$1" | sed 's/[][\/.^$*&]/\\&/g'; }
old='old.example.com'
new='new.example.com/v2&beta'
sed "s/$(sed_escape "$old")/$(sed_escape "$new")/" app.conf

url=https://new.example.comold.example.combeta/api
url=https://new.example.com/v2&beta/api

& in the replacement means "the matched text", so new.example.com&beta inserted old.example.com in the middle. A / in the data would end the replacement early — sed reports an error, which macOS words as a bad flag in substitute command and GNU as an unknown option to the s command — and a \ would start an escape. On the pattern side, . in old.example.com matches any character. sed_escape puts a backslash before every character that is special on either side, and with both halves escaped the substitution is literal. It covers basic regular expressions and does not handle a newline in the data, which a sed replacement cannot contain unescaped; for arbitrary data, the replacement should come in through awk's ENVIRON (below) or — for one value — through a parameter expansion, which has none of these problems.

Editing a file in place with sed -i differs between GNU and BSD sed — GNU takes an optional suffix attached to the option, BSD requires a suffix argument, even an empty one — and Linux §5.4 has the details. A script that must run on both can avoid the flag entirely:

printf 'port=80\nhost=a\n' > app.conf
tmp=$(mktemp app.conf.XXXXXX) || exit
sed 's/^port=.*/port=8080/' app.conf > "$tmp" && mv -- "$tmp" app.conf
cat app.conf

port=8080
host=a

Write to a temporary file in the same directory, and replace the original only if sed succeeded. The && means a failed sed leaves the original untouched; creating the temporary file beside the original keeps the final mv a rename on the same filesystem, which replaces the file in a single step, so a reader never sees half a file. §12.4's cleanup trap removes the temporary file if the script is interrupted between the two.

awk in a script: data goes in through -v, or better, ENVIRON

awk has variables, so data can be passed in as data rather than spliced into the program. There are two ways, and they are not equivalent:

pattern='C:\temp\new'
awk -v p="$pattern" 'BEGIN { print "-v:      " p }'
P=$pattern awk 'BEGIN { print "ENVIRON: " ENVIRON["P"] }'

-v:      C:	emp
ew
ENVIRON: C:\temp\new

-v p=… processes escape sequences in the value, as if it were an awk string literal: \t became a tab and \n a newline, and C:\temp\new came out on two lines. That is specified by POSIX and done by every awk measured here (macOS's awk and Debian's mawk). ENVIRON["P"] reads the environment variable unchanged. For a value that might contain a backslash — a Windows path, a regular expression, a password — ENVIRON is the one to use; -v is fine for values the script controls, such as a number or a key from a fixed list.

What must never happen is to build the awk program itself from data:

printf 'ada:admin\nlinus:dev\n' > users.txt
role='nobody" || 1 || "'
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # building the program from data is the bug being shown
awk -F: '$2 == "'"$role"'" { print $1 }' users.txt
echo '---'
awk -F: -v role="$role" '$2 == role { print $1 }' users.txt
echo "(nothing matched, correctly)"

ada
linus
---
(nothing matched, correctly)

The role was spliced into the program text, where its quotes closed the string and its || 1 || became code, so the condition was true for every line and both users were printed — an injection into awk, of the same kind §18 covers for the shell itself. With -v role=… the value is compared as a string, nothing matched, and the output is correctly empty. The program stays in single quotes, and every value comes in through -v or ENVIRON.

A readable awk program

§5.9 set the limit for parameter expansion: when it needs three chained steps, or one you have to run to understand, write a sed or awk call with a comment instead. That call is only better if it is readable, which means formatting it as the program it is:

cat > access.log <<'EOF'
10.0.0.1 GET /index.html 200 5120
10.0.0.2 GET /missing 404 312
10.0.0.1 POST /api/login 200 890
10.0.0.3 GET /index.html 200 5120
10.0.0.2 GET /admin 403 150
EOF

# Requests and bytes per status code, most requests first.
# Fields: 1 client, 2 method, 3 path, 4 status, 5 bytes.
summarise() {
  awk '
    { requests[$4]++; bytes[$4] += $5 }       # tally by status
    END {
      for (s in requests)
        printf "%s %d %d\n", s, requests[s], bytes[s]
    }
  ' "$@" | sort -k2,2nr -k1,1
}
summarise access.log

200 3 11130
403 1 150
404 1 312

The awk program is laid out over several lines inside the single quotes, with a comment on what each part does, and the comment above the function records what the input fields are, which is the thing a reader cannot see from the code. Wrapping it in a function with "$@" as the input makes it a filter like any other — summarise access.log, or … | summarise. The sort is outside the awk program because for (s in requests) visits keys in an unspecified order, the same caveat as bash's associative arrays (§6.7).

The last awk idiom a script needs is the exit status. awk exits 0 unless told otherwise, so to use it as a test, set a flag and exit with it:

printf 'alpha 1\nbeta 2\n' > table.txt
has_key() { awk -v k="$1" '$1 == k { found = 1; exit } END { exit !found }' "$2"; }
has_key beta table.txt && echo 'beta: present'
has_key gamma table.txt || echo 'gamma: absent'

beta: present
gamma: absent

exit in the main block stops reading at the first match, and still runs the END block, where exit !found returns 0 when the key was found and 1 when it was not. That is a grep -q for a condition on a field.

15.9 Joining an Array

Joining an array — the inverse of §15.4 — has three forms, and §14.12 already taught the most general one: printf -v out '%s,' "${a[@]}" followed by ${out%,}. Here are the other two, and the traps in each:

hosts=(web-1 web-2 db-1)
(IFS=,; echo "${hosts[*]}")
joined=$(IFS=', '; echo "${hosts[*]}")
echo "$joined"

web-1,web-2,db-1
web-1,web-2,db-1

"${hosts[*]}" joins the elements with the first character of IFS (§3.5), so IFS=, gives a comma-separated list and IFS=', ' gives the same list, not a comma-and-space one — only the comma is used. It is the fastest join, and it is limited to a single-character separator. The subshell keeps the IFS change from escaping; inside a function, local IFS=, does the same (§15.4).

A join function

For a separator of any length, a function:

# join_by SEPARATOR [ITEM...]: prints the items with SEPARATOR between them
join_by() {
  local sep=$1 first=${2-}
  shift 2 || return 0
  printf '%s' "$first" "${@/#/"$sep"}"
}
join_by ', ' web-1 web-2 db-1; echo
join_by ' & ' salt pepper; echo
join_by ', ' only; echo
join_by ', '; echo "[empty]"

web-1, web-2, db-1
salt & pepper
only
[empty]

join_by prints the first item, then every remaining item with the separator put in front of it — ${@/#/"$sep"} applies a substitution to each positional parameter in turn, with /# anchoring the empty pattern at the start, so each one gains a prefix. It handles one item (no separator at all) and none (the shift 2 fails, and the function returns without printing). The quotes around "$sep" are not decoration. Here is the same function without them:

naive_join() { local sep=$1; shift; local first=$1; shift; printf '%s' "$first" "${@/#/$sep}"; echo; }
naive_join ', ' a b c
naive_join ' & ' salt pepper

a, b, c
salt  pepper

, survived, and & became two spaces: & in an unquoted replacement is the matched text (§15.5), and the matched text of an empty anchored pattern is empty. This version of join_by was a widely copied snippet, and it was correct until bash 5.2 turned patsub_replacement on — which is the general lesson of §15.5 made concrete.

The printf join, and a separator in the format

§14.12's join puts the separator in printf's format. That is safe for a constant separator and not for a variable one, because the format is code (§14.11):

hosts=(web-1 web-2 db-1)
sep=' | '
printf -v out "%s$sep" "${hosts[@]}"
echo "[${out%"$sep"}]"
sep=' %s '
# shellcheck disable=SC2059  # a separator in the format is the bug being shown
printf -v out "%s$sep" "${hosts[@]}"
echo "[${out%"$sep"}]"
printf -v out '%s' "${hosts[@]/%/"$sep"}"
echo "[${out%"$sep"}]"

[web-1 | web-2 | db-1]
[web-1 web-2 db-1  ]
[web-1 %s web-2 %s db-1]

The first join, with |, worked. The second separator, %s, contains a conversion; placed in the format, each round consumed two arguments, the output lost its separators, and the final trim found no %s to remove, leaving two trailing spaces. The third form keeps the separator out of the format: ${hosts[@]/%/"$sep"} appends it to every element, printf '%s' prints them, and the final ${out%"$sep"} — quoted, so the separator is matched literally — removes the last one. When joining an array with a separator that comes from a caller or from data, use the function or this form.

Joining the lines of a file

printf 'web-1\nweb-2\ndb-1\n' > hosts.txt
paste -sd, hosts.txt
mapfile -t h < hosts.txt
(IFS=,; echo "${h[*]}")

web-1,web-2,db-1
web-1,web-2,db-1

paste -sd, file joins all the lines of a file with commas in one process, and is the tool for a stream; mapfile followed by "${h[*]}" does it in the shell when the lines are wanted as an array anyway.

15.10 Maps as Data: Writing an Associative Array to a File

§5's fourth exercise snapshotted a map with ${map[@]@K} and eval, and left two caveats: the snapshot is in bash's hash order, so it is for restoring and never for comparing, and @K needs bash 5.1. The question behind it is how to keep an associative array beyond the life of the script that built it — to cache it, to hand it to another script, to reload it tomorrow. A map is data, and it belongs in a file format with a parser. The shell has three reasonable choices, and the choice depends on what the keys and values may contain.

Tab-separated lines

When no key contains a tab or a newline and no value contains a newline, one key<TAB>value line per entry is the simplest format that other tools can read:

declare -A port=([web]=8080 [db]=5432 [cache]=6379)

for k in "${!port[@]}"; do
  printf '%s\t%s\n' "$k" "${port[$k]}"
done | sort > ports.tsv
cat ports.tsv

declare -A loaded=()
while IFS=$'\t' read -r k v; do
  loaded[$k]=$v
done < ports.tsv
echo "db is on ${loaded[db]}, ${#loaded[@]} entries"

cache	6379
db	5432
web	8080
db is on 5432, 3 entries

The keys are written through sort, so the file does not depend on bash's hash order (§6.7) and two dumps of the same map are identical — which makes the file diffable, a property worth having whenever it is checked in or compared. Reading it back is a read loop with IFS=$'\t' and two names: the last name takes the rest of the line, so a value may contain tabs. The format's limits are the delimiters themselves:

declare -A note=([ada]=$'first line\nsecond line' [linus]=$'tab\there')
for k in "${!note[@]}"; do printf '%s\t%s\n' "$k" "${note[$k]}"; done | sort > notes.tsv
declare -A back=()
while IFS=$'\t' read -r k v; do back[$k]=$v; done < notes.tsv
mapfile -t keys < <(printf '%s\n' "${!back[@]}" | sort)
for k in "${keys[@]}"; do printf '%-12s = %q\n' "$k" "${back[$k]}"; done

ada          = first\ line
linus        = $'tab\there'
second line  = ''

linus's value kept its tab, as predicted. ada's value contained a newline, so the file had a line second line of its own, which was read back as a key with an empty value, and ada's value was cut to its first line. TSV is right for maps whose content the script controls — ports, counts, host names — and wrong for anything that holds free text.

NUL-delimited pairs

The only byte that cannot occur in a shell string is NUL (§14.9), so it is the only delimiter that works for every key and value:

declare -A note=([ada]=$'first line\nsecond line' [linus]=$'tab\there' [grace]='')
save_map() {
  local -n _m=$1
  local k
  for k in "${!_m[@]}"; do printf '%s\0%s\0' "$k" "${_m[$k]}"; done
}
load_map() {
  local -n _m=$1
  local k v
  _m=()
  # shellcheck disable=SC2004  # _m is associative; ShellCheck cannot see through the nameref
  while IFS= read -r -d '' k && IFS= read -r -d '' v; do _m[$k]=$v; done
}
save_map note > notes.map
declare -A back
load_map back < notes.map
for k in ada grace linus; do printf '%-6s = %q\n' "$k" "${back[$k]}"; done
echo "${#back[@]} entries, the same as ${#note[@]}"

ada    = $'first line\nsecond line'
grace  = ''
linus  = $'tab\there'
3 entries, the same as 3

save_map writes each key and each value followed by a NUL; load_map reads them back two at a time with read -r -d '', into a map named by the caller (both use a nameref, §5.7). The newline, the tab and the empty value all survived. The file is not human-readable, and it does not need to be: it is the shell's safe interchange format, and xargs -0, sort -z and find -print0 speak it. The one thing to add in real use is a check that the loop ended at a clean end of file — an odd number of fields means the file was truncated.

declare -p, and why it is code

declare -p writes a variable as the command that would recreate it, and source runs that command:

declare -A port=([web]=8080 [db]=5432)
declare -p port > ports.sh
cat ports.sh
unset port
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source ./ports.sh
echo "db is on ${port[db]}"

declare -A port=([db]="5432" [web]="8080" )
db is on 5432

It is the shortest round trip and it handles every value. It is also executing a file: whatever the file contains runs with the script's privileges, so it is safe only for a file that only this script can write, in a directory that only this user controls. A cache under ~/.cache qualifies; a file in /tmp, or one downloaded, does not. §18 returns to reading configuration without source.

JSON, when another program is the reader

When the reader is a program in another language, or a person with a JSON viewer, the format should be JSON, and it should be produced by a tool that understands JSON rather than by printf and hope:

declare -A note=([ada]=$'first line\nsecond "quoted"' [linus]='tab	here' [grace]='')
args=()
for k in "${!note[@]}"; do args+=(--arg "$k" "${note[$k]}"); done
jq -n -S '$ARGS.named' "${args[@]}" > notes.json
cat notes.json

declare -A back=()
while IFS= read -r -d '' k && IFS= read -r -d '' v; do
  back[$k]=$v
done < <(jq -j 'to_entries[] | .key, "\u0000", .value, "\u0000"' notes.json)
[[ ${back[ada]} == "${note[ada]}" ]] && echo "round trip: ${#back[@]} entries, values intact"

{
  "ada": "first line\nsecond \"quoted\"",
  "grace": "",
  "linus": "tab\there"
}
round trip: 3 entries, values intact

jq --arg NAME VALUE passes each value in as a string, and $ARGS.named is the object built from all of them — jq does the escaping, so the newline, the quotes and the tab came out as valid JSON. -S sorts the keys, for the same diffability as the TSV file. Reading back, jq -j prints each key and value followed by a NUL, which is the format the loop above already reads. jq 1.7.1 ships with current macOS as /usr/bin/jq; on Debian it is the jq package, which is not installed by default, so a script that uses it should check command -v jq and say what is missing. Building JSON with printf '{"%s": "%s"}' works until the first value contains a quote, and then produces invalid JSON or, worse, JSON that parses into something else.

15.11 File Names: Spaces, Newlines and a Leading Dash

A Unix file name may contain any byte except / and NUL. Spaces, tabs, newlines, a leading dash, glob characters, invalid UTF-8 — all legal, all possible in a directory a script is asked to process, and all ignored by the code that works on the author's own files. This subsection collects the rules for handling file names in a script; §8.4 covered looping over a glob and §14.9 NUL-delimited streams, and both are applied here.

Do not parse ls

ls formats names for a person. Its output separates names with newlines, which a name may contain, and it is word-split and globbed again when captured unquoted:

mkdir d && cd d || exit
touch -- -n.txt 'report 2024.txt' $'two\nlines.txt' plain.txt
echo "--- ls | wc -l"
# shellcheck disable=SC2012  # counting ls output is the bug being shown
ls | wc -l | tr -d ' '
echo "--- for f in \$(ls)"
# shellcheck disable=SC2045  # iterating over ls is the bug being shown
for f in $(ls); do printf '[%s]\n' "$f"; done

--- ls | wc -l
5
--- for f in $(ls)
[-n.txt]
[plain.txt]
[report]
[2024.txt]
[two]
[lines.txt]

Four files; ls | wc -l counted five, because one name contains a newline and ls, writing to a pipe, printed it raw. for f in $(ls) produced six "names", because the output was split on every space and newline — report 2024.txt became two words and two⏎lines.txt two more. Both are the reason for the rule do not parse ls: its output is for reading, not for splitting. On a terminal, ls may show ? in place of the newline, or quote the name; to a pipe, it prints the raw bytes; and the GNU and BSD versions differ in both, so no parser can undo it. ShellCheck reports SC2012 and SC2045 for the two forms.

The replacement is always a glob, which hands the names to the script as separate words with no parsing step:

mkdir d && cd d || exit
touch -- -n.txt 'report 2024.txt' $'two\nlines.txt' plain.txt
shopt -s nullglob
files=(*)
echo "${#files[@]} files"
for f in "${files[@]}"; do printf '%q\n' "$f"; done

4 files
-n.txt
plain.txt
report\ 2024.txt
$'two\nlines.txt'

files=(*) collects exactly four names, each whole, including the one with the newline. nullglob (§4.7) makes an empty directory an empty array instead of one literal *. %q prints each name unambiguously. For a recursive listing, or selection by type, size or age, find -print0 into mapfile -d '' or a read -d '' loop (§14.9) is the equivalent. That is the whole of do not parse ls: everything ls would be parsed for, a glob, a test or find can give directly.

Filenames with spaces, and filenames with newlines

Filenames with spaces are handled by quoting: every expansion of a variable holding a name is "$f", and every list of names is an array expanded as "${files[@]}" (§6.5). That is enough for filenames with spaces and tabs, and it costs nothing — the code that handles them is simply the correctly quoted code.

Filenames with newlines need one more rule: a list of names must never be newline-separated, because the separator can occur inside a name. Any pipeline that emits names one per line has this bug:

mkdir d && cd d || exit
touch -- -n.txt 'report 2024.txt' $'two\nlines.txt' plain.txt
echo "find | wc -l says $(find . -type f | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"
mapfile -t -d '' found < <(find . -type f -print0)
echo "find -print0 into an array says ${#found[@]}"

find | wc -l says 5
find -print0 into an array says 4

find | wc -l counted five lines for four files; find -print0 into an array counted four. Newline-separated lists of names — find's default output, ls, grep -l, a while read loop over paths — are correct only for names without newlines, and a script that processes names it did not create cannot assume that. The NUL-delimited forms are: find -print0, grep -l --null (the long option works on both GNU and macOS; the short -Z means something else to BSD grep), sort -z, xargs -0, read -d '', mapfile -d ''. Filenames with newlines are rare, and are exactly what someone crafting a hostile directory would use, which is why §18 returns to them.

The leading dash filename

A leading dash filename is a name that a command parses as an option:

mkdir d && cd d || exit
printf 'b\n' > -r
printf 'a\nc\n' > letters.txt
echo '--- sort *'
# shellcheck disable=SC2035  # the unprotected glob is the bug being shown
sort * | paste -sd' ' -
echo '--- sort -- *'
sort -- * | paste -sd' ' -
echo '--- sort ./*'
sort ./* | paste -sd' ' -

--- sort *
c a
--- sort -- *
a b c
--- sort ./*
a b c

The directory holds letters.txt and a file called -r. sort * expanded to sort -r letters.txt: the file name became the "reverse" option, so the output came out backwards, the file -r was never read, and nothing reported an error. With a name that is not a valid option the failure is at least loud — wc -c * with a file -n.txt fails with illegal option -- n on macOS and invalid option -- 'n' on GNU — but the silent case is the one that matters, and the classic of the kind is a file named -rf in a directory where someone runs rm *.

Two fixes, and they are both worth using. -- ends option parsing for any command that follows the POSIX guidelines (§13.5), so sort -- * read both files. And ./* makes every name start with ./, so no expanded name can begin with a dash, whatever the command's parser does — which is the more robust of the two, because it also protects commands that do not support -- and it is visible in every name a script later prints. For a leading dash filename that arrives as data rather than from a glob — an argument, a line in a list — -- is the only fix, which is why §13.1 made it one of the guidelines every script should honour.

What ls was being parsed for

Scripts parse ls for three things beyond the names: the newest file, a size, and a modification time. Each has a replacement that does not parse anything:

mkdir d && cd d || exit
printf 'old\n' > 'old log.txt'
touch -t 202601010000 'old log.txt'
printf 'newest, and a longer one\n' > $'new\nlog.txt'
printf 'mid\n' > -middle.txt
touch -t 202605010000 -- -middle.txt

newest=
for f in ./*; do
  [[ -z $newest || $f -nt $newest ]] && newest=$f
done
printf 'newest: %q\n' "${newest#./}"

for f in ./*; do
  printf '%4d bytes  %q\n' "$(wc -c < "$f")" "${f#./}"
done

newest: $'new\nlog.txt'
   4 bytes  -middle.txt
  25 bytes  $'new\nlog.txt'
   4 bytes  old\ log.txt

The newest file comes from -nt (§7.6), comparing modification times in a loop over the glob — which found the file with the newline in its name, where ls -t | head -1 would have printed its first half. A size comes from wc -c < "$f", which prints only a number because the name is not given to wc. (stat also gives sizes and times, but its options are entirely different between GNU, stat -c %s, and BSD, stat -f %z, which makes it a portability decision of its own, §19.) And the -middle.txt name went through the loop as ./-middle.txt, where no command could mistake it for an option; ${f#./} removes the prefix for display.

15.12 The Text Processing Table

Each job, the in-shell way, and the rule that is easiest to get wrong.

Job
In the shell, and the rule that is easiest to get wrong
Cost of a tool
An expansion is free, $(…) forks, an external command forks and starts a program; count per item, not per script (§15.1).
Output without a fork
${ cmd; } and ${| cmd; } — bash 5.3 only; printf -v on older versions (§15.1).
Read a file
$(<file) runs no program and strips every trailing newline; IFS= read -r -d '' keeps them and returns 1 (§15.2).
Feed a file to a command
cmd file or < file cmd; cat is for concatenating, and cat -- "$@" in a filter (§15.2).
Trim whitespace
${s#"${s%%[![:space:]]*}"} and its mirror, or extglob; read stops at a newline (§15.3).
Strip a prefix or suffix
${s#"$prefix"} — quote it, or it is a pattern; test that it was there (§15.3).
basename, dirname
Drop trailing slashes first; a bare name's directory is .; the root is / (§15.3).
Split into fields
Append one delimiter, then mapfile -d or read -a; never arr=($s) (§15.4).
Change IFS
local IFS in a function; a saved-and-restored unset IFS comes back empty (§15.4).
Contains
[[ $s == *"$sub"* ]] or case; the quotes make it literal (§15.5).
Replace all
${s//"$old"/"$new"}; since 5.2 an unquoted & in the replacement is the match (§15.5).
Length
${#s} counts characters of the locale; pin LC_ALL for bytes (§15.5).
Each character
${s:i:1} in a UTF-8 locale; read -N 1 from a stream (§15.6).
Sort an array
printf '%s\0' | sort -z | mapfile -d ''; guard the empty array; LC_ALL=C for a stable order (§15.7).
grep
Status 2 is an error, not "no match"; -F for data, -e and --; -P is GNU only (§15.8).
sed
Escape / & \ in a replacement from data; write to a temporary file instead of -i (§15.8).
awk
Values through ENVIRON (or -v, which processes escapes); never splice data into the program (§15.8).
Join
"${a[*]}" for one character; a function with a quoted "$sep" for more (§15.9).
Store a map
TSV for controlled content, NUL pairs for anything, jq for JSON; declare -p is code (§15.10).
File names
Do not parse ls; quote every name; NUL between names; ./* or -- against a leading dash (§15.11).

And the rule behind the table: text is data until something interprets it — a pattern, a regular expression, a format string, a sed replacement, an awk program, an unquoted expansion — and every trap in this section is a place where it was interpreted without anyone deciding it should be. Quote it, pass it as data, or delimit it with the one byte it cannot contain.

Exercises

1. A slug from a title. Write slugify TITLE, which prints a lowercase URL slug: letters and digits kept, every run of other characters turned into a single -, no - at either end, and untitled if nothing is left. Use only parameter expansion — no sed, no tr. What happens to Café au lait?

Solution 
slugify() {
  local s=${1,,}
  local LC_ALL=C
  s=${s//[^a-z0-9]/-}                  # everything else becomes a dash
  while [[ $s == *--* ]]; do s=${s//--/-}; done
  s=${s#-}; s=${s%-}
  printf '%s\n' "${s:-untitled}"
}
for t in 'Hello, World!' '  Q3 Report (FINAL)  ' 'bash 5.3 & you' '---' 'Café au lait'; do
  printf '%s -> %s\n' "[$t]" "$(slugify "$t")"
done

[Hello, World!] -> hello-world
[  Q3 Report (FINAL)  ] -> q3-report-final
[bash 5.3 & you] -> bash-5-3-you
[---] -> untitled
[Café au lait] -> caf-au-lait

${1,,} lowercases (§5.6). ${s//[^a-z0-9]/-} replaces every other character with a dash (§15.5), and the while loop squeezes runs of dashes by replacing -- with - until none is left — a fixed point, because one pass of // over --- leaves --. ${s#-} and ${s%-} strip one leading and one trailing dash (§15.3), which is enough after squeezing. ${s:-untitled} supplies the fallback for ---, which squeezes to - and then strips to nothing (§5.2).

local LC_ALL=C matters twice. [a-z] in a bracket expression is a range, and outside the C locale a range can include characters that are not ASCII letters, depending on the collation (§15.7); in the C locale it is exactly the 26 letters. And it makes the result deterministic on every machine. Its cost is what Café au lait shows: in the C locale é is two bytes, neither of them in [a-z0-9], so they became dashes and the word became caf. Transliterating accents (é to e) needs a table, or iconv -t ASCII//TRANSLIT, whose output was measured three ways for Café: Caf'e from macOS's libiconv, Cafe from glibc in a UTF-8 locale, and Caf? from glibc in the C locale. That is a case for a real library in another language, if slugs of non-English titles matter.

2. Ten programs for five lines. This script totals sales by region. It is correct, and it runs two programs per line of input. Rewrite it twice: once in pure bash, running no program for the loop, and once with a single awk.

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the labels passed to calls are literal text
# Spies: each logs its own name to calls.log, then runs the real tool
mkdir spy
for tool in cut awk; do
  printf '#!/bin/sh\necho %s >> "%s/calls.log"\nexec %s "$@"\n' \
    "$tool" "$PWD" "$(command -v "$tool")" > "spy/$tool"
  chmod +x "spy/$tool"
done
PATH=$PWD/spy:$PATH
: > calls.log
calls() {
  mapfile -t log < calls.log; : > calls.log
  printf '%-34s %d program(s) run\n' "$1" "${#log[@]}"
}

cat > sales.csv <<'EOF'
region,product,amount
north,widget,120
south,widget,80
north,gadget,200
south,gadget,50
north,widget,30
EOF

declare -A total=()
{
  read -r _
  while IFS= read -r line; do
    region=$(cut -d, -f1 <<< "$line")
    amount=$(cut -d, -f3 <<< "$line")
    (( total[$region] += amount ))
  done
} < sales.csv
for r in "${!total[@]}"; do echo "$r ${total[$r]}"; done | sort
calls 'the loop above'
Solution

The original, counted with the spies of §15.1:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the labels passed to calls are literal text
# Spies: each logs its own name to calls.log, then runs the real tool
mkdir spy
for tool in cut awk; do
  printf '#!/bin/sh\necho %s >> "%s/calls.log"\nexec %s "$@"\n' \
    "$tool" "$PWD" "$(command -v "$tool")" > "spy/$tool"
  chmod +x "spy/$tool"
done
PATH=$PWD/spy:$PATH
: > calls.log
calls() {
  mapfile -t log < calls.log; : > calls.log
  printf '%-34s %d program(s) run\n' "$1" "${#log[@]}"
}

cat > sales.csv <<'EOF'
region,product,amount
north,widget,120
south,widget,80
north,gadget,200
south,gadget,50
north,widget,30
EOF

declare -A total=()
{
  read -r _
  while IFS= read -r line; do
    region=$(cut -d, -f1 <<< "$line")
    amount=$(cut -d, -f3 <<< "$line")
    (( total[$region] += amount ))
  done
} < sales.csv
for r in "${!total[@]}"; do echo "$r ${total[$r]}"; done | sort
calls 'the loop above'

north 350
south 130
the loop above                     10 program(s) run

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the labels passed to calls are literal text
# Spies: each logs its own name to calls.log, then runs the real tool
mkdir spy
for tool in cut awk; do
  printf '#!/bin/sh\necho %s >> "%s/calls.log"\nexec %s "$@"\n' \
    "$tool" "$PWD" "$(command -v "$tool")" > "spy/$tool"
  chmod +x "spy/$tool"
done
PATH=$PWD/spy:$PATH
: > calls.log
calls() {
  mapfile -t log < calls.log; : > calls.log
  printf '%-34s %d program(s) run\n' "$1" "${#log[@]}"
}

cat > sales.csv <<'EOF'
region,product,amount
north,widget,120
south,widget,80
north,gadget,200
south,gadget,50
north,widget,30
EOF

# Pure bash: read splits each line, arithmetic accumulates
declare -A total=()
{
  read -r _
  while IFS=, read -r region _ amount; do
    (( total[$region] += amount ))
  done
} < sales.csv
for r in "${!total[@]}"; do echo "$r ${total[$r]}"; done | sort
calls 'read and arithmetic'

# One awk: NR > 1 skips the header
awk -F, 'NR > 1 { total[$1] += $3 } END { for (r in total) print r, total[r] }' sales.csv | sort
calls 'one awk'

north 350
south 130
read and arithmetic                0 program(s) run
north 350
south 130
one awk                            1 program(s) run

The pure-bash version keeps the structure and the arithmetic — (( total[$region] += amount )), where an unset element counts as 0 — and replaces the two cut calls with read splitting each line on commas, with _ for the unwanted product (§15.4). It runs no programs for the loop. The awk version does the whole job, header skipping included (NR > 1), in one program. Both print the same totals as the original.

Which to prefer depends on the size. For a file of a few hundred lines, the bash loop is fine and keeps everything in one language. For a file of a million lines, the awk version is the right one: bash's read reads a pipe or file in small pieces (§14.7 measured it), and awk's loop is compiled. In both rewrites the sort is there only because both bash's associative arrays and awk's for (r in total) visit keys in an unspecified order (§6.7).

3. The newest log without ls. Write newest FILE..., which prints the most recently modified regular file among its arguments, so that newest ./*.log works for any file names — spaces, newlines, a leading dash — and returns status 1 when there are none. How should it deliver the name to the caller?

Solution 
mkdir logs && cd logs || exit
printf 'a\n' > 'app 1.log';        touch -t 202601010000 'app 1.log'
printf 'b\n' > $'app\n2.log';      touch -t 202603010000 $'app\n2.log'
printf 'c\n' > -app3.log;          touch -t 202602010000 -- -app3.log
printf 'd\n' > notes.txt

# newest PATTERN...: the most recently modified of the given files, NUL-terminated
newest() {
  local f best=
  for f; do
    [[ -f $f ]] || continue
    [[ -z $best || $f -nt $best ]] && best=$f
  done
  [[ -n $best ]] || return 1
  printf '%s\0' "$best"
}

IFS= read -r -d '' latest < <(newest ./*.log) && printf 'newest log: %q\n' "${latest#./}"
IFS= read -r -d '' latest < <(newest ./*.none) || echo 'no match: status 1'

newest log: $'app\n2.log'
no match: status 1

newest compares modification times with -nt (§7.6) and skips anything that is not a regular file, which also skips the unexpanded pattern ./*.none when nothing matched (nullglob would be the alternative). It delivers the name NUL-terminated, because that is the only terminator a file name cannot contain, and the caller reads it with IFS= read -r -d '' (§14.9) — which got app⏎2.log whole. A newline-terminated name read back with $(newest …) would have handled this case too, but would silently strip a trailing newline from a name that ended in one (§15.2), and a NUL cannot be captured by $(…) at all (§14.9). The caller passes ./*.log, so a name like -app3.log arrives as ./-app3.log (§15.11), and ${latest#./} removes the prefix only for display. The status of the read is the status of the lookup: when newest prints nothing, read finds end of file and returns 1.

4. An INI file into a map. Write ini_load FILE MAP, which reads an INI file into an associative array with keys section.key (keys before any section have no prefix). Trim whitespace around keys and values; skip blank lines and lines starting with # or ;, even when indented; treat everything after the first = as the value; and report a line that is none of these with its line number, returning 1.

Solution 
cat > app.ini <<'EOF'
; global settings
name = demo app

[server]
host = 0.0.0.0
port=8080
  # indented comment
[database]
url = postgres://db:5432/app
pool = 5 ; not a comment - values keep everything
EOF

# ini_load FILE MAP: fills MAP with "section.key" -> value
ini_load() {
  local -n _ini=$2
  local line section='' key value n=0
  while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n $line ]]; do
    (( ++n ))
    line=${line#"${line%%[![:space:]]*}"}       # trim leading whitespace
    line=${line%"${line##*[![:space:]]}"}       # trim trailing whitespace
    case $line in
      '' | '#'* | ';'*) continue ;;
      '['*']')  section=${line:1:${#line}-2}; continue ;;
      *=*)      ;;
      *)        echo "$1:$n: not a setting: $line" >&2; return 1 ;;
    esac
    key=${line%%=*}   key=${key%"${key##*[![:space:]]}"}
    value=${line#*=}  value=${value#"${value%%[![:space:]]*}"}
    _ini[${section:+$section.}$key]=$value
  done < "$1"
}

declare -A cfg=()
ini_load app.ini cfg
for k in $(printf '%s\n' "${!cfg[@]}" | sort); do printf '%-14s = [%s]\n' "$k" "${cfg[$k]}"; done

database.pool  = [5 ; not a comment - values keep everything]
database.url   = [postgres://db:5432/app]
name           = [demo app]
server.host    = [0.0.0.0]
server.port    = [8080]

Each line is trimmed at both ends with the portable idiom (§15.3) — which also removes the trailing spaces after the database URL and the indentation of the comment — and then classified by a case on its shape. [server] sets the section, with ${line:1:${#line}-2} taking everything between the brackets (§5.3). For a setting, ${line%%=*} is the key and ${line#*=} the value, split at the first =, so a value may contain = signs; the key has its trailing whitespace and the value its leading whitespace removed. ${section:+$section.} adds the prefix only when there is a section (§5.2). The value of pool keeps its ; not a comment part, because INI has no single standard for inline comments and a value containing ; — a connection string, a password — is more common than a comment after one. The loop uses the || [[ -n $line ]] form, so a file without a final newline loses nothing (§14.3), and the map is filled through a nameref (§5.7).

A malformed line is reported with the file name and line number, in the format compilers use, and the function returns 1:

printf '[server]\nport = 80\nthis line is wrong\n' > bad.ini
ini_load() {
  local -n _ini=$2
  local line section='' key value n=0
  while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n $line ]]; do
    (( ++n ))
    line=${line#"${line%%[![:space:]]*}"}
    line=${line%"${line##*[![:space:]]}"}
    case $line in
      '' | '#'* | ';'*) continue ;;
      '['*']')  section=${line:1:${#line}-2}; continue ;;
      *=*)      ;;
      *)        echo "$1:$n: not a setting: $line" >&2; return 1 ;;
    esac
    key=${line%%=*}   key=${key%"${key##*[![:space:]]}"}
    value=${line#*=}  value=${value#"${value%%[![:space:]]*}"}
    _ini[${section:+$section.}$key]=$value
  done < "$1"
}
declare -A cfg=()
ini_load bad.ini cfg || echo "status $?, ${#cfg[@]} setting(s) loaded before the error"

bad.ini:3: not a setting: this line is wrong
status 1, 1 setting(s) loaded before the error

The loader never executes anything from the file, which is the point of writing it: source app.ini would have run each line as a command (§15.10, §18).

SECTION 16

Processes, Subshells and the Environment

Every shell script is a program that starts other programs, and most of the surprises in shell scripting come from one fact about how it does that: a new process begins as a copy of the one that started it, and nothing it does afterwards is copied back. A variable set inside a loop at the end of a pipeline is gone when the loop ends. A cd inside $(…) changes nothing. An array exported to a child arrives as nothing at all. A function the script defined is unknown to the bash -c it runs. None of these is a bug in bash; each is a precise consequence of which process a piece of code runs in, and what that process was given when it started.

This section is about that boundary. It starts with what the shell carries around — the command execution environment — and what an external program is handed from it when it starts (§16.1). It then follows the two system calls behind every command, fork() and exec (§16.2); the difference between a shell variable and an environment variable, and the builtins that move a name from one to the other (§16.3); what the environment actually is — a list of strings — and what that makes impossible (§16.4). Then subshells: what they are, what they inherit, and how to tell you are in one (§16.5); the three places bash creates one without being asked — pipelines, $(…) and <(…) (§16.6); the shell's options, which are part of the environment a subshell inherits, and how to change them without leaking the change (§16.7); the variable lost in a pipeline, which is the most reported problem in all of shell scripting, and its four fixes (§16.8); and process substitution set against a pipeline, including the exit status it hides (§16.9).

The editorial boundary: §9 owns functions and local, and §9.6 the ways a function returns data. §10 owns exec with only redirections, which changes the current shell's descriptors and replaces nothing. §12 owns traps and signals. §17 owns background jobs, wait in general, process groups and locking. This section uses each of them where the boundary between processes is the point.

Every example was measured under bash 5.3 on macOS and bash 5.2 on Debian, and the two agree byte for byte except for one diagnostic whose wording 5.3 extended, labelled where it appears (§16.7). Two claims about interactive shells — what exit does with jobs running — were measured on a real terminal rather than in a script, and are reported in the prose. No example prints a process ID: they differ on every run, so every example compares them instead, and the comparison is the claim.

16.1 The Command Execution Environment

A running shell carries a set of state around with it, and the bash manual gives the whole set a name: the command execution environment. It is longer than people expect:

  • the open files, meaning every file descriptor the shell has, including those opened with exec (§10);
  • the current working directory, set by cd;
  • the file creation mask, set by umask;
  • the traps, set by trap (§12);
  • the shell parameters: every variable, whether exported or not, and the positional parameters;
  • the functions defined so far;
  • the options set with set and shopt (§16.7);
  • the aliases;
  • and a handful of process properties: $$, $PPID, the jobs the shell is tracking.

The command execution environment matters because of what happens when the shell runs something. It runs one of two very different kinds of thing, and each receives a different part of that list. A subshell (§16.5) gets a copy of all of it. An external program — ls, grep, another bash — gets only a small part, because it is a new program with its own memory, and the only things that cross into it are the ones the operating system knows how to carry.

What a child inherits

The first example sets one item of each kind, then starts a separate bash program and asks it what it can see:

# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # greeting is set to show that a child does not see it
# What a child program is given, and what it is not
umask 027
greeting=hello                      # a shell variable
export GREETING=exported            # an environment variable
f() { :; }                          # a function
trap 'echo caught' USR1             # a caught signal
trap '' USR2                        # an ignored signal
exec 3> fd3.txt                     # an open file descriptor
cd /tmp || exit

bash -c '
  echo "umask:      $(umask)"
  echo "directory:  $PWD"
  echo "greeting:   ${greeting-<not set>}"
  echo "GREETING:   ${GREETING-<not set>}"
  echo "function f: $(type -t f || echo "<not defined>")"
  echo "traps:      $(trap -p | tr "\n" " ")"
  { true >&3; } 2>/dev/null && echo "descriptor 3: open"
'

umask:      0027
directory:  /tmp
greeting:   <not set>
GREETING:   exported
function f: <not defined>
traps:      trap -- '' SIGUSR2 
descriptor 3: open

That output is the whole answer to what a child inherits, and it is worth reading line by line:

  • The umask arrived: 0027. It is a property of the process, and every new process starts with its parent's.
  • The working directory arrived: /tmp. So did the open descriptor 3 — a child program starts with every descriptor its parent had open, which is why exec 3> file before running a command lets the command write to it.
  • GREETING arrived and greeting did not. The difference is the export: only exported variables are passed on, as the child's environment (§16.3).
  • The function did not arrive. A function lives in the shell's memory, and the new program has its own. type -t f found nothing.
  • The ignored signal arrived and the caught one did not. trap '' USR2 asks the operating system to discard USR2, and that setting survives into a new program. trap 'echo caught' USR1 installs a handler, which is code in the shell's memory; the new program cannot run code it does not have, so its USR1 is back to the default. §12.8 used the same rule to explain why a background job in a script ignores SIGINT.

Run the same list in a subshell instead of a new program, and every line comes through, because a subshell is a copy of the shell rather than a new program:

# The same list, seen from a subshell instead of a child program
umask 027
greeting=hello
f() { echo "f ran"; }
exec 3> fd3.txt
cd /tmp || exit

(
  echo "umask:      $(umask)"
  echo "directory:  $PWD"
  echo "greeting:   ${greeting-<not set>}"
  echo "function f: $(f)"
  { true >&3; } 2>/dev/null && echo "descriptor 3: open"
)

umask:      0027
directory:  /tmp
greeting:   hello
function f: f ran
descriptor 3: open

The non-exported greeting and the function f are both there. That contrast — a subshell gets everything, a child program gets what the operating system carries — is the most useful single fact in this section, and §16.5 and §16.6 develop it. The one exception inside a subshell is the traps, which is subtle enough to have its own example in §16.5.

The practical rule for what a child inherits: if a program the script runs needs a value, export it or pass it as an argument; if it needs a function, pass the function's work as a script or use export -f (§16.4); and if it must not inherit something — a secret in an environment variable, a descriptor holding a lock — remove it for that command (env -u, §16.3, or 3>&-, §10).

16.2 fork() and exec: How a Command Runs

Every external command starts the same way, in two steps, and the two steps are two system calls.

fork() makes a copy of the running process. The copy — the child process — has a new process ID, but otherwise holds the same memory, the same open files, the same working directory: at that moment it is a second bash, one line into running the command. exec (strictly, one of the execve family) then replaces the program in a process with a different one. The child calls it with /bin/ls, say, and from that point the process is ls: bash's memory, its variables and its functions are gone, and only what the operating system carries across an exec remains — the environment, the open descriptors, the directory, the umask, the ignored signals. That is exactly the list §16.1 measured, and now it has a reason: the list is what survives exec. Meanwhile the parent, the original shell, waits for the child to finish and collects its exit status.

So a command costs a fork() and an exec, and a subshell costs only the fork() — which is why a subshell sees everything and a child program does not. That subshell cost is smaller than a program's, and still a whole process: §15.1 counted it in a loop. The child process is a different process from the script, and its parent is the script:

# Every external command runs in a new process, whose parent is this script
bash -c '
  echo "the child is a different process: $([[ $$ != "$1" ]] && echo yes)"
  echo "its parent is the script:        $([[ $PPID == "$1" ]] && echo yes)"
' _ "$$"

the child is a different process: yes
its parent is the script:        yes

The child receives the script's $$ as an argument (_ "$$" makes it $1) and compares: its own $$ is different, and its $PPID — the parent's process ID — is the script's.

The exec builtin: replacing the shell process

The exec builtin runs the second step without the first. exec command does not fork: it replaces the shell itself with the command, in the same process, and the shell is gone. Replacing the shell process has two consequences, and the example shows both:

# exec does not start a child: the program takes over this process
echo "before exec"
exec bash -c '
  echo "same process as the script: $([[ $$ == "$1" ]] && echo yes)"
  exit 7
' _ "$$"
echo "this line is never reached"

before exec
same process as the script: yes

The new program has the same process ID as the script — it is the script's process now. And the last line of the script never ran, because there was no script left to run it; the exit status of the whole run is the new program's, 7. Everything after an exec that succeeds is dead code.

That makes exec the right last line of a wrapper script: a script whose job is to set up an environment and then start the real program. Without exec, the wrapper stays alive as a parent that does nothing but wait; with it, the program takes over the wrapper's process:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # $report is expanded by the child bash, not here
# A wrapper that sets up the environment, then gets out of the way
printf '%s\n' '#!/usr/bin/env bash' 'export APP_MODE=production' 'exec "$@"' > with-exec.sh
printf '%s\n' '#!/usr/bin/env bash' 'export APP_MODE=production' '"$@"' > without-exec.sh
chmod +x with-exec.sh without-exec.sh

report='echo "  APP_MODE=$APP_MODE; parent is the caller: $([[ $PPID == "$1" ]] && echo yes || echo no)"'
echo "with exec:"
./with-exec.sh bash -c "$report" _ "$$"
echo "without exec:"
./without-exec.sh bash -c "$report" _ "$$"

with exec:
  APP_MODE=production; parent is the caller: yes
without exec:
  APP_MODE=production; parent is the caller: no

In both versions APP_MODE reached the program, because it was exported before the program started. The difference is the process tree. With exec, the program's parent is the caller — the wrapper is gone. Without it, the wrapper is still there, in between. That matters in practice for three reasons. A signal sent to the wrapper's PID — by a service manager, a container runtime, or Ctrl-C's kill to the process group — reaches the real program directly, instead of a bash that may or may not pass it on (§12). The exit status the caller sees is the program's own, with no chance of a wrapper line that changes it. And one fewer process is running. Container entrypoint scripts end with exec "$@" for exactly this reason: the program becomes the container's main process and receives its stop signal.

exec in a subshell replaces the subshell, not the script — ( exec cmd ) is a way to run a command in a child without a second fork — and exec with only redirections (exec 3> file, exec > log) replaces nothing at all: it changes the current shell's descriptors, which is §10's subject.

When exec fails

If the program cannot be found or run, there is no new program to take over the process, and a non-interactive shell's response is severe: it exits.

# If the program cannot be found, a non-interactive shell exits
shopt -s execfail
exec no-such-program
echo "with execfail, the script carries on (status $?)"
shopt -u execfail
exec no-such-program
echo "this line is never reached"

example.sh: line 3: exec: no-such-program: not found
with execfail, the script carries on (status 127)
example.sh: line 6: exec: no-such-program: not found

With shopt -s execfail, the failed exec reported not found and the script carried on with status 127, so the script can fall back to something else. With the option off — the default — the same failure ended the script on the spot, with status 127 and the last line unreached. An interactive shell does not exit on a failed exec; a script does. For a wrapper whose exec is its last line that makes no difference, but a script that tries exec and means to handle failure needs execfail, or a command -v test first.

exec -c and exec -a

exec takes two options worth knowing. exec -c runs the command with an empty environment, which is a quick way to prove a program does not depend on anything it happened to inherit:

# exec -c runs the program with an empty environment
export TOKEN=secret
( exec -c bash -c 'echo "TOKEN=${TOKEN-<not set>}"' )
echo "the script still has it: TOKEN=$TOKEN"

TOKEN=<not set>
the script still has it: TOKEN=secret

The exec ran inside ( … ), so it replaced a subshell and the script carried on with its own TOKEN intact. exec -a name sets the name the new program sees as its argv[0] — what ps shows (measured on both systems: ( exec -a renamed sleep 2 ) & appears in ps as renamed 2), and what a program like busybox reads to decide which tool to be. Both have more general equivalents: env -i for the empty environment (§16.3), and nothing else for argv[0].

16.3 Shell Variables and Environment Variables

A variable in bash is one of two kinds, and the difference is exactly the difference §16.1 measured. A shell variable exists only in the shell's own memory: it is visible to the shell, to its functions and to its subshells, and to nothing else. An environment variable is a shell variable that has been marked for export, and is therefore copied into the environment of every program the shell starts. Shell variable versus environment variable is not a difference in the value, or the syntax, or the name — it is one attribute, the -x attribute, and the export builtin sets it.

The distinction between a shell variable versus environment variable is visible in declare -p, which prints the attribute:

show() { bash -c 'echo "  child sees: level=${level-<not set>}"'; }

level=debug
echo "a shell variable:"; show
export level
echo "after export:"; show
declare -p level
export -n level
echo "after export -n:"; show
declare -p level

a shell variable:
  child sees: level=<not set>
after export:
  child sees: level=debug
declare -x level="debug"
after export -n:
  child sees: level=<not set>
declare -- level="debug"

level=debug made a shell variable, and the child saw nothing. After export level, the child saw debug, and declare -p printed declare -x, where x is the export attribute. export -n level removed the attribute again: the variable is still set in the script (declare --), and the child no longer sees it. An exported variable is therefore not a copy stored somewhere else — it is the same variable, with the attribute that says "include me when starting a program". Change its value later and the next child sees the new value.

The ways to create an exported variable are all equivalent: export name=value, export name after an assignment, and declare -x name=value. The export builtin also takes -p, which lists every exported variable as a declare -x line, and -f, which exports functions (§16.4). By convention, environment variables are named in UPPERCASE and shell variables in lowercase, and the convention protects something: the names a script uses for its own purposes cannot then collide with PATH, HOME, IFS or any other variable the system gives meaning to.

The variable assignment prefix

Setting a variable for one command only does not need export at all. A variable assignment prefix — NAME=value written in front of a command — puts the variable in that command's environment and nowhere else:

# NAME=value in front of a command: for that command only
level=info
level=debug bash -c 'echo "child: level=$level"'
echo "script: level=$level"

TZ=UTC0 date -d @0 +%H:%M 2>/dev/null || TZ=UTC0 date -r 0 +%H:%M

child: level=debug
script: level=info
00:00

The child saw level=debug; the script still has info. The last line uses the prefix in its best-known form: TZ=UTC0 sets the time zone for one date command, and the epoch prints as 00:00 whatever zone the machine is in. (The line tries GNU date -d @0 and falls back to BSD date -r 0, so it runs on both.) The var=x command form is how most environment variables are actually set in practice — LC_ALL=C sort, DEBUG=1 ./run, GIT_DIR=… git log — because it scopes the change to exactly the command that needs it. §2 introduced the prefix as part of a simple command's grammar; here is what it does to the processes.

Three details of the var=x command form catch people, and the next example shows each:

# shellcheck disable=SC2097,SC2098  # the gotcha being shown
level=info
# 1. The prefix is not visible to the command's own arguments
level=debug echo "echo was given: $level"

# 2. On a function, the assignment lasts for the call, and is exported during it
f() { echo "inside f: level=$level, child sees: $(bash -c 'echo "${level-<not set>}"')"; }
level=debug f
echo "after f: level=$level"

# 3. On a special builtin in POSIX mode, the assignment stays
set -o posix
level=debug :
echo "after ': ' in POSIX mode: level=$level"

echo was given: info
inside f: level=debug, child sees: debug
after f: level=info
after ': ' in POSIX mode: level=debug

The prefix does not apply to the command's own arguments. level=debug echo "$level" printed info, because $level is expanded before the command runs, while the prefix only takes effect when it runs. ShellCheck reports this as SC2097 and SC2098. The prefix is for the command's environment: a program that reads $level itself would see debug; an argument written on the same line does not.

On a function, the assignment lasts for the call, and is exported during it. Inside f, level was debug, and even a child started from inside f saw it. After the call, level was back to info. So the prefix works on functions too — which is what makes LC_ALL=C my_function useful.

On a special builtin in POSIX mode, the assignment stays. POSIX says that a prefix on a special builtin — :, ., eval, export, readonly, set, shift, trap, unset, exec, exit, return, break, continue — persists after it. Bash follows that only in POSIX mode, and the example shows it: after set -o posix, level=debug : left level set to debug. In bash's normal mode it would not have. The lesson is to not rely on either behaviour: write the assignment on its own line when it is meant to last.

The unset builtin

The unset builtin removes a variable — its value and its attributes, including the export attribute, so an unset variable leaves the environment too. It also removes functions, and a name can be both:

# shellcheck disable=SC2034,SC2329  # LOCKED and name() exist to be unset
export TOKEN=secret
unset TOKEN
bash -c 'echo "child: TOKEN=${TOKEN-<not set>}"'

name=value
name() { echo "the function"; }
unset name                   # removes the variable first
echo "variable: ${name-<not set>}"; name
unset name                   # no variable left, so now the function
type -t name || echo "function: <not defined>"

readonly LOCKED=1
unset LOCKED
echo "status $?"

child: TOKEN=<not set>
variable: <not set>
the function
function: <not defined>
example.sh: line 14: unset: LOCKED: cannot unset: readonly variable
status 1

After unset TOKEN, the child saw no TOKEN: unsetting an exported variable is how to stop passing it on. The middle part shows the lookup order when a name is both a variable and a function: the first unset name removed the variable and left the function, which still ran; the second, with no variable left, removed the function. That order is why scripts that mean one or the other should say so — unset -v name touches only a variable, unset -f name only a function — because a plain unset removes whichever it finds first. And unset cannot remove a readonly variable: it printed cannot unset: readonly variable and returned 1. A value marked readonly is fixed for the life of the shell.

Unsetting a variable is different from setting it to empty. x= leaves x set, with an empty value, and exported if it was — the child sees x with nothing in it, and ${x-default} does not use the default. unset x makes it not exist at all. §5.2 made the same distinction for expansions: ${x-…} tests for set, ${x:-…} for set and non-empty.

The env command

The env command is an external program — /usr/bin/env — that prints the environment it was given, or runs a command in a modified one:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # expanded by the child bash
export APP_HOME=/srv/app
env | grep '^APP_'
printenv APP_HOME

env APP_HOME=/opt/app bash -c 'echo "with env NAME=value:   $APP_HOME"'
env -u APP_HOME bash -c 'echo "with env -u:           ${APP_HOME-<not set>}"'
echo "variables bash adds under env -i: $(env -i bash -c 'env' | cut -d= -f1 | sort | tr '\n' ' ')"

APP_HOME=/srv/app
/srv/app
with env NAME=value:   /opt/app
with env -u:           <not set>
variables bash adds under env -i: PWD SHLVL _

Without arguments the env command prints every environment variable as a name=value line, which is why env | grep '^APP_' is the quick way to see what a script is really passing on. printenv NAME prints one value. env NAME=value command does what the prefix does, from any program rather than only from a shell — which is why #!/usr/bin/env bash works: env finds bash on PATH and runs it. env -u NAME runs the command with one variable removed, the one-command form of unset. And env -i starts from an empty environment: the last line ran bash under env -i and listed what bash had anyway, which was only the three variables bash creates itself when it starts — PWD, SHLVL and _. Everything else, PATH and HOME included, was gone. env -i is how to test that a script does not depend on anything it did not set.

16.4 The Environment Is a List of Strings

The environment a program receives is not a structure of typed variables. It is a list of strings, each of the form name=value, handed to the new program by exec alongside its arguments. The program — bash, Python, ls — reads that list when it starts and makes whatever it likes of it. That one fact explains everything the environment cannot carry.

declare -i count=5
export count
bash -c 'count+=1; echo "the integer attribute is gone:   $count"'

readonly MODE=safe
export MODE
bash -c 'MODE=changed; echo "readonly did not travel:       $MODE"'

list=(a b c)
export list
bash -c 'echo "an array is not exported at all: ${list-<not set>}"'

the integer attribute is gone:   51
readonly did not travel:       changed
an array is not exported at all: <not set>

The integer attribute did not travel. declare -i count made count+=1 arithmetic in the script; in the child, count arrived as the string 5, so count+=1 appended and printed 51. readonly did not travel either: the child changed MODE without complaint. Attributes are the shell's bookkeeping about a variable, and the list holds only the text. And the array was not exported at all — not even as its first element. export list was accepted without complaint and did nothing, because a list of name=value strings has no way to represent a list. §6.15 showed the consequence for arrays and the workaround: serialise the array into a string, with declare -p or a delimited format, and rebuild it on the other side.

export -f: a function as a string

Functions are not variables, and yet export -f exports them — by turning the function into a string:

greet() { echo "hello, $1"; }
export -f greet
bash -c 'greet world'
env | grep -A1 '^BASH_FUNC_greet'

hello, world
BASH_FUNC_greet%%=() {  echo "hello, $1"
}

The child ran greet, and env shows how it got there: a variable called BASH_FUNC_greet%% whose value is the function's source code. A child bash that finds a variable with that shape in its environment defines the function from it. The strange name is deliberate: % cannot appear in a shell variable's name, so the entry can never collide with an ordinary variable, and nothing but bash will try to interpret it. Any other program simply passes it along. (Before 2014 the name was plain greet, and bash parsed any environment value starting with () { as a function definition — including, through a bug in that parser, commands appended after it. That was Shellshock, CVE-2014-6271, and the BASH_FUNC_ prefix and %% suffix are its fix.)

export -f is useful for exactly one situation: a function that must run in a child bash, typically one started by xargs, find -exec or parallel, which start programs rather than subshells. find . -name '*.log' -exec bash -c 'compress_one "$1"' _ {} \; works only if compress_one was exported with export -f.

Names bash cannot use

Because the environment is just strings, it can contain names that are not valid shell identifiers, and bash does something careful with them:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # expanded by the child bash
# A name bash cannot use is still passed on to the next program
env 'my-var=1' 'my_var=2' bash -c '
  echo "bash can read my_var=$my_var"
  env | grep "^my-var"
'

bash can read my_var=2
my-var=1

my-var cannot be a bash variable — - is not allowed in a name — so bash did not import it. But when bash started env, the entry my-var=1 was still in the list, passed through untouched. Bash keeps entries it cannot use and hands them to its children, so a script does not silently strip settings that a program further down the line expects. Some programs do use such names; docker and many CI systems have variables with dots or dashes in them.

The size limit

The environment shares a size limit with the arguments of the command being started, and when the limit is exceeded, the program does not start at all:

# The environment and the arguments share one limit when a program starts
for size in 100000 2000000; do
  big=$(printf "%${size}s" '')
  export big
  if bash -c 'true' 2> err.txt; then
    echo "$size bytes in the environment: the child started"
  else
    status=$? msg=$(< err.txt)
    echo "$size bytes in the environment: status $status, ${msg##*: }"
    ls > /dev/null 2>&1 || echo "  and while it is exported, ls cannot start either"
  fi
done
unset big
ls > /dev/null && echo "after unset big, ls runs again"

100000 bytes in the environment: the child started
2000000 bytes in the environment: status 126, Argument list too long
  and while it is exported, ls cannot start either
after unset big, ls runs again

A 100 KB value was fine. A 2 MB value made the exec fail with Argument list too long — the same error as a glob that expands to too many file names, because it is the same limit: ARG_MAX, the total size of arguments plus environment that exec accepts. The failure is not in bash: it is the operating system refusing to start the program, and bash reports it with status 126, "found but could not be run".

The example's third line is the trap. While the 2 MB variable was exported, every program failed to start — not only the bash -c, but ls, and anything else — because every one of them would have been handed the same oversized environment. The script's builtins still worked, which is why the message was read with $(< err.txt) rather than with sed: an earlier version of this example used sed, and sed failed too. unset big made everything work again.

The limits differ between systems and were measured on both. macOS has ARG_MAX of 1,048,576 bytes for everything together, and a single 1,000,000-byte variable still started a program. Linux had ARG_MAX of 2,097,152 bytes here, but also a separate limit on each single string of 131,072 bytes: a name=value of 131,000 bytes started a program and one of 131,072 did not. So on Linux a single 200 KB variable fails, well below the total. The environment is for small settings — a path, a flag, a URL — and anything larger belongs in a file whose name is in the environment.

16.5 Subshells

A subshell is a copy of the shell running in a child process. Bash creates one with fork() and never calls exec: the child is still bash, still in the middle of the same script, with the same memory. So a subshell sees everything the parent had at the moment of the fork — every variable exported or not, every array, every function, every option, the directory, the descriptors — and the parent sees nothing the subshell does afterwards. Parentheses create one explicitly:

# shellcheck disable=SC2030,SC2031  # losing the changes is the point
count=1
list=(a b c)
start=$PWD
mkdir build
(
  count=2
  list+=(d)
  cd build || exit
  echo "inside:  count=$count, ${#list[@]} elements, in ${PWD#"$start"/}"
)
echo "outside: count=$count, ${#list[@]} elements, $([[ $PWD == "$start" ]] && echo "still where it started")"

inside:  count=2, 4 elements, in build
outside: count=1, 3 elements, still where it started

Inside the parentheses, count became 2, the array gained an element, and the directory was build. Outside, all three were as before. The rule that a subshell inherits everything has an exact counterpart: it gives back nothing but an exit status and whatever it writes to its descriptors. Every change inside — assignments, cd, set, shopt, umask, trap, new functions — is discarded when it exits.

That is precisely what makes a subshell useful as a boundary. A cd in a subshell is the standard way to run commands somewhere else without having to come back: (cd build && make) leaves the script where it was even if make fails halfway, with no saved directory and no cd -. A cd in a subshell also cannot fail in a way that strands the script: if cd build fails, the && skips make, and the script is still in its own directory. The same goes for anything the subshell sets: an option, an IFS, a variable. A subshell inherits everything and gives nothing back, so it cannot leak.

Knowing you are in a subshell: $$, BASHPID and BASH_SUBSHELL

A subshell is a different process, and yet $$ does not change in it. $$ in a subshell still holds the process ID of the original script — deliberately, so that a temporary file named /tmp/job.$$ means the same file wherever in the script it is written. The variable that tells the processes apart is BASHPID, which is always the ID of the process actually running. And BASH_SUBSHELL counts how deep the nesting is:

same() { if [[ $1 == "$2" ]]; then echo same; else echo different; fi; }
top=$$ mine=$BASHPID
echo "script:   BASH_SUBSHELL=$BASH_SUBSHELL, \$\$ and BASHPID are the $(same "$top" "$mine")"
( a=$$ b=$BASHPID
  echo "subshell: BASH_SUBSHELL=$BASH_SUBSHELL, \$\$ is the $(same "$a" "$top") number, BASHPID is $(same "$b" "$top")"
  ( echo "nested:   BASH_SUBSHELL=$BASH_SUBSHELL" )
)
{ echo "a brace group: BASH_SUBSHELL=$BASH_SUBSHELL"; }

script:   BASH_SUBSHELL=0, $$ and BASHPID are the same
subshell: BASH_SUBSHELL=1, $$ is the same number, BASHPID is different
nested:   BASH_SUBSHELL=2
a brace group: BASH_SUBSHELL=0

In the script, $$ and BASHPID are the same. In the subshell, $$ is the same number as before, and BASHPID is different. So $$ in a subshell identifies the script, never the subshell — use BASHPID whenever the process itself matters, as in kill "$BASHPID" in §16.5's traps example. BASH_SUBSHELL went 0, 1, 2 with each level of parentheses. A brace group { …; } stayed at 0: it groups commands without creating a process, which is the whole difference between the two (§9.1).

The example is careful in one way that is worth copying: it reads $$ and BASHPID into variables before comparing them inside $(…). A comparison written as $(same "$$" "$BASHPID") would have expanded BASHPID inside the command substitution — which is itself a subshell (§16.6) — and reported "different" even in the main script. That is also the most common mistake when checking for a subshell, and §16.6 shows it on its own.

The subshell exit status

A subshell returns a status like any command, and the subshell exit status is the status of the last command it ran, or the argument of an exit inside it:

( exit 3 )
echo "( exit 3 ):          status $?"
( false; true )
echo "( false; true ):     status $?"
( set -e; false; echo "not reached" )
echo "( set -e; false ):   status $?, and the script carries on"

( exit 3 ):          status 3
( false; true ):     status 0
( set -e; false ):   status 1, and the script carries on

( exit 3 ) returned 3 — and only the subshell exited, not the script. ( false; true ) returned 0, because true ran last. ( set -e; false ) returned 1: set -e inside the subshell made the subshell exit at the false, and the script, which does not have set -e, carried on. That combination is useful: exit and set -e inside a subshell stop the subshell, so a block of commands can be made to fail as a unit and its status tested like one command. It is also why exit inside $(…) or on the right of a | never ends the script.

Waiting for a subshell

A subshell can run in the background like any command, and the script can wait for a subshell and collect its status:

( sleep 0.2; exit 4 ) &
worker=$!
echo "started a subshell in the background"
wait "$worker"
echo "wait returned its status: $?"

started a subshell in the background
wait returned its status: 4

( … ) & started the subshell without waiting; $! held its process ID; wait "$worker" waited for that process and returned its exit status, 4. Waiting for a subshell is how a script runs several blocks of work at once and still checks each one's result — §17's subject, where wait -n, job control and collecting many statuses are developed. Two details matter already. $! must be saved straight after the &, because the next background command overwrites it. And wait with no argument waits for every background job but returns 0 whatever they returned, so to wait for a subshell and know whether it succeeded, pass its PID.

Traps in a subshell

The one item a subshell does not inherit in working order is a caught trap. The manual says traps caught by the shell are reset to their original values in a subshell, and a script can see that — but trap -p makes it easy to believe the opposite:

trap 'echo "the script caught TERM"' TERM
{
  (
    echo "listed in the subshell: $(trap -p TERM)"
    kill -TERM "$BASHPID"
    echo "not reached: the handler is not active here"
  )
} 2> /dev/null
status=$?
echo "the subshell was killed by SIG$(kill -l "$status") (status $status)"
kill -TERM "$$"

listed in the subshell: trap -- 'echo "the script caught TERM"' SIGTERM
the subshell was killed by SIGTERM (status 143)
the script caught TERM

Inside the subshell, trap -p still listed the script's handler for TERM. Yet when the subshell sent itself TERM, the handler did not run: the subshell was killed by SIGTERM, with status 143 (128 + 15). Then the same signal sent to the script ran the handler. Both halves are documented behaviour. The reset is what the manual promises — a handler is code in the shell's memory, and running it in a copy of the shell would run it in the wrong process. The listing is a POSIX provision, so that saved=$(trap) — a command substitution, which is a subshell — can capture the parent's traps to restore them later. The effect is that trap -p inside a subshell reports handlers that are not active there. A subshell that needs a handler must set its own. (The group { … } 2> /dev/null around the subshell only hides bash's report of the killed process, whose wording differs between systems.)

16.6 Pipelines, $( ) and <( ) Are Subshells

Parentheses are the one way to ask for a subshell explicitly. Bash also creates them without being asked, in three places that between them account for nearly every "my variable disappeared" problem.

A pipeline runs in subshells

In bash, a pipeline runs in subshells: every command in a pipeline that is more than one command long runs in a subshell of its own, the last one included. This example has a function report which process it runs in, from each side of a |:

top=$BASHPID
where() {
  if [[ $BASHPID == "$top" ]]; then echo "$1: the script"; else echo "$1: a subshell"; fi
}
where "left of |" | { where "right of |"; cat; }
where "no pipeline"

right of |: a subshell
left of |: a subshell
no pipeline: the script

Both sides of the pipe reported a subshell; the same function called outside a pipeline ran in the script. (The right-hand side printed first because it wrote its own line before cat passed on the left-hand side's.) The reason is mechanical: the commands of a pipeline run at the same time, connected by a pipe, so each must be a separate process, and bash does not treat the last one specially. Other shells do: ksh and zsh run the last command of a pipeline in the current shell. POSIX allows either. shopt -s lastpipe makes bash behave like ksh, under a condition §16.8 explains. So in bash a pipeline runs in subshells on both sides by default, which is why cmd | while read …; done loses every variable the loop sets. §16.8 is devoted to that.

Command substitution is a subshell

Command substitution is a subshell too: the command inside $(…) runs in a child, with its output captured through a pipe. So is process substitution:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016,SC2030,SC2031  # labels are literal; the lost n is the point
top=$BASHPID
where() {
  if [[ $BASHPID == "$top" ]]; then echo "$1: the script"; else echo "$1: a subshell"; fi
}
n=0
out=$(n=5; where 'inside $( )')
echo "$out; n is still $n"
read -r line < <(n=7; where 'inside <( )')
echo "$line; n is still $n"

inside $( ): a subshell; n is still 0
inside <( ): a subshell; n is still 0

Inside $( ), the function reported a subshell, and the assignment n=5 there did not reach the script: n is still 0. Process substitution is a subshell in the same way: <( … ) ran in a subshell, and n=7 was lost just the same. That process substitution is a subshell is harmless in the usual pattern, while read …; done < <(cmd), because only cmd is inside it — the loop is not, which is the whole point (§16.8). For command substitution this is rarely a problem, because the point of $(…) is its output. But it catches functions that both print a result and set a variable (§9.6 — the "return data" rule), and a cd or exit written inside $(…), which affects only the copy. Bash 5.3's ${ command; } form runs the command in the current shell instead, and §15.1 measured it: no fork, and the variables stick.

Even the arguments are inside

One consequence trips up careful people. Everything between $( and ) is expanded in the subshell — including expansions that look as if they are just arguments:

# shellcheck disable=SC2116  # the echo is the experiment
here=$BASHPID
inside=$(echo "$BASHPID")
[[ $inside == "$here" ]] || echo "even an argument inside \$( ) is expanded in the subshell"

even an argument inside $( ) is expanded in the subshell

$(echo "$BASHPID") printed the subshell's PID, not the script's, because $BASHPID was expanded inside the command substitution. So a check written as [[ $(echo "$BASHPID") == … ]], or a $(report "$BASHPID"), measures the wrong process. §16.5's example read the value into a variable first for exactly this reason.

A copy is not an environment

A subshell and a child program are both child processes, and it is tempting to think of them the same way. They are not, and one example makes the difference concrete — an associative array and a function, both of which §16.4 showed cannot be passed through the environment:

# A subshell is a copy of the shell, so it sees what the environment cannot carry
declare -A port=([http]=80 [https]=443)
greet() { echo "hello from a function"; }
echo "subshell:      ${port[https]}, $(greet)"
bash -c 'echo "child program: ${port[https]-<not set>}, $(greet 2>/dev/null || echo "<no function>")"'

subshell:      443, hello from a function
child program: <not set>, <no function>

The subshell read ${port[https]} and called greet without any export, because it is a copy of the script's memory. The child program saw neither. That is the practical test for which kind of boundary a piece of code crosses: a ( … ), a pipeline, a $( ) or a <( ) gets a copy of everything; a program started by name — bash -c, xargs, find -exec, sudo, env — gets the environment, which is strings (§16.4).

16.7 Shell Options: set and shopt

Bash's behaviour is adjusted by options, and it has two separate sets of them, managed by two builtins, for historical reasons. The set builtin manages the options that come from the Bourne shell and POSIX — errexit, nounset, pipefail, noglob, xtrace — each with a long name for set -o name and most with a single letter too (set -e, set -u, set -f, set -x). The single letters are the older form: the Bourne shell had only those, and the long names came later, from ksh. The shopt builtin manages bash's own additions — nullglob, extglob, globstar, lastpipe and about fifty more — which have only long names. The shopt builtin also covers a few options that are not switches at all but read-only reports, such as login_shell. A shell option is a switch in either table, and both tables are part of the command execution environment: a subshell inherits them, and a child program does not (with one exception, below).

The two tables are read and written with different commands:

set -o | grep -E '^(errexit|noglob|pipefail) '
