shopt -p nullglob extglob
echo "set -o names in \$-: $-"
set -f
shopt -s nullglob
echo "after set -f and shopt -s nullglob:"
set -o | grep '^noglob '
shopt -p nullglob
[[ -o noglob ]] && echo "[[ -o noglob ]] is true"
shopt -q nullglob && echo "shopt -q nullglob is true"

errexit        	off
noglob         	off
pipefail       	off
shopt -u nullglob
shopt -u extglob
set -o names in $-: hB
after set -f and shopt -s nullglob:
noglob         	on
shopt -s nullglob
[[ -o noglob ]] is true
shopt -q nullglob is true

set -o with no argument lists the first table as name on|off; the example filtered it to three rows. shopt -p prints the second table's settings as commands — shopt -u nullglob — which is more useful than the plain shopt listing, for a reason the next part shows. The letters in $- are the single-letter set options currently on: h (hashall, remembering where commands were found) and B (braceexpand) are on by default in a script. After set -f and shopt -s nullglob, both tables changed. Each has its own test: [[ -o noglob ]] for the set kind (§7.6), shopt -q nullglob for the shopt kind. shopt -s turns an option on and shopt -u turns it off; shopt -p shows the setting and shopt -q tests it without printing. set has the equivalent pair set -o name / set +o name, where + means off.

The set builtin itself

The set builtin does two more jobs besides options, and a script uses both:

# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # greeting is only listed by set
set -- one "two words" three
echo "set -- replaced the positional parameters: $# of them, \$2 is '$2'"
set --
echo "set -- with nothing cleared them: $#"
greeting=hi
set | grep -E '^greeting='

set -- replaced the positional parameters: 3 of them, $2 is 'two words'
set -- with nothing cleared them: 0
greeting=hi

set -- … replaces the positional parameters: after set -- one "two words" three, $# is 3 and $2 is two words. set -- with nothing after it clears them. The -- is there so that an argument beginning with - is taken as a parameter and not as an option — set -- -x sets $1 to -x rather than turning on tracing. And set with no arguments at all prints every shell variable and function, which is why set | grep '^greeting=' found greeting even though it was never exported — env would not have shown it.

Saving and restoring options

An option is global state, and a function that changes one changes it for its caller too (§7.12 made this point about nocasematch). Changing an option temporarily therefore means saving and restoring it, and both tables can print themselves as commands that restore the current state:

saved_set=$(set +o)
saved_shopt=$(shopt -p)
echo "set +o prints commands:"; grep -E 'noglob|nounset' <<< "$saved_set"
echo "shopt -p prints commands:"; grep -E 'nullglob' <<< "$saved_shopt"

set -f -u
shopt -s nullglob
eval "$saved_set"
eval "$saved_shopt"
[[ -o noglob || -o nounset ]] || echo "set options restored"
shopt -q nullglob || echo "shopt options restored"

set +o prints commands:
set +o noglob
set +o nounset
shopt -p prints commands:
shopt -u nullglob
set options restored
shopt options restored

set +o — with a plus and no name — prints the set table as set -o … and set +o … commands, one per option. shopt -p prints the shopt table the same way. Saving both into variables, changing options, and eval-ing the saved text put every option back: noglob, nounset and nullglob were all off again. This is the same idea as declare -p in §6.15 — output that is valid shell input — and the same caution applies: eval runs whatever the text says, so it must be text the shell itself produced.

For the set table there is a shorter way inside a function: local -. Written in a function, it makes the set options local to the call, the way local name makes a variable local: every option changed with set after that line is put back to its previous value when the function returns, whichever return it leaves by. It covers only the set table, and the next example measures that, against the alternative of a function whose body is a subshell — f() ( … ) with parentheses instead of braces:

with_local_dash() {
  local -
  set -f
  shopt -s nullglob
}
with_subshell() (
  set -f
  shopt -s nullglob
)
with_local_dash
echo "after local -: noglob $([[ -o noglob ]] && echo on || echo off), nullglob $(shopt -q nullglob && echo on || echo off)"
shopt -u nullglob
with_subshell
echo "after a subshell body: noglob $([[ -o noglob ]] && echo on || echo off), nullglob $(shopt -q nullglob && echo on || echo off)"

after local -: noglob off, nullglob on
after a subshell body: noglob off, nullglob off

After the function with local -, noglob was restored to off but nullglob was still on: local - does not cover shopt options. After the function with a subshell body, both were off, because the subshell's changes were thrown away with the subshell. So the choice is: local - plus a saved shopt -p for a function that must change the caller's variables, and a subshell body — which restores everything, options, cd, IFS and all, at the cost of a fork and of losing every variable it sets — for one that need not.

SHELLOPTS and BASHOPTS: options into a child bash

A child program does not inherit shell options — it is a new program, and options are the shell's memory. There is one deliberate exception. Bash keeps two read-only variables listing the options that are on: SHELLOPTS for the set table and BASHOPTS for the shopt table. If either is exported, a child bash reads it at startup and turns those options on:

set -o noglob
bash -c 'echo "a child without SHELLOPTS: noglob $([[ -o noglob ]] && echo on || echo off)"'
export SHELLOPTS
bash -c 'echo "a child with SHELLOPTS:    noglob $([[ -o noglob ]] && echo on || echo off)"'

a child without SHELLOPTS: noglob off
a child with SHELLOPTS:    noglob on

With noglob on and nothing exported, the child bash had noglob off. After export SHELLOPTS, the child had it on. That is how to make every bash a script starts run with, say, errexit and nounset — and also a way for a setting to leak into scripts that did not expect it, which is why it is rarely the right tool. A script that needs options in a child should say so in the child: bash -eu -c …, or a set line at the top of the child script.

The options worth knowing individually

Most options are covered where they matter: errexit, nounset and pipefail in §11, noclobber in §10, nullglob, failglob, dotglob, globstar and extglob in §4 and §7, xtrace in §20. The rest of this subsection takes the ones that belong to processes and to how the shell reads a script.

allexport

allexport, or set -a, marks every variable assigned while it is on for export. Its one common use is loading a file of settings into the environment of the programs a script starts:

# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # LOCAL_ONLY is set to show it is not exported
printf '%s\n' 'DB_HOST=db.internal' 'DB_PORT=5432' > app.env
set -a
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source ./app.env
set +a
LOCAL_ONLY=1
bash -c 'echo "child: DB_HOST=$DB_HOST DB_PORT=$DB_PORT LOCAL_ONLY=${LOCAL_ONLY-<not set>}"'

child: DB_HOST=db.internal DB_PORT=5432 LOCAL_ONLY=<not set>

The two variables assigned by source ./app.env while set -a was on were exported, and the child saw them. LOCAL_ONLY, assigned after set +a, was not. The set -a / source / set +a sandwich is the standard way to load a .env file — with the caution that source runs the file as shell code, so a value such as $(rm …) in it would run too. For a file whose contents are not trusted, parse it as data with read (§14) and export each name explicitly; allexport is for files you control.

noglob

noglob — set -f — turns off pathname expansion, so an unquoted * stays a *. It is the tool for splitting a string on IFS without the words being taken as patterns (§3.6), and it is the option the save-and-restore examples above used. set -f must be undone with set +f, or saved with local -, because a script that forgets it has lost globbing everywhere after that point.

noexec: set -n and bash -n

noexec, or set -n, makes the shell read commands and check their syntax without running any of them. Nobody turns it on in the middle of a script — nothing after it would run, including set +n — but bash -n script runs a whole file under noexec, and that is a real tool:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the quoted lines are the scripts' contents
printf '%s\n' 'echo "this would run"' 'if true; then' '  echo "missing fi"' > broken.sh
printf '%s\n' 'echo "this would run"' 'touch ran.txt' > fine.sh
bash -n fine.sh && [[ ! -e ran.txt ]] && echo "fine.sh: syntax is valid, and nothing ran"
bash -n broken.sh
echo "broken.sh: status $?"

fine.sh: syntax is valid, and nothing ran
broken.sh: line 4: syntax error: unexpected end of file from `if' command on line 2
broken.sh: status 2

bash -n fine.sh returned 0 and ran nothing — its echo printed nothing, and ran.txt was never created, so the touch was only parsed. The same would hold for an rm. bash -n broken.sh found the missing fi and returned 2. That makes bash -n a cheap syntax check before running a script that would be expensive or dangerous to run half of. It checks only what the parser checks: a misspelled command or a wrong variable name is valid syntax, which is what ShellCheck (§20) is for. The diagnostic's wording differs by version: bash 5.3 adds from `if' command on line 2 to the message, as shown; bash 5.2 stops at unexpected end of file.

The monitor option

The monitor option, set -m, turns on job control: each background job runs in a process group of its own, the shell reports when jobs finish, and fg, bg and Ctrl-Z work. It is on by default in an interactive shell and off in a script, and the difference is visible in the process groups:

sleep 1 &
job=$!
(( $(ps -o pgid= -p "$job") == $(ps -o pgid= -p "$$") )) && echo "monitor off: the job is in the script's process group"
kill "$job"
set -m
sleep 1 &
job=$!
(( $(ps -o pgid= -p "$job") == job )) && echo "monitor on:  the job leads a process group of its own"
kill "$job"
set +m

monitor off: the job is in the script's process group
monitor on:  the job leads a process group of its own

With the monitor option off, the background sleep was in the script's own process group; with it on, the job led a process group of its own. That matters for signals: Ctrl-C at a terminal sends SIGINT to the terminal's foreground process group, and with job control on, background jobs are not in it. §17 develops process groups and the job-control commands; the fact this section needs is that the monitor option changes how commands are grouped into processes, and that one feature — lastpipe, §16.8 — refuses to work while it is on.

huponexit and checkjobs

Two options change what happens to running jobs when an interactive shell exits, and both were measured on a real terminal, because a script is never interactive.

huponexit makes an interactive login shell send SIGHUP to all of its jobs when it exits. Measured: in a login shell with huponexit on, a background sleep 300 was killed when the shell exited; with huponexit off, it survived; and in an interactive shell that was not a login shell, huponexit on made no difference — the job survived. So huponexit is off by default, which is why a job started with & in a login session can outlive the session. nohup and disown (§17) are the explicit ways to make sure a job survives; huponexit is the way to make sure it does not.

checkjobs makes an interactive shell refuse the first exit while jobs are running. Measured: with checkjobs on and a sleep 300 in the background, the first exit printed There are running jobs. and the shell stayed; a second exit left. With checkjobs off, the first exit left at once. (Stopped jobs always get this warning, with There are stopped jobs.; checkjobs extends it to running ones.) It is a protection for people who start long jobs at a terminal, and it has no effect in a script.

extdebug

extdebug turns on features meant for debuggers, and one of them is useful on its own: declare -F reports where a function was defined.

deploy() {
  echo "deploying"
}
declare -F deploy
shopt -s extdebug
declare -F deploy

deploy
deploy 1 example.sh

Without extdebug, declare -F deploy printed only the name. With it, the same command printed deploy 1 example.sh: the name, the line of the definition, and the file. In a large script, or one that sources several libraries, that answers "which definition of this function is running?" in one command. The other extdebug features — a DEBUG trap that can skip commands, BASH_ARGV and BASH_ARGC filled in for every call — are what bashdb is built on, and they change behaviour enough that extdebug should be switched on only for the command that needs it.

expand_aliases

expand_aliases is why aliases do not work in scripts. It is on in an interactive shell and off in a non-interactive one, so an alias a script defines is simply ignored:

# shellcheck disable=SC2262,SC2263  # the failure is the point
mkdir demo && cd demo || exit
alias ll='ls -1'
ll 2>&1
shopt -s expand_aliases
alias ll='ls -1'
touch a.txt
ll

example.sh: line 4: ll: command not found
a.txt

The first ll failed with command not found: the alias was defined, and not expanded. After shopt -s expand_aliases, an alias defined on a later line worked. The "later line" matters. Aliases are expanded when a line is read, not when it runs, so an alias defined and used in the same line — or inside the same function body, or the same if block — is not yet defined when its use is read. In a script, a function does everything an alias does, takes arguments properly and has none of these rules, so expand_aliases is mostly for sourcing a file of interactive aliases and needing them to work.

16.8 The Variable Lost in a Pipeline

This is the problem the rest of the section has been leading to. A loop reads lines and counts them, and after the loop the count is zero:

# shellcheck disable=SC2030,SC2031  # this is the bug being shown
printf 'alpha\nbeta\ngamma\n' > names.txt
count=0
cat names.txt | while read -r _; do
  (( ++count ))
done
echo "after the pipeline: count=$count"

after the pipeline: count=0

The loop ran three times. Each time it incremented count — in the subshell that the right-hand side of the pipeline runs in (§16.6). When the pipeline finished, that subshell exited, and its count went with it. The script's own count was never touched. This is the variable lost in a pipeline, and it is the most frequently reported problem in shell scripting because nothing about it looks wrong: no error, no warning at run time, a plausible-looking result of 0.

ShellCheck does warn about it. It reports SC2030, "Modification of count is local (to subshell caused by pipeline)", on the assignment inside the loop, and SC2031, "count was modified in a subshell. That change might be lost", on the use after it. The example above disables both with a directive, because the bug is its point; in a real script, SC2030 and SC2031 together are nearly always this bug. The same pair fires for an assignment inside $(…) or ( … ) that is used outside, which is the same problem in another shape.

The four fixes

A variable lost in a pipeline has four standard fixes, and they differ in what they cost:

printf 'alpha\nbeta\ngamma\n' > names.txt

count=0
while read -r _; do (( ++count )); done < names.txt
echo "redirect the file:        count=$count"

count=0
while read -r _; do (( ++count )); done < <(grep -v beta names.txt)
echo "process substitution:     count=$count"

grep -v beta names.txt | {
  count=0
  while read -r _; do (( ++count )); done
  echo "use it inside the group:  count=$count"
}

mapfile -t names < names.txt
echo "mapfile, then loop:       count=${#names[@]}"

redirect the file:        count=3
process substitution:     count=2
use it inside the group:  count=2
mapfile, then loop:       count=3

Redirect the file into the loop. while …; done < names.txt has no pipeline at all, so the loop runs in the script and the count, 3, survives. When the input is a file, this is the right fix, and cat file | was never needed (§15.2).

Process substitution. When the input is a command's output, done < <(grep -v beta names.txt) feeds it to the loop through a redirection instead of a pipe. The grep runs in a subshell, and the loop does not, so the count, 2, survives. This is the usual fix, and §16.9 compares it with the pipeline it replaces.

Use the result inside the group. If the value is only needed for something printed or decided right after the loop, put that code in the same subshell: … | { while …; done; echo "$count"; }. The count is correct inside the braces and still lost after them, which is fine when nothing after them needs it.

Read everything first. mapfile -t names < names.txt (§6.12) reads the lines into an array in the script, and the count is simply ${#names[@]}, 3. When the whole input fits in memory, loading it first and looping over the array afterwards removes the problem and often simplifies the loop.

shopt -s lastpipe

There is a fifth fix, which changes the rule instead of avoiding it. lastpipe makes bash run the last command of a pipeline in the current shell, as ksh and zsh do:

printf 'alpha\nbeta\ngamma\n' > names.txt
shopt -s lastpipe

count=0
grep -v beta names.txt | while read -r _; do (( ++count )); done
echo "lastpipe, monitor off:  count=$count, status of grep kept in PIPESTATUS: ${PIPESTATUS[0]}"

set -m
count=0
grep -v beta names.txt | while read -r _; do (( ++count )); done
echo "lastpipe, monitor on:   count=$count"

lastpipe, monitor off:  count=2, status of grep kept in PIPESTATUS: 0
lastpipe, monitor on:   count=0

With shopt -s lastpipe, the pipeline version kept its count: 2. PIPESTATUS still reported grep's status, 0, so nothing about the pipeline's status handling was lost. But lastpipe works only when the monitor option (§16.7) is off. In the second half, after set -m, the same pipeline lost the count again — silently, with lastpipe still on. Job control is off by default in a script, so shopt -s lastpipe works in scripts; it is on by default in an interactive shell, so the same code pasted at a prompt does not work, and neither does a script that turns on set -m.

Weighed against the other fixes, lastpipe is attractive because it lets the natural cmd | while … form be correct. Its costs are that it is bash-specific (and works in ksh and zsh anyway, while POSIX sh has no equivalent), that it fails without a sound under job control, and that a reader who does not know the script set it will see a pipeline that looks like the classic bug and "fix" it. Process substitution is explicit at the place it is used. The recommendation, therefore: process substitution or a redirection as the default; lastpipe in a script that sets it once at the top, says why, and never turns on job control.

16.9 Process Substitution versus a Pipeline

<(cmd) looks like a way of writing a pipeline backwards, and in one respect it is: the command's output reaches the loop either way. The differences are in which process each part runs in, and in what happens to the exit statuses. §4.6 introduced process substitution as an expansion that produces a file name; here are the process-level consequences.

Which side runs in a subshell. In producer | loop, both sides run in subshells. In loop < <(producer), the producer runs in a subshell and the loop runs in the script. That is the property §16.8's second fix relies on: process substitution moves the subshell to the side that does not need to set variables.

What happens to the producer's status. A pipeline keeps every component's status in PIPESTATUS, and pipefail (§11) can make the pipeline fail when any component does. Process substitution keeps nothing, unless the script asks for it:

producer() { printf 'a\nb\n'; return 3; }

producer | while read -r _; do :; done
echo "pipeline:             PIPESTATUS=(${PIPESTATUS[*]})"

while read -r _; do :; done < <(producer)
echo "process substitution: loop status $?, and \$! is the producer's PID"
wait "$!"
echo "wait \"\$!\":            status $?"

pipeline:             PIPESTATUS=(3 0)
process substitution: loop status 0, and $! is the producer's PID
wait "$!":            status 3

The pipeline's PIPESTATUS was (3 0): the producer's failure was recorded. With process substitution, the loop's status was 0 and the producer's 3 appeared nowhere — pipefail does not see it either, because the producer is not part of a pipeline. The way to recover it is $!, which holds the process ID of the last process substitution, and wait "$!", which returned 3. That has worked since bash 4.4 (measured on 4.4, 5.0, 5.1, 5.2 and 5.3). It covers only the last process substitution, so a script with two needs to save $! after each. A script that must notice a failing producer and uses process substitution needs that wait; otherwise the failure is silent — the loop simply sees fewer lines than it should.

Sending output to a log and the terminal

Process substitution also works for output, with >(…), and its best-known use is giving a whole script a log file while still printing to the terminal. §10.7 redirected a script's output into a log with exec; with tee in a process substitution, the output goes to both:

# shellcheck disable=SC2164  # the failing cd is the error being logged
exec 3>&1 4>&2                    # keep the originals
exec > >(tee -a run.log) 2>&1     # from here on, everything goes through tee
tee_pid=$!

echo "a normal line"
cd no-such-directory
echo "another line"

exec >&3 2>&4 3>&- 4>&-           # restore, which closes tee's input
wait "$tee_pid"                   # and let it finish writing
mapfile -t logged < run.log
echo "run.log holds ${#logged[@]} lines, the error included"

a normal line
example.sh: line 7: cd: no-such-directory: No such file or directory
another line
run.log holds 3 lines, the error included

exec > >(tee -a run.log) 2>&1 sends standard output into a tee running in a subshell, and standard error to the same place, so everything the script prints — the cd error included — reaches both the terminal and run.log. The rest of the example is what makes it reliable. The script saved the original descriptors in 3 and 4 first, and restored them at the end, which closed the pipe into tee; then wait "$tee_pid" waited for tee to write the last lines and exit. Without that wait, the script could finish — and the next command read run.log — before tee had written everything, because tee runs as a separate process at its own pace. That race is the one flaw of the pattern, and at the end of a script it shows up as output appearing after the prompt has returned. Waiting for tee removes it.

Standard output and standard error arrive in tee through one pipe, in the order they were written, so the log keeps them in order. Sending them to two different tees — > >(tee out.log) 2> >(tee err.log >&2) — loses that order, because the two processes run independently.

16.10 The Process Table

Each place code runs, what it gets, and what it gives back.

Where
What it gets, and what comes back
An external program
fork() then exec: the environment (exported variables only, as strings), descriptors, directory, umask, ignored signals. No functions, arrays, attributes or caught traps. Back: an exit status (§16.1, §16.2).
exec cmd
No fork: the command replaces the shell, keeps its PID, and nothing after the line runs; a failed exec ends a script unless execfail is on (§16.2).
NAME=value cmd
For that command only; not seen by its own arguments; lasts for a function call; persists after a special builtin in POSIX mode (§16.3).
The environment
A list of name=value strings: no arrays, no -i, no readonly; functions only as BASH_FUNC_name%%; shares ARG_MAX with the arguments, and one string over 128 KiB fails on Linux (§16.4).
( … )
A copy of everything, except that caught traps are reset (though trap -p still lists them); $$ unchanged, BASHPID new; nothing comes back but the status (§16.5).
{ …; }
No new process: the current shell; changes stick (§16.5).
a | b
Every part in a subshell, the last included; lastpipe runs the last in the shell when the monitor option is off (§16.6, §16.8).
$( … )
A subshell, arguments included; only the output comes back; ${ …; } in 5.3 avoids the fork (§16.6).
<( … ), >( … )
A subshell; the loop that reads it stays in the shell; its status is lost unless you wait "$!" (§16.6, §16.9).
Shell options
Two tables: set -o / set +o and shopt -s / -u / -p; save both to restore; local - covers only set; SHELLOPTS exported reaches a child bash (§16.7).

And the rule behind the table: a process begins as a copy and gives nothing back but a status and its output. Every "lost" variable is a value set in a copy; every "missing" function is a function asked for across an exec. Decide which side of the boundary each piece of code must run on, and choose the construct — a redirection, a process substitution, a brace group, a subshell, an export — that puts it there.

Exercises

1. The total that is always zero. This script adds up a list of sizes, and it prints total=0:

# shellcheck disable=SC2030,SC2031  # the bug the exercise asks about
printf '%s\n' 120 45 300 > sizes.txt
total=0
cat sizes.txt | while read -r n; do
  (( total += n ))
done
echo "total=$total"

Explain exactly why, naming the process each part runs in. Then fix it three ways — with the file redirected into the loop, with a filter (grep -v '^45$') in front of the loop that still preserves the total, and with lastpipe — and say which you would use in a script that other people maintain.

Solution

cat sizes.txt | while … is a pipeline, and in bash every part of a pipeline runs in a subshell (§16.6), the while loop included. The loop added 120, 45 and 300 to the total in its subshell, which then exited, taking that total with it. The script's own total was never changed, and printed its initial 0. ShellCheck reports SC2030 and SC2031 on it (§16.8).

printf '%s\n' 120 45 300 > sizes.txt

total=0
while read -r n; do (( total += n )); done < sizes.txt
echo "1. redirect into the loop:     total=$total"

total=0
while read -r n; do (( total += n )); done < <(grep -v '^45$' sizes.txt)
echo "2. process substitution:       total=$total (45 filtered out)"

shopt -s lastpipe
total=0
grep -v '^45$' sizes.txt | while read -r n; do (( total += n )); done
echo "3. lastpipe:                   total=$total (45 filtered out)"

1. redirect into the loop:     total=465
2. process substitution:       total=420 (45 filtered out)
3. lastpipe:                   total=420 (45 filtered out)

1. Redirecting the file into the loop removes the pipeline and the subshell: 465. 2. With a command in front, process substitution moves the command into the subshell and leaves the loop in the script: 420 once 45 is filtered out. 3. shopt -s lastpipe runs the loop in the script, since job control is off in a script: also 420.

For shared code, the first and second: they are correct where they are written, whatever options are in force. lastpipe makes the pipeline form correct only while the monitor option is off (§16.8), and it leaves code that looks exactly like the bug to anyone who does not know the option was set at the top.

2. Settings for one command. Write run_with_env FILE COMMAND…, which runs COMMAND with the variables from a KEY=VALUE file in its environment, without changing any variable in the calling script, and returns the command's exit status. What should happen if FILE does not exist? What is the danger in the approach, and when would you parse the file instead?

Solution 
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # expanded by the child bash
run_with_env() (
  set -a
  # shellcheck source=/dev/null
  source "$1" || exit
  set +a
  shift
  exec "$@"
)

printf '%s\n' 'DB_HOST=db.internal' 'LOG_LEVEL=debug' > app.env
LOG_LEVEL=info

run_with_env app.env bash -c 'echo "child:  DB_HOST=$DB_HOST LOG_LEVEL=$LOG_LEVEL"'
echo "script: DB_HOST=${DB_HOST-<not set>} LOG_LEVEL=$LOG_LEVEL"
run_with_env app.env false
echo "the command's status comes back: $?"
run_with_env missing.env true
echo "a missing file: status $?"

child:  DB_HOST=db.internal LOG_LEVEL=debug
script: DB_HOST=<not set> LOG_LEVEL=info
the command's status comes back: 1
example.sh: line 5: missing.env: No such file or directory
a missing file: status 1

The function's body is a subshell — run_with_env() ( … ), parentheses instead of braces — so everything it does, including set -a and every variable the file assigns, disappears when it returns (§16.5, §16.7). set -a exports each assignment in the file (allexport, §16.7), and exec "$@" replaces the subshell with the command (§16.2), so the command's status is the function's status, with no extra process left waiting. The child saw DB_HOST and the file's LOG_LEVEL=debug; the script still had no DB_HOST and its own LOG_LEVEL=info. false returned 1 through it. A missing file made source fail, and || exit ended the subshell before running anything, returning 1 with source's own message.

The danger is that source runs the file as bash code, so LOG_LEVEL=$(curl …) in it would run curl. That is fine for a file the script's own author controls. For a file written by someone else — or one that should simply be data — read it line by line with IFS='=' read -r key value (§14), check key against ^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$, and export "$key=$value" inside the same subshell.

3. Turning globbing off for one command. Write without_globbing COMMAND…, which runs a command with noglob on and nullglob on, then restores both to what they were, and returns the command's status — and must not use a subshell, because the command may be a function that sets variables in the script. Then test it, and explain why without_globbing echo *.txt still prints file names.

Solution 
# shellcheck disable=SC2035  # the bare glob in the call is the point
without_globbing() {
  local -                          # restores set options (noglob) on return
  set -f
  local restore
  restore=$(shopt -p nullglob)     # local - does not cover shopt options
  shopt -s nullglob
  "$@"
  local status=$?
  eval "$restore"
  return "$status"
}

mkdir demo && cd demo || exit
touch a.txt b.txt
show() { echo "$1" *.txt; }
without_globbing show "expanded inside the call:"
without_globbing echo "written in the call itself:" *.txt
without_globbing bash -c 'exit 3'
echo "status passed through: $?"
echo "afterwards: noglob $([[ -o noglob ]] && echo on || echo off), nullglob $(shopt -q nullglob && echo on || echo off), and *.txt is" *.txt

expanded inside the call: *.txt
written in the call itself: a.txt b.txt
status passed through: 3
afterwards: noglob off, nullglob off, and *.txt is a.txt b.txt

local - restores the set table when the function returns, which covers noglob, but not the shopt table (§16.7 measured it), so nullglob is saved with shopt -p nullglob before the change and put back with eval afterwards. The status is saved in status before the eval, which would otherwise overwrite $?. Afterwards both options were off again and *.txt expanded normally.

The call without_globbing echo "…" *.txt still printed a.txt b.txt, because *.txt in the call is expanded by the caller, before without_globbing has run a single line — the option was off at that moment. Only an expansion that happens inside the call — like the one in show — sees the changed option. That is the general rule for every option-changing wrapper: it affects what the command does, not how its arguments were expanded. To pass a pattern through unexpanded, the caller has to quote it.

4. Am I in a subshell? Write in_subshell, which succeeds when the code calling it runs in a subshell, and use it to check every construct in §16.10's table: a plain call, ( ), $( ), both sides of a pipeline, { } and a background job.

Solution 
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # '$( )' is a label
in_subshell() { [[ $BASHPID != "$$" ]]; }
report() { if in_subshell; then echo "$1: in a subshell"; else echo "$1: in the script"; fi; }

report "plain call"
( report "( )" )
out=$(report '$( )'); echo "$out"
report "left of |" | cat
echo x | report "right of |"
{ report "{ }"; }
report "background &" & wait

plain call: in the script
( ): in a subshell
$( ): in a subshell
left of |: in a subshell
right of |: in a subshell
{ }: in the script
background &: in a subshell

in_subshell compares BASHPID, the ID of the process actually running, with $$, which is the script's ID in every subshell (§16.5). BASH_SUBSHELL would work too ((( BASH_SUBSHELL > 0 ))). The test has to be run where it is called — in a function, as here, or directly — and never by passing $BASHPID into a $( ), whose arguments are expanded in the subshell (§16.6).

The results match the table: ( ), $( ), both sides of the pipeline and the background job are subshells, and a plain call and a brace group are not. The background job is one because & must run the command while the script carries on, which needs a second process; §17 builds on that.

SECTION 17

Concurrency, Parallelism and Locking

A shell script is a natural coordinator of work: it starts programs, and nothing obliges it to start them one at a time. Put & after a command and the script carries on while the command runs, and a script that compresses forty log files, checks twenty hosts or builds six packages can do them side by side instead of in a queue. That is parallelism in the shell, and bash has everything it needs built in — background jobs, $!, the wait builtin, and since bash 5.1 wait -n -p, which is enough to write a proper job pool without any outside tool.

Running things at once brings three problems that a sequential script never has, and this section is organised around them. The first is accounting: a background job's exit status does not arrive by itself, and a script that starts ten jobs and never asks how they ended has quietly given up error handling (§17.1–§17.3). The second is control: how many jobs run at once, what a script can do with job control, and what the standard tools — xargs -P and GNU parallel — offer instead of a hand-written loop (§17.4–§17.6). The third is sharing: two processes that touch the same file, directory or temporary name can interleave in ways neither expected. That is a race condition, and the defences are operations the kernel performs in one step, lock files built on them, the kernel locks behind flock and lockf, and temporary files that no one else can predict (§17.7–§17.10). The section ends with the longer-lived kinds of process a script can start: coprocesses and named pipes, which a script talks to while they run (§17.11); jobs that must outlive the script, with nohup, disown, setsid and the daemon question (§17.12); and a bound on how long anything may take, with timeout (§17.13).

The editorial boundary: §12 owns signals, kill, trap and process groups, and §12.7 already showed how wait behaves when a trapped signal arrives; §16 owns subshells, what a child inherits, and the monitor option's effect on process groups (§16.7). This section uses all of them. Security is §18's, but one attack belongs here, because it is the reason mktemp exists: the symlink attack on a predictable temporary name (§17.10).

Every example was measured under bash 5.3 on macOS and bash 5.2 on Debian. They agree except in three places, each labelled where it appears: the padding of jobs output, which 5.3 widened (§17.1); a warning 5.2 prints when a second coprocess starts (§17.11); and the exit status xargs reports, which BSD and GNU define differently (§17.6). Three tools are not on every system — flock and setsid are Linux's util-linux, macOS ships lockf instead, and GNU parallel is a separate package everywhere — and each example that needs one says so in its first line. Concurrency is the one subject where the thing being taught is nondeterminism, so every example here was run twice and had to print the same thing both times. Where the order of events is the point, the jobs sleep for durations far enough apart that the durations decide the order, not the scheduler; where a race is the point, the example widens the window on purpose so that the losing interleaving happens every time. No example prints a duration or a process ID.

17.1 Background Jobs: & and $!

A background job is a command the shell starts without waiting for it to finish. The & operator — the control operator §2 introduced as a list terminator — is what makes one: where ; or a newline says "run this, wait for it, then go on", & says "run this, and go on at once".

# & starts a command and moves on without waiting for it
{ sleep 0.5; echo "background: finished"; } &
echo "script: carried on at once"
wait
echo "script: after wait"

script: carried on at once
background: finished
script: after wait

The script printed its own line first, although it came second in the source, because & did not wait for the brace group. The group ran in a subshell of its own, slept, and printed; wait, the subject of §17.2, held the script back until it had. Without that wait the script would have reached its end while the job was still sleeping — and a script that ends does not stop its background jobs (§12.4 measured three orphaned sleeps left running that way).

A background job always runs in a separate process: sleep 1 & forks a child for sleep, and { …; } & forks a subshell for the group, exactly as ( … ) would (§16.5). That has two consequences worth stating before anything else. Nothing a background job does to variables, the directory or options comes back to the script, because it is a copy. And the script's next line runs while the job may still be running, so the two share whatever they both touch — the terminal, files, the network — from then on.

Because the & operator ends a command the way ; does, it can separate several on one line, and each one it ends becomes its own job:

# & ends one command of a list, so each of these is its own background job
sleep 0.6 & sleep 0.3 & echo "three commands, two of them in the background"
jobs
wait

three commands, two of them in the background
[1]-  Running                    sleep 0.6 &
[2]+  Running                    sleep 0.3 &

sleep 0.6 & sleep 0.3 & echo … is three commands: two background jobs and one foreground one. The jobs builtin (§17.4) then listed the two jobs, numbered [1] and [2]. (bash 5.2 pads the Running column two spaces narrower than 5.3; the content is the same.) Mixing & with && needs care: a && b & puts the whole AND-list a && b in the background, because the & operator ends a whole list of commands joined by && and || (§2), which is usually what is meant — and a & && b is a syntax error.

The $! last background PID

When the shell starts a background job, it stores the job's process ID in the special parameter $!. The $! last background PID is the handle the script needs to wait for that job, signal it, or check whether it is still running, and it has one property that decides how every script must use it: each & overwrites it.

# $! is the PID of the most recent background job, and every & replaces it
echo "before any job: ${!-<not set>}"
sleep 0.2 & first=$!
sleep 0.2 & second=$!
echo "the first job is still known by the saved PID: $([[ $first != "$second" ]] && echo yes)"
true                            # a foreground command does not touch $!
[[ $! == "$second" ]] && echo "\$! still holds the second job's PID"
wait "$first" "$second"

before any job: <not set>
the first job is still known by the saved PID: yes
$! still holds the second job's PID

Before any job, $! was not set at all. Each & replaced it: the first PID survived only because the script copied it into first on the same line. A foreground command such as true leaves $! alone, so the value lasts until the next & — and in a loop, that means the next iteration. The rule is therefore to save $! immediately, on the same line as the & or the next one, into a variable or an array: worker & pids+=("$!"). Code that starts two jobs and then reads $! has lost the first one.

For a background pipeline, $! holds the PID of the pipeline's last command:

# For a background pipeline, $! is the LAST command in it
sleep 0.3 | bash -c 'echo "$$" > last.pid; sleep 0.3' &
sleep 0.1
[[ $! == "$(<last.pid)" ]] && echo "\$! is the pipeline's last command"
wait

$! is the pipeline's last command

The last command wrote its own $$ — its own PID, since it is a separate bash — to last.pid, and it matched $!. That is consistent with the way a pipeline's exit status is its last command's (§11.7): wait "$!" on a background pipeline returns the last command's status.

A background job reads /dev/null

A background job in a script does not share the script's standard input. The bash manual: when a command is run asynchronously and job control is not active, its standard input is redirected from /dev/null. Measured:

# A background job in a script reads /dev/null, not the script's standard input
printf 'cat & wait\n' > plain.sh
printf 'cat < /dev/stdin & wait\n' > explicit.sh
echo "from the pipe" | bash plain.sh;    echo "[plain &: read nothing]"
echo "from the pipe" | bash explicit.sh; echo "[explicit < /dev/stdin]"

[plain &: read nothing]
from the pipe
[explicit < /dev/stdin]

The script plain.sh was given a line on its standard input and started cat &, and cat read nothing: its input was /dev/null. The rule exists because a background job and the foreground script reading the same input would take lines from each other unpredictably. With an explicit redirection — cat < /dev/stdin &, or < file — the job reads what it was given, and the line arrived. So a background job that is meant to consume input needs that input redirected into it explicitly, and a background job that prompts a person will find no one there.

17.2 The wait Builtin

The wait builtin is how a script collects its background jobs: it blocks until a job finishes and returns that job's exit status. The wait builtin is a builtin by necessity, since only the shell knows its own children. A process's exit status is delivered to its parent, and only to its parent, so wait is not a convenience — it is the only way the script ever learns how a job ended. §16.5 used it for one subshell, and §12.7 showed how a trapped signal interrupts it. This subsection covers its forms.

wait with no arguments

With no arguments, wait waits for every background job the shell started, and then returns 0 — whatever the jobs returned:

# wait with no arguments waits for every job, and returns 0 whatever they returned
( sleep 0.2; exit 3 ) &
( sleep 0.1; exit 5 ) &
wait
echo "wait returned $?"

wait returned 0

Both jobs failed, with 3 and 5, and wait returned 0. That is documented behaviour, and it is the single most common mistake in parallel shell scripts: for f in *.log; do gzip "$f" & done; wait looks like it checks something and checks nothing. A bare wait is right for "let everything finish before the script goes on", and wrong wherever the outcome matters. The outcome needs a PID.

How to wait for a specific PID

wait PID waits for one job and returns its exit status. To wait for a specific PID is how a script gets an exit status back from a background job, and the example shows its three details:

# wait PID returns that job's exit status
( sleep 0.2; exit 3 ) & slow=$!
( exit 5 ) & fast=$!
sleep 0.4                     # both have finished before either wait runs
wait "$slow"; echo "wait for the slow job:          $?"
wait "$fast"; echo "wait for the fast job:          $?"
wait "$fast"; echo "wait for it again:              $?"
wait "$slow" "$fast"; echo "wait for both (the last one's): $?"

wait for the slow job:          3
wait for the fast job:          5
wait for it again:              5
wait for both (the last one's): 5

The status is kept after the job ends. Both jobs had finished before either wait ran, and both statuses — 3 and 5 — were still reported: bash records a finished job's status until the script collects it, so there is no race between a job ending and the script asking. Asking again returns the same status: bash 5.3 and 5.2 both answered 5 to a second wait for the same PID. POSIX only promises the first answer, so a script should collect each status once and store it, not rely on asking twice. And wait with several PIDs waits for all of them and returns the status of the last one named — 5 here, although the first failed with 3. So wait "$a" "$b" is fine for "both have finished" and no good for "both succeeded".

wait can only wait for the shell's own children:

# Only the shell's own children can be waited for
sleep 0.2 & pid=$!
bash -c 'wait "$1" 2>/dev/null; echo "a different shell waiting for it: status $?"' _ "$pid"
wait 1; echo "PID 1: status $?"
wait "$pid"; echo "the script's own child:            status $?"

a different shell waiting for it: status 127
example.sh: line 4: wait: pid 1 is not a child of this shell
PID 1: status 127
the script's own child:            status 0

A second bash, given the script's job PID, could not wait for it: wait returned 127, the status for "no such child". PID 1 got the same answer, with the diagnostic pid 1 is not a child of this shell. A process can only collect the exit status of a process it started itself — which is also why a job started in a subshell, ( job & ), cannot be waited for by the script: its parent was the subshell, and the subshell is gone (§17.12 uses that on purpose).

wait -n: the next job to finish

wait -n (bash 4.3) waits for whichever job finishes next, and returns that job's status. It is the building block of a job pool, because it lets a script react to each job as it finishes instead of in the order they were started:

# wait -n returns when the NEXT job finishes, with that job's status
( sleep 0.9; exit 3 ) &
( sleep 0.3; exit 5 ) &
( sleep 0.6; exit 0 ) &
wait -n; echo "first to finish:  status $?"
wait -n; echo "second to finish: status $?"
wait -n; echo "third to finish:  status $?"
wait -n; echo "nothing left:     status $?"

first to finish:  status 5
second to finish: status 0
third to finish:  status 3
nothing left:     status 127

Three jobs were started in the order 3, 5, 0 and finished in the order of their durations — the one that exited 5 first. Each wait -n returned the next status in finishing order. When nothing was left, wait -n returned 127.

wait -n -p: which job finished

A status on its own does not say which job it belongs to. wait -p NAME (bash 5.1) stores the PID of the job whose status is being returned in the variable NAME, and with an associative array (§6) mapping PIDs to names, the script knows exactly what finished:

# wait -n -p NAME also says WHICH job finished (bash 5.1+)
declare -A name
( sleep 0.9; exit 3 ) & name[$!]=backup
( sleep 0.3; exit 5 ) & name[$!]=upload
( sleep 0.6; exit 0 ) & name[$!]=report

while true; do
  wait -n -p pid; status=$?
  [[ -n ${pid-} ]] || break               # no job was left to wait for
  echo "${name[$pid]} finished with status $status"
  unset pid
done
echo "loop ended: wait -n returned $status and set no PID"

upload finished with status 5
report finished with status 0
backup finished with status 3
loop ended: wait -n returned 127 and set no PID

wait -p needs bash 5.1; on an older bash wait -n alone returns statuses with no way to tell whose they are. name[$!]=backup on the same line as the & records each job under its PID the moment it starts. Each wait -n -p pid then set pid, and ${name[$pid]} turned it back into a name. The loop's exit test is [[ -n ${pid-} ]], not the status, for a reason the next example proves; unset pid at the end of each pass makes sure a stale value from the last job cannot pass the test.

wait -n also accepts PIDs, and then waits for the first of those to finish (bash 5.1):

# wait -n with PIDs waits for the first of THOSE to finish, ignoring the rest
( sleep 0.2; exit 4 ) & quick=$!
( sleep 0.8; exit 6 ) & a=$!
( sleep 0.5; exit 7 ) & b=$!
wait -n "$a" "$b"; echo "first of a and b: status $?"
wait "$quick"; echo "the quick job, collected later: status $?"
wait

first of a and b: status 7
the quick job, collected later: status 4

The quick job finished first, but wait -n "$a" "$b" ignored it and returned 7, from b, the first of the two it was asked about. The quick job's status, 4, was still there to collect later.

127 is ambiguous

wait -n returns 127 when there is nothing left to wait for. But 127 is also what a job returns when its command is not found (§11.4), so the status alone cannot tell the two apart:

# A job can itself return 127, so the status alone cannot mean "nothing left"
no-such-command 2>/dev/null &
wait -n -p pid; echo "status $?, pid set: ${pid:+yes}"
unset pid
wait -n -p pid; echo "status $?, pid set: ${pid:-no}"

status 127, pid set: yes
status 127, pid set: no

The first wait -n returned 127 because the job's command did not exist — and set pid. The second returned 127 because nothing was left, and set nothing. That is why a loop over wait -n should end on "no PID was set", as the wait-n-p example did, and never on while wait -n, which also stops at the first job that fails — every non-zero status ends a while — and leaves the rest uncollected.

17.3 Launching Is Not Succeeding: Collecting Exit Statuses

The status of a & is 0: it reports that the launch succeeded, not the program. §2 stated that in its table; here is the measurement:

# The status of `cmd &` says the launch worked, never what the command did
no-such-command 2>/dev/null &
echo "status of the & line: $?"
wait "$!"; echo "status from wait:    $?"
false &
echo "status of the & line: $?"
wait "$!"; echo "status from wait:    $?"

status of the & line: 0
status from wait:    127
status of the & line: 0
status from wait:    1

A command that does not exist, started with &, gave the & line a status of 0. So did false. The real statuses — 127 and 1 — only arrived through wait. The consequence reaches every part of error handling: set -e cannot fail on a background job, because the line that started it succeeded; if cmd & is always true; || after a & never runs. §11.8 showed the one place set -e does act — on wait "$!"'s status. A background job's status exists only where the script waits for it, so collecting exit statuses is not an optional extra of parallel scripting, it is the error handling.

Wait for each PID, in launch order

The simplest correct pattern starts every job, records each PID in an array alongside what it was, then waits for each PID in turn:

# Start every job, then wait for each one by PID and keep its status
work() { sleep "$2"; [[ $1 != bad ]]; }       # a job that fails when its name is "bad"

declare -a pids names
for job in alpha bad gamma; do
  work "$job" 0.2 &
  pids+=("$!") names+=("$job")
done

failed=0
for i in "${!pids[@]}"; do
  if wait "${pids[i]}"; then
    echo "${names[i]}: ok"
  else
    echo "${names[i]}: FAILED with status $?"
    failed=$(( failed + 1 ))
  fi
done
echo "$failed of ${#pids[@]} jobs failed"
(( failed == 0 ))

alpha: ok
bad: FAILED with status 1
gamma: ok
1 of 3 jobs failed

pids and names are parallel indexed arrays, filled on the same line as the & so that no PID is lost. The second loop waits for each PID in the order the jobs were started — not the order they finish, but that does not matter, because a finished job's status is kept (§17.2) and waiting for a job that has already ended returns at once. if wait "${pids[i]}" tests the status directly, and $? inside else is still that status. The script counted one failure, reported it by name, and the final (( failed == 0 )) gave the script an exit status of 1 — so whatever called this script learns that part of the work failed, which a bare wait would have hidden.

This is collecting exit statuses in its plainest form, and for a fixed, modest number of jobs it is the one to use: it works in every bash since 3, and it reports results in a stable order. Its limit is that it reports nothing until the first job in the list finishes, however long that takes.

Report each job as it finishes

With wait -n -p the same collection reports each job the moment it ends:

# The same, reporting each job the moment it finishes
work() { sleep "$2"; [[ $1 != bad ]]; }

declare -A name
work alpha 0.9 & name[$!]=alpha
work bad   0.3 & name[$!]=bad
work gamma 0.6 & name[$!]=gamma

failed=()
while (( ${#name[@]} > 0 )); do
  wait -n -p pid; status=$?
  (( status == 0 )) || failed+=("${name[$pid]}")
  echo "${name[$pid]} finished (status $status)"
  unset 'name[$pid]'
done
echo "failed: ${failed[*]:-none}"

bad finished (status 1)
gamma finished (status 0)
alpha finished (status 0)
failed: bad

The associative array name holds exactly the jobs still running: each is added at & and removed with unset 'name[$pid]' when collected, so ${#name[@]} counts the jobs outstanding and the loop ends when it reaches zero. The quotes in unset 'name[$pid]' stop the shell from treating the subscript as a glob pattern (§6.6). The report came in finishing order, the failing job first, and the failures were gathered into their own array for the summary. Collecting exit statuses this way costs one line more than the first pattern, and it is the basis of the job pool in §17.5.

Give each job its own output

Jobs that run at the same time and print to the same terminal interleave their output in whatever order the scheduler produces. A line printed by one echo or printf usually arrives whole, but lines from different jobs mix, and a job's error message ends up beside another job's progress report. The fix that keeps collecting exit statuses simple is to give each job its own output file, and print the files in a fixed order once everything has finished:

# Parallel jobs writing to one terminal interleave; give each its own file
fetch() { echo "$1: start"; sleep "$2"; echo "$1: done"; }
fetch first 0.6 > first.log 2>&1 & a=$!
fetch second 0.3 > second.log 2>&1 & b=$!
wait "$a" "$b"
cat first.log second.log

first: start
first: done
second: start
second: done

second finished first, but its output was printed second, after first's, because the files were printed in launch order. The job's standard error goes to the same file (2>&1), so its messages stay next to its output. In a real script the files belong in a mktemp -d directory that a trap removes (§12.3, §17.10); exercise 1 does exactly that.

17.4 Job Control in a Script

Job control is the shell feature that lets an interactive user stop a program with Ctrl-Z, send it to the background with bg, bring it back with fg, and see what is running with jobs. It is on in an interactive shell and off in a script, and job control in a script is best understood by what it takes away and what is left. Nearly everything a script needs from its jobs works without it; job control in a script adds only the commands that hand a terminal back and forth.

The jobs builtin and job specifications

The jobs builtin works with or without job control. It lists the shell's background jobs, each with a job number:

# The jobs builtin lists the shell's jobs, with a number for each
sleep 3 & sleep 3 & sleep 0.1 &
sleep 0.4
jobs
echo "--- jobs -r, running only:"
jobs -r
echo "--- the current job, %%:"
jobs %%
echo "--- jobs -p gives one PID per job: $(jobs -p | wc -l | tr -d ' ') PIDs"
kill %1 %2
wait

[1]   Running                    sleep 3 &
[2]-  Running                    sleep 3 &
[3]+  Done                       sleep 0.1
--- jobs -r, running only:
[1]-  Running                    sleep 3 &
[2]+  Running                    sleep 3 &
--- the current job, %%:
[2]+  Running                    sleep 3 &
--- jobs -p gives one PID per job: 2 PIDs

Each line shows the job number in brackets, a marker, the state and the command. + marks the current job — the most recently started — and - the previous one. The third job had finished by the time jobs ran, so it was listed once as Done and then dropped from the table: the second jobs call listed only the two still running. (As in §17.1, bash 5.2 pads the state column differently.) The options select and reshape: jobs -r lists only running jobs, jobs -s only stopped ones, jobs -l adds each PID, and jobs -p prints only PIDs, one per job, which is the form §12.4's cleanup trap passed to kill.

A job specification names a job where a PID would go, in kill, wait, fg, bg, disown and jobs: %1 is job 1, %% or %+ is the current job, %- the previous one, and %sleep the job whose command starts with sleep — which is an error if two do, as here, where all three commands were sleep. The script's kill %1 %2 used job specifications to stop the two long sleeps before waiting. They are convenient at a prompt; in a script, a saved PID is clearer and does not depend on how many jobs were started before it.

fg and bg need job control

The job-control commands proper — fg, which moves a job to the foreground and waits for it, and bg, which resumes a stopped job in the background — refuse to run in a script:

# fg and bg need job control, which a script does not have
sleep 0.3 &
fg %1; echo "fg: status $?"
bg %1; echo "bg: status $?"
wait

example.sh: line 3: fg: no job control
fg: status 1
example.sh: line 4: bg: no job control
bg: status 1

Both printed no job control and returned 1. In a script there is no terminal to hand to a foreground job and no user to press Ctrl-Z, so the commands have nothing to do. The monitor option, set -m, turns job control on, and then they work:

# set -m turns job control on, and fg, bg and stopped jobs work
set -m
sleep 0.3 &
fg %1; echo "fg waited for the job, and returned $?"

sleep 5 &
kill -s STOP %1; sleep 0.2
jobs
bg %1; sleep 0.2
jobs
kill %1
wait

sleep 0.3
fg waited for the job, and returned 0
[1]+  Stopped                    sleep 5
[1]+ sleep 5 &
[1]+  Running                    sleep 5 &

With set -m, fg %1 printed the job's command, as it does at a prompt, then waited for it and returned its status. kill -s STOP %1 stopped the second job — the signal Ctrl-Z sends is SIGTSTP, and SIGSTOP is its uncatchable twin — and jobs showed it as Stopped. bg %1 sent it SIGCONT, printed the job with an & the way an interactive shell does, and jobs showed it Running again. Measured on a real terminal as well: Ctrl-Z on a foreground sleep 300 reported Stopped, bg printed [1]+ sleep 300 &, and jobs then showed it running.

Job control in a script: what set -m changes

So a script can turn job control on. It rarely should, and it helps to know exactly what set -m changes, because each change is something §12 or §16 measured:

  • Each job runs in a process group of its own (§16.7 measured the process group IDs). A signal the terminal sends to its foreground group — Ctrl-C's SIGINT — reaches only that group, not these jobs.
  • Background jobs stop ignoring SIGINT and SIGQUIT, which a script's jobs otherwise do (§12.8), so a SIGINT sent to them directly now works, and they read their real standard input rather than /dev/null (§17.1).
  • lastpipe stops working (§16.8).

The genuine uses in a script are two. A script that wants to send a signal to a job and all its descendants benefits from the job being a process group: §12.9 used set -m for exactly that, then kill -- -"$pid". And a script that drives an interactive program may need the terminal handed over. For everything else — starting work, waiting for it, collecting statuses — a script needs no job control at all: &, $!, wait and jobs all work without it. Leave job control in a script off unless one of those two needs is the reason, and when it is, turn it on for the lines that need it (set -m; … & pid=$!; set +m), as §12.9 did.

17.5 Limiting Concurrency: a Job Pool in Bash

The first parallel loop anyone writes puts & inside a for loop, and it starts one job per item — all at once:

# One & per item starts everything at once, however many items there are
for n in $(seq 1 40); do sleep 0.5 & done
echo "jobs running at once: $(jobs -r | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"
wait

jobs running at once: 40

Forty items gave forty jobs running at the same moment. For forty sleeps that is harmless. For forty image conversions it means forty processes fighting over the same CPUs, each going slower than if they had queued, with forty times the memory in use; for four hundred downloads it means four hundred connections to one server, which is a denial-of-service attack by accident. Limiting concurrency — running at most N jobs at a time, and starting the next the moment one finishes — is what makes a parallel loop safe to point at a list of unknown length.

A job pool with wait -n

The structure is a counter of running jobs and one rule: before starting a job, if N are already running, wait for one to finish. With wait -n -p (§17.2), a job pool in bash is a dozen lines:

# A job pool: never more than max_jobs running; start the next as one finishes
max_jobs=2
declare -A name

reap() {                               # wait for one job, report it, forget it
  local pid
  wait -n -p pid
  echo "  ${name[$pid]} finished (status $?)"
  unset 'name[$pid]'
}

for spec in a:1.5 b:0.3 c:0.3 d:0.3 e:0.3; do
  (( ${#name[@]} < max_jobs )) || reap
  sleep "${spec#*:}" & name[$!]=${spec%%:*}
  echo "started ${spec%%:*}, ${#name[@]} running"
done
while (( ${#name[@]} > 0 )); do reap; done

started a, 1 running
started b, 2 running
  b finished (status 0)
started c, 2 running
  c finished (status 0)
started d, 2 running
  d finished (status 0)
started e, 2 running
  e finished (status 0)
  a finished (status 0)

name again holds exactly the running jobs, so ${#name[@]} is the count. Before each start, (( ${#name[@]} < max_jobs )) || reap waits for one job whenever the pool is full. Read the events against the durations: a takes five times as long as the others, and it never held anything up. b finished, and c started in its place; c finished, and d started; then e; and a, started first, finished last. The pool never had more than two jobs running — the count after every start was 2 — and it was never idle while there was work left. After the loop, while (( ${#name[@]} > 0 )); do reap; done collects the jobs still running.

The obvious simpler design is batches: start N, wait for all of them, start the next N.

# The simpler alternative: batches of max_jobs, each waiting for its slowest job
max_jobs=2
batch=0
for spec in a:1.5 b:0.3 c:0.3 d:0.3 e:0.3; do
  sleep "${spec#*:}" & batch=$(( batch + 1 ))
  if (( batch == max_jobs )); then
    wait; echo "batch done after ${spec%%:*}"; batch=0
  fi
done
wait; echo "last batch done"

batch done after b
batch done after d
last batch done

It is correct, and it is slow in exactly the case that matters. The first batch held a and b, and wait held the script until a, the slow one, finished, while one slot sat idle; every batch takes as long as its slowest job. Here that makes the whole run take the 1.5 seconds of a plus two more batches of 0.3, against the pool's 1.5 in total. A pool built on wait -n needs bash 4.3; -p needs 5.1. On an older bash, the portable fallback is a pool that polls — while (( $(jobs -rp | wc -l) >= max )); do sleep 0.1; done before each start — which works anywhere and costs a process and a pause per check.

How many at once: parallelism in the shell

The right N depends on what the jobs wait for. CPU-bound jobs — compression, image conversion, compiling — are limited by processor cores, and the usual starting point is one job per core:

# How many jobs? One per CPU is the usual start for CPU-bound work
cpus=$(getconf _NPROCESSORS_ONLN)
(( cpus > 0 )) && echo "getconf _NPROCESSORS_ONLN: a positive number, on macOS and Linux alike"
command -v nproc >/dev/null && (( $(nproc) == cpus )) && echo "nproc (GNU coreutils) agrees"

getconf _NPROCESSORS_ONLN: a positive number, on macOS and Linux alike
nproc (GNU coreutils) agrees

getconf _NPROCESSORS_ONLN prints the number of online processors on both macOS and Linux, and it is the portable spelling. nproc is GNU coreutils' command for the same number: present on Linux, absent from a stock macOS (this machine has it from Homebrew's coreutils, and the example checks for it before using it). The example prints no number, because the count differs on every machine; the probe asserts it is positive and that the two agree.

I/O-bound jobs — downloads, remote commands, database queries — spend their time waiting, so more of them than cores can run usefully, and the limit is set by what they wait on: a server's connection limit, an API's rate limit, a disk's throughput. Parallelism in the shell has one more cost worth measuring before choosing a large N: every job is at least one fork(), which §15.1 counted, so a thousand tiny jobs spend more time being started than working. Parallelism pays when each job is substantial. For a thousand tiny ones, one process that loops over all of them — an awk script, or a find -exec … + — beats any pool.

The pool as a function

A pool that is written once and reused keeps the running set, the failures and the status in one place:

# The pool as a reusable function: run_pool MAX COMMAND ARG..., one job per ARG
run_pool() {
  local max=$1 cmd=$2 arg pid status failed=0
  shift 2
  local -A running=()
  for arg in "$@"; do
    if (( ${#running[@]} >= max )); then
      wait -n -p pid; status=$?
      (( status == 0 )) || { echo "$cmd ${running[$pid]}: status $status" >&2; failed=1; }
      unset 'running[$pid]'
    fi
    "$cmd" "$arg" & running[$!]=$arg
  done
  while (( ${#running[@]} > 0 )); do
    wait -n -p pid; status=$?
    (( status == 0 )) || { echo "$cmd ${running[$pid]}: status $status" >&2; failed=1; }
    unset 'running[$pid]'
  done
  return "$failed"
}

check_host() { sleep 0.2; [[ $1 != *.invalid ]]; }
run_pool 3 check_host a.example b.example c.invalid d.example e.example
echo "run_pool returned $?"

check_host c.invalid: status 1
run_pool returned 1

run_pool 3 check_host a.example b.example … runs check_host once per argument, three at a time. The running set is local -A (§9), so nothing leaks into the caller. Each failure is reported on standard error the moment it is collected, with the argument that caused it, and the function returns 1 if anything failed — so run_pool … || exit works the way a single command would. The command runs in the background as a subshell of the script, so it can be a function (check_host is one) — the advantage a bash pool has over xargs, which §17.6 shows.

17.6 xargs -P and GNU parallel

Two standard tools run a command over a list in parallel, and both are worth knowing before writing a pool by hand.

xargs -P

xargs reads items from its standard input and runs a command with them as arguments. xargs -P N runs up to N of those commands at once, and with -n 1 each command gets one item:

# xargs -P runs up to N commands at once; -n 1 gives each one argument
cat > work.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
sleep 0.2
echo "processed $1"
EOF
chmod +x work.sh
printf '%s\n' alpha beta gamma delta | xargs -P 3 -n 1 ./work.sh | sort

processed alpha
processed beta
processed delta
processed gamma

Four items ran three at a time. The output is sorted in the example because xargs -P makes no promise about order: each command's output goes straight to the shared standard output as it is produced, and the finishing order decides the rest. Both GNU and BSD xargs support -P, and -P 0 means "as many at once as possible" in both — the unbounded loop of §17.5 again, so avoid it.

xargs's error reporting is where it falls short of a pool. It reports failure as one status for the whole run:

# xargs fails if any command failed, but cannot say which one
cat > work.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
[[ $1 != beta ]]
EOF
chmod +x work.sh
if printf '%s\n' alpha beta gamma | xargs -P 2 -n 1 ./work.sh; then echo "xargs succeeded"
else echo "one command failed, so xargs failed"; fi
if printf '%s\n' alpha gamma | xargs -P 2 -n 1 ./work.sh; then echo "none failed: xargs succeeded"; fi
printf '%s\n' alpha | xargs -n 1 ./no-such-script 2>/dev/null
echo "the command could not be found: xargs status $?"

one command failed, so xargs failed
none failed: xargs succeeded
the command could not be found: xargs status 127

When one command failed, xargs failed; when none did, it succeeded; when the command could not be found, it returned 127 — the same on both systems. But the non-zero status for "a command failed" is not portable. GNU xargs returns 123, and BSD xargs, which macOS ships, returns 1 (measured: the same run gave 123 on Debian and 1 on macOS; the BSD manual says so). A command that exits with 255 makes both stop reading input and start no more commands — GNU then returns 124, BSD 1 — and so does a command killed by a signal (GNU 125, BSD 1). None of those statuses says which item failed. When that matters, have each command report its own failure on standard error, or use a pool.

Items that are file names need the NUL-separated form, because xargs otherwise splits its input on blanks and newlines and treats quotes specially (§14.9):

# With file names, -0 and find -print0, so a space or newline cannot split a name
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # $1 is expanded by the child bash
mkdir in && cd in || exit
touch 'plain.txt' 'with space.txt' $'with\nnewline.txt'
find . -name '*.txt' -print0 | xargs -0 -P 2 -n 1 bash -c 'printf "%q\n" "${1#./}"' _ | sort

$'with\nnewline.txt'
plain.txt
with\ space.txt

find -print0 ends each name with a NUL byte, and xargs -0 splits on NUL and nothing else, so the name with a space and the name with a newline each arrived whole; %q shows them unambiguously. This pairing is the one safe way to feed file names to xargs, with or without -P.

xargs runs programs, found on PATH; it cannot see the script's functions, because it is a separate process that execs what it runs (§16.2):

# xargs runs programs, not functions; export the function and run it in bash -c
process() { echo "processed $1"; }
printf '%s\n' a b | xargs -n 1 process 2>&1 | sed 's/^[^:]*xargs: /xargs: /'
export -f process
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # $1 is expanded by the child bash
printf '%s\n' a b | xargs -P 2 -n 1 bash -c 'process "$1"' _ | sort

xargs: process: No such file or directory
processed a
processed b

xargs -n 1 process failed with No such file or directory: there is no program called process. The fix is export -f (§16.4) and a bash -c wrapper that receives the item as $1, which also keeps the item out of the command string — writing bash -c "process {}" with -I {} would paste the file name into code, which is an injection hole (§18). The function then runs in a new bash per item, which costs a process each time.

GNU parallel

GNU parallel is a separate program — not part of GNU coreutils or findutils — installed as the parallel package on Linux distributions and from Homebrew on macOS. (Debian's moreutils package also ships a different, much simpler command called parallel; check parallel --version.) It does what xargs -P does, with three differences that matter:

# Linux only: GNU parallel is a separate package on every system
parallel --will-cite -j 3 'sleep 0.{}; echo "job {} done"' ::: 3 1 2
echo "--- with --keep-order:"
parallel --will-cite -j 3 --keep-order 'sleep 0.{}; echo "job {} done"' ::: 3 1 2

job 1 done
job 2 done
job 3 done
--- with --keep-order:
job 3 done
job 1 done
job 2 done

{} is replaced by each argument after :::, and -j 3 is the limit. Without options, output comes out in finishing order, like xargs; --keep-order prints each job's output in the order of the arguments instead, although the jobs still run in parallel. --will-cite silences the request to cite the program in academic work, which parallel otherwise prints until it has been acknowledged once with parallel --citation.

The second difference is that parallel groups output: it holds each job's output until the job finishes, and prints it in one piece, so two jobs never interleave:

# Linux only: GNU parallel is a separate package on every system
job() { echo "$1: start"; sleep "$2"; echo "$1: end"; }
export -f job
parallel --will-cite -j 2 --colsep ' ' job '{1}' '{2}' ::: 'slow 0.4' 'fast 0.1'

fast: start
fast: end
slow: start
slow: end

The slow job started first and printed slow: start long before fast finished, but that line was held back until slow was done, so each job's lines came out together. --colsep ' ' split each argument into the fields {1} and {2}, and the exported function job ran in the shell parallel starts for each job.

The third difference is the exit status, which counts failures:

# Linux only: GNU parallel is a separate package on every system
parallel --will-cite -j 2 '[[ {} != *bad* ]]' ::: ok1 bad1 ok2 bad2
echo "two jobs failed:       parallel status $?"
parallel --will-cite -j 1 --halt now,fail=1 'echo "ran {}"; [[ {} != bad ]]' ::: a bad c 2>/dev/null
echo "--halt now,fail=1:     parallel status $?"

two jobs failed:       parallel status 2
ran a
ran bad
--halt now,fail=1:     parallel status 1

Two jobs failed, and parallel returned 2 — the number of failed jobs; its manual reserves 101 for "more than 100 failed" and 255 for other errors. --halt now,fail=1 stops everything at the first failure, killing running jobs, so c never ran; --halt soon,fail=1 would let running jobs finish instead. All three examples were measured with GNU parallel 20240222 on Debian.

Which to use

For a list of files and a command that is a program, find -print0 | xargs -0 -P "$(getconf _NPROCESSORS_ONLN)" -n 1 cmd is available everywhere and needs nothing installed. When output must stay grouped or ordered, when failures must be counted, or when the work is spread over several machines (parallel's -S), GNU parallel is the tool — on systems where installing it is acceptable. When the work is a shell function, when each failure must be reported by name, or when nothing may be installed, the pool of §17.5 is short enough to write and does all three.

17.7 Race Conditions and Atomicity

A race condition is a bug whose outcome depends on the timing of two things that run at the same time. Two scripts, two parallel jobs, or a script and a copy of itself started by cron a minute later each do something correct on their own; run together, they interleave, and the result is one that neither would produce alone. Race conditions are the defining bug of concurrent code, because the interleaving that breaks things may happen once in ten thousand runs, and every test before that one passes.

Every example in this subsection widens the window on purpose: a sleep between two steps turns a gap of microseconds, which a race needs luck to hit, into one of a fifth of a second, which it hits every time. That is how a race is demonstrated rather than hoped for, and it is also the fastest way to test for one in a script of your own: put a sleep between the check and the act, run two copies, and see whether the result is still right.

The lost update

The classic race is two processes updating a shared value by reading it, changing it, and writing it back:

# Two jobs add 1 to a counter file; the sleep widens the gap between read and write
echo 0 > counter
increment() {
  local n
  n=$(<counter)          # read
  sleep 0.2              # ... anything that takes time ...
  echo $(( n + 1 )) > counter    # write
}
increment & increment &
wait
echo "two increments, counter is $(<counter)"

two increments, counter is 1

Two increments, and the counter says 1. Both jobs read 0, both waited, both wrote 0 + 1. The second write did not add to the first; it replaced it. That is a lost update, and the sleep did not create it — it only made it certain. Without the sleep the two jobs would usually run one after the other and the counter would usually say 2, which is the dangerous version: correct in testing, wrong in production under load.

Check, then act

The second classic race is deciding on stale information. "If nobody holds the lock, take it" looks like one step and is two — a check and an act — and another process can pass the same check in between:

# "If nobody holds the lock, take it" is two steps, and both jobs pass the check
claim() {
  if [[ ! -e run.lock ]]; then          # check
    sleep 0.2
    echo "$1" > run.lock                 # act
    echo "$1: I hold the lock"
  fi
}
{ claim first & claim second & wait; } | sort      # sorted: which prints first varies

first: I hold the lock
second: I hold the lock

Both jobs checked that run.lock did not exist, both found it absent, and both created it and believed they held the lock. §10.5 pointed at exactly this line: [[ -e run.lock ]] || echo "$$" > run.lock has a gap between the test and the redirection, and a lock with a gap in it is not a lock. The same shape — test for a file, then create it; test a directory is empty, then remove it; test a process is running, then signal it — is behind most race conditions in shell scripts. §18 returns to it as a security problem, the TOCTOU ("time of check to time of use") bug, where the second process is an attacker.

Atomicity: one step, for exactly one caller

The fix for check-then-act is to have no gap: an operation that checks and acts in one indivisible step, so that when several processes attempt it at once, exactly one succeeds and every other one fails and knows it. That property is atomicity, and a shell script does not implement it — it cannot, since each line is a separate system call — but it can use operations the kernel already performs atomically:

# Operations the kernel does in one step: each succeeds for exactly one caller
mkdir lock.d && echo "mkdir:            created"
mkdir lock.d 2>/dev/null || echo "mkdir again:      refused (status $?)"

set -o noclobber
echo 1 > lock.f && echo "> with noclobber: created"
# shellcheck disable=SC2320  # $? is the brace group's status
{ echo 2 > lock.f; } 2>/dev/null || echo "> again:          refused (status $?)"
set +o noclobber

ln -s target lock.l && echo "ln -s:            created"
ln -s target lock.l 2>/dev/null || echo "ln -s again:      refused (status $?)"

mkdir:            created
mkdir again:      refused (status 1)
> with noclobber: created
> again:          refused (status 1)
ln -s:            created
ln -s again:      refused (status 1)

Each of the three created something the first time and was refused the second, with a non-zero status:

  • mkdir creates a directory, or fails if the name exists. The kernel does the check and the creation as one operation.
  • > with noclobber (§10.5) opens a file with O_CREAT|O_EXCL: create it, or fail if it exists. Plain > has no such check.
  • ln -s (and ln) creates a link, or fails if the name exists.

A fourth atomic operation is the one that makes replacing a file safe: rename(), which is what mv does when source and destination are on the same filesystem. It changes which file a name refers to in one step, so anyone opening the name gets either the old file or the new one, never a mixture. Across filesystems, mv has to copy and delete instead, and that is not atomic — which is why a temporary file meant to replace another must be created in the same directory as its target, not in /tmp.

Readers and half-written files

That last point deserves its own example, because it is the race a single script meets most often, with no second copy of itself involved: a program reads a configuration file at the moment another rewrites it.

# A reader can see a file half-written, because > empties it first
echo "port=80 host=old" > config
{ echo "port=8080"; sleep 0.4; echo "host=new"; } > config &
sleep 0.2
echo "while writing in place: $(tr '\n' ' ' < config)"
wait

echo "port=80 host=old" > config
{
  tmp=$(mktemp config.XXXXXX)
  { echo "port=8080"; sleep 0.4; echo "host=new"; } > "$tmp"
  mv -f -- "$tmp" config                # rename: the name changes in one step
} &
sleep 0.2
