echo "while writing a copy:   $(tr '\n' ' ' < config)"
wait
echo "after the rename:       $(tr '\n' ' ' < config)"

while writing in place: port=8080 
while writing a copy:   port=80 host=old 
after the rename:       port=8080 host=new

In the first half the writer rewrote config in place, and a reader that looked in the middle saw port=8080 and no host line — a file that was never valid. > empties the file before the first byte is written (§10.2), so for the whole time the writer is working, the file is incomplete. In the second half the writer built the new content in a temporary file beside it and then renamed that over config. A reader in the middle saw the complete old file; afterwards, the complete new one. Write to a temporary file in the same directory, then mv it into place — that is atomicity applied to file contents, and it is how configuration management tools, package managers and editors save files. §17.10 adds the details that make the temporary file safe, and exercise 3 turns it into a function.

The rename has a consequence that surprises people once:

# A reader that opened the old file keeps reading the old file
printf 'version 1\n' > config
exec {r}< config                      # a reader opens it, then is slow
printf 'version 2\n' > new && mv -f new config
echo "already open:   $(cat <&"$r")"
echo "opened again:   $(<config)"
exec {r}<&-

already open:   version 1
opened again:   version 2

A reader that had opened config before the rename kept reading the old file. The rename changed which file the name refers to; a descriptor refers to the file itself, which lives on (unnamed) until its last descriptor is closed. That is why a long-running program must be told to reopen its configuration — the job §12.11's HUP handler does — and why a log file renamed by a rotation tool keeps receiving lines from any program that still has it open.

17.8 Lock Files: mkdir, noclobber and PID Files

A lock file is an agreement between cooperating processes: whoever creates a certain name first may proceed, and everyone else backs off or waits. It is the usual way to stop a cron job from overlapping a still-running copy of itself, or two deployments from running at once. The agreement is only as good as the operation that takes it, so a lock file must be created with one of the atomic operations of §17.7 — and cleaned up in a way that survives the script failing.

mkdir as a lock

Using mkdir as a lock is the most portable form: mkdir works identically on every Unix, needs no option, and fails if the directory exists.

# mkdir as a lock: exactly one of the contenders creates the directory
job() {
  if mkdir run.lock 2>/dev/null; then
    sleep 0.3
    echo "$1: got the lock and did the work"
    rmdir run.lock
  else
    echo "$1: the lock is taken, giving up"
  fi
}
job A & sleep 0.1; job B
wait

B: the lock is taken, giving up
A: got the lock and did the work

A created run.lock and did its work; B, starting while A held it, failed to create it and gave up. When A finished, it removed the directory with rmdir, releasing the lock. A directory also has room for information about the holder — a file inside it can record who holds the lock, which the full version below uses.

The noclobber lock

The noclobber lock uses set -o noclobber (set -C) so that > refuses to overwrite, and it writes the holder's PID into the lock file in the same step that creates it:

# noclobber lock: create the file only if it does not exist, and write the PID into it
lock=run.lock
take_lock() { ( set -o noclobber; echo "$BASHPID" > "$lock" ) 2>/dev/null; }

take_lock && echo "first attempt:  got it; the file holds a PID: $([[ $(<"$lock") =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] && echo yes)"
take_lock || echo "second attempt: refused, the lock is held"

first attempt:  got it; the file holds a PID: yes
second attempt: refused, the lock is held

The subshell keeps noclobber from leaking into the rest of the script (§16.7), and 2>/dev/null hides the cannot overwrite existing file message on failure. $BASHPID rather than $$ is written because the redirection runs in the subshell, and the two are the same only at the top level (§12.9) — a script that wants its own PID in the file writes $$ instead. The first attempt created the file and recorded a PID; the second was refused. Unlike mkdir, noclobber is a shell feature, so this works in any POSIX shell but not from a program that is not a shell.

Signal-safe cleanup with a lock

A lock that is never released blocks every later run, so a lock is always paired with a trap that releases it (§12.3). The trap has to be set in the right place, and the wrong place is the natural one:

# Register the cleanup only AFTER taking the lock, or the loser removes the winner's
cat > wrong.sh <<'EOF'
trap 'rm -f run.lock' EXIT
( set -o noclobber; echo "$$" > run.lock ) 2>/dev/null || exit 1
sleep 0.4
EOF
cat > right.sh <<'EOF'
( set -o noclobber; echo "$$" > run.lock ) 2>/dev/null || exit 1
trap 'rm -f run.lock' EXIT
sleep 0.4
EOF
for script in wrong.sh right.sh; do
  bash "$script" & sleep 0.1
  bash "$script"; echo "$script: the second copy exited $?"
  [[ -e run.lock ]] && echo "  and the first copy's lock is still there" \
                    || echo "  and removed the first copy's lock on its way out"
  wait
done

wrong.sh: the second copy exited 1
  and removed the first copy's lock on its way out
right.sh: the second copy exited 1
  and the first copy's lock is still there

wrong.sh sets its EXIT trap first and then tries for the lock. The second copy failed to get the lock and exited — and its EXIT trap ran, and deleted the lock file, which belonged to the first copy. The first copy was still running, now unprotected: a third copy would have walked straight in. right.sh sets the trap only after the lock is taken, so a copy that never held the lock never removes it. Signal-safe cleanup with a lock follows two rules. Register the release only after acquiring, as right.sh does. And make the release an EXIT trap, which bash runs on exit, on a set -e failure and after a trapped signal (§12.3, §12.5), so that Ctrl-C or a kill does not leave the lock behind. The one thing no trap survives is SIGKILL (§12.1), which is where stale locks come from.

PID files

A PID file records the process ID of a running program so that other processes can find it — to signal it, or to see whether it is running. It is closely related to a lock file, and often the same file:

# A PID file records who is running; kill -0 decides whether it still is
cat > daemon.sh <<'EOF'
echo "$$" > daemon.pid
trap 'rm -f daemon.pid' EXIT
sleep 5
EOF
bash daemon.sh & sleep 0.2
pid=$(<daemon.pid)
kill -0 "$pid" && echo "daemon.pid names a running process"
kill "$pid"; wait
[[ -e daemon.pid ]] || echo "stopped with TERM: the EXIT trap removed daemon.pid"

daemon.pid names a running process
stopped with TERM: the EXIT trap removed daemon.pid

daemon.sh wrote its $$ to daemon.pid and registered its removal. Another process read the PID, confirmed with kill -0 (§12.9) that the process was running, and stopped it with SIGTERM; the trap removed the PID file on the way out. The classic weakness of a PID file is PID reuse: once a process has exited, the kernel may give its number to an unrelated process, and a stale PID file then points at a stranger. kill -0 would say "running", and a kill would signal the wrong program. Keeping the PID file only while the process is alive — removing it in the trap — is the main defence; checking that the process with that PID is the right program (ps -o comm= -p "$pid") is the second.

Stale locks

A stale lock is a lock whose holder has died without releasing it, usually because it was killed with SIGKILL, or the machine lost power. A lock file with a PID in it can detect that:

# A lock left by a process that died is stale: kill -0 says nobody is behind it
lock=run.lock
{ bash -c 'echo "$$" > run.lock; kill -s KILL "$$"'; } 2>/dev/null   # a holder dies uncleanly
echo "the lock file survived its owner: $([[ -e $lock ]] && echo yes)"

take_lock() {
  local pid
  ( set -o noclobber; echo "$BASHPID" > "$lock" ) 2>/dev/null && return 0
  pid=$(<"$lock") || return 1
  if kill -0 "$pid" 2>/dev/null; then
    return 1                                    # the holder is alive
  fi
  echo "stale lock: PID $([[ -n $pid ]] && echo '<pid>') is not running; removing it"
  rm -f -- "$lock"
  ( set -o noclobber; echo "$BASHPID" > "$lock" ) 2>/dev/null
}
take_lock && echo "lock taken"

the lock file survived its owner: yes
stale lock: PID <pid> is not running; removing it
lock taken

The holder wrote its PID and then died from SIGKILL, with no chance to clean up, and the lock file survived it. The next contender found the lock held, read the PID, and kill -0 failed: no such process. So the lock was stale, and it was removed and taken again. This is how most tools that use PID lock files recover.

The recovery has a race of its own, and it is worth being honest about. If two contenders find the same stale lock at the same moment, both decide it is stale; the first removes it and creates a new one; the second then removes that one — a live lock — and creates its own. Both proceed. The window is small, and for a cron job that runs every few minutes it is usually accepted, but it cannot be closed with file operations alone. The complete answer is a lock that the kernel releases when its holder dies, so that no lock is ever stale — which is what flock provides, in §17.9.

A complete portable lock

Put together — mkdir for atomicity, the holder's PID inside, stale detection, and the trap set only after acquiring — the lock is short enough to include in a script, and it runs unchanged on every Unix:

# A complete portable lock: mkdir, the owner's PID inside, stale detection, cleanup
lockdir=run.lock
acquire() {
  local pid
  if mkdir -- "$lockdir" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "$$" > "$lockdir/pid"
    trap 'rm -rf -- "$lockdir"' EXIT
    return 0
  fi
  pid=$(cat -- "$lockdir/pid" 2>/dev/null)
  if [[ -n $pid ]] && ! kill -0 "$pid" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "removing a stale lock" >&2
    rm -rf -- "$lockdir"
    acquire
    return
  fi
  return 1
}

cat > job.sh <<'EOF'
source ./lock.sh
acquire || { echo "$1: already running, skipping this run"; exit 0; }
echo "$1: working"; sleep "$2"; echo "$1: done"
EOF
declare -f acquire > lock.sh; echo "lockdir=$lockdir" >> lock.sh

bash job.sh first 0.5 & sleep 0.2
bash job.sh second 0
wait
bash job.sh third 0

first: working
second: already running, skipping this run
first: done
third: working
third: done

first took the lock and began its work. second, started while first was working, found the lock held by a live process and skipped its run with status 0, which is the right answer for a cron job — overlap is expected, not an error. third, after first had finished and its trap had removed the directory, took the lock normally. The function stores the PID inside the directory with $$, since this is the script's own lock; a caller that runs acquire in a subshell would need $BASHPID. Exercise 2 builds the same lock into a run_once wrapper.

17.9 flock and lockf: Locks the Kernel Releases

A lock file is a convention: the lock is the file's existence, and a process that dies uncleanly leaves the convention behind it. A kernel lock is different in kind. The process asks the kernel to lock an open file (the flock(2) system call), and the kernel records the lock against that open file. When the last descriptor to it closes — because the process closed it, exited, or was killed with SIGKILL — the kernel releases the lock itself. There is no stale lock to detect and no cleanup to register, because there is nothing left over.

Two commands expose this to scripts, one per platform. flock is part of Linux's util-linux package, present on every mainstream distribution and absent from macOS. lockf ships with macOS and FreeBSD, and uses the same flock(2) call underneath. The two have different options but the same two forms: lock a file while running a command, or lock a descriptor the script holds open.

flock on Linux

The form to use in a script locks a descriptor that the script opens itself, and keeps it for as long as the script runs:

# Linux only: flock is util-linux, which macOS does not ship
cat > nightly.sh <<'EOF'
exec {lock_fd}>> nightly.lock
flock -n "$lock_fd" || { echo "$1: another run holds the lock"; exit 1; }
echo "$1: working"
sleep 0.4
echo "$1: done"
EOF
bash nightly.sh first & sleep 0.1
bash nightly.sh second; echo "second exited $?"
wait
bash nightly.sh third

first: working
second: another run holds the lock
second exited 1
first: done
third: working
third: done

exec {lock_fd}>> nightly.lock opens the lock file for the rest of the script on a descriptor bash chooses (§10.8); >> rather than > so that opening it never empties anything, which matters if the file doubles as a PID file. flock -n "$lock_fd" asks for an exclusive lock on that descriptor and, because of -n, fails at once if it is held instead of waiting. first took it; second, started while first held it, was refused and exited 1; third, after first had exited, took it. Nothing released the lock explicitly — first exiting closed the descriptor, and the kernel did the rest. That is the whole of it: two lines at the top of a script, no trap, no stale locks.

flock's options cover the other behaviours a lock needs:

# Linux only: flock is util-linux, which macOS does not ship
flock app.lock sleep 0.5 &
sleep 0.1
flock -n app.lock echo "never printed";            echo "-n, busy:            status $?"
flock -n -E 75 app.lock echo "never printed";      echo "-n -E 75, busy:      status $?"
flock -w 0.1 app.lock echo "never printed";        echo "-w 0.1, timed out:   status $?"
flock -w 2 app.lock echo "waited, then ran";       echo "-w 2:                status $?"
flock app.lock false;                              echo "the command's own:   status $?"
flock -s shared.lock sleep 0.3 &
sleep 0.1
flock -n -s shared.lock echo "a second shared lock is granted at once"
flock -n    shared.lock echo "never printed" || echo "an exclusive lock is refused while it is shared"
wait

-n, busy:            status 1
-n -E 75, busy:      status 75
-w 0.1, timed out:   status 1
waited, then ran
-w 2:                status 0
the command's own:   status 1
a second shared lock is granted at once
an exclusive lock is refused while it is shared

Here flock FILE COMMAND, the second form, holds the lock for the duration of one command. flock -n fails immediately with status 1 when the lock is held. -E 75 changes that status, so that "busy" can be told apart from the command's own failure — 75 is EX_TEMPFAIL, the conventional "try again later". -w SECONDS waits up to that long: 0.1 seconds was not enough, 2 was, and the command then ran. Without -n or -w, flock waits as long as it takes. Once the lock is taken, flock's status is the command's, 1 for false. And -s takes a shared lock: any number of processes may hold one together — readers, typically — while an exclusive lock, the default, waits for all of them to finish.

The kernel releasing the lock is the point, so it is worth seeing happen:

# Linux only: flock is util-linux, which macOS does not ship
cat > holder.sh <<'EOF'
exec {fd}>> app.lock
flock -n "$fd" && echo "holder: locked"
exec sleep 5                      # the holder becomes sleep, still holding the descriptor
EOF
bash holder.sh & holder=$!
sleep 0.2
flock -n app.lock true; echo "while the holder runs:  status $?"
kill -s KILL "$holder"; wait "$holder" 2>/dev/null
flock -n app.lock true; echo "after SIGKILL:          status $?"

holder: locked
while the holder runs:  status 1
after SIGKILL:          status 0

The holder locked the file and then exec'd sleep — the process became sleep, still holding the descriptor (§16.2). While it ran, the lock was refused. After SIGKILL, which no trap can catch, the lock was free at once: the kernel closed the dead process's descriptors and released the lock with them.

lockf on macOS

macOS's lockf has the same two forms and different spellings:

# macOS: lockf FILE COMMAND holds a kernel lock on FILE while COMMAND runs
lockf -k app.lock sleep 0.4 &
sleep 0.1
lockf -t 0 app.lock echo "never printed"; echo "busy, -t 0:        status $?"
lockf -k -t 2 app.lock echo "waited for the lock, then ran"; echo "waited, -t 2:      status $?"
lockf -k app.lock false; echo "the command's own: status $?"

lockf: app.lock: already locked
busy, -t 0:        status 75
waited for the lock, then ran
waited, -t 2:      status 0
the command's own: status 1

lockf FILE COMMAND held the lock while sleep ran. -t 0 is lockf's flock -n: fail at once if the lock is held, with status 75 (EX_TEMPFAIL) and a message; -t 2 waited up to two seconds and then ran the command. When the lock is taken, the status is the command's own, 1 here. -k keeps the file after the command finishes. Without it lockf deletes the lock file on the way out — which reintroduces a race of the kind §17.8 described, since a newcomer may create a fresh file while another waiter still holds the old one open, so pass -k whenever several processes contend for one lock. -s makes it silent, reporting only through the status.

The descriptor form is lockf -t 0 FD, which locks a descriptor the script already has open, exactly like flock -n "$fd":

# macOS: lock a descriptor the script holds open, for the rest of the script
cat > nightly.sh <<'EOF'
exec {lock_fd}>> nightly.lock
lockf -s -t 0 "$lock_fd" || { echo "$1: another run holds the lock"; exit 1; }
echo "$1: working"
sleep 0.4
echo "$1: done"
EOF
bash nightly.sh first & sleep 0.1
bash nightly.sh second; echo "second exited $?"
wait
bash nightly.sh third

first: working
second: another run holds the lock
second exited 1
first: done
third: working
third: done

The script is the same as the flock one line for line, with lockf -s -t 0 "$lock_fd" in place of flock -n "$lock_fd", and the result is the same: first worked, second was refused and exited 1, third worked. And the kernel releases it the same way:

# The kernel releases the lock when its holder dies, however it dies
cat > holder.sh <<'EOF'
exec {fd}>> app.lock
lockf -s -t 0 "$fd" && echo "holder: locked"
exec sleep 5                      # the holder becomes sleep, still holding the descriptor
EOF
bash holder.sh & holder=$!
sleep 0.2
lockf -s -k -t 0 app.lock true; echo "while the holder runs:  status $?"
kill -s KILL "$holder"; wait "$holder" 2>/dev/null
lockf -s -k -t 0 app.lock true; echo "after SIGKILL:          status $?"

holder: locked
while the holder runs:  status 75
after SIGKILL:          status 0

A script meant to run on both systems can pick whichever command exists:

lock_or_exit() {        # lock_or_exit FD: take an exclusive lock on FD, or exit
  if command -v flock >/dev/null; then
    flock -n "$1" || { echo "${0##*/}: another copy is running" >&2; exit 1; }
  elif command -v lockf >/dev/null; then
    lockf -s -t 0 "$1" || { echo "${0##*/}: another copy is running" >&2; exit 1; }
  else
    echo "${0##*/}: neither flock nor lockf is available" >&2; exit 1
  fi
}
exec {lock_fd}>> "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/nightly.lock"
lock_or_exit "$lock_fd"

A child inherits the lock

A kernel lock belongs to the open file, and every process holding a descriptor to that file shares it. A background process started by the script inherits the descriptor (§16.1) — and with it, the lock:

# A background child inherits the locked descriptor, and keeps the lock
cat > leaky.sh <<'EOF'
exec {fd}>> app.lock
lockf -s -t 0 "$fd" || { echo "$1: busy"; exit 1; }
sleep 0.5 &                       # inherits $fd, so it holds the lock too
echo "$1: finished"
EOF
cat > careful.sh <<'EOF'
exec {fd}>> app.lock
lockf -s -t 0 "$fd" || { echo "$1: busy"; exit 1; }
sleep 0.5 {fd}>&- &               # closed in the child: the lock stays with the script
echo "$1: finished"
EOF
bash leaky.sh first;    bash leaky.sh second;    wait; sleep 0.6
bash careful.sh first;  bash careful.sh second

first: finished
second: busy
first: finished
second: finished

leaky.sh started a background sleep and exited, and the second copy found the lock held: the sleep had inherited the locked descriptor and kept the lock alive after the script that took it was gone. For a sleep that is half a second of confusion; for a server started by a deployment script, it is a lock held until the server stops, and every later deployment refused. careful.sh closed the descriptor for that one child with {fd}>&- in the command's own redirections (§10.6), so the child held nothing, and the second copy ran as soon as the first had finished. Measured the same way with flock on Linux:

# Linux only: flock is util-linux, which macOS does not ship
cat > leaky.sh <<'EOF'
exec {fd}>> app.lock
flock -n "$fd" || { echo "$1: busy"; exit 1; }
sleep 0.5 &                       # inherits $fd, so it holds the lock too
echo "$1: finished"
EOF
cat > careful.sh <<'EOF'
exec {fd}>> app.lock
flock -n "$fd" || { echo "$1: busy"; exit 1; }
sleep 0.5 {fd}>&- &               # closed in the child: the lock stays with the script
echo "$1: finished"
EOF
bash leaky.sh first;    bash leaky.sh second;    wait; sleep 0.6
bash careful.sh first;  bash careful.sh second

first: finished
second: busy
first: finished
second: finished

flock has an option for its command form that does the same thing: flock -o FILE COMMAND closes the lock's descriptor before running the command, so that the command's own children do not inherit it.

Two limits apply to every kernel lock. It is advisory: it stops only processes that also ask for it, and a program that opens the file and writes to it without calling flock is not prevented from doing so. The lock is a protocol between cooperating scripts, not a permission. And flock(2) locks on network filesystems have varied by system and version, so a lock meant to coordinate several machines belongs in a service designed for it rather than a file on NFS.

17.10 Temporary Files Done Securely

§12.3 introduced mktemp for the cleanup it needs. This subsection is about the name itself: why a temporary file must have an unpredictable name, where it should go, and what permissions it gets.

mktemp and mktemp -d

mktemp creates a new, empty file with a name no other process can predict, and prints the name; mktemp -d does the same for a directory:

# mktemp creates a new file with an unpredictable name, readable only by its owner
f=$(mktemp)
d=$(mktemp -d)
echo "file:      ${f##*/}" | sed 's/\.[^.]*$/.XXXXXX/'
echo "directory: ${d##*/}" | sed 's/\.[^.]*$/.XXXXXX/'
[[ -n $(find "$f" -perm 600) ]] && echo "the file's mode is 600, and it is ours: $([[ -O $f ]] && echo yes)"
[[ -n $(find "$d" -prune -perm 700) ]] && echo "the directory's mode is 700"
rm -f -- "$f"; rmdir -- "$d"

file:      tmp.XXXXXX
directory: tmp.XXXXXX
the file's mode is 600, and it is ours: yes
the directory's mode is 700

Both names ended in a random suffix (shown here as XXXXXX, since it changes every run). The file was created with mode 600 — readable and writable by its owner only — and owned by the user who ran the script; the directory with mode 700. Those modes are not from the umask; mktemp sets them, so a temporary file holding data from a private file does not become readable by other users on the way through. And mktemp creates the file with the same exclusive-create operation noclobber uses (§17.7), so if the random name already existed it would try another, rather than open what was there.

TMPDIR and the template form

By convention, the TMPDIR environment variable names the directory temporary files belong in, and /tmp is the default when it is unset. On a shared server TMPDIR often points to a per-user or per-job directory, and a container may set it to a writable volume, so honouring it matters. The portable way to honour it is a template:

# A template names the directory and the file, and every mktemp obeys it
mkdir scratch
TMPDIR=$PWD/scratch
f=$(mktemp "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/report.XXXXXX")
[[ $f == "$PWD"/scratch/report.* ]] && echo "the template put the file in \$TMPDIR: ${f##*/}" | sed 's/\.[^.]*$/.XXXXXX/'
[[ -k /tmp/ ]] && echo "/tmp has the sticky bit: only a file's owner can delete or rename it"

the template put the file in $TMPDIR: report.XXXXXX
/tmp has the sticky bit: only a file's owner can delete or rename it

mktemp "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/report.XXXXXX" names the directory and the file explicitly, replaces the Xs with random characters, and does the same on every system. The name also says what the file is, which helps whoever finds it after a crash.

The plain forms do not agree across systems, and the difference was measured, not assumed. With TMPDIR set to a directory of the script's choosing, GNU mktemp (Debian) created the file there; macOS's mktemp created it in the per-user directory under /var/folders/…/T/ instead, ignoring TMPDIR. Its manual says why: macOS prefers the per-user directory named by the system setting _CS_DARWIN_USER_TEMP_DIR, and falls back to TMPDIR only if that is unavailable. mktemp -t disagrees too: on macOS -t report is a prefix, and GNU rejects the same command, since its -t takes a template that must contain Xs. The template form avoids all of it. The last line of the example checked something else about /tmp: it has the sticky bit, so although anyone may create files there, only a file's owner may delete or rename it — which stops another user from removing your temporary file, and does nothing to stop the attack that follows.

The symlink attack

/tmp is shared by every user on the machine, and anyone may create any name in it that does not yet exist. That is the whole of the problem with a predictable temporary name, and the symlink attack is how it is exploited:

# A predictable name in a shared directory lets someone else choose where you write
mkdir shared                       # stands in for /tmp: anyone can create names here
echo "important data" > precious.txt

ln -s ../precious.txt shared/report.tmp      # another user plants a link first

echo "report output" > shared/report.tmp     # the script writes its "temporary" file
echo "precious.txt now holds: $(<precious.txt)"

precious.txt now holds: report output

The directory shared stands in for /tmp. The script meant to write its report to shared/report.tmp, a name it always uses. Another user, knowing that, created a symbolic link at that name first, pointing at precious.txt. The script's > opened the name, followed the link, and truncated and overwrote the file the link pointed to. On a real system the target is any file the victim can write — its own ~/.bashrc, or, for a script run as root, /etc/passwd — and the attacker never needed permission to touch it. A name built from $$ is no better: process IDs are small numbers that an attacker can plant links for in advance.

The defences are the ones already met, and the example measures them:

# mktemp never reuses a name; noclobber refuses to follow a planted link
mkdir shared
echo "important data" > precious.txt
ln -s ../precious.txt shared/report.tmp
ln -s ../not-yet.txt shared/other.tmp

tmp=$(mktemp shared/report.XXXXXX)
echo "report output" > "$tmp"
echo "with mktemp:              precious.txt holds: $(<precious.txt)"

set -o noclobber
# shellcheck disable=SC2320  # $? is the brace group's status
{ echo "report output" > shared/report.tmp; } 2>/dev/null || echo "noclobber, existing target: refused (status $?)"
# shellcheck disable=SC2320  # $? is the brace group's status
{ echo "report output" > shared/other.tmp; } 2>/dev/null || echo "noclobber, dangling link:   refused (status $?)"
[[ -e not-yet.txt ]] || echo "and not-yet.txt was not created"

with mktemp:              precious.txt holds: important data
noclobber, existing target: refused (status 1)
noclobber, dangling link:   refused (status 1)
and not-yet.txt was not created

mktemp chose a fresh name that did not exist, created it exclusively, and wrote there; the planted link was never touched and precious.txt kept its content. noclobber refused both planted links: the one pointing at an existing file (it would have overwritten it) and the dangling one pointing at a file that did not yet exist (bash's exclusive create fails on any existing name, links included), and not-yet.txt was not created. Of the two, mktemp is the one to use, since it also picks the name; noclobber is the protection for a name the script cannot choose. A secure temporary file is one whose name no one else could have created first, and a secure temporary file therefore comes down to three rules: create it with mktemp, never with a fixed or $$-based name in a shared directory; use the name mktemp printed, and never recreate the file by name after deleting it; and clean it up with a trap (§12.3). For many temporary files, create one mktemp -d directory — mode 700, so no one else can create names inside it — and put fixed names inside that.

Replacing a file through mktemp

§17.7's atomic replace — write a temporary file beside the target, then mv it over — has one trap, and it comes from the secure mode:

# Replacing a file through mktemp gives it mode 600; restore the mode you meant
printf 'port=80\n' > config; chmod 644 config
tmp=$(mktemp config.XXXXXX)
printf 'port=8080\n' > "$tmp"
mv -f -- "$tmp" config
[[ -n $(find config -perm 600) ]] && echo "after mv: config is mode 600, and other users can no longer read it"

tmp=$(mktemp config.XXXXXX)
printf 'port=9090\n' > "$tmp"
chmod 644 "$tmp" && mv -f -- "$tmp" config
[[ -n $(find config -perm 644) ]] && echo "chmod before mv: config is mode 644 again"

after mv: config is mode 600, and other users can no longer read it
chmod before mv: config is mode 644 again

The temporary file was created with mode 600, and mv moved that file into place, mode and all: config, which had been 644 and readable by other users, became private. A service running as a different user could then no longer read its own configuration. chmod on the temporary file before the mv gave the result mode 644 again. When the mode to keep is whatever the old file had, copy it with cp -p into the temporary file before writing, as exercise 3 does, since reading a mode portably needs stat, whose options differ between GNU and BSD.

17.11 Coprocesses and Named Pipes

The background jobs so far run on their own and report back once, through wait. Two mechanisms let a script talk to a process while it runs: a coprocess, which bash connects with two pipes, and a named pipe, which any processes can open by name.

The coproc keyword

The coproc keyword (bash 4.0) starts a command in the background, like &, with one pipe connected to its standard input and another to its standard output, and gives the script both ends:

# coproc starts a command with a pipe to its input and a pipe from its output
coproc UPPER { while IFS= read -r line; do printf '%s\n' "${line^^}"; done; }
upper_job=$UPPER_PID upper_in=${UPPER[1]}      # saved while they exist (see below)
echo "descriptors: write to ${UPPER[1]}, read from ${UPPER[0]}; the PID is in UPPER_PID" |
  sed 's/[0-9][0-9]*/N/g'

printf '%s\n' "hello" >&"${UPPER[1]}"
IFS= read -r reply <&"${UPPER[0]}"
echo "reply: $reply"

printf '%s\n' "and again" >&"${UPPER[1]}"
IFS= read -r reply <&"${UPPER[0]}"
echo "reply: $reply"

exec {upper_in}>&-            # close its input: the loop reads end-of-file and exits
wait "$upper_job"; echo "the coprocess exited $?"

descriptors: write to N, read from N; the PID is in UPPER_PID
reply: HELLO
reply: AND AGAIN
the coprocess exited 0

coproc UPPER { …; } created an array UPPER: ${UPPER[1]} is a descriptor that writes to the coprocess's input, and ${UPPER[0]} one that reads from its output. UPPER_PID holds its PID. The script wrote a line with >&"${UPPER[1]}", read the answer with read … <&"${UPPER[0]}", and did it again — one long-lived process, many exchanges. The first line after coproc saved the PID and the write descriptor's number in ordinary variables, for a reason the next example shows. Closing the write end with exec {upper_in}>&- — the {var}>&- form of §10.8, which closes the descriptor whose number is in upper_in — gave the loop end-of-file, it exited, and wait collected its status. (exec {UPPER[1]}>&-, naming the array element directly, also works in bash, but ShellCheck 0.11 does not recognise it: it reports the braces as literal text (SC1083) and the line as an exec of a command, so the examples close through a copy of the number.) The manual recommends the form coproc NAME { command; }: a name is required to have more than one, and with a simple command instead of a group, no name is allowed at all and the array is always called COPROC.

That is the pattern of a coproc for a background filter: start a program once, feed it and read it many times, instead of starting it once per item. A calculator is the usual illustration:

# A long-lived calculator: one bc process, many questions
coproc BC { bc -l; }
bc_job=$BC_PID bc_in=${BC[1]}
ask() { printf '%s\n' "$1" >&"${BC[1]}"; IFS= read -r answer <&"${BC[0]}"; echo "$1 = $answer"; }
ask 'scale=4; 22/7'
ask '2^64'
ask 'sqrt(2)'
exec {bc_in}>&-; wait "$bc_job"

scale=4; 22/7 = 3.1428
2^64 = 18446744073709551616
sqrt(2) = 1.4142

A coproc for a background filter pays off exactly here. One bc process answered three questions; its state carried between them, which is why scale=4 still applied to sqrt(2). Starting bc once per question would cost a process each time (§15.1). bc is present on macOS and on most Linux installations, though not all: it was absent from the minimal Debian image used for these measurements until installed.

Save the PID and the output descriptor

The coproc variables have a lifetime, and it catches almost everyone once. When a coprocess exits, bash unsets its array and its _PID variable, and closes its descriptors — including the one holding output the script has not read yet:

# When a coprocess exits, bash unsets its variables AND closes its descriptors
coproc LAST { sleep 0.1; echo "the last words"; }
sleep 0.4                     # it has finished by now
echo "LAST_PID is ${LAST_PID-<unset>}, LAST is ${LAST[0]-<unset>}: its output is gone"

coproc LAST { sleep 0.1; echo "the last words"; }
exec {out}<&"${LAST[0]}"      # a copy of the read end, which bash does not manage
last_job=$LAST_PID            # and the PID, saved while it exists
sleep 0.4
IFS= read -r words <&"$out"; echo "read through the copy: $words"
exec {out}<&-
wait "$last_job"; echo "the saved PID can still be waited for: status $?"

LAST_PID is <unset>, LAST is <unset>: its output is gone
read through the copy: the last words
the saved PID can still be waited for: status 0

The first coprocess printed its line and exited while the script was sleeping. By the time the script looked, LAST_PID and LAST were gone, and so was the descriptor that held the last words: the output was lost. The second time, the script made a copy of the read end straight away with exec {out}<&"${LAST[0]}" — a descriptor bash does not manage, so bash does not close it — and saved the PID in an ordinary variable. After the coprocess exited, the copy still read its output, and the saved PID could still be waited for. So the rule for any coprocess whose output is read after it may have finished: save NAME_PID in a variable, and duplicate NAME[0], as soon as the coprocess starts. Every example in this subsection saves the PID and the write descriptor's number; the examples that read after closing the input also copy the read end.

Buffering: the answer that never comes

The coprocess above answered because its loop is bash, and bash's printf writes each line as it is produced. Most programs do not. A program using the C library's standard output writes line by line when its output is a terminal, and in blocks of several kilobytes when it is a pipe — and a coprocess's output is always a pipe:

# Most filters buffer their output when it is a pipe, so a line may never come back
coproc TR { tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]'; }
exec {tr_out}<&"${TR[0]}"; tr_job=$TR_PID tr_in=${TR[1]}
printf 'hello\n' >&"${TR[1]}"
if IFS= read -r -t 1 reply <&"$tr_out"; then echo "tr answered: $reply"
else echo "tr has not answered after a second (read status $?)"; fi

exec {tr_in}>&-               # end of input makes tr flush what it holds, and exit
IFS= read -r reply <&"$tr_out"; echo "after closing its input: $reply"
exec {tr_out}<&-; wait "$tr_job"

coproc UC { perl -pe 'BEGIN { $| = 1 } $_ = uc'; }     # $| = 1: flush every line
uc_job=$UC_PID uc_in=${UC[1]}
printf 'hello\n' >&"${UC[1]}"
IFS= read -r -t 1 reply <&"${UC[0]}" && echo "a program that flushes each line answered: $reply"
exec {uc_in}>&-; wait "$uc_job"

tr has not answered after a second (read status 142)
after closing its input: HELLO
a program that flushes each line answered: HELLO

tr received hello and converted it, then kept the result in its output buffer, waiting to fill a block: after a second, read -t 1 gave up with status 142 (above 128, the timeout, §14.6). Closing tr's input made it flush and exit, and the line arrived. The one-exchange-at-a-time conversation a coprocess is for only works with a program that flushes after each line. The example's second coprocess is perl with $| = 1, which does. For other programs, measured on both systems: macOS's awk answered when the program called fflush() after each print, but Debian's default awk, which is mawk, did not even then, because mawk also reads its input in blocks — it answered with awk -W interactive. GNU sed -u and BSD sed -l are those seds' line-buffered modes. And stdbuf -oL, from GNU coreutils, makes many standard C-library programs line-buffered from outside: stdbuf -oL tr a-z A-Z answered at once on Debian. stdbuf is not on macOS. Exercise 4 is a coprocess that can never answer early, however it is buffered.

Two details of coprocess descriptors

The manual states that a coprocess's descriptors are not available in subshells, and the example checks it:

# A coprocess's descriptors are not available in a subshell; copy them first
coproc CAT { cat; }
cat_job=$CAT_PID cat_in=${CAT[1]}
( printf 'from a subshell\n' >&"${CAT[1]}" ) 2>&1 | sed 's/^.*line [0-9]*: /  /'
exec {to_cat}>&"${CAT[1]}"
( printf 'through a copy\n' >&"$to_cat" )
IFS= read -r line <&"${CAT[0]}"; echo "cat echoed: $line"
exec {to_cat}>&- {cat_in}>&-
wait "$cat_job"

  "${CAT[1]}": Bad file descriptor
cat echoed: through a copy

( printf … >&"${CAT[1]}" ) failed with Bad file descriptor: bash closes coprocess descriptors in every subshell it forks, so that a stray child does not keep the coprocess's input open (which would stop it ever seeing end-of-file). A copy made with exec {to_cat}>&"${CAT[1]}" is an ordinary descriptor, and the subshell could use it. That applies to $( … ) and pipelines too, since both are subshells (§16.6).

A script may run more than one coprocess, each with its own name:

# Two coprocesses at once, each with its own name
coproc ONE { while IFS= read -r l; do echo "one: $l"; done; }
coproc TWO { while IFS= read -r l; do echo "two: $l"; done; }
one_in=${ONE[1]} two_in=${TWO[1]}
echo a >&"${ONE[1]}"; IFS= read -r r <&"${ONE[0]}"; echo "$r"
echo b >&"${TWO[1]}"; IFS= read -r r <&"${TWO[0]}"; echo "$r"
exec {one_in}>&- {two_in}>&-
wait

one: a
two: b

Both answered. Bash 5.2 ran them too, but printed warning: execute_coproc: coproc [PID:ONE] still exists when the second started; bash 5.3 enabled multiple coprocesses by default (its NEWS lists it) and prints nothing.

Named pipes: mkfifo

A named pipe, or FIFO ("first in, first out"), is a pipe with a name in the filesystem. mkfifo NAME creates it; any process that opens the name for writing is connected to any process that opens it for reading, and data passes through the kernel without ever being stored on disk. A named pipe in a script connects processes that were not started together in one pipeline, which is its whole reason to exist:

# mkfifo makes a named pipe: a file name that two processes open to talk
mkfifo queue
[[ -p queue ]] && echo "queue is a named pipe"

{ for job in build test deploy; do echo "$job"; done > queue; } &
while IFS= read -r job; do
  echo "worker: got $job"
done < queue
wait

queue is a named pipe
worker: got build
worker: got test
worker: got deploy

[[ -p queue ]] is the test for a FIFO (§7.6). A background writer sent three jobs into queue, and the loop read them out in order. The same thing could have been a pipeline, and when it can, it should be; a named pipe in a script earns its place when the two ends are started separately — by different scripts, at different times, or when the reader must stay in the current shell.

Opening a FIFO blocks until the other end is opened too:

# Opening a FIFO for writing waits until someone opens it for reading
mkfifo pipe
{ echo "writer: opening"; exec 3> pipe; echo "writer: opened, a reader exists"; echo data >&3; } &
sleep 0.3
echo "reader: about to open"
IFS= read -r line < pipe
echo "reader: read $line"
wait

writer: opening
reader: about to open
writer: opened, a reader exists
reader: read data

The writer printed opening and then stopped inside exec 3> pipe until the reader opened the other end; only then did opened appear. A FIFO with no reader holds a writer forever, which is the first way FIFO scripts hang.

The second way is end-of-file. A reader sees end-of-file when the last writer closes, and the next write needs a new open — which, with the reader gone, blocks:

# Each open of the FIFO ends at the writer's close; hold one descriptor open instead
mkfifo inbox
reader() { while IFS= read -r msg; do echo "got: $msg"; done < inbox; echo "reader: end of file"; }
reader &
echo "first"  > inbox
sleep 0.2
echo "second" > inbox 2>/dev/null &   # the reader already left; this write would block
sleep 0.2
kill $! 2>/dev/null; wait 2>/dev/null
echo "---"
reader &
exec {w}<> inbox              # read-write: does not wait for a reader, and never closes
echo "first"  >&"$w"
echo "second" >&"$w"
sleep 0.2
exec {w}>&-                   # the last writer closes: now the reader sees end of file
wait

got: first
reader: end of file
---
got: first
got: second
reader: end of file

In the first half the reader's loop received first and then end-of-file, because the echo that wrote it opened the FIFO, wrote and closed. The reader left, and the second echo blocked on its open with no one to read — the script had to kill it. In the second half the script opened the FIFO once with <>, read-write, on its own descriptor. Opening a FIFO read-write does not wait for another party, because the opener is both (§10.7 noted that a FIFO is inherently two-way; POSIX leaves opening one read-write undefined, and both Linux and macOS allow it, measured). As long as the script held that descriptor there was always a writer, so the reader kept reading through both messages; closing it delivered end-of-file, and the reader finished. That is the shape of a long-lived FIFO consumer: hold the write side open for as long as messages may come, and close it to say "no more".

A FIFO is a file name, so it needs the same care as a temporary file (§17.10): create it inside a mktemp -d directory, not at a predictable path in /tmp, and remove it with the directory in the cleanup trap.

17.12 Outliving the Script: nohup, disown, setsid and Daemons

A background job normally lives and dies with the session that started it. Sometimes it must not: a long job started from an SSH session should survive the connection dropping, and a service should keep running after the script that started it is gone. Four tools address this, and they solve different problems.

What kills a job when the terminal goes away

When a terminal closes — the window shut, the SSH connection lost — the kernel sends SIGHUP to the terminal's session leader, the interactive shell. Bash then resends SIGHUP to every job in its job table and exits. The default action for SIGHUP is to terminate, so a job started with a plain & dies with the terminal. Measured on a pseudo-terminal, with SIGHUP sent to an interactive bash that had a background sleep 300: the plain job was killed; a job protected in each of the three ways below survived. (That is separate from huponexit, §16.7, which concerns an ordinary exit from a login shell, and is off by default.)

nohup

nohup runs a command with SIGHUP ignored. An ignored signal is inherited across exec (§16.1), so the command, and anything it starts, is immune:

# nohup runs a command with SIGHUP ignored
nohup bash -c 'trap -p HUP' 2>/dev/null
nohup bash -c 'kill -s HUP $$; echo "survived its own SIGHUP"' 2>/dev/null
[[ -e nohup.out ]] || echo "no nohup.out: output was not a terminal, so it went where it was sent"

trap -- '' SIGHUP
survived its own SIGHUP
no nohup.out: output was not a terminal, so it went where it was sent

Under nohup, the child bash reported SIGHUP as ignored, and sending itself SIGHUP did nothing. nohup also redirects output that would go to a terminal: when its standard output is a terminal it appends it to nohup.out (in the current directory, or $HOME), and says so on standard error. Measured on a pseudo-terminal, nohup echo … wrote the line into nohup.out. In the example the output was not a terminal, so no nohup.out was created and the output went where it was sent. The idiom for a job that must survive a session is therefore nohup command > job.log 2>&1 & — the redirections chosen by the script, not by nohup.

disown

disown is a bash builtin that removes a job from the shell's job table. A job the shell no longer lists is a job it will not send SIGHUP to:

# disown removes a job from the shell's table
sleep 0.5 & pid=$!
jobs
disown
jobs
echo "jobs lists nothing now"
wait "$pid"; echo "wait returned $? at once, without waiting"
kill -0 "$pid" && echo "and the process is still running"

[1]+  Running                    sleep 0.5 &
jobs lists nothing now
wait returned 0 at once, without waiting
and the process is still running

jobs listed the sleep, and after disown it listed nothing. The process itself was untouched and still running. But disown has a cost inside a script, and the example shows it: wait for a disowned PID returned 0 at once, without waiting, while the process was still running. The shell had forgotten the job, so it had nothing to wait for — and it did not say so. A script that disowns a job has given up its exit status and any way of waiting for it.

disown -h is the version that keeps both:

# disown -h keeps the job, but marks it not to receive the shell's SIGHUP
sleep 0.4 &
disown -h %1
jobs
wait %1; echo "still waitable: status $?"

[1]+  Running                    sleep 0.4 &
still waitable: status 0

The job stayed in the table and could be waited for, and its status came back; it is only marked so that the shell will not send it SIGHUP. Measured on a pseudo-terminal, a disown -h job survived its terminal's hang-up just as a disowned one did. disown -a applies to every job, and disown -r to the running ones. The difference between nohup and disown: nohup is decided when a command starts, and protects it from SIGHUP from any sender; disown can be applied afterwards to a job already running — the "I forgot to use nohup" rescue at a prompt — and only stops the shell's own SIGHUP.

setsid

setsid runs a command in a new session: the process becomes a session leader and a process group leader, with no controlling terminal. A terminal hang-up is delivered to the session attached to that terminal, and this one is attached to none. setsid is util-linux, on Linux only:

# Linux only: setsid is util-linux, which macOS does not ship
ps -o sid= -p $$ > script.sid
setsid bash -c 'ps -o sid=,pgid=,tty= -p $$ > child.ids; echo "$$" > child.pid'
read -r sid pgid tty < child.ids
[[ $sid == "$(<child.pid)" && $pgid == "$sid" ]] && echo "setsid: the child leads a new session and a new process group"
[[ $sid != "$(tr -d ' ' < script.sid)" ]] && echo "which is not the script's session"
[[ $tty == "?" ]] && echo "and it has no controlling terminal"

setsid: the child leads a new session and a new process group
which is not the script's session
and it has no controlling terminal

The child's session ID and process group ID were both its own PID, neither was the script's session, and ps showed ? for its terminal. On macOS there is no setsid command; the same effect needs a small program in another language (perl -e 'use POSIX; setsid(); exec @ARGV', for instance), and in practice a service manager (below).

Daemonising a script

A daemon is a process that runs in the background, detached from any terminal, not the child of whoever started it. Daemonising a script by hand is a sequence of steps, each undoing one tie to the starting environment: change to / so the daemon does not keep a directory (and its filesystem) in use; redirect standard input, output and error away from the terminal; start a new session with setsid; and fork twice, so that the process that started it can exit and the daemon is adopted by another process. In bash the double fork is a background command inside a subshell:

# Double fork: the subshell starts the daemon and exits, so the daemon is adopted
here=$PWD
(
  cd / || exit
  echo "$BASHPID" > "$here/subshell.pid"
  bash -c 'sleep 0.1; echo "$PPID" > "$1"; sleep 0.3' _ "$here/daemon.ppid" </dev/null >/dev/null 2>&1 &
)
wait; echo "wait returned $? at once: the daemon is not the script's child"
sleep 0.3
parent=$(<daemon.ppid)
[[ $parent != "$$" && $parent != "$(<subshell.pid)" ]] && echo "its parent is neither the script nor the subshell that started it"

wait returned 0 at once: the daemon is not the script's child
its parent is neither the script nor the subshell that started it

The subshell ( … & ) started the command in the background and exited immediately, so wait in the script returned at once — the daemon was never the script's child, and the script could not wait for it (§17.2). The daemon's parent was then neither the script nor the subshell: when the subshell exited, its orphaned child was adopted. On macOS and in a Linux container the adoptive parent was PID 1 (launchd, docker-init), measured; on a Linux desktop it is often a per-user service manager registered to adopt orphans. Adding setsid in front of bash -c on Linux completes the recipe.

That recipe works, and daemonising a script by hand is almost always the wrong design. A daemon started this way has no supervisor: nothing restarts it when it crashes, nothing collects its logs, nothing stops it cleanly at shutdown, and the only handle on it is a PID file with all the weaknesses §17.8 described. Every modern system has a service manager built to do exactly this — systemd on Linux, launchd on macOS — and the right way to run a script as a service is to write it as an ordinary foreground program that logs to standard output and handles SIGTERM (§12.5, §12.7), and let the service manager start, restart, log and stop it. For one-off jobs on Linux, systemd-run --user starts a command as a transient service with the same supervision. The nohup … & idiom remains the right tool for the smaller problem: keeping a job alive past an SSH session.

17.13 timeout: Bounding How Long Something Runs

Any command that waits on the network, a lock, a person or another process can wait forever, and a script that runs unattended — from cron, CI or a deployment — must decide how long is too long. The timeout command runs a command and stops it if it has not finished in time. The timeout command is GNU coreutils, present on every Linux distribution, and not part of macOS, where Homebrew's coreutils provides it (as it did on this machine).

# timeout runs a command, and stops it if it takes too long
timeout 5 true;     echo "finished in time:      status $?"
timeout 5 false;    echo "failed in time:        status $?"
timeout 0.3 sleep 5; echo "ran out of time:       status $?"
timeout 0.3 bash -c 'sleep 0.1; exit 3'; echo "the command's own:     status $?"

finished in time:      status 0
failed in time:        status 1
ran out of time:       status 124
the command's own:     status 3

A command that finished in time returned its own status, 0 or 1. One that ran out of time was sent SIGTERM, and timeout returned 124, its "timed out" status. That is the whole contract, and 124 is the number to test for: timeout 30 fetch || { (( $? == 124 )) && echo "fetch timed out"; }. The duration takes a suffix — s, m, h, d — and decimals.

Choosing the signal, and making sure

SIGTERM can be caught or ignored, so timeout has options for a command that does not stop when asked:

# -s chooses the signal; -k sends KILL if the first one is ignored
timeout -s INT 0.3 sleep 5;          echo "-s INT:               status $?"
timeout 0.3 bash -c 'trap "" TERM; sleep 2';   echo "TERM ignored:         status $? (it ran to the end)"
{ timeout -k 0.3 0.3 bash -c 'trap "" TERM; sleep 2'; } 2>/dev/null; echo "-k 0.3:               status $?"
timeout --preserve-status 0.3 sleep 5; echo "--preserve-status:    status $?"

-s INT:               status 124
TERM ignored:         status 124 (it ran to the end)
-k 0.3:               status 137
--preserve-status:    status 143

-s INT sent SIGINT instead, and still reported 124. The second line is a command that ignored SIGTERM and ran to its end: timeout still returned 124, because the time limit had been reached, whatever the command then did. -k 0.3 sends SIGKILL if the command is still running that long after the first signal, and the status became 137, 128 + 9 — SIGKILL cannot be ignored (§12.1). And --preserve-status returns the command's own status even after a timeout: 143, 128 + 15, for a sleep killed by SIGTERM. For a script, timeout -k 10 60 command — ask politely after 60 seconds, insist 10 seconds later — is the usual shape.

A function cannot be timed out directly

timeout is an external program that runs another program, so, like xargs (§17.6), it cannot see the script's functions:

# timeout runs a program, so it cannot see the script's functions
slow_check() { sleep 5; }
timeout 0.3 slow_check; echo "status $?"
export -f slow_check
timeout 0.3 bash -c slow_check; echo "through bash -c: status $?"

timeout: failed to run command 'slow_check': No such file or directory
status 127
through bash -c: status 124

timeout 0.3 slow_check failed with 127 and failed to run command 'slow_check'. After export -f, timeout 0.3 bash -c slow_check ran the function in a child bash, and it was timed out properly.

timeout stops more than the one process it started. It runs the command in a process group of its own, and sends the signal to the whole group:

# timeout signals the command's whole process group, children included
timeout 0.3 bash -c 'sleep 5 & echo "$!" > child.pid; wait'
echo "timeout: status $?"
sleep 0.2
kill -0 "$(<child.pid)" 2>/dev/null || echo "the command's own background child was stopped too"

timeout: status 124
the command's own background child was stopped too

The command started a background sleep 5 of its own and waited for it. When the time ran out, that sleep was stopped too, although timeout had never heard of it. This is what makes timeout safe to wrap around a script that starts children. The same process-group design has one side effect: a command run under timeout from a script is moved out of the terminal's foreground process group, so if it reads from the terminal it is stopped when it tries; timeout --foreground is the option for that case, and it gives up the signalling of children.

Without the timeout command

Where timeout is not available, or the thing to bound is a shell function that must run in the current shell's context, a watchdog does the same job in bash:

# Without timeout(1): a watchdog in the background, stopped once the command finishes
with_timeout() {
  local secs=$1 pid watchdog status
  shift
  "$@" & pid=$!
  ( sleep "$secs"; kill -s TERM "$pid" 2>/dev/null ) & watchdog=$!
  wait "$pid"; status=$?
  kill "$watchdog" 2>/dev/null; wait "$watchdog" 2>/dev/null
  (( status == 128 + 15 )) && return 124     # report a timeout the way timeout(1) does
  return "$status"
}
slow() { sleep 5; }
with_timeout 0.3 slow;          echo "a function that ran out of time: status $?"
with_timeout 2 bash -c 'exit 3'; echo "a command that finished:         status $?"

a function that ran out of time: status 124
a command that finished:         status 3

The command runs in the background, and a second background job — the watchdog — sleeps for the limit and then sends SIGTERM to it. If the command finishes first, the script kills the watchdog. wait then returns the command's status, and a status of 143 (128 + 15, killed by the watchdog's SIGTERM) is translated to 124, so that callers can test it exactly as they would test timeout's. It timed out a function directly — no export -f, because "$@" & forks the current shell. Its limitation is the one timeout solved: the watchdog signals one PID, not a process group, so a command that starts children of its own needs set -m around the launch and kill -- -"$pid" in the watchdog (§12.9).

For waiting on input, the shell already has a timeout: read -t (§14.6).

# For input, read -t is timeout built into the shell
if IFS= read -r -t 0.3 answer < <(sleep 5); then echo "got: $answer"
else echo "no answer in time: read returned $?"; fi

no answer in time: read returned 142

read -t 0.3 gave up after 0.3 seconds with status 142 — above 128, which is how read reports a timeout, as distinct from end-of-file's 1.

17.14 The Concurrency Table

Each tool, what it does, and the detail that bites.

Tool
What it does, and the detail that bites
cmd &, $!
Runs cmd in a separate process without waiting; its status is 0 whatever cmd does. $! is replaced by every &: save it at once. A script's background job reads /dev/null (§17.1, §17.3).
wait
No arguments: waits for all, returns 0 regardless. wait PID: that job's status, kept after it ends; several PIDs: the last one's status. 127: not a child (§17.2).
wait -n -p var
The next job to finish, and its PID in var (4.3; -p 5.1). 127 with var unset means nothing left; loop on var, never on the status (§17.2, §17.3).
jobs, fg, bg, set -m
jobs -r/-s/-l/-p work in a script; fg and bg need set -m, which also gives jobs their own process groups and stops lastpipe (§17.4).
Job pool
Count running jobs in an associative array; wait -n -p before each start once full. Batches waste a slot on every slow job (§17.5).
xargs -P N
No order; one failure status for the run: 123 on GNU, 1 on BSD; 255 stops it. Runs programs, not functions. Use -0 with find -print0 (§17.6).
GNU parallel
Separate install. Groups each job's output; --keep-order; status = number of failed jobs; --halt now,fail=1 (§17.6).
Atomic operations
mkdir, set -C; > f, ln -s and mv within one filesystem each succeed for exactly one caller. Write a temporary file beside the target, then mv (§17.7).
Lock files
mkdir or noclobber, PID inside, trap set only after acquiring; kill -0 detects a stale lock, with a small race (§17.8).
flock / lockf
Kernel locks on an open file, released when the last descriptor closes — never stale. Linux flock -n "$fd", macOS lockf -s -t 0 "$fd". Children inherit the lock: close it with {fd}>&-. Advisory only (§17.9).
mktemp
Unpredictable name, mode 600 (700 for -d), exclusive create. Use a template to honour TMPDIR everywhere; restore the mode when replacing a file (§17.10).
coproc
Two pipes to a background command. Save NAME_PID and copy NAME[0] at once: bash unsets and closes them when it exits. Needs a program that flushes each line. Not visible in subshells (§17.11).
mkfifo
Opening blocks until both ends are open; each writer's close is an end-of-file. Hold a <> descriptor to keep it open (§17.11).
nohup, disown, setsid
nohup: SIGHUP ignored from the start. disown: forgotten by the shell, and wait then returns 0 at once. disown -h: kept, but not hung up. setsid: new session, no terminal (Linux). For a service, use the service manager (§17.12).
timeout
124 on timeout; -k for SIGKILL (137); signals the whole process group; cannot run a function without export -f and bash -c (§17.13).

And the rule behind the table: concurrency in the shell is easy to start and easy to lose track of. Every job is started with & and must be finished with a wait that reads its status; every resource two processes share needs one atomic operation to decide who owns it; and every name in a shared place must be one no one else could have predicted.

Exercises

1. Checksums in parallel. Write checksum_all MAX FILE…, which runs cksum on every file, at most MAX at a time, prints the results in the order the files were given whatever order they finish in, includes the error message for any file that fails, and returns non-zero if any failed. Explain why the results cannot simply be printed as each job finishes.

Solution 
# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # results is read through the nameref below
checksum_all() {
  local max=$1 dir pid status i=0 failed=0
  shift
  dir=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/checksums.XXXXXX") || return 2
  local -A index=()
  for file in "$@"; do
    if (( ${#index[@]} >= max )); then
      wait -n -p pid; status=$?
      (( status == 0 )) || failed=1
      unset 'index[$pid]'
    fi
    cksum -- "$file" > "$dir/$i" 2>&1 & index[$!]=$i
    i=$(( i + 1 ))
  done
  while (( ${#index[@]} > 0 )); do
    wait -n -p pid; status=$?
    (( status == 0 )) || failed=1
    unset 'index[$pid]'
  done
  for (( i = 0; i < $#; i++ )); do cat -- "$dir/$i"; done
  rm -rf -- "${dir:?}"
  return "$failed"
}

printf 'alpha\n' > a.txt; printf 'beta\n' > b.txt; printf 'gamma\n' > c.txt
checksum_all 2 a.txt b.txt missing.txt c.txt
echo "checksum_all returned $?"

3650393976 6 a.txt
3703342344 5 b.txt
cksum: missing.txt: No such file or directory
3677655623 6 c.txt
checksum_all returned 1

Each job writes to its own numbered file in a private mktemp -d directory (§17.10), and the files are printed in number order once every job has been collected — so the output is in argument order even though the jobs finished in whatever order their sizes and the scheduler decided (§17.3). Printing as each job finishes would interleave the jobs' output and put the results in finishing order, which changes from run to run and makes the output useless to anything that parses it. The pool is §17.5's: index maps each running job's PID to its number, wait -n -p collects one whenever MAX are running, and the loop after it collects the rest. The failing file's error message went into its own result file through 2>&1, so it appears in its place in the list, and the function returned 1. ${dir:?} guards the rm -rf against an empty variable (§12.3).

2. The cron job that must not overlap. A report runs from cron every five minutes and occasionally takes longer than five minutes. Write run_once LOCKDIR COMMAND…, portable to macOS and Linux, which runs the command only if no other copy is running, skips with status 0 if one is, recovers from a lock left by a copy that was killed with SIGKILL, and always removes its own lock when the command ends. Then say what flock would change.

Solution 
run_once() {
  local lockdir=$1 pid
  shift
  if ! mkdir -- "$lockdir" 2>/dev/null; then
    pid=$(cat -- "$lockdir/pid" 2>/dev/null)
    if [[ -n $pid ]] && kill -0 "$pid" 2>/dev/null; then
      echo "run_once: already running as another process; skipping" >&2
      return 0
    fi
    echo "run_once: removing a stale lock" >&2
    rm -rf -- "$lockdir"
    mkdir -- "$lockdir" 2>/dev/null || { echo "run_once: lost the race; skipping" >&2; return 0; }
  fi
  echo "$BASHPID" > "$lockdir/pid"
  (
    trap 'rm -rf -- "$lockdir"' EXIT
    "$@"
  )
}

report() { echo "report $1: working"; sleep "$2"; echo "report $1: done"; }

run_once report.lock report first 0.5 & sleep 0.2
run_once report.lock report second 0
wait

mkdir report.lock
{ bash -c 'echo "$$" > report.lock/pid; kill -s KILL "$$"'; } 2>/dev/null
run_once report.lock report third 0
[[ -e report.lock ]] || echo "the lock was removed after the third run"

report first: working
run_once: already running as another process; skipping
report first: done
run_once: removing a stale lock
report third: working
report third: done
the lock was removed after the third run

The lock is a directory, created by mkdir, which is atomic on every Unix (§17.8). If it exists, the PID inside is checked with kill -0: a live holder means skip, with status 0, since overlap is expected rather than an error; a dead one means the lock is stale, so it is removed and taken again — and if another contender got there first, mkdir fails a second time and this run skips instead of fighting over it. The PID is written with $BASHPID, the process actually running run_once. The command runs in a subshell whose EXIT trap removes the lock directory, so the trap is registered only after the lock is held (§17.8) and fires however the command ends — success, failure, exit or a trapped signal — without replacing any EXIT trap the calling script has set. The run showed all three cases: second skipped while first held the lock, third found a lock whose holder had been killed with SIGKILL, removed it, ran, and left no lock behind.

With flock (Linux) or lockf (macOS) on a descriptor, almost all of this disappears: exec {fd}>> "$lockfile"; flock -n "$fd" || exit 0 at the top of the job, and the kernel releases the lock when the process ends, however it ends, so there is no stale lock to detect, no PID to check, no trap to register and no race in the recovery (§17.9). The price is that the command is not on stock macOS — hence the lockf alternative — and that any long-lived child the job starts must be run with {fd}>&-, or it will hold the lock after the job has finished.

3. Replacing a file safely. Write write_atomic FILE COMMAND…, which replaces FILE with the output of COMMAND, so that a reader of FILE sees either the old content or the complete new content and never a mixture, which leaves FILE untouched if COMMAND fails, which keeps FILE's permissions, and which leaves no temporary file behind. Why does it take a command, rather than reading its standard input like producer | write_atomic FILE?

Solution 
# write_atomic FILE COMMAND [ARG...]: FILE gets COMMAND's output, or is left untouched
write_atomic() {
  local file=$1 tmp status
  shift
  tmp=$(mktemp "$(dirname -- "$file")/.${file##*/}.XXXXXX") || return
  if [[ -e $file ]]; then
    cp -p -- "$file" "$tmp" || { rm -f -- "$tmp"; return 1; }    # copies the mode too
  fi
  if "$@" > "$tmp"; then
    mv -f -- "$tmp" "$file"
  else
    status=$?
    rm -f -- "$tmp"
    return "$status"
  fi
}

printf 'port=80\n' > app.conf; chmod 644 app.conf
write_atomic app.conf printf 'port=8080\n'
echo "replaced: $(<app.conf), mode still 644: $([[ -n $(find app.conf -perm 644) ]] && echo yes)"

half_written() { printf 'port=9'; return 1; }
write_atomic app.conf half_written
echo "a failing command: status $?, app.conf still holds $(<app.conf)"
echo "temporary files left behind: $(find . -name '.app.conf.*' | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"

replaced: port=8080, mode still 644: yes
a failing command: status 1, app.conf still holds port=8080
temporary files left behind: 0

The temporary file is created by mktemp in the same directory as the target, so the final mv is a rename() within one filesystem, which replaces the name in one step (§17.7), and its name is unpredictable, so no one can plant a link at it (§17.10). Because mktemp creates the file with mode 600, the old file is copied onto it first with cp -p, which carries the mode across portably — the replaced app.conf was still 644. The command's output then overwrites the copy. If the command fails, the temporary file is removed and its status returned, and app.conf still held port=8080: the half-written port=9 was never visible to anyone. find confirmed nothing was left behind.

It takes a command because a function at the end of a pipeline cannot see whether the producer succeeded. producer | write_atomic FILE runs the two in separate processes (§16.6); write_atomic would read whatever arrived before the producer failed — port=9 — reach end-of-file, see a successful read, and install the half-written file. The failure is in PIPESTATUS in the caller, after it is too late. Running the command itself, with its output redirected to the temporary file, puts its exit status exactly where the decision to rename is made.

4. The coprocess that never answers. This script hangs forever at the read:

coproc SORT { sort; }
printf '%s\n' pear apple fig >&"${SORT[1]}"
IFS= read -r first <&"${SORT[0]}"
echo "first: $first"

Explain why no amount of buffering control would fix it. Then rewrite it to get all three lines, sorted, and make sure it cannot lose them however quickly sort exits.

Solution 
coproc SORT { sort; }
exec {sorted_fd}<&"${SORT[0]}"; sort_job=$SORT_PID sort_in=${SORT[1]}
printf '%s\n' pear apple fig >&"${SORT[1]}"
if ! IFS= read -r -t 1 _ <&"$sorted_fd"; then
  echo "nothing after a second: sort cannot print until its input ends"
fi
exec {sort_in}>&-
mapfile -t sorted <&"$sorted_fd"
exec {sorted_fd}<&-
wait "$sort_job"
echo "after closing its input: ${sorted[*]}"

nothing after a second: sort cannot print until its input ends
after closing its input: apple fig pear

sort cannot print its first line until it has read its last: the smallest item may be the final one it is sent. So it writes nothing until its input ends, and the script's input end is still open — the script is waiting for sort, and sort is waiting for the script. stdbuf, -u options and fflush() all control when output is written after it is produced; sort has produced nothing (§17.11). The solution's read -t 1 proves it without hanging: nothing arrived in a second. Closing the write end with exec {sort_in}>&- gives sort its end-of-file; it sorts, writes everything, and exits — and, having exited, has its variables unset and its descriptors closed by bash. That is why the read end was copied to sorted_fd, and the PID saved to sort_job, straight after coproc (§17.11): mapfile then read all three lines from the copy, whenever sort happened to exit, and wait collected its status through the saved PID. For a one-shot filter like this, a coprocess is more machinery than the job needs — mapfile -t sorted < <(printf '%s\n' pear apple fig | sort) does it in one line — and a coprocess earns its place only with a program that answers each line as it arrives.

SECTION 18

Security and Injection

A shell script is an interpreter for text, and most of what it interprets arrives from somewhere else: its arguments, its environment, the files it reads, the names of the files it finds, the output of the programs it runs. Every one of those is data, and the defining failure of shell security is data being parsed as code. The rest of the course has been teaching the defences without always naming them — quoting (§3), arrays for commands (§6.14), read -r (§14.4), -- (§13.5), a format string that never contains data (§14.11). This section names the attacks those habits prevent, measures each one, and adds the defences that are not about quoting at all: the environment a script inherits, the PATH it searches, the files it creates, the races it runs, the secrets it handles and the privileges it holds.

It is organised from the inside out. §18.1 defines untrusted input and shows the property the shell gives you for free. §18.2–§18.5 are the injection family: splicing a value into a command string, an unquoted expansion, the arithmetic context, and a value used as a pattern or as part of another program. §18.6 is option injection and --. §18.7 and §18.8 are the inherited attack surface, PATH and the environment, including shellshock. §18.9–§18.11 are eval — what it does, how to replace it, and the other places the shell runs text later. §18.12–§18.14 are validation: allowlists, set -f, and file names that climb out of a directory. §18.15 is secrets, §18.16 permissions, §18.17 the TOCTOU race, §18.18 deleting safely, §18.19 setuid scripts and the restricted shell, and §18.20 sudo. §18.21 is the table.

The editorial boundary: web application security — cross-site scripting, SQL injection, authentication — belongs to the websec course, and this section says nothing about it beyond the shell's part. The linux course owns permissions, users, sudo administration and file ownership as system facts; §1.4 owns the choice of interpreter line; claude_code §5.2 owns an agent's shell permission rules. What this section owns is what a script must do so that the values passing through it cannot take control of it.

Every demonstration here is harmless by construction. A value that "injects" does one of two things: it creates an empty file named pwned in the example's own temporary directory, or it prints a line. Where the section must talk about deleting files, a stand-in rm function prints the arguments it was given and deletes nothing, and the same device stands in for sudo and ssh. Every vulnerable form is followed by its fix, because the pair is the lesson. The examples were run under bash 5.3 on macOS and bash 5.2 on Debian, and they print the same thing on both except where a block is marked as Linux only.

18.1 Untrusted Input, and the Property Quoting Buys

Untrusted input is any value the script's author did not write. That is a wider category than it sounds. Command-line arguments are the obvious case. So are the environment (every variable the caller exported), standard input, the contents of any file the script reads, the names of files in any directory someone else can write to, the output of any command whose input someone else controls, and a remote system's replies. A value is not trusted because it came from a colleague or from a configuration file in the repository; it is trusted when the script would still be correct if the value were chosen by someone trying to break it.

That definition sounds paralysing, and it would be if the shell re-parsed values as a matter of course. It does not, and the most important security property of the shell is this one:

# A file name that looks like code is still only a name, as long as it is only ever expanded
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the $( ) inside single quotes is the payload, literal on purpose
touch 'report $(touch pwned).txt' 'notes; touch pwned.txt'
for f in *; do
  printf 'found: %s\n' "$f"
done
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists" || echo "no file called pwned: the names stayed data"

found: example.sh
found: notes; touch pwned.txt
found: report $(touch pwned).txt
no file called pwned: the names stayed data

Both names look like shell code — one contains a command substitution, the other a ; and a second command — and neither ran. The loop expanded $f, and expansion produces text; the result of an expansion is never parsed again for $( ), ;, | or quotes (§4.8 measured this: expansion is one pass). A quoted expansion is also not split and not globbed (§3.6). So "$f" delivers exactly the bytes of the name to printf as one argument, and that is the whole of it.

Where the property ends

Everything in this section is a way of losing that property. There are only a few, and they are worth learning as a list, because each one has the same shape — a value that has been expanded once reaches something that parses it a second time:

  • A string handed to another shell: bash -c, sh -c, ssh host, su -c, sudo sh -c, xargs -I with a command string, find -exec sh -c (§18.2).
  • An unquoted expansion, which is split into words and globbed (§18.3).
  • An arithmetic context, whose array subscripts can run commands (§18.4).
  • A pattern, or the text of another program — sed, awk, a regular expression, a printf format (§18.5).
  • A leading dash, which a command reads as an option (§18.6).
  • eval, source, trap, declare and friends, which exist to parse text (§18.9–§18.11).

Keep that list in mind as a reading habit. When reviewing a script, the question is never "is this value dangerous?" — any value can be — but "does this value reach anything that parses?"

Untrusted input and arbitrary code execution

The consequence of losing the property is usually called arbitrary code execution: the person who chose the value chooses a command, and the command runs with the script's privileges, in its directory, with its credentials in the environment. In a script run by a developer that is the developer's account. In a CI job it is the job's deploy key. In a script run by cron as root, or through sudo, or by a web server's hook, it is everything. The severity of an injection bug is set by who runs the script, not by how obscure the vector looks, which is why the fixes here are habits applied everywhere rather than precautions saved for the scripts that seem important.

18.2 Command Injection: Building a Command String

Command injection is the textbook case: a value is pasted into the text of a command, and a shell parses the result. When the parser is a shell it is also called shell injection, and it is the shell's version of SQL injection, and it has the same cause and the same cure — code and data travel in the same string, so keep them in separate strings.

# ❌ The value is pasted into the text of a command, so the inner shell parses it as code
name='world; touch pwned'
bash -c "echo hello $name"
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists: the value ran as a command"

hello world
pwned exists: the value ran as a command

The outer double quotes expanded $name before bash ever started, so the program bash -c received was the text echo hello world; touch pwned. The inner shell parsed that text, saw two commands separated by ;, and ran both. Nothing about the value was exotic: shell injection needs only a character the shell treats as syntax, and a ; is enough.

Passing the value as an argument instead

The fix is to make the program text a constant and pass the value as a positional parameter. bash -c takes the words after the command string as $0, $1, $2 and so on:

# The command text is a constant; the value arrives as $1 and is never parsed
name='world; touch pwned'
bash -c 'echo "hello $1"' _ "$name"
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists" || echo "no pwned: the value stayed an argument"

hello world; touch pwned
no pwned: the value stayed an argument

The command string is in single quotes, so the outer shell did not touch it: the inner bash received the literal text echo "hello $1", which contains no data at all. The value arrived separately as $1, and inside the inner shell it was an expansion — which, by §18.1, is never parsed. The _ fills $0, which bash -c uses for its own name in error messages. This is the single most useful pattern in the section. Whenever a second shell must run something, the text it parses is a constant, and every value travels as an argument.

xargs -I and find -exec

§17.6 used xargs to run a function in parallel and warned that the bash -c "process {}" form is an injection hole. Here it is:

# ❌ xargs -I pastes each item into the command string before bash parses it
printf '%s\n' 'a.txt' 'b$(touch pwned).txt' > list
xargs -I{} bash -c 'echo "processing {}"' < list
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists: a line of the list ran as a command"

processing a.txt
processing b.txt
pwned exists: a line of the list ran as a command

xargs -I{} substitutes each input line for {} inside the command string, before bash parses it. The second line of the list was b$(touch pwned).txt, so the program was echo "processing b$(touch pwned).txt", and the substitution ran — printing b.txt because touch prints nothing. Anyone who can create a file whose name ends up in that list can run a command. The argument form is the same fix as before:
