# The item is passed to bash as $1, so it is never part of the program text
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the $( ) inside single quotes is the payload, literal on purpose
printf '%s\n' 'a.txt' 'b$(touch pwned).txt' > list
xargs -I{} bash -c 'echo "processing $1"' _ {} < list
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists" || echo "no pwned: each item stayed an argument"

processing a.txt
processing b$(touch pwned).txt
no pwned: each item stayed an argument

Now {} is a separate word after the program text, so xargs passes each item as $1 and the program never contains it. find -exec has the same two forms, and the same one is wrong:

# The same rule for find: {} inside the sh -c text is spliced; {} after it is an argument
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the $( ) inside single quotes is the payload, literal on purpose
touch 'x$(touch pwned).log'
# shellcheck disable=SC2156  # the spliced form is the defect being shown
find . -name '*.log' -exec sh -c 'echo "spliced: {}"' \;
[[ -e pwned ]] && { echo "pwned exists after the spliced form"; rm -f pwned; }
find . -name '*.log' -exec sh -c 'for f; do echo "argument: $f"; done' sh {} +
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists" || echo "no pwned after the argument form"

spliced: ./x.log
pwned exists after the spliced form
argument: ./x$(touch pwned).log
no pwned after the argument form

POSIX leaves it implementation-defined whether find replaces a {} that is only part of an argument; GNU and BSD find both do, and a {} inside the sh -c text is therefore the spliced form. With sh {} + after the text, find passes the names as $1, $2 …, and for f; do loops over them. The + form also batches many names into one sh, so it is faster as well as safe. ShellCheck reports the spliced form as SC2156, "Injecting filenames is fragile and insecure. Use parameters."

A remote command line

ssh host command args… does not run command with those arguments. It joins all of them with spaces into a single string and sends that to the remote user's shell, which parses it. That is bash -c "$*" — a splice — and the local shell's quotes are gone by the time the remote shell reads the text. Here run_remotely stands in for ssh, doing exactly what ssh does on the far side:

# A remote command runner joins its arguments with spaces and hands the result to a shell,
# which is what ssh does on the far side.  run_remotely stands in for it here.
run_remotely() { bash -c "$*"; }
file='my notes.txt'
touch "$file"
run_remotely ls -l "$file" > /dev/null 2>&1 || echo "quoted locally, split remotely: 'my' and 'notes.txt'"
run_remotely ls "${file@Q}"                   # quoted for the second parse
name='x; touch pwned'
run_remotely echo "$name" > /dev/null
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists: the remote shell parsed the value"

quoted locally, split remotely: 'my' and 'notes.txt'
my notes.txt
pwned exists: the remote shell parsed the value

Three results. A file name with a space, quoted correctly on the local side, arrived at the remote shell as the two words my and notes.txt. ${file@Q} fixed it, because it produces the value quoted for one more parse (§5.8), which is exactly what a remote shell will do. And a value containing ; ran a second command on the remote side, which is command injection across a network. The rule for ssh: quote every argument for the remote shell with ${var@Q} (or pass the whole command as "${cmd[@]@Q}", as exercise 3 does), or send the values on standard input rather than on the command line. su -c, sudo sh -c, docker exec … sh -c and kubectl exec … -- sh -c all have the same shape.

18.3 An Unquoted Variable in a Command

The second way to lose the property is not to quote. An unquoted variable in a command is split at every IFS character and each piece is globbed (§3.6), so one value becomes any number of arguments — and some of those arguments can be options or actions the author never wrote:

# ❌ An unquoted value is split into words, and the words can be options
touch report.txt
# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # the missing quotes are the defect being shown
pattern='report.txt -exec touch pwned ;'
find . -name $pattern
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists: the value became a -exec action"

pwned exists: the value became a -exec action

The value was meant as a file name to search for. Unquoted, it became five arguments: report.txt, -exec, touch, pwned and ;. find read those as a name test followed by an -exec action, and ran it for the matching file. Nothing in the value was a shell metacharacter; splitting on spaces was enough to turn data into a program, because find's arguments are a program. The same is true of awk, sed, git -c, tar's --to-command and any tool whose options can name another program to run.

touch report.txt
pattern='report.txt -exec touch pwned ;'
find . -name "$pattern"
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists" || echo "no pwned: one argument, a name that matches nothing"

no pwned: one argument, a name that matches nothing

Quoted, the value is one argument, the name to test; it matches no file and find prints nothing. The quotes are the whole fix.

Globbing is the other half

Word splitting gets the attention, but pathname expansion is half of what an unquoted variable in a command does, and it has its own failure:

# ❌ The words are also globbed: a value of * becomes every file in the directory
touch keep.txt other.txt
remove() { printf 'would remove:'; printf ' %s' "$@"; echo; }
# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # the missing quotes are the defect being shown
choice='*'; remove $choice
remove "$choice"

would remove: example.sh keep.txt other.txt
would remove: *

A value of * became every name in the directory — including the script itself — and a function that removes its arguments would have removed all of them. Quoted, the function received the one-character string *. §18.13 shows how to split deliberately without globbing, for the rare case where splitting is the point; everywhere else, the rule is §3.8's: every expansion is double-quoted unless there is a reason, and the reason is written down in a # shellcheck disable=SC2086 comment next to it.

18.4 Arithmetic Injection

§7.13 showed the most surprising vector in bash, and every arithmetic example since has validated its input first because of it. An arithmetic context evaluates its operands as expressions; a name inside an expression is looked up and its value evaluated too (§4.5); and an array subscript is itself an arithmetic expression, which may contain a command substitution. So the string x[$(touch pwned)], reaching arithmetic, runs a command — through ordinary bash semantics, with no eval anywhere.

Here it is in each context bash evaluates arithmetically:

# A value used in an arithmetic context is evaluated, and a subscript may run a command
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the $( ) inside single quotes is the payload, literal on purpose
n='x[$(touch pwned)]'
check() { [[ -e pwned ]] && echo "$1: ran the command" || echo "$1: safe"; rm -f pwned; }
(( n > 0 ));              check '(( n > 0 ))'
: $(( n + 1 ));           check '$(( n + 1 ))'
[[ $n -gt 0 ]];           check '[[ $n -gt 0 ]]'
declare -i i; i=$n;       check 'declare -i'
a=(zero one); : "${a[$n]}"; check '${a[$n]}'
[ "$n" -gt 0 ] 2>/dev/null; check '[ "$n" -gt 0 ]'

(( n > 0 )): ran the command
$(( n + 1 )): ran the command
[[ $n -gt 0 ]]: ran the command
declare -i: ran the command
${a[$n]}: ran the command
[ "$n" -gt 0 ]: safe

Five of the six ran the command: (( )), $(( )), [[ … -gt … ]] (whose numeric operators evaluate their operands as arithmetic, §7.4), an assignment to a declare -i variable, and an indexed-array subscript. Only [ "$n" -gt 0 ] was safe, because [ is an ordinary command that parses its operands as decimal integers and rejects anything else with an error. That is also why it is not a fix: it is safe for an unrelated reason, and the next reader who "modernises" it to [[ ]] opens the hole.

The value does not have to reach arithmetic directly. (( n > 0 )) with n='x[$(cmd)]' works because arithmetic looked up n, found text, and evaluated that text as an expression. A value that is stored in a variable and used by name later is as dangerous as one used in place.

Validate before arithmetic

The fix is to prove the value is a number, with a test that does no arithmetic, before any arithmetic sees it:

# Validate first: only digits may reach arithmetic
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the $( ) inside single quotes is the payload, literal on purpose
count() {
  [[ $1 =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || { echo "not a number: ${1@Q}" >&2; return 2; }
  echo "doubled: $(( 10#$1 * 2 ))"
}
count 21
count 'x[$(touch pwned)]'
count 010
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists" || echo "no pwned"

doubled: 42
not a number: 'x[$(touch pwned)]'
doubled: 20
no pwned

[[ $1 =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] is a regular-expression match, not an arithmetic context, so the hostile value was rejected without being evaluated. Two details matter. The anchors ^ and $ are required — an unanchored [0-9]+ accepts any string that contains a digit, which exercise 4 measures. And 10#$1 forces base ten after validation, so 010 means ten rather than the octal eight (§7.10); without it, a leading zero is a correctness bug rather than a security one, and 08 is an error. For a signed value the pattern is ^-?[0-9]+$; for a range, validate the digits first and compare second, as §9.5's is_port did.

18.5 Data Inside a Pattern or Another Program

A pattern is a small program: * and ? and […] mean something. So is a sed script, an awk program, a regular expression and a printf format (§14.11). A value pasted into any of them is interpreted by that language's rules.

A value used as a pattern

In ${var#pattern}, [[ $x == pattern ]] and case, an unquoted expansion on the pattern side is itself a pattern. §5.4 made the point for trimming; here is what it costs when the value is a directory prefix that happens to contain a *:

# ❌ A value used unquoted as a pattern is a pattern: * matches everything
path='/srv/app/a*b/file'
prefix='/srv/app/a*b'
other='/srv/app/axyzb/file'
# shellcheck disable=SC2295  # the missing quotes are the defect being shown
echo "unquoted: ${other#$prefix}"
echo "quoted:   ${other#"$prefix"}"
echo "quoted:   ${path#"$prefix"}"

unquoted: /file
quoted:   /srv/app/axyzb/file
quoted:   /file

${other#$prefix} was supposed to strip the literal prefix /srv/app/a*b and should have left /srv/app/axyzb/file untouched, since that path does not start with it. Unquoted, a*b was a pattern matching axyzb, and the prefix was stripped from the wrong path. Quoting the expansion inside the pattern — ${other#"$prefix"} — makes its characters literal. The same applies to the right-hand side of == in [[ ]] (§7.5) and to a case pattern: quote the part that is data, leave unquoted only the wildcards you wrote. For path prefixes the mistake is realistic — directory names with [ in them are common enough on shared drives.

A value used as a replacement

The replacement side of ${var/pattern/replacement} gained a meaning in bash 5.2: with patsub_replacement on (the default), an unquoted & in the replacement stands for the matched text (§15.5).

# In a replacement, an unquoted & is the matched text (bash 5.2+, patsub_replacement)
template='Dear NAME,'
name='Tom & Jerry'
echo "${template/NAME/$name}"
echo "${template/NAME/"$name"}"

Dear Tom NAME Jerry,
Dear Tom & Jerry,

Tom & Jerry became Tom NAME Jerry, because & was replaced by the text that matched, NAME. Quoting the variable inside the replacement makes it literal. It is a small bug, but the same template-filling code is often used to build shell or HTML text, and a replacement that silently rewrites its data is not something to discover in production.

A value spliced into a sed or awk program

sed and awk are programming languages, and both can write files and run commands. A value pasted into the program text is code in that language:

# ❌ A value pasted into a sed program is sed code; its w command writes a file
printf 'Dear NAME,\n' > letter
name=$'x/w pwned\n#'
sed "s/NAME/$name/" letter
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists: sed wrote a file the data named"

Dear x,
pwned exists: sed wrote a file the data named

The value contained a / that ended the s command early, a w pwned that told sed to write the pattern space to a file named pwned, and a newline followed by # that commented out the rest. sed did exactly what its program said. GNU sed also has an e command that runs a shell command; awk has system() and print | "cmd". The fixes are the ones §15.8 gave: pass values to awk with -v or ENVIRON, never inside the program; for sed, escape the value for its context or, better, do the substitution in the shell with a quoted ${var//…/…}, which has no command language to escape from.

18.6 Option Injection, and --

A command reads its arguments from left to right, and until it sees an operand — or the special argument -- — any argument starting with - is an option. So a value that starts with a dash, placed where an operand should be, becomes an option. This is option injection, and it needs no shell metacharacter at all. The most common source is a glob, because a file name can start with a dash.

Here a stand-in rm parses its arguments with getopts, exactly as the real rm does, and prints what it would have done:

# rm stands in for the real one: it parses its arguments the way rm does and deletes nothing
rm() {
  local opt flags='' OPTIND=1
  while getopts 'fiRrv' opt 2>/dev/null; do flags+=$opt; done
  shift $(( OPTIND - 1 ))
  printf 'options: %-5s operands:' "${flags:-none}"; printf ' %s' "$@"; echo
}
mkdir work && cd work || exit
touch -- -rf important.txt notes.txt
# shellcheck disable=SC2035  # the unguarded glob is the defect being shown
rm *              # ❌ the first file name is read as options
rm -- *           # -- ends the options: every word after it is an operand
rm ./*            # or make every name start with ./

options: rf    operands: important.txt notes.txt
options: none  operands: -rf important.txt notes.txt
options: none  operands: ./-rf ./important.txt ./notes.txt

The glob expanded to -rf important.txt notes.txt, and the first word was parsed as the options r and f. With the real rm, a directory that someone else can write to becomes a way to make your rm * recursive and forced — or to add -i, -v, or, for other commands, options that name output files and programs. There are two fixes, and both appear in the output. -- ends option parsing, so everything after it is an operand. ./* makes every name start with ./, so none can start with a dash; it also works for commands that do not understand --.

This is not specific to rm. Here is the real cat:

# A file called -n changes what cat does, with the real cat
mkdir work && cd work || exit
printf 'alpha\nbeta\n' > a.txt
touch -- -n
# shellcheck disable=SC2035  # the unguarded glob is the defect being shown
cat *
echo ---
cat -- *

     1	alpha
     2	beta
---
alpha
beta

A file named -n made cat * number its output, and the file itself was never read — it was consumed as an option. After --, -n is a file (an empty one) and the output is plain.

GNU tools find options anywhere

On Linux the hazard is wider. GNU's option parser permutes its arguments by default: an option is recognised even after an operand, so a hostile name does not have to sort first.

# Linux only: GNU tools find options after the operands too
printf 'alpha\n' > a
touch -- -n
cat a -n                 # GNU: -n is an option even here
cat -- a -n 2>&1 || true # after --, -n is a file name

     1	alpha
alpha

cat a -n numbered its output — on GNU, -n after the file name is still an option. BSD cat, following POSIX's syntax guidelines, stops looking for options at the first operand: on macOS the same command prints alpha unnumbered, having read -n as a file. After --, both agree. The rule that holds on every system is §13.1's: put -- before operands that come from data, every time.

A value that becomes an option

A variable is exposed in the same way as a glob:

printf '%s\n' 'use -v for verbose' 'use -q for quiet' > help.txt
word='-v'
grep "$word" help.txt < /dev/null; echo "status $?: grep read -v as an option and help.txt as the pattern"
grep -e "$word" help.txt          # -e: the next argument is the pattern, whatever it looks like
grep -- "$word" help.txt          # or end the options first

status 1: grep read -v as an option and help.txt as the pattern
use -v for verbose
use -v for verbose

The user searched for the text -v. grep read it as the invert option and took help.txt as the pattern, then read standard input — here empty — and exited 1 without looking at the file. grep -e "$word" says "the next argument is the pattern, whatever it looks like"; grep -- "$word" ends the options first. Both found the line. Most tools that take a pattern have an -e-style option for exactly this, and most take --; the few that take neither (echo is the famous one, §14.14) are why printf '%s\n' "$x" exists.

18.7 PATH: Which Program a Name Means

When a script runs ls, the kernel is not asked for ls; bash searches the directories in PATH, in order, and runs the first executable file called ls it finds. PATH is inherited from whoever started the script. So the caller decides which program every bare command name in the script refers to.

Path injection

Path injection is putting a directory you control ahead of the real ones:

# The script calls ls by name; whoever sets PATH decides which program that is
cat > report.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
ls report.sh
EOF
chmod +x report.sh
mkdir trap
cat > trap/ls <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
echo "not the real ls"
touch pwned
EOF
chmod +x trap/ls
./report.sh
PATH="$PWD/trap:$PATH" ./report.sh
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists: the caller's PATH chose the program"

report.sh
not the real ls
pwned exists: the caller's PATH chose the program

The script did not change. Called normally it ran /bin/ls; called with a planted directory first in PATH it ran the planted ls, which printed a line and created a file. For a script a developer runs that is not an attack — the developer can already run anything. It becomes one when the person setting PATH is not the person whose privileges the script uses: a script run through sudo with an environment-preserving rule, a setuid wrapper, a service that runs hooks from a writable directory, a CI system that puts a project's own bin/ first. §1.4's advice to use #!/bin/bash rather than env for privileged scripts is the same observation applied to the interpreter.

Path hygiene: set PATH first

Path hygiene means the script decides its own search path before it runs a command by name:

# The fix: the script sets its own PATH before it runs any command by name
cat > report.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
PATH=/usr/bin:/bin
export PATH
ls report.sh
EOF
chmod +x report.sh
mkdir trap
printf '#!/bin/sh\necho "not the real ls"\ntouch pwned\n' > trap/ls
chmod +x trap/ls
PATH="$PWD/trap:$PATH" ./report.sh
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists" || echo "no pwned: the script chose its own PATH"

report.sh
no pwned: the script chose its own PATH

The first two lines set PATH to the system directories and export it, so every command the script runs — and every child of those commands — searches only there. The caller's planted directory was never consulted. For a script that runs with privileges, or on behalf of someone else, this is the first line of defence and it costs one line; the right value is the system's own (/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin on most Linux systems, with /usr/local/bin added only if the script needs something from there). Setting PATH is also the natural place for path hygiene's other half: a script should never rely on the caller's PATH containing a tool at all, which is what command -v tool || die "needs tool" at the top checks (§19.13).

Path ordering and the empty element

Path ordering matters because the first match wins, and one detail of the syntax makes the current directory part of PATH without anyone writing a dot:

# An empty element in PATH means the current directory, wherever the script happens to be
mkdir work && cd work || exit
# shellcheck disable=SC2238  # a file named ls is the point
printf '#!/bin/sh\necho "the ls in the current directory"\n' > ls
printf '#!/bin/sh\necho "the backup in the current directory"\n' > backup
chmod +x ls backup
for p in '/usr/bin:/bin' ':/usr/bin:/bin' '.:/usr/bin:/bin' '/usr/bin:/bin:'; do
  printf '%-16s ls: %-32s backup: %s\n' "$p" "$(PATH=$p ls ls)" "$(PATH=$p backup 2>&1 | sed 's/.*: //')"
done

/usr/bin:/bin    ls: ls                               backup: command not found
:/usr/bin:/bin   ls: the ls in the current directory  backup: the backup in the current directory
.:/usr/bin:/bin  ls: the ls in the current directory  backup: the backup in the current directory
/usr/bin:/bin:   ls: ls                               backup: the backup in the current directory

An empty element — a leading colon, a trailing one, or two colons together — means the current directory, exactly as . does. With the current directory first, the local ls shadowed the real one. With it last (a trailing colon), the real ls still won, but a name that exists nowhere else — a typo, or a tool that is not installed — ran whatever file of that name was in the directory the script happened to be in. Both forms appear in the wild, usually from a line like PATH=$PATH:$EXTRA where EXTRA was empty. A script that sets PATH itself, as above, is immune; one that extends it should do so with ${EXTRA:+:$EXTRA}, which adds nothing when the variable is empty.

The interpreter line searches PATH too

#!/usr/bin/env bash asks env to find bash on PATH:

# ❌ #!/usr/bin/env bash searches PATH for bash, so a caller-controlled PATH picks the interpreter
mkdir trap
cat > trap/bash <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
echo "a fake bash was given $1"
touch pwned
EOF
chmod +x trap/bash
printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\necho "the real bash"\n' > via-env.sh
printf '#!/bin/bash\necho "the real bash"\n' > absolute.sh
chmod +x via-env.sh absolute.sh
PATH="$PWD/trap:/usr/bin:/bin" ./via-env.sh
PATH="$PWD/trap:/usr/bin:/bin" ./absolute.sh

a fake bash was given ./via-env.sh
the real bash

The script said env bash, so the planted bash ran, and it received the script's path as its argument. The absolute interpreter line ignored PATH. That is the trade §1.4 described: env finds a newer bash on a developer's machine, and for the same reason it lets whoever controls PATH choose the interpreter. Privileged scripts name their interpreter absolutely.

An absolute path for a command, and command -p

The other form of path hygiene is to name a command absolutely where it matters. An absolute path for a command — /usr/bin/tar, /bin/rm — does not consult PATH at all. It is the right choice for the handful of security-relevant commands in a privileged script, and the wrong choice everywhere else, because commands move between /bin, /usr/bin and /usr/local/bin across systems (macOS has ls in /bin, Debian in /usr/bin). The portable middle ground is command -p, which searches the system's default path — the value of getconf PATH — whatever PATH says:

# command -p searches the system's default PATH, whatever PATH says
mkdir trap
printf '#!/bin/sh\necho "not the real date"\n' > trap/date
chmod +x trap/date
PATH="$PWD/trap:$PATH"
date -u -r 0 +%Y 2>/dev/null || date
command -p date -u -d @0 +%Y 2>/dev/null || command -p date -u -r 0 +%Y

not the real date
1970

With the planted directory first, date ran the fake; command -p date ran the system's date, which printed the year of the epoch. (The || fallbacks exist because GNU date spells "from this timestamp" as -d @0 and BSD date as -r 0, §19.12.)

The hash table

bash remembers where it found each command, so it does not search PATH on every call. The table is cleared whenever PATH is assigned, which is why setting PATH at the top of a script is enough. What it does not notice is a new executable appearing earlier in an unchanged PATH:

# bash remembers where it found a command. Assigning PATH forgets everything; a program
# appearing earlier in an unchanged PATH is not noticed until hash -r
mkdir a b
printf '#!/bin/sh\necho from b\n' > b/greeter
chmod +x b/greeter
PATH="$PWD/a:$PWD/b:/usr/bin:/bin"
greeter
printf '#!/bin/sh\necho from a\n' > a/greeter
chmod +x a/greeter
greeter
hash -r
greeter

from b
from b
from a

The first call found b/tool and remembered it. When a/tool appeared — earlier in the same PATH — bash kept running b/tool until hash -r cleared the table. That is rarely a security problem, but it explains a confusing class of "I fixed PATH and it still runs the old one" reports, and it is the reason a script that installs a tool and then calls it should run hash -r in between.

18.8 The Environment as Input

PATH is one environment variable. A script inherits every exported variable from its caller, and a handful of them change what bash itself does before the first line of the script runs. That makes the environment a second argument list, one most scripts never validate. An environment variable attack is a value placed in one of those variables to change what a script does without touching its arguments.

Exported functions: the simplest environment variable attack

§9.9 taught export -f, which passes a function to child bash processes through the environment. The child imports it at startup — and an imported function takes precedence over a command of the same name:

# ❌ An exported function beats a command of the same name inside the script it reaches
printf '#!/bin/bash\nls report.sh\n' > report.sh
chmod +x report.sh
ls() { echo "an inherited function called ls"; touch pwned; }
export -f ls
./report.sh
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists: the caller's function ran inside the script"

an inherited function called ls
pwned exists: the caller's function ran inside the script

The script ran ls. The caller had exported a function called ls, so the script's ls was the caller's function. For a script whose caller already has the same privileges that proves nothing; for one run on behalf of someone else, it is complete control over every command the script names. Two defences:

# bash -p does not import functions from the environment; command bypasses any that exist
printf '#!/bin/bash -p\nls report.sh\n' > p.sh
printf '#!/bin/bash\ncommand ls report.sh\n' > cmd.sh
touch report.sh
chmod +x p.sh cmd.sh
ls() { echo "an inherited function called ls"; touch pwned; }
export -f ls
./p.sh
./cmd.sh
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists" || echo "no pwned"

report.sh
report.sh
no pwned

#!/bin/bash -p starts bash in privileged mode. The manual's description of what that does at startup is exact: shell functions are not inherited from the environment; SHELLOPTS, BASHOPTS, CDPATH and GLOBIGNORE from the environment are ignored; and no startup files are read — the last is what matters for BASH_ENV, below. (Without -p, bash does all of that automatically when its effective user ID differs from its real one, and then also drops the effective ID.) The other defence is command ls, which bypasses functions and aliases for one call; it is useful in a library that must be robust to its caller, but it has to be written on every call, which is why the privileged-mode interpreter line is the better tool.

Shellshock

Shellshock is the name given to CVE-2014-6271, disclosed in September 2014 and one of the most serious vulnerabilities in the history of Unix software. Exported functions were then passed as ordinary environment variables whose value began with () {. bash, starting up, scanned its environment for such values and parsed each one as a function definition — and its parser kept going after the closing brace, executing whatever came next. Any program that put untrusted text into an environment variable and then ran bash was therefore vulnerable, and many did: web servers passing HTTP headers to CGI scripts as HTTP_* variables, DHCP clients passing server-supplied options to hook scripts, ssh passing SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND to restricted accounts. An attacker needed only to send a request with a header like User-Agent: () { :; }; command.

The classic test is still the clearest demonstration of what changed:

# The 2014 test: a variable whose value starts with () { was once parsed as a function
# definition, and any command after the closing brace ran as the new shell started
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the $( ) inside single quotes is the payload, literal on purpose
env 'probe=() { :; }; echo VULNERABLE' bash -c 'echo "bash started; probe is a plain variable: ${probe@Q}"'

bash started; probe is a plain variable: '() { :; }; echo VULNERABLE'

On a fixed bash the variable is just a variable whose value happens to begin with () {; nothing is parsed and nothing runs. The fix had two parts. bash stopped executing anything after a function body, and — because the parser itself was the attack surface, and further bugs were found in it within days — the encoding changed, so that bash only imports functions from variables with a name no ordinary variable can have:

# How bash passes a function through the environment since 2014
greet() { echo hi; }
export -f greet
env | grep -A1 '^BASH_FUNC_greet'

BASH_FUNC_greet%%=() {  echo hi
}

A web server copying a header chooses the variable's name itself (HTTP_USER_AGENT), so it can never produce BASH_FUNC_greet%%; and no shell assignment can either, because % is not allowed in a variable name. Only export -f produces it. The lesson outlives the bug: the environment is untrusted input, and a program that parses it is an attack surface. Shellshock was fixed by a series of bash patches in the weeks after the disclosure, and every maintained distribution has shipped them for years, but the pattern that made it catastrophic — privileged software that copies attacker-chosen strings into the environment of a shell — is still common, and the other variables in this subsection are still live.

BASH_ENV

A non-interactive bash — which is what runs every script — reads the file named by BASH_ENV before running the script. It is meant for setting up an environment for scripts; it is also a variable the caller controls:

# ❌ A non-interactive bash sources the file named by BASH_ENV before running the script
printf 'echo "BASH_ENV ran first"; touch pwned\n' > startup.sh
printf '#!/bin/bash\necho "the script"\n' > job.sh
chmod +x job.sh
BASH_ENV=./startup.sh ./job.sh
[[ -e pwned ]] && { echo "pwned exists"; rm -f pwned; }
printf '#!/bin/bash -p\necho "the script"\n' > job.sh
BASH_ENV=./startup.sh ./job.sh
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists" || echo "no pwned under -p"
printf '#!/bin/bash\necho "the script"\n' > job.sh
BASH_ENV='$(touch pwned)' ./job.sh           # the value itself is expanded, $( ) included
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists: BASH_ENV's value was expanded"

BASH_ENV ran first
the script
pwned exists
the script
no pwned under -p
the script
pwned exists: BASH_ENV's value was expanded

The file named by BASH_ENV ran before the script's first line, and could have redefined anything. Under bash -p it was not read. The last case is worse than it looks: the manual says BASH_ENV's value "is subjected to parameter expansion, command substitution, and arithmetic expansion before being interpreted as a filename", so the value itself is code, and a $( ) in it ran without any file existing at all. ENV is the POSIX equivalent, read by an interactive sh.

The IFS attack, and SHELLOPTS

The IFS attack is the historical ancestor of all of these. Early Bourne shells imported IFS from the environment, so a caller could set IFS=/ and turn /bin/ls into the command bin with argument ls — found on PATH, and chosen by the attacker. Modern shells close it by ignoring the inherited value:

# IFS, PS4 and the rest: which values does a new shell take from its environment?
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the $( ) inside single quotes is the payload, literal on purpose
IFS=/ bash -c 'printf "IFS: %q\n" "$IFS"'
IFS=/ /bin/dash -c '[ "$IFS" = / ] && echo "dash took IFS=/" || echo "dash reset IFS"'
env SHELLOPTS=xtrace bash -c 'echo "a plain echo"' 2>&1

IFS: $' \t\n'
dash reset IFS
+ echo 'a plain echo'
a plain echo

Both bash and dash started with the default IFS of space, tab and newline, whatever the environment said. But the same probe shows that the principle is not universal: bash does import SHELLOPTS from the environment, and a caller who sets SHELLOPTS=xtrace turns on tracing inside the script, printing every command and its expanded arguments to standard error — secrets included (§18.15). BASHOPTS does the same for shopt options, CDPATH changes where cd goes (and makes it print), and GLOBIGNORE changes what a glob matches. -p ignores all four.

Starting from a clean environment

When a script runs another program on someone else's behalf, the simplest defence is to give it an environment built on purpose instead of an inherited one:

# env -i starts a program with an empty environment; pass back only what it needs
export SECRET_TOKEN=abc123 BASH_ENV=/nonexistent
cd / && env -i PATH=/usr/bin:/bin HOME=/tmp/probe bash -c 'env | sort'

HOME=/tmp/probe
PATH=/usr/bin:/bin
PWD=/
SHLVL=1
_=/usr/bin/env

env -i cleared everything, including a token and a BASH_ENV that were exported just before, and passed back only PATH and HOME. The child bash added PWD, SHLVL and _ itself. This is the right shape for a hook runner or a privilege boundary: list what the child needs and pass exactly that. sudo does something similar by default (env_reset, §18.20), which is one reason that a script which works in a shell and fails under sudo usually needed a variable it did not declare.

18.9 The eval Builtin: Parsing Text a Second Time

The eval builtin joins its arguments with spaces and runs the result as a shell command — parsing it, expanding it, and executing it, as if it had been typed. It is the explicit version of every injection above, and the reason for the proverb that eval is dangerous: it exists to do the one thing §18.1 said the shell never does, which is to parse a value. Eval is dangerous not because it is buggy but because it does exactly what it says.

# eval joins its arguments and parses the result as a new command: a second parse
x='hello; touch pwned'
eval "echo $x"                    # ❌ $x expanded first; its ; is a separator on the second parse
[[ -e pwned ]] && { echo "pwned exists: the value ran"; rm -f pwned; }
eval 'echo "$x"'                  # the text eval parses is echo "$x": the value is expanded once
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists" || echo "no pwned: eval saw a variable, not its value"

hello
pwned exists: the value ran
hello; touch pwned
no pwned: eval saw a variable, not its value

With double quotes, the outer shell expanded $x first, so eval received the text echo hello; touch pwned and parsed a ;. With single quotes, eval received the text echo "$x", which contains no data: parsing it produced an expansion of $x, and expansions are not parsed again. The difference is when the value is expanded — before eval builds its text, or while running it — and it is the whole of eval safety. A value that is part of the string eval parses is code; a reference to a variable in that string is safe, because eval expands it only once.

Why eval looks like the answer

It is worth seeing why people reach for eval, because the temptation is always the same:

# The second parse is what makes eval look useful: quotes inside the string mean something again
# shellcheck disable=SC2089  # quotes kept in a string are the point
cmd='printf [%s] "two words" three'
# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # the unquoted expansion is the point
# shellcheck disable=SC2090  # the quotes being ignored is the point
$cmd; echo                        # word splitting only: the quotes are ordinary characters
eval "$cmd"; echo                 # parsed as shell: the quotes group

["two][words"][three]
[two words][three]

A command kept in a string does not work when expanded: $cmd is split into words, and the quotes inside it are ordinary characters by then (§6.14 measured the same failure). eval "$cmd" makes it work, because the second parse gives the quotes their meaning back — and gives ;, $( ) and backticks theirs, too, if any arrive in the data. Eval does not fix the problem of keeping a command in a variable; §18.10 does, with an array.

When eval is unavoidable, or acceptable

There are a few cases where eval is the right tool, and they have one thing in common: every byte of the text it parses was either written by the script's author or produced by something designed to produce safe shell code.

Text quoted by the shell itself. printf %q and ${var@Q} produce a representation that one parse turns back into exactly the original value (§5.8, §14.13). Text built from constants plus quoted values can be eval'd:

# Acceptable: every piece of the text eval parses was quoted by the shell itself
name=$'it\'s a $(touch pwned) "test"'
printf -v line 'printf "%%s\\n" %q' "$name"
echo "the text:  $line"
eval "$line"
line="printf '%s\n' ${name@Q}"
eval "$line"
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists" || echo "no pwned"

the text:  printf "%s\n" it\'s\ a\ \$\(touch\ pwned\)\ \"test\"
it's a $(touch pwned) "test"
it's a $(touch pwned) "test"
no pwned

The value contained a single quote, double quotes, a space and a command substitution, and came back from eval exactly as it went in, with nothing run. This is the pattern for quoting for eval: any value that is going to be parsed again is quoted with %q or @Q at the moment it is inserted, never by hand. Quoting for eval by hand — wrapping a value in single quotes and hoping it contains none — fails on the first value that does.

Output designed for eval. Some programs exist to print shell assignments for the caller to evaluate — ssh-agent -s, gpg-agent, dircolors, direnv, pyenv init, brew shellenv, and util-linux getopt (§13.8). Evaluating their output is using them as documented:

# Acceptable: a program whose documented job is to print shell code for eval
cat > agent <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
# stands in for ssh-agent -s, gpg-agent, dircolors, direnv, getopt: prints assignments
echo 'AGENT_SOCK=/tmp/agent.1234/sock; export AGENT_SOCK;'
echo 'AGENT_PID=1234; export AGENT_PID;'
EOF
chmod +x agent
eval "$(./agent)"
echo "socket $AGENT_SOCK, pid $AGENT_PID"

socket /tmp/agent.1234/sock, pid 1234

The trust here is in the program, not the eval: the output is as safe as the program that produced it and the inputs it was given. eval "$(ssh-agent -s)" is fine; eval "$(curl …)" is running whatever the server sends.

When eval is unavoidable in the strict sense is now rare. Indirect assignment, dynamic variable names, delayed expansion and building commands all have better tools in bash 4.3 and later (§18.10). What remains is old-shell portability — bash 3.2 on macOS lacks namerefs, and POSIX sh has no indirection at all — and generated code, such as a completion system or a test framework defining functions whose names are not known until run time (§9.8). In both, the discipline is the same: build the text from constants and %q-quoted values, and nothing else.

18.10 Replacing eval, and ${var@Q} for Safe Reuse

Almost every eval in a real script does one of four jobs, and each has a replacement that does not parse data.

Reading and writing a variable by name

# Reading and writing a variable whose name is in another variable, without eval
set_var() { printf -v "$1" '%s' "$2"; }
get_var() { printf '%s\n' "${!1}"; }
set_var colour 'dark blue'
get_var colour
declare -n ref=colour             # a nameref: ref is another name for colour
# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # assigning the nameref sets colour
ref='light green'
echo "$colour"

dark blue
light green

printf -v name assigns to the variable whose name is in $name (§14.12); ${!name} reads it (§5.7); declare -n makes a nameref, a second name for the same variable (§5.7, §9.6). None of them parse the value. But all three do something with the name, and a name is not a string of letters by definition:

# ❌ The name itself is still code: a subscript is arithmetic, and arithmetic runs $( )
declare -a a=(x)
name='a[$(touch pwned)0]'
printf -v "$name" '%s' value;  [[ -e pwned ]] && echo "printf -v:  ran the command"; rm -f pwned
: "${!name}";                  [[ -e pwned ]] && echo "\${!name}:   ran the command"; rm -f pwned
declare -n r=$name; : "$r";    [[ -e pwned ]] && echo "declare -n: ran the command"; rm -f pwned

printf -v:  ran the command
${!name}:   ran the command
declare -n: ran the command

A variable name may carry an array subscript, and an indexed-array subscript is arithmetic, and arithmetic runs $( ) (§18.4). All three indirection forms evaluated the subscript. So a name that came from data must be validated as a name before it is used as one:

# So a name that comes from data is checked before it is used as a name
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the $( ) inside single quotes is the payload, literal on purpose
is_name() { [[ $1 =~ ^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$ ]]; }
set_var() {
  is_name "$1" || { printf 'set_var: not a variable name: %q\n' "$1" >&2; return 2; }
  printf -v "$1" '%s' "$2"
}
set_var colour red && echo "colour=$colour"
set_var 'a[$(touch pwned)0]' value
set_var PATH /tmp/probe && echo "PATH was accepted: a valid name can still be the wrong one"

colour=red
set_var: not a variable name: a\[\$\(touch\ pwned\)0\]
PATH was accepted: a valid name can still be the wrong one

The pattern ^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$ accepts exactly the names bash allows for a plain variable and rejects subscripts. But the last line is the real lesson: PATH is a perfectly valid name, and letting data choose which variable to overwrite is still letting data change PATH, IFS or PS4. Validating that a name is well-formed only proves it is a name.

Keys in a map, not names

The better design is not to let data choose variable names at all. An associative array is a namespace the script owns, and a key is only ever a key:

# Better still: data selects a key in one associative array, never a variable name
declare -A setting=()
while IFS='=' read -r key value; do
  setting[$key]=$value
done <<'EOF'
colour=blue
a[$(touch pwned)0]=x
PATH=/tmp
EOF
declare -p setting
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists" || echo "no pwned; PATH is untouched: $([[ $PATH == /tmp ]] && echo no || echo yes)"

declare -A setting=(["a[\$(touch pwned)0]"]="x" [PATH]="/tmp" [colour]="blue" )
no pwned; PATH is untouched: yes

Three lines of hostile input became three keys: a subscript-shaped string, PATH, and an ordinary colour. Nothing ran and the script's own PATH was untouched. This is why §6.7 introduced associative arrays as "the reason a script no longer has to build variable names with eval". It is also safe in the way that matters most: bash 5.2 and 5.3 expand an associative-array key only once, whether it is used in an assignment, an expansion, [[ -v ]] or (( )):

# Is a key that came from data expanded again when it is used as a subscript?
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the $( ) inside single quotes is the payload, literal on purpose
declare -A seen=()
k='$(touch pwned)'
check() { [[ -e pwned ]] && echo "$1: ran the command" || echo "$1: safe"; rm -f pwned; }
seen[$k]=1;              check 'seen[$k]=1'
: "${seen[$k]}";         check '${seen[$k]}'
[[ -v seen[$k] ]];       check '[[ -v seen[$k] ]]'
(( seen[$k] ));          check '(( seen[$k] ))'
[[ -v 'seen[$k]' ]];     check "[[ -v 'seen[\$k]' ]]"
(( seen[\$k] ));         check '(( seen[\$k] ))'

seen[$k]=1: safe
${seen[$k]}: safe
[[ -v seen[$k] ]]: safe
(( seen[$k] )): safe
[[ -v 'seen[$k]' ]]: safe
(( seen[\$k] )): safe

(This was not always so. bash 5.0's NEWS introduces assoc_expand_once as an option that "attempts to expand associative array subscripts only once", which says what earlier versions did by default. On bash 5.2 and 5.3, measured here, every form expands a key once; a script that must run on an older bash should keep data-derived keys out of (( )) and [[ -v ]].)

A command as an array

The third job — keeping a command to run later — is §6.14's array:

# A command built at run time lives in an array; each element is one argument, never re-parsed
cmd=(printf '[%s]\n')
cmd+=("two words" 'x; touch pwned')
"${cmd[@]}"
printf 'logged as: %s\n' "${cmd[*]@Q}"
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists" || echo "no pwned"

[two words]
[x; touch pwned]
logged as: 'printf' '[%s]\n' 'two words' 'x; touch pwned'
no pwned

Each element is one argument and is never parsed, so the element x; touch pwned was passed to printf as text. The last line shows the fourth job: logging a command so that a person, or a later eval, can reproduce it exactly. "${cmd[*]@Q}" quotes each element for one parse and joins them with spaces.

${var@Q} for safe reuse

${var@Q} for safe reuse is the general tool for that last job, and printf %q is its equivalent:

# ${var@Q} and printf %q quote a value so that one parse gives it back exactly
v=$'tab\there, a \'quote\', a $(touch pwned) and a newline\nend'
echo "${v@Q}"
printf '%q\n' "$v"
eval "copy=${v@Q}"
[[ $copy == "$v" ]] && echo "round trip exact"
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists" || echo "no pwned"

$'tab\there, a \'quote\', a $(touch pwned) and a newline\nend'
$'tab\there, a \'quote\', a $(touch pwned) and a newline\nend'
round trip exact
no pwned

Both produced the same representation: bash's $'…' quoting, which can represent a tab, a newline and a single quote, and in which $(touch pwned) is plain text. Evaluating the quoted form gave back a string byte-for-byte identical to the original. Use @Q whenever a value must survive a second parse — an ssh command line, a line in a generated script, a trap string, a log entry meant to be copied and pasted — and remember that its output is for bash: $'…' is not POSIX in any shell older than the 2024 standard (§19.7), so a value quoted for sh on another machine needs the '\'' method instead.

18.11 Other Places Data Becomes Code

Eval is the explicit parser. Several other builtins parse text as part of their job, and each one is an eval when the text contains data.

Reading configuration without source

The most common is source (or .), which runs a file as a script in the current shell. Using it to load a configuration file is convenient, and it means the configuration file is a program:

# ❌ source runs a configuration file as a script, with everything in it
cat > app.conf <<'EOF'
name=demo
port=8080
greeting="hello $(touch pwned)"
EOF
source ./app.conf
echo "name=$name port=$port"
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists: the config file ran a command"

name=demo port=8080
pwned exists: the config file ran a command

Every line of the file ran, including the command substitution inside a value. That is acceptable when the file is part of the program — a library, or a configuration file with the same owner and permissions as the script itself — and wrong when the file comes from a user, a download, a shared directory or a system someone else administers. §15 promised a loader that reads such a file as data:

# Read the file as data: split each line at the first =, and accept only known keys
load_config() {
  local line key value n=0
  while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n $line ]]; do
    (( ++n ))
    [[ $line =~ ^[[:space:]]*(#|$) ]] && continue
    [[ $line == *=* ]] || { echo "$1:$n: not key=value" >&2; return 1; }
    key=${line%%=*} value=${line#*=}
    case $key in
      name|port|greeting) config[$key]=$value ;;
      *) printf '%s:%d: unknown key %q\n' "$1" "$n" "$key" >&2; return 1 ;;
    esac
  done < "$1"
}
cat > app.conf <<'EOF'
# the same file, read as data
name=demo
port=8080
greeting="hello $(touch pwned)"
EOF
declare -A config=()
load_config app.conf && declare -p config
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists" || echo "no pwned: the value is text"
printf 'PATH=/tmp\n' > bad.conf
load_config bad.conf || echo "status $?"

declare -A config=([port]="8080" [greeting]="\"hello \$(touch pwned)\"" [name]="demo" )
no pwned: the value is text
bad.conf:1: unknown key PATH
status 1

The loader reads each line with read -r, skips blank lines and comments, splits at the first =, and accepts only the keys it knows. The hostile value was stored as text — including its double quotes, which a data reader does not strip, because quoting is a shell concept and this is not shell. An unknown key stopped the load with a line number rather than being silently ignored, since a key the script does not know is either a typo or an attack. The || [[ -n $line ]] handles a last line without a newline (§14.3), and config is an associative array, so no key can become a variable name (§18.10).

declare, local, export and readonly parse assignments

A tempting shortcut for a loader is declare "$line", which turns key=value into an assignment. But declare's argument is an assignment, with an assignment's syntax — including a subscript:

# ❌ declare evaluates a subscript too, so "key=value" from a file is not safe with declare
line='a[$(touch pwned)0]=x'
declare -a a
declare "$line"
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists: declare evaluated the subscript"

pwned exists: declare evaluated the subscript

declare evaluated the arithmetic subscript and ran the command, just as printf -v did in §18.10. local, export, readonly and typeset take the same syntax and have the same property. Using one of them with a name chosen by the script and a value from data — export "APP_PORT=$port" — is safe, because the value is not part of the name; letting data supply the name side is not, unless the name is validated first (exercise 2 does both).

Strings run later: trap, PS4, PROMPT_COMMAND

trap stores a string and parses it when the signal arrives. A value expanded into that string is parsed then:

# A string the shell runs later is code too: trap, PS4, PROMPT_COMMAND
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the $( ) inside single quotes is the payload, literal on purpose
file='x$(touch pwned).tmp'
# shellcheck disable=SC2064  # expanding now is the defect being shown
( trap "echo cleaning $file" EXIT )      # ❌ the value is inside the trap's text
[[ -e pwned ]] && { echo "pwned exists: the trap text was parsed at exit"; rm -f pwned; }
( trap 'echo cleaning "$file"' EXIT )    # the trap's text names the variable instead
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists" || echo "no pwned: the value was expanded once, as data"

cleaning x.tmp
pwned exists: the trap text was parsed at exit
cleaning x$(touch pwned).tmp
no pwned: the value was expanded once, as data

With double quotes, $file was expanded when the trap was set, so the trap's text contained $(touch pwned), and it ran at exit. With single quotes, the trap's text was echo cleaning "$file", and the value was expanded once, as data, when the trap ran. §12.2 already recommended single-quoted trap strings for a different reason — they see the variable's value at the time of the signal, not at the time of the trap — and this is a second one. PS4 (expanded on every traced line), PROMPT_COMMAND and PS1 (parsed for every prompt), complete -C and bind -x all store text to parse later, and none of them should ever contain data.

Other interpreters

Anything that interprets text is on this list when a script puts data into it: awk's program (§15.8), sed's script (§18.5), printf's format (§14.11), a regular expression (where the danger is a denial of service or a match that is wider than meant, rather than execution), a find expression (§18.3), python -c, perl -e, psql -c, jq's filter (pass values with --arg), and a /dev/tcp/$host/$port path (§10.12), which is an outbound connection the data chooses. The rule is the same in every language: the program text is a constant, and values travel through that language's own argument mechanism.

18.12 Allowlist Validation

Quoting keeps data from becoming code. Validation decides whether the data is acceptable at all, and it is needed wherever a value's meaning matters: a port that must be a number, an environment that must be one of three, a file name that must stay in one directory. There are two ways to validate, and one of them does not work.

Sanitising input by removing characters

Sanitising input usually means removing the characters thought to be dangerous. It fails because the list is always incomplete:

# ❌ Sanitising by removing dangerous characters: each fix leaves another way in
sanitise() { local v=${1//;/}; v=${v//&/}; v=${v//|/}; printf '%s' "$v"; }
for input in 'a; touch pwned' 'a$(touch pwned)' 'a`touch pwned`' $'a\ntouch pwned'; do
  bash -c "echo $(sanitise "$input")" > /dev/null 2>&1
  printf '%-18q -> %s\n' "$input" "$([[ -e pwned ]] && echo ran || echo blocked)"
  rm -f pwned
done

a\;\ touch\ pwned  -> blocked
a\$\(touch\ pwned\) -> ran
a\`touch\ pwned\`  -> ran
$'a\ntouch pwned'  -> ran

The sanitiser removed ;, & and |, and blocked the one attack its author thought of. Command substitution in either spelling, and a plain newline — which is a command separator exactly like ; — all got through. Every blocked character has a substitute, and the set of characters a shell treats specially depends on the context: inside double quotes it is $, `, \ and "; in a pattern it is *, ? and [; at the start of a word it is - and ~; in IFS it is whatever IFS says. Any denylist is a bet that you have enumerated a language's syntax correctly. The practical conclusion is that sanitising input is the wrong model: a value that needs characters removed from it before it is safe to use is being used in the wrong way, and the fix is to pass it as an argument, not to scrub it.

Allowlist validation

Allowlist validation inverts the question: describe what a valid value looks like, and reject everything else. Unknown attacks fail because they are not on the list:

# Describe what is allowed, and reject everything else
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the $( ) inside single quotes is the payload, literal on purpose
valid_env()  { case $1 in dev|staging|prod) return 0 ;; *) return 1 ;; esac; }
valid_port() { [[ $1 =~ ^[0-9]{1,5}$ ]] && (( 10#$1 >= 1 && 10#$1 <= 65535 )); }
valid_file() { [[ $1 =~ ^[A-Za-z0-9_][A-Za-z0-9._-]*$ ]]; }
for v in prod Prod 'prod; touch pwned'; do valid_env "$v" && r=ok || r=rejected; printf '%-24q %s\n' "$v" "$r"; done
for v in 8080 0 65536 08080 '1+1' 'x[$(touch pwned)]'; do valid_port "$v" && r=ok || r=rejected; printf '%-24q %s\n' "$v" "$r"; done
for v in report.txt .hidden -rf ../up 'a b' $'a\nb'; do valid_file "$v" && r=ok || r=rejected; printf '%-24q %s\n' "$v" "$r"; done
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists" || echo "no pwned"

prod                     ok
Prod                     rejected
prod\;\ touch\ pwned     rejected
8080                     ok
0                        rejected
65536                    rejected
08080                    ok
1+1                      rejected
x\[\$\(touch\ pwned\)\]  rejected
report.txt               ok
.hidden                  rejected
-rf                      rejected
../up                    rejected
a\ b                     rejected
$'a\nb'                  rejected
no pwned

Each validator is one line. An enumerated value is a case with its members listed — Prod is not prod, and that is correct. A number is an anchored regular expression followed by a range check that runs only after the pattern has proved there is nothing but digits (§18.4); 08080 passes as eight thousand and eighty because of 10#, and whether a leading zero should be accepted at all is a policy decision the validator makes explicit. A file name is a short character class — letters, digits, dot, underscore and dash — with the first character restricted so that it cannot be - (an option, §18.6) or . (a hidden file, ..). The hostile values were rejected without the validators knowing anything about shell syntax. That is the property allowlist validation buys: it does not need to know what an attack looks like.

Two principles make validation reliable. Reject, do not repair: a value that fails is an error with a message that names it (${v@Q}, so a newline in it is visible), not a value to be adjusted until it passes. And validate once, at the boundary: check each value where it enters the script — argument parsing (§13.10), the configuration loader, the line read from a file — and let everything after that assume a valid value, rather than scattering partial checks through the code.

Character classes follow the locale

[[:alnum:]] means "letters and digits in the current locale", and in a UTF-8 locale that includes a great many letters:

# A character class follows the locale: pin it while validating
v='café'
LC_ALL=C;           [[ $v =~ ^[[:alnum:]]+$ ]] && echo "C:           accepted" || echo "C:           rejected"
LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8; [[ $v =~ ^[[:alnum:]]+$ ]] && echo "en_US.UTF-8: accepted" || echo "en_US.UTF-8: rejected"

C:           rejected
en_US.UTF-8: accepted

Under the C locale, café was rejected, because é is two bytes and neither is alphanumeric in C. Under en_US.UTF-8 it was accepted. Neither is wrong, but a validator that means "ASCII letters and digits" must say so: either spell the class out as [A-Za-z0-9] under LC_ALL=C, or set LC_ALL=C for the script, as §19.8 recommends for data processing generally. The same caution applies to ranges like [a-z], whose meaning outside the C locale is unspecified by POSIX.

18.13 set -f Before an Unquoted Expansion

Occasionally a script splits a value into words on purpose — a line of a log file into fields, a list of flags into arguments. That needs an unquoted expansion, and an unquoted expansion globs as well as splits (§18.3). §3 promised a defensive use of set -f (noglob) for exactly this:

# Splitting a line on purpose: an unquoted expansion both splits AND globs
mkdir work && cd work || exit
touch a.log b.log
line='INFO *.log rotated'
# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # splitting is intended here
set -- $line
echo "without set -f: $# words: $*"
set -f
# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # splitting is intended here
set -- $line
set +f
echo "with set -f:    $# words: $*"

without set -f: 4 words: INFO a.log b.log rotated
with set -f:    3 words: INFO *.log rotated

Without set -f, the word *.log in the data matched two files in the directory, and the line had four "fields" instead of three — the count depended on what was in the current directory, which is both a bug and, in a directory an attacker can write to, a way to inject arguments. With set -f before the unquoted expansion, the pattern stayed a word. The rule this section adds is short: set -f before an unquoted expansion that is deliberately unquoted, and set +f straight after, or scope it:

# In a function, local - restores every set option when the function returns (bash 4.4+)
words() {
  local -
  set -f
  # shellcheck disable=SC2086  # splitting is intended here
  printf '[%s]' $1; echo
}
mkdir work && cd work || exit
touch a.log
words 'x *.log y'
[[ $- == *f* ]] && echo "noglob still on" || echo "noglob is off again in the caller"

[x][*.log][y]
noglob is off again in the caller

local - (bash 4.4 and later) saves the shell's set options and restores them when the function returns, so set -f inside the function cannot leak into the caller however the function exits (§16.7 covered saving and restoring options in general). For splitting into an array, read -a does not glob at all, and is usually the better tool:

# Or split without any unquoted expansion at all: read -a never globs
mkdir work && cd work || exit
touch a.log
line='INFO *.log rotated'
read -ra words <<< "$line"
declare -p words

declare -a words=([0]="INFO" [1]="*.log" [2]="rotated")

read -ra split on IFS and stored *.log as the literal word. It needs no option changes, and its only limit is that it stops at a newline (§14.2). Between them, read -a for data and a scoped set -f for the unusual case cover every place a script needs to split on purpose; neither leaves globbing to the contents of the directory.

18.14 Path Traversal and Hostile File Names

Path traversal

Path traversal is a value used as part of a path that walks out of the directory it was meant for, using .. or an absolute path:

# ❌ A name that contains / or .. leaves the directory it was meant for
mkdir -p srv/uploads
save() { printf 'data\n' > "srv/uploads/$1"; }
save report.txt
save ../escaped.txt
find srv -type f | sort

srv/escaped.txt
srv/uploads/report.txt

The function meant to save files into srv/uploads, and ../escaped.txt wrote one into srv. With enough ../, a value reaches any directory the script can write to; an absolute name is harmless inside "$dir/$name", which becomes srv/uploads//etc/…, but not in code that uses the name on its own, as an archive extractor does with a member name. The same shape appears in reading (a cat "$docs/$page" that serves ../../etc/…), in archive extraction (a tar member named ../../.bashrc), and in deletion (§18.18).

There are two defences, and a script handling untrusted names needs both:

# Two defences: refuse names with a slash, and check where a path really resolves
mkdir -p srv/uploads srv/private
ln -s ../private srv/uploads/link
base_name_ok() { [[ -n $1 && $1 != */* && $1 != . && $1 != .. ]]; }
inside() {                       # is directory $2, resolved, inside directory $1?
  local root dir
  root=$(cd -P -- "$1" && pwd -P) || return 1
  dir=$(cd -P -- "$2" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P) || return 1
  [[ $dir == "$root" || $dir == "$root"/* ]]
}
for n in report.txt ../escaped.txt .. link/x; do
  base_name_ok "$n" && echo "name ok:   $n" || echo "refused:   $n"
done
for d in srv/uploads srv/uploads/link srv/uploads/../private; do
  inside srv/uploads "$d" && echo "inside:    $d" || echo "outside:   $d"
done

name ok:   report.txt
refused:   ../escaped.txt
refused:   ..
refused:   link/x
inside:    srv/uploads
outside:   srv/uploads/link
outside:   srv/uploads/../private

base_name_ok refuses a name that is not a single path component: anything with a /, and the two names . and .. that refer to directories rather than entries. That is the right check when a value is supposed to be a plain file name, and it rejected all three hostile values. inside is the check for a path that may legitimately have several components: it resolves both paths with cd -P and pwd -P — the portable way to resolve symbolic links and .., as §19's exercise 3 wrote it — and compares the resolved directory with the resolved root. It caught the symbolic link srv/uploads/link, which is textually inside uploads and physically in private; a check on the text alone would have accepted it. On Linux, realpath -m or readlink -f does the same resolution in one command.

Filename injection

Filename injection is using a file name as the vector: a name crafted so that a script which handles it carelessly does something the name chose. The earlier subsections have shown most of the ways — a name that is a command substitution reaching bash -c (§18.2), a name beginning with a dash reaching a command (§18.6), a name containing a glob or a space reaching an unquoted expansion (§18.3). One more has nothing to do with execution:

# A name with a newline in it can forge a line of output
f=$'old.txt\nOK: all 42 checks passed'
echo "removed $f"                 # ❌ the reader sees two lines
printf 'removed %q\n' "$f"        # %q shows the name as one unambiguous word

removed old.txt
OK: all 42 checks passed
removed $'old.txt\nOK: all 42 checks passed'

A name containing a newline forged a second line of output that looks like the script's own. In a log that someone reads, or a report that another program parses line by line, that is a lie told on the script's behalf. %q makes the name one unambiguous word. Names can contain terminal escape sequences as well, which can recolour, retitle or rewrite what a terminal shows, and %q renders those visibly too.

What a script handling names from a directory it does not control should expect:

# Names a script should expect in any directory it did not create
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the $( ) inside single quotes is the payload, literal on purpose
mkdir work && cd work || exit
touch -- -n ' lead' 'trail ' $'new\nline' '*' 'a$(b)' $'tab\tx'
for f in *; do printf '%q\n' "$f"; done

\ lead
\*
-n
a\$\(b\)
$'new\nline'
$'tab\tx'
trail\

A leading dash, leading and trailing spaces, a newline, a literal *, a command substitution and a tab — every one a legal file name, and every one handled correctly by a quoted "$f" in a glob loop. The habits that make a script safe against filename injection are the ones §15.11 collected: glob instead of parsing ls, quote every expansion, -- before names, NUL-delimited lists (§14.9) when names pass between programs, and %q when they are shown to a person.

18.15 Secrets

A script that deploys, backs up or calls an API holds a credential, and the shell offers several ways to leak one. Each has a better alternative.

Secrets in a script

Secrets in a script — a token written into the source — are the first to avoid. The file is in version control, in backups, in editor swap files, in the output of bash -x and cat, and readable by anyone who can read the script. The script should instead name where the secret comes from and read it at run time: a file with restricted permissions, standard input, the environment of a single command, or the system's secret store.

Secrets on the command line, and /proc/PID/cmdline

Secrets on the command line are visible to every user on the machine for as long as the process runs:

# Any user on the machine can read every process's arguments: ps shows them
token=hunter2
sh -c 'sleep 2; exit' client --token="$token" &
sleep 0.5
ps -o args= -p "$!"
wait

sh -c sleep 2; exit client --token=hunter2

ps printed the full argument list of the background process, token included, and ps does not need any privilege to do that — on macOS and on Linux, an ordinary user can list the arguments of other users' processes. On Linux the arguments live in /proc/PID/cmdline, which is world-readable:

# Linux only: /proc/PID/cmdline holds a process's arguments, NUL-separated, readable by anyone
sh -c 'sleep 2; exit' client --token=hunter2 &
sleep 0.5
tr '\0' ' ' < "/proc/$!/cmdline"; echo
ls -l "/proc/$!/cmdline" | cut -c1-10
ls -l "/proc/$!/environ" | cut -c1-10
wait

sh -c sleep 2; exit client --token=hunter2 
-r--r--r--
-r--------

The arguments are NUL-separated in the file, turned into spaces here by tr. cmdline is mode r--r--r--, readable by every user; environ, which holds the environment, is r--------, readable only by the process's owner (and root). Linux can hide other users' processes altogether with the hidepid mount option for /proc, but a script cannot assume that. So a program that takes a password as an argument is exposing it to the whole machine, and a script calling it inherits the leak. Look for a --password-file, --password-stdin or --token-fd option; most tools that take secrets have one.

A builtin is different, because it runs inside the shell and starts no program:

# A builtin runs inside the shell and starts no program, so its arguments are never listed
token=hunter2
{ printf '%s\n' "$token"; sleep 2; } > /dev/null &
sleep 0.5
ps -o args= -p "$!" | sed 's|^[^ ]*/||'     # the program's directory differs between systems
wait

bash example.sh

The background job's command line was the script's own — bash example.sh — because printf is a builtin and the token never became the argument of a new process. That is why printf '%s\n' "$token" | tool --password-stdin is safe where tool --password "$token" is not, and why a here-string or here-document (tool <<< "$token") is a good way to deliver a secret on standard input. (echo is a builtin too; /bin/echo is not.)

Tracing prints secrets

set -x prints every command after expansion, which means it prints every secret the command was given:

# ❌ set -x prints every expanded command, secrets included
token=hunter2
set -x
printf 'Authorization: Bearer %s\n' "$token" > request.txt
set +x
# Trace around the secret, not through it
set -x
: sending request
{ set +x; } 2>/dev/null
printf 'Authorization: Bearer %s\n' "$token" > request.txt
set -x
: request sent
{ set +x; } 2>/dev/null

+ printf 'Authorization: Bearer %s\n' hunter2
+ set +x
+ : sending request
+ : request sent

The first trace line contains the token, and in a CI log that line is kept, indexed and readable by everyone with access to the job. The second half shows how to trace around a secret: turn tracing off before the line, inside a group whose standard error is discarded so that the set +x itself is not traced, and back on afterwards. A caller can turn tracing on from outside with SHELLOPTS (§18.8), so a script that handles secrets and cannot run under -p should end with the secret-handling lines guarded this way regardless.

Secrets in the environment

Secrets in the environment are safer than on the command line — the environment is private to the owner — but they are inherited by every program the script starts, and every program those start:

# A secret in the environment reaches every program the script starts, and each one's children
export API_TOKEN=hunter2
bash -c 'bash -c "env | grep -c API_TOKEN"'
# Give it to the one command that needs it, for that command only
unset API_TOKEN
token=hunter2
API_TOKEN=$token bash -c 'echo "the command sees ${API_TOKEN:+a token}"'
bash -c 'echo "the next one sees: ${API_TOKEN:-nothing}"'

1
the command sees a token
the next one sees: nothing

An exported API_TOKEN reached a grandchild. Every tool the script runs can read it, and some tools write their environment into crash reports, debug logs or error pages. The better form is a prefix assignment, which puts the variable into the environment of that one command only (§2.3): the command saw the token, and the next command did not. The Twelve-Factor convention of passing configuration in the environment is reasonable for a service, whose process tree is small and known; for a script that runs dozens of other programs, scope each secret to the command that needs it.

Reading a secret from a file

# Read the secret from a file only its owner can read, or from standard input
umask 077
printf 'hunter2\n' > token.txt
ls -l token.txt | cut -c1-10
IFS= read -r token < token.txt
echo "read ${#token} characters"
printf '%s\n' "$token" | bash -c 'IFS= read -r t; echo "the child got ${#t} characters on stdin"'

-rw-------
read 7 characters
the child got 7 characters on stdin

umask 077 before creating the file made it -rw------- from the start (§18.16 shows why the order matters). read -r loaded the token into a variable without running any program, and a pipe delivered it to a child on standard input, where no other user can see it. For a person typing a secret, read -rs (§14.8) reads it without echoing it.

18.16 Permissions: umask, World-Writable Files, and Setuid

umask in a script

A new file's permissions are the mode the program asked for — 666 for a file, 777 for a directory — with the bits in the umask removed. The usual umask, 022, removes write permission for the group and others:

# A file's mode is 666 masked by the umask; a directory's is 777 masked by it
mkdir work && cd work || exit
umask 022; touch shared; mkdir shared.d
umask 077; touch private; mkdir private.d
ls -ld shared shared.d private private.d | awk '{print substr($1, 1, 10), $NF}'

-rw------- private
drwx------ private.d
-rw-r--r-- shared
drwxr-xr-x shared.d

With 022, a file is rw-r--r--, readable by everyone; with 077, it is rw-------, readable by its owner alone. A script that creates anything private — a key, a token file, a log with personal data, a temporary directory of intermediate results — should set umask in a script before creating it, rather than fixing the mode afterwards:

# ❌ Create first, restrict second: between the two the file has the default mode
umask 022
printf 'hunter2\n' > token
ls -l token | cut -c1-10        # this is the window another user can open it in
chmod 600 token
ls -l token | cut -c1-10
rm -f token
( umask 077; printf 'hunter2\n' > token )   # created 600: there is no window
ls -l token | cut -c1-10
umask

-rw-r--r--
-rw-------
-rw-------
0022

The first file existed with mode rw-r--r-- between the redirection that created it and the chmod that restricted it. Another user who opens it in that window keeps the open descriptor after the chmod, because permissions are checked when a file is opened, not when it is read. Creating it under umask 077 leaves no window at all. The subshell keeps the tighter umask to the one command, and the last line shows the script's own umask was unchanged. mktemp already creates files 600 and directories 700 for the same reason (§17.10).

World-writable files, and finding them

A world-writable file is one any user can modify, and a world-writable directory is one in which any user can create, rename and delete entries. The first means the file's contents are untrusted input to anything that reads it; the second means every name in the directory is — including names that are symbolic links to somewhere else (§18.17). The one legitimate kind of world-writable directory is a sticky one, like /tmp, where the sticky bit restricts deletion and renaming to each entry's owner. find locates the rest, and §7.6's file tests read the special bits:

# Find what anyone can modify, and what runs with its owner's privileges
mkdir work && cd work || exit
touch ok.conf open.conf tool helper
mkdir drop shared
chmod 644 ok.conf; chmod 666 open.conf; chmod 1777 shared; chmod 777 drop
chmod 4755 tool; chmod 2755 helper
echo "world-writable, not sticky:"
find . -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000 | sort
echo "setuid or setgid:"
find . -type f \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) | sort
for f in *; do
  flags=''
  [[ -u $f ]] && flags+=' setuid'; [[ -g $f ]] && flags+=' setgid'; [[ -k $f ]] && flags+=' sticky'
  [[ -n $flags ]] && echo "$f:$flags"
done

world-writable, not sticky:
./drop
./open.conf
setuid or setgid:
./helper
./tool
helper: setgid
shared: sticky
tool: setuid

-perm -0002 matches modes with the world-write bit set, and ! -perm -1000 excludes sticky directories, so the list is the open file and the open directory and not shared, the sticky one. The second find is the classic setuid sweep: -perm -4000 is setuid, -perm -2000 is setgid, and on a real system find / -xdev -type f \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) lists every program that runs with its owner's or group's privileges — a list an administrator should know by heart, and which should change only when a package is installed. [[ -u f ]], [[ -g f ]] and [[ -k f ]] test the setuid, setgid and sticky bits one file at a time.

Before trusting a file

A script that reads configuration, sources a library or runs a hook should check that nobody else can change it:

# Before trusting a file, check who can change it
trust() {
  local f=$1
  [[ -f $f && ! -L $f ]] || { echo "$f: not a regular file" >&2; return 1; }
  [[ -O $f ]] || { echo "$f: not owned by me" >&2; return 1; }
  if [[ -n $(find "$f" -prune \( -perm -0020 -o -perm -0002 \)) ]]; then
    echo "$f: writable by group or others" >&2; return 1
  fi
  echo "$f: ok"
}
umask 022
touch good.conf loose.conf; chmod 664 loose.conf
ln -s good.conf link.conf
for f in good.conf loose.conf link.conf; do trust "$f" || echo "  refused"; done

good.conf: ok
loose.conf: writable by group or others
  refused
link.conf: not a regular file
  refused

trust accepts a file only if it is a regular file and not a symbolic link, is owned by the user running the script (-O, §7.6), and is not writable by its group or by others. The permission check is a find because the shell has no test for "writable by someone other than me"; -perm -0020 -o -perm -0002 means "the group-write bit or the world-write bit", where -perm -0022 would have meant both. The link was refused because a link's target could be anywhere. A script run as root would accept root as the owner instead, and the same check should be applied to every directory on the path, since a writable parent directory lets its owner replace the file. OpenSSH makes a similar check before trusting ~/.ssh and refuses a private key that others can read, which is why its complaints about permissions are worth heeding rather than silencing.

18.17 TOCTOU: the Race Between Checking and Using

§17.7 measured check-then-act races between two copies of a script. The same race is a security hole when the second party is an attacker. TOCTOU — "time of check to time of use" — is the name for it: a script checks a property of a path, then uses the path, and between the two someone changes what the path refers to.

# ❌ Check, then use: the path can change between the two
printf 'keep me\n' > victim
mkfifo checked swapped
attacker() {                     # waits for the check, then swaps the path
  read -r < checked
  rm -f out; ln -s victim out
  echo > swapped
}
attacker &
touch out
if [[ -f out && ! -L out ]]; then          # the check: a plain file, not a link
  echo > checked; read -r < swapped         # the window, made visible
  printf 'report\n' > out                   # the use: follows whatever out is now
fi
wait
printf 'victim now holds: %s\n' "$(cat victim)"

victim now holds: report

The script checked that out was a regular file and not a link. It was. Then, in the window between the check and the write — made visible here with two FIFOs, which let the "attacker" act at exactly that moment every time — out was replaced by a symbolic link to victim. The redirection followed the link, and victim's contents were overwritten. In real life the window is microseconds wide, and an attacker who can create files in the directory runs the swap in a loop until it lands. The race is in the design, not the timing: any sequence that checks a path and then opens it by name has two separate lookups, and the path can be different each time.

The race in a temp file, and the symlink race

The race in a temp file is the classic instance. A script that writes to /tmp/myscript.log, or even /tmp/myscript.$$, uses a name that another user can predict and create first, as a symbolic link to a file the script's user can write — a symlink race. When the script runs, its > follows the link and overwrites the target with the script's privileges. §17.10 measured the attack and its defence, and the defence is the rule: never create a file with a predictable name in a shared directory; use mktemp, which creates a new file with a random name and fails if anything already exists there. Checking first — [[ -e $f ]] || … — does not fix the symlink race, for the reason the probe above just showed.

Operations that check and act at once

The general fix for TOCTOU is to replace "check, then act" with one operation that does both atomically, so there is no gap. The shell has a few:

# noclobber opens a new file with O_EXCL, which refuses any existing name, a link included
printf 'keep me\n' > victim
ln -s victim out
ln -s nowhere dangling
set -o noclobber
printf 'report\n' > out
printf 'report\n' > dangling
set +o noclobber
printf 'victim holds: %s; nowhere exists: %s\n' "$(cat victim)" "$([[ -e nowhere ]] && echo yes || echo no)"

example.sh: line 6: out: cannot overwrite existing file
example.sh: line 7: dangling: cannot overwrite existing file
victim holds: keep me; nowhere exists: no

With noclobber set (§10.5), > opens a new file with O_CREAT|O_EXCL, which the kernel refuses if the name exists in any form — and a symbolic link counts, even a dangling one that points at a file which does not yet exist.
