Both writes failed, victim was untouched, and no file called nowhere was created through the dangling link. mkdir is atomic in the same way (it fails if the name exists), which is why §17.8 built locks on it, and mv within one filesystem replaces a name atomically (§17.7).

The strongest fix is to remove the attacker's ability to change the path at all:

# The real fix is a directory nobody else can write: then no one can swap anything in it
work=$(mktemp -d) || exit
ls -ld "$work" | cut -c1-10
printf 'report\n' > "$work/out"
mv -- "$work/out" final.txt
rmdir -- "$work"
cat final.txt

drwx------
report

mktemp -d created a directory with mode drwx------, so no other user can create, rename or delete anything in it. Inside it, check-then-use is safe again, because nobody else can change a path between the two steps. The finished file was moved into place with mv, which makes the complete file appear at once. That is the shape of every temp-file-and-output problem in a script: work in a private directory, then publish atomically.

18.18 Safe rm: Deleting Without Surprises

rm -rf is the one command whose mistakes are unrecoverable, and it combines every hazard in this section: an expansion that can be empty, a glob that can match the wrong things, arguments that can be options, and a directory that may not be the one you think. Safe rm is not a single option but a set of guards, each against a specific failure. The examples use the stand-in rm, which prints what it would have done.

The rm -rf hazard: an empty variable

The rm -rf hazard that has deleted the most data is a path built from a variable that turned out to be empty:

# rm stands in for the real one and only prints what it was given
rm() { printf 'rm'; printf ' %s' "$@"; echo; }
prefix=''                          # unset, empty, or a typo in its name: the same result
rm -rf "$prefix/build"             # ❌ becomes /build
rm -rf "${prefix:?}/build"          # an error, and a non-interactive shell exits on it
echo "not reached"

rm -rf /build
example.sh: line 5: prefix: parameter null or not set

"$prefix/build" with an empty prefix is /build — an absolute path at the root of the filesystem. With a trailing /*, as in rm -rf "$dir/"*, it is every top-level directory. The variable does not need to be set to empty on purpose: a typo in its name, a failed command substitution, or a function called without an argument all produce the same thing, and Steam's Linux client once shipped the line rm -rf "$STEAMROOT/"* and deleted the files of users for whom the variable came out empty. ${prefix:?} makes an empty or unset value an error, and — measured here — a non-interactive shell exits on that error, so rm never ran and nothing after it did either. That is what you want. set -u (§11.2) catches the unset case everywhere, but not the empty one; :? catches both, on the one expansion where it matters.

ShellCheck knows the pattern:

cat > clean.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
rm -rf "$build_dir/"*
cd $target
rm -rf *
EOF
shellcheck -f gcc clean.sh || true

clean.sh:2:8: warning: Use "${var:?}" to ensure this never expands to /* . [SC2115]
clean.sh:2:9: warning: build_dir is referenced but not assigned. [SC2154]
clean.sh:3:1: warning: Use 'cd ... || exit' or 'cd ... || return' in case cd fails. [SC2164]
clean.sh:3:4: warning: target is referenced but not assigned. [SC2154]
clean.sh:3:4: note: Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting. [SC2086]
clean.sh:4:8: note: Use ./*glob* or -- *glob* so names with dashes won't become options. [SC2035]

SC2115 is the empty-variable guard; SC2164 is a cd whose failure is ignored; SC2035 is a glob that can produce an option. Every one of them is a way to delete the wrong thing, and a script that deletes anything should be ShellCheck-clean before it runs (§20).

cd that fails

# ❌ If cd fails, the next command runs in the directory you were already in
rm() { printf 'rm %s in %s\n' "$*" "${PWD##*/}"; }
mkdir -p home/project
cd home/project || exit
target=cache                       # does not exist
cd "$target" 2>/dev/null; rm -rf ./*
cd "$target" 2>/dev/null && rm -rf ./*
echo "status $?: nothing removed"

rm -rf ./* in project
status 1: nothing removed

The cd failed, the script carried on, and rm -rf ./* ran in the directory it was already in — here project, in real life often the user's home. With &&, a failed cd stops the command. A script under set -e is protected by that too, but only outside the many contexts where set -e does not apply (§11.5), so the explicit form is still the one to write: cd -- "$dir" || exit.

Quoting a glob for rm

Quoting a glob for rm follows one rule: quote the variable, leave the glob outside the quotes.

rm() { printf 'rm'; printf ' [%s]' "$@"; echo; }
mkdir -p 'my logs' && touch 'my logs/a.tmp' 'my logs/b.tmp'
dir='my logs'
# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # the missing quotes are the defect being shown
rm -f $dir/*.tmp                   # ❌ split at the space: my, then logs/*.tmp (no match)
rm -f "$dir/*.tmp"                 # ❌ the * is quoted: a file literally named *.tmp
rm -f -- "$dir"/*.tmp              # quote the variable, leave the glob outside the quotes
shopt -s nullglob
rm -f -- "$dir"/*.log              # no match: nullglob gives no words at all

rm [-f] [my] [logs/*.tmp]
rm [-f] [my logs/*.tmp]
rm [-f] [--] [my logs/a.tmp] [my logs/b.tmp]
rm [-f] [--]

Unquoted, the directory name my logs split into my and logs/*.tmp, so rm was asked to remove a file called my and a pattern that matched nothing. Fully quoted, the * was quoted too, and rm received the literal name my logs/*.tmp — a file that does not exist, or, worse, one that does. "$dir"/*.tmp quotes exactly the part that is data and leaves the glob to expand, and -- stops a name from being an option. The last line shows a fourth case: a glob that matches nothing is passed through literally by default, and with nullglob (§4.7) it produces no words at all, so rm -f -- received nothing to delete — correct, but a command that treats "no operands" as "the current directory" (find, ls, du) must be guarded against it with a check that the array of matches is not empty.

A guarded deletion function

A script that deletes directories chosen at run time should route every deletion through one function that refuses the classic mistakes:

# A deletion function that refuses the classic mistakes before calling rm
rm() { printf 'rm'; printf ' %s' "$@"; echo; }
remove_tree() {                    # remove_tree DIR ROOT: DIR must resolve strictly inside ROOT
  local target=$1 root=$2 real
  [[ -n $target && -n $root ]] || { echo "usage: remove_tree DIR ROOT" >&2; return 2; }
  real=$(cd -P -- "$target" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P) || { echo "not a directory: $target" >&2; return 1; }
  root=$(cd -P -- "$root" && pwd -P) || return 1
  [[ $real == "$root"/?* ]] || { echo "refusing: $target is not inside $2" >&2; return 1; }
  rm -rf -- "$real"
}
mkdir -p srv/cache/old srv/other
here=$(pwd -P)
remove_tree srv/cache/old srv/cache | sed "s|$here|.|"
remove_tree srv/cache srv/cache
remove_tree srv/cache/../other srv/cache
remove_tree srv/cache/missing srv/cache
remove_tree '' srv/cache
echo "status $?"

rm -rf -- ./srv/cache/old
refusing: srv/cache is not inside srv/cache
refusing: srv/cache/../other is not inside srv/cache
not a directory: srv/cache/missing
usage: remove_tree DIR ROOT
status 2

remove_tree resolves both the target and the permitted root with cd -P, so .. and symbolic links cannot disguise where the target really is (§18.14), and removes the target only if it is strictly inside the root — "$root"/?* requires at least one character after the slash, so the root itself is refused. The four refusals are the four accidents: deleting the whole root, climbing out of it with .., a target that does not exist, and an empty argument. It checks its arguments explicitly instead of with ${1:?}, because :? would have exited the whole script from inside the function. rm has guards of its own, and they are narrower than they look. POSIX requires rm to refuse an operand that "resolves to the root directory", and an operand whose last component is . or ..; GNU calls the first --preserve-root and turns it on by default. But rm -rf "$dir/"* with an empty dir is not an operand of /: the glob has already expanded to /bin, /etc, /home and the rest, and each of those is an ordinary directory. Only the script's own guards stop that. GNU --one-file-system and BSD -x refuse to cross into another mounted filesystem, which keeps a recursive delete out of a bind mount or a network share; they are spelled differently, so a portable script checks which one exists (§19.13).

18.19 Setuid Scripts and the Restricted Shell

§1.4 stated the Google Shell Style Guide's flattest rule — never make a shell script setuid or setgid — and promised the reasons. There are two: the kernel does not honour the bit, and if it did, the script could not defend itself.

A setuid shell script: the kernel ignores the bit

# Linux only: run as root in a throwaway container. The kernel honours setuid on a binary
# and ignores it on a script, whatever the script's mode says
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the $( ) inside single quotes is the payload, literal on purpose
(( EUID == 0 )) || { echo "this probe needs root"; exit 3; }
chmod 755 .
printf '#!/bin/bash\necho "script: uid $(id -ru), effective uid $(id -u)"\n' > who.sh
cp "$(command -v id)" ./id-copy
chmod 4755 who.sh id-copy
ls -l who.sh id-copy | cut -c1-10
su nobody -s /bin/bash -c './who.sh'
su nobody -s /bin/bash -c 'echo "binary: uid $(./id-copy -ru), effective uid $(./id-copy -u)"'

-rwsr-xr-x
-rwsr-xr-x
script: uid 65534, effective uid 65534
binary: uid 65534, effective uid 0

Both files are owned by root and carry the setuid bit (s in the owner's execute position), and both were run by the unprivileged user nobody (65534). The copy of id — a compiled program — ran with an effective user ID of 0, root, as setuid asks. The script ran as nobody: Linux ignores the setuid and setgid bits on any file that starts with #!, so a suid script is not privileged at all — it only looks as if it is in ls -l. The reason is the race this section has already described. The kernel opens the script to read the #! line, then starts the interpreter, which opens the script again by name; between the two, a user could replace a symbolic link to the script with a link to their own file, and the privileged interpreter would run it. Some Unix systems close that race by passing the interpreter an already-open descriptor; Linux refuses the bit instead.

And even on a system that honoured a suid script, §18.7 and §18.8 are the list of what the caller controls: PATH, exported functions, BASH_ENV, SHELLOPTS, IFS on older shells, the current directory, the umask, open file descriptors, resource limits and signal dispositions. A privileged program must distrust all of them, and a shell script, which consults most of them implicitly on every line, cannot. The right tools for running something with privileges are sudo with a narrow rule (§18.20), a small compiled wrapper, or a service with its own account.

rbash, the restricted shell

rbash — bash started as rbash or with -r — is a shell that refuses a fixed list of actions. It is sometimes offered as a way to give an account limited access:

# A restricted shell refuses a fixed list of things
for cmd in 'cd /' 'PATH=/tmp' '/bin/ls' 'echo x > f' 'exec ls' 'command -p ls'; do
  printf '%-16s ' "$cmd"
  bash -r -c "$cmd" 2>&1 | sed 's/^bash: line 1: //'
  if (( PIPESTATUS[0] == 0 )); then echo allowed; fi
done

cd /             cd: restricted
PATH=/tmp        PATH: readonly variable
/bin/ls          /bin/ls: restricted: cannot specify `/' in command names
echo x > f       f: restricted: cannot redirect output
exec ls          exec: restricted
command -p ls    command: -p: restricted

The manual's list includes those six: changing directory, changing PATH (and SHELL, ENV, BASH_ENV, HISTFILE), running a command by a name containing /, redirecting output, replacing the shell with exec, and command -p. It also refuses importing functions from the environment, parsing SHELLOPTS, and turning the restrictions off. The list sounds strict. The restrictions, however, apply only to the restricted shell itself:

# ❌ It restricts only itself: any program it may run that can start a shell ends it
bash -r -c 'cd / 2>&1; bash -c "cd / && echo \"a child shell is in \$PWD\""'
printf 'cd /\necho "a script run from rbash is in $PWD"\n' > s.sh
bash -r -c 'bash s.sh'

bash: line 1: cd: restricted
a child shell is in /
a script run from rbash is in /

The restricted shell could not cd, but it could run bash, found on PATH, and that child shell was not restricted. The manual is explicit that a shell script run from rbash runs without restrictions, too. So rbash is only as strong as the set of programs its PATH reaches, and almost every useful program — an editor, a pager, find, awk, git, ssh, python — can start a shell or write a file. A working rbash setup therefore means a PATH pointing at a directory of hand-picked links, each program audited for escapes, and a startup file that cannot be changed. That is a real design, but it is a narrow one, and it is not a security boundary to rely on for untrusted users: use a container, a separate account with filesystem permissions, or an SSH forced command (command="…" in authorized_keys, which runs one program whatever the client asks) instead.

18.20 sudo in a Script

sudo runs one command as another user, usually root, if a rule in /etc/sudoers permits it. Scripts meet it in two ways: a script that needs root, and a script that calls sudo for one step. Both have characteristic mistakes.

Decide at the top whether the script needs root

A script that needs root throughout should say so on its first lines and stop if it does not have it, rather than calling sudo on every other line and prompting for a password halfway through:

# Decide once at the top whether the script has the privileges it needs
need_root() {
  (( EUID == 0 )) && return 0
  echo "${0##*/}: must be run as root (try: sudo ${0##*/})" >&2
  exit 1
}
need_root
echo "not reached"

example.sh: must be run as root (try: sudo example.sh)

EUID is the effective user ID, and 0 is root. The message tells the user how to run the script instead of failing obscurely at the first privileged step. A script that needs root for only one step should keep the rest unprivileged and call sudo for that step, with sudo -n, which fails instead of prompting when a password would be needed, so that an unattended run fails cleanly rather than hanging.

The redirection belongs to the calling shell

The best-known sudo mistake is a redirection. The shell sets up redirections before running the command, in its own process, with its own privileges:

# sudo stands in for the real one: it prints what it would run
sudo() { printf 'sudo runs:'; printf ' %s' "$@"; echo; }
mkdir locked && chmod 555 locked
# shellcheck disable=SC2024  # the redirection outside sudo is the defect being shown
sudo echo setting > locked/app.conf     # ❌ the redirection is the calling shell's, not sudo's
echo "status $?: sudo never ran"
printf 'setting\n' | sudo tee locked/app.conf
chmod 755 locked

example.sh: line 5: locked/app.conf: Permission denied
status 1: sudo never ran
sudo runs: tee locked/app.conf

sudo echo setting > locked/app.conf failed with "Permission denied", and the stand-in sudo shows it was never even started: the calling shell tried to open the file, failed, and skipped the command. With the real sudo the result is the same — echo would have run as root and written to standard output, and the unprivileged shell could not open the file. The fix is to make the privileged process open the file: printf … | sudo tee file, where tee runs as root and opens the file itself, or sudo tee -a for appending.

sudo sh -c is command injection again

The other common fix for the redirection problem is sudo sh -c "…", which brings back §18.2:

# ❌ sudo sh -c "…$var…" is bash -c splicing again, now as root; pass the value as an argument
sudo() { "$@"; }                        # stand-in: runs the command without changing user
name='app; touch pwned'
sudo sh -c "echo restarting $name"
[[ -e pwned ]] && { echo "pwned exists: the value ran as root would have"; rm -f pwned; }
sudo sh -c 'echo restarting "$1"' sh "$name"
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists" || echo "no pwned"

restarting app
pwned exists: the value ran as root would have
restarting app; touch pwned
no pwned

The value was spliced into the text that the root shell parses, and its second command ran — as root, with the real sudo. The argument form is the same fix as always: a constant program in single quotes, and the value as $1.

Sudo in a script: a narrowly written rule

Most scripts that run unattended need a sudoers rule that allows one command without a password. Sudo in a script is only as safe as that rule, and a rule is narrow when it names the full path of the command, the exact arguments permitted, and the user it runs as:

# Linux only: run as root in a throwaway container, since it writes /etc/sudoers.d. A rule
# that names the command, its exact arguments and the user it runs as
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the $( ) inside single quotes is the payload, literal on purpose
[[ -f /.dockerenv ]] || { echo "this probe edits /etc/sudoers.d: container only"; exit 3; }
id deploy > /dev/null 2>&1 || useradd -m deploy
printf '#!/bin/sh\necho "restarting app as $(id -un)"\n' > /usr/local/sbin/restart-app
chmod 755 /usr/local/sbin/restart-app
printf 'deploy ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/sbin/restart-app ""\n' > rule
visudo -c -q -f rule && echo "rule parses"
install -m 440 rule /etc/sudoers.d/restart-app
su deploy -c 'sudo -n /usr/local/sbin/restart-app'
su deploy -c 'sudo -n /usr/local/sbin/restart-app --now' 2>&1 | sed 's/^sudo: //'
su deploy -c 'sudo -n /bin/sh -c id' 2>&1 | sed 's/^sudo: //'
su deploy -c 'sudo -n -l' | sed -n '/may run/,$p' | sed 's/ on [^ ]*:$/ on this host:/'
rm -f /etc/sudoers.d/restart-app

rule parses
restarting app as root
a password is required
a password is required
User deploy may run the following commands on this host:
    (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/sbin/restart-app ""

That was run as root in a disposable Debian container, because it edits /etc/sudoers.d. visudo -c -f checks a rule's syntax before it is installed, which matters because a broken sudoers file can lock everyone out of sudo; the file is installed with mode 440. The "" at the end of the rule means no arguments: restart-app alone ran as root without a password, while restart-app --now did not match the rule — sudo -n then needed a password it could not ask for, and refused. So did a shell. Every part of the rule is doing work. A rule without "" would allow any arguments, and a program whose arguments can name files or commands (tar, find, vi, less, git, rsync) is a root shell with extra steps. A rule naming a script the deploy user can edit — or one in a directory it can write to — lets deploy replace the script with anything. And the command should be one that reads nothing its caller controls: sudo resets the environment by default (env_reset) and sets PATH from secure_path on most distributions, but a rule with SETENV or env_keep for PATH, LD_PRELOAD, PYTHONPATH or BASH_ENV undoes that.

18.21 The Security Table

Each place a value can be parsed or trusted, and the habit that closes it.

Where data becomes code
What a script does instead
bash -c "… $v …", ssh host cmd $v
A constant program in single quotes, the value as $1; ${v@Q} for a remote shell (§18.2).
xargs -I{} sh -c '… {} …', find -exec sh -c '… {} …'
sh -c '… "$1" …' _ {}, or 'for f; do …; done' sh {} +. ShellCheck SC2156 (§18.2).
Unquoted $v
Quote it. The value was split into options and actions, and globbed (§18.3).
(( n )), $((n)), [[ $n -gt 0 ]], declare -i, a[$n]
Validate with an anchored [[ $n =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] first, then 10#$n. A subscript runs $( ) (§18.4).
${x#$p}, [[ $x == $p ]], ${t/X/$v}
Quote the data inside the pattern or replacement: ${x#"$p"} (§18.5).
sed "s/X/$v/", awk "… $v …"
awk -v or ENVIRON; a quoted ${var//…/…} instead of sed (§18.5, §15.8).
cmd *, cmd "$v" with a leading dash
cmd -- *, cmd ./*, grep -e "$v". GNU finds options after operands too (§18.6).
A bare command name
Set PATH at the top; no empty elements; absolute paths or command -p where it matters; #!/bin/bash when privileged (§18.7).
The environment
#!/bin/bash -p ignores exported functions, BASH_ENV, SHELLOPTS, BASHOPTS, CDPATH, GLOBIGNORE; env -i for a child (§18.8).
eval "… $v …"
Remove it: namerefs, printf -v, arrays for commands, maps for dynamic names. If it stays, every value is %q/@Q-quoted (§18.9, §18.10).
printf -v "$name", ${!name}, declare -n
Validate the name, since a subscript is code; better, use keys of an associative array (§18.10).
source config, declare "$line"
A read -r loader with an allowlist of keys (§18.11).
trap "… $v …", PS4, PROMPT_COMMAND
Single quotes: the text names the variable, and the value is expanded once (§18.11).
Removing bad characters
An allowlist: case for enumerations, anchored patterns under LC_ALL=C; reject, do not repair (§18.12).
Deliberate splitting
read -ra, or set -f scoped with local - (§18.13).
"$dir/$name"
Refuse /, ., .. in a name; resolve with cd -P/pwd -P and compare with the root; %q when showing a name (§18.14).
A secret
Not in the script, not on a command line (ps, /proc/PID/cmdline), not in set -x, not exported to everything: a 600 file, stdin, a prefix assignment (§18.15).
Creating a private file
umask 077 first, not chmod after; check owner and write bits before trusting a file (§18.16).
Check, then use a path
One atomic operation (noclobber, mkdir, mv), or a mktemp -d directory nobody else can write (§18.17, §17.10).
rm -rf "$dir/"*
${dir:?}, cd … || exit, "$dir"/* with --, one guarded deletion function; ShellCheck SC2115 (§18.18).
A setuid script, rbash
Linux ignores setuid on scripts; rbash is escaped by any program that starts a shell. Use sudo, an account, a container (§18.19).
sudo
Check EUID at the top; sudo tee for redirections; no sudo sh -c "$v"; a rule with a full path and exact arguments, checked with visudo -c (§18.20).

The principle behind every row is §18.1's: an expansion is data, and stays data, until something parses it. Find everything in a script that parses — another shell, an unquoted expansion, arithmetic, a pattern, another language, an option parser, eval and its relatives — and make sure that nothing a caller chose reaches it as text. Then treat the rest of what the script inherits — PATH, the environment, the current directory, the permissions of what it reads, the names in the directories it walks — as input too.

Exercises

1. Audit a script. tag.sh below prints numbered tags for a name, with a prefix from a configuration file. Find every way a caller can make it run a command of their choosing — through its first argument, its second argument and its configuration file — demonstrate each with a harmless payload, and rewrite it so that all three fail with a clear message while ordinary use prints the same output.

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the $( ) inside single quotes is the payload, literal on purpose
cat > tag.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
# tag.sh NAME COUNT: print COUNT numbered tags for NAME, using settings from tag.conf
name=$1 count=$2
source ./tag.conf
for (( i = 1; i <= count; i++ )); do
  eval "echo $prefix-$name-$i"
done
bash -c "echo tagged $name"
EOF
chmod +x tag.sh
printf 'prefix=rel\n' > tag.conf
./tag.sh api 2
check() { [[ -e pwned ]] && echo "   -> pwned: $1"; rm -f pwned; }
./tag.sh 'x;touch pwned' 1 > /dev/null;         check 'NAME through eval and bash -c'
./tag.sh api 'x[$(touch pwned)]' > /dev/null;   check 'COUNT through arithmetic'
printf 'prefix=$(touch pwned)rel\n' > tag.conf
./tag.sh api 1 > /dev/null;                     check 'the config file through source'
Solution

All three vectors, demonstrated:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the $( ) inside single quotes is the payload, literal on purpose
cat > tag.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
# tag.sh NAME COUNT: print COUNT numbered tags for NAME, using settings from tag.conf
name=$1 count=$2
source ./tag.conf
for (( i = 1; i <= count; i++ )); do
  eval "echo $prefix-$name-$i"
done
bash -c "echo tagged $name"
EOF
chmod +x tag.sh
printf 'prefix=rel\n' > tag.conf
./tag.sh api 2
check() { [[ -e pwned ]] && echo "   -> pwned: $1"; rm -f pwned; }
./tag.sh 'x;touch pwned' 1 > /dev/null;         check 'NAME through eval and bash -c'
./tag.sh api 'x[$(touch pwned)]' > /dev/null;   check 'COUNT through arithmetic'
printf 'prefix=$(touch pwned)rel\n' > tag.conf
./tag.sh api 1 > /dev/null;                     check 'the config file through source'

rel-api-1
rel-api-2
tagged api
   -> pwned: NAME through eval and bash -c
   -> pwned: COUNT through arithmetic
   -> pwned: the config file through source

The name reached two parsers: eval, whose text was built with the value inside it (§18.9), and bash -c, whose program text was built the same way (§18.2). The count reached the arithmetic of the for ((…)) loop, where an array subscript runs a command (§18.4). And source ran the configuration file as a script (§18.11). The rewrite:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the $( ) inside single quotes is the payload, literal on purpose
cat > tag.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# tag.sh NAME COUNT: print COUNT numbered tags for NAME, using settings from tag.conf
set -euo pipefail
die() { printf 'tag.sh: %s\n' "$1" >&2; exit 2; }
(( $# == 2 )) || die 'usage: tag.sh NAME COUNT'
name=$1 count=$2
[[ $name =~ ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$ ]] || die "invalid name: ${name@Q}"
[[ $count =~ ^[0-9]{1,3}$ ]] || die "invalid count: ${count@Q}"
prefix=tag
while IFS='=' read -r key value; do
  case $key in
    prefix) [[ $value =~ ^[a-z0-9-]+$ ]] || die "invalid prefix in tag.conf"; prefix=$value ;;
    ''|'#'*) ;;
    *) die "unknown setting in tag.conf: ${key@Q}" ;;
  esac
done < ./tag.conf
for (( i = 1; i <= 10#$count; i++ )); do
  printf '%s-%s-%d\n' "$prefix" "$name" "$i"
done
printf 'tagged %s\n' "$name"
EOF
chmod +x tag.sh
printf 'prefix=rel\n' > tag.conf
./tag.sh api 2
./tag.sh 'x;touch pwned' 1
./tag.sh api 'x[$(touch pwned)]'
printf 'prefix=$(touch pwned)rel\n' > tag.conf
./tag.sh api 1
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists" || echo "no pwned"

rel-api-1
rel-api-2
tagged api
tag.sh: invalid name: 'x;touch pwned'
tag.sh: invalid count: 'x[$(touch pwned)]'
tag.sh: invalid prefix in tag.conf
no pwned

Each fix removes a parser rather than guarding one. The eval and the bash -c are gone, replaced by printf with a constant format, so the name is never code. The name and count are validated against allowlists before anything uses them (§18.12), with the rejected value shown by ${name@Q}. The count's check is a regular expression, which does no arithmetic, and 10# keeps a leading zero decimal. The configuration file is read as data, and only the one key the script knows is accepted, with its own allowlist. die exits with status 2, the usage-error convention (§11.4).

2. A safe environment-file loader. Write load_env FILE, which reads KEY=VALUE lines (with blank lines and # comments allowed) and exports each variable. It must never run anything in the file, must refuse a file that is not a regular file owned by the caller or that others can write, must accept only names made of capital letters, digits and underscores, and must refuse to set variables that change how the shell or the dynamic linker behaves.

Solution 
# load_env FILE: export KEY=VALUE lines from FILE, safely
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the $( ) inside single quotes is the payload, literal on purpose
load_env() {
  local file=$1 line key value n=0
  [[ -f $file && ! -L $file && -O $file ]] || { echo "load_env: $file: not a regular file I own" >&2; return 1; }
  if [[ -n $(find "$file" -prune \( -perm -0020 -o -perm -0002 \)) ]]; then
    echo "load_env: $file: writable by others" >&2; return 1
  fi
  while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n $line ]]; do
    (( ++n ))
    [[ $line =~ ^[[:space:]]*(#|$) ]] && continue
    [[ $line =~ ^([A-Z_][A-Z0-9_]*)=(.*)$ ]] || { echo "load_env: $file:$n: malformed" >&2; return 1; }
    key=${BASH_REMATCH[1]} value=${BASH_REMATCH[2]}
    case $key in
      PATH|IFS|HOME|SHELL|ENV|BASH_ENV|SHELLOPTS|BASHOPTS|PS4|CDPATH|GLOBIGNORE|PROMPT_COMMAND|LD_*|DYLD_*|BASH_FUNC_*)
        echo "load_env: $file:$n: refusing to set $key" >&2; return 1 ;;
    esac
    export "$key=$value"
  done < "$file"
}
umask 022
cat > app.env <<'EOF'
# settings for the app
APP_PORT=8080
APP_GREETING=hello $(touch pwned) world
EOF
load_env app.env && printf '%s=%s\n' APP_PORT "$APP_PORT" APP_GREETING "$APP_GREETING"
printf 'BASH_ENV=./evil.sh\n' > bad.env;  load_env bad.env
printf 'a[$(touch pwned)0]=x\n' > worse.env; load_env worse.env
chmod 666 app.env; load_env app.env
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists" || echo "no pwned"

APP_PORT=8080
APP_GREETING=hello $(touch pwned) world
load_env: bad.env:1: refusing to set BASH_ENV
load_env: worse.env:1: malformed
load_env: app.env: writable by others
no pwned

The file checks are §18.16's trust. Each line is matched against one anchored regular expression that splits it into a name and a value and proves the name is a plain uppercase identifier, so a subscript-shaped name was rejected as malformed and never reached export (§18.11). A denylist of dangerous names follows — which is not a contradiction of §18.12: the allowlist decides what is well-formed, and the denylist removes well-formed names that are too powerful to set from a file, BASH_ENV among them (§18.8). A stricter loader would instead allow only names with the application's own prefix, APP_*, which is an allowlist and needs no denylist at all. export "$key=$value" is safe because the name side has been validated and the value is never parsed; the command substitution in APP_GREETING was stored as text. When the file was made world-writable, the loader refused it.

3. A remote command runner. ssh host cmd args… joins its arguments and sends them to the remote shell (§18.2). Write remote_run COMMAND ARG… on top of the stand-in run_remotely, so that every argument arrives at the remote side as exactly one word, whatever it contains.

Solution 
# run_remotely stands in for ssh HOST: it joins its arguments and gives them to a shell
run_remotely() { bash -c "$*"; }
umask 022
remote_run() {                   # remote_run COMMAND ARG...: every word arrives intact
  run_remotely "${@@Q}"
}
touch 'my notes.txt'
remote_run ls -l 'my notes.txt' | cut -c1-10
remote_run printf '[%s]\n' 'two words' 'x; touch pwned' "it's"
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "pwned exists" || echo "no pwned"

-rw-r--r--
[two words]
[x; touch pwned]
[it's]
no pwned

"${@@Q}" quotes each positional parameter for one parse, so when run_remotely joins them with spaces and the remote shell parses the result, each argument comes back as it was: the name with a space, the two-word argument, the ; argument as plain text and the single quote in it's. With the real ssh the call is the same: ssh host "${cmd[@]@Q}" for a command held in an array. Two caveats. @Q produces bash's quoting, and a remote login shell that is not bash — dash, or a user's fish — needs POSIX quoting (§19.7) instead. And for data of any size, sending it on standard input (ssh host 'cat > file' < data) avoids the command line entirely.

4. Four validators that look right. Each of these was meant to reject bad input. Find a value that each one accepts wrongly, or that makes it do something worse than accept.

is_num()  { [[ $1 =~ [0-9]+ ]]; }
is_name() { [[ $1 != *..* ]]; }
is_port() { (( $1 > 0 && $1 < 65536 )); }
is_safe() { [[ $1 != *';'* && $1 != *'|'* ]]; }
Solution 
# Four validators that look right and are not
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the $( ) inside single quotes is the payload, literal on purpose
is_num_a()  { [[ $1 =~ [0-9]+ ]]; }                   # unanchored
is_num_b()  { [[ $1 =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; }
is_name_a() { [[ $1 != *..* ]]; }                     # checks one spelling of "up"
is_port_a() { (( $1 > 0 && $1 < 65536 )) 2>/dev/null; } # arithmetic before any check
for v in 42 'x42y' $'42\nrm'; do
  printf '%-10q a:%s b:%s\n' "$v" "$(is_num_a "$v" && echo ok || echo no)" "$(is_num_b "$v" && echo ok || echo no)"
done
mkdir -p work/base/sub && ln -s ../.. work/base/sub/up
is_name_a '../secret' || echo "../secret refused"
is_name_a 'sub/up' && echo "sub/up accepted, and it holds: $(ls work/base/sub/up)"
is_port_a 'x[$(touch pwned)]'
[[ -e pwned ]] && echo "is_port_a ran the command"

42         a:ok b:ok
x42y       a:ok b:no
$'42\nrm'  a:ok b:no
../secret refused
sub/up accepted, and it holds: base
is_port_a ran the command

is_num is unanchored, so it accepts any string containing a digit: x42y, and a value with a newline and a second line. With ^ and $ it rejects both — in bash's =~, $ matches only at the true end of the string, unlike some other languages where it also matches before a final newline. is_name blocks one spelling of "go up" and misses a symbolic link: sub/up contains no .. but leads out of base, which only resolving the path catches (§18.14). is_port is worse than wrong, because it does arithmetic on the value to decide whether the value is safe for arithmetic, and a subscript ran a command during the check itself (§18.4). is_safe is §18.12's denylist: $(…), backticks, & and a newline all pass it. The fixes are the ones this section has used throughout: anchor every pattern; resolve a path before judging it; prove a value is digits before any arithmetic sees it; and describe the values that are allowed instead of the ones that are not.

SECTION 19

POSIX Portability

Every script in this course so far has started with #!/usr/bin/env bash or #!/bin/bash, and has used arrays, [[ ]], local, ${var@Q} and the rest of bash freely. That was a deliberate choice, argued in §1: bash is installed almost everywhere a script runs, and it is a far better language than the one underneath it. This section is about the language underneath it — the POSIX shell, the command language the POSIX standard specifies and every /bin/sh claims to implement — and about the scripts that have to be written in it.

Those scripts exist. A script run by /bin/sh because some other program chose the interpreter — a Makefile recipe, a Debian package's maintainer script, a RUN line in a container build, a system() call from C or Python, a hook a tool runs with sh -c — is a POSIX script whether its author knew it or not. A script for a minimal container image with no bash in it, or for an embedded system with only BusyBox, has no choice either. And a script that is shared widely enough — an installer piped from a web page, a tool's bootstrap script — earns its portability by running on systems its author never saw.

The section is organised around one question: which parts of what this course has taught are bash, and what does a portable script write instead? §19.1 says what sh actually is on the systems a script meets, and why "it works when I run it with sh" proves nothing on a Mac. §19.2 is about finding a bashism mechanically, with ShellCheck, checkbashisms and dash itself. §19.3–§19.11 then go through the language construct by construct — tests, strings, arrays, functions, quoting and output, the locale, redirection and sourcing, arithmetic and loops, options, traps and read — measuring each bash form under dash and giving the portable replacement. §19.12 and §19.13 leave the shell for the utilities it calls, where GNU and BSD disagree more than any two shells do, and show how a script detects a capability instead of guessing from the operating system. §19.14 collects everything that fails under dash in one table, §19.15 writes a complete portable script and checks it four ways, and §19.16 is the summary.

The editorial boundary: the linux course owns sh as the interactive shell a person types into; §1 owns the decision between #!/bin/sh and #!/usr/bin/env bash; §13 owns getopts, which is POSIX and is used here without being re-taught. This section owns what changes in the language when a script must be POSIX.

Every example here was run under bash 5.3 on macOS and bash 5.2 on Debian, and each script under test was run with dash, which is /bin/dash on macOS and /bin/sh on Debian and Ubuntu. The two platforms print the same thing everywhere except where a line runs sh itself, because sh is a different program on each — those places say so. Claims about what POSIX requires are quoted from POSIX.1-2024, the current edition (IEEE Std 1003.1-2024, "Issue 8"), which changed more of the shell than any edition in twenty years; where a feature became standard only in 2024, the section says so, because a standard that was published in 2024 is not yet what most systems ship.

19.1 What POSIX sh Is, and When Portability Matters

POSIX is a standard, not a program. It specifies a shell command language and a set of utilities, and a shell that implements that language is a POSIX shell. No shell implements only that language: bash, dash, ksh, zsh in its sh emulation and BusyBox's ash all add extensions, and they add different ones. So a script is portable not because it runs under one POSIX shell, but because it uses nothing any of them adds.

POSIX compliance, and what sh is on each system

POSIX compliance of a script means exactly that: every construct in it is one the standard specifies, so any conforming shell runs it the same way. POSIX compliance of a shell is a weaker property than it sounds, because compliance is about what the shell must accept, not what it must reject. bash is a largely compliant shell, and it will run [[ ]] under the name sh without a murmur. A script can therefore only be checked for POSIX compliance by something that rejects extensions, and §19.2 is about those tools.

What /bin/sh actually is depends on the system:

System
What /bin/sh runs
Debian, Ubuntu
dash, the Debian Almquist shell: small, fast, and close to the bare standard. The version measured here is 0.5.12.
macOS
bash 3.2.57 in POSIX mode — the same 2007 bash as /bin/bash, started under the name sh. macOS also ships /bin/dash.
Alpine, BusyBox systems
BusyBox ash, another Almquist descendant, with a few bash extensions compiled in and many left out.
Fedora, RHEL, Arch
bash in POSIX mode, a current version.
FreeBSD
FreeBSD's own sh, also an Almquist shell.

Dash as /bin/sh: Ubuntu /bin/sh is dash

Debian and Ubuntu made dash their /bin/sh long ago, and the reason is visible in its size: dash is a fraction of bash, starts faster, and a system runs a great many sh scripts. Ubuntu /bin/sh is dash, as is Debian's, and so are the debian and ubuntu container images that a large share of the world's CI runs in. Dash as /bin/sh is therefore the case that matters most in practice, and it is the shell this section measures against.

Here is what the difference looks like. The same four lines, run by three interpreters:

# The same four lines under three interpreters
cat > greet.sh <<'EOF'
name=world
if [[ $name == w* ]]; then
  echo "hello, ${name^}"
fi
EOF
for shell in bash sh dash; do
  echo "== $shell"; "$shell" greet.sh 2>&1; echo "status $?"
done

== bash
hello, World
status 0
== sh
greet.sh: line 3: hello, ${name^}: bad substitution
status 1
== dash
greet.sh: 2: [[: not found
status 0

Three shells, three different outcomes, and only one of them an honest failure. bash ran it. macOS sh — bash 3.2 — accepted the [[ ]] test, which bash 3.2 has, and failed on ${name^}, which arrived in bash 4.0. dash did not know [[ at all: it looked for a command called [[, found none, printed [[: not found, and the if took its false branch. The script's exit status was 0, because an if whose condition fails and which has no else succeeds. A bashism under dash does not always crash; sometimes it silently takes the wrong branch and reports success. (On Debian, where sh is dash, the middle block prints what the dash block prints.)

sh compatibility is not bash in POSIX mode

bash has a POSIX mode, turned on by --posix, by set -o posix, or by being started under the name sh. It is tempting to think that running a script under it checks the script's sh compatibility. It does not:

# POSIX mode changes the behaviours POSIX specifies differently; it does not remove bash's extensions
cat > extras.sh <<'EOF'
list=(one two three)
[[ ${list[1]} == t* ]] && echo "arrays and [[ ]] still work: ${list[1]^^}"
EOF
bash --posix extras.sh
dash extras.sh 2>&1; echo "dash: status $?"

arrays and [[ ]] still work: TWO
extras.sh: 1: Syntax error: "(" unexpected
dash: status 2

In POSIX mode bash still has arrays, still has [[ ]] and still has ${var^^}. The bash manual lists what POSIX mode changes, and every item on that list is a place where bash's default behaviour contradicts the standard — how . searches for a file, whether a failed special builtin exits the shell, what echo does with backslashes on some builds. POSIX mode makes bash obey the standard where the two conflict; it does not make bash forget its extensions, because an extension is not a conflict. That is why sh script.sh on a Mac, or bash --posix script.sh anywhere, is not a test of sh compatibility. dash is.

When portability matters

Portability is a cost, and it should be paid only when something requires it. The portable language has no arrays, no local, no [[ ]], no ${var//old/new} and no (( )), and §19.3–§19.11 show what each costs to live without. When portability matters is therefore a decision to make deliberately, and these are the cases that force it:

  • The interpreter is chosen for you. make runs recipes with /bin/sh; system() and popen() in C, os.system and subprocess.run(..., shell=True) in Python, exec in many tools, and a Dockerfile's shell-form RUN all use sh -c. Whatever is written there is a POSIX script.
  • bash may not be installed. Alpine, distroless and BusyBox-based images, initramfs scripts, routers and embedded boards. A script that must run before packages are installed — a bootstrap, an installer — belongs here too.
  • The script is distributed to systems you do not control, and you cannot say which shell or which bash version is on them. macOS's /bin/bash 3.2 is the standing example: a "bash script" that uses mapfile or associative arrays fails there.
  • A convention demands it. Debian maintainer scripts must be /bin/sh scripts (Debian Policy §10.4 allows five extensions, §19.2 lists them), as must scripts sourced by several different shells, such as a profile fragment.

When none of these applies, the answer is the one §1 gave: write #!/usr/bin/env bash, use bash properly, and do not pretend otherwise with a #!/bin/sh line. The worst script is the one that says sh and means bash — it works on the author's Mac and on Fedora, where sh is bash, and fails on the first Ubuntu machine it meets. §19.15 ends with a guard that makes such a script at least fail loudly, or re-run itself under bash.

19.2 Finding a Bashism

A bashism is a construct bash accepts and POSIX does not specify. Finding them by reading is unreliable, because many of them look like ordinary shell: == in a test, echo -n, local, source, function. They are found mechanically, and there are three instruments, each blind where another sees.

Running the script under dash, and why that is not enough

The most direct check is to run the script with dash. That catches everything dash rejects on the lines it executes, and nothing else. It is tempting to go one step further and use dash -n, which parses a script without running it:

# dash -n checks syntax only, and [[ is not a syntax error to dash: it is a command name
cat > check.sh <<'EOF'
if [[ -f config ]]; then
  echo found
fi
EOF
dash -n check.sh && echo "dash -n: no complaint"
dash check.sh; echo "dash: status $?"

dash -n: no complaint
check.sh: 1: [[: not found
dash: status 0

dash -n found nothing, because [[ -f config ]] is not a syntax error to dash — [[ is just a word, and a word at the start of a command is a command name. Most bashisms are like that: local, source, let, declare, [[ and == are all syntactically fine and fail only when executed, and only on the path that reaches them. A run under dash is still worth doing, but it tests the branches the run happened to take. The static tools read every line.

shellcheck -s sh and the SC3000 portability warnings

ShellCheck knows several dialects — sh, bash, dash, ksh, busybox — and reads the script against the one its shebang names. For a #!/bin/sh script it switches on the SC3000 family of checks: every code from SC3001 upwards is one of the portability warnings, and each one names a construct POSIX sh does not have.

cat > report.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
name=$1
if [[ $name == admin ]]; then
  echo "${name^^} may proceed"
fi
local count=0
echo -n "done"
EOF
shellcheck -f gcc report.sh

report.sh:3:4: warning: In POSIX sh, [[ ]] is undefined. [SC3010]
report.sh:3:13: warning: In POSIX sh, == in place of = is undefined. [SC3014]
report.sh:4:9: warning: In POSIX sh, case modification is undefined. [SC3059]
report.sh:6:1: warning: In POSIX sh, 'local' is undefined. [SC3043]
report.sh:6:7: warning: count appears unused. Verify use (or export if used externally). [SC2034]
report.sh:7:6: warning: In POSIX sh, echo flags are undefined. [SC3037]

Every bashism in the script has its own code: SC3010 for [[ ]], SC3014 for == in place of =, SC3059 for case modification, SC3043 for local and SC3037 for echo's flags. Each code has a wiki page explaining the construct and its portable replacement, which is why the portability warnings are the best single place to learn this material. The -f gcc format prints one line per finding, file:line:column:, which is what an editor or a CI log wants. SC2034 in the middle is not a portability warning — it is the ordinary unused-variable check, and it would appear in a bash script too.

shellcheck -s sh overrides the shebang. It is how to check a file that is going to be run by sh although it says bash, or has no shebang at all — a Makefile recipe extracted to a file, a snippet from a Dockerfile:

# ShellCheck picks the dialect from the shebang; -s overrides it
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the $ belongs to the script being written, not to this one
printf '#!/bin/bash\narr=(a b)\necho "${arr[0]}"\n' > tool.sh
shellcheck tool.sh && echo "as bash: clean"
shellcheck -s sh -f gcc tool.sh

as bash: clean
tool.sh:2:5: warning: In POSIX sh, arrays are undefined. [SC3030]
tool.sh:3:7: warning: In POSIX sh, array references are undefined. [SC3054]

The same file is clean as bash and has two portability warnings as sh. The dialect can also be set inside a file with a directive, # shellcheck shell=sh, which is how to mark a library that has no shebang because it is only ever sourced. ShellCheck as a gate — severities, suppressions, running it in CI — is §20's subject; here it is used for the one question of portability.

checkbashisms

checkbashisms comes from Debian's devscripts package, written for exactly this job: Debian maintainer scripts must run under /bin/sh, and the tool checks them. It is a pattern matcher, not a parser, so its messages are phrased as suspicions:

cat > report.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
name=$1
if [[ $name == admin ]]; then
  echo "${name^^} may proceed"
fi
local count=0
echo -n "done"
EOF
checkbashisms report.sh

possible bashism in report.sh line 3 (alternative test command ([[ foo ]] should be [ foo ])):
if [[ $name == admin ]]; then
possible bashism in report.sh line 3 (should be 'b = a'):
if [[ $name == admin ]]; then
possible bashism in report.sh line 4 (${parm,[,][pat]} or ${parm^[^][pat]}):
  echo "${name^^} may proceed"

It found three of the problems and missed two: local and echo -n are not reported. That is not a bug but a policy. Debian Policy §10.4 lets /bin/sh scripts assume POSIX.1-2017 plus five extensions — echo -n, local, test's -a and -o, kill -SIGNAL and numeric signals in trap — so by default checkbashisms checks against Debian's sh, not against POSIX. Its -p option (--posix) checks against the standard:

# -p (--posix) also reports what Debian Policy allows in /bin/sh but POSIX does not
cat > report.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
f() {
  local count=0
  echo -n "done"
}
EOF
checkbashisms report.sh && echo "default: no report"
checkbashisms -p report.sh

default: no report
possible bashism in report.sh line 3 (local foo=bar):
  local count=0
possible bashism in report.sh line 4 (echo -n):
  echo -n "done"

With -p both are reported. The two tools overlap heavily, and where they differ the difference is useful: ShellCheck understands the grammar, so it does not report a bashism inside a quoted string or a here-document meant as data; checkbashisms sometimes does, but it also knows a few runtime details ShellCheck does not model. A portable script should pass shellcheck -s sh and checkbashisms -p and a run under dash, and §19.15 does all three.

19.3 Tests: [[ is not POSIX

§7 taught [[ ]] as the test to use in bash, and gave the reasons: no word splitting inside it, pattern matching with ==, regular expressions with =~, and && and || inside the brackets. None of that exists in POSIX sh. POSIX 2024 lists [[ and ]] among the words that "may be recognized as reserved words on some implementations", with results that are unspecified — which is the standard's way of saying that a portable script must not use them. [[ is not POSIX, and in dash it is not anything at all:

cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
answer=yes
if [[ $answer = yes ]]; then echo "matched"; else echo "did not match"; fi
EOF
dash t.sh; echo "status $?"

t.sh: 2: [[: not found
did not match
status 0

The same silent failure §19.1 showed, from the other side: [[ was not found, the test "failed", and the else branch ran — the script printed did not match for a value that matched, and exited 0. The portable test is [ (the test builtin), with every variable double-quoted, since word splitting and globbing apply inside [ ] exactly as they do on any command line (§7.2).

== in test is not POSIX

== in test is not POSIX either. POSIX test compares strings with a single =; bash's [ accepts == as a synonym, and dash's does not:

# == inside [ ] is a bash extension; POSIX test has only =
cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
a=x
if [ "$a" == x ]; then echo "== matched"; else echo "== did not match"; fi
if [ "$a" = x ];  then echo "=  matched"; fi
EOF
echo "bash:"; bash t.sh
echo "dash:"; dash t.sh

bash:
== matched
=  matched
dash:
t.sh: 2: [: x: unexpected operator
== did not match
=  matched

dash's [ saw three arguments, x, == and x, did not recognise == as an operator, and reported unexpected operator — then the if took its false branch. This is the most common bashism in scripts written by people who know the portable rules, because == is what every other language uses and bash never complains. The fix is one character.

Patterns without [[ ]]: case

[[ $x == pattern ]] matched a glob pattern, and POSIX has a construct built for exactly that: case. Every pattern [[ == ]] can take, case can take, including bracket expressions and alternatives with |:

# [[ $x == pattern ]] has a portable replacement: case
cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
for file in notes.txt photo.JPG script.sh; do
  case $file in
    *.txt)       echo "$file: text" ;;
    *.[Jj][Pp][Gg]) echo "$file: image" ;;
    *)           echo "$file: other" ;;
  esac
done
EOF
dash t.sh

notes.txt: text
photo.JPG: image
script.sh: other

*.[Jj][Pp][Gg] matched photo.JPG case-insensitively, with no shopt -s nocasematch. case is also the portable answer to "does this string contain that one" (§19.4) and "is this a number" below, and it has two properties that make it better than it looks: it never splits or globs the word being tested, so case $x in needs no quotes, and it is a single builtin with no subprocess.

Joining tests: && and ||, not -a and -o

Inside [[ ]], bash lets && and || join conditions. POSIX test had -a and -o for this, marked obsolescent for years because expressions using them are ambiguous — [ "$a" -a "$b" ] parses differently when $a is ! or (. POSIX.1-2024 removed them, along with test's ( and ). The portable form joins separate tests with the shell's own && and ||:

# Join tests with && and ||, not -a and -o (which POSIX.1-2024 removed from test)
cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
x=5
if [ "$x" -gt 1 ] && [ "$x" -lt 10 ]; then echo "between 1 and 10"; fi
empty=
if [ -z "$empty" ] || [ "$empty" = none ]; then echo "empty or none"; fi
EOF
dash t.sh

between 1 and 10
empty or none

Each [ ] is a complete command, and && joins commands. dash still accepts -a, and Debian Policy still promises it to Debian's scripts (§19.2), but a script written today for POSIX should not use it.

Regular expressions without =~

[[ $x =~ regex ]] has no POSIX spelling. For the most common use — checking that a value is made of allowed characters — a case pattern with a negated bracket expression is exact:

# [[ =~ ]] has no POSIX spelling; case or expr covers most uses
cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
for port in 8080 80a ''; do
  case $port in
    ''|*[!0-9]*) echo "${port:-(empty)}: not a number" ;;
    *)           echo "$port: a number" ;;
  esac
done
EOF
dash t.sh

8080: a number
80a: not a number
(empty): not a number

*[!0-9]* matches any string containing at least one character that is not a digit; together with '' for the empty string, the remaining case is "one or more digits and nothing else". Note ! for negation inside a bracket expression: POSIX specifies [!…], and [^…] is an extension that most shells accept and a portable script avoids. For a pattern that genuinely needs a regular expression, expr "$x" : 'regex' and printf '%s\n' "$x" | grep -Eq 'regex' both work, at the cost of a subprocess each. And the < and > string comparisons, which [[ ]] has always had, were added to POSIX test only in 2024, together with -nt, -ot and -ef; dash supports all five, but a script for older systems should compare with sort or expr instead.

19.4 Strings: ${var^^} is not POSIX

§5 taught more than twenty forms of parameter expansion. POSIX specifies a subset of them, and a portable script lives within it. ${var^^} is not POSIX, and neither is any case modification:

cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
name='Ada Lovelace'
echo "${name^^}"
EOF
dash t.sh; echo "status $?"
cat > t2.sh <<'EOF'
name='Ada Lovelace'
upper=$(printf '%s' "$name" | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]')
lower=$(printf '%s' "$name" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')
echo "$upper / $lower"
EOF
dash t2.sh

t.sh: 2: Bad substitution
status 2
ADA LOVELACE / ada lovelace

dash rejected the expansion with Bad substitution and exit status 2, and a non-interactive shell stops at a bad substitution, so nothing after it ran. The portable replacement is tr with the POSIX character classes, which is what §5 pointed to: tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]' converts to upper case, and the classes follow the locale, so letters outside ASCII are converted where the locale knows them. It costs a subprocess and a pipe per conversion, which is the price of portability for almost everything in this subsection. printf '%s' rather than echo feeds the pipe, for the reasons §19.7 measures.

The expansions POSIX does have

What remains is more than it sounds. These are all POSIX, and all ran under dash:

# The parameter expansions POSIX does have, all under dash
cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
path=/srv/app/logs/app.log.gz
echo "length:      ${#path}"
echo "no dir:      ${path##*/}"
echo "dir:         ${path%/*}"
echo "no suffix:   ${path%%.*}"
echo "default:     ${unset_var:-fallback}"
echo "alternative: ${path:+set}"
: "${port:=8080}"; echo "assigned:    $port"
EOF
dash t.sh

length:      24
no dir:      app.log.gz
dir:         /srv/app/logs
no suffix:   /srv/app/logs/app
default:     fallback
alternative: set
assigned:    8080

Length with ${#var}; the four prefix and suffix removals #, ##, % and %%, which take patterns; and the defaults family — :-, :=, :+ and :?, with and without the colon (§5.2). That covers path manipulation, extension handling, defaults and required variables, which is most of what scripts do with strings. : "${port:=8080}" is the portable idiom for "give this a default and keep it": : is the null command, and the expansion assigns as a side effect.

Substrings and replacement

${var:offset:length} and ${var/old/new} are both bash, and both fail the same way:

cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
word=portable
echo "${word:0:4}"
EOF
dash t.sh; echo "status $?"
cat > t2.sh <<'EOF'
word=portable
first4=$(printf '%s\n' "$word" | cut -c1-4)
rest=${word#????}
echo "$first4 + $rest"
EOF
dash t2.sh

t.sh: 2: Bad substitution
status 2
port + able

The portable substring has several spellings, none as neat as bash's. cut -c1-4 takes characters by position — except that GNU cut counts bytes, not characters: measured on Debian under en_US.UTF-8, cut -c1-4 of café keeps half of the é, where macOS cut keeps the whole character. A prefix removal with ? wildcards takes a fixed number of characters off the front without a subprocess: ${word#????} removes exactly four, whatever they are. And printf '%.4s' truncates, counting bytes. Replacement goes to tr for single characters and sed for strings:

cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
csv='a,b,c'
echo "${csv//,/ }"
EOF
dash t.sh; echo "status $?"
cat > t2.sh <<'EOF'
csv='a,b,c'
printf '%s\n' "$csv" | tr ',' ' '
printf '%s\n' "$csv" | sed 's/,/ and /g'
EOF
dash t2.sh

t.sh: 2: Bad substitution
status 2
a b c
a and b and c

Both cost a subprocess. In a loop over thousands of lines, that is the moment to process the whole file with one sed or awk instead of one per line, which is §21's subject; for a handful of values, it does not matter.

Case conversion as a function

A script that converts case more than once should wrap the pipe in a function, so that the portable spelling is written once and the call site reads like the bash one:

upper() { printf '%s\n' "$1" | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]'; }
lower() { printf '%s\n' "$1" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]'; }
name=$(upper "$name")

The function writes a newline and the command substitution strips it, so name gets exactly the converted text. §19.15's complete script and the exercises build a small library of such functions — trim, contains, starts_with — all without a subprocess, using only the expansions above and case.

19.5 Arrays Are Not POSIX

Arrays are not POSIX. POSIX sh has no indexed arrays and no associative arrays, and the syntax that creates one is a syntax error, not a runtime error — which means dash rejects the whole script before running a line of it, when the assignment is at the top level:

cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
files=(a.txt b.txt)
echo "${files[0]}"
EOF
dash t.sh; echo "status $?"

t.sh: 1: Syntax error: "(" unexpected
status 2

This is the largest single loss, because §6 made arrays the answer to so much: a list of file names that may contain spaces, a command assembled piece by piece, a set of options passed through. The portable language has exactly one list that keeps its elements intact, and it is the positional parameters.

"$@" as the one array

"$@" expands to every positional parameter as a separate word, spaces and all (§3.5), and set -- replaces the whole list. Together they make a usable list, including an append:

# "$@" is POSIX sh's one array: build it with set --, read it with "$@"
cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
set --                                  # start empty
for f in 'first file.txt' second.txt 'third  file.txt'; do
  set -- "$@" "$f"                      # append one element
done
echo "count: $#"
for f in "$@"; do printf '[%s]\n' "$f"; done
EOF
dash t.sh

count: 3
[first file.txt]
[second.txt]
[third  file.txt]

set -- "$@" "$f" re-sets the positional parameters to all the old ones plus one more. The file names with a space and with two spaces came through intact, because nothing was ever unquoted. $# is the length, for f in "$@" (or just for f) iterates, shift removes from the front and "$1" reads the first element. What is missing is random access by index, deletion from the middle, and a second list: there is only one "$@" at a time.

Two lists: functions have their own positional parameters

There is one more "$@" available: every function call has its own. Setting a function's positional parameters does not touch the script's:

# Using "$@" as a list overwrites the script's own arguments; a function has its own
cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
list_logs() {
  set --
  for f in app.log 'old app.log'; do set -- "$@" "$f"; done
  printf '<%s>' "$@"; echo " ($# items)"
}
echo "script arguments before: $*"
list_logs
echo "script arguments after:  $*"
EOF
dash t.sh --verbose target

script arguments before: --verbose target
<app.log><old app.log> (2 items)
script arguments after:  --verbose target

list_logs built a two-element list with set -- and the script's own arguments, --verbose target, were still there afterwards. So a second list is a function call away, and a function that needs a scratch list can use its own "$@" freely. What does not work is returning a list: a function's output is text, so a list comes back as lines of text — which is safe only for elements that cannot contain a newline.

Reading a list in pairs

shift N removes several elements at once, which makes a flat list of pairs a workable substitute for an associative array when the data is small and ordered:

# Reading a list two at a time with shift
cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
set -- host1 22 host2 2222 host3 22
while [ "$#" -ge 2 ]; do
  echo "$1 listens on $2"
  shift 2
done
EOF
dash t.sh

host1 listens on 22
host2 listens on 2222
host3 listens on 22

while [ "$#" -ge 2 ] stops when fewer than two remain, so an odd trailing element is ignored rather than read as a pair with an empty second half. For lists that must hold arbitrary strings and outlive a function call, the portable answers are the ones bash scripts use across process boundaries (§6.15): a temporary file with one element per line, or NUL-delimited where the elements may contain newlines and the tools support it (§14.9), or a string quoted for eval — which §19.7 builds, without printf %q, which dash does not have.

19.6 Functions Without bash

POSIX functions are the name() compound-command form §9 started with, and they work the same way in every shell: arguments in "$@", a return status from return, and definitions that can be redefined. What POSIX lacks is the two things bash adds to them.

The function keyword is not POSIX

bash accepts function name { … } as well as name() { … }. The function keyword is not POSIX — it is one of the words the standard says may be reserved with unspecified results — and dash does not know it:

cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
function greet {
  echo "hello"
}
greet
EOF
dash t.sh; echo "status $?"

t.sh: 1: function: not found
hello
t.sh: 3: Syntax error: "}" unexpected
status 2

The output shows how dash reads a script: one complete command at a time, executing each before parsing the next. function greet { was not a definition to dash, so it parsed function greet { as a simple command, ran it, and reported function: not found. Then it ran echo "hello" — the body, now just a line of the script — and only on line 3 did it meet a } with nothing to close and stop with a syntax error. So a script can do real work before a bashism further down stops it, which is one more reason to check scripts statically rather than by running them. The fix is mechanical: name() {, which bash also accepts and which ShellCheck's SC2113 asks for.

local is not POSIX

local is not POSIX, and this one is subtle, because dash has it. dash, BusyBox ash, bash, zsh and FreeBSD's sh all implement local, and Debian Policy requires it, so a script using it runs on most systems. POSIX.1-2024 still does not specify it: it appears only in the standard's list of command names whose results are unspecified. The shell that proves the point is ksh93, the Korn shell that POSIX's shell was largely modelled on, which scopes variables with typeset instead:

# dash has local; POSIX does not, and ksh93 does not either
cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
count=outer
f() { local count=inner; echo "in f: $count"; }
f; echo "after f: $count"
EOF
echo "dash:"; dash t.sh
echo "ksh93:"; ksh t.sh 2>&1 | sed 's/^.*: local:/local:/'

dash:
in f: inner
after f: outer
ksh93:
local: not found
in f: outer
after f: outer

Under dash, local scoped the variable as expected. Under ksh93 — /bin/ksh on macOS, the ksh package on Debian — local was an unknown command, so the assignment written as its argument never happened: the function printed outer, the global value. Nothing stopped; the script just computed with the wrong variable. Whether that matters depends on the list of shells a script must support. For "every sh on Linux and the BSDs", local is safe in practice; for "POSIX", it is not, and there are two portable ways to get the same effect.

Scope by subshell: a function body in parentheses

A function's body may be any compound command, including a subshell ( … ). Then everything the function changes — variables, the working directory, options, traps — belongs to a subshell and disappears when it returns:

# A function whose body is ( ... ) runs in a subshell: nothing it changes leaks out
cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
count=outer
f() (
  count=inner
  cd /tmp || exit 1
  echo "in f: count=$count, directory=$PWD"
)
f
echo "after f: count=$count, directory unchanged: $([ "$PWD" = "$start" ] && echo yes)"
EOF
start=$PWD dash t.sh

in f: count=inner, directory=/tmp
after f: count=outer, directory unchanged: yes

f changed count and the directory, and neither change reached the caller. This is complete isolation, and it costs a fork per call (§16.5) — nothing for a function called a few times, noticeable in a loop of thousands. It also means the function can only communicate through its output and its exit status, which is often exactly the discipline wanted. Exercise 3 uses it for abspath, which must cd without moving the caller.

Scope by convention: prefixed names

The other answer costs nothing at run time and works in every shell: give each function's working variables a prefix no one else will use, and unset them before returning:

# Without local, name a function's variables so they cannot collide, and unset them
cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
i=keep
count_lines() {
  _cl_n=0
  while IFS= read -r _cl_line; do _cl_n=$((_cl_n + 1)); done < "$1"
  echo "$_cl_n"
  unset _cl_n _cl_line
}
printf 'a\nb\nc\n' > three
count_lines three
echo "i is still: $i; _cl_n is ${_cl_n-unset}"
EOF
dash t.sh

3
i is still: keep; _cl_n is unset

_cl_ is short for count_lines, so _cl_n cannot collide with the caller's i, n or line, and after unset the function has left nothing behind. It is not real scoping — a recursive call would share the variables — but for the library functions a portable script needs, it is the usual technique, and many widely used POSIX scripts are written this way.

19.7 Quoting and Output

$'...' is not POSIX — or was not, before 2024

bash's ANSI-C quoting, $'\t', $'\n', $'\x1b', is the only way in bash to write a control character in a script literally (§3.1). For its whole history the rule was simple: $'...' is not POSIX. POSIX.1-2024 changed that — section 2.2.4, "Dollar-Single-Quotes", now specifies it — but a standard published in 2024 is not what systems ship, and neither dash measured here has it:

cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
tab=$'\t'
case $tab in
  "$(printf '\t')") echo "a tab character" ;;
  *)               printf 'not a tab: the %s characters %s\n' "${#tab}" "$tab" ;;
esac
EOF
echo "bash: $(bash t.sh)"
echo "dash: $(dash t.sh)"
cat > t2.sh <<'EOF'
tab=$(printf '\t')
newline='
'
printf '[%s][%s]\n' "$tab" "$newline" | sed -n l
EOF
echo "portable, under dash:"; dash t2.sh

bash: a tab character
dash: not a tab: the 3 characters $\t
portable, under dash:
[\t][$
]$

bash stored a tab. dash read $ as a literal dollar sign followed by an ordinary single-quoted string, so tab held three characters, $, \ and t — and nothing reported a problem. (It is worth noticing how the probe had to print that result: with printf '%s', because dash's echo would have turned the \t back into a tab and hidden the evidence — the subject of the next few paragraphs.) The portable way to get a control character into a variable is printf inside a command substitution. That works for everything but a newline, since command substitution strips trailing newlines (§4.4); a newline is written literally, inside quotes, across two lines, as t2.sh does.

echo -n portability

echo is the least portable command in common use. POSIX says that if the first operand is -n, or if any operand contains a backslash, "the results are implementation-defined" — and the implementations differ. echo -n portability is the famous case, but backslashes are the more dangerous one:

# The same echo lines under three shells
cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
echo -n "no newline"; echo "|"
echo 'a\tb'
echo -e 'c'
EOF
for shell in bash dash sh; do echo "== $shell"; "$shell" t.sh; done

== bash
no newline|
a\tb
c
== dash
no newline|
a	b
-e c
== sh
-n no newline
|
a	b
-e c

Three shells, three different outputs from three lines. bash's echo took -n and -e as options and printed backslashes literally. dash's echo took -n as an option but printed -e as text, and turned \t into a real tab — dash follows the XSI rule that echo interprets backslash escapes always. macOS sh, which is bash 3.2 in POSIX mode with xpg_echo on, printed -n as text and interpreted the backslash (§14.14 measured the same). So echo -n is portable to neither macOS sh nor POSIX, and echo "$var" is not safe for any value that might contain a backslash — a Windows path, a regular expression, a user's input — under dash. (On Debian, sh is dash, so the third block prints what dash prints.)

printf is portable

POSIX's own advice, in the echo page: "New applications are encouraged to use printf instead of echo." printf is portable because its behaviour is fully specified: the first argument is a format, the rest are data, and data is never interpreted:

cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
value='-n'
printf '%s' "no newline"; printf '|\n'
printf '%s\n' "$value"
printf '%s\t%s\n' a b
printf '%5.2f|%-4s|%x|%o\n' 3.14159 ab 255 8
EOF
for shell in bash dash sh; do echo "== $shell"; "$shell" t.sh; done

== bash
no newline|
-n
a	b
 3.14|ab  |ff|10
== dash
no newline|
-n
a	b
 3.14|ab  |ff|10
== sh
no newline|
-n
a	b
 3.14|ab  |ff|10

All three shells printed the same thing, byte for byte. printf '%s\n' "$value" prints a value exactly, even when the value is -n. The conversions POSIX specifies — %s, %d, %i, %u, %o, %x, %X, %c, %b, %e, %f, %g with widths, precisions and the - flag — are available everywhere. The rule for a portable script is short: use echo only for a constant string with no backslashes and no leading dash, and printf for everything else.

Quoting a value for re-use without printf %q

printf %q and ${var@Q} produce a value quoted so the shell can read it back (§5.8, §14.13), and both are bash:

cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
printf '%q\n' 'a b'
EOF
dash t.sh; echo "status $?"
cat > t2.sh <<'EOF'
# Single-quote a value for reuse: close the quote, add an escaped quote, reopen
quote() { printf "'%s'\n" "$(printf '%s' "$1" | sed "s/'/'\\\\''/g")"; }
quote "it's here"
eval "set -- $(quote "it's here")"; printf '[%s]\n' "$1"
EOF
dash t2.sh

t.sh: 1: printf: %q: invalid directive
status 2
'it'\''s here'
[it's here]

The portable technique is the one those operators implement: wrap the value in single quotes, and turn every single quote inside it into '\'' — close the quoted string, add an escaped quote, open a new one. A single-quoted string can contain anything else, so the result is always one word that reads back as the original value. The sed expression is the whole algorithm, and the eval line proves the round trip under dash: it's here came back as one argument, apostrophe intact. This is the function a portable script uses whenever it must build a command as a string — for su -c, for a remote shell, for a file of commands to run later.

19.8 Locale and the POSIX Character Class

The locale decides how characters are classified, how strings sort and compare, and how many bytes a character is. Scripts inherit it from whoever runs them, so a script's output can differ between two machines, or two users on one machine, for no reason visible in the code — §5.3 measured ${#var}, §14.10 measured printf, §15.7 measured three different sort orders of the same words.

The POSIX character class

A bracket expression can name a class of characters instead of a range: [[:alpha:]], [[:digit:]], [[:alnum:]], [[:upper:]], [[:lower:]], [[:space:]], [[:blank:]], [[:punct:]], [[:print:]], [[:cntrl:]], [[:graph:]] and [[:xdigit:]]. The POSIX character class works in case patterns, in globs, in tr, in grep, sed and awk regular expressions, and in every shell:

# POSIX character classes work in case, in tr and in grep, under every shell
cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
for word in Ada 42 'x y' ''; do
  case $word in
    '')                     echo "(empty): empty" ;;
    *[![:alnum:]]*)         echo "$word: has a non-alphanumeric character" ;;
    [[:upper:]]*)           echo "$word: starts with a capital" ;;
    *[![:digit:]]*)         echo "$word: letters" ;;
    *)                      echo "$word: digits only" ;;
  esac
done
printf 'Mixed Case\n' | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]'
printf 'a1\nb\n22\n' | grep -c '^[[:digit:]]*$'
EOF
dash t.sh

Ada: starts with a capital
42: digits only
x y: has a non-alphanumeric character
(empty): empty
mixed case
1

Why prefer [[:lower:]] to [a-z]? Because POSIX says, in its chapter on regular expressions, that outside the POSIX locale "a range expression has unspecified behavior: strictly conforming applications shall not rely on whether the range expression is valid, or on the set of collating elements matched." In some locales, on some systems, [a-z] has matched upper-case letters, because the collation order interleaves them — a A b B …. Neither macOS nor Debian did so in the measurements made for this section (bash has globasciiranges on by default since 5.0), but that is an observation about two systems, not a guarantee. A class means exactly what it says in every locale, and a character outside ASCII is classified by the locale's rules — where the tool understands multibyte characters at all. Measured under en_US.UTF-8, é matched [[:alpha:]] in a bash case and in grep, and did not match in a dash case: dash treats text as bytes, and the two bytes of é are not letters in any locale. Under C nothing matched é. So classes make ASCII handling exact everywhere, and non-ASCII handling depends on the shell as well as the locale.

Pinning the locale

A script whose output must not depend on who runs it sets the locale itself, once, at the top, and exports it, so every command it runs sees the same one:

# Pin the locale once, at the top, and every tool that follows the locale agrees everywhere
cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
LC_ALL=C
export LC_ALL
printf '%s\n' banana Apple cherry apple | sort | tr '\n' ' '; echo
printf '%s' 'café' | wc -c | tr -d ' '
EOF
for shell in bash dash; do echo "== $shell"; LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 "$shell" t.sh; done

== bash
Apple apple banana cherry 
5
== dash
Apple apple banana cherry 
5

The caller asked for en_US.UTF-8, and the script overrode it with LC_ALL=C. Under C, sort compares bytes, so upper-case letters sort before lower-case ones, and wc -c counts café as 5 bytes — the same result under bash and dash, on macOS and on Debian, whatever the caller's settings. LC_ALL overrides every other locale variable (LANG, LC_COLLATE, LC_CTYPE, …), which is why it is the one to set. Choose C when the script processes data — log files, configuration, machine-readable output — and reliability matters more than language rules; leave the locale alone when the script's job is to present text to a person in their own language. Setting LC_ALL=C in the middle of a script, or for one command as LC_ALL=C sort, is also correct, and is the usual way to make one comparison byte-exact without affecting the rest.

19.9 Redirection and Sourcing

POSIX redirection is the core of §10: >, >>, <, 2>&1, >&2, <>, >|, here-documents with << and <<-, and descriptors 0–9. What bash adds on top is mostly shorthand, and one of the shorthands fails in a particularly quiet way.

&> in a POSIX shell

&> file is bash's shorthand for > file 2>&1. dash has no such operator, and it reads the characters as two separate things — & ending the command and running it in the background, then > file as an empty command that truncates the file:

cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
echo "to the file" &> out.txt
wait
printf 'out.txt holds: [%s]\n' "$(cat out.txt)"
EOF
echo "bash:"; bash t.sh
echo "dash:"; dash t.sh

bash:
out.txt holds: [to the file]
dash:
to the file
out.txt holds: []

Under bash the text went to the file. Under dash, echo ran in the background with its output still on standard output, and out.txt was created empty. No error, no non-zero status — §10.4 measured the same thing, and it is the most dangerous kind of bashism for exactly that reason. The portable spelling is > file 2>&1, in that order (§10.4).

A here string is not POSIX

<<< word feeds a string to a command's standard input (§10.10). A here string is not POSIX, and dash rejects it as a syntax error:

cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
read -r first rest <<< "one two three"
echo "$first"
EOF
dash t.sh; echo "status $?"
cat > t2.sh <<'EOF'
line="one two three"
read -r first rest <<EOF2
$line
EOF2
echo "first=$first rest=$rest"
EOF
dash t2.sh

t.sh: 1: Syntax error: redirection unexpected
status 2
first=one rest=two three

The portable form is a here-document containing the expansion. It behaves like <<< in the way that matters — the command reads the value followed by a newline — and works for read, which is the most common use. printf '%s\n' "$line" | read -r first rest does not work as a replacement in bash or dash, because read would run in a pipeline subshell and its variables would vanish (§16.6); the here-document runs read in the current shell.

source is not POSIX

bash has two names for the command that reads a file into the current shell: . and source. source is not POSIX, and dash has only .. There is a second difference, less well known, in where . looks for the file:

# source is bash's name for . ; and . without a slash searches PATH, not the current directory
printf 'echo "lib loaded"\n' > lib.sh
cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
source lib.sh
EOF
echo "source under dash:"; dash t.sh; echo "status $?"
echo ". lib.sh under dash:";         dash -c '. lib.sh'; echo "status $?"
echo ". lib.sh under bash --posix:"; bash --posix -c '. lib.sh'; echo "status $?"
echo ". lib.sh under bash:";         bash -c '. lib.sh'
echo ". ./lib.sh under dash:";       dash -c '. ./lib.sh'

source under dash:
t.sh: 1: source: not found
status 127
. lib.sh under dash:
dash: 1: .: lib.sh: not found
status 2
. lib.sh under bash --posix:
bash: line 1: .: lib.sh: file not found
status 1
. lib.sh under bash:
lib loaded
. ./lib.sh under dash:
lib loaded

POSIX says that if the file name given to . "does not contain a , the shell shall use the search path specified by PATH to find the directory containing file" — PATH, not the current directory. dash does exactly that, so . lib.sh failed although lib.sh was right there, and a non-interactive shell aborts when . fails. bash in its default mode also looks in the current directory after PATH, which is why . lib.sh works in a bash script and nowhere else; in POSIX mode bash follows the standard. So a portable script always gives . a path with a slash: . ./lib.sh, or better, a path built from where the script lives.

Sourcing a library relative to the script
