./lib.sh is relative to the caller's directory, not the script's, so it breaks as soon as the script is run from somewhere else. bash scripts use ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} for the script's own path (§9.10); POSIX sh has only $0, which is the path the script was run by — good enough for a script executed as a file, though not for one that is itself sourced:

# A library next to the script, found whatever the caller's directory is
mkdir -p app/lib
printf 'greet() { echo "hello from the library"; }\n' > app/lib/greet.sh
cat > app/run.sh <<'EOF'
here=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")" && pwd) || exit 1
. "$here/lib/greet.sh"
greet
EOF
cd /tmp && dash "$OLDPWD/app/run.sh"

hello from the library

The script was run from /tmp with an absolute path, and still found its library. CDPATH= stops a CDPATH variable in the environment from redirecting the cd (and from making cd print the directory, which would corrupt the output); -- protects a directory name beginning with -; dirname and cd … && pwd turn whatever $0 was into an absolute path. The whole line is the portable equivalent of the ${BASH_SOURCE[0]%/*} idiom.

19.10 Arithmetic and Loops

$(( expression )) is POSIX: arithmetic expansion with the C operators — + - * / %, comparisons, &&, ||, bit operators, shifts, the ternary operator and assignment operators such as += — on signed integers of at least 32 bits (the shells measured here use 64). Almost everything else in §7's arithmetic is bash.

(( )) is not arithmetic in dash

(( expression )) as a command is bash (and ksh). POSIX specifies what an application must write instead: two parentheses with a space between them, because "shells which implement an extension whereby ((expression)) is evaluated as an arithmetic expression may treat the (( as introducing as an arithmetic evaluation instead of a grouping command." dash does not implement that extension, so it reads (( as two nested subshells — with a redirection in the middle:

cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
count=3
if (( count < 5 )); then echo "small"; fi
EOF
dash t.sh; echo "status $?"
ls

t.sh: 2: cannot open 5: No such file
status 0
example.sh
t.sh

To dash, (( count < 5 )) was the command count with its standard input redirected from a file named 5, inside two subshells. The file did not exist, so the redirection failed, the if took its false branch, and the script exited 0. Nothing was created — < only opens for reading — but a > in the same position would have created a file named after the number. The portable spellings are [ "$count" -lt 5 ] for a comparison, or [ "$((count < 5))" -eq 1 ] for an expression, since $(( )) yields 1 for true and 0 for false:

cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
count=3
if [ "$((count < 5))" -eq 1 ]; then echo "small"; fi
if [ "$count" -lt 5 ]; then echo "small, the usual way"; fi
count=$((count + 1)); echo "count is $count"
echo "power of two: $(( 1 << 10 )), remainder: $(( 17 % 5 )), hex: $(( 0x1F ))"
EOF
dash t.sh

small
small, the usual way
count is 4
power of two: 1024, remainder: 2, hex: 31

Everything there is POSIX, including <<, % and hexadecimal constants. One trap is shared by every shell: a number with a leading zero is octal in arithmetic, so $((010)) is 8 under dash as under bash, and bash's 10# prefix for forcing decimal (§7.10) is not POSIX. A portable script strips leading zeros with a loop, while :; do case $n in 0?*) n=${n#0} ;; *) break ;; esac; done, before doing arithmetic on input that may have them.

What is missing

Four more arithmetic forms from §7 and §8 are bash, and dash rejects each in a different way:

# Four bash arithmetic forms, one line each, under dash
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # each snippet is code for dash to run, so it must not expand here
for snippet in 'let n=1' 'n=1; echo $((n++))' 'for ((i=0; i<2; i++)); do :; done' 'echo "[$RANDOM]"'; do
  printf '%-40s -> ' "$snippet"
  dash -c "$snippet" 2>&1 | sed 's/^dash: 1: //'
done

let n=1                                  -> let: not found
n=1; echo $((n++))                       -> arithmetic expression: expecting primary: "n++"
for ((i=0; i<2; i++)); do :; done        -> Syntax error: Bad for loop variable
echo "[$RANDOM]"                         -> []

let is not a command in dash. ++ and -- are optional in POSIX arithmetic and dash does not implement them; write n=$((n + 1)). The C-style for (( ; ; )) loop is a syntax error. And $RANDOM is an ordinary unset variable, so it expands to nothing — silently, which makes it the one that gets past a test run. A portable random number comes from awk 'BEGIN { srand(); print int(rand() * 32768) }' (seeded by the time, so not for anything secret) or from reading /dev/urandom with od.

Counting loops

{1..3} brace expansion is bash, and in dash it is just a word:

cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
for i in {1..3}; do printf '%s ' "$i"; done; echo "(brace range)"
i=1
while [ "$i" -le 3 ]; do printf '%s ' "$i"; i=$((i + 1)); done; echo "(while loop)"
EOF
dash t.sh

{1..3} (brace range)
1 2 3 (while loop)

dash printed {1..3} as the loop's only value, once — no error. seq is not a POSIX utility either (it is on both macOS and GNU systems, but not on every system), so the portable counting loop is while with a counter, exactly as written above.

19.11 Options, Traps and read

set -o pipefail and its replacement

§11 introduced set -o pipefail, and noted that POSIX added it only in the 2024 edition. The shells have not all caught up: Debian's dash 0.5.12 accepts it, and the dash that ships with macOS rejects it with Illegal option -o pipefail — and because set is a special builtin, a non-interactive shell exits on that error. Where a pipeline's first command must be checked without pipefail, its status can be carried out through a spare file descriptor:

# Without pipefail: carry the first command's status through a file descriptor
cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
run() {
  { { "$@"; echo "$?" >&3; } | sort; } 3>&1 >&4 | { read -r status; return "$status"; }
} 4>&1
run sh -c 'printf "b\na\n"; exit 3'
echo "status of the producer: $?"
EOF
dash t.sh

a
b
status of the producer: 3

The technique needs reading from the inside out. Inside the braces, the command runs with its output going down the pipe to sort, and then its exit status is written to descriptor 3. The redirections after the group, 3>&1 >&4, point descriptor 3 at the outer pipe and the group's normal output at descriptor 4 — which the function's own 4>&1 attached to the real standard output. So sort's output goes to the terminal, the status alone goes down the outer pipe to read, and return "$status" hands it back. It is not pretty, and it is one of the strongest arguments in this section for simply requiring bash; but it is how the standard allows the question to be answered.

Signal names in trap

Traps are POSIX, including EXIT (also spelled 0), and §12 is almost entirely portable. The one bashism that recurs is the SIG prefix:

cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
trap 'echo caught' SIGINT
EOF
dash t.sh; echo "status $?"
cat > t2.sh <<'EOF'
trap 'echo "cleanup"' EXIT
trap 'echo caught; exit 130' INT
kill -s INT $$
EOF
dash t2.sh; echo "status $?"

trap: SIGINT: bad trap
status 1
caught
cleanup
status 130

POSIX specifies signal names without the prefix — HUP, INT, QUIT, TERM — and says an implementation "may permit names with the SIG prefix". bash does; dash does not, and trap … SIGINT was an error that stopped the script. Written as INT, the same trap ran, and so did the EXIT trap afterwards — under dash an exit inside a signal handler still runs the EXIT trap. But a death by a re-raised signal is different: measured here, bash 5 runs the EXIT trap afterwards, and dash and bash 3.2 do not (§12.5 made the same observation). That is why the portable cleanup pattern §12.5 promised does its cleanup in the signal handler, then removes both traps and re-raises the signal:

# The portable cleanup-and-re-raise: EXIT is not guaranteed after a signal, so clean up in the handler
cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
tmp=$(mktemp -d) || exit 1
cleanup() { rm -rf -- "$tmp"; echo "cleaned up"; }
trap 'cleanup' EXIT
trap 'cleanup; trap - EXIT INT; kill -s INT "$$"' INT
kill -s INT "$$"
echo "not reached"
EOF
for shell in bash dash; do echo "== $shell"; "$shell" t.sh; echo "status $?"; done

== bash
cleaned up
status 130
== dash
cleaned up
status 130

Both shells cleaned up once, and both exited with status 130 — killed by SIGINT, as a caller such as make needs to see (§12.5). trap - EXIT INT resets both traps before the re-raise, so the cleanup cannot run a second time and the second SIGINT takes the default action, which is to die. kill -s INT rather than kill -INT is the POSIX spelling; both work in every shell measured here.

read: -r and -d, and nothing else

POSIX's read is read [-r] [-d delim] var... — -d new in 2024 — and it requires at least one variable name. Every other option §14 taught is bash:

for snippet in 'read -r a b' 'read -p "name? " a' 'read -a list' 'read' ; do
  printf '%-22s -> ' "$snippet"
  printf 'x y\n' | dash -c "$snippet && echo ok" 2>&1 | sed 's/^dash: 1: //'
done

read -r a b            -> ok
read -p "name? " a     -> ok
read -a list           -> read: Illegal option -a
read                   -> read: arg count

read -r is the portable form, and it should always be used, for the reasons §14.4 measured. dash also accepts -p — so a prompt with read -p works under dash but is not POSIX, and fails in shells that do not implement it; the portable prompt is printf 'name? ' >&2; read -r name. -a does not exist, since there are no arrays. And a bare read with no variable, which in bash fills REPLY, is an error in dash. -s, -n, -t and -u have no POSIX equivalent: silent input needs stty -echo (restored in a trap, §14.8), and a timeout needs a background sleep and kill.

19.12 GNU and BSD Utilities

A POSIX shell script is only as portable as the programs it runs, and the utilities differ between systems far more than the shells do. Linux distributions ship the GNU versions — coreutils, GNU sed, grep, find, date — and macOS and the BSDs ship BSD versions, and each family has options the other lacks or spells differently. Every option below was measured on macOS (BSD tools, PATH=/usr/bin:/bin so that nothing installed by a package manager could stand in) and on Debian (GNU):

Task
GNU (Debian)
BSD (macOS)
Edit a file in place
sed -i 's/…/…/' f; sed -i '' … fails: the empty string is taken as the script
sed -i '' 's/…/…/' f; sed -i 's/…/…/' f fails: the script is taken as a backup suffix
Date arithmetic
date -d '2026-01-31 +1 day', date -d @0
date -j -v+1d -f %F 2026-01-31, date -r 0 (-r on GNU names a file)
File size
stat -c %s f
stat -f %z f
Perl regex in grep
grep -P
absent: status 2, "invalid option"
Formatted find output
find … -printf '%s\n'
absent: "unknown primary or operator"
Decode base64
base64 -d; -D fails
base64 -d and -D
Empty input to xargs
runs the command once with no arguments unless -r
does not run the command; -r accepted
Lines in reverse
tac; tail -r fails
tail -r; no tac
CPU count
nproc, getconf _NPROCESSORS_ONLN
getconf _NPROCESSORS_ONLN; no nproc
Both, measured
sed -E, grep -E, grep -o, sort -V, readlink -f, realpath, seq, mktemp -d, mktemp with a template, head -n, tail -n +N, find -print0, xargs -0

The last row is the dangerous one to trust. Everything in it works on the two systems measured, and several items are not POSIX (sort -V, readlink -f, seq, -print0, mktemp itself), so they are exactly the options that fail on a BusyBox image, an older macOS, or a commercial Unix. A tool being present on every machine you have tried is evidence, not a specification.

Writing to the intersection

The first strategy is to use only what both families accept, which is usually possible with a little restructuring. In-place editing has one spelling both seds read the same way — a suffix attached to -i, which makes a backup, which the script then deletes:

# The one in-place sed spelling GNU and BSD both read the same way: a suffix attached to -i
PATH=/usr/bin:/bin
printf 'port=80\n' > app.conf
sed -i.bak 's/80/8080/' app.conf && rm -f app.conf.bak
cat app.conf; ls

port=8080
app.conf
example.sh

Better still is not to edit in place at all. sed -i is not POSIX, and it replaces the file by writing a new one and renaming it anyway (§15.8), so doing that explicitly is both portable and clearer:

# Or avoid -i: write a temporary file and move it into place, which every sed supports
PATH=/usr/bin:/bin
printf 'port=80\n' > app.conf
tmp=$(mktemp app.conf.XXXXXX) && sed 's/80/8080/' app.conf > "$tmp" && mv -- "$tmp" app.conf
cat app.conf

port=8080

The temporary file is created by mktemp next to the target, so the mv is a rename within one filesystem and a reader sees the old file or the new one, never half of each (§17.7). The same thinking covers the rest of the table. A file's size is wc -c < file, which every wc supports; the $((size)) strips the leading spaces BSD wc pads its number with:

# stat's options differ between GNU and BSD; wc -c counts bytes on both
PATH=/usr/bin:/bin
printf 12345 > five
size=$(wc -c < five)
echo "size: $((size)) bytes"

size: 5 bytes

xargs with possibly empty input gets a guard rather than -r:

# GNU xargs runs the command once on empty input; BSD does not. A guard makes both agree.
PATH=/usr/bin:/bin
: > empty.list
if [ -s empty.list ]; then xargs echo "ran with:" < empty.list; else echo "nothing to do"; fi

nothing to do

And date arithmetic is done in seconds since the epoch, where it is plain integer arithmetic, leaving only the final formatting to the platform-specific options — tried in turn, BSD first, with the error from the one that does not apply discarded:

# Date arithmetic is where GNU and BSD date differ most; seconds since the epoch are portable
PATH=/usr/bin:/bin
now=$(date +%s)
later=$((now + 86400))
echo "one day is $((later - now)) seconds"
TZ=UTC date -u -r 0 +%Y-%m-%d 2>/dev/null || TZ=UTC date -u -d @0 +%Y-%m-%d

one day is 86400 seconds
1970-01-01

date +%s is not POSIX either, but it is in both GNU and BSD date, which makes it about as close to universal as an extension gets. For anything more, a script that must do real date arithmetic portably is a script that should call awk, Python or Perl, and §21 discusses when to make that move.

19.13 Feature Detection

The second strategy is to find out what the system offers and choose an implementation to match. Feature detection means testing for the capability itself — does this sed accept --version, does this date accept -d — rather than for the name of the operating system. The reason is that the name is a poor proxy: a Mac with GNU coreutils installed and first on PATH has GNU tools, a Linux container built on BusyBox has neither family, and uname says nothing about which sed is first on PATH.

Choosing an implementation once, at load time

The pattern is to test once, near the top of the script, and define a function whose body fits the answer; the rest of the script calls the function and never asks again:

# Detect the capability, not the operating system
PATH=/usr/bin:/bin
if sed --version >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  sed_inplace() { sed -i "$@"; }
else
  sed_inplace() { sed -i '' "$@"; }
fi
printf 'port=80\n' > app.conf
sed_inplace 's/80/8080/' app.conf
cat app.conf; ls

port=8080
app.conf
example.sh

GNU sed answers --version; BSD sed rejects it, and the test's status picks the branch. Run on Debian the same code takes the other branch, and prints the same result. This is the portable in-place edit for a script that wants one: the test is a real property of the program that will run, so it gives the right answer on a Mac with GNU sed first on PATH, which a uname test would get wrong.

The same shape works for date formatting, testing the GNU option directly:

# One function, two implementations, chosen once by trying the GNU form
PATH=/usr/bin:/bin
if date -d @0 +%s >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  day_of() { TZ=UTC date -d "@$1" +%Y-%m-%d; }
else
  day_of() { TZ=UTC date -r "$1" +%Y-%m-%d; }
fi
day_of 0
day_of 1000000000

1970-01-01
2001-09-09

Does the command exist?

The portable test for whether a command is available is command -v, which POSIX specifies: it prints how the name would be resolved and returns non-zero if it would not be:

# command -v is POSIX; which is not, and its output and status vary
PATH=/usr/bin:/bin
for tool in awk jq-does-not-exist; do
  if command -v "$tool" >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo "$tool: available"; else echo "$tool: missing"; fi
done

awk: available
jq-does-not-exist: missing

which is not POSIX; it is an external program whose output and exit status vary between systems, and on some it prints a message on standard output when the command is missing. type is POSIX but its output is meant for people. command -v is the one to use in scripts, with its output discarded when only the answer is needed (§7.7 used it the same way).

Does the shell have a feature?

A shell feature can be tested the same way, but with one precaution: trying an unsupported construct may be a syntax error, which would stop the script. Running the attempt in a subshell, through eval so that it is parsed only when run, contains the failure:

# Test a shell feature by trying it in a subshell, where a syntax error cannot stop the script
cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
if (eval 'set -o pipefail') 2>/dev/null; then echo "pipefail: available"; else echo "pipefail: missing"; fi
if (eval 'x=$(( 1 ))') 2>/dev/null;       then echo "arithmetic: available"; fi
if (eval 'a=(1)') 2>/dev/null;            then echo "arrays: available"; else echo "arrays: missing"; fi
EOF
echo "== bash"; bash t.sh
echo "== dash"; dash t.sh

== bash
pipefail: available
arithmetic: available
arrays: available
== dash
pipefail: missing
arithmetic: available
arrays: missing

Under bash every feature is present. Under the dash that ships with macOS, pipefail is missing and the script can fall back to §19.11's descriptor technique; under Debian's dash 0.5.12 the same test prints pipefail: available, which is exactly the point of testing rather than assuming. Arrays are missing under both, and the test reports it without the syntax error reaching the script. This is how a script can use set -o pipefail where it exists and still run where it does not: (set -o pipefail) 2>/dev/null && set -o pipefail.

19.14 What Fails Under dash

This subsection collects the section's constructs into one table, measured the only way that settles the question: each line is valid bash, and each was run by dash.

# Each line is valid bash; here is what dash makes of it
while IFS= read -r snippet; do
  printf '%-38s ' "$snippet"
  out=$(dash -c "$snippet" 2>&1); status=$?
  printf '%-3s %s\n' "$status" "$(printf '%s' "$out" | sed 's/^dash: 1: //' | head -n 1)"
done <<'EOF'
cat <(echo hi)
cat <<< hi
[[ a == a ]] && echo yes
[ a == a ] && echo yes
a=(1 2); echo "${a[0]}"
function f { :; }
x=abc; echo "${x^^}"
x=abc; echo "${x:1}"
x=abc; echo "${x/b/B}"
echo {1..3}
(( 1 < 2 )) && echo yes
let x=1
source /dev/null
echo $'a\tb'
declare x=1
select x in a; do :; done </dev/null
echo "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}"
EOF

cat <(echo hi)                         2   Syntax error: "(" unexpected
cat <<< hi                             2   Syntax error: redirection unexpected
[[ a == a ]] && echo yes               127 [[: not found
[ a == a ] && echo yes                 2   [: a: unexpected operator
a=(1 2); echo "${a[0]}"                2   Syntax error: "(" unexpected
function f { :; }                      2   Syntax error: "}" unexpected
x=abc; echo "${x^^}"                   2   Bad substitution
x=abc; echo "${x:1}"                   2   Bad substitution
x=abc; echo "${x/b/B}"                 2   Bad substitution
echo {1..3}                            0   {1..3}
(( 1 < 2 )) && echo yes                2   cannot open 2: No such file
let x=1                                127 let: not found
source /dev/null                       127 source: not found
echo $'a\tb'                           0   $a	b
declare x=1                            127 declare: not found
select x in a; do :; done </dev/null   2   Syntax error: "do" unexpected
echo "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}"               2   Bad substitution

The status column divides them into three kinds. 2 is a hard failure: a syntax error or a bad substitution, which stops a non-interactive shell there and then. 127 is a missing command — [[, let, source, declare — which prints a message and carries on, so the script continues with a wrong result and may still exit 0, as §19.1 and §19.3 showed. 0 is the dangerous kind: {1..3} stayed a literal word and $'a\tb' became a dollar sign and an ordinary string (which dash's echo then printed with a real tab), and nothing reported anything. §19.9's &> belongs with them — it was left out of the table only because its output arrives from a background job in no fixed order.

Process substitution is not POSIX

The first line of the table deserves a word of its own, because process substitution is one of the most useful things bash has (§4.6, §16.9): <(command) names the command's output as a file, so diff <(sort a) <(sort b) needs no temporary files. Process substitution is not POSIX, and dash rejects it as a syntax error. The portable replacements are a temporary file per stream (made with mktemp, removed by a trap — §17.10), or, for one stream, an ordinary pipe; for two streams at once, named pipes made with mkfifo, which are POSIX but need the same care about cleanup and blocking that §17.11 described.

19.15 Writing for POSIX sh

Writing for POSIX sh comes down to a short discipline: a #!/bin/sh shebang, the language of §19.3–§19.11, the utilities of §19.12, and the three checks of §19.2 before the script is trusted. Here is a complete script written that way — logsum, which counts the levels in log files, with an option, validation, a temporary file and cleanup — run by four different shells:

cat > logsum <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
# logsum - count log lines by level.  POSIX sh: runs under dash, ksh, bash and macOS sh.
set -euf                               # -f: no globbing; the lines below split on purpose
LC_ALL=C
export LC_ALL

usage() { printf 'usage: %s [-l LEVEL] FILE...\n' "${0##*/}" >&2; exit 2; }

level=
while getopts 'l:h' opt; do
  case $opt in
    l) level=$OPTARG ;;
    h) usage ;;
    *) usage ;;
  esac
done
shift $((OPTIND - 1))
[ "$#" -gt 0 ] || usage

case $level in
  ''|ERROR|WARN|INFO) ;;
  *) printf '%s: unknown level: %s\n' "${0##*/}" "$level" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac

tmp=$(mktemp) || exit 1
trap 'rm -f -- "$tmp"' EXIT
trap 'rm -f -- "$tmp"; trap - EXIT INT; kill -s INT "$$"' INT

for file in "$@"; do
  while IFS= read -r line || [ -n "$line" ]; do
    # shellcheck disable=SC2086        # splitting is the point, and set -f stops globbing
    set -- $line
    [ "$#" -ge 2 ] || continue
    case $2 in ERROR|WARN|INFO) printf '%s\n' "$2" ;; esac
  done < "$file"
done > "$tmp"

if [ -n "$level" ]; then
  printf '%s %s\n' "$level" "$(grep -c -x -- "$level" "$tmp" || true)"
else
  sort "$tmp" | uniq -c | while read -r count name; do printf '%s %s\n' "$name" "$count"; done
fi
EOF
printf '%s\n' '10:00 INFO start' '10:01 WARN disk 91%' '10:02 ERROR *.tmp not found' '10:03 INFO done' > app.log
chmod +x logsum
for shell in dash sh ksh 'bash --posix'; do
  echo "== $shell"; $shell ./logsum app.log; $shell ./logsum -l ERROR app.log
done

== dash
ERROR 1
INFO 2
WARN 1
ERROR 1
== sh
ERROR 1
INFO 2
WARN 1
ERROR 1
== ksh
ERROR 1
INFO 2
WARN 1
ERROR 1
== bash --posix
ERROR 1
INFO 2
WARN 1
ERROR 1

Four shells, identical output. Everything in it has appeared earlier in this section, and it is worth reading once for what it avoids. There are no arrays: the file list is "$@" after getopts has consumed the options (§13.3), and each log line is split into fields with set -- $line, reusing the positional parameters as the one list POSIX has (§19.5). That line deliberately leaves $line unquoted, which is why the script sets -f: with globbing off, the third log line's *.tmp stayed three characters instead of expanding to whatever .tmp files the current directory held. The directive above it tells ShellCheck the unquoted expansion is intended. There is no [[ ]]: level validation is a case. There is no local, because nothing needs it. The locale is pinned. The temporary file is cleaned up by an EXIT trap and by an INT trap that cleans, resets and re-raises (§19.11). And the || [ -n "$line" ] on the read handles a final line with no newline (§14.3).

The script passes the two static checks as well:

cat > logsum <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
set -euf
for file in "$@"; do
  while IFS= read -r line || [ -n "$line" ]; do
    # shellcheck disable=SC2086        # splitting is the point, and set -f stops globbing
    set -- $line
    [ "$#" -ge 2 ] || continue
    printf '%s\n' "$2"
  done < "$file"
done
EOF
shellcheck -f gcc logsum && echo "shellcheck: clean"
checkbashisms -p logsum && echo "checkbashisms -p: clean"

shellcheck: clean
checkbashisms -p: clean

ShellCheck reads the dialect from the #!/bin/sh line and reports nothing; checkbashisms -p reports nothing. With a run under dash, that is the full check §19.2 recommended, and it is the check to put in CI for any script that claims to be POSIX.

The other answer: say bash, and make sure bash runs

Sometimes the honest conclusion is that a script needs bash — associative arrays, pipefail everywhere, mapfile — but will occasionally be started with sh script by someone who did not read the shebang. A guard at the top turns that mistake into a re-run under bash instead of a strange failure halfway down:

# The other answer: say bash, and make sure bash is what runs
cat > tool <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
if [ -z "${BASH_VERSION:-}" ]; then
  exec bash "$0" "$@"
fi
declare -A seen=()
for word in "$@"; do seen[$word]=1; done
echo "running under bash ${BASH_VERSINFO[0]}: ${#seen[@]} distinct words"
EOF
dash tool a b a

running under bash 5: 2 distinct words

dash started the script, found BASH_VERSION unset, and replaced itself with bash running the same file with the same arguments (exec, §16.2); from then on it was a bash script, and the associative array worked. The guard itself is POSIX — it has to be, since it runs under whatever shell was used — and it must come before any bashism, because dash would stop at a syntax error in a line it parses before reaching the guard. It is the right tool when bash is available but might be bypassed; where bash might not exist at all, it only moves the failure to the exec, and the script should have been POSIX.

19.16 The Portability Table

Each bash construct, whether POSIX has it, and what a portable script writes instead.

bash
Portable replacement, and the detail that bites
[[ … ]]
[ … ] with every expansion quoted; case for patterns; a missing [[ is status 127 and the if takes its false branch (§19.3).
== in [ ]
=. dash says "unexpected operator" and the test fails (§19.3).
-a, -o in test
[ … ] && [ … ]. Removed in POSIX.1-2024, still promised by Debian Policy (§19.3).
=~
case with *[!0-9]*-style patterns; grep -E or expr for a real regex (§19.3).
${v^^}, ${v:o:l}, ${v//a/b}
tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]'; cut -c (bytes on GNU) or ${v#??}; sed. #, %, :-, :=, :+, :? and ${#v} are POSIX (§19.4).
Arrays
"$@" with set -- "$@" x; a function's own "$@" as a second list; files for anything more (§19.5).
function f, local
f() {; a ( … ) body or prefixed names. dash has local, ksh93 does not (§19.6).
$'\t'
$(printf '\t'); a literal newline in quotes. POSIX since 2024; neither dash measured has it (§19.7).
echo -n, echo -e
printf. dash's echo interprets backslashes; macOS sh prints -n (§19.7).
printf %q, ${v@Q}
Single-quote the value and replace each ' with '\'' (§19.7).
Locale
[[:alpha:]] classes, not ranges; LC_ALL=C; export LC_ALL for data (§19.8).
&> f
> f 2>&1. dash backgrounds the command and empties the file, silently (§19.9).
<<< word
A here-document holding $word (§19.9).
source f, . f
. ./f or an absolute path: . without a slash searches PATH only (§19.9).
(( … )), let, ++
[ "$n" -lt 5 ], n=$((n + 1)). dash reads ((a < 5)) as a redirection from a file named 5 (§19.10).
{1..3}, for ((…)), $RANDOM
A while loop with a counter; awk's rand(). The brace range stays a word, silently (§19.10).
set -o pipefail
POSIX since 2024; not in macOS's dash. Test with (set -o pipefail) 2>/dev/null, or carry the status on a spare descriptor (§19.11).
trap … SIGINT
trap … INT. Clean up in the handler, reset both traps, re-raise (§19.11).
read -p/-a/-s/-t
read -r (and -d, 2024); a prompt with printf … >&2 (§19.11).
<(cmd)
A temporary file or mkfifo (§19.14).
GNU/BSD options
Write to the intersection; detect the capability, not the OS; command -v, not which (§19.12, §19.13).

And the rule behind the table: decide first whether the script must be POSIX. If it must, write it for dash, check it with shellcheck -s sh and checkbashisms -p, and run it under dash; if it need not, say bash in the shebang and use bash properly. The one script that is always wrong is the one whose first line says sh and whose body is bash.

Exercises

1. Port a script. This script says #!/bin/bash and must now run as /bin/sh on a minimal image. Find every bashism in it, first by reading and then with a tool, and rewrite it so that it passes shellcheck as sh and checkbashisms -p, and prints the same results under dash. Which of the findings would a run under dash have missed?

printf 'dest=saved\n' > settings.sh
cat > backup.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
source ./settings.sh
function backup_one {
  local src=$1
  [[ -f $src ]] || { echo -e "skip:\t$src"; return; }
  cp -- "$src" "$dest/${src##*/}.bak"
  echo "saved ${src^^}"
}
files=("$@")
for f in "${files[@]}"; do backup_one "$f"; done
read -r first _ <<< "$*"
echo "first was $first"
EOF
shellcheck -x -s sh -f gcc backup.sh | sed 's/^backup.sh://'
Solution

ShellCheck, run as sh, finds every construct:

printf 'dest=saved\n' > settings.sh
cat > backup.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
source ./settings.sh
function backup_one {
  local src=$1
  [[ -f $src ]] || { echo -e "skip:\t$src"; return; }
  cp -- "$src" "$dest/${src##*/}.bak"
  echo "saved ${src^^}"
}
files=("$@")
for f in "${files[@]}"; do backup_one "$f"; done
read -r first _ <<< "$*"
echo "first was $first"
EOF
shellcheck -x -s sh -f gcc backup.sh | sed 's/^backup.sh://'

2:1: warning: In POSIX sh, 'source' in place of '.' is undefined. [SC3046]
2:1: warning: In POSIX sh, 'source' in place of '.' is undefined. [SC3051]
3:1: warning: 'function' keyword is non-standard. Use 'foo()' instead of 'function foo'. [SC2113]
4:3: warning: In POSIX sh, 'local' is undefined. [SC3043]
4:13: note: Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting. [SC2086]
5:3: warning: In POSIX sh, [[ ]] is undefined. [SC3010]
5:27: warning: In POSIX sh, echo flags are undefined. [SC3037]
7:15: warning: In POSIX sh, case modification is undefined. [SC3059]
9:7: warning: In POSIX sh, arrays are undefined. [SC3030]
10:11: warning: In POSIX sh, array references are undefined. [SC3054]
11:17: warning: In POSIX sh, here-strings are undefined. [SC3011]

The port:

printf 'dest=saved\n' > settings.sh
mkdir saved; printf 'x\n' > a.txt
cat > backup.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
. ./settings.sh
backup_one() {
  _src=$1
  [ -f "$_src" ] || { printf 'skip:\t%s\n' "$_src"; return 0; }
  cp -- "$_src" "$dest/${_src##*/}.bak"
  printf 'saved %s\n' "$(printf '%s' "$_src" | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]')"
}
for f in "$@"; do backup_one "$f"; done
first=${1-}
echo "first was $first"
EOF
shellcheck -x -f gcc backup.sh && checkbashisms -p backup.sh && echo "both checkers: clean"
dash backup.sh a.txt missing.txt
ls saved

both checkers: clean
saved A.TXT
skip:	missing.txt
first was a.txt
a.txt.bak

Each change maps to a finding: . for source (§19.9), name() for function, a prefixed _src for local (§19.6), [ -f "$_src" ] for [[ ]] (§19.3), printf with \t in the format for echo -e (§19.7), tr for ${src^^} (§19.4), "$@" directly for the array (§19.5), and ${1-} for the here-string that only extracted the first word — which also removes the need for read at all. SC2086 on local src=$1 is worth understanding. POSIX does not define local, so nothing guarantees that a shell parses its arguments as assignments rather than as ordinary words, which would be split and globbed; both dash versions measured here do treat them as assignments (local a=$1 with x y keeps x y whole), and quoting costs nothing, so ShellCheck asks for the quotes.

A run under dash would have reported almost nothing:

printf 'dest=saved\n' > settings.sh
mkdir saved; printf 'x\n' > a.txt
cat > backup.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
source ./settings.sh
function backup_one {
  local src=$1
  [[ -f $src ]] || { echo -e "skip:\t$src"; return; }
  cp -- "$src" "$dest/${src##*/}.bak"
  echo "saved ${src^^}"
}
files=("$@")
for f in "${files[@]}"; do backup_one "$f"; done
read -r first _ <<< "$*"
echo "first was $first"
EOF
dash backup.sh a.txt missing.txt; echo "status $?"

backup.sh: 2: source: not found
backup.sh: 3: function: not found
backup.sh: 4: local: not in a function
status 2

It printed three lines and stopped: source: not found (line 2), function: not found (line 3, the keyword read as a command, as §19.6 showed), and then local: not in a function on line 4 — because without a function definition, the body was being run as top-level code, and dash's local is an error outside a function. That error stopped the script with status 2. The [[ ]], echo -e, ${src^^}, the array and the here-string were never reached, so a run would have needed five more rounds of fix-and-rerun to find what one static check listed at once.

2. A portable string library. Write trim, contains and starts_with for POSIX sh, without any subprocess. trim removes leading and trailing whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines) and keeps inner whitespace; contains STRING SUB and starts_with STRING PREFIX return 0 or 1 and must treat SUB and PREFIX literally, even if they contain * or ?.

Solution 
cat > strings.sh <<'EOF'
# Portable string helpers: no bash, no subprocess
trim() {
  _t=${1#"${1%%[![:space:]]*}"}     # strip the leading whitespace
  _t=${_t%"${_t##*[![:space:]]}"}   # strip the trailing whitespace
  printf '%s\n' "$_t"
}
contains() { case $1 in *"$2"*) return 0 ;; *) return 1 ;; esac; }
starts_with() { case $1 in "$2"*) return 0 ;; *) return 1 ;; esac; }
EOF
cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
. ./strings.sh
printf '[%s]\n' "$(trim '   two  words   ')"
printf '[%s]\n' "$(trim '')"
printf '[%s]\n' "$(trim '    ')"
contains 'report.txt' '.tx' && echo "contains .tx"
contains 'report.txt' '*'   || echo "does not contain a literal *"
starts_with '--verbose' '--' && echo "starts with --"
EOF
dash t.sh
shellcheck -s sh -f gcc strings.sh && echo "shellcheck -s sh: clean"

[two  words]
[]
[]
contains .tx
does not contain a literal *
starts with --
shellcheck -s sh: clean

trim uses two nested expansions. ${1%%[![:space:]]*} removes everything from the first non-space character to the end, leaving only the leading whitespace; ${1#"…"} then removes exactly that from the front — quoted, so the whitespace is matched literally. The second line does the same at the end. An empty or all-whitespace string gives an empty result, because the inner expansion is then the whole string. [![:space:]] is the portable negated class (§19.3, §19.8).

contains and starts_with are case patterns, with the argument quoted inside the pattern: *"$2"* matches the characters of $2 literally, so contains 'report.txt' '*' correctly says no. Unquoted, *$2* would make * a wildcard and match everything — the same quoting rule §5.4 taught for ${var#pattern}.

3. An absolute path without readlink -f. readlink -f is not POSIX, and older systems lack it. Write abspath DIR, which prints the physical absolute path of a directory — symbolic links resolved, .. removed — or fails if it does not exist, without changing the caller's current directory.

Solution 
cat > abspath.sh <<'EOF'
# abspath DIR: the physical absolute path of a directory, without readlink -f
abspath() ( CDPATH= cd -P -- "$1" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P )
EOF
mkdir -p real/inner; ln -s real/inner shortcut
cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
. ./abspath.sh
base=$(pwd -P)
for d in shortcut real/inner/.. . nowhere; do
  if p=$(abspath "$d"); then printf '%-14s <here>%s\n' "$d" "${p#"$base"}"; else printf '%-14s (no such directory)\n' "$d"; fi
done
EOF
dash t.sh

shortcut       <here>/real/inner
real/inner/..  <here>/real
.              <here>
nowhere        (no such directory)

The function's body is a subshell (§19.6), so its cd cannot move the caller. cd -P resolves symbolic links as it changes directory, and pwd -P prints the physical path, both POSIX. CDPATH= stops an inherited CDPATH from sending cd somewhere else and printing it; -- protects a directory named -x; the error from a missing directory is discarded and the non-zero status is the answer. It works for directories only — for a file, split off the last component with ${f##*/} and ${f%/*}, resolve the directory, and add the name back.

4. Joining without arrays. bash joins an array with (IFS=,; echo "${a[*]}") (§15.9). Write the POSIX version, join SEP WORD..., and explain why it only works for a single-character separator. Then write join_str for any separator, including an empty list, without changing the caller's IFS.

Solution 
cat > t.sh <<'EOF'
# join SEP WORD...: POSIX sh has no arrays, but "$*" joins on the first character of IFS
join() ( IFS=$1; shift; printf '%s\n' "$*" )
# A separator longer than one character needs a loop
join_str() {
  _sep=$1; shift
  _out=${1-}; [ "$#" -gt 0 ] && shift
  for _w in "$@"; do _out=$_out$_sep$_w; done
  printf '%s\n' "$_out"
}
old_ifs=$IFS
join , a 'b c' d
join_str ' | ' a 'b c' d
join_str ' | '
[ "$IFS" = "$old_ifs" ] && echo "IFS is untouched"
EOF
dash t.sh

a,b c,d
a | b c | d

IFS is untouched

"$*" joins the positional parameters with the first character of IFS (§3.5), and that is POSIX; join sets IFS to its separator in a subshell body, so the caller's IFS is untouched. Only the first character is used, which is why a ' | ' separator would become a single space. join_str builds the string itself: the first word, then the separator and each remaining word. ${1-} and the [ "$#" -gt 0 ] && shift guard make an empty list print an empty line rather than fail under set -u or shift an empty list. Its variables carry the _ prefix of §19.6, because there is no local.

SECTION 20

Static Analysis, Testing and Debugging

Every section so far has ended the same way: an example that was run, with the output pasted underneath. That habit is the subject of this section. A script that nobody has checked is a script whose author is hoping, and a shell script is worse placed than most for hope: it has no compiler, no type checker, an expansion pipeline that silently changes the meaning of a line, and a failure mode — a wrong answer reported with status 0 — that no exception will ever flag. §11 taught a script to fail loudly when it fails; this section is about finding out, before anyone depends on it, whether it does what it was meant to.

There are three ways to find a defect in a script, and they find different things. Static analysis reads the code without running it and reports patterns that are known to cause bugs; it is fast, it needs no test data and no fixtures, and it is the only method that sees a branch nobody has executed. Tests run the code against inputs whose right answer is known, which finds what a linter cannot — a wrong boundary, a missing case, a function that does what it says but not what was meant. Debugging is what you do once either has told you there is a defect and you do not yet know where. §20.1–§20.6 are static analysis, and nearly all of that is one tool, ShellCheck: what it reports, the checks that matter most, how to silence one honestly, and how to make it a gate that a change cannot pass without satisfying. §20.7–§20.11 are testing: how to write a script so that it can be tested, the bats-core framework, how to replace the commands a script calls, shunit2, and running all of it in CI. §20.12–§20.14 are debugging: set -x and everything that makes its output readable, stepping through a script and the bashdb debugger, and the printf-and-logging habits that make the next bug cheaper. §20.15 is the summary table, and the exercises use all three.

Several neighbours already own part of the ground, and this section does not repeat them. The main guard that lets a test load a file's functions without running the script is §9.14's; here it is used, and its cost when missing is measured. The ERR trap, caller and the stack-trace handler are §11.10, §9.10 and §12.6; trap DEBUG, functrace and extdebug are §12.10; bash -n was introduced in §2.7 and §16.7. shellcheck -s sh as a portability check is §19.2, and the security checks a linter finds are §18.18's. This section owns the discipline that connects them: what to run, in what order, and what a failing run means.

Every example here was run: ShellCheck 0.11.0, bats-core 1.14.0, shunit2 2.1.8 and bashdb 5.2-1.2.0 on macOS under bash 5.3, and the same commands on Debian under bash 5.2. The tools' own messages — ShellCheck's wording and its severity for each check, bats's report format, shunit2's summary line — are quoted from those runs, because they change between releases and no one can write them correctly from memory. Where a version matters, the section says which.

20.1 What Static Analysis Is, and What ShellCheck Reports

Static analysis: reading a script without running it

Static analysis examines a program's source and reports defects without executing it. For a language with a compiler it usually means the type checker and a linter; for shell there is no compiler, so the linter is the whole of it. The value of the method is where it looks: a static analyser reads every line of every branch, including the error path nobody has taken since the day it was written, and it does not need the input that would trigger the defect. What it cannot do is know what you meant. It reports a pattern — an unquoted expansion, a cd whose failure is ignored, an if [ $? -eq 0 ] — and leaves the decision about whether this instance is a bug to you. That is the reason every serious linter has a way to say "I know, and here is why", and it is what §20.3 and §20.4 are about.

ShellCheck is the linter for shell: a program written in Haskell, GPL-licensed, that parses a script the way the shell would, tracks which variables are assigned and quoted, and reports a numbered finding — SC2086, SC2164 — for each pattern it recognises. It knows sh, bash, dash, ksh and BusyBox's sh, and takes the dialect from the script's #! line. Every code has a page at shellcheck.net/wiki/SC followed by the number that explains what is wrong, when the warning is a false alarm, and what to write instead; the tool prints the addresses of the pages for the codes it reported. It is packaged for every system this course targets — brew install shellcheck, apt install shellcheck, and a shellcheck-py package on PyPI that carries the binary — and it belongs on every developer's machine and in every CI runner (§20.6).

Here is a first run, on a script written the way most first drafts are:

cat > backup.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
# Copy every log into the archive, then report.
archive=/var/tmp/archive
for f in $(ls *.log); do
  cp $f $archive
done
cd $archive
if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "archived"
fi
EOF
shellcheck backup.sh

In backup.sh line 4:
for f in $(ls *.log); do
         ^---------^ SC2045 (error): Iterating over ls output is fragile. Use globs.
              ^-- SC2035 (info): Use ./*glob* or -- *glob* so names with dashes won't become options.


In backup.sh line 5:
  cp $f $archive
     ^-- SC2086 (info): Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting.

Did you mean:
  cp "$f" $archive


In backup.sh line 7:
cd $archive
^---------^ SC2164 (warning): Use 'cd ... || exit' or 'cd ... || return' in case cd fails.

Did you mean:
cd $archive || exit


In backup.sh line 8:
if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then
     ^-- SC2181 (style): Check exit code directly with e.g. 'if mycmd;', not indirectly with $?.

For more information:
  https://www.shellcheck.net/wiki/SC2045 -- Iterating over ls output is fragi...
  https://www.shellcheck.net/wiki/SC2164 -- Use 'cd ... || exit' or 'cd ... |...
  https://www.shellcheck.net/wiki/SC2035 -- Use ./*glob* or -- *glob* so name...

Five findings, and each one is a real defect, not a matter of taste. SC2045 says that for f in $(ls *.log) iterates over the output of a command that prints names, so any name containing a space is split into two; the fix is a glob, for f in *.log, or find -exec (§8.4). SC2035 notes that a glob starting with * can match a name beginning with -, which ls will then take for an option; ./*.log fixes it. SC2086 is the quoting warning that §3 spent a section on: cp $f $archive splits on whitespace and expands globs in both operands. SC2164 says cd $archive may fail, and if it does the script carries on in whatever directory it was in. SC2181 says the if [ $? -eq 0 ] on line 8 tests the status of the cd, which is right, but indirectly, and anything added between the two lines would silently change what it tests (§11.6).

Each finding carries its check number, its level in brackets, and — where the tool knows the fix — a Did you mean: line showing it. The level is the next thing to understand.

ShellCheck severity: the error level, warning level, info level and style level

ShellCheck grades every finding into one of four levels, and the grade decides what a gate does with it. An error level finding is a script that cannot do what it says: a syntax error, or a construct that is wrong in a way the tool is sure of. A warning level finding is very likely a bug — a cd without a fallback, a variable that is set and never used. An info level finding is code that works today and breaks on unexpected input, the largest class being unquoted expansions. A style level finding is a suggestion, of which the $? test is the usual example. The levels are the tool's judgement and they are not always the ones a reader would guess:

cat > levels.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
local scratch=/tmp/x
cd /tmp
if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then echo ok; fi
echo $1
EOF
echo "== every finding, with its level"
shellcheck levels.sh | grep -o 'SC[0-9]* ([a-z]*)'
echo "== the same findings in gcc format: info and style are both a note"
shellcheck --format=gcc levels.sh | cut -d: -f2-4
for level in error warning info style; do
  printf '== --severity=%-7s ' "$level"
  shellcheck --severity="$level" --format=gcc levels.sh | grep -c .
done

== every finding, with its level
SC2168 (error)
SC2034 (warning)
SC2164 (warning)
SC2181 (style)
SC2086 (info)
== the same findings in gcc format: info and style are both a note
2:1: error
2:7: warning
3:1: warning
4:6: note
5:6: note
== --severity=error   1
== --severity=warning 3
== --severity=info    4
== --severity=style   5

Read the first block as the lint report of one five-line script: SC2168 is an error (local outside a function is not valid), SC2034 and SC2164 are warnings, SC2181 is style, and SC2086 is info. Two details are worth having in mind. The gcc output format that editors and CI systems parse has only three words, error, warning and note, so it reports info and style alike as note; to see which is which, use the default format, as the first block did. And --severity — -S for short — is a minimum: --severity=warning keeps warnings and errors and drops the two lower levels, which is why the counts grow as the threshold falls, from 1 at error to 5 at style. A finding's level is also fixed per check by the ShellCheck version: SC2045 was an error in the run above, and nothing in the tool's contract says it must stay one, which is a reason to pin the version in CI (§20.6).

That last property matters more than it looks, because the severity threshold also decides the exit status, and so what a gate lets through:

cat > unquoted.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
cp $1 backup/
EOF
shellcheck --format=gcc unquoted.sh;                       echo "default:            exit $?"
shellcheck --severity=warning unquoted.sh;                 echo "--severity=warning: exit $?"
shellcheck --severity=info --format=gcc unquoted.sh;       echo "--severity=info:    exit $?"

unquoted.sh:2:4: note: Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting. [SC2086]
default:            exit 1
--severity=warning: exit 0
unquoted.sh:2:4: note: Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting. [SC2086]
--severity=info:    exit 1

The unquoted $1 is the most valuable single finding the tool has, and it is only info level. A gate written shellcheck --severity=warning exits 0 on this script and lets it through; the gate has to be shellcheck --severity=info to catch it. Choosing the threshold is therefore a policy decision, not a default, and §20.4 and §20.6 return to it.

Output formats, and a fix you can apply

--format selects how findings are written: tty (the default, with the source line and a caret), gcc (one line per finding, file:line:column: level: message [SCnnnn], which editors and CI log parsers understand), json and json1 (for tools), checkstyle (XML, for the systems that read it) and quiet (nothing; only the exit status). The odd one out is diff, which writes the fixes ShellCheck is sure of as a unified diff that patch can apply:

cat > loop.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
for f in $(ls); do
  cp $f /backup
done
EOF
echo "== gcc"; shellcheck --format=gcc loop.sh
echo "== diff"; shellcheck --format=diff loop.sh
shellcheck --format=diff loop.sh | patch -p1 > /dev/null
echo "== after patch"; cat loop.sh

== gcc
loop.sh:2:10: error: Iterating over ls output is fragile. Use globs. [SC2045]
loop.sh:3:6: note: Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting. [SC2086]
== diff
--- a/loop.sh
+++ b/loop.sh
@@ -1,4 +1,4 @@
 #!/bin/bash
 for f in $(ls); do
-  cp $f /backup
+  cp "$f" /backup
 done

== after patch
#!/bin/bash
for f in $(ls); do
  cp "$f" /backup
done

Only the changes ShellCheck can make safely are in the patch — the quoting on line 3 — and it left the $(ls) loop alone, because the right replacement there depends on what the loop is for. shellcheck --format=diff file | patch -p1 is a reasonable way to clear a backlog of SC2086 in an old script; read the diff before applying it, since it edits the file in place.

What a clean run does not mean

ShellCheck knows what shell code tends to get wrong; it does not know what your script is for. A script can pass with no findings and still be wrong:

cat > retry.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
# Try the job up to $max times.
max=3
for ((attempt = 1; attempt < max; attempt++)); do
  echo "attempt $attempt of $max"
done
EOF
shellcheck retry.sh && echo "shellcheck: clean"
bash retry.sh

shellcheck: clean
attempt 1 of 3
attempt 2 of 3

The comment says "try the job up to $max times" and the loop tries it twice: attempt < max should be attempt <= max, and every construct is legal and idiomatic, so there is nothing for a pattern-matcher to report. Only running the code against a case whose answer is known — here, that three attempts means three lines — finds it. That is the argument for testing, and the next five subsections are the tools for it. Static analysis and tests are not alternatives: the linter finds the class of mistakes no one should be spending a test on, and the tests find the ones no linter can define.

20.2 The Checks You Will Meet Most

A script of any size will draw the same ten or twelve warnings again and again. Knowing what each one means — the defect, not just the wording — is what lets you tell a real finding from a false alarm at a glance, and it is the difference between a linter that is obeyed and one that is silenced wholesale. This subsection takes them in the pairs they usually arrive in. Each example shows the tool's report and then the script's behaviour, because a warning is only convincing next to the bug it predicts.

SC2086 and SC2046: the unquoted variable warning

The unquoted variable warning is SC2086, "Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting", and SC2046 is its twin for command substitution, "Quote this to prevent word splitting". They are the same defect in two spellings, and §3 explains the mechanism: an unquoted expansion is split on whitespace into words and each word is then expanded as a glob, so the number of arguments a command receives depends on the data.

cat > split.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
count() { echo "$# argument(s)"; }
name='my notes.txt'
listing=$(printf 'one two\nthree\n')
count $name
count "$name"
count $(printf 'one two\nthree\n')
count "$listing"
EOF
shellcheck --format=gcc split.sh
bash split.sh

split.sh:5:7: note: Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting. [SC2086]
split.sh:7:7: warning: Quote this to prevent word splitting. [SC2046]
2 argument(s)
1 argument(s)
3 argument(s)
1 argument(s)

count reports how many arguments it received. With name='my notes.txt' the unquoted call passed two, and the quoted call one; $(printf 'one two\nthree\n') unquoted gave three arguments from what was one command's output, and quoted, one. That is all SC2086 and SC2046 mean, and it is why they are the most valuable checks in the tool. ShellCheck reported the two unquoted lines and left the two quoted ones alone. The two are not equally severe: SC2086 on line 5 is only info, and SC2046 on line 7 is a warning — the reason a --severity=warning gate misses the first and catches the second. A quoted expansion is right; an unquoted one is right only when word splitting is the intent, and then it deserves a comment (§20.3, §18.13).

SC2181 and SC2155: a status that gets lost

Two checks are about $?, and each is about a status that was replaced before anyone read it.

cat > masked.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
fetch() { echo "fetching"; return 3; }

fetch
echo "done fetching"
if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then echo "fetch worked"; else echo "fetch failed"; fi

load() {
  local out=$(false)
  echo "status of the assignment: $?"
  local separate
  separate=$(false)
  echo "status of the assignment when split: $?"
}
load
EOF
shellcheck --format=gcc masked.sh
bash masked.sh

masked.sh:6:6: warning: This $? refers to echo/printf, not a previous command. Assign to variable to avoid it being overwritten. [SC2320]
masked.sh:6:6: note: Check exit code directly with e.g. 'if mycmd;', not indirectly with $?. [SC2181]
masked.sh:9:9: warning: out appears unused. Verify use (or export if used externally). [SC2034]
masked.sh:9:9: warning: Declare and assign separately to avoid masking return values. [SC2155]
masked.sh:12:3: warning: separate appears unused. Verify use (or export if used externally). [SC2034]
fetching
done fetching
fetch worked
status of the assignment: 0
status of the assignment when split: 1

SC2181 flags if [ $? -eq 0 ]: testing the previous command's status indirectly. The script above shows why it is worth fixing rather than a matter of style. Between fetch, which returned 3, and the test, someone added echo "done fetching", and now $? is the status of that echo — 0 — so the script announced "fetch worked". ShellCheck reported the pair together, as SC2320 (the $? "refers to echo/printf, not a previous command") and SC2181. The fix is to test the command itself, if fetch; then …, which cannot drift (§11.6).

SC2155, "Declare and assign separately to avoid masking return values", is §9.4's and §11.5's local x=$(cmd) trap. The status of local out=$(false) is the status of local, which is 0, and the failure of the command substitution is gone; the same assignment split into local separate and separate=$(false) returned 1, as printed. The check applies to export too, and it is the reason a set -e script can appear to ignore a failing command: the failure was thrown away on the same line it happened.

SC2164 and SC2115: cd and rm

A pair that goes together because a failed cd is what makes a later rm destructive (§18.18).

cat > clean.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
build=./build
cd "$build"
touch cleaned.marker
EOF
shellcheck --format=gcc clean.sh
mkdir keep && cd keep && bash ../clean.sh; ls

clean.sh:3:1: warning: Use 'cd ... || exit' or 'cd ... || return' in case cd fails. [SC2164]
../clean.sh: line 3: cd: ./build: No such file or directory
cleaned.marker

SC2164, "Use cd … || exit or cd … || return in case cd fails", is the warning that predicts this: cd ./build failed — there was no such directory — and the script went on to touch cleaned.marker in the directory it was already in, which is where the marker appears. Replace touch with a command that removes files and the script has emptied the wrong directory. The fix is one of cd "$dir" || exit 1, cd -- "$dir" || return, or set -e (§11.3).

cat > wipe.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
build=$1
rm -r "$build"/
EOF
shellcheck --format=gcc wipe.sh

wipe.sh:3:7: warning: Use "${var:?}" to ensure this never expands to / . [SC2115]

SC2115 fires on rm -r "$build"/ — quoted, and still flagged — because if $build is empty the argument is /, and the command tries to delete the root of the filesystem. The message names the guard: "${build:?}" makes the shell stop with an error when the variable is empty or unset, and §18.18 measured what happens to a script that uses it. A variable followed by / inside an rm -r is the pattern to distrust.

SC2034, SC2128 and SC2162: names and arrays

Three checks about variables and arrays, all of which report a mistake that runs without error.

cat > names.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
retries=3
for attempt in 1 2 3; do
  echo "attempt $attempt of $retires"
done
servers=(alpha beta gamma)
echo "first: $servers"
echo "all: ${servers[*]}"
printf 'C:\\temp\\new\n' > paths.txt
read line < paths.txt
echo "$line"
EOF
shellcheck --format=gcc names.sh
bash names.sh

names.sh:2:1: warning: retries appears unused. Verify use (or export if used externally). [SC2034]
names.sh:4:29: warning: retires is referenced but not assigned. [SC2154]
names.sh:7:14: warning: Expanding an array without an index only gives the first element. [SC2128]
names.sh:10:1: note: read without -r will mangle backslashes. [SC2162]
attempt 1 of 
attempt 2 of 
attempt 3 of 
first: alpha
all: alpha beta gamma
C:tempnew

SC2034, "appears unused", is the check that finds typos: retries=3 was assigned and never read, and line 4 reads $retires, which is what SC2154, "referenced but not assigned", reports. The script ran without complaint and printed attempt 1 of with nothing after of, because the misspelt name expanded to an empty string. SC2034 alone is a warning about a variable that might be exported or used by a sourced file, and §20.3's source= directive is what tells ShellCheck about those. SC2128, "Expanding an array without an index only gives the first element", is §6.4's bare array name: $servers is ${servers[0]}, so line 7 printed first: alpha. The plural form, ${servers[*]}, is the array as one string and printed all three, and the tool has no opinion about which was meant. SC2162 is read without -r, which §14.4 covers: C:\temp\new came back as C:tempnew, the backslashes consumed as escapes.

SC2016: single quotes that do not expand

SC2016, "Expressions don't expand in single quotes, use double quotes for that", is the most common false alarm, and the most instructive, because the same message is right on one line and wrong on the next.

cat > quotes.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
echo 'the price is $5'
envsubst '$USER $HOME' < /dev/null
psql -c 'SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = $1' /dev/null
sed 's/$HOME/~/' /dev/null
awk '{ print $1 }' /dev/null
EOF
shellcheck --format=gcc quotes.sh

quotes.sh:2:6: note: Expressions don't expand in single quotes, use double quotes for that. [SC2016]
quotes.sh:3:10: note: Expressions don't expand in single quotes, use double quotes for that. [SC2016]
quotes.sh:4:9: note: Expressions don't expand in single quotes, use double quotes for that. [SC2016]
quotes.sh:5:5: note: Expressions don't expand in single quotes, use double quotes for that. [SC2016]

Four findings. Line 2 is a real bug: echo 'the price is $5' prints $5, and the author probably wanted the shell to expand it (though here they may have wanted the literal, which is the point — the tool cannot know). Lines 3, 4 and 5 are false alarms: envsubst reads $USER $HOME from its own argument, and needs the dollar signs literal; a SQL text with $1 is a placeholder for a database driver; and in sed 's/$HOME/~/' the pattern is the literal text $HOME, which the author wants sed to find. ShellCheck stays silent for awk, jq, perl, find -exec sh -c and a few others, because it recognises that those programs take a script in quotes, and reports the ones it has no model for. Each of the three false alarms is the same shape: the quotes are single on purpose, because the receiving program, not the shell, is meant to interpret the dollar sign. §20.3 shows how to say so, and §20.4 how to decide whether a given finding is one.

20.3 The ShellCheck Directive: Scope, Sourced Files and Dialects

The ShellCheck directive: # shellcheck disable

A ShellCheck directive is a comment of the form # shellcheck key=value that changes how ShellCheck reads the code that follows it. The one used most is # shellcheck disable=SC2086, which switches a check off. What a directive covers depends on where it is written, and the rules are worth stating exactly because a directive that covers too much hides real bugs:

cat > scope.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
echo $1
# shellcheck disable=SC2086
echo $2
echo $3
f() {
  # shellcheck disable=SC2086
  echo $4
  echo $5
}
# shellcheck disable=SC2086
g() {
  echo $6
  echo $7
}
EOF
shellcheck --format=gcc scope.sh

scope.sh:2:6: note: Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting. [SC2086]
scope.sh:5:6: note: Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting. [SC2086]
scope.sh:9:8: note: Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting. [SC2086]

Three of the seven $n were reported, on lines 2, 5 and 9. A directive before a simple command covered just that command: line 4's echo $2 was silent, and line 5's echo $3 right after it was not. A directive inside a function body covered the next command in the body: line 8 was silent, line 9 not. A directive before a compound command — the function g — covered everything inside it, so $6 and $7 were both silent. The rule is: the directive applies to the next command, and a command that contains other commands takes its whole body with it. A function is a compound command, which makes a directive above a long function a wide suppression, and the reason to put it inside the function, on the line it is about.

There is a second position, the top of the file:

cat > wide.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
# shellcheck disable=SC2086
echo $1
echo $2
EOF
cat > late.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
set -u
# shellcheck disable=SC2086
echo $1
echo $2
EOF
echo "== directive before the first command"; shellcheck --format=gcc wide.sh; echo "exit $?"
echo "== directive after one"; shellcheck --format=gcc late.sh

== directive before the first command
exit 0
== directive after one
late.sh:5:6: note: Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting. [SC2086]

A directive before the first command applies to the whole file, and one after even a single command applies only to what follows. That makes the top of a file the place for a decision that is really about the whole script (# shellcheck disable=SC2034 for a file of exported settings, say), and everywhere else the place for a decision about one line.

A directive may list several codes, and may carry a reason on the same line, after a second #:

cat > multi.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
# shellcheck disable=SC2086,SC2016  # $1 is awk's, and the word list is meant to split
awk '{ print $1 }' $1
EOF
shellcheck multi.sh; echo "exit $?"

exit 0

The script exited 0, so ShellCheck read both codes and ignored the comment after them. Write the reason. A suppression with no explanation cannot be reviewed, and in a year no one will know whether the warning was silenced because it was wrong or because it was inconvenient. §20.4 makes that an enforced rule.

SC1090 and shellcheck source=: files ShellCheck cannot follow

When a script sources a file, ShellCheck needs to see that file to know what variables and functions it defines; otherwise every use of them looks like an undefined name. It will read a sourced file only if it is told to, with -x (--external-sources), and only if it can work out the file's name.

mkdir lib
cat > lib/common.sh <<'EOF'
greet() { echo "hello, $1"; }
EOF
cat > main.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
here=$(dirname "$0")
source "$here/lib/common.sh"
greet world
EOF
echo "== default";         shellcheck --format=gcc main.sh
echo "== with -x";          shellcheck --format=gcc -x main.sh
cat > main2.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
here=$(dirname "$0")
os=linux
source "$here/lib/$os.sh"
greet world
EOF
echo "== a name built from a variable"; shellcheck --format=gcc -x main2.sh

== default
main.sh:3:8: note: Not following: ./lib/common.sh was not specified as input (see shellcheck -x). [SC1091]
== with -x
== a name built from a variable
main2.sh:4:8: warning: ShellCheck can't follow non-constant source. Use a directive to specify location. [SC1090]

source "$here/lib/common.sh" is written with a variable in front, and ShellCheck treats a leading $var/ as "some directory", reading it as ./lib/common.sh; without -x it reported SC1091, "Not following: … was not specified as input", and with -x it followed the file and was silent. source "$here/lib/$os.sh" has a variable in the middle of the name, which cannot be resolved without running the script, and the tool reported SC1090, "ShellCheck can't follow non-constant source. Use a directive to specify location." The directive that says where is # shellcheck source=, and source=/dev/null says "there is nothing worth reading":

mkdir lib
cat > lib/common.sh <<'EOF'
lib_version=2
greet() { echo "hello, $1"; }
EOF
cat > unlocated.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
here=$(dirname "$0")
os=linux
source "$here/lib/$os.sh"
echo "library version $lib_version"
EOF
cat > located.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
here=$(dirname "$0")
os=linux
# shellcheck source=lib/common.sh
source "$here/lib/$os.sh"
echo "library version $lib_version"
EOF
cat > skipped.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
here=$(dirname "$0")
os=linux
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source "$here/lib/$os.sh"
echo "library version $lib_version"
EOF
cat > searched.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
# shellcheck source-path=SCRIPTDIR/lib
source common.sh
echo "library version $lib_version"
EOF
echo "== no directive";                   shellcheck --format=gcc -x unlocated.sh
echo "== source=lib/common.sh, no -x";    shellcheck --format=gcc located.sh
echo "== source=lib/common.sh, with -x";  shellcheck --format=gcc -x located.sh
echo "== source=/dev/null";               shellcheck --format=gcc -x skipped.sh
echo "== source-path=SCRIPTDIR/lib";      shellcheck --format=gcc -x searched.sh
echo "== the same, without -x";           shellcheck --format=gcc searched.sh

== no directive
unlocated.sh:4:8: warning: ShellCheck can't follow non-constant source. Use a directive to specify location. [SC1090]
unlocated.sh:5:23: warning: lib_version is referenced but not assigned. [SC2154]
== source=lib/common.sh, no -x
located.sh:5:8: note: Not following: lib/common.sh was not specified as input (see shellcheck -x). [SC1091]
located.sh:6:23: warning: lib_version is referenced but not assigned. [SC2154]
== source=lib/common.sh, with -x
== source=/dev/null
skipped.sh:6:23: warning: lib_version is referenced but not assigned. [SC2154]
== source-path=SCRIPTDIR/lib
== the same, without -x
searched.sh:3:8: note: Not following: common.sh was not specified as input (see shellcheck -x). [SC1091]
searched.sh:4:23: warning: lib_version is referenced but not assigned. [SC2154]

Six runs of nearly the same script. The first, with no directive, reported SC1090 on the source line and SC2154 on $lib_version, because ShellCheck did not know the library defined it. # shellcheck source=lib/common.sh named the file, but without -x ShellCheck still would not read it: SC1091, and the SC2154 again. With -x as well the report was empty, which is the proof the library was read: lib_version=2 is set in it. source=/dev/null kept the SC1090 quiet but did nothing for $lib_version, because nothing was read. And # shellcheck source-path=SCRIPTDIR/lib — the directive form of --source-path, with SCRIPTDIR standing for the checked script's own directory — let source common.sh resolve, again only with -x. The two halves are separate: the directive says where the file is, and -x gives permission to open it. A project's lint command therefore carries -x, and each dynamic source carries a source= directive (§9.13).

shellcheck shell=: files with no shebang

ShellCheck chooses its dialect from the #! line. A file with none — a library that is only ever sourced, a fragment of a profile — has no dialect, and ShellCheck will not guess:

cat > colors.sh <<'EOF'
# colors.sh: sourced by other scripts, never run
palette=(red green blue)
echo "${palette[@]}"
EOF
cat > colors-directive.sh <<'EOF'
# shellcheck shell=bash
palette=(red green blue)
echo "${palette[@]}"
EOF
cat > posix-lib.sh <<'EOF'
# shellcheck shell=sh
palette=(red green blue)
echo "${palette[@]}"
EOF
echo "== no shebang";       shellcheck --format=gcc colors.sh
echo "== shell=bash";       shellcheck --format=gcc colors-directive.sh
echo "== shell=sh";         shellcheck --format=gcc posix-lib.sh
echo "== -s bash, no directive"; shellcheck --format=gcc -s bash colors.sh

== no shebang
colors.sh:1:1: error: Tips depend on target shell and yours is unknown. Add a shebang or a 'shell' directive. [SC2148]
== shell=bash
== shell=sh
posix-lib.sh:2:9: warning: In POSIX sh, arrays are undefined. [SC3030]
posix-lib.sh:3:7: warning: In POSIX sh, array references are undefined. [SC3054]
== -s bash, no directive

The bare file drew SC2148, an error: "Tips depend on target shell and yours is unknown". # shellcheck shell=bash on the first line fixed it, and -s bash on the command line has the same effect for every file in the run. The directive is the better tool for a library, because it travels with the file and documents which dialect the file is written in: # shellcheck shell=sh marks a library that has to be POSIX, and it caught the two array constructs as SC3030 and SC3054, §19.2's checks. A file without a shebang and without the directive is the commonest cause of "ShellCheck says everything is an error" on a first run.

20.4 False Positives, Suppressing a Check, and Project Settings

A linter that is obeyed on every finding has to be right on every finding, and no pattern-matcher is. The alternative to obeying it blindly is silencing it wholesale, which is worse: a suppressed check finds nothing, and the next real instance of the pattern passes without a word. What is needed is a way to say "this instance is intended" that is narrow, visible and explained. This subsection is that discipline.

A ShellCheck false positive: how to recognise one

A ShellCheck false positive is a finding whose premise does not hold for the code it points at. The tool assumed something — that the single quotes were a mistake, that the variable was meant to be split, that the sourced file did not matter — and here the assumption is wrong. Before deciding that a finding is one, ask three questions in order:

  1. Is the code doing what I think? Most findings that feel like false alarms are not. SC2086 on a variable that "never has spaces in it" is the classic: it has never had one yet, and the check exists for the day it does. The retires typo in §20.2 was an SC2154 that looked like noise.
  2. Can the code be written so the finding cannot arise, and is that clearer? An unquoted $flags that is meant to split into several options is SC2086, and the honest fix is an array (§6): flags=(-l -a) and ls "${flags[@]}" is both quiet and correct with values that contain spaces. An SC2016 on a long awk program can go away by moving the program into a file and calling awk -f. Rewriting is better than suppressing whenever the result is no harder to read.
  3. If not, is the premise really wrong? The wiki page for each check has a section on when the warning does not apply. envsubst '$USER $HOME', a SQL text with a $1 placeholder and an unquoted expansion that must split are the three that recur, and §20.2 showed the first two. That is when a directive is honest.

A false positive is worth reporting to the ShellCheck project when the tool has a model of the construct and gets it wrong, but it is a bug in a specific version, and the script has to pass its gate today. That is what the next tools are for.

Suppressing a check: narrowly, with a reason

Suppressing a check means writing # shellcheck disable=SCnnnn (§20.3). The rules that keep suppression from eroding the tool are these:

  • Put it on the line, not on the file. A directive before a single command covers that command. The same directive at the top of the file covers every present and future instance of the pattern. Use the wide form only for a decision that is genuinely about the file, such as a settings file every variable of which is read by the script that sources it.
  • Name the code and the reason. # shellcheck disable=SC2086 # $flags is a space-separated list by design. The reason is what a reviewer weighs; without it the only question left is whether the author was lazy.
  • Never disable an error-level check to get a clean run. SC2148 (no shebang) is fixed with a directive that supplies the dialect (§20.3), not one that hides the message; an error-level finding that has to be suppressed is a script the tool cannot analyse, and the rest of its report is unreliable.

A suppression also outlives its cause, and the tool does nothing about it:

cat > stale.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
# shellcheck disable=SC2086
echo "$1"
EOF
shellcheck stale.sh; echo "exit $? (a directive that no longer matches anything is never reported)"

exit 0 (a directive that no longer matches anything is never reported)

stale.sh quotes its variable, so there is nothing for SC2086 to say, and the directive sitting above it still disables the check for the next command anyone adds there. ShellCheck 0.11 does not report a directive that no longer matches anything. Cleaning them up is a job for a person or a script, and the last subsection here is that script.

Project settings: .shellcheckrc, --exclude and --include

Options that belong to a whole project, not a file, go in a .shellcheckrc — plain key=value lines, the directive syntax without the comment marker. ShellCheck looks for one in the directory of each file it checks and in every directory above it, so a .shellcheckrc at the repository root applies to the whole tree:

mkdir -p project/bin
cat > project/.shellcheckrc <<'EOF'
shell=bash
disable=SC2086
EOF
cat > project/bin/run <<'EOF'
list=(a b)
echo $list
echo ${list[@]}
EOF
cp project/bin/run outside
echo "== no rc file in reach";  shellcheck --format=gcc outside
echo "== the rc file is found from the script's directory upward";  shellcheck --format=gcc project/bin/run
echo "== --norc";  shellcheck --norc --format=gcc project/bin/run
mkdir home
printf 'shell=bash\n' > home/.shellcheckrc
echo "== a .shellcheckrc in the home directory applies to every script"
HOME=$PWD/home shellcheck --format=gcc outside

== no rc file in reach
outside:1:1: error: Tips depend on target shell and yours is unknown. Add a shebang or a 'shell' directive. [SC2148]
outside:2:6: warning: Expanding an array without an index only gives the first element. [SC2128]
outside:2:6: note: Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting. [SC2086]
outside:3:6: error: Double quote array expansions to avoid re-splitting elements. [SC2068]
== the rc file is found from the script's directory upward
project/bin/run:2:6: warning: Expanding an array without an index only gives the first element. [SC2128]
project/bin/run:3:6: error: Double quote array expansions to avoid re-splitting elements. [SC2068]
== --norc
project/bin/run:1:1: error: Tips depend on target shell and yours is unknown. Add a shebang or a 'shell' directive. [SC2148]
project/bin/run:2:6: warning: Expanding an array without an index only gives the first element. [SC2128]
project/bin/run:2:6: note: Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting. [SC2086]
project/bin/run:3:6: error: Double quote array expansions to avoid re-splitting elements. [SC2068]
== a .shellcheckrc in the home directory applies to every script
outside:2:6: warning: Expanding an array without an index only gives the first element. [SC2128]
outside:2:6: note: Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting. [SC2086]
outside:3:6: error: Double quote array expansions to avoid re-splitting elements. [SC2068]

The first run had no rc file in reach, and outside, which has no shebang, drew SC2148, SC2128 and SC2086 and the array-quoting error SC2068. The second run, on the same content but in a directory with a .shellcheckrc above it, had shell=bash (so no SC2148) and disable=SC2086 (so no SC2086), and the SC2128 and SC2068 remained. --norc ignored the file and brought all four back. A .shellcheckrc in the home directory is read too, and applied shell=bash to a file far from any project. That is convenient and worth knowing about: a script that is clean on your machine because of a personal rc file is not clean in CI, so a project sets what it needs in its own .shellcheckrc and CI runs with it.

The command line has the same controls. --exclude=SC2086,SC2164 (-e) removes checks for one run, and its opposite, --include (-i), restricts a run to only the codes listed:

cat > flags.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
cd /tmp
echo $1
EOF
shellcheck --format=gcc flags.sh
echo "== --exclude=SC2086"; shellcheck --format=gcc --exclude=SC2086 flags.sh
echo "== -e SC2086,SC2164"; shellcheck --format=gcc -e SC2086,SC2164 flags.sh; echo "exit $?"

flags.sh:2:1: warning: Use 'cd ... || exit' or 'cd ... || return' in case cd fails. [SC2164]
flags.sh:3:6: note: Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting. [SC2086]
== --exclude=SC2086
flags.sh:2:1: warning: Use 'cd ... || exit' or 'cd ... || return' in case cd fails. [SC2164]
== -e SC2086,SC2164
exit 0

The first run reported both findings, --exclude=SC2086 left the SC2164 warning, and excluding both exited 0. Exclusion is the blunt instrument: it removes a check for every file in the run.

cat > strict.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
list=(a b)
echo ${list[@]}
cd /tmp
echo $1
EOF
echo "== everything at the default severity"; shellcheck --format=gcc strict.sh
echo "== --include: only these checks";       shellcheck --format=gcc --include=SC2068 strict.sh
echo "== --include, and the exit status";     shellcheck --include=SC2164 strict.sh > /dev/null; echo "exit $?"
echo "== an --include for a check that does not fire"; shellcheck --include=SC2016 strict.sh; echo "exit $?"

== everything at the default severity
strict.sh:3:6: error: Double quote array expansions to avoid re-splitting elements. [SC2068]
strict.sh:4:1: warning: Use 'cd ... || exit' or 'cd ... || return' in case cd fails. [SC2164]
strict.sh:5:6: note: Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting. [SC2086]
== --include: only these checks
strict.sh:3:6: error: Double quote array expansions to avoid re-splitting elements. [SC2068]
== --include, and the exit status
exit 1
== an --include for a check that does not fire
exit 0

The --include form is how to make one check a hard gate without adopting a whole severity level. §6.5 said SC2068, the unquoted ${list[@]}, is worth treating as an error: ShellCheck 0.11 already reports it at the error level, as the first block shows, so any gate at --severity=error catches it.
