A check that is only info, like SC2086, needs one of two things: a gate at --severity=info (every finding in the tree must be fixed or suppressed), or, for a project not ready for that, a second command that runs --include=SC2086 on the files that have been cleaned. shellcheck --include=SC2164 above exited 1 because that one check fired, and --include=SC2016 exited 0 because it did not.

Auditing the suppressions

A suppression without a reason is a promise nobody can check, so check it mechanically. This script fails on any directive that lacks the # reason that §20.4's rules require, and it is short enough to run in the same gate as ShellCheck:

mkdir src
cat > audit-directives.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Fail on any "shellcheck disable" that gives no reason.
status=0
while IFS= read -r line; do
  [[ $line == *'shellcheck disable='* ]] || continue
  if [[ $line != *'  # '?* ]]; then
    echo "no reason: $line" >&2
    status=1
  fi
done < <(grep -rn --include='*.sh' '^ *# *shellcheck disable=' . || true)
exit "$status"
EOF
cat > src/good.sh <<'EOF'
# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # the word list is meant to split
EOF
cat > src/bad.sh <<'EOF'
# shellcheck disable=SC2086
EOF
cd src && bash ../audit-directives.sh; echo "exit $?"

no reason: ./bad.sh:1:# shellcheck disable=SC2086
exit 1

good.sh carries a reason and passes; bad.sh has a bare directive and is reported by file and line, with status 1. The grep pattern '^ *# *shellcheck disable=' matches only lines that begin with the directive, so the audit script's own mentions of the words in its test and in its pattern are not counted. Extend the loop to print the code list and reason together and the output is a reviewable inventory of every exception the project has made.

20.5 Optional Checks

Some checks are off by default because they are opinions, not defects. Reasonable people disagree about whether every variable reference should have braces, and a linter that reported hundreds of style choices on a first run would be uninstalled. ShellCheck keeps these as optional checks, and ships a list:

shellcheck --list-optional | grep '^name:' | cut -d: -f2 | tr -d ' '

add-default-case
avoid-negated-conditions
avoid-nullary-conditions
check-extra-masked-returns
check-set-e-suppressed
check-unassigned-uppercase
deprecate-which
quote-safe-variables
require-double-brackets
require-variable-braces
useless-use-of-cat

That is the whole list for 0.11.0: eleven checks, each of which shellcheck --list-optional documents with an example and a fix. What each does, and the code it reports:

  • quote-safe-variables (SC2248): quote even a variable ShellCheck can prove holds nothing special, like v=hello; echo $v.
  • require-variable-braces (SC2250): write ${v} rather than $v, everywhere.
  • require-double-brackets (SC2292): prefer [[ ]] to [ ] in a bash script.
  • avoid-nullary-conditions (SC2244): write [ -n "$v" ] rather than [ "$v" ].
  • avoid-negated-conditions (SC2335): write -ne rather than ! … -eq.
  • add-default-case (SC2249): a case should end with a *) arm, even if it only fails.
  • deprecate-which (SC2230): use command -v, not which (§19.13).
  • useless-use-of-cat (SC2002): cat file | cmd should be cmd < file.
  • check-unassigned-uppercase (SC2154 for uppercase names): the default check skips names in capitals on the assumption that they come from the environment.
  • check-extra-masked-returns (SC2312): a command whose status is lost inside a $( ) in an argument.
  • check-set-e-suppressed (SC2310, SC2311): a function called in a position where set -e is switched off.

There are four ways to switch them on: --enable=name (or -o name) on the command line, --enable=all for every one, a # shellcheck enable=name directive, and enable=name in a .shellcheckrc:

cat > opt.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
v=hello
echo $v
[ $v ]
which ls
case $v in hello) echo hi ;; esac
EOF
echo "== default";                         shellcheck --format=gcc opt.sh; echo "exit $?"
echo "== --enable=all";                    shellcheck --format=gcc --enable=all opt.sh
echo "== --enable=require-variable-braces"; shellcheck --format=gcc --enable=require-variable-braces opt.sh

== default
exit 0
== --enable=all
opt.sh:3:6: note: Prefer double quoting even when variables don't contain special characters. [SC2248]
opt.sh:3:6: note: Prefer putting braces around variable references even when not strictly required. [SC2250]
opt.sh:4:1: note: Prefer [[ ]] over [ ] for tests in Bash/Ksh/Busybox. [SC2292]
opt.sh:4:3: note: Prefer explicit -n to check non-empty string (or use =/-ne to check boolean/integer). [SC2244]
opt.sh:4:3: note: Prefer double quoting even when variables don't contain special characters. [SC2248]
opt.sh:4:3: note: Prefer putting braces around variable references even when not strictly required. [SC2250]
opt.sh:5:1: note: 'which' is non-standard. Use builtin 'command -v' instead. [SC2230]
opt.sh:6:1: note: Consider adding a default *) case, even if it just exits with error. [SC2249]
opt.sh:6:6: note: Prefer putting braces around variable references even when not strictly required. [SC2250]
== --enable=require-variable-braces
opt.sh:3:6: note: Prefer putting braces around variable references even when not strictly required. [SC2250]
opt.sh:4:3: note: Prefer putting braces around variable references even when not strictly required. [SC2250]
opt.sh:6:6: note: Prefer putting braces around variable references even when not strictly required. [SC2250]

The script has one variable, v=hello, and the default run found nothing (exit 0). With everything on, the same six lines produced nine findings, and with only require-variable-braces — the check the next paragraph discusses — the three places a variable is expanded without braces. The enable= directive is scoped exactly as disable= is, so # shellcheck enable=quote-safe-variables in a file turns the check on for that file:

cat > opt2.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
# shellcheck enable=quote-safe-variables
v=hello
echo $v
EOF
shellcheck --format=gcc opt2.sh

opt2.sh:4:6: note: Prefer double quoting even when variables don't contain special characters. [SC2248]

require-variable-braces and quote-safe-variables: two that divide teams

Two of the eleven cause disagreement. require-variable-braces asks for ${name} everywhere. The Google Shell Style Guide asks for braces on every variable except the single-character specials and the positional parameters, and this check enforces the first half of that (§5.1); this course's own rule is to brace when the syntax needs it and not otherwise. Both are defensible, and a project should choose one and let the tool enforce it, because an inconsistent style is the thing a reviewer ends up correcting by hand. quote-safe-variables asks for "$v" even when v was just assigned a constant. That is not a bug today; it is a bug the day someone changes the assignment to a value containing a space, and the cost of the extra quotes is nothing. A project that wants "quote everything" as a rule turns it on and never thinks about SC2086 again.

The two checks that pay for themselves in any script that uses set -e are the last two:

cat > more.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
set -e
get_dir() { echo /tmp; }
check() { cp a b; rm c; }
n=3
[ ! "$n" -eq 1 ]
cp "$(get_dir)/data" backup
cat file.txt | grep word
echo "$UNSET_UPPER"
if check; then echo ok; fi
EOF
shellcheck --format=gcc more.sh; echo "== default exit: $?"
echo "== --enable=all"
shellcheck --format=gcc --enable=all more.sh

== default exit: 0
== --enable=all
more.sh:6:1: note: Prefer [[ ]] over [ ] for tests in Bash/Ksh/Busybox. [SC2292]
more.sh:6:3: note: Use a -ne b instead of ! a -eq b. [SC2335]
more.sh:6:6: note: Prefer putting braces around variable references even when not strictly required. [SC2250]
more.sh:7:7: note: Bash implicitly disabled set -e for this function invocation because it's inside a command substitution. Add set -e; before it or enable inherit_errexit. [SC2311]
more.sh:7:7: note: Consider invoking this command separately to avoid masking its return value (or use '|| true' to ignore). [SC2312]
more.sh:8:1: note: Consider invoking this command separately to avoid masking its return value (or use '|| true' to ignore). [SC2312]
more.sh:8:5: note: Useless cat. Consider 'cmd < file | ..' or 'cmd file | ..' instead. [SC2002]
more.sh:9:7: warning: UNSET_UPPER is referenced but not assigned. [SC2154]
more.sh:9:7: note: Prefer putting braces around variable references even when not strictly required. [SC2250]
more.sh:10:4: note: This function is invoked in an 'if' condition so set -e will be disabled. Invoke separately if failures should cause the script to exit. [SC2310]

check-set-e-suppressed is §11.5's trap made visible. SC2310 says the function check, called as an if condition on line 10, runs with set -e disabled, so the cp failing inside it will not stop the script; SC2311 says the same about a function called inside $( ) on line 7. SC2312 says the cp "$(get_dir)/data" on line 7 and the cat file.txt | grep pipeline on line 8 lose the status of their first command. None of these is a wrong program; each is a place where set -e does not do what the reader of set -e assumes, which is the argument for having them in a project that relies on it.

20.6 ShellCheck as a Gate

A linter that people run when they remember to is a suggestion. ShellCheck as a gate means the change cannot go in until the tool is satisfied: the exit status of a command decides whether a commit is made, a pull request is mergeable, a release is cut. The tool's exit status is the interface, and the work is in choosing what the gate covers and where it runs.

shellcheck --severity and the exit status

cat > clean.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
echo "$1"
EOF
printf '#!/bin/bash\ncd /tmp\n' > warns.sh
printf '#!/bin/bash\nif then\n' > broken.sh
shellcheck clean.sh;                          echo "clean file:          $?"
shellcheck warns.sh > /dev/null;              echo "a warning:          $?"
shellcheck --severity=error warns.sh;         echo "warning, gated at error: $?"
shellcheck broken.sh > /dev/null;             echo "a syntax error:     $?"
shellcheck no-such-file.sh 2> /dev/null;      echo "a file it cannot read: $?"
shellcheck --severity=fatal clean.sh 2> /dev/null; echo "a bad option:      $?"

clean file:          0
a warning:          1
warning, gated at error: 0
a syntax error:     1
a file it cannot read: 2
a bad option:      4

ShellCheck exits 0 when it found nothing, 1 when it found something at or above the threshold, 2 when it could not read a file, and 4 when the command line was wrong. A syntax error in the script is a finding, so it exits 1. The threshold is shellcheck --severity, and §20.1 showed its effect: --severity=warning on a script that has only info findings exits 0. A gate therefore has three settings to choose deliberately:

  • The severity. For a new project, --severity=info (everything but style) costs nothing and catches SC2086. For an existing one, start at --severity=warning, clear the backlog, and lower it.
  • The file list. Every file in the repository that is a shell script — not just the ones ending in .sh (see below).
  • The ShellCheck version. New versions add checks and change levels, so a CI run that installs "the latest" fails on a day nobody touched the code. Pin the version (§20.6 below, and §20.11).

ShellCheck as a gate: linting a whole tree

Shell scripts do not always end in .sh. A tool in bin/ is called deploy, a git hook has no extension at all, and a library is .sh or .bash. A gate that lists files with find -name '*.sh' checks a fraction of a project. This script asks git for the tracked files and picks the shell ones by extension or by their shebang:

mkdir project && cd project
git init -q -b main
mkdir bin lib
cat > bin/deploy <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "$1"
EOF
printf '#!/bin/sh\ncd /tmp\n'                   > bin/cleanup
cat > lib/util.sh <<'EOF'
greet() { echo "hi $1"; }
EOF
printf '#!/usr/bin/env python3\nprint(1)\n'     > bin/report
printf 'notes, not a script\n'                  > NOTES.md
printf 'shell=bash\n'                           > .shellcheckrc
chmod +x bin/*
cat > lint.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Lint every tracked file that is a shell script, by extension or by shebang.
set -euo pipefail

is_shell() {
  case $1 in *.sh | *.bash) return 0 ;; esac
  local first
  IFS= read -r first < "$1" || return 1
  [[ $first =~ ^'#!'.*(ba|da|k)?sh([[:space:]]|$) ]]
}

status=0
while IFS= read -r -d '' file; do
  is_shell "$file" || continue
  echo "lint $file"
  shellcheck -x --severity=warning --format=gcc -- "$file" || status=1
done < <(git ls-files -z)
exit "$status"
EOF
git add .
bash lint.sh; echo "exit $?"

lint bin/cleanup
bin/cleanup:2:1: warning: Use 'cd ... || exit' or 'cd ... || return' in case cd fails. [SC2164]
lint bin/deploy
lint lib/util.sh
lint lint.sh
exit 1

Four files were checked, and bin/report (Python) and NOTES.md were skipped, because their first lines are not a shell shebang. bin/cleanup has a #!/bin/sh line and an unguarded cd, and the gate reported SC2164 for it and returned 1, which is the whole job. lib/util.sh has no shebang at all: the .shellcheckrc at the root supplied shell=bash (§20.4), or it would have drawn SC2148. lint.sh was checked too — a project's tools are scripts, and a gate that skips them is exempting the part most likely to be changed in a hurry. Reading the first line with read in the shell keeps it to one process per file; git ls-files -z with read -d '' is the NUL-safe loop of §14.9, and -x lets each script's source lines resolve.

A pre-commit hook

Local enforcement catches a defect before it is in the history. A git hook is an executable file in .git/hooks/; pre-commit runs before a commit is made and a non-zero exit stops it:

git init -q -b main repo && cd repo
git config user.name "Test User"; git config user.email "test@example.com"
cat > .git/hooks/pre-commit <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Check the staged version of each shell script; refuse the commit on any finding.
status=0
while IFS= read -r -d '' file; do
  case $file in *.sh) ;; *) continue ;; esac
  git show ":$file" | shellcheck --severity=warning --format=gcc --shell=bash - || status=1
done < <(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM -z)
exit "$status"
EOF
chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit
printf '#!/bin/bash\ncd /tmp\n' > job.sh
git add job.sh
git commit -q -m "add job"; echo "commit exit: $?"
git rev-parse --verify --quiet HEAD > /dev/null || echo "no commit was made"
printf '#!/bin/bash\ncd /tmp || exit\n' > job.sh
git add job.sh
git commit -q -m "add job"; echo "commit exit: $?"
git log --format=%s

-:2:1: warning: Use 'cd ... || exit' or 'cd ... || return' in case cd fails. [SC2164]
commit exit: 1
no commit was made
commit exit: 0
add job

The first commit was refused: the hook read the staged version of job.sh with git show ":$file" (the index, not the working tree, so a fix that is unstaged does not pass), ShellCheck reported SC2164 for -, its name for standard input, and the hook's status 1 aborted the commit, leaving no history. The second commit, with cd /tmp || exit, went through. A hook is a courtesy, not a control: it lives in .git/, which is not versioned, and anyone can skip it with git commit --no-verify. That is why it is the fast local check and the CI job is the enforcement.

ShellCheck in CI: make check

ShellCheck in CI should be as small as possible, because the less a CI configuration knows, the fewer places there are for it to disagree with a developer's machine. The way to arrange that is to put the whole check in one command that lives in the repository and run that command in both places. A Makefile is the traditional home:

mkdir -p bin test
cat > bin/greet <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "hello, ${1:?name required}"
EOF
chmod +x bin/greet
cat > test/greet.bats <<'EOF'
@test "greets" {
  run bin/greet grace
  [ "$output" = "hello, grace" ]
}
EOF
cat > Makefile <<'EOF'
SCRIPTS := bin/greet

.PHONY: lint test check
lint:
	shellcheck -x --severity=warning $(SCRIPTS)
test:
	bats test
check: lint test
EOF
make check; echo "make exit: $?"

shellcheck -x --severity=warning bin/greet
bats test
1..1
ok 1 greets
make exit: 0

make check linted the script and then ran the bats suite (§20.8), and both passed. The recipe lines begin with a tab, as make requires, and the two targets are .PHONY because they name actions, not files. The point of the Makefile is that the CI system's own file can then do nothing but install the tools at pinned versions and run make check, so that "passes locally" and "passes in CI" are the same statement; §20.11 gives that file, and the pinning rule that goes with it. The linter's version matters more than it seems: new versions add checks and change levels, so a CI run that installs whatever is newest fails on a day nobody touched the code.

20.7 Making a Script Testable

Static analysis needs nothing from the script. A test needs a great deal: it has to be able to load the code without running it, call one piece of it with chosen input, look at what came out, and do all of that without disturbing the next test. Most shell scripts as first written give none of that, and the reason is structural, not a shortage of a framework. This subsection is the structure; the frameworks come after it.

Unit testing a shell script: what a unit is

Unit testing a shell script has two natural levels, and a script needs both. The outer level treats the whole script as a black box: run it with arguments and input in a temporary directory, and check three things — its exit status, what it wrote to standard output and to standard error, and what it left on disk. Nothing about the script has to change for this, and it is the level at which a test suite starts. The inner level treats each function as a unit: source the file, call slugify "Two Words", compare the result. It is faster, it pins a failure to a function, and it is possible only when the file is written so that loading it runs nothing.

The unit that matters is the behaviour at a boundary. A function's boundary is its arguments, the global variables it reads, its standard output and its return status; a script's is its command line, its environment, its files and its three streams. A test that reaches past a boundary — reading a variable a function happens to use internally — breaks when the function is refactored, which is the moment tests are supposed to help. Writing to standard output and returning a status, as §9.5 and §9.6 recommended for functions, is what makes a function testable at all: a function that only sets a global and prints nothing can be tested only by reading the global.

The main guard: what a test needs from a script

The first requirement is that loading the file must not run it. §9.14 develops the main guard that arranges this, if [[ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} == "$0" ]]; then main "$@"; fi, and here is what goes wrong without one:

cat > rot13.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
rot13() { printf '%s' "$1" | tr 'A-Za-z' 'N-ZA-Mn-za-m'; }
echo "$(rot13 "$1")"
exit 0
EOF
echo "== run it";      bash rot13.sh hello
echo "== source it, then call the function"
bash -c 'source ./rot13.sh hello; echo "after source: $(rot13 uryyb)"'
echo "(the second command printed nothing: exit ended the shell that sourced the script)"

== run it
uryyb
== source it, then call the function
uryyb
(the second command printed nothing: exit ended the shell that sourced the script)

Run as a script, rot13.sh printed uryyb. Sourced, it printed uryyb again — its top-level echo ran, using the hello that the test had passed as an argument for no reason but to call the function — and then exit 0 ran in the shell that had sourced it, so after source: never appeared and the calling shell was gone. A test harness written in bash would have ended at that line and reported nothing. A file meant to be loaded therefore has no top-level exit, no top-level read and no top-level work at all: its statements are definitions, and everything else is in main.

The guard is a test on how the file was started, and §9.14's (return 0 2>/dev/null) variant works where the BASH_SOURCE comparison does not (bash < file). Neither is portable to every shell, and the difference matters when the code under test is meant for sh:

cat > guard.sh <<'EOF'
main() { echo "main ran"; }
# (return 0) succeeds only where `return` is legal: in a sourced file, or inside a function
if (return 0 2> /dev/null); then
  echo "sourced: defining functions only"
else
  main "$@"
fi
EOF
cat > guard-posix.sh <<'EOF'
main() { echo "main ran"; }
case ${0##*/} in
  guard-posix.sh) main "$@" ;;
  *) echo "sourced: defining functions only" ;;
esac
EOF
echo "== (return 0) guard"
printf 'bash run:    '; bash guard.sh
printf 'bash source: '; bash -c '. ./guard.sh'
printf 'dash run:    '; dash guard.sh
printf 'dash source: '; dash -c '. ./guard.sh'
echo "== \$0 guard"
printf 'bash run:    '; bash guard-posix.sh
printf 'bash source: '; bash -c '. ./guard-posix.sh'
printf 'dash run:    '; dash guard-posix.sh
printf 'dash source: '; dash -c '. ./guard-posix.sh'

== (return 0) guard
bash run:    main ran
bash source: sourced: defining functions only
dash run:    sourced: defining functions only
dash source: sourced: defining functions only
== $0 guard
bash run:    main ran
bash source: sourced: defining functions only
dash run:    main ran
dash source: sourced: defining functions only

Under bash both forms are right. Under dash, the (return 0) guard reported "sourced" when the file was run: dash accepts a return at the top level of a script it is running, so the test succeeds in the wrong place, and main would never run. The portable guard has to be a comparison of $0 with the file's own name, case ${0##*/} in guard-posix.sh) main "$@" ;; esac, which was right in all four cases. It depends on the file keeping its name, which is the price of running a guard in a shell that has no BASH_SOURCE.

Sourcing a script for test: what it must not do

Sourcing a script for test runs its top-level statements in the test's own shell, and everything they change is changed there. Three things leak, and each was in this file:

cat > strict.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
cd /
trap 'echo "the trap set by strict.sh ran"' EXIT
counter=0
bump() { counter=$((counter + 1)); }
EOF
cat > harness.sh <<'EOF'
here=$PWD
[[ $- == *e* ]] && echo "before: errexit is on" || echo "before: errexit is off"
source ./strict.sh
[[ $- == *e* ]] && echo "after:  errexit is on" || echo "after:  errexit is off"
[[ $PWD == "$here" ]] && echo "after:  same directory" || echo "after:  the directory changed to $PWD"
false
echo "the harness carries on after a failed check"
EOF
bash harness.sh
echo "exit $?"

before: errexit is off
after:  errexit is on
after:  the directory changed to /
the trap set by strict.sh ran
exit 1

strict.sh began as a good script: set -euo pipefail, a cd / so its paths were absolute, and an EXIT trap. Sourced, the options went into the harness (errexit is off before, on after), the current directory changed to /, and a trap the harness did not ask for was installed on the harness's exit. Then the test's false — an assertion that failed on purpose — ended the harness under the errexit the script had switched on, and the trap ran as it died. Each of those is right in a script and wrong in a library. The rule for a file that will be sourced: at its top level it defines functions and sets nothing global — no set -e, no cd, no trap, no variable that anything else reads. Options go inside main, where they run only when the file is run; a function that needs a different directory does ( cd "$dir" && … ) in a subshell or cd - afterwards.

Testing a function in isolation

Testing a function in isolation means calling it so that nothing from a previous call can influence it, and nothing it does can reach the next:

cat > counter.sh <<'EOF'
count=0
bump() { count=$((count + 1)); echo "$count"; }
EOF
source ./counter.sh
echo "== two checks in the same shell"
bump; bump
echo "count is now $count"
echo "== each check in its own subshell"
( bump ); ( bump )
echo "count is still $count"

== two checks in the same shell
1
2
count is now 2
== each check in its own subshell
3
3
count is still 2

In the same shell the two calls counted 1 then 2 and left count at 2: the function's state is in a global, and a test suite that runs its checks in one shell has checks that depend on their order. In a subshell — ( bump ) — each call started from the parent's value of 2, counted up to 3, and the parent's count was unchanged, because a subshell's assignments die with it (§16). That is the isolation a test needs, and it is what every framework arranges for you: bats runs each test in its own process and shunit2 runs each test after a fresh setUp. A function that is hard to isolate is telling you something about its design: one that reads $config_file set three calls ago should take it as an argument, and one that runs cd should not.

A test with no framework

Everything a framework does can be done in ten lines, and doing it once shows what the frameworks are for:

cat > slug.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
slugify() {
  local s=${1,,}
  s=${s//[^a-z0-9]/-}
  printf '%s\n' "$s"
}
[[ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} == "$0" ]] && slugify "$@"
EOF
cat > test-slug.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
source ./slug.sh
failures=0
check() {   # check DESCRIPTION EXPECTED ACTUAL
  if [[ $2 == "$3" ]]; then
    echo "ok   $1"
  else
    echo "FAIL $1: expected '$2', got '$3'"
    failures=$((failures + 1))
  fi
}
check "lowercases"        "hello"      "$(slugify Hello)"
check "spaces to dashes"  "two-words"  "$(slugify 'Two Words')"
check "runs of junk"      "a-b"        "$(slugify 'A !! B')"
exit "$((failures > 0))"
EOF
bash test-slug.sh; echo "exit $?"

ok   lowercases
ok   spaces to dashes
FAIL runs of junk: expected 'a-b', got 'a----b'
exit 1

The harness sourced the file under test, defined check to compare and count, ran three checks, and exited with a status that says whether any failed. It worked, and found a real defect: slugify 'A !! B' returned a----b, because each of the four non-alphanumeric characters became its own dash, while the intended result is one. What it does not do is what a suite of forty tests needs: it cannot run a single test by name, cannot give each test a clean directory, has no setup or teardown and no report of which of forty checks failed and where. Those are the gaps bats fills, and they are the next section.

20.8 bats-core: a Test Framework for Shell

bats and bats-core: installing and running

bats, the Bash Automated Testing System, is the test framework for shell scripts that most projects choose, and bats-core is its maintained continuation — the project on GitHub under the bats-core organisation, and the one packaged as bats-core in Homebrew and as bats in most Linux distributions. The command it installs is bats. The version measured here is 1.14.0; the distribution packages are often older, which matters for the features below that name a minimum version.

A test file ends in .bats and looks like a shell script with a special block:

cat > greet.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
greet() { printf 'hello, %s\n' "${1:?name required}"; }

main() {
  case ${1-} in
    -h) echo "usage: greet NAME"; return 0 ;;
    '') echo "greet: missing name" >&2; return 2 ;;
  esac
  greet "$1"
}

if [[ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} == "$0" ]]; then
  main "$@"
fi
EOF
chmod +x greet.sh
cat > greet.bats <<'EOF'
@test "greets by name" {
  run ./greet.sh grace
  [ "$status" -eq 0 ]
  [ "$output" = "hello, grace" ]
}

@test "no argument is a usage error" {
  run ./greet.sh
  [ "$status" -eq 2 ]
  [ "$output" = "greet: missing name" ]
}

@test "capitalises the name" {
  run ./greet.sh ada
  [ "$output" = "hello, Ada" ]
}

@test "the help flag is not written yet" {
  skip "-h is not tested yet"
  run ./greet.sh -h
}
EOF
bats greet.bats; echo "exit $?"

1..4
ok 1 greets by name
ok 2 no argument is a usage error
not ok 3 capitalises the name
# (in test file greet.bats, line 15)
#   `[ "$output" = "hello, Ada" ]' failed
ok 4 the help flag is not written yet # skip -h is not tested yet
exit 1

Four tests: two passed, one failed and one was skipped, and bats exited 1 because a test failed. The report is TAP, the Test Anything Protocol: a plan line 1..4 first, then one line per test, ok or not ok with the test's number and description. For a failing test bats adds comment lines beginning #: the file, the line number, and the command that failed — [ "$output" = "hello, Ada" ] on line 15, which is the assertion, not the run before it. A skip builtin marks a test as not run, with a reason after # skip. The TAP form is what bats prints when standard output is not a terminal; on a terminal the default is a coloured pretty formatter, and --formatter (-F) picks tap, tap13, junit or pretty explicitly — junit is the one CI systems that draw test-result tables consume.

The @test block

@test "description" { … } is not bash syntax. bats reads the file first and rewrites each block into a function, so the description is an ordinary string and may contain anything; the body is bash. Each test runs in its own process, and inside it the shell is set up so that the first command to return non-zero ends the test, and the test fails at that line. That is why the tests above are just [ … ] commands one after another: a false [ is a failed test, with no assert function needed. The rule has the same holes as set -e (§11.3), and one that surprises: a command on the left of && or ||, or in an if, does not fail the test, which is why bats tests avoid [ … ] && … chains. The third test of bats-run-subshell, below, shows the simple case: a bare false fails the test at its own line.

The run helper: the status variable and the lines array

The tests above called the script with run. The run helper executes a command in a subshell and records what happened instead of letting a failure end the test. After it, three variables describe the run: $status is the exit status (the status variable), $output is everything the command wrote, standard output and standard error together, with the trailing newline removed, and ${lines[@]} is $output split into lines (the lines array), so ${lines[0]} is the first. run itself always succeeds, which is what lets a test check a command that is expected to fail.

mkdir -p src test
cat > src/wc-words <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: wc-words FILE...
set -euo pipefail
for f in "$@"; do
  [[ -r $f ]] || { echo "wc-words: cannot read $f" >&2; exit 1; }
  printf '%s %s\n' "$(tr -s '[:space:]' '\n' < "$f" | grep -c .)" "$f"
done
EOF
chmod +x src/wc-words
cat > test/wc-words.bats <<'EOF'
bats_require_minimum_version 1.5.0

setup() {
  cd "$BATS_TEST_TMPDIR"
  printf 'one two three\n' > a.txt
  printf 'four five\nsix\n' > b.txt
  PATH="$BATS_TEST_DIRNAME/../src:$PATH"
}

@test "counts one file" {
  run wc-words a.txt
  [ "$status" -eq 0 ]
  [ "$output" = "3 a.txt" ]
}

@test "prints one line per file" {
  run wc-words a.txt b.txt
  [ "${#lines[@]}" -eq 2 ]
  [ "${lines[0]}" = "3 a.txt" ]
  [ "${lines[1]}" = "3 b.txt" ]
}

@test "a missing file is an error on stderr" {
  run --separate-stderr wc-words nope.txt
  [ "$status" -eq 1 ]
  [ -z "$output" ]
  [ "$stderr" = "wc-words: cannot read nope.txt" ]
}

@test "a clean run writes nothing to stderr" {
  run --separate-stderr wc-words a.txt
  [ "$status" -eq 0 ]
  [ -z "$stderr" ]
}

@test "run ! expects a failure" {
  run ! wc-words nope.txt
}

@test "a test can leave files behind" {
  touch leftover.txt
}

@test "the next test starts in a fresh directory" {
  [ ! -e leftover.txt ]
}
EOF
bats test; echo "exit $?"

1..7
ok 1 counts one file
ok 2 prints one line per file
ok 3 a missing file is an error on stderr
ok 4 a clean run writes nothing to stderr
ok 5 run ! expects a failure
ok 6 a test can leave files behind
ok 7 the next test starts in a fresh directory
exit 0

Seven tests, all passing. prints one line per file uses ${#lines[@]} and ${lines[0]}. a missing file is an error on stderr uses run --separate-stderr, which keeps the two streams apart: $output held only standard output (empty here), and $stderr held the message. a clean run writes nothing to stderr is the assertion §5.7 asked for — a test that captures standard error and demands it be empty, which is how a suite treats warnings a function printed and then returned success on. And run ! inverts: the test passes only if the command fails. Its neighbour run -N expects exactly status N:

mkdir -p test
cat > check <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "checking $1"
exit "${2:-0}"
EOF
chmod +x check
cat > test/flags.bats <<'EOF'
@test "run without a flag never fails the test" {
  run ./check x 3
  [ "$status" -eq 3 ]
}

@test "run ! expects any failure" {
  run ! ./check x 3
}

@test "run -3 expects exactly status 3" {
  run -3 ./check x 3
}

@test "run -2 expects status 2, and gets 3" {
  run -2 ./check x 3
}
EOF
echo "== without bats_require_minimum_version"
bats test/flags.bats 2>&1 | grep -m1 '^BW02' | cut -c1-105
echo "== with it"
{ echo 'bats_require_minimum_version 1.5.0'; cat test/flags.bats; } > test/flags-versioned.bats
bats test/flags-versioned.bats

== without bats_require_minimum_version
BW02: Using flags on `run` requires at least BATS_VERSION=1.5.0. Use `bats_require_minimum_version 1.5.0`
== with it
1..4
ok 1 run without a flag never fails the test
ok 2 run ! expects any failure
ok 3 run -3 expects exactly status 3
not ok 4 run -2 expects status 2, and gets 3
# (in test file test/flags-versioned.bats, line 16)
#   `run -2 ./check x 3' failed, expected exit code 2, got 3
# checking x

Without the declaration bats printed a BW02 warning that flags on run need at least 1.5.0. Putting bats_require_minimum_version 1.5.0 at the top of the file is how a test file states what it needs, and it is correct to do so, because an older bats — distribution packages lag the project — would not understand the flags. The last test asked for status 2 and got 3, and the message names both numbers and the command. Note also that the failing test shows the command's output, checking x, which bats collected for the failure report.

run is a subshell

The most confusing thing about run is a consequence of what it is:

cat > subshell.bats <<'EOF'
counter=0
bump() { counter=$((counter + 1)); echo "bumped"; }

@test "run executes the command in a subshell" {
  run bump
  echo "counter after run: $counter"
  [ "$counter" -eq 0 ]
}

@test "a direct call changes the test's variables" {
  bump
  echo "counter after a direct call: $counter"
  [ "$counter" -eq 1 ]
}

@test "and a direct call that fails fails the test at once" {
  false
  echo "never printed"
}
EOF
bats subshell.bats

1..3
ok 1 run executes the command in a subshell
ok 2 a direct call changes the test's variables
not ok 3 and a direct call that fails fails the test at once
# (in test file subshell.bats, line 17)
#   `false' failed

run bump executed the function in a subshell, so counter in the test never changed and the first test's [ "$counter" -eq 0 ] passed. A direct call bump ran in the test's own shell, and the second test's counter is 1. The rule follows: use run for anything whose status or output is the point, and call a function directly when the point is the state it changes. The third test shows the price of a direct call: a failing command with no run fails the test on that line (false' failed), and theecho` after it never ran.

An assert helper

A test file that only uses [ gets a report of the form [ "$output" = "lines: 3" ]' failed — which line, but not what the values were. An assert helper turns that into a message, and it needs no library:

mkdir -p test
cat > test/test_helper.bash <<'EOF'
assert_equal() {
  if [[ $1 != "$2" ]]; then
    {
      echo "expected: $1"
      echo "actual:   $2"
    } >&2
    return 1
  fi
}

assert_output() {
  assert_equal "$1" "$output"
}

assert_success() {
  if [[ $status -ne 0 ]]; then
    echo "expected success, got status $status; output: $output" >&2
    return 1
  fi
}
EOF
cat > test/greet.bats <<'EOF'
setup() {
  load test_helper
}

@test "passes" {
  run echo hello
  assert_success
  assert_output "hello"
}

@test "fails with a message" {
  run echo hello
  assert_output "goodbye"
}

@test "reports a bad status" {
  run bash -c 'echo trouble; exit 4'
  assert_success
}
EOF
bats test/greet.bats

1..3
ok 1 passes
not ok 2 fails with a message
# (from function `assert_equal' in file test/test_helper.bash, line 7,
#  from function `assert_output' in file test/test_helper.bash, line 12,
#  in test file test/greet.bats, line 13)
#   `assert_output "goodbye"' failed
# expected: goodbye
# actual:   hello
not ok 3 reports a bad status
# (from function `assert_success' in file test/test_helper.bash, line 18,
#  in test file test/greet.bats, line 18)
#   `assert_success' failed
# expected success, got status 4; output: trouble

load test_helper sourced test/test_helper.bash, and the three functions in it gave the failing tests a message: the second printed expected: goodbye and actual: hello, the third printed the status and the output. A helper prints its explanation to standard error and returns 1, and the returned status fails the test; bats adds the call chain. Two libraries from the same project supply this ready-made: bats-support and bats-assert, which provide assert_success, assert_failure, assert_output, refute_output, assert_line, refute_line, assert_regex, assert_equal and stderr variants, and print a formatted "output differs" block. They are cloned or vendored into a project (a git submodule is the usual way) and loaded with load. Write the three-line helper yourself until a project's tests need more than that.

The setup function and the teardown function

The setup function runs before every test, in the test's own process, and the teardown function runs after every test, whether it passed or failed. setup_file and teardown_file run once per file:

mkdir -p test
cat > test/helpers.bash <<'EOF'
make_repo() {
  git init -q "$1"
}
EOF
cat > test/files.bats <<'EOF'
setup_file() {
  export SHARED="$BATS_FILE_TMPDIR/shared"
  echo "setup_file: $(basename "$BATS_TEST_FILENAME")" >&3
  mkdir "$SHARED"
}

teardown_file() {
  echo "teardown_file: removing the shared directory" >&3
}

setup() {
  load helpers
  echo "setup for: $BATS_TEST_DESCRIPTION" >&3
}

teardown() {
  echo "teardown for: $BATS_TEST_DESCRIPTION" >&3
}

@test "first" {
  [ -d "$SHARED" ]
  make_repo "$BATS_TEST_TMPDIR/r"
  [ -d "$BATS_TEST_TMPDIR/r/.git" ]
}

@test "second" {
  [ -d "$SHARED" ]
  [ ! -e "$BATS_TEST_TMPDIR/r" ]
}

@test "third fails, and teardown still runs" {
  false
}
EOF
bats test/files.bats

1..3
setup_file: files.bats
setup for: first
teardown for: first
ok 1 first
setup for: second
teardown for: second
ok 2 second
setup for: third fails, and teardown still runs
teardown for: third fails, and teardown still runs
not ok 3 third fails, and teardown still runs
# (in test file test/files.bats, line 32)
#   `false' failed
teardown_file: removing the shared directory

The order is exactly what the output shows: setup_file once, then for each test setup, the test, teardown, and finally teardown_file once. teardown ran for the third test, which failed. That guarantee is the reason to clean up there and not at the end of the test body, which a failing assertion skips. >&3 writes to the terminal directly, because bats captures a test's own standard output; it is how a helper shows something on a passing run. setup calls load helpers, which sourced test/helpers.bash and defined make_repo, and $BATS_TEST_DESCRIPTION holds the current description. Variables exported from setup_file reach every test; a variable set in setup reaches only its test, since each test has its own process.

Test fixtures and a temporary directory per test

Test fixtures are the data and the files a test starts from. A good test builds its own: in setup, write the two-line input file, and know exactly what is in it. bats supplies directories to build them in, and the first tests in bats-run used one:

  • $BATS_TEST_TMPDIR is a temporary directory per test: empty when the test begins, removed when it ends. bats-run's "a test can leave files behind" created a file there and the next test, "starts in a fresh directory", did not see it.
  • $BATS_FILE_TMPDIR lives for the whole file, and is where setup_file puts what all its tests share.
  • $BATS_TEST_DIRNAME is the directory of the test file, which is how a test finds the script under test ($BATS_TEST_DIRNAME/../src) without depending on the current directory.

Larger fixtures — a sample configuration, a saved response — live in a test/fixtures directory in the repository and are copied into $BATS_TEST_TMPDIR by setup, so that a test that modifies one modifies its own copy. A test that writes anywhere else is a test that fails the second time it runs or, worse, corrupts the machine.

Running a subset, and reading a failure

A suite grows, and the useful options are those that run less of it:

mkdir -p test/slow
cat > test/quick.bats <<'EOF'
# bats test_tags=unit
@test "parses a flag" { true; }

# bats test_tags=unit,parser
@test "parses an option" { true; }

@test "fails on purpose" { false; }

@test "never reached with --abort" { true; }
EOF
cat > test/slow/deep.bats <<'EOF'
# bats test_tags=integration
@test "deep test" { true; }
EOF
echo "== --count";                         bats --count test/quick.bats
echo "== --recursive --count";             bats --recursive --count test
echo "== --filter 'parses'";               bats --filter 'parses' test/quick.bats
echo "== --filter-tags parser";            bats --filter-tags parser test/quick.bats
echo "== --filter-tags unit,!parser";      bats --filter-tags 'unit,!parser' test/quick.bats
echo "== --abort";                         bats --abort test/quick.bats

== --count
4
== --recursive --count
5
== --filter 'parses'
1..2
ok 1 parses a flag
ok 2 parses an option
== --filter-tags parser
1..1
ok 1 parses an option
== --filter-tags unit,!parser
1..1
ok 1 parses a flag
== --abort
1..4
ok 1 parses a flag
ok 2 parses an option
not ok 3 fails on purpose
# (in test file test/quick.bats, line 7)
#   `@test "fails on purpose" { false; }' failed
# bats warning: Executed 3 instead of expected 4 tests

--count printed the number of tests without running any: 4 in one file, and 5 with --recursive, which descends into subdirectories. --filter selects by a regular expression on the description, and --filter-tags by tags written above a test in a # bats test_tags= comment; unit,!parser means "tagged unit but not parser". --abort stopped at the first failure — the fourth test never ran, and bats said so in its warning. What a failure shows is worth reading closely:

cat > count.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
printf 'lines: 3\nwords: 12\n'
EOF
chmod +x count.sh
cat > count.bats <<'EOF'
@test "silent failure" {
  run ./count.sh
  [ "$output" = "lines: 3" ]
}

@test "failure that shows the output" {
  run ./count.sh
  echo "output was: $output"
  echo "status was: $status"
  [ "$output" = "lines: 3" ]
}
EOF
bats count.bats
echo "== --print-output-on-failure"
bats --print-output-on-failure count.bats

1..2
not ok 1 silent failure
# (in test file count.bats, line 3)
#   `[ "$output" = "lines: 3" ]' failed
not ok 2 failure that shows the output
# (in test file count.bats, line 10)
#   `[ "$output" = "lines: 3" ]' failed
# output was: lines: 3
# words: 12
# status was: 0
== --print-output-on-failure
1..2
not ok 1 silent failure
# (in test file count.bats, line 3)
#   `[ "$output" = "lines: 3" ]' failed
# Last output:
# lines: 3
# words: 12
not ok 2 failure that shows the output
# (in test file count.bats, line 10)
#   `[ "$output" = "lines: 3" ]' failed
# output was: lines: 3
# words: 12
# status was: 0
# Last output:
# lines: 3
# words: 12

A test that prints nothing gives only the failing line, and the values that mattered are gone. Two ways to see them. Print them in the test: bats shows a failing test's output as # comment lines, and shows nothing for passing tests, so echo "output was: $output" before an assertion costs nothing on a green run. Or run with --print-output-on-failure, which appends the last run's $output to every failure, as the "Last output:" block shows. The second is the better default in CI, where a failure is often read hours later from a log.

20.9 Mocking a Command

Mocking a command: what it is for

A script's tests run in an environment the script did not choose — it may have no network, no mail, no root — and often the behaviour under test depends on something that cannot be produced on demand: a disk at 95%, a date that says December 31st, a service that fails twice before it works. Mocking a command means putting a stand-in where the real one would be, one that prints what the test says and records that it was called. It has three purposes, and each is a different kind of test. It makes a test fast and safe: no email is sent, nothing is deleted. It makes a test deterministic: date always says the same. And it makes a failure path reachable: the df that fails is a branch no real system will take when asked.

Stubbing PATH

A shell script finds every external command by searching PATH in order, so the stand-in only has to be an executable of the same name in a directory that comes first. That is stubbing PATH, and it needs no library:

cat > alert.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Mail the admin when a filesystem is nearly full.
threshold=${THRESHOLD:-90}

usage_percent() { df -P "$1" | awk 'NR == 2 { gsub("%", "", $5); print $5 }'; }

check_disk() {
  local mount=$1 pct
  pct=$(usage_percent "$mount") || return 3
  if (( pct >= threshold )); then
    mail -s "disk $mount at ${pct}%" admin@example.com <<< "usage is ${pct}%"
    return 1
  fi
}

if [[ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} == "$0" ]]; then
  check_disk "${1:-/}"
fi
EOF
mkdir stubs
cat > stubs/df <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
echo "df $*" >> "$STUB_LOG"
printf 'Filesystem 1024-blocks Used Available Capacity Mounted on\n'
printf '/dev/sda1 1000 %s %s %s%% %s\n' "$STUB_USED" "$((1000 - STUB_USED))" "$STUB_USED" "$1"
EOF
cat > stubs/mail <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
echo "mail $*" >> "$STUB_LOG"
cat >> "$STUB_LOG"
EOF
chmod +x stubs/*
export STUB_LOG=$PWD/calls.log PATH=$PWD/stubs:$PATH
: > "$STUB_LOG"
STUB_USED=42 bash alert.sh /data; echo "status at 42%: $?"
STUB_USED=95 bash alert.sh /data; echo "status at 95%: $?"
echo "== what the stubs saw"; cat "$STUB_LOG"

status at 42%: 0
status at 95%: 1
== what the stubs saw
df -P /data
df -P /data
mail -s disk /data at 95% admin@example.com
usage is 95%

alert.sh reads a disk's usage with df -P and mails the administrator above a threshold. The two stubs are three-line shell scripts in stubs/. The df stub ignores what it is asked and prints a table whose usage comes from $STUB_USED; the mail stub appends its arguments and its standard input to a log. With PATH=$PWD/stubs:$PATH, nothing in alert.sh had to change. At 42% the script exited 0 and the log held only the two df calls; at 95% it exited 1 and the log recorded mail -s disk /data at 95% admin@example.com with the body usage is 95%. The log is the spy: the test can assert both that the mail was sent and what it said, and, at 42%, that it was not.

A function as a stub

When the code under test is sourced into the test's shell, a stub can be a shell function, because bash looks for a function before it looks in PATH:

cat > alert.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
usage_percent() { df -P "$1" | awk 'NR == 2 { gsub("%", "", $5); print $5 }'; }
notify() { mail -s "disk alert" admin@example.com <<< "$1"; }
report() { echo "$1 is at $(usage_percent "$1")%"; notify "check $1"; }
EOF
cat > stub-in-process.sh <<'EOF'
source ./alert.sh
df()   { printf 'Filesystem 1 2 3 4 5\n/dev/x 100 80 20 80%% %s\n' "$2"; }
mail() { echo "  [mail stub] args: $*"; cat | sed 's/^/  [mail stub] body: /'; }
report /data
echo "== a child process does not see the functions"
echo "type -t df in a child bash: $(bash -c 'type -t df')"
echo "== export -f hands them to a child bash"
export -f df mail
bash -c 'source ./alert.sh; report /data'
EOF
bash stub-in-process.sh

/data is at 80%
  [mail stub] args: -s disk alert admin@example.com
  [mail stub] body: check /data
== a child process does not see the functions
type -t df in a child bash: file
== export -f hands them to a child bash
/data is at 80%
  [mail stub] args: -s disk alert admin@example.com
  [mail stub] body: check /data

df and mail were defined as functions in the test script, and report called them without knowing. A function stub is easier to write — it can print from the test's own variables — but it reaches only the shell it is defined in. A child bash did not see it (type -t df says file: the real /bin/df), which means the technique cannot stub a command called by a script that the test runs rather than sources. export -f, a bash feature, hands functions down to a child bash, as the last block shows; it does not reach sh, dash or a program that is not a shell.

What a stub cannot intercept

A stub is found by name, so a call that does not go through the name does not find it:

mkdir stubs
printf '#!/bin/sh\necho "stub date"\n' > stubs/date
chmod +x stubs/date
PATH=$PWD/stubs:$PATH
echo "== plain name:      $(date)"
echo "== absolute path:   $(/bin/date +%Y | sed 's/[0-9]/N/g')"
echo "== command -p:      $(command -p date +%Y | sed 's/[0-9]/N/g')"
echo "== env:             $(env date)"
date() { echo "function date"; }
echo "== a function wins: $(date)"
echo "== command skips it: $(command date)"

== plain name:      stub date
== absolute path:   NNNN
== command -p:      NNNN
== env:             stub date
== a function wins: function date
== command skips it: stub date

A stub named date was found by the plain name and by env date, which searches PATH. It was not found by the absolute path /bin/date, nor by command -p date, which searches the system default path. A function named date beat the stub, since functions come first, and command date skipped the function but still found the stub. So a script that calls its commands by full path — as a script that must not trust PATH does (§18.7) — cannot be stubbed by PATH; the test either accepts that or the script reads the path from a variable the test can set.

Stubs that fail: testing a retry

A stub that always succeeds is the easy case. The valuable ones fail:

cat > fetch.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Run a command up to three times; report which attempt worked.
retry() {
  local attempt
  for attempt in 1 2 3; do
    if "$@"; then echo "worked on attempt $attempt"; return 0; fi
    sleep "${RETRY_DELAY:-1}"
  done
  echo "gave up after 3 attempts" >&2
  return 1
}
EOF
mkdir stubs
cat > stubs/flaky <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
# Fail until it has been called $FAIL_TIMES times, counting in $COUNTER.
n=$(($(cat "$COUNTER" 2> /dev/null || echo 0) + 1))
echo "$n" > "$COUNTER"
[ "$n" -gt "$FAIL_TIMES" ]
EOF
cat > stubs/sleep <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
echo "slept $*" >> "$STUB_LOG"
EOF
chmod +x stubs/*
export PATH=$PWD/stubs:$PATH COUNTER=$PWD/count STUB_LOG=$PWD/calls.log
source ./fetch.sh
for fails in 0 2 3; do
  : > "$STUB_LOG"; rm -f "$COUNTER"
  export FAIL_TIMES=$fails
  printf 'fails %s time(s): ' "$fails"; retry flaky; echo "  -> status $?, sleeps: $(grep -c slept "$STUB_LOG")"
done

fails 0 time(s): worked on attempt 1
  -> status 0, sleeps: 0
fails 2 time(s): worked on attempt 3
  -> status 0, sleeps: 2
fails 3 time(s): gave up after 3 attempts
  -> status 1, sleeps: 3

retry runs a command up to three times with a sleep between attempts. Testing it against a real flaky command would take seconds and would not be repeatable, so the test supplied two stubs. flaky counts its calls in a file and fails until it has been called $FAIL_TIMES times; sleep is replaced by a stub that only records the request, so the test takes no time and can count the waits. The output shows the three paths: success on the first attempt with no sleeps, success on the third after two, and giving up after three failures and returning 1. Much of the value of a retry function is its last line, and no real system will fail three times on demand.

A stub helper in bats

In a bats file the same pieces are a helper and a setup:

mkdir -p src test
cat > src/alert.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
threshold=${THRESHOLD:-90}
usage_percent() { df -P "$1" | awk 'NR == 2 { gsub("%", "", $5); print $5 }'; }
check_disk() {
  local mount=$1 pct
  pct=$(usage_percent "$mount") || return 3
  if (( pct >= threshold )); then
    mail -s "disk $mount at ${pct}%" admin@example.com <<< "usage is ${pct}%"
    return 1
  fi
}
if [[ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} == "$0" ]]; then check_disk "${1:-/}"; fi
EOF
cat > test/alert.bats <<'EOF'
# stub NAME [STATUS] -- put a command called NAME first on PATH; it logs its arguments
stub() {
  mkdir -p "$BATS_TEST_TMPDIR/stubs"
  cat > "$BATS_TEST_TMPDIR/stubs/$1" <<STUB
#!/bin/sh
echo "$1 \$*" >> "$BATS_TEST_TMPDIR/calls"
[ -n "\${STUB_STDOUT-}" ] && printf '%s\n' "\$STUB_STDOUT"
exit ${2:-0}
STUB
  chmod +x "$BATS_TEST_TMPDIR/stubs/$1"
  PATH="$BATS_TEST_TMPDIR/stubs:$PATH"
}

setup() {
  stub mail
  source "$BATS_TEST_DIRNAME/../src/alert.sh"
  DF_LINE='/dev/x 100 95 5 95% /data'
}

df() { printf 'Filesystem 1 2 3 4 5\n%s\n' "$DF_LINE"; }

@test "no mail below the threshold" {
  DF_LINE='/dev/x 100 40 60 40% /data'
  run check_disk /data
  [ "$status" -eq 0 ]
  [ ! -e "$BATS_TEST_TMPDIR/calls" ]
}

@test "mails the admin at the threshold" {
  run check_disk /data
  [ "$status" -eq 1 ]
  [ "$(cat "$BATS_TEST_TMPDIR/calls")" = "mail -s disk /data at 95% admin@example.com" ]
}

@test "the threshold is configurable" {
  THRESHOLD=99 run check_disk /data
  [ "$status" -eq 0 ]
}

@test "a df that fails is status 3" {
  df() { return 1; }
  run check_disk /data
  [ "$status" -eq 3 ]
}
EOF
echo "== first run"
bats test
cat > src/alert.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
usage_percent() {
  local out
  out=$(df -P "$1") || return 1
  awk 'NR == 2 { gsub("%", "", $5); print $5 }' <<< "$out"
}
check_disk() {
  local mount=$1 pct
  pct=$(usage_percent "$mount") || return 3
  if (( pct >= ${THRESHOLD:-90} )); then
    mail -s "disk $mount at ${pct}%" admin@example.com <<< "usage is ${pct}%"
    return 1
  fi
}
if [[ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} == "$0" ]]; then check_disk "${1:-/}"; fi
EOF
echo "== after fixing the script"
bats test

== first run
1..4
ok 1 no mail below the threshold
ok 2 mails the admin at the threshold
not ok 3 the threshold is configurable
# (in test file test/alert.bats, line 37)
#   `[ "$status" -eq 0 ]' failed
not ok 4 a df that fails is status 3
# (in test file test/alert.bats, line 43)
#   `[ "$status" -eq 3 ]' failed
== after fixing the script
1..4
ok 1 no mail below the threshold
ok 2 mails the admin at the threshold
ok 3 the threshold is configurable
ok 4 a df that fails is status 3

stub NAME [STATUS] writes an executable into $BATS_TEST_TMPDIR/stubs that logs its arguments to $BATS_TEST_TMPDIR/calls, and puts that directory first on PATH; the test's df is a function stub, because the test sources alert.sh. Four tests, and the first run failed two of them, which is what testing is for. the threshold is configurable failed because alert.sh read THRESHOLD when the file was sourced, so setting it later did nothing. a df that fails is status 3 failed because usage_percent was df | awk, a pipeline whose status is awk's (§11.7), so df failing made pct empty, the comparison 0 >= 90 false, and the function returned 0 — a disk-space alert that reports "fine" when it cannot read the disk. ShellCheck did not report either, because neither is a pattern; the second is what the optional check-extra-masked-returns check points at — with --enable=all it reports SC2312 on the df | awk line, and only then. The fixed script assigns df's output first, so its status counts, and reads the threshold inside the function, and the second run passed all four.

Two habits keep stubs honest. Assert that the stub was called, as the mail test did, because a stub that is never reached makes a test pass for the wrong reason. And stub the boundary, not the logic: stub df, mail, date and curl, the commands that touch the outside world, and let everything the script itself does run for real.

20.10 shunit2

shunit2 is the other framework worth knowing. It is an xUnit-style library — a test is a function named test…, and assertions are functions like assertEquals — written in portable sh, so a test file runs under bash, dash, ksh and zsh. That property is what it is for. It is packaged as shunit2 in Homebrew and in Debian (2.1.8 in Debian 12 as well as on macOS), and the version measured here is 2.1.8.

shunit2: tests are functions, and the framework is sourced last

cat > slug.sh <<'EOF'
slugify() {
  local s=${1,,}
  s=${s//[^a-z0-9]/-}
  printf '%s\n' "$s"
}
EOF
cat > test_slug.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
oneTimeSetUp() { source ./slug.sh; }
setUp()        { WORK=$(mktemp -d); }
tearDown()     { rm -rf "$WORK"; }

testLowercases() {
  assertEquals "lowercases" "hello" "$(slugify Hello)"
}

testSpacesBecomeDashes() {
  assertEquals "spaces become dashes" "two-words" "$(slugify 'Two Words')"
}

testRunOfJunkIsOneDash() {
  assertEquals "a run of junk is one dash" "a-b" "$(slugify 'A !! B')"
}

testExitStatus() {
  slugify ok > /dev/null
  assertTrue "slugify succeeds" $?
}

testWorkDirectory() {
  assertTrue "the work directory exists" "[ -d '$WORK' ]"
}

source shunit2
EOF
bash test_slug.sh; echo "exit $?"

testLowercases
testSpacesBecomeDashes
testRunOfJunkIsOneDash
ASSERT:a run of junk is one dash expected:<a-b> but was:<a----b>
shunit2:ERROR testRunOfJunkIsOneDash() returned non-zero return code.
testExitStatus
testWorkDirectory

Ran 5 tests.

FAILED (failures=2)
exit 1

A shunit2 file defines its setUp, tearDown and test functions and then sources shunit2 as its last line; sourcing runs the tests. oneTimeSetUp runs once before the first test (here it loads the code under test), setUp before each test (a fresh work directory), tearDown after each, and each test… function is a test, run in the order defined. The report is plainer than bats's: the name of each test as it starts, a line ASSERT: for a failed assertion with the message, expected and actual values, a count and FAILED or OK. The available assertions, from the source of 2.1.8, are assertEquals, assertNotEquals, assertContains, assertNotContains, assertNull, assertNotNull, assertSame, assertNotSame, assertTrue, assertFalse and fail. assertTrue takes either a status ($?) or a condition to evaluate: the last test, [ -d '$WORK' ], is an expression.

What the failure count counts

cat > test_count.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
testTwoAssertionsOneTest() {
  assertEquals "first"  "a" "b"
  assertEquals "second" "c" "d"
}

testOneAssertionEndingTheTest() {
  assertEquals "only"   "a" "b"
}

testPlainFailure() {
  [ 1 -eq 2 ]
}

source shunit2
EOF
bash test_count.sh; echo "exit $?"

testTwoAssertionsOneTest
ASSERT:first expected:<a> but was:<b>
ASSERT:second expected:<c> but was:<d>
shunit2:ERROR testTwoAssertionsOneTest() returned non-zero return code.
testOneAssertionEndingTheTest
ASSERT:only expected:<a> but was:<b>
shunit2:ERROR testOneAssertionEndingTheTest() returned non-zero return code.
testPlainFailure
shunit2:ERROR testPlainFailure() returned non-zero return code.

Ran 3 tests.

FAILED (failures=6)
exit 1

Three tests, all failing, and failures=6. The number is not the count of failed tests. Every failed assertion counts one, and so does every test function that returns non-zero — and a failed assertion returns 1, so a test whose last command is a failed assertion counts twice: testOneAssertionEndingTheTest shows ASSERT: and shunit2:ERROR … returned non-zero return code. The first test has two failed assertions and the non-zero return: three. A plain failing [ 1 -eq 2 ] counts once. Read the lines, not the total, and treat FAILED as the fact; the exit status is non-zero whenever a test failed.

Setup, teardown, and running one test

cat > test_teardown.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
oneTimeSetUp()    { echo "oneTimeSetUp"; }
oneTimeTearDown() { echo "oneTimeTearDown"; }
setUp()           { echo "  setUp"; }
tearDown()        { echo "  tearDown"; }
testOne() { assertEquals 1 1; }
testTwo() { assertEquals 2 2; }
source shunit2
EOF
bash test_teardown.sh
echo "== only the named tests"
bash test_teardown.sh -- testTwo

oneTimeSetUp
  setUp
testOne
  tearDown
  setUp
testTwo
  tearDown
oneTimeTearDown

Ran 2 tests.

OK
  tearDown
oneTimeTearDown
== only the named tests
oneTimeSetUp
  setUp
testTwo
  tearDown
oneTimeTearDown

Ran 1 test.

OK
  tearDown
oneTimeTearDown

The order is oneTimeSetUp, then for each test setUp, the test, tearDown, and oneTimeTearDown, as in bats. One behaviour of 2.1.8 is easy to miss: after the OK, tearDown and oneTimeTearDown ran a second time. The framework's exit handler runs them again, so a teardown that is not safe to run twice — one that fails on an already-removed directory — misbehaves at the end of an otherwise green run. Write teardowns as rm -rf "$WORK", not rmdir "$WORK". Naming tests after -- runs only those: bash test_teardown.sh -- testTwo.

One suite, several shells

The reason to choose shunit2 over bats is that the same test file runs under different shells:

cat > count.sh <<'EOF'
# words FILE: print the number of words in FILE
words() { wc -w < "$1" | tr -d ' '; }
EOF
cat > test_count.sh <<'EOF'
oneTimeSetUp() { . ./count.sh; }
setUp() { printf 'one two three\n' > sample.txt; }

testCountsWords() {
  assertEquals 3 "$(words sample.txt)"
}

testEmptyFile() {
  : > empty.txt
  assertEquals 0 "$(words empty.txt)"
}

. shunit2
EOF
for sh in bash dash; do
  echo "== $sh"
  $sh test_count.sh 2>&1 | grep -v '^$'
done

== bash
testCountsWords
testEmptyFile
Ran 2 tests.
OK
== dash
testCountsWords
testEmptyFile
Ran 2 tests.
OK

The code under test, words, is POSIX sh; the test file sources it with . and shunit2 with . shunit2 (a path-less . searches PATH in both shells), and the loop runs it under bash and under dash. Both passed. bats tests are bash by definition — the @test syntax is bash — so they cannot check that a script works under dash. Choose bats for bash scripts, where its run, its temporary directories and its failure output earn their keep, and shunit2 for code that has to be portable (§19). A project of POSIX shell scripts is the natural home for shunit2, run once per shell it supports.

20.11 CI for Shell Scripts

CI for shell scripts is three commands run in order, cheapest first: a syntax check, the linter, the tests. The order is the point: bash -n is the fastest and fails first on a script that would not parse, ShellCheck is next and fails on a defect it can see, and the test suite comes last, because it is the slowest and needs a working script to run. A failure stops the run at the first stage that found it, and the log ends on the reason.

The commands themselves belong in the repository, in the Makefile that §20.6 built, so that a developer runs exactly what CI runs. What CI adds is an environment that is the same on every run, and a set of shells that is wider than one machine.

Pinning the tools

The tools' versions change what they report. A CI run that installs "the newest ShellCheck" turns red the day a release adds a check, with no change to the code; one that installs the distribution's package is behind a developer's laptop — Debian 12 packages ShellCheck 0.9.0 and bats 1.8.2, against 0.11.0 and 1.14.0 here — and the two disagree. The fix is to install the exact version the project was written against, and the workflow for GitHub Actions does that with two downloads:

name: check
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Install pinned tools
        run: |
          curl -sSL https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck/releases/download/v0.11.0/shellcheck-v0.11.0.linux.x86_64.tar.xz | tar -xJ
          sudo install shellcheck-v0.11.0/shellcheck /usr/local/bin/
          git clone --depth 1 --branch v1.14.0 https://github.com/bats-core/bats-core.git
          sudo bats-core/install.sh /usr/local
      - run: make check

Those install commands were run on a clean Ubuntu 24.04 image and printed version: 0.11.0 and Bats 1.14.0. actions/checkout@v7 is the major version current when this was written (v7.0.1, July 2026); a CI action has its own release schedule, so check the tag rather than copying it. The same three steps — get the tools at pinned versions, run make check, fail on a non-zero status — translate to any CI system.

Testing across bash versions

A script that says #!/usr/bin/env bash runs under whichever bash is first on the machine that runs it: 3.2 on a Mac that has not installed another (§1), 4.x on old enterprise Linux, 5.x on everything current. A feature that the developer's bash 5.3 has and the user's bash 3.2 lacks is a failure that only the user will see. CI can see it first, because the official bash container images carry a tag for each release series — 3.2, 4.2, 4.4 and 5.3 are the four used here:

cat > needs-new-bash.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
mapfile -t names < <(printf 'ada\ngrace\n')
echo "${#names[@]} names, last is ${names[-1]}"
EOF
for v in 3.2 4.2 4.4 5.3; do
  printf 'bash %s: ' "$v"
  docker run --rm -i --pull=never "bash:$v" bash -c 'cat > needs-new-bash.sh; bash needs-new-bash.sh 2>&1' < needs-new-bash.sh
done

bash 3.2: needs-new-bash.sh: line 2: mapfile: command not found
needs-new-bash.sh: line 3: names: bad array subscript
0 names, last is 
bash 4.2: 2 names, last is grace
bash 4.4: 2 names, last is grace
bash 5.3: 2 names, last is grace

The four lines are four runs of the same three-line script in four containers. Under bash 3.2 it failed twice — mapfile: command not found (mapfile arrived in 4.0), and names: bad array subscript, because ${names[-1]} is a negative index that 3.2 does not have — and printed 0 names, then carried on. Under 4.2, 4.4 and 5.3 it worked. The lesson is not that every script must run on 3.2; it is that the oldest bash you support should be an explicit, tested decision, and a matrix job is what makes it one. The same check, written into the script, turns a confusing failure into a clear one:

cat > guarded.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
if ((BASH_VERSINFO[0] < 4 || (BASH_VERSINFO[0] == 4 && BASH_VERSINFO[1] < 4))); then
  echo "guarded.sh needs bash 4.4 or newer; this is bash $BASH_VERSION" >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "running under bash ${BASH_VERSINFO[0]}.${BASH_VERSINFO[1]}"
EOF
for v in 3.2 4.2 4.4 5.3; do
  printf 'bash %s: ' "$v"
  docker run --rm -i --pull=never "bash:$v" bash -c 'cat > guarded.sh; bash guarded.sh 2>&1' < guarded.sh
done

bash 3.2: guarded.sh needs bash 4.4 or newer; this is bash 3.2.57(1)-release
bash 4.2: guarded.sh needs bash 4.4 or newer; this is bash 4.2.53(1)-release
bash 4.4: running under bash 4.4
bash 5.3: running under bash 5.3

The guard compares BASH_VERSINFO and refuses to run. It is an ordinary version test at the top of main, and the two failing lines show the message as a user on 3.2 or 4.2 would see it. Then a matrix job in CI is a loop over the tags you support.

What a test in CI must not do

A test that passes on a laptop and fails in CI, or the reverse, is usually one of a small number of things. It reads the real environment: the home directory, the current directory, $TERM, the machine's PATH — bats's temporary directories and PATH stubs exist so it need not. It depends on time: a date that changes, a sleep that is too short on a loaded runner; stub the clock and count the sleeps, as §20.9 did. It depends on order: one test leaving a file for the next, which the per-test directory prevents. It uses the network, which a stub replaces. And it prints a duration, which differs on every run and turns any comparison against saved output into noise; a test asserts what a run did, not how long it took. When a CI job needs a report in a format its dashboard understands, bats --formatter junit writes JUnit XML; that is the only output of the framework not meant for a human reader.

20.12 Debugging a Shell Script with Tracing

Static analysis and tests say that something is wrong. Debugging a shell script starts from a script that misbehaves and a question — what did it actually run? — and shell has an unusually good answer to it, because the shell can print each command after all its expansions, exactly as it is about to execute it. Most shell bugs are expansion bugs (§4): a variable that was empty, a word that split, a glob that matched something unexpected. A trace shows the result of every expansion, so it shows those bugs directly.

Debugging a shell script: set -x, and reading xtrace output

set -x, also set -o xtrace, makes the shell write each command to standard error before running it, prefixed with the trace prompt +. Starting a script as bash -x script.sh turns it on from the first line, and set -x inside the script turns it on from that point (§1.5 lists bash -x among the ways to start a script):

cat > trace.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
total=0
add() { total=$((total + $1)); }
for n in 1 2 3; do
  add "$n"
done
first=$(printf '%s\n' b a | sort | head -n 1)
echo "total=$total first=$first"
EOF
bash -x trace.sh

+ total=0
+ for n in 1 2 3
+ add 1
+ total=1
+ for n in 1 2 3
+ add 2
+ total=3
+ for n in 1 2 3
+ add 3
+ total=6
++ printf '%s\n' b a
++ sort
++ head -n 1
+ first=a
+ echo 'total=6 first=a'
total=6 first=a

That is xtrace output, and it is worth reading line by line. Every command appears after expansion: the loop's add "$n" was traced as add 1, add 2, add 3, and the assignment inside the function as total=1, total=3, total=6 — the values, not the $(( total + $1 )) that produced them. The for n in 1 2 3 line appears once per iteration, with the loop variable already set. Commands inside a command substitution are traced with two + characters, ++ printf, ++ sort and ++ head, one for each level of nesting, because the first character of the prompt is repeated to show depth. And the final echo shows its argument with the quoting the shell would need to re-read it, 'total=6 first=a'.

That last property is what makes a trace useful for the commonest bug:

cat > words.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
count() { echo "$# argument(s)"; }
name='my notes.txt'
count $name
count "$name"
count "$name" 'it'\''s' "a\$b" ''
EOF
bash -x words.sh

+ name='my notes.txt'
+ count my notes.txt
+ echo '2 argument(s)'
2 argument(s)
+ count 'my notes.txt'
+ echo '1 argument(s)'
1 argument(s)
+ count 'my notes.txt' 'it'\''s' 'a$b' ''
+ echo '4 argument(s)'
4 argument(s)

The unquoted call was traced as count my notes.txt — two words — and the quoted one as count 'my notes.txt' — one, in quotes. Quotes appear in a trace only where the word needs them, so an unquoted expansion that split shows as separate words with no quotes and a correct one as a single quoted word. The single quote in it's was written as 'it'\''s', a$b as 'a$b', and the empty string as '': each is exactly what a person would type to get that word, so a trace line can be copied back to a prompt and run. §20.2's SC2086 predicts the split; the trace shows it happening.

The PS4 prompt: file, line and function in every trace line

The + is the value of PS4, the PS4 prompt — the trace's counterpart of PS1. Bash expands PS4 afresh for every trace line, so it can hold variables that change, and the useful ones say where the command is:

cat > trace.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
total=0
add() { total=$((total + $1)); }
for n in 1 2; do
  add "$n"
done
echo "total=$total"
EOF
export PS4='+ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]##*/}:${LINENO}:${FUNCNAME[0]:+${FUNCNAME[0]}():} '
bash -x trace.sh

+ trace.sh:2: total=0
+ trace.sh:4: for n in 1 2
+ trace.sh:5: add 1
+ trace.sh:3:add(): total=1
+ trace.sh:4: for n in 1 2
+ trace.sh:5: add 2
+ trace.sh:3:add(): total=3
+ trace.sh:7: echo total=3
total=3

PS4='+ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]##*/}:${LINENO}:${FUNCNAME[0]:+${FUNCNAME[0]}():} ' gives each line the file, the line number and — for a command inside a function — the function's name: + trace.sh:3:add(): total=1 is the assignment on line 3, run inside add. In a script of any size that is the difference between a trace and a map. Three details. PS4 must be in single quotes, or the shell expands it once, when it is assigned, and every line carries the same file and line. Its first character is the one repeated to show nesting depth, so keep the + first. And because the value is expanded at each trace line, it is code: a PS4 taken from an untrusted environment runs commands (§18.11).

BASH_XTRACEFD: sending the trace somewhere else

Standard error is where the trace goes, which is also where the script's own errors go, and in a long run the two interleave until neither can be read. BASH_XTRACEFD names a file descriptor for the trace and takes it out of standard error:

cat > quiet.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
exec 5> trace.log
BASH_XTRACEFD=5
PS4='+ ${LINENO}: '
set -x
x=1
echo "stdout is untouched: $x" >&2
echo "and so is stderr" >&2
set +x
exec 5>&-
EOF
bash quiet.sh 2> err.txt
echo "== err.txt (stderr, no trace in it)"; cat err.txt
echo "== trace.log"; cat trace.log

== err.txt (stderr, no trace in it)
stdout is untouched: 1
and so is stderr
== trace.log
+ 6: x=1
+ 7: echo 'stdout is untouched: 1'
+ 8: echo 'and so is stderr'
+ 9: set +x

The script opened trace.log on descriptor 5, set BASH_XTRACEFD=5, and traced a region. Standard error, captured to err.txt, held only the script's own two messages, and the trace, with its ${LINENO} prompt, went to the log. The feature exists in bash 4.1 and later; an older bash ignores the variable:

cat > quiet.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
exec 5> trace.log
BASH_XTRACEFD=5
PS4='+ ${LINENO}: '
set -x
x=1
set +x
exec 5>&-
EOF
for v in 3.2 4.4; do
  echo "== bash $v: standard error, then trace.log"
  docker run --rm -i --pull=never "bash:$v" bash -c 'cat > quiet.sh; bash quiet.sh 2>&1; echo "-- trace.log:"; cat trace.log' < quiet.sh
done

== bash 3.2: standard error, then trace.log
+ 6: x=1
+ 7: set +x
-- trace.log:
== bash 4.4: standard error, then trace.log
-- trace.log:
+ 6: x=1
+ 7: set +x

Under bash 3.2 the trace lines appeared on standard error and trace.log was empty; under 4.4 it went to the file. That is the macOS system bash again (§1), and a reason to write the log-file form only in scripts that already require bash 4 — or to test for it, as §20.11's guard does.

Turning tracing on for a region, and on demand

Tracing everything of a 500-line script is noise; tracing the ten lines in question is a diagnosis. set -x and set +x bracket a region, a subshell confines it, and an environment variable turns the whole facility on without editing the file:

cat > region.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
setup() { a=1; b=2; }
compute() { c=$((a + b)); }
setup
set -x
compute
set +x
echo "c=$c"
( set -x; echo "traced only inside the subshell" )
echo "not traced"
if [[ -n ${TRACE-} ]]; then set -x; fi
echo "traced when TRACE is set"
EOF
echo "== plain";      bash region.sh
echo "== TRACE=1";    TRACE=1 bash region.sh

== plain
+ compute
+ c=3
+ set +x
c=3
+ echo 'traced only inside the subshell'
traced only inside the subshell
not traced
traced when TRACE is set
== TRACE=1
+ compute
+ c=3
+ set +x
c=3
+ echo 'traced only inside the subshell'
traced only inside the subshell
not traced
+ echo 'traced when TRACE is set'
traced when TRACE is set

The trace covered compute and the assignment inside it, then set +x itself (the last traced command is the set +x that turned it off). ( set -x; echo … ) traced only inside the parentheses, since the subshell's option dies with it. And the last two lines — if [[ -n ${TRACE-} ]]; then set -x; fi — traced nothing in the plain run and the final echo under TRACE=1: a script that carries this line can be debugged in a place where its source cannot be edited, by running TRACE=1 script.

xtrace and secrets

A trace prints what the shell is about to run, and the shell has, by then, expanded every variable. Anything secret that was ever a variable is in the trace:

cat > login.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -x
password=$(printf 'hunter2')
echo "connecting with a token of ${#password} characters"
EOF
cat > login-safe.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -x
{ set +x; } 2> /dev/null
password=$(printf 'hunter2')
echo "connecting with a token of ${#password} characters"
set -x
EOF
echo "== leaks";  bash login.sh
echo "== quiet around the secret"; bash login-safe.sh

== leaks
++ printf hunter2
+ password=hunter2
+ echo 'connecting with a token of 7 characters'
connecting with a token of 7 characters
== quiet around the secret
connecting with a token of 7 characters

The traced script leaked the password twice: ++ printf hunter2 for the command substitution, and + password=hunter2 for the assignment. In CI, where logs are kept and read by many people, that is a credential in a build log. The second script turned tracing off around the secret with { set +x; } 2> /dev/null: the braces and the redirection hide the + set +x line that would otherwise be printed, and nothing of the assignment appeared. Turn set -x back on afterwards if it was on. §14.8 and §18.15 make the same point from the other side — read -s hides a value from the terminal, not from a trace — and the rule is the one here: a script that handles secrets does not run under set -x in a shared log, and one that must does so with the secret's lines excluded.

xtrace and child scripts

bash -x traces the script it starts and not the scripts that script starts:

cat > child.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "in the child"
EOF
cat > parent.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "in the parent"
bash child.sh
EOF
echo "== bash -x: the child is not traced"; bash -x parent.sh
echo "== env SHELLOPTS=xtrace: it is";       env SHELLOPTS=xtrace bash parent.sh

== bash -x: the child is not traced
+ echo 'in the parent'
in the parent
+ bash child.sh
in the child
== env SHELLOPTS=xtrace: it is
+ echo 'in the parent'
in the parent
+ bash child.sh
+ echo 'in the child'
in the child

bash -x parent.sh traced parent.sh's two commands, including the call to bash child.sh, and then the child ran untraced. Passing SHELLOPTS=xtrace through the environment — with env, since the variable is read-only inside a running bash — traced the child as well, because bash reads SHELLOPTS at startup and applies it to every bash process the variable reaches (§18.8). That is the way to trace a build system that calls dozens of scripts, and the reason not to leave SHELLOPTS in an environment.

set -v, and the bash -n syntax check

set -v is the older cousin of set -x: it prints each line as the shell reads it, before any expansion and before it runs. For a script it echoes the source, and an entire for loop appears at once, because the parser reads the whole compound command before running it:

cat > loop.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
for n in 1 2; do
  echo "n is $n"
done
EOF
echo "== bash -v (echo each line as it is read)"; bash -v loop.sh
echo "== bash -vx"; bash -vx loop.sh 2>&1
cat > broken.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "about to start"
if [[ -f data ]]; then
  echo "found"
echo "end"
EOF
echo "== bash -n reads without running"; bash -n broken.sh; echo "exit $?"
cat > runtime.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "started"
no_such_command_here
EOF
echo "== bash -n cannot see a missing command"; bash -n runtime.sh; echo "exit $?"

== bash -v (echo each line as it is read)
#!/usr/bin/env bash
for n in 1 2; do
  echo "n is $n"
done
n is 1
n is 2
== bash -vx
#!/usr/bin/env bash
for n in 1 2; do
  echo "n is $n"
