That is negligible at the top of a script and a hundred programs inside a loop that runs a hundred times, which is the shape of the table's last row: an outer loop over {1..100} with for n in $(seq 1 5) inside it, a hundred seq processes against none for the version that writes {1..5}. seq also is not POSIX, and it exists in GNU and BSD forms that differ.

The other cost is memory, and it is a surprise. Every form that expands a range into a list of words holds the whole list; only the C-style loop holds a counter:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the snippets are code for a fresh shell, not text to expand
n=5
# shellcheck disable=SC2051  # brace expansion does not see $n: that is the point
echo {1..$n}

# growth SNIPPET: how much the resident memory of a fresh shell grew, in KB
growth() {
  bash -c 'rss() { ps -o rss= -p $$; }
           before=$(rss); eval "$1"; after=$(rss); echo $(( after - before ))' _ "$1"
}
yn() { if (( $1 )); then echo yes; else echo no; fi; }

g=$(growth 'for i in {1..1000000}; do :; done')
echo "for i in {1..1000000}      grows the shell by 100 MB or more: $(yn "$(( g >= 100 * 1024 ))")"
g=$(growth 'for i in $(seq 1 1000000); do :; done')
echo "for i in \$(seq 1 1000000)  grows the shell by 20 MB or more:  $(yn "$(( g >= 20 * 1024 ))")"
g=$(growth 'for ((i = 1; i <= 1000000; i++)); do :; done')
echo "for ((i = 1; i <= ...; ))  grows the shell by under 2 MB:     $(yn "$(( g < 2 * 1024 ))")"

{1..5}
for i in {1..1000000}      grows the shell by 100 MB or more: yes
for i in $(seq 1 1000000)  grows the shell by 20 MB or more:  yes
for ((i = 1; i <= ...; ))  grows the shell by under 2 MB:     yes

{1..n} cannot take a variable, because brace expansion happens before parameter expansion (§4.1): {1..$n} is printed as it is, which is the reason seq and eval are so often reached for, and the reason the C-style for ((i = 1; i <= n; i++)) is the right loop for a count that is not a literal. A million words as a brace expansion grew the shell by more than a hundred megabytes — about 180 MB on macOS and 270 MB on Debian — a million words from $(seq) by about half of that or less, and the C-style loop by nothing at all. The advice in §4's exercises to use the C-style loop stands, and now has a measurement behind it: it needs no process, holds no list and needs no quoting decisions. seq earns its place for a step that is not an integer, and for output that is data rather than a loop.

expr, bc and awk: arithmetic by process

Arithmetic is where the process habit is oldest, because the Bourne shell had no arithmetic of its own and expr was how anything got added. expr is a program, so n=$(expr "$n" + 1) is a fork and an exec to add one, and the table put a number on it. $((n + 1)) is the replacement, and it is POSIX; (( n++ )) and let do the same in bash; and none of them starts anything. For fractions there is nothing in the shell, and the two tools to reach for are awk, which is everywhere, and bc, which does arbitrary precision. Both are programs, so the discipline is the same as for any program: do the arithmetic once, over the whole dataset, not once per iteration. A loop that calls awk -v x="$x" 'BEGIN { print x * 1.07 }' per line is the shape to remove: the fix is a single awk '{ print $1 * 1.07 }' over the file, and §21.5 does exactly that.

When the subprocess is the right call

None of this is an argument that an external command is a mistake. The cost of a process is a fixed overhead — about a millisecond on the macOS machine measured, about 0.2 ms on Linux — and whether it matters depends on how much work the process does for it. A loop whose body runs ffmpeg on a video, rsync on a directory or curl on a URL does tens or hundreds of milliseconds of real work per item, and the overhead is one percent of that: replacing the process would change nothing and there is nothing to replace it with. The rule is that a process is worth replacing when the work it does is smaller than the cost of starting it — a string operation on one short value, an integer sum, a file name split, a comparison — and worth keeping when the work is larger, or when the program's behaviour is what you want: sort on a big input, grep across many files, date -d for date arithmetic the shell cannot do. That is also why the expansion is only the first cure. When the work is a whole file rather than one value per iteration, the right process is a single one that does all of it, which is §21.5.

21.5 Reading a File with a Loop Is Slow, and Using a Single awk Instead of a Loop

Reading a file with a loop is slow: what read does for every line

A while read loop pays even when its body does nothing, and the cost has a cause that can be seen. The strace example below counts the system calls the shell makes while reading a 1,000-line file of 8,893 bytes, different ways:

# Linux only: strace shows what the shell asks the kernel for while it reads a 1,000-line file
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the snippets are code for bash -c, not text to expand
seq 1 1000 | sed 's/^/line /' > lines.txt
echo "$(wc -c < lines.txt) bytes"
calls() {
  strace -f -c -e trace=read,lseek,openat,write -o trace.txt bash -c "$1" > /dev/null 2>&1
  awk -v body="$1" '
    $NF ~ /^(read|lseek|openat|write)$/ { n[$NF] = $4 }
    END { printf "%-56s read %5d  lseek %5d  open %5d\n", body, n["read"], n["lseek"], n["openat"] }' trace.txt
}
calls ':'
calls 'while read -r l; do :; done < lines.txt'
calls 'cat lines.txt | while read -r l; do :; done'
calls 'mapfile -t a < lines.txt'
calls 'cat lines.txt | { mapfile -t a; }'
calls 'while read -r l; do echo "$l" >> out.txt; done < lines.txt'
calls 'while read -r l; do echo "$l"; done < lines.txt > out.txt'

8893 bytes
:                                                        read     2  lseek     0  open     4
while read -r l; do :; done < lines.txt                  read  1003  lseek  2000  open     5
cat lines.txt | while read -r l; do :; done              read  8899  lseek  1001  open     7
mapfile -t a < lines.txt                                 read     6  lseek     1  open     5
cat lines.txt | { mapfile -t a; }                        read  8899  lseek     1  open     7
while read -r l; do echo "$l" >> out.txt; done < lines.txt read  1003  lseek  2000  open  1005
while read -r l; do echo "$l"; done < lines.txt > out.txt read  1003  lseek  2000  open     6

The first row is the shell starting and stopping, the baseline. Reading the file with while read … < file made about a thousand read calls and two thousand lseek calls for a thousand lines: one read and two lseeks per line. The shell cannot read a large block and keep it, because the file descriptor is shared with whatever the loop's body runs — a read inside the loop, a child process that inherits standard input — and a byte the shell had read ahead would be lost to them. So for a file it can seek in, it reads a block, takes the first line from it and moves the descriptor back to just after that line, so that the next reader starts in the right place.

When the input is a pipe, it cannot seek back, and the only way to avoid consuming bytes that belong to someone else is to read one byte at a time. The second row shows it: 8,899 read calls for 8,893 bytes. A while read loop fed by a pipe — cat file | while read, command | while read, while read … < <(command) — costs a system call per byte, where the same loop reading a file redirected on its standard input costs one per line. mapfile behaves the same way: from the file it made six reads for the whole file, from the pipe 8,899. The remedy for a pipe is not to fight the shell but to notice that a pipe delivers a stream and a stream is what awk, grep and sort are for; the loop belongs where the data is a file.

The last two rows are the cost of the output side. Redirecting on every iteration (echo "$l" >> out.txt) opened and closed the file a thousand times — 1,005 openat calls — where redirecting the loop as a whole (done < lines.txt > out.txt) opened it once. §21.6 measures that as a ratio.

The loop against the tool

A loop costs a per-line overhead even with no external command in its body, and the tools that do the same work run a compiled loop of their own. This block sums one column of a 20,000-line file, counts the lines matching a pattern and loads a file into an array, each with a loop and with the tool built for it:

# micros COMMAND...: the best of three runs, in microseconds
micros() {
  local i start took best=
  for i in 1 2 3; do
    start=${EPOCHREALTIME//[!0-9]/}
    "$@" > /dev/null
    took=$(( ${EPOCHREALTIME//[!0-9]/} - start ))
    if [[ -z $best ]] || (( took < best )); then best=$took; fi
  done
  echo "$best"
}
# yn NUMBER: yes if the number is not zero, no if it is
yn() { if (( $1 )); then echo yes; else echo no; fi; }

awk 'BEGIN { for (i = 1; i <= 20000; i++) printf "id%d,%s,%d\n", i, (i % 5 == 0 ? "ERROR" : "INFO"), i * 3 }' > log.csv

sum_loop() { local total=0 n; while IFS=, read -r _ _ n; do (( total += n )); done < log.csv; echo "$total"; }
sum_awk()  { awk -F, '{ total += $3 } END { print total }' log.csv; }

count_loop() { local count=0 level; while IFS=, read -r _ level _; do [[ $level == ERROR ]] && (( count++ )); done < log.csv; echo "$count"; }
count_grep() { grep -c ',ERROR,' log.csv; }

load_loop()    { local line lines=(); while IFS= read -r line; do lines+=("$line"); done < log.csv; echo "${#lines[@]}"; }
load_mapfile() { local lines; mapfile -t lines < log.csv; echo "${#lines[@]}"; }

versus() {  # versus LABEL SLOW FAST FACTOR
  local agree slow fast
  if [[ $("$2") == "$("$3")" ]]; then agree=yes; else agree=NO; fi
  slow=$(micros "$2"); fast=$(micros "$3")
  printf '%-20s same result: %-3s  %2dx faster or more: %s\n' "$1" "$agree" "$4" "$(yn "$(( slow >= $4 * fast ))")"
}
versus 'sum a column'       sum_loop   sum_awk       5
versus 'count matches'      count_loop count_grep   10
versus 'load into an array' load_loop  load_mapfile 10

sum a column         same result: yes   5x faster or more: yes
count matches        same result: yes  10x faster or more: yes
load into an array   same result: yes  10x faster or more: yes

The results agree in each case, and the tool wins by a margin. awk was at least five times faster than the loop for the sum and grep -c ten times faster for the count, and mapfile ten times faster than the while read loop that appends each line to an array. On the machine measured the actual factors were about 10 and 30 for the sum, 20 and 150 for the count and 40 and 30 for the array, on macOS and Debian in that order — for the array, of an appending loop against mapfile. The empty loop — while read; do :; done over the same file — cost about three microseconds per line on macOS, which is small next to a process and large next to what awk spends on a line. So a while read loop is right when the body is the point — each line drives a different command, or needs the shell's own state — and slow when the body is a comparison or a sum that a tool would do in the same pass.

mapfile and the array instead of the loop

When the goal is only to get a file's lines into an array, mapfile -t lines < file (§14.7) does what the appending loop does in a single builtin, and it is the fastest way there is to read a file in bash. -t strips the trailing newline from each element, as read does. What it costs is memory, and §21.9 measures it: an array holds each element with a fixed overhead, and a million-line file takes several times its own size. mapfile is the right choice for files that fit comfortably in memory and are wanted as a whole — to be sorted, indexed or looped over twice — and the wrong one for a file that is only to be scanned once, where a streaming while read < file or a tool holds one line at a time.

Walking a string is quadratic

The other loop that looks harmless is one over the characters of a string, indexing each with ${s:i:1}. The cost of each index is proportional to the length of the string, so a loop over all of it is proportional to the length squared, and the way to see it is to lengthen the string and watch the time:

# micros COMMAND...: the best of three runs, in microseconds
micros() {
  local i start took best=
  for i in 1 2 3; do
    start=${EPOCHREALTIME//[!0-9]/}
    "$@" > /dev/null
    took=$(( ${EPOCHREALTIME//[!0-9]/} - start ))
    if [[ -z $best ]] || (( took < best )); then best=$took; fi
  done
  echo "$best"
}
# yn NUMBER: yes if the number is not zero, no if it is
yn() { if (( $1 )); then echo yes; else echo no; fi; }

walk_index() { local s=$1 i n=${#1}; for ((i = 0; i < n; i++)); do : "${s:i:1}"; done; }
walk_read()  { while IFS= read -r -n 1 _; do :; done <<< "$1"; }

string() { printf '%*s' "$1" '' | tr ' ' x; }
short=$(string 5000);  long=$(string 20000)
t1=$(micros walk_index "$short"); t2=$(micros walk_index "$long")
echo "\${s:i:1}: a string four times as long takes 8 times the time or more: $(yn "$(( t2 >= 8 * t1 ))")"
t1=$(micros walk_read "$short");  t2=$(micros walk_read "$long")
echo "read -n 1: a string four times as long takes less than 8 times:       $(yn "$(( t2 < 8 * t1 ))")"

${s:i:1}: a string four times as long takes 8 times the time or more: yes
read -n 1: a string four times as long takes less than 8 times:       yes

Making the string four times as long multiplied the time by eight or more for the indexed walk, and by less than eight for the read -n 1 walk. Quadratic growth turns a factor of four in length into sixteen in time, and linear growth into four; the threshold sits between, and a factor of four rather than two keeps the noise of a timer well inside it. On the machine measured, a 10,000-character string took about 0.12 seconds to walk by index and a 40,000-character string 1.6 seconds, where the read -n 1 loop took 85 milliseconds for the 40,000. The walk is quadratic in the C locale and in a UTF-8 one, where it was about three times slower again on multibyte characters, and it is consistent with the shell producing the whole value of $s before it takes the substring. §15.6 introduced iterating over characters; this is why to prefer read -n 1 from a here-string, or an array built once (mapfile -t chars < <(grep -o . <<< "$s"), one process) and looped over, or a single awk with substr, over an index into a long string. A string of a few hundred characters is too short for any of it to matter.

Using a single awk instead of a loop

A loop that reads each line and runs tools on it is the most expensive form a shell script takes, and the fix that removes the most is to hand the whole file to one program. This example totals the bytes served per status code in a 500-line access log, three ways: with a tool per field, with builtins only, and with one awk. The spies count the programs each starts:

# shellcheck disable=SC2003  # expr is the process being counted
# Spies: each logs its own name to calls.log, then runs the real tool
mkdir spy
for tool in cut expr awk sort; do
  printf '#!/bin/sh\necho %s >> "%s/calls.log"\nexec %s "$@"\n' \
    "$tool" "$PWD" "$(command -v "$tool")" > "spy/$tool"
  chmod +x "spy/$tool"
done
: > calls.log
programs() { mapfile -t log < calls.log; : > calls.log; echo "${#log[@]}"; }

# 500 requests: address, status, path, bytes
awk 'BEGIN { for (i = 1; i <= 500; i++)
  printf "10.0.0.%d %d /page/%d %d\n", i % 250, (i % 7 == 0 ? 404 : 200), i % 25, (i * 37) % 5000 }' > access.log

# Bytes served per status, three ways.  Each prints "status total" lines, sorted.
with_tools() {
  local line status bytes
  declare -A total
  while IFS= read -r line; do
    status=$(echo "$line" | cut -d' ' -f2)
    bytes=$(echo "$line" | cut -d' ' -f4)
    total[$status]=$(expr "${total[$status]:-0}" + "$bytes")
  done < access.log
  for status in "${!total[@]}"; do echo "$status ${total[$status]}"; done | sort
}
with_builtins() {
  local status bytes
  declare -A total
  while read -r _ status _ bytes; do
    (( total[$status] += bytes ))
  done < access.log
  for status in "${!total[@]}"; do echo "$status ${total[$status]}"; done | sort
}
with_awk() {
  awk '{ total[$2] += $4 } END { for (status in total) print status, total[status] }' access.log | sort
}

for variant in with_tools with_builtins with_awk; do
  PATH=$PWD/spy:$PATH "$variant" > "$variant.out"
  printf '%-14s %4d programs\n' "$variant" "$(programs)"
done
echo "--- the three results, one line each:"
cat with_awk.out
cmp with_tools.out with_awk.out && cmp with_builtins.out with_awk.out && echo "identical"

with_tools     1501 programs
with_builtins     1 programs
with_awk          2 programs
--- the three results, one line each:
200 1017246
404 167004
identical

with_tools started 1,501 programs: three per line (two cuts and an expr) times 500, and the final sort. with_builtins started one, the sort. with_awk started two, its own and the sort. All three printed the same two lines, which cmp confirmed. The first is the mistake §21.4 described. The second and third are both fixes, and they are fixes for different reasons: the builtins version stays in the shell and is the right size when the loop's body needs the shell, and the awk version is shortest and, by the previous subsection's measurement, faster when the body is arithmetic on fields.

The question of which single tool is not one to settle from memory. awk is not always faster than a pipeline of small programs, and the answer changes with the machine. Counting the values in a column of a 200,000-line file with awk '{ n[$1]++ }' and with cut | sort | uniq -c, measured with hyperfine, the pipeline won on the macOS machine, 1.6 times faster than macOS's own awk. On Debian in a container awk won: 2.3 times faster with mawk, which is what Debian installs, and 1.36 times faster with gawk. Three different programs answer to the name awk, and a machine with a fast sort may prefer to let it do the grouping. Both were an order of magnitude faster than any loop, which is the difference that matters. Choose between the tools with hyperfine, on the machine that will run the script, and choose between a loop and a tool by counting processes first.

21.6 Batching Work, I/O Buffering and stdbuf

Batching work: many arguments per program

When each item really does need a program, the cost that remains is one process per item — unless the program accepts many items at once, which most of the tools that take file names do. Batching work means handing a program a hundred or a thousand arguments in a single run instead of one. The stand-in program below records each time it is started and how many arguments it received, and the loop tries every way of running it over a thousand files:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016,SC2038  # the quoted labels are text, and the unsafe pipe is one of the forms compared
# A stand-in program that records each time it is started and how many arguments it got
cat > tool <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
echo "$#" >> calls.log
EOF
chmod +x tool
mkdir files
for ((i = 1; i <= 1000; i++)); do : > "files/f$i"; done

runs() { local n; n=$(grep -c . calls.log); : > calls.log; printf '%-40s %4d run(s)\n' "$1" "$n"; }
: > calls.log

for f in files/*; do ./tool "$f"; done;                     runs 'for f in files/*; do tool "$f"; done'
./tool files/*;                                             runs 'tool files/*'
find files -type f -exec ./tool {} \;;                      runs 'find -exec tool {} \;'
find files -type f -exec ./tool {} +;                       runs 'find -exec tool {} +'
find files -type f | xargs -n 1 ./tool;                     runs 'xargs -n 1 tool'
find files -type f | xargs -n 100 ./tool;                   runs 'xargs -n 100 tool'
find files -type f -print0 | xargs -0 ./tool;               runs 'xargs -0 tool'

for f in files/*; do tool "$f"; done     1000 run(s)
tool files/*                                1 run(s)
find -exec tool {} \;                    1000 run(s)
find -exec tool {} +                        1 run(s)
xargs -n 1 tool                          1000 run(s)
xargs -n 100 tool                          10 run(s)
xargs -0 tool                               1 run(s)

The for loop, find -exec … \; and xargs -n 1 each started the program a thousand times. Passing the glob directly (tool files/*), find -exec … {} + and a plain xargs each started it once. And xargs -n 100 started it ten times, which is the tool's way of capping the batch. The + form of find -exec and xargs are the two batchers, and they are the same idea: collect arguments until the command line is as long as the system allows, run the command, repeat. find … -print0 | xargs -0 is the form that survives any file name (§15.11, §18.14); xargs -P N runs several batches in parallel (§17.6), which is what to add once the batching is right and not before.

There is a limit, and it is why xargs exists at all. The kernel restricts how much can be passed to a program in one exec — the arguments and the environment together, ARG_MAX — and a command line larger than that fails outright:

printf '#!/bin/sh\necho "$# arguments"\n' > tool; chmod +x tool
big=(); for ((i = 0; i < 300000; i++)); do big+=("argument-number-$i"); done

echo "a builtin takes them all: $(printf '%s\n' "${big[@]}" | grep -c .) lines"
./tool "${big[@]}" 2>&1 | sed 's/^.*: //'
printf '%s\n' "${big[@]}" | xargs ./tool > runs.txt
echo "xargs split them into more than one run, fewer than a hundred: $(
  awk 'END { print (NR > 1 && NR < 100) ? "yes" : "no" }' runs.txt)"
echo "and none was lost: $(awk '{ n += $1 } END { print n }' runs.txt) arguments"

a builtin takes them all: 300000 lines
Argument list too long
xargs split them into more than one run, fewer than a hundred: yes
and none was lost: 300000 arguments

The builtin printf took all 300,000 arguments, because a builtin is never exec'd and so never meets the limit. The external program refused: Argument list too long, the message for the error the kernel returns, E2BIG. xargs split the same list into batches that fit — more than one run, fewer than a hundred, and no argument lost. The number of runs was 60 on macOS and 52 on Debian, since the limit differs (getconf ARG_MAX reports 1,048,576 on the macOS machine and 2,097,152 in the Debian container), which is why the block prints only that it was in between. A script that builds a very long list of names and passes it to an external command is one that will work on the developer's machine and fail on a bigger tree; xargs and find -exec … + are what make it work at any size.

Output in a loop: open the file once

The mirror image of a program per item is a file opened per item. echo "$n" >> out.txt inside a loop opens out.txt, appends and closes it on every iteration; the strace table in §21.5 counted 1,005 openat calls for it against 6 for the version that redirects the loop as a whole. Timed:

# micros COMMAND...: the best of three runs, in microseconds
micros() {
  local i start took best=
  for i in 1 2 3; do
    start=${EPOCHREALTIME//[!0-9]/}
    "$@" > /dev/null
    took=$(( ${EPOCHREALTIME//[!0-9]/} - start ))
    if [[ -z $best ]] || (( took < best )); then best=$took; fi
  done
  echo "$best"
}
# yn NUMBER: yes if the number is not zero, no if it is
yn() { if (( $1 )); then echo yes; else echo no; fi; }

seq 1 20000 > numbers.txt
open_each_time() { local n; while read -r n; do echo "$n" >> out.txt; done < numbers.txt; : > out.txt; }
open_once()      { local n; while read -r n; do echo "$n"; done < numbers.txt > out.txt; : > out.txt; }

a=$(micros open_each_time); b=$(micros open_once)
echo "opening the file on every iteration costs 1.5 times as much or more: $(yn "$(( 2 * a >= 3 * b ))")"

opening the file on every iteration costs 1.5 times as much or more: yes

Opening the file on every iteration cost at least one and a half times as much as opening it once — about 4.5 times on macOS and 1.9 on Debian, on 20,000 lines. The cure is to move the redirection to the loop, done > out.txt (§10.11), or to a group around it, or to change the shell's own descriptor once with exec > out.txt (§10.7). It also gives the correct semantics when the file must not be truncated and appended to by someone else halfway through, but that is §17's subject.

I/O buffering: why a pipeline says nothing

Some pipelines are slow for a reason that no count of processes reveals: they are not slow, they are buffered. A program that writes to a terminal is usually line-buffered — the C library flushes at each newline, so the output appears as it is produced. The same program writing to a pipe or a file is usually fully buffered: it collects its output in a block, several kilobytes, and writes only when the block is full or the program exits. That is a sound decision for throughput, since one large write is cheaper than a thousand small ones. It is a surprise the first time a tail -f log | grep ERROR | cut -d' ' -f3 sits silent for minutes because grep is holding what it has found until it has enough. I/O buffering is the library's, not the shell's: the shell only connects file descriptors (§10.1), and each program decides when to write.

The experiment that shows it needs a producer that writes a line, waits a second, says so on standard error and writes another line. A consumer that delivers the first line before the announcement is streaming; one that delivers it after is holding back:

# The producer writes a line, waits a second, says so on stderr, and writes another line.
# A consumer that receives "one" before the announcement is streaming; one that receives it
# after is holding its output back until it has a full buffer or its input ends.
producer() { printf 'one\n'; sleep 1; echo '-- the producer waited' >&2; printf 'two\n'; }

verdict() {
  local out
  out=$( { producer | "$@" | while read -r line; do echo "got $line"; done; } 2>&1 )
  if [[ ${out,,} == "got one"* ]]; then verdict=streams; else verdict='holds back'; fi
  printf '%-24s %s\n' "$*" "$verdict"
}
verdict cat
verdict grep .
verdict grep --line-buffered .
verdict stdbuf -oL grep .
verdict cut -c1-3
verdict stdbuf -oL cut -c1-3
verdict tr a-z A-Z
verdict stdbuf -o0 tr a-z A-Z
verdict sed -u p
verdict sort
verdict stdbuf -oL sort

cat                      streams
grep .                   holds back
grep --line-buffered .   streams
stdbuf -oL grep .        streams
cut -c1-3                holds back
stdbuf -oL cut -c1-3     streams
tr a-z A-Z               holds back
stdbuf -o0 tr a-z A-Z    streams
sed -u p                 streams
sort                     holds back
stdbuf -oL sort          holds back

cat streams because it does not use the C library's buffering: it writes each block it reads as soon as it reads it. grep, cut and tr hold their output back. sort holds it back for a reason of its own — it cannot print a first line until it has read every line, since the smallest may be the last — and nothing in the buffering can change that (§17.11). grep --line-buffered and sed -u stream, because each tool has an option that asks it to; cut and tr have none. And stdbuf, the last topic of this section, makes grep, cut and tr stream when the tool has no option. awk is left out of that table, because the answer depends on which awk it is:

producer() { printf 'one\n'; sleep 1; echo '-- the producer waited' >&2; printf 'two\n'; }
verdict() {
  local out
  out=$( { producer | "$@" | while read -r line; do echo "got $line"; done; } 2>&1 )
  if [[ ${out,,} == "got one"* ]]; then verdict=streams; else verdict='holds back'; fi
  printf '%-30s %s\n' "$*" "$verdict"
}
verdict awk '{ print }'
verdict awk '{ print; fflush() }'

awk { print }                  holds back
awk { print; fflush() }        streams

On this machine awk streams with an fflush() after each print and holds back without one. Not every awk does. The examples run on Debian, where awk is mawk, measured the other three:

# Linux only: the same test with the tools that ship as `awk` on Debian and Ubuntu, and with python3
producer() { printf 'one\n'; sleep 1; echo '-- the producer waited' >&2; printf 'two\n'; }
verdict() {   # verdict LABEL COMMAND...
  local label=$1 out
  shift
  out=$( { producer | "$@" | while read -r line; do echo "got $line"; done; } 2>&1 )
  if [[ ${out,,} == "got one"* ]]; then verdict=streams; else verdict='holds back'; fi
  printf '%-32s %s\n' "$label" "$verdict"
}
cat > filter.py <<'EOF'
import sys
for line in sys.stdin:
    print(line, end="")
EOF
verdict 'mawk (fflush)'              mawk '{ print; fflush() }'
verdict 'mawk -W interactive'        mawk -W interactive '{ print }'
verdict 'stdbuf -oL mawk'            stdbuf -oL mawk '{ print }'
verdict 'gawk (fflush)'              gawk '{ print; fflush() }'
verdict 'python3'                    python3 filter.py
verdict 'python3 -u'                 python3 -u filter.py
verdict 'stdbuf -oL python3'         stdbuf -oL python3 filter.py

mawk (fflush)                    holds back
mawk -W interactive              streams
stdbuf -oL mawk                  holds back
gawk (fflush)                    streams
python3                          holds back
python3 -u                       streams
stdbuf -oL python3               holds back

mawk reads its input in blocks, so calling fflush() on its output is not enough: mawk -W interactive is its option, and gawk and macOS's awk stream with fflush(). Python buffers its own output rather than using the C library's, so python3 needs -u. And note the last row of each group: stdbuf did nothing for mawk or python3, which brings the next question.

stdbuf: changing another program's buffering

stdbuf runs a command with its standard streams' buffering changed: -o for output, -i for input and -e for error, each with 0 for unbuffered, L for line-buffered (not for input, where the tool says it is invalid), or a size such as 4K for fully buffered with that block. stdbuf -oL cut -d' ' -f3 is cut with a line-buffered output, and it is the one to use when the program has no option of its own. It has no magic of its own either, and the mechanism is visible:

# stdbuf changes nothing itself: it sets an environment variable and starts the command
stdbuf -oL env | grep '^_STDBUF'
stdbuf -o0 -e0 env | grep '^_STDBUF' | sort

_STDBUF_O=L
_STDBUF_E=0
_STDBUF_O=0

stdbuf sets an environment variable, _STDBUF_O for output, _STDBUF_E for error, and runs the command. On Linux, GNU's version also sets LD_PRELOAD to load a small library, libstdbuf.so, into the command, and that library reads the variable and calls setvbuf for the process before it starts. Both versions rest on the same fact: the program must be using the C library's standard I/O, and must not override it. GNU's own help says as much: a command that adjusts the buffering of its streams itself, tee for one, overrides stdbuf, and filters like dd and cat do not use streams for I/O and are unaffected. That is why the table showed it working on grep, cut and tr, and not on mawk or python3, which manage their own output; and it cannot make sort write before it has read.

The last rule is the one that surprises people: it changes one command's buffering, the one it starts, and a pipeline is a chain in which every stage that buffers holds the data up. This is the tail-and-filter pipeline from above, four ways:

producer() { printf 'ERROR one\n'; sleep 1; echo '-- the producer waited' >&2; printf 'ERROR two\n'; }
verdict() {
  local out
  out=$( { producer | "$@" | while read -r line; do echo "got $line"; done; } 2>&1 )
  if [[ $out == "got"* ]]; then echo "streams"; else echo "holds back"; fi
}
echo "grep | cut:                              $(verdict sh -c "grep ERROR | cut -d' ' -f2")"
echo "grep --line-buffered | cut:              $(verdict sh -c "grep --line-buffered ERROR | cut -d' ' -f2")"
echo "grep | stdbuf -oL cut:                   $(verdict sh -c "grep ERROR | stdbuf -oL cut -d' ' -f2")"
echo "both stages line-buffered:               $(verdict sh -c "grep --line-buffered ERROR | stdbuf -oL cut -d' ' -f2")"

grep | cut:                              holds back
grep --line-buffered | cut:              holds back
grep | stdbuf -oL cut:                   holds back
both stages line-buffered:               streams

Adding --line-buffered to the first stage, or stdbuf -oL to the second, left the chain holding back; only both together made it stream. Each stage passes the data on when its own buffer says to, and the last stage's output reaches the reader only after every earlier stage has released it.

Buffering is a throughput optimisation, and turning it off costs what it saved: a write per line instead of one per block. Use stdbuf, --line-buffered and fflush() where a person or a program is waiting for each line — a log being followed, a progress display, a coprocess that needs one answer per question (§17.11) — and leave a batch pipeline alone. It is also, incidentally, the reason a log that captures both output and error from a program can show an error before the output that led to it (§10.3): the error stream is unbuffered and the output stream is not.

21.7 When a Shell Script Is Too Slow: Criteria for Rewriting

Finding out where the time goes

A script that is too slow needs a diagnosis before a remedy, and the shell can give one. The xtrace of §20.12 prints every command as it runs, and a PS4 that begins with EPOCHREALTIME prefixes each line with the time it started, so a command lasts from its own timestamp to the next. The script below has three phases, one of which waits, and the awk program that follows reports the command before the longest gap:

cat > job.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
prepare() { local i; for ((i = 0; i < 300; i++)); do :; done; }
fetch()   { sleep 0.3; }
report()  { echo done; }
prepare
fetch
report
EOF

# Every traced command starts with the time it began, in microseconds
PS4='+ ${EPOCHREALTIME//[!0-9]/} ' bash -x job.sh 2> trace.txt > /dev/null

# A command lasts until the next one starts: report the line before the longest gap
awk '
  NR > 1 && $2 - previous > longest { longest = $2 - previous; line = text }
  { previous = $2; $1 = $2 = ""; text = substr($0, 3) }
  END { print "slowest command:", line }' trace.txt

slowest command: sleep 0.3

The slowest command was sleep 0.3 — a wait, not work, and something no rewrite would change. A profile like this answers the first question of §21.1 directly: is the script waiting, or working, and on what. For a loop, the gaps between lines are small and many, so the sum over identical commands is what matters, and Exercise 2 makes that change. strace -c gives the same picture for system calls on Linux, and time per phase is the cheapest version of all.

The order of remedies

There is an order in which to try things, and it is the order of how much each changes and how little it costs. First, decide whether the script is waiting or working (§21.1). Second, count the programs it starts (§15.1, §21.4), and remove every process that does less work than starting it costs. Third, batch what remains (§21.6): a program that takes many arguments should be given many. Fourth, replace a loop that reads a file with one tool that reads it (§21.5). Fifth, stop holding what can be streamed (§21.9). Sixth, add parallelism (§17): it multiplies throughput by the number of cores when the work is many independent items, and does nothing for a script whose cost is one process per item — that just starts the same processes on more cores. Only after these does the question of leaving shell come up, and it comes up much less often than it would have without them: a script that started ten thousand processes and now starts three does not need a rewrite.

A shell script that is too slow to fix: compute-bound work

Some slowness survives every remedy above because the work is computation, and the shell's interpreter is slow at computation. Bash parses a script into a tree of commands and walks the tree, expanding every word again each time a command runs; there is no compilation to machine code, no bytecode and no optimisation of a loop, and a loop that does arithmetic pays for that walk on every iteration. The example sums the squares of the first 300,000 integers in a bash loop and in one awk:

# micros COMMAND...: the best of three runs, in microseconds
micros() {
  local i start took best=
  for i in 1 2 3; do
    start=${EPOCHREALTIME//[!0-9]/}
    "$@" > /dev/null
    took=$(( ${EPOCHREALTIME//[!0-9]/} - start ))
    if [[ -z $best ]] || (( took < best )); then best=$took; fi
  done
  echo "$best"
}
# yn NUMBER: yes if the number is not zero, no if it is
yn() { if (( $1 )); then echo yes; else echo no; fi; }

sum_bash() { local i total=0; for ((i = 1; i <= 300000; i++)); do (( total += i * i )); done; echo "$total"; }
sum_awk()  { awk 'BEGIN { for (i = 1; i <= 300000; i++) total += i * i; printf "%d\n", total }'; }

echo "the same answer: $([[ $(sum_bash) == "$(sum_awk)" ]] && echo yes || echo no)"
slow=$(micros sum_bash); fast=$(micros sum_awk)
echo "the awk program is 10 times faster or more: $(yn "$(( slow >= 10 * fast ))")"

the same answer: yes
the awk program is 10 times faster or more: yes

The answers agree, and the awk program was at least ten times faster. The measured factor was about 30, and bash ran that loop at roughly a million iterations per second on both machines: 340 milliseconds for 300,000, a little over a microsecond for each one-statement iteration. That figure is the ceiling for computation written in shell, and a task that needs a hundred million operations is a task for another language, or for a tool that does the loop for you.

The cost of the replacement's own start-up

The natural next step is to move the slow part to Python, and here is the trap that a count of processes shows. A Python interpreter takes milliseconds to start; a shell loop that calls a Python one-liner per item pays that cost per item, which is worse than the basename it replaced:

# Linux only: what starting another interpreter costs, and what it buys
# micros COMMAND...: the best of three runs, in microseconds
micros() {
  local i start took best=
  for i in 1 2 3; do
    start=${EPOCHREALTIME//[!0-9]/}
    "$@" > /dev/null
    took=$(( ${EPOCHREALTIME//[!0-9]/} - start ))
    if [[ -z $best ]] || (( took < best )); then best=$took; fi
  done
  echo "$best"
}
# yn NUMBER: yes if the number is not zero, no if it is
yn() { if (( $1 )); then echo yes; else echo no; fi; }

loop_bash()   { local i total=0; for ((i = 1; i <= 300000; i++)); do (( total += i * i )); done; echo "$total"; }
loop_python() { python3 -c 'print(sum(i * i for i in range(1, 300001)))'; }
start_bash()   { bash -c :; }
start_python() { python3 -c pass; }
start_basename() { basename /a/b/c.txt; }

echo "python3 starts 3 times slower than bash or more: $(yn "$(( $(micros start_python) >= 3 * $(micros start_bash) ))")"
echo "python3 starts 5 times slower than basename or more: $(yn "$(( $(micros start_python) >= 5 * $(micros start_basename) ))")"
echo "the same answer: $([[ $(loop_bash) == "$(loop_python)" ]] && echo yes || echo no)"
echo "python3 does the loop 10 times faster or more: $(yn "$(( $(micros loop_bash) >= 10 * $(micros loop_python) ))")"

python3 starts 3 times slower than bash or more: yes
python3 starts 5 times slower than basename or more: yes
the same answer: yes
python3 does the loop 10 times faster or more: yes

On Debian, starting python3 cost about 6 ms against about 0.35 ms for bash — eighteen times as much — and the same loop that took bash 340 ms took Python about 13. The lesson is that the boundary matters. Move the loop, not the body: a python3 -c per line is a slower version of basename per line, and one Python program that reads the whole input and does all the work is a version 26 times faster than the shell loop. Start-up is paid once, and Python does the loop at its own speed.

The criteria for rewriting

A shell script is worth rewriting in another language when one of the following holds, and slowness alone is rarely enough, since the remedies above usually fix slowness. Each is a signal that the work has stopped being what shell is for (§1.6), and each has a threshold worth checking against the script in front of you:

The cost survives the remedies. After the process counts are down, the files are read once and the work is batched, the script still misses a budget — and the time is user, not waiting. Measure with §21.1's tools against a stated budget: a nightly job that takes three minutes is fine, and the same script inside a request that must answer in a second is not.
The data has structure the shell cannot hold. A list inside a map, a record with fields, a tree: §6.9's "one string per key" is the signal. When the answer to "how do I store this?" is a delimiter and a promise, the data has outgrown the language.
The numbers are not integers. Fractions, money, percentages, dates as arithmetic, or anything beyond 64 bits (§7.9). Each use of awk or bc for a calculation is a small admission; when the script is mostly those, it is a program in awk that is hiding in shell.
The input is a structured format. JSON, YAML, XML and CSV with quoting are formats to be parsed, not split. jq is the right tool for JSON inside a script that orchestrates; a script that spends most of its lines picking JSON apart is a reason to move.
It is long and it has logic. §1.6's hundred lines, counting lines that make decisions and not lines that run commands in order. Past that, the defects are in the interactions among parts, and shell is the language in which those are hardest to see and test.
Errors need context. A failure must carry the item, the step and the cause up to a caller that decides what to do. Shell has an exit status and a message on stderr (§11); a script that works around set -e in more than a few places is one whose error handling wants exceptions.
Concurrency shares state. A job pool of independent items is shell's (§17.5). Workers that share results, need a queue, or must be cancelled and retried independently are not.

Two things are not on the list. "The script is old" is not a criterion, and neither is "the team prefers another language" unless the team is the one that will maintain it, in which case it is a legitimate cost of the script's ownership and belongs on the list. And a slow script under its budget is not a script to rewrite: the effort is the cost, and the measurement is the evidence that it buys anything.

21.8 Rewriting in Another Language: Where to Cut

The honest test, applied

§1.6 gave the test: if the script's interesting content is which commands to run in what order, shell is right; if it is what to do with the data those commands produced, it is time to leave. The test rarely says to leave the whole script, because most scripts contain both. The log summariser of §21.5 does: reading the arguments, checking that the log is readable, choosing an exit status on failure and starting the program are all "which commands in what order"; counting bytes per status is "what to do with the data". They are different work and they have a seam between them.

The thin wrapper and the one program

The shape that follows is a thin wrapper: the shell keeps the interface — arguments, error messages, exit statuses, the environment — and starts one program that does the data work, once, on the whole input. The wrapper below keeps the command line of the shell versions from §21.5 and delegates the counting to Python:

cat > summarise.py <<'EOF'
import sys
from collections import defaultdict

totals = defaultdict(int)
for line in sys.stdin:
    ip, status, path, nbytes = line.split()
    totals[status] += int(nbytes)
for status in sorted(totals):
    print(status, totals[status])
EOF

cat > summarise.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# summarise.sh LOGFILE: bytes served per status. The shell keeps the interface; Python does the counting.
set -euo pipefail
usage() { echo "usage: ${0##*/} LOGFILE" >&2; exit 2; }
(( $# == 1 )) || usage
[[ -r $1 ]] || { echo "${0##*/}: cannot read $1" >&2; exit 1; }
exec python3 "${0%/*}/summarise.py" < "$1"
EOF
chmod +x summarise.sh

awk 'BEGIN { for (i = 1; i <= 500; i++)
  printf "10.0.0.%d %d /page/%d %d\n", i % 250, (i % 7 == 0 ? 404 : 200), i % 25, (i * 37) % 5000 }' > access.log

./summarise.sh access.log
awk '{ total[$2] += $4 } END { for (s in total) print s, total[s] }' access.log | sort > expected.txt
./summarise.sh access.log | cmp - expected.txt && echo "same output as the awk version"

./summarise.sh; echo "status $?"
./summarise.sh missing.log; echo "status $?"

200 1017246
404 167004
same output as the awk version
usage: summarise.sh LOGFILE
status 2
summarise.sh: cannot read missing.log
status 1

The wrapper is nine lines, and it does what shell is good at: it checks its arguments and gives a usage message and status 2, it checks that the file is readable and says which one isn't, and it execs the program so that Python's exit status is its own. The Python program is eight lines, and it does what Python is good at, on the whole input in one process. The three outputs show the contract: the same two lines for the same input as the awk version, cmp silent, and the two failures with the statuses and messages they had before.

Keep the seam narrow. Pass the input on standard input, and any option as a plain argument, not spliced into the source of a python3 -c string: building program text out of shell variables is the injection problem of §18.2 in a new costume. Let the program read and write the streams and return an exit status, and it can be tested, benchmarked and replaced without the wrapper knowing.

Rewriting safely: the old script is the test

The strongest test a rewrite has is the script it replaces. Run both on the same real inputs and compare the output byte for byte, as the example did with cmp; keep the old script beside the new one until they have agreed on a representative set, including the inputs that were awkward the first time. Write the wrapper's tests in the framework of §20.8 — arguments, statuses and messages are what the callers depend on — and time both with hyperfine (§21.1) so that the rewrite is shown to be faster rather than assumed to be. Rewrite the hot part first: the profile of §21.7 says which part it is, and often one function is the whole cost. A rewrite that replaces the loop that took 95 per cent of the time and leaves the other 400 lines of shell alone is a smaller change, a cheaper review and a smaller thing to get wrong.

What not to rewrite

The opposite mistake is as expensive. A script that runs six tools in order, checks each status and cleans up is a shell script, and turned into Python it becomes six subprocess.run calls with their arguments, checks and cleanup written out longer than before. The rewrite pays for itself where there is data to process, and does not where there is none. And a script whose slowness §21.4 through §21.6 would have removed should have those applied first: nothing is gained by porting a loop that starts ten thousand processes into a language where it is a loop that starts ten thousand processes.

21.9 Memory Use of a Shell Script

What a shell holds in memory

A shell script's memory is what its variables hold, and the shell holds them differently from the way the file on disk did. Two things multiply the size of data as it enters the shell. A command substitution builds the command's whole output in a buffer, then copies it into the variable. And an array stores each element as its own allocation with bookkeeping around it, so an array of small strings costs many times what its text does. The measurement uses a file of the numbers 1 to 1,000,000 — 6.9 megabytes — and a fresh shell for each snippet, so that memory freed by an earlier one is not reused and hides the growth of a later one. ps -o rss= reports the shell's resident memory in kilobytes, and only the comparison is printed:

# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the snippets are code for a fresh shell, not text to expand
seq 1 1000000 > numbers.txt
size=$(( $(wc -c < numbers.txt) / 1024 ))          # the file's size in KB

# growth SNIPPET: how much the resident memory of a fresh shell grew, in KB
growth() {
  bash -c 'rss() { ps -o rss= -p $$; }
           before=$(rss); eval "$1"; after=$(rss); echo $(( after - before ))' _ "$1"
}
yn() { if (( $1 )); then echo yes; else echo no; fi; }

g=$(growth 'x=$(< numbers.txt)')
echo "x=\$(< file)      holds the whole file:            $(yn "$(( g >= size ))")"
g=$(growth 'while read -r line; do :; done < numbers.txt')
echo "while read       grows by under 2 MB:             $(yn "$(( g < 2048 ))")"
g=$(growth 'mapfile -t lines < numbers.txt')
echo "mapfile          grows by 5 times the file or more: $(yn "$(( g >= 5 * size ))")"
g=$(growth 'declare -A seen; while read -r line; do seen[$line]=1; done < numbers.txt')
echo "associative map  grows by 8 times the file or more: $(yn "$(( g >= 8 * size ))")"
g=$(growth 'sort numbers.txt | tail -n 1 > /dev/null')
echo "sort | tail      grows by under 2 MB:             $(yn "$(( g < 2048 ))")"
g=$(growth 's=; for ((i = 0; i < 1000000; i++)); do s+=x; done')
echo "a 1 MB string    grows by under 3 MB:             $(yn "$(( g < 3072 ))")"

x=$(< file)      holds the whole file:            yes
while read       grows by under 2 MB:             yes
mapfile          grows by 5 times the file or more: yes
associative map  grows by 8 times the file or more: yes
sort | tail      grows by under 2 MB:             yes
a 1 MB string    grows by under 3 MB:             yes

The variable holding the file cost at least the file's size, and the measured figure was about twice it: 15 MB on macOS and 13 on Debian, for a 6.9 MB file. mapfile cost at least five times the file's size; the measured growth was 46 MB and 76 MB, seven to eleven times. An associative array of the same lines cost at least eight times; it was 72 MB and 114 MB, ten to seventeen times. The overhead is per element and not per byte: an array of a million one-character strings, built with a+=(x), grew the shell by 46 MB on macOS and 76 MB on Debian — 46 to 76 bytes to hold each character. A million-character string, built by appending, grew it by one megabyte. So a value costs about what it looks like when it is one string, and many times more when it is many elements. The same tool that made a script fast in §21.5 costs memory here: mapfile is the fastest way to read a file, and holds the most of it.

Streaming instead of holding

The cure is the one that has run through this section: process the data where it flows instead of collecting it. The while read loop over the file grew the shell by under two megabytes — it holds one line at a time, the file's size is irrelevant — and sort numbers.txt | tail -n 1 grew the shell by the same, because the data moves through the pipe and the sorting happens in another process. A pipeline's stages each hold what they need, and the pipe between them is bounded, so the shell that connects them stays small however large the data. That is a design rule as much as an optimisation: a script that reads a file to summarise it should stream it, and reserve the array for data that is to be indexed or looped over more than once.

Exercise 3 is exactly that change, on a file of 300,000 lines: the script that loads the file into an array grows by more than three times the file, the one that reads it a line at a time by less than the file, and both print the same totals.

Memory that is freed is not returned

unset frees a variable, and the shell can reuse the memory, but it does not necessarily hand it back to the system, so the resident size does not fall:

seq 1 1000000 > numbers.txt
bash -c '
  rss() { ps -o rss= -p $$; }
  mapfile -t lines < numbers.txt
  peak=$(rss)
  unset lines
  after=$(rss)
  if (( 10 * after >= 9 * peak )); then echo "after unset, the shell still holds 90% of its peak: yes"; else echo "after unset, the shell still holds 90% of its peak: no"; fi
  echo "the array is gone: ${#lines[@]} elements"
'

after unset, the shell still holds 90% of its peak: yes
the array is gone: 0 elements

After the array was unset, the shell still held 90 per cent of its peak. That is measured for the array on both macOS and Debian; a large string was returned on Debian and kept on macOS, since it depends on how the system's allocator treats big blocks. The consequence is for long-running scripts: a script that loads a large structure, uses it and unsets it has a resident size that stays at its peak, and a daemon that does this repeatedly stays at the peak. The way to give the memory back is to do the work in a subshell or a child process, which exits and returns everything it held: ( mapfile … ) for a step that needs a big array once.

Limits: ulimit -v, and what bash does when an allocation fails

ulimit -v caps a process's virtual memory in kilobytes, which is a way to make a runaway script fail rather than exhaust the machine. It works on Linux, and what happens at the limit is worth seeing, because bash does not recover:

# Linux only: cap the shell's address space at about 40 MB and load a 1,000,000-line file
# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # the data is loaded only to see whether it fits
seq 1 1000000 > numbers.txt
( ulimit -v 40000; mapfile -t lines < numbers.txt; echo "mapfile finished" ); echo "exit status $?"
( ulimit -v 40000; x=$(< numbers.txt); echo "\$(< file) finished: ${#x} characters" ); echo "exit status $?"
( ulimit -v 40000; while read -r _; do :; done < numbers.txt; echo "the loop finished" ); echo "exit status $?"

example.sh: xmalloc: cannot allocate 32 bytes
exit status 2
$(< file) finished: 6888895 characters
exit status 0
the loop finished
exit status 0

With about 40 MB of address space, loading a million-line file into an array died: xmalloc: cannot allocate 32 bytes, exit status 2, and no chance for the script to handle it — bash aborts when an allocation fails, since nothing it holds can be trusted after that. The same file read into one string fitted, and the streaming loop did not notice the limit. On macOS the experiment cannot be run: ulimit -v, -m and -d refuse to be lowered (Invalid argument), so a memory cap there is a job for the process supervisor and not for the script. The other limit on memory is ARG_MAX, which is the subject of §21.6: arguments passed to a program are held in the kernel's copy, and there is a ceiling.

Measuring memory

Three ways, in order of convenience. ps -o rss= -p PID prints a running process's resident set size in kilobytes and works the same on macOS and Linux; a script can ask about itself with $$, as the examples do. The /usr/bin/time program reports the peak for a command it runs: on macOS, /usr/bin/time -l command prints "maximum resident set size" in bytes, and on Linux GNU time, packaged as time, prints it with -v in kilobytes, as "Maximum resident set size". Peak is the number to watch: the resident size at any moment can be lower than the highest it reached, as unset showed. And hyperfine reports times only, so memory is measured separately from speed; the two need not agree, and the faster form is often the one that holds more.

21.10 The Performance Table

Cost or technique
What it means, and the detail that bites
time, TIMEFORMAT
A reserved word: times pipelines, compound commands, builtins and functions. real far above user + sys means waiting, not working; -p is the POSIX layout (§21.1).
${EPOCHREALTIME//[!0-9]/}
Microseconds since 1970 in any locale; the locale's decimal separator breaks ${EPOCHREALTIME/./}, and $(( )) reads a comma as the comma operator (§21.1).
Best of several, then a ratio
Noise only adds time, so keep the minimum; compare a factor, not a duration; check the outputs agree (§21.1).
hyperfine -N
Warm-up, runs, mean ± σ and a summary; -N skips the shell and its calibration; a failing command stops it unless -i (§21.1).
fork and exec
A builtin costs microseconds, a substitution a fork, a program a fork and an exec; about 0.4 ms and 1 ms on the macOS machine measured (§21.2).
The environment
Every exec copies it: 600 KB exported doubled the cost of a program. On Linux a fork also costs more the more the shell holds (§21.2).
type -t, enable -n, enable -f
Which of builtin and program a name is; a loadable builtin saves the exec, not the fork of a substitution (§21.3).
$(< f), printf -v, read <<<
The forms that make no fork: at least 10 to 50 times cheaper than $(cat f), $(printf) and echo | read (§21.3).
f() ( … ), ( … ), a pipeline stage
A fork each. Worth it for isolation, not inside a loop of a hundred thousand (§21.3).
A process per item
10,000 lines: 11 s with basename, 50 ms with ${p##*/}, 6 ms with one sed (macOS). Replace a process that does less work than starting it costs (§21.4).
seq, {1..n}, for ((…))
seq is one program per loop, {1..1000000} holds 180–270 MB, the C-style loop holds nothing; brace ranges cannot take variables (§21.4).
expr, bc, awk per iteration
$(( )) for integers; one awk or bc over the whole dataset for the rest (§21.4, §21.5).
while read < file and | while read
A file: one read and two lseek per line. A pipe: one read per byte, and mapfile too (§21.5).
mapfile
30 to 40 times faster than an appending loop, and several times the file's size in memory (§21.5, §21.9).
${s:i:1} in a loop
Quadratic: doubling the string quadruples the time. read -n 1, or an array built once, is linear (§21.5).
One awk, grep -c, sort | uniq -c
1,501 programs became 1 or 2 with the same output. Which single tool is fastest depends on the machine: measure it (§21.5).
find -exec … +, xargs, -n
A thousand files: a thousand runs with \; or -n 1, one with +. ARG_MAX is why xargs exists (§21.6).
>> file inside a loop
An open per iteration: 1,005 against 6. Redirect the loop (§21.6).
stdio buffering
A pipe is block-buffered. grep --line-buffered, sed -u, fflush(), python3 -u, mawk -W interactive, stdbuf -oL (not for python3, mawk, sort); every stage must stream (§21.6).
A PS4 with EPOCHREALTIME
A profile from bash -x: a command lasts until the next timestamp; add identical commands up (§21.7).
The order of remedies
Waiting or working; count programs; batch; one tool per file; stream; parallelise (§17); only then leave shell (§21.7).
When to leave shell
Cost survives the remedies; data with structure; non-integers; structured formats; long with logic; errors that need context; concurrency that shares state (§21.7).
Thin wrapper, one program
The shell keeps arguments, messages and exit statuses; one program does the data, once, on stdin. The old script is the test (§21.8).
ps -o rss= -p, time -l, time -v
Resident size in KB; peak in bytes on macOS, in KB with GNU time. A string is what it looks like; an array element costs 46–76 bytes; unset does not return memory; ulimit -v works on Linux and bash aborts at it (§21.9).

The order of use, when a script is slow: measure whether it is waiting or working, count the programs it starts, remove or batch them, give a file to one tool instead of a loop, stream what does not need holding, and only then ask whether the work is still the kind shell is for. Each step is cheap, each is measured with a count or a ratio and not a stopwatch, and together they turn most "too slow for shell" scripts into ordinary ones.

Exercises

1. Count, then remove. original.sh reads a manifest and prints each path's directory and its lower-cased file name. Count the programs it starts on a 100-line manifest, then write a version that starts none and prints exactly the same output. A colleague proposes piping the whole loop's output through a single tr instead — is that a fix?

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# original.sh MANIFEST
while read -r path; do
  dir=$(dirname "$path")
  file=$(basename "$path")
  lower=$(echo "$file" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')
  echo "$dir $lower"
done < "$1"
Solution

The spies count programs (§15.1) for the original, the fixed script and the colleague's proposal, and cmp compares what each prints:

# Spies: each logs its own name to calls.log, then runs the real tool
mkdir spy
for tool in basename dirname tr; do
  printf '#!/bin/sh\necho %s >> "%s/calls.log"\nexec %s "$@"\n' \
    "$tool" "$PWD" "$(command -v "$tool")" > "spy/$tool"
  chmod +x "spy/$tool"
done
: > calls.log
programs() { mapfile -t log < calls.log; : > calls.log; echo "${#log[@]}"; }

for ((i = 1; i <= 100; i++)); do echo "/srv/Media/Photos/IMG_$i.JPG"; done > manifest.txt

cat > original.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
while read -r path; do
  dir=$(dirname "$path")
  file=$(basename "$path")
  lower=$(echo "$file" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')
  echo "$dir $lower"
done < "$1"
EOF

cat > fixed.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
while read -r path; do
  file=${path##*/}
  echo "${path%/*} ${file,,}"
done < "$1"
EOF

# The tempting fix lowercases the whole line: one tr for the file, but the directory changes too
cat > tempting.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
while read -r path; do
  echo "${path%/*} ${path##*/}"
done < "$1" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]'
EOF

for version in original fixed tempting; do
  PATH=$PWD/spy:$PATH bash "$version.sh" manifest.txt > "$version.out"
  printf '%-9s %3d programs   first line: %s\n' "$version" "$(programs)" "$(head -n 1 "$version.out")"
done
for version in fixed tempting; do
  if cmp -s original.out "$version.out"; then echo "$version output is identical"; else echo "$version output DIFFERS"; fi
done

original  300 programs   first line: /srv/Media/Photos img_1.jpg
fixed       0 programs   first line: /srv/Media/Photos img_1.jpg
tempting    1 programs   first line: /srv/media/photos img_1.jpg
fixed output is identical
tempting output DIFFERS

The original started 300 programs: dirname, basename and tr for every line of the manifest, a hundred in all. The fixed version started none, using ${path%/*} for the directory, ${path##*/} for the file name and ${file,,} to lower-case it — the parameter expansions of §5.4 and §5.6 — and its output is identical. The colleague's proposal starts one program and is not a fix: tr sees the whole line, so it lower-cased the directory too (/srv/media/photos where the original printed /srv/Media/Photos), and the output differs. It is the classic trap of a performance change: the count went down and the answer changed. A rewrite is right only when the output is compared, which is what cmp -s in the last lines did. (${file,,} needs bash 4; §19.4 has the POSIX alternative for sh scripts.)

2. Find the command that costs the most. The trace-and-report of §21.7 named the longest single gap, which is the wrong question for a loop. nightly.sh adds 2,000 numbers with expr and then sleeps briefly. Extend the report so that it adds up the time of identical commands (treat digits as interchangeable), and say which command costs the most in total.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# shellcheck disable=SC2003  # expr is the process being profiled
total=0
for ((i = 0; i < 2000; i++)); do total=$(expr "$total" + "$i"); done
sleep 0.05
echo "$total"
Solution

Charge each command the time until the next one starts, mask the digits so that expr 1 + 1 and expr 2 + 1 are the same command, add up, and print the largest:

cat > nightly.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# shellcheck disable=SC2003  # expr is the process being profiled
total=0
for ((i = 0; i < 2000; i++)); do total=$(expr "$total" + "$i"); done
sleep 0.05
echo "$total"
EOF

PS4='+ ${EPOCHREALTIME//[!0-9]/} ' bash -x nightly.sh 2> trace.txt > /dev/null

# Charge each command the time until the next one starts, and add up identical commands
awk '
  function charge() { if (text != "") cost[text] += $2 - began }
  { charge(); began = $2; $1 = $2 = ""; text = substr($0, 3); gsub(/[0-9]+/, "N", text) }
  END { for (t in cost) print cost[t], t }' trace.txt | sort -rn | head -n 1 |
  awk '{ $1 = ""; print "the command that took longest in total:" $0 }'

the command that took longest in total: expr N + N

expr N + N — 2,000 programs started in the loop — cost more in total than the single sleep, although no one of them was the longest gap. That is the answer the loop hides from a per-line report, and the remedy is §21.4's: total=$((total + i)). A profile of a loop is the sum over lines, not the maximum. Note what the trace itself does to the timing: bash -x writes a line per command, so a traced run is slower than a plain one, and the ranking is what a profile gives you, not the durations.

3. Stream it. loaded.sh totals the second column per key, and on a 300,000-line file it holds the entire file in an array first. Rewrite it so its memory does not grow with the file, and show — with ps -o rss= and the growth helper of §21.9 — that it did not, and that the totals are unchanged.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Total per key, holding the whole file in an array first
mapfile -t lines < "$1"
declare -A total
for line in "${lines[@]}"; do
  read -r key value <<< "$line"
  (( total[$key] += value ))
done
for key in "${!total[@]}"; do echo "$key ${total[$key]}"; done | sort -n
Solution

Read the file a line at a time, and keep only the totals — one entry per key, a thousand keys, not 300,000 lines:

seq 1 300000 | awk '{ printf "%d %d\n", $1 % 1000, $1 }' > pairs.txt
size=$(( $(wc -c < pairs.txt) / 1024 ))

cat > loaded.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Total per key, holding the whole file in an array first
mapfile -t lines < "$1"
declare -A total
for line in "${lines[@]}"; do
  read -r key value <<< "$line"
  (( total[$key] += value ))
done
for key in "${!total[@]}"; do echo "$key ${total[$key]}"; done | sort -n
EOF

cat > streamed.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# The same totals, one line at a time
declare -A total
while read -r key value; do
  (( total[$key] += value ))
done < "$1"
for key in "${!total[@]}"; do echo "$key ${total[$key]}"; done | sort -n
EOF

growth() {
  bash -c 'rss() { ps -o rss= -p $$; }
           before=$(rss); source "$1" pairs.txt > "$2"; after=$(rss); echo $(( after - before ))' _ "$1" "$2"
}
yn() { if (( $1 )); then echo yes; else echo no; fi; }
a=$(growth ./loaded.sh loaded.out); b=$(growth ./streamed.sh streamed.out)
echo "loaded:   grew by more than 3 times the file: $(yn "$(( a > 3 * size ))")"
echo "streamed: grew by less than the file:        $(yn "$(( b < size ))")"
cmp -s loaded.out streamed.out && echo "identical output"
head -n 2 streamed.out

loaded:   grew by more than 3 times the file: yes
streamed: grew by less than the file:        yes
identical output
0 45150000
1 44850300

The loaded version grew the shell by more than three times the file's size and the streamed one by less than the file's size, and the two printed identical totals. The rewrite also removed a read <<< per line, so it is faster as well as smaller. The associative array is still there, and correctly: what it holds is the answer, which is bounded by the number of distinct keys, and not the input.

4. Why does the monitor say nothing? watch.sh follows a log and prints the first word of each error, in capitals. It prints nothing until minutes after the errors happen. Explain why, and make it print each line as it arrives, changing as little as possible.

tail -f app.log | grep ERROR | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]' | cut -c1-9
Solution

tail writes each line as it is appended, but every stage after it writes to a pipe, and a program writing to a pipe buffers its output until a block is full (§21.6). grep, tr and cut each do, so the first errors sit in the first buffer until enough have accumulated, and whatever is in the last buffer is what the reader sees. The producer here writes a line, waits, and writes another; the four versions differ in how many stages have been told not to hold back:

producer() { printf 'ERROR disk\n'; sleep 1; echo '-- the producer waited' >&2; printf 'ERROR net\n'; }
verdict() {
  local out
  out=$( { producer | sh -c "$1" | while read -r line; do echo "got $line"; done; } 2>&1 )
  if [[ $out == "got"* ]]; then echo "streams"; else echo "holds back"; fi
}
echo "original:                    $(verdict "grep ERROR | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]' | cut -c1-9")"
echo "grep fixed:                  $(verdict "grep --line-buffered ERROR | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]' | cut -c1-9")"
echo "grep and tr fixed:           $(verdict "grep --line-buffered ERROR | stdbuf -oL tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]' | cut -c1-9")"
echo "every stage fixed:           $(verdict "grep --line-buffered ERROR | stdbuf -oL tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]' | stdbuf -oL cut -c1-9")"

original:                    holds back
grep fixed:                  holds back
grep and tr fixed:           holds back
every stage fixed:           streams

Fixing grep was not enough, and neither was fixing grep and tr: the chain streamed only when every buffering stage did. The version to write is tail -f app.log | grep --line-buffered ERROR | stdbuf -oL tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]' | stdbuf -oL cut -c1-9. tail needs no change because it writes each line as it reads it; and the last stage matters because its output is a pipe to whatever reads the result. sed -u in place of tr would also work if the transformation could be written as a substitution, and stdbuf is the general tool. And when the reader is a person at a terminal, the last stage is line-buffered already, since a terminal is not a pipe.

SECTION 22

Style, Architecture and the Capstone

Every earlier section taught a piece: how a line is parsed, how to quote, how to fail, how to test. A script that uses all of them correctly can still be miserable to inherit, because the pieces have to fit together in a shape someone else can read, change and trust. That shape is what this section is about, in two halves. Style is the part a machine can mostly enforce: how a file is laid out, indented and wrapped, what names mean, what comments say and where. Architecture is the part it cannot: what a script's functions are for, where its input and output happen, how it behaves when it is run twice, how a caller can tell what it did. Both come down to one aim, that the next person to open the file — including you, in a year — can predict what a line does before running it.

The style half follows one document. The Google Shell Style Guide is the most complete public statement of how a large organisation writes shell, and §1.6 already used its rule about when to stop, and §9.12 its naming and layout. It was fetched again for this section on 2026-09-25, and every rule attributed to it below was checked against its text rather than remembered. It is a set of decisions somebody made so that nobody has to argue about them again, and its own closing section says so: many of its rules "boil down to 'Just pick one and stop worrying about it'". The course follows it except where it says so, and §22.1 lists the places.

The architecture half is built by doing it. §22.6 writes an idempotent deployment script with a dry run — the run wrapper that §6.14 promised — §22.7 writes library files that are safe to source, §22.8 tests a command's contract, and §22.9 and §22.10 take a tangled script apart and prove, with a recorded output, that the pieces still do what it did. §22.11 is the decision to stop using shell, which §1.6 and §21.7 prepared. §22.12 is the capstone: logsum, a complete command with a library, options, tests, formatting rules and a Makefile, built to everything in the course and checked by five tools that all have to be quiet.

Some ground is owned elsewhere and is used here without repeating it. §9.12 has the naming and function-comment rules as a list, and §9.14 the main guard; §11.4 has exit-status conventions and sysexits.h; §13.6 has the long-option parser the capstone uses and §13.9 the help text; §16.3 has the environment; §20 has ShellCheck, bats-core and the debugging tools. This section adds what they lacked: the measurements that show why each rule exists, the tool that enforces it, and the places the rules interact.

Every example was run. The tools are ShellCheck 0.11.0, bats-core 1.14.0 and shfmt 3.14.1 on macOS under bash 5.3, and the same commands on Debian under bash 5.2 with shfmt 3.8.0.

22.1 The Google Shell Style Guide, and Where This Course Departs from It

The Google shell style guide: what it covers

The guide has nine parts, and it helps to have them in one list because the rest of this section is organised around the same ground. Background says which shell to use and when to use shell at all. Shell Files and Interpreter Invocation covers file extensions and bans SUID. Environment is one rule: error messages go to standard error. Comments covers the file header, function comments, implementation comments and TODOs. Formatting covers indentation, line length, pipelines, control flow, case, variable expansion and quoting. Features and Bugs is the longest: ShellCheck, $(…) over backticks, [[ … ]], string tests, wildcards, eval, arrays, pipes to while, arithmetic. Aliases, Naming Conventions and Calling Commands (return values, builtins over external commands) follow, and a last section says to be consistent.

Nothing in it is a language feature. It is advice about which of the many equivalent spellings to use, and where it gives a reason the reason is almost always one this course has measured: [[ because no word splitting or pathname expansion happens inside it (§7.2), a pipe into while because it creates a subshell (§16.8), ./* because a file may be named -r (§15.11), arithmetic because expr is a program (§21.4). That is why the course can follow it without arguing each rule again.

When to use shell, and when not to use shell

The guide's answer to when to use shell is four sentences long and is the shortest statement of §1.6. Shell should only be used for small utilities or simple wrapper scripts. If you are mostly calling other utilities and doing relatively little data manipulation, shell is an acceptable choice. If performance matters, use something other than shell. And "if you are writing a script that is more than 100 lines long, or that uses non-straightforward control flow logic, you should rewrite it in a more structured language now. Bear in mind that scripts grow. Rewrite your script early to avoid a more time-consuming rewrite at a later date." A last guideline asks for the judgement to be made by considering whether the code is easily maintainable by people other than its author.

Each of those is a rule about shell as a language, and each has a place in this course. Shell as a language has one data type and a process for a function call, which is why the rules exist; as a glue language it is unmatched, and the first rule says what a glue language is for: its job is to connect programs that do the work, and it is best when it is nearly all glue, connecting and little else. The second and third are the decision §21 measured: the performance rule is right about computation and too strong about the rest, because §21.4 through §21.6 removed most of what makes a script slow without leaving shell, and what remains is the compute-bound work of §21.7. The fourth is the structured language the guide wants a long script rewritten in — one with data structures, exceptions and a type checker — and §21.7 turned the vague "non-straightforward" into criteria. The guide's last clause is the one to hold on to: scripts grow. A shell prototype is a fine thing to write, and the mistake is not writing it but leaving it in production while it acquires requirements: a shell prototype that works is the dangerous kind, because it is the one that never gets its rewrite.

The 100 lines rule

The 100 lines rule is a heuristic, and the useful question is what it counts. Comments and blank lines are not complexity, and a hundred lines of case branches that each run one command are simpler than forty lines that nest three loops. Counting lines that are neither blank nor comments is the fairer measure, and §22.12 does it for the capstone: its command is 77 such lines and its library 42, so a tool that does something real and is written to this section's standards crosses the guide's hundred lines. That is not a contradiction of the rule, and §22.11 returns to what to conclude from it. The rule says rewrite now, and the honest use of it is as an alarm: when a script passes a hundred lines, ask §21.7's questions on purpose, once, and record the answer.

Bash as the portability target

The guide says "Bash is the only shell scripting language permitted for executables", and that executables must start with #!/bin/bash and use set for their options, so that bash script_name does not change what they do. From that it concludes that there is no need to strive for POSIX compatibility or to avoid bashisms, because bash is installed on every machine it cares about. Both halves depend on a fact about the fleet. On a fleet where /bin/bash is one known version, #!/bin/bash is right and a portability target narrower than bash is wasted effort. On a laptop, /bin/bash may be 3.2 from 2007 (§1.2), and #!/usr/bin/env bash finds the first bash on PATH instead (§1.4). The course's position is the guide's with the premise stated: pick the target for the machines you control, write down which it is, and use sh and §19's discipline only where a script must run under a shell you did not choose.

Script file extension: executable script and library

The rule for the script file extension is short and has three cases. An executable script should have a .sh extension or none. If a build rule renames it, use .sh in the source so that foo.sh builds to foo; if it is going straight onto a user's PATH, use none, since "it is not necessary to know what language a program is written in when executing it". Libraries "must have a .sh extension and should not be executable". That is the layout of the capstone, bin/logsum and lib/logsum.sh, and it makes the two roles visible in a directory listing. The guide also forbids SUID and SGID on shell scripts, for the reasons §18.19 measured: use sudo instead.

Which tool checks which rule

Most of the guide can be checked mechanically, and by different tools, so a project that wants its rules kept needs to know which tool keeps which. This script breaks the guide in several ways at once — a tab, backticks, unquoted variables, a test of $?, a line over 80 columns, a TODO with no owner, no header comment, no main — and asks the three standard tools what they see:

# A script that breaks the guide in several ways; the third line is indented with a tab
cat > backup.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/bin/bash
function backup {
	files=`ls $1`
  for f in $files; do cp $f /backup/$f; done
  if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then echo ok; fi
  echo "a message that runs on past the eightieth column of the terminal and keeps on"
}
backup /data  # TODO clean up
END_OF_FILE

echo "ShellCheck:       $(shellcheck -f gcc backup.sh | sed 's/.*\[\(SC[0-9]*\)\]$/\1/' | sort -u | paste -sd' ' -)"
echo "shfmt -i 2 -d:    $(shfmt -i 2 -d backup.sh | grep -c '^-[^-]') lines would change"
echo "awk, 80 columns:  $(awk 'length > 80' backup.sh | wc -l | tr -d ' ') line too long"

ShellCheck:       SC2006 SC2086 SC2181
shfmt -i 2 -d:    2 lines would change
awk, 80 columns:  1 line too long

ShellCheck found the three things it is built for: backticks (SC2006), the unquoted expansions (SC2086) and the indirect test of $? (SC2181). shfmt would rewrite two lines: it fixed the tab, turned the backticks into $(…) (so it also cleared the SC2006 that ShellCheck reported), and put the trailing comment one space from the command. A four-line awk found the one line that is too long. Nobody found the missing file header, the missing function comment, the missing main, or the TODO with no owner. Those need a tool that is not on the standard list, or a reviewer; §22.4 and §22.5 measure the rules, and §22.12 writes the small checker that covers them.
