The point to take from this subsection is the division: ShellCheck for the language, shfmt for the layout, a length check and a custom lint for the conventions, and a person for the rest.

22.2 Formatting: Indentation of Two Spaces, Line Length 80, Pipelines and Control Flow

Indentation of two spaces

The guide's rule is "Indent 2 spaces. No tabs", with the single exception that the body of a <<- here document is indented with tabs. Nobody should apply it by hand. shfmt rewrites a shell file into a canonical layout, and its default is not this one: with no options it indents with tabs. Three settings turn it into the guide's, and this messy script shows all three:

# The first line of the body is indented with a tab, the rest with assorted spaces
cat > messy.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/bin/bash
main(){
	if [[ -f $1 ]];then
    echo yes
      fi
  case $1 in
  a) echo a;;
  b)
   echo b
   ;;
  esac
  cat access.log | grep -v health | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq -c > counts.txt
}
main "$@"
END_OF_FILE

echo "== shfmt with no options (tabs shown as <tab>)"
shfmt messy.sh | awk '{ gsub(/\t/, "<tab>") } 1' | sed -n 2,7p
echo "== shfmt -i 2: two spaces"
shfmt -i 2 messy.sh | sed -n 2,7p
echo "== shfmt -i 2 -ci -sr: case alternatives indented, a space after > and <"
shfmt -i 2 -ci -sr messy.sh | sed -n 5,12p

== shfmt with no options (tabs shown as <tab>)
main() {
<tab>if [[ -f $1 ]]; then
<tab><tab>echo yes
<tab>fi
<tab>case $1 in
<tab>a) echo a ;;
== shfmt -i 2: two spaces
main() {
  if [[ -f $1 ]]; then
    echo yes
  fi
  case $1 in
  a) echo a ;;
== shfmt -i 2 -ci -sr: case alternatives indented, a space after > and <
  fi
  case $1 in
    a) echo a ;;
    b)
      echo b
      ;;
  esac
  cat access.log | grep -v health | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq -c > counts.txt

With no options the body was indented with tabs, and a case alternative sat level with the case. -i 2 changed the indentation to two spaces. -ci indented the alternatives one level under case, which is the guide's layout, and -sr put a space after > and <, the way this course writes > file. Notice what shfmt did not do: the long pipeline on the last line was left long, since it fixes layout and never wraps.

The flags are better kept in a file than remembered. shfmt reads an .editorconfig, the format most editors already honour, so the same settings apply in the editor, in the pre-commit hook and in CI:

cat > .editorconfig <<'END_OF_FILE'
root = true

[*]
indent_style = space
indent_size = 2
switch_case_indent = true
binary_next_line = true
space_redirects = true
END_OF_FILE
cat > tool.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/bin/bash
main(){
    case $1 in
    a) echo a;;
    esac
    echo done>log
}
END_OF_FILE

shfmt -l tool.sh
shfmt -d tool.sh > /dev/null; echo "-d finds a difference; exit $?"
shfmt -w tool.sh
shfmt -d tool.sh; echo "after -w: exit $?"
cat tool.sh

tool.sh
-d finds a difference; exit 1
after -w: exit 0
#!/bin/bash
main() {
  case $1 in
    a) echo a ;;
  esac
  echo done > log
}

-l lists a file that would change, and -d prints the difference and exits 1 when there is one. (Bash-side detail that depends on the version: shfmt 3.14, on macOS, also exits 1 for -l, and the 3.8 that Debian packages does not, so gate on -d.) -w rewrites the file, and after it -d is silent and exits 0. Those exit statuses are what make it a gate (§20.6): shfmt -d in a Makefile fails the build on a badly formatted file. The <<- exception keeps working, since shfmt leaves a tab-indented here-document body alone:

# <<- removes leading tabs from the body and the delimiter, and nothing else
printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' 'usage() {' > usage.sh
printf '\tcat <<-END_OF_USAGE\n\t\tusage: tool FILE\n\t\t  -h  show this help\n\tEND_OF_USAGE\n}\nusage\n' >> usage.sh
bash usage.sh
echo "shfmt -i 2 leaves the tab-indented body alone: $(shfmt -i 2 usage.sh | grep -c "$(printf '\t\tusage')")"

usage: tool FILE
  -h  show this help
shfmt -i 2 leaves the tab-indented body alone: 1

<<- removed the leading tabs from the body and from the delimiter line, and only tabs, so an editor that turned them into spaces would break the here document. That is the one place the guide permits a tab, and it is the reason shfmt -i 2 does not touch those lines.

There is one place where shfmt and the guide's own examples disagree, and the tool wins in a repository that enforces it. The guide writes (( x > 3 )) and $(( 2 + 2 )) with spaces inside the parentheses. shfmt removes them:

cat > arith.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/bin/bash
if (( $# > 1 )); then echo "two or more"; fi
x=$(( 2 + 2 ))
END_OF_FILE
shfmt -i 2 arith.sh

#!/bin/bash
if (($# > 1)); then echo "two or more"; fi
x=$((2 + 2))

(($# > 1)) and $((2 + 2)) are what the formatter writes, and the capstone's code is written that way. The guide's own advice for a case like this is the last of its rules: be consistent, and let automation decide a matter no argument settles.

Line length 80

"Maximum line length is 80 characters." The reason is practical: an 80-column file can be read in a terminal, in two panes side by side and in a diff without wrapping. The guide allows two exceptions, for a word that cannot sensibly be split, such as a path or a URL, and a string that is best written as a here document or with an embedded newline. shfmt does not enforce the limit, so the check is one line of awk, and the file below fails it three times and its rewrite not at all:

cat > long.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
main() {
  cat access.log | grep -v health | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 10 > top.txt
  first_step && second_step || echo "one of the two steps failed and here is a long message"
  echo "I am an exceptionally long string that goes well past the eightieth column."
}
END_OF_FILE

cat > wrapped.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
main() {
  cat access.log \
    | grep -v health \
    | cut -d' ' -f1 \
    | sort \
    | uniq -c \
    | sort -rn \
    | head -n 10 > top.txt
  first_step \
    && second_step \
    || echo "one of the two steps failed and here is a long message"
  cat << END_OF_TEXT
I am an exceptionally long string that goes well past the eightieth
column, and a here document is where it belongs.
END_OF_TEXT
}
END_OF_FILE

for file in long.sh wrapped.sh; do
  printf '%s: %s line(s) over 80 columns\n' "$file" "$(awk 'length > 80' "$file" | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"
done
echo "shfmt -i 2 -d would rewrite the wrapped form:    $(shfmt -i 2 -d wrapped.sh > /dev/null && echo no || echo yes)"
echo "shfmt -i 2 -sr -bn -d accepts it as it is: $(shfmt -i 2 -sr -bn -d wrapped.sh > /dev/null && echo yes || echo no)"

long.sh: 3 line(s) over 80 columns
wrapped.sh: 0 line(s) over 80 columns
shfmt -i 2 -d would rewrite the wrapped form:    yes
shfmt -i 2 -sr -bn -d accepts it as it is: yes

Three ways to shorten a line, and each is the one to use in its case. A long pipeline is split one stage per line, with the pipe at the start of the continuation, and the same for a chain of && and ||; that layout is shfmt's -bn ("binary operators at the beginning of the next line"), and without it shfmt rewrites the pipes to the end of each line, which the last line of the output shows. A long string goes in a here document, where the line breaks are the text's own. And a long path or URL that cannot be split goes on a line of its own or into a variable. The limit applies to comments as well, and the capstone's stylecheck reports any line over 80.

Pipelines and control flow

The remaining formatting rules are shorter, and shfmt enforces all of them. A pipeline that fits on one line is on one line; otherwise it is split with one segment per line, each continuation starting with the operator (above). Control flow puts ; then and ; do on the same line as the if, for or while, else on a line of its own, and fi and done on lines of their own, aligned with the opening keyword. A case indents its alternatives one level, has no opening parenthesis before a pattern, and puts a one-line action, a space and ;; on the pattern's line, or splits a long one over several lines with the pattern, the actions and ;; on separate lines. The guide adds two things that the course's earlier sections argued for on their own: a for loop over the arguments writes in "$@" for clarity though it can be omitted, and it avoids the ;& and ;;& case terminators, which few readers know.

22.3 Naming Convention: Function Names, Variable Names and Constants

Naming convention: what the case of a name says

The guide's naming convention has one idea: the case of a name tells the reader what kind of thing it is. Functions and variables are lower case, with underscores between words. Constants and anything exported to the environment are upper case, separated with underscores, and declared at the top of the file. So PATH_TO_FILES is a constant, files is a variable, and load_config is a function, and no reader has to look up a definition to know which. §9.12 listed the rules; this section measures what each one prevents.

Function naming

Function naming has two more rules than the case. A library's functions carry a package prefix separated by :: — logsum::aggregate — which is the only namespace bash has, and the guide notes that auto-completion in an interactive shell does not cope well with colons, so it says to avoid namespacing in those contexts. And "parentheses are required after the function name": the function keyword is optional, but "must be used consistently throughout a project". Neither is portable, and the difference is measured:

try() {
  printf '%-28s ' "$1"
  "${@:2}" 2>&1 | sed 's|^.*Syntax error|Syntax error|'
}
try 'bash: pkg::my_func' bash -c 'pkg::my_func() { echo works; }; pkg::my_func'
try 'bash: my-func' bash -c 'my-func() { echo works; }; my-func'
try 'bash --posix: pkg::my_func' bash --posix -c 'pkg::my_func() { echo works; }; pkg::my_func'
try 'dash: pkg::my_func' dash -c 'pkg::my_func() { echo works; }; pkg::my_func'
try 'dash: my-func' dash -c 'my-func() { echo works; }; my-func'
try 'dash: my_func' dash -c 'my_func() { echo works; }; my_func'

bash: pkg::my_func           works
bash: my-func                works
bash --posix: pkg::my_func   works
dash: pkg::my_func           Syntax error: Bad function name
dash: my-func                Syntax error: Bad function name
dash: my_func                works

Bash accepts pkg::my_func and my-func. In POSIX mode, where POSIX defines a function name as a plain name of letters, digits and underscores, bash 5.3 still accepts the colons, as the third row shows, and bash 5.2 does not: it answers not a valid identifier. dash rejects both spellings with Bad function name. That is a real limit on where the naming rule holds: a script that must run under sh (§19.6) uses plain lower_case names, prefixed with the library's name and an underscore if it needs a prefix at all. A script that declares bash in its shebang can use the :: prefix, which is why the capstone does.

Variable naming

Variable naming is the same rule, "same as for function names", with one addition: the variable of a loop is named after what it loops over. for zone in "${zones[@]}" names one element of zones in the singular, so the loop body reads as prose, where for i in "${arr[@]}" makes the reader look back. A single letter is fine for a counter and for nothing else. Declare the loop variable local inside a function, as the guide's example does, so that it does not leak into the caller (§9.4).

Lowercase for locals

Lowercase for locals is the half of the case rule that prevents a real failure, and not only an untidy one. The names that the shell and its programs read are upper case: PATH, HOME, IFS, LANG, PS4, TZ. A local variable that happens to share one of those names changes how commands run inside the function. The example gives a function a local named PATH, and then a local named path:

narrow_path() {
  local PATH=/nonexistent
  date > /dev/null
  echo "date status: $?"
}
narrow_path

# The lower-case spelling cannot collide with anything the shell or a program reads
narrow_dirs() {
  local path=/nonexistent
  date > /dev/null
  echo "date status: $?  (path is only a variable: $path)"
}
narrow_dirs

example.sh: line 3: date: command not found
date status: 127
date status: 0  (path is only a variable: /nonexistent)

With local PATH=/nonexistent, date was not found: status 127, inside a function whose author only wanted a variable holding a directory. With the lower-case name the same code was harmless. Nothing in the shell warns of it, since PATH is an ordinary variable that commands happen to consult. The rule that keeps it from happening is the case convention itself: a script's own variables are lower case and so cannot collide with the upper-case ones the environment defines.

Constant naming, the readonly builtin and declare -r

Constant naming is upper case with underscores, at the top of the file; a constant that has to be set at run time or in a conditional is made readonly immediately afterwards. The readonly builtin is what makes it a constant and not merely a variable that is not supposed to change, and there is a second way to spell it, declare -r, that is not equivalent:

config() {
  readonly FROM_READONLY=1
  declare -r FROM_DECLARE=2
  declare -gr FROM_DECLARE_G=3
}
config
echo "readonly:    ${FROM_READONLY-unset}"
echo "declare -r:  ${FROM_DECLARE-unset}"
echo "declare -gr: ${FROM_DECLARE_G-unset}"

readonly:    1
declare -r:  unset
declare -gr: 3

Inside a function, readonly made a global constant and declare -r made a local one: FROM_DECLARE was gone as soon as config returned. declare -gr is the global form. The guide recommends readonly and export over the equivalent declare commands "for the sake of clarity", and this is a second reason: the two look alike and behave differently in a function. For a constant that is also exported, declare -xr NAME=value is one command, and readonly NAME=value followed by export NAME is two that read more plainly.

What an attempt to change a constant does is worth seeing once:

readonly LIMIT=3
LIMIT=4
echo "after the failed assignment, LIMIT=$LIMIT"
unset LIMIT
echo "status of unset: $?"
readonly -p | grep LIMIT

# An assignment error ends the rest of its line, not the script
readonly PLACE=here
PLACE=there; echo "this echo is never reached"
echo "the next line runs, and PLACE=$PLACE"

example.sh: line 2: LIMIT: readonly variable
after the failed assignment, LIMIT=3
example.sh: line 4: unset: LIMIT: cannot unset: readonly variable
status of unset: 1
declare -r LIMIT="3"
example.sh: line 10: PLACE: readonly variable
the next line runs, and PLACE=here

Assigning to a readonly variable printed an error and did not change it. It also skipped the rest of that line — the echo after PLACE=there; was never reached — but not the script, which carried on at the next line. unset failed with status 1, and readonly -p lists every constant in a form that can be sourced back. The skipped rest of the line is the behaviour to remember: a script that puts a check after an assignment on the same line has not checked anything.

The constant has a second trap, for libraries. A file that declares readonly names cannot be loaded twice:

cat > constants.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
readonly LIB_VERSION=1
constants::show() { echo "version $LIB_VERSION"; }
END_OF_FILE
source ./constants.sh
source ./constants.sh
echo "status of the second source: $?"
constants::show

# The guard that makes a second load a no-op
cat > guarded.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
[[ -n ${GUARDED_LOADED:-} ]] && return 0
readonly GUARDED_LOADED=1
readonly GUARDED_VERSION=1
END_OF_FILE
source ./guarded.sh
source ./guarded.sh
echo "guarded, status $?"

./constants.sh: line 1: LIB_VERSION: readonly variable
status of the second source: 0
version 1
guarded, status 0

The second source printed LIB_VERSION: readonly variable and returned 0 anyway, because the error ended only that line and the next line, the function definition, ran and succeeded. A library whose constants are readonly needs a guard at the top that returns when it has already been loaded, and the second half of the example shows it: the guarded file sourced twice printed nothing. §22.7 makes that part of the sourcing conventions.

Uppercase for environment variables

Uppercase for environment variables is the other half of the upper-case rule: a name exported to child processes is upper case, and by extension every name a script reads from its environment (§16.3). Two practices follow. Give a script's own exported names a prefix — LOGSUM_VERSION, LOGSUM_LIB_LOADED in the capstone — so that they cannot collide with a variable some program the script starts also reads. And export only what a child needs: an exported variable is copied into every process the script starts (§21.2 measured what that costs at scale), and is visible to every one of them (§18.15 on where secrets leak). A constant that only the script uses is readonly and not export.

22.4 Comments: File Header, Function Comment, Implementation Comment and TODO Comment

File header comment

The guide's rule for the file header comment is that every file starts with "a description of its contents": a top-level comment with "a brief overview". A copyright notice and author information are optional. It is the first thing a reader sees, so it says what the file is for and, for an executable, how to call it, which is also the text §13.9's help function can print. The capstone's command opens like this:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# Summarise a web access log: requests and bytes per status, top paths.
#
# Usage: logsum [-n N] [-f text|tsv] [-o FILE] [-D] [-v] LOGFILE

The comment starts on the second line, after the shebang and an empty comment line, and describes the file in one sentence. stylecheck, the checker of §22.12, requires exactly that: a comment in the first three lines.

Function comment

A function comment is required, by the guide's rule, for "any function that is not both obvious and short", and for every function in a library "regardless of length or complexity". Its purpose is that someone can use the function by reading the comment and not the code. The guide's format has five headings — a description, then Globals (those the function reads or modifies), Arguments, Outputs (what goes to standard output or standard error) and Returns (a status other than the default one of the last command). The capstone's aggregating function, which reads its input from standard input and writes tab-separated lines, is documented that way (the function's own line follows the comment):

#######################################
# Count requests and bytes per status, and requests per path.
# Globals:
#   None
# Arguments:
#   None. Reads the log from standard input.
# Outputs:
#   Tab-separated lines on stdout, unsorted:
#     S status requests bytes
#     P path requests
#   A diagnostic on stderr for each malformed line.
# Returns:
#   0, or 1 if any line did not have four fields.
#######################################

Two things about the format are easy to miss. A heading is listed even when it is empty — Globals: None — so that a reader can tell "none" from "forgot". And input is documented as well as output: Arguments: None. Reads the log from standard input, because for a filter the standard input is the interface.

"Not both obvious and short" is a judgement, and a judgement is what a tool cannot make. The course's mechanical version of it is that a function longer than five lines needs a comment, and the check is a few lines of awk. It reports the one function below that has no header, and ignores the short is_old:

cat > rotate <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# Rotate application logs.

#######################################
# Print a message to stderr.
# Arguments:
#   The message words.
#######################################
err() {
  echo "$*" >&2
}

is_old() { [[ $1 -gt 30 ]]; }

older_than() {
  local dir=$1 days=$2
  local f
  for f in "$dir"/*; do
    [[ -f $f ]] || continue
    find "$f" -mtime "+$days" -print
  done
}
END_OF_FILE

# A function longer than five lines needs a header comment; a short, obvious one does not
awk '
  /^[a-z_:]+\(\) *\{/ { opened = FNR; func_name = $1; commented = (prev ~ /^#/) }
  /^}/ && opened {
    if (FNR - opened > 6 && !commented) {
      printf "rotate:%d: %s is %d lines long and has no header comment\n",
        opened, func_name, FNR - opened - 1
    }
    opened = 0
  }
  $0 !~ /^[ \t]*$/ { prev = $0 }' rotate

rotate:16: older_than() is 6 lines long and has no header comment

The threshold is arbitrary and the point is not: some rule that a machine can apply is better than none, because the comment that gets skipped is always on the function someone thought was obvious.

Implementation comment

An implementation comment is for the tricky, the non-obvious, the interesting and the important, and the guide adds the qualifier that matters: "Don't comment everything". A comment that repeats the code — # increment i above ((i++)) — is noise that will go stale. A useful one says why: what a reader could not see by reading the line. The capstone has two. # Loading the file twice is harmless. above its guard explains a line that would otherwise look like a mistake, and # shellcheck disable=SC2034 # read by the script that sources this file gives the reason a warning is being silenced, as §20.4 required of every suppression. When you find yourself writing a comment that explains what a block does, that is usually a sign the block wants to be a function with a name.

TODO comment

A TODO comment marks code that is temporary, a short-term solution or good enough but not perfect. The format is TODO, in capitals, then the name, e-mail address or other identifier of "the person with the best context about the problem" in parentheses and a colon: TODO(ada): handle compressed logs (bug 1234). Its purpose is to make the marker searchable; the guide is explicit that "a TODO is not a commitment that the person referenced will fix the problem". A convention that can be searched can be checked, and the two searches are one line each:

cat > rotate <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# Rotate application logs.

# TODO(ada): handle compressed logs (bug 1234)
# TODO fix the date format
# TODO(grace): add --dry-run
# TODO(ada): read the retention from a file
END_OF_FILE

echo "== TODOs with no owner"
grep -n 'TODO' rotate | grep -v 'TODO([a-z][a-z0-9_.-]*):'
echo "== TODOs per owner"
sed -n 's/.*TODO(\([a-z][a-z0-9_.-]*\)):.*/\1/p' rotate | sort | awk '{ n[$1]++ } END { for (o in n) print o, n[o] }' | sort

== TODOs with no owner
6:# TODO fix the date format
== TODOs per owner
ada 2
grace 1

The first search found the TODO with no owner, and the second counted the rest per owner. Both run in a hook or a CI job, which is how the convention stays a convention.

22.5 Script Layout, Function Ordering and the main Function

Script layout

The guide's script layout is one order, and the capstone's command shows it from the top: the interpreter line and the file header, then the set options, then constants, then anything sourced, then all the functions, then a function called main, and as the last line main "$@":

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # an excerpt: the rest of the file uses these
#
# Summarise a web access log: requests and bytes per status, top paths.
#
# Usage: logsum [-n N] [-f text|tsv] [-o FILE] [-D] [-v] LOGFILE

set -o errexit -o nounset -o pipefail

readonly PROG=${0##*/}
readonly EX_USAGE=64 EX_DATAERR=65 EX_NOINPUT=66 EX_CANTCREAT=73

# shellcheck source=lib/logsum.sh
source "${BASH_SOURCE[0]%/*}/../lib/logsum.sh"

set comes first because it changes how everything after it behaves, and it takes the options as set -o errexit -o nounset -o pipefail, which reads as prose where -euo does not. The guide's wording is that executables use set "so that calling your script as bash script_name does not break its functionality" — options set inside the file travel with it, and options on the shebang line do not. Constants come next, readonly and upper case (§22.3), and the sourced file after them, so that a reader finds every name the script depends on before the first function.

Function ordering

Function ordering in the guide is a rule about executable code: "put all functions together in the file just below constants. Don't hide executable code between functions." Only includes, set statements and constants may come before the functions. The reason is that a function exists only from the moment its definition runs (§9.2), so code interleaved with definitions works or fails depending on the order of the file:

echo "-- a function can call one that is defined later, if the call happens later"
caller() { callee; }
callee() { echo "callee ran"; }
caller

echo "-- but not if the call happens before the definition has run"
early() { late; }
early
late() { echo "late ran"; }
early

-- a function can call one that is defined later, if the call happens later
callee ran
-- but not if the call happens before the definition has run
example.sh: line 7: late: command not found
late ran

A function can call one that is defined later in the file, as long as the call happens later: caller ran callee although callee came second. What fails is a call that runs before the definition has: the first early printed late: command not found, and the second, after late had been defined, worked. The layout rule is a way of never having to reason about this: all definitions first, then one call.

The main function

The main function is what makes the last sentence of that rule true. The guide says a function called main is required "for scripts long enough to contain at least one other function", that it should be the bottom-most function, and that the last non-comment line of the file is main "$@". It also gives the two reasons: it makes the start of the program easy to find, and it lets the code in it use local, which only works inside a function. What happens when it is not done is subtle:

cat > main-last.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
main() { helper "$@"; }
helper() { echo "helper got $*"; }
main "$@"
END_OF_FILE

cat > main-early.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
main() { helper "$@"; }
main "$@"
helper() { echo "helper got $*"; }
END_OF_FILE

bash main-last.sh a b; echo "status $?"
bash main-early.sh a b; echo "status $?"

helper got a b
status 0
main-early.sh: line 2: helper: command not found
status 0

main-last.sh defined main and helper, then called main. main-early.sh called main before helper was defined: the error is printed, as helper: command not found, and the script's exit status is 0. The last command in the file was the definition of helper, which succeeded, so the status of the failed call was lost. A script whose calls are all at the bottom cannot do this, and one that puts a call in the middle can fail and report success. The rule is short enough to be a lint: the stylecheck of §22.12 reports an executable whose last line is not main "$@".

A file that is both a library and a command replaces the unconditional call with the guard of §9.14, if [[ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} == "$0" ]]; then main "$@"; fi, so that a test can source the file to reach its functions; §22.10's refactored script does that. The capstone's command has no guard, because its functions live in the library file, which a test sources directly.

22.6 Idempotent Scripts and the Dry Run Flag

Idempotent script

An idempotent script is one that leaves the system in the same state whether it runs once or ten times. That property is not a luxury. Scripts are re-run after a failure halfway through, by a scheduler that fires twice, by a colleague who did not know it had already run, and by configuration-management tools that run everything on every cycle. A script that fails on the second run, or worse, succeeds and duplicates its work, turns each of those into an incident. The technique is always the same: state what should be true, test whether it already is, and act only if it is not. Most of the commands a script needs have a form that is already idempotent, or a test that makes it so:

  • mkdir -p dir succeeds if the directory exists; plain mkdir fails.
  • ln -sfn target link replaces a link and does not create a second one inside a directory the link points to; plain ln -s fails on the second run, or nests.
  • install -m 644 src dest, guarded by cmp -s src dest, writes only when the content differs.
  • grep -qxF "$line" file || echo "$line" >> file appends a line only if it is not already there; plain >> adds it again on every run.
  • A test before a destructive command, [[ -e $file ]] && …, and command || true where "already done" is a normal outcome (§11.5).

The deployment script below is built from these. It installs the files of a release into a target directory, and it is safe to run twice:

cat > deploy.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# Install the files of a release into a target directory.
# Safe to run twice: it changes only what differs.
#
# Usage: deploy.sh [--dry-run] RELEASE_DIR TARGET_DIR

set -o errexit -o nounset -o pipefail

dry_run=0
changes=0

# Log a command, and run it unless this is a dry run.
run() {
  printf '+'
  printf ' %q' "$@"
  printf '\n'
  changes=$((changes + 1))
  ((dry_run)) || "$@"
}

ensure_dir() {
  [[ -d $1 ]] || run mkdir -p "$1"
}

ensure_file() {
  cmp -s "$1" "$2" 2> /dev/null || run install -m 644 "$1" "$2"
}

ensure_link() {
  [[ $(readlink "$2" 2> /dev/null) == "$1" ]] || run ln -sfn "$1" "$2"
}

main() {
  [[ ${1:-} == --dry-run ]] && { dry_run=1; shift; }
  local release=${1:?usage: deploy.sh [--dry-run] RELEASE TARGET} target=${2:?}
  local file
  ensure_dir "${target}/current"
  for file in "${release}"/*; do
    ensure_file "${file}" "${target}/current/${file##*/}"
  done
  ensure_link current "${target}/live"
  if ((dry_run)); then
    echo "${changes} change(s) would be made"
  else
    echo "${changes} change(s) made"
  fi
}

main "$@"
END_OF_FILE

mkdir release
echo 'port=80' > release/app.conf
echo 'binary' > release/app.bin
tree() { [[ -d target ]] && find target | sort || echo "(no target directory)"; }

echo "== dry run"; bash deploy.sh --dry-run release target
tree
echo "== first run"; bash deploy.sh release target
tree
echo "== second run"; bash deploy.sh release target
echo "== after changing one file"
echo 'port=8080' > release/app.conf
bash deploy.sh release target

== dry run
+ mkdir -p target/current
+ install -m 644 release/app.bin target/current/app.bin
+ install -m 644 release/app.conf target/current/app.conf
+ ln -sfn current target/live
4 change(s) would be made
(no target directory)
== first run
+ mkdir -p target/current
+ install -m 644 release/app.bin target/current/app.bin
+ install -m 644 release/app.conf target/current/app.conf
+ ln -sfn current target/live
4 change(s) made
target
target/current
target/current/app.bin
target/current/app.conf
target/live
== second run
0 change(s) made
== after changing one file
+ install -m 644 release/app.conf target/current/app.conf
1 change(s) made

Read the output as four runs of the same script. The dry run printed the four commands it would have run, said "4 change(s) would be made", and created nothing: the tree after it found no target directory. The first run made the four changes and the tree shows their result. The second run printed no commands at all and made no changes, which is the definition. And after one file in the release was edited, a third run did exactly one thing, installing that file. Each ensure_ function is one of the tests above: ensure_dir checks the directory, ensure_file compares content with cmp -s and ensure_link reads the link with readlink, and none of them acts if the state is already right.

The dry run flag

The run function in that script is the dry run flag in the form §6.14 promised: a wrapper through which every command that changes something passes.

# Log a command, and run it unless this is a dry run.
run() {
  printf '+'
  printf ' %q' "$@"
  printf '\n'
  changes=$((changes + 1))
  ((dry_run)) || "$@"
}

It prints the command, in a form that can be copied and run — %q quotes each argument, so a name with a space prints as one word (§20.14) — counts it as a change, and runs it unless dry_run is set. That is all a dry run needs, because the script's decisions are made by the ensure_ functions, which only read state. That division is the design rule: reads always happen, so the script can decide; writes go through run, so they can be suppressed. A dry run that also suppressed reads could not tell what would change.

There is a limit worth knowing. A dry run predicts the commands a script would run from the current state, and a script whose later decisions depend on what its earlier commands would have done cannot be predicted this way: in a dry run the directory ensure_dir did not create does not exist, so a cd into it, or a cmp of a file inside it, behaves differently from the real run. The two cures are to make every decision from state that exists before the script starts, as deploy.sh does, or to have the dry run say so where it cannot know. A dry run is documentation of intent and not a proof, and the honest wording is the one the script uses: "would be made".

Idempotent is not atomic

Two things a script that passes the second-run test still does not promise. It does not promise that two copies running at the same moment are safe: both can see the file missing, and both can create it. That is the race of §17.7, and the answer is a lock (§17.8), not more tests. And it does not promise that an interruption halfway leaves the target usable: the install of a large file can be cut off, so writing to a temporary name and renaming it into place (§17.10) is what makes a change all-or-nothing. Idempotence answers "what if I run it again"; atomicity and locking answer "what if it is interrupted" and "what if two run at once".

22.7 Library Files, Sourcing Conventions and Avoiding Side Effects on Source

Library file

A library file holds definitions and nothing else, and the guide's rules for it are two: it must have a .sh extension, and "should not be executable". The second is a protection. A file that has no executable bit cannot be run by mistake, and one that does is a command that happens to define functions, which is the difference between lib/logsum.sh and bin/logsum. The conventions beyond that come from earlier sections and are gathered here: functions carry the library's package prefix, logsum::aggregate (§22.3); constants are upper case and carry a prefix too; and the file begins with a guard, so that loading it twice is harmless (§22.3 measured why):

# Functions for logsum. Source this file; it does nothing on its own.
# A log line has four fields: address, status, path and bytes.

# Loading the file twice is harmless.
[[ -n ${LOGSUM_LIB_LOADED:-} ]] && return 0
readonly LOGSUM_LIB_LOADED=1
# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # read by the script that sources this file
readonly LOGSUM_VERSION='1.0.0'

The guard's line, [[ -n ${LOGSUM_LIB_LOADED:-} ]] && return 0, returns from the sourcing without running the rest, and is written as ${LOGSUM_LIB_LOADED:-} so that it works under set -u (§11.2). A return at the top of a file is legal only when the file is being sourced, which is the situation it protects against.

Sourcing conventions

The sourcing convention that matters most is where the library is looked for. A path such as source lib/strings.sh is relative to the directory the caller is in, not to the script, so it works from the project's root and fails from anywhere else. The convention is to name the library relative to the script's own location, which BASH_SOURCE gives (§9.13):

mkdir -p project/bin project/lib other

cat > project/lib/strings.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
strings::shout() { echo "${1^^}!"; }
END_OF_FILE

cat > project/bin/tool <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
source "${BASH_SOURCE[0]%/*}/../lib/strings.sh"
strings::shout "$1"
END_OF_FILE

cat > project/bin/naive <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
source lib/strings.sh
strings::shout "$1"
END_OF_FILE
chmod +x project/bin/tool project/bin/naive

(
  cd other
  ../project/bin/tool hello
  ../project/bin/naive hello 2>&1 | sed 's|^.*naive: ||'
)
echo "library is executable: $([[ -x project/lib/strings.sh ]] && echo yes || echo no)"

HELLO!
line 2: lib/strings.sh: No such file or directory
line 3: strings::shout: command not found
library is executable: no

The script that sourced "${BASH_SOURCE[0]%/*}/../lib/strings.sh" printed HELLO! from a directory it does not live in. The naive source lib/strings.sh failed there: No such file or directory, then strings::shout: command not found, with the script carrying on. The last line confirms the library is not executable. ShellCheck follows such a source only if it is told where to look, and the capstone tells it once, in a .shellcheckrc next to the code — source-path=SCRIPTDIR/.. and external-sources=true (§20.3) — so that the directive above each source is a plain # shellcheck source=lib/logsum.sh and no command-line flag is needed.

Avoiding side effects on source

The last rule is the one that makes the others safe: sourcing a library must have no side effects. A library is loaded into the shell of whoever sources it, so anything it does happens to them: a set -e changes their error handling, a cd moves them, an exit ends their script, a trap replaces theirs, and output nobody asked for goes to their standard output. Three small files show what the sourcing shell looks like afterwards:

cat > noisy.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
echo "loading noisy.sh"
set -e
cd /
END_OF_FILE

cat > exits.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
echo "loading exits.sh"
exit 3
END_OF_FILE

cat > quiet.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
quiet::hello() { echo hello; }
END_OF_FILE

# report what a script that sources FILE looks like afterwards
after() {
  bash -c 'cd /tmp; source "$1"; echo "afterwards: directory $PWD, errexit ${-//[!e]/}"' _ "$PWD/$1"
  echo "  exit status $?"
}
after noisy.sh
after exits.sh
after quiet.sh

loading noisy.sh
afterwards: directory /, errexit e
  exit status 0
loading exits.sh
  exit status 3
afterwards: directory /tmp, errexit 
  exit status 0

noisy.sh printed a message, turned on errexit and changed the caller's directory to /: after sourcing it the shell was in / with errexit set, and nothing had been asked for. exits.sh ended the whole calling script with its own status, 3, and nothing after the source ran. quiet.sh, which only defined a function, left the directory and the options as they were. A library's top level may define functions and readonly constants, and may return early from its guard; everything else belongs in a function that the caller chooses to call. §20.7 made the same point about testing, and it is the same rule seen from the other side: a file that can be sourced without consequences is a file that can be tested.

22.8 The --help Convention, the Version Flag and Semantic Exit Codes

The --help convention

The --help convention has three parts, and nearly every command-line tool keeps them. --help and -h print the usage text and exit 0, since the user asked for it and it worked. The text goes to standard output, so that tool --help | less and tool --help | grep -i output work; the guide's rule that "all error messages should go to STDERR" is about errors, and a help request is not one. And a wrong invocation prints a short message to standard error and exits non-zero, with a pointer to --help. §13.9 built the function; the convention is what makes it something a script can depend on.

The version flag

The version flag, --version or -V, prints one line, the tool's name and its version, to standard output and exits 0: logsum 1.0.0. One line makes it parseable by another script deciding whether a tool is new enough (§20.11 pinned tool versions in CI). The version lives in one place — a constant in the library, LOGSUM_VERSION — and the command and the tests both read it.

Semantic exit codes

Semantic exit codes are exit statuses with a meaning that a caller can act on. §11.4 listed the conventions: 0 success, 1 a general failure, 2 or 64 a usage error, and sysexits.h for the specific ones. The capstone uses the last: 64 for a usage error, 65 for malformed input data, 66 for an input file that is missing or unreadable, 73 for an output file that cannot be created. A caller can then tell "you called it wrongly" from "the file is not there" from "the file is corrupt" without parsing a message, and the codes are part of the help text, because a status nobody documented is one nobody can rely on.

A contract test

A command's conventions are testable, and worth testing once, generically, because they are the same for every tool. The function below takes a command and checks the five behaviours above: --help exits 0 with the usage on standard output only, --version does the same, an unknown option and a missing operand exit 64 with a message on standard error only, and an unreadable file exits 66. It is run on two tools, one that keeps the contract and one that does not:

cat > good <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
case ${1:-} in
  --help) echo "Usage: good FILE"; exit 0 ;;
  --version) echo "good 1.0"; exit 0 ;;
  -*) echo "good: unknown option: $1" >&2; exit 64 ;;
  '') echo "good: expected a FILE" >&2; exit 64 ;;
esac
[[ -r $1 ]] || { echo "good: cannot read $1" >&2; exit 66; }
cat "$1"
END_OF_FILE

cat > sloppy <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
case ${1:-} in
  --help) echo "Usage: sloppy FILE" >&2; exit 1 ;;
  -*) echo "unknown option"; exit 1 ;;
  '') echo "sloppy: no file"; exit 1 ;;
esac
cat "$1"
END_OF_FILE
chmod +x good sloppy

describe() { if [[ -n $1 ]]; then echo text; else echo empty; fi; }

# check LABEL STATUS STREAM COMMAND...: the status is right, and only STREAM (out or err) has text
check() {
  local label=$1 want=$2 stream=$3 out err status
  shift 3
  out=$("$@" 2> stderr.txt); status=$?
  err=$(< stderr.txt)
  local here=$out there=$err
  [[ $stream == err ]] && { here=$err; there=$out; }
  if ((status == want)) && [[ -n $here && -z $there ]]; then
    printf '  pass  %s\n' "$label"
  else
    printf '  FAIL  %s: status %d, stdout %s, stderr %s\n' "$label" "$status" \
      "$(describe "$out")" "$(describe "$err")"
  fi
}

for tool in good sloppy; do
  echo "$tool:"
  check '--help exits 0, usage on stdout only' 0 out ./$tool --help
  check '--version exits 0, on stdout only' 0 out ./$tool --version
  check 'an unknown option exits 64, message on stderr only' 64 err ./$tool --bogus
  check 'a missing operand exits 64, message on stderr only' 64 err ./$tool
  check 'an unreadable file exits 66, message on stderr only' 66 err ./$tool missing.txt
done

good:
  pass  --help exits 0, usage on stdout only
  pass  --version exits 0, on stdout only
  pass  an unknown option exits 64, message on stderr only
  pass  a missing operand exits 64, message on stderr only
  pass  an unreadable file exits 66, message on stderr only
sloppy:
  FAIL  --help exits 0, usage on stdout only: status 1, stdout empty, stderr text
  FAIL  --version exits 0, on stdout only: status 1, stdout text, stderr empty
  FAIL  an unknown option exits 64, message on stderr only: status 1, stdout text, stderr empty
  FAIL  a missing operand exits 64, message on stderr only: status 1, stdout text, stderr empty
  FAIL  an unreadable file exits 66, message on stderr only: status 1, stdout empty, stderr text

good passes all five. sloppy fails all five, each for a different reason that the failure line names: its help goes to standard error and exits 1, its version does not exist and the error goes to standard output, and its errors exit 1 and land on the wrong stream or are cat's own message. Each of those is a thing that breaks a script that calls the tool: a pipeline that captures the help text, a check that --version succeeded, a wrapper that distinguishes exit statuses. The capstone's own tests, in §22.12, check exactly these.

22.9 Script Architecture: Separating Logic from I/O and Testable Shell Code

Script architecture: the layers

Script architecture is the answer to a question a ten-line script does not need to ask: which parts of this program are deciding something, and which are touching the world? A script that mixes the two is hard to change and hard to test, because every decision can only be exercised by arranging the world that it touches. The layers that work for shell are the same four in almost every script. Parse: turn the command line and the environment into a small set of settings, or refuse with a usage error. Validate: check that the inputs exist and are what was promised, before anything is changed. Compute: turn input into output — the part with the logic in it. Act: write files, print, call other programs. The first, second and fourth touch the world; only the third is an idea, and it is the one worth being able to test.

Here is a script that has all four in one place. It totals the sales per region from a file it finds in the current directory, and writes and prints a report:

cat > report.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Total the sales in sales.csv by region.
echo "Reading sales.csv"
total=0
declare -A by_region
while IFS=, read -r region amount; do
  [ "$region" = region ] && continue
  by_region[$region]=$((${by_region[$region]:-0} + amount))
  total=$((total + amount))
done < sales.csv
{
  for r in $(printf '%s\n' "${!by_region[@]}" | sort); do
    printf '%-8s %6d\n' "$r" "${by_region[$r]}"
  done
  printf '%-8s %6d\n' total "$total"
} | tee report.txt
echo "Wrote report.txt"
END_OF_FILE

printf '%s\n' region,amount north,120 south,80 north,30 east,55 south,10 > sales.csv
bash report.sh
echo "== the same script, run where there is no sales.csv"
mkdir elsewhere
(cd elsewhere && bash ../report.sh 2>&1 | sed 's|^.*report.sh: ||'; echo "exit status ${PIPESTATUS[0]}")

Reading sales.csv
east         55
north       150
south        90
total       295
Wrote report.txt
== the same script, run where there is no sales.csv
Reading sales.csv
line 10: sales.csv: No such file or directory
total         0
Wrote report.txt
exit status 0

It works, on the day it is written, and the second half of the output is what is wrong with it. Run in a directory with no sales.csv, it printed the No such file or directory error from the shell, then a table with a total of 0, then "Wrote report.txt", and exited 0: a report was produced and reported as a success from no data at all. Nothing in the script decides what a missing input means, because nothing in it separates reading the input from totalling it. Every fault in it follows from that one fact: the file name is fixed inside the loop, progress messages go to the same stream as the report, the result cannot be tested without creating sales.csv in the right directory, and the for r in $(printf … | sort) line splits on whitespace (§3.3) and would break on a region with a space in its name.

Separating logic from I/O

Separating logic from I/O means the compute layer is made of functions that take their input as arguments or on standard input, write their output to standard output, read no files and change no globals. Call such a function pure, though shell only approximates it: its result depends on its input and on nothing else. In shell the natural form is a filter, as in the pipelines of §15 and §21.5: report::totals reads lines and writes lines, and report::render reads those and writes a table. Anything that touches the world — opening the file, choosing where the report goes, saying what is happening — is the job of main, the one function that does I/O, and is written at the edge.

The gain is a division of labour that also divides the failure modes. A bug in the arithmetic is in a pure function and can be found by calling it with a string. A bug in a file name or a missing input is in main, which has almost no logic to get wrong. And the two can be changed independently: the output format is one function, the input source is one line.

Testable shell code

Testable shell code is code shaped like that, plus two things that §20.7 established: the file can be sourced without running the script (the main guard of §9.14), and its functions have no effects at load time (§22.7). With both, a test needs no fixtures and no working directory. The functions of the refactored report below are called with a here-string in place of a file:

# The original, and the report it wrote: the script's contract, recorded before any change
cat > original.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "Reading sales.csv"
total=0
declare -A by_region
while IFS=, read -r region amount; do
  [ "$region" = region ] && continue
  by_region[$region]=$((${by_region[$region]:-0} + amount))
  total=$((total + amount))
done < sales.csv
{
  for r in $(printf '%s\n' "${!by_region[@]}" | sort); do
    printf '%-8s %6d\n' "$r" "${by_region[$r]}"
  done
  printf '%-8s %6d\n' total "$total"
} | tee report.txt
echo "Wrote report.txt"
END_OF_FILE
printf '%s\n' region,amount north,120 south,80 north,30 east,55 south,10 > sales.csv
bash original.sh > /dev/null
cp report.txt golden.txt

cat > report.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# Total sales by region.
#
# Usage: report.sh [CSV_FILE]   (default: sales.csv)

set -o errexit -o nounset -o pipefail

#######################################
# Add up the amounts for each region.
# Arguments:
#   None. Reads "region,amount" lines, with a header, on standard input.
# Outputs:
#   One "region total" line per region, sorted by region.
#######################################
report::totals() {
  awk -F, '
    NR > 1 { total[$1] += $2 }
    END { for (r in total) print r, total[r] }' | sort
}

#######################################
# Format totals as a table with a grand total.
# Arguments:
#   None. Reads "region total" lines on standard input.
# Outputs:
#   The table on stdout.
#######################################
report::render() {
  awk '
    { printf "%-8s %6d\n", $1, $2; sum += $2 }
    END { printf "%-8s %6d\n", "total", sum }'
}

main() {
  local csv=${1:-sales.csv}
  echo "Reading ${csv}" >&2
  report::totals < "${csv}" | report::render | tee report.txt
  echo "Wrote report.txt" >&2
}

# Run main only when executed, so that a test can source the functions
if [[ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} == "$0" ]]; then
  main "$@"
fi
END_OF_FILE

bash report.sh > /dev/null 2>&1
cmp -s report.txt golden.txt && echo "report.txt is identical to the golden copy" || echo "report.txt DIFFERS"

echo "== with no sales.csv, the original and the refactored script"
mkdir empty
(cd empty && bash ../original.sh > /dev/null 2>&1; echo "original:   exit status $?")
(cd empty && bash ../report.sh > /dev/null 2>&1; echo "refactored: exit status $?")

echo "== the functions, tested with no files and no directory"
source ./report.sh
printf '%s\n' region,amount a,1 b,2 a,3 | report::totals
printf '%s\n' 'a 4' 'b 2' | report::render

report.txt is identical to the golden copy
== with no sales.csv, the original and the refactored script
original:   exit status 0
refactored: exit status 1
== the functions, tested with no files and no directory
a 4
b 2
a             4
b             2
total         6

The second half of the output is a test with no files: report::totals was given a small CSV as a here-string and printed the totals, and report::render was given two lines and printed the table with a grand total. Neither created a file or depended on the directory it was run in. A test written this way is short enough to write while the function is being written, and a suite of them (§20.8) runs in milliseconds; the tests of the monolith would each need a directory and a file.

22.10 Refactoring a Shell Script

Refactoring a shell script: record the behaviour first

Refactoring a shell script is changing its structure without changing what it does, and the second half of that sentence is the one that fails. The discipline is to record the behaviour before touching the code: run the script on representative input and keep its output. That recording is the golden copy, and it is the only test the original ever had. Each change to the structure is then followed by a comparison against it, and a change that alters the output is either a mistake or a decision you should be making on purpose.

The block above is that discipline applied to report.sh. It ran original.sh on the fixture and copied the report it wrote to golden.txt. Then it ran the refactored script and compared report.txt with golden.txt with cmp -s, and printed identical. That comparison is what the whole exercise rests on, and it took one line.

The steps, and what each is checked by

The order of steps is the point. Each is small enough that a failure has one possible cause, and each is followed by the comparison and by the two static checks, ShellCheck and shfmt. The refactoring of report.sh was four steps:

  1. Wrap what exists in functions, without changing a line inside them: main holds the old body. Run the comparison. Nothing has changed, and the code now has places to put things.
  2. Extract the pure part. The loop that totals becomes report::totals, reading standard input and writing region total lines; the formatting becomes report::render. Replace the bash loop and associative array with one awk while there, since the tool is right for it (§21.5). Run the comparison.
  3. Push the I/O to the edge. main takes the file name as an argument with a default, opens it in one place, and writes progress to standard error. This step changes behaviour on purpose — progress no longer goes to standard output — so the comparison is against report.txt, the deliverable, and not against everything the script printed. Say so in the commit message.
  4. Add the guard and the tests, and turn on set -o errexit -o nounset -o pipefail now that failure paths are explicit. This step also changes a behaviour on purpose: a missing input file is now an error with a non-zero status, where the original reported success — the block measures both, exit status 0 for the original and 1 for the refactored script.

Two of the four steps are deliberate changes of behaviour, and both are improvements the monolith's own output pointed at. That is normal. What refactoring adds is that the deliberate changes are separate, named and few, and that everything else is proven unchanged.

Small steps and the checks between them

Three practices make the steps safe. Keep the golden copy in the repository, next to the script, so that the comparison can be run by anyone and by CI. Run ShellCheck after each step (§20.6), because extracting a function is the moment a variable stops being visible where it is used. And when a step changes the output, resist fixing it in the same commit: revert, make the change alone, and record the new golden copy with its reason. A refactoring that cannot say what it changed is a rewrite, and a rewrite of a script with no tests is exactly the job §21.8 said to do behind a comparison.

22.11 When to Stop Using Shell

The decision, restated

When to stop using shell is a decision the course has approached three times, and each time from a different side. §1.6 gave the test: is the interesting content which commands run in what order, or what happens to the data? §21.7 gave the criteria for the second: cost that survives the remedies, data with structure, non-integers, structured formats, length with logic, errors that need context, and concurrency that shares state. And the guide gives the alarm: more than a hundred lines, or non-straightforward control flow, means rewrite it now. This section's addition is a way to use them, which is to ask the questions on a schedule and not when the script has already become a problem: when it first passes a hundred lines of logic (§22.1), when a requirement is added that names data rather than commands, and when a fix needs a workaround for something shell is bad at.

A worked case: the requirements that arrive

logsum is a good specimen, because it is at a decision point today and it is easy to see what the next requirements do to it. Take four, each plausible: report the 95th percentile of response time per path, which needs the log to have a latency field and the tool to sort within groups; emit the report as JSON for a dashboard; join each address with an inventory file to name the host; and alert when the error rate of a path over a sliding window passes a threshold.

Read them against §21.7's criteria. The percentile is a numeric task with a sort inside each group: it is an awk program, and a longer one, and it starts to want floating-point rounding that §7.9 said shell does not have. JSON output is a structured format to be written, where shell will happily build a string that is not valid JSON the first time a path contains a quote. The join is a data problem — two inputs, keyed — that join or awk does in one process and that is a dictionary lookup in any structured language. The sliding window is state over time, which is where shell's one-string-per-key maps (§6.9) run out. Each of the four adds a criterion, and by the fourth the tool is a program that happens to be written in shell.

The decision that follows is not "rewrite it all". It is §21.8's: keep the command line, the options, the exit statuses and the tests in shell, where they are correct and small, and move the data work behind the seam, into one program that takes the log on standard input. The tests that already exist, the contract checks and the golden output, are what tells the rewritten part is still logsum.

Refactor before rewriting

The last question is whether to refactor first, and the answer is usually yes, in the sense of §22.10: a tangled script cannot be rewritten safely, because nobody knows what it does, and the first step of any rewrite is the golden copy. The costs are not symmetrical. A refactoring is cheap and reversible and leaves a script that is easier to reason about, and it is what turns "rewrite it" from a plan into a series of small, checked moves. A script that has been separated into layers, with its logic in pure functions and its edges thin, can have those functions replaced one at a time, and a script that has not can only be replaced whole.

22.12 Capstone: logsum

The specification

The capstone is a small command that summarises a web access log, chosen because it has all the pieces the course taught and none of the bulk. logsum reads a log whose lines are address status path bytes, and prints the requests and bytes for each status and the busiest paths. It has short and long options — --top N, --format text|tsv, --output FILE, --dry-run, --verbose, --help and --version — with the exit statuses of §22.8. It is written to this section's rules and to the rest of the course's: a library and a command (§22.7), functions with header comments (§22.4), a main at the bottom (§22.5), the counting done in one awk and not a loop (§21.5), the long-option loop of §13.6, and tests in bats (§20.8). The tree has seven files:

  • bin/logsum, the command: option parsing, validation, the pipeline and the output.
  • lib/logsum.sh, the library: logsum::aggregate (one awk), logsum::statuses, logsum::top_paths and the two renderers.
  • test/logsum.bats, twelve tests.
  • tools/stylecheck, the checker for the rules no standard tool has (§22.1).
  • Makefile, .editorconfig and .shellcheckrc, which say how the tools are run and configured.

The library

The library holds the logic and none of the I/O. logsum::aggregate is the only function that reads the log's format, and it does the whole counting in one awk process, which is what §21.5 showed a loop could not match. It writes two kinds of tab-separated line, S for status and P for path, and everything else works on those:

logsum::aggregate() {
  awk '
    NF != 4 {
      printf "line %d: expected 4 fields, found %d\n", NR, NF > "/dev/stderr"
      bad = 1
      next
    }
    { requests[$2]++; bytes[$2] += $4; hits[$3]++ }
    END {
      for (s in requests) printf "S\t%s\t%d\t%d\n", s, requests[s], bytes[s]
      for (p in hits) printf "P\t%s\t%d\n", p, hits[p]
      exit bad
    }'
}

Its only side effect on the outside is a diagnostic, on standard error, for a line that does not have four fields, and it returns 1 if there was one — the raw material for the command's exit status 65. The renderers, logsum::render_text and logsum::render_tsv, take aggregated lines and print a report, so a new output format is a new function with the same shape, and the command chooses one by name.

The command

main in the command is where the layers of §22.9 are visible. The first half parses (a while over the arguments with a case, in the shape §13.6 built) and the second validates, refusing early with a status that means something:

  (($# == 1)) || die "${EX_USAGE}" 'expected one LOGFILE (try --help)'
  log=$1
  [[ ${top} =~ ^[1-9][0-9]*$ ]] || die "${EX_USAGE}" "bad count: ${top}"
  [[ ${format} == text || ${format} == tsv ]] \
    || die "${EX_USAGE}" "unknown format: ${format}"
  [[ -r ${log} ]] || die "${EX_NOINPUT}" "cannot read ${log}"

Each die names its status by a constant from sysexits.h, so the exit codes are documented in one place and used by name. The rest of main is the compute-and-act layers, in five lines: the pipeline from the log through aggregate and one renderer into a variable, an || that turns a failed aggregation into status 65, and then one of three ways to deliver the report — print it, say what would be written, or write it. The command never opens the log with a loop: the library reads it once, through one redirection.

The tests

The tests are the contract of §22.8 and the behaviour of the report, twelve of them in all. Each starts with a setup that writes a four-line log into a temporary directory that bats gives every test, so no test depends on another or on the state of the machine:

# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # an excerpt: the rest of the file uses these
setup() {
  ROOT=$(cd "${BATS_TEST_DIRNAME}/.." && pwd)
  LOGSUM="${ROOT}/bin/logsum"
  cd "${BATS_TEST_TMPDIR}"
  printf '%s\n' \
    '10.0.0.1 200 /a 100' \
    '10.0.0.2 200 /b 200' \
    '10.0.0.3 404 /a 50' \
    '10.0.0.4 200 /a 10' > access.log
}

Four tests check the contract — version, help on standard output only, usage errors and their statuses — two the failure statuses 65 and 66, four the report and where it goes (text, tab-separated with --top, the dry run and the output file), and two the library directly, without the command line: that logsum::aggregate counts a line from a here-string, and that sourcing the file twice is harmless. The last is the guard of §22.3 under test.

The checks

make check runs five checks in order, and the stylecheck at the fourth is the one written for this section, since nothing standard checks a file header, a main at the bottom or a TODO without an owner:

check_file() {
  awk -v file="$1" '
    function report(line, message) {
      printf "%s:%d: %s\n", file, line, message
      found = 1
    }
    /\t/ { report(FNR, "tab character") }
    length > 80 { report(FNR, "line is " length " columns; the limit is 80") }
    FNR <= 3 && /^# / { header = 1 }
    /TOD[O]/ && !/TOD[O]\([a-z][a-z0-9_.-]*\):/ {
      report(FNR, "TODO needs an owner: TODO(name):")
    }
    /^[a-z_:]+\(\) \{$/ {
      opened = FNR
      func_name = $1
      commented = (prev ~ /^#/)
    }
    /^}$/ && opened {
      if (FNR - opened > 6 && !commented) {
        report(opened, func_name " is long and has no header comment")
      }
      opened = 0
    }
    $0 !~ /^[ \t]*$/ { prev = $0 }
    $0 !~ /^[ \t]*(#.*)?$/ { last = $0 }
    END {
      if (!header) report(1, "no header comment describing the file")
      if (file !~ /[.]sh$/ && last != "main \"$@\"") {
        report(FNR, "the last line of a script should be: main \"$@\"")
      }
      exit found
    }' "$1"
}

The Makefile names them once, so that the developer, the pre-commit hook and CI run the same thing: bash -n on each file for syntax, shellcheck for the language, shfmt -d for layout, stylecheck for the conventions and bats for behaviour. Any of them failing fails the build. The next block builds the whole tree and runs it. It is long, since it is the whole program, and every file in it is the one excerpted above:

mkdir -p lib
cat > lib/logsum.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# Functions for logsum. Source this file; it does nothing on its own.
# A log line has four fields: address, status, path and bytes.

# Loading the file twice is harmless.
[[ -n ${LOGSUM_LIB_LOADED:-} ]] && return 0
readonly LOGSUM_LIB_LOADED=1
# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # read by the script that sources this file
readonly LOGSUM_VERSION='1.0.0'

#######################################
# Count requests and bytes per status, and requests per path.
# Globals:
#   None
# Arguments:
#   None. Reads the log from standard input.
# Outputs:
#   Tab-separated lines on stdout, unsorted:
#     S status requests bytes
#     P path requests
#   A diagnostic on stderr for each malformed line.
# Returns:
#   0, or 1 if any line did not have four fields.
#######################################
logsum::aggregate() {
  awk '
    NF != 4 {
      printf "line %d: expected 4 fields, found %d\n", NR, NF > "/dev/stderr"
      bad = 1
      next
    }
    { requests[$2]++; bytes[$2] += $4; hits[$3]++ }
    END {
      for (s in requests) printf "S\t%s\t%d\t%d\n", s, requests[s], bytes[s]
      for (p in hits) printf "P\t%s\t%d\n", p, hits[p]
      exit bad
    }'
}

#######################################
# Keep the status lines of aggregated data, sorted by status.
# Outputs:
#   The S lines on stdout. Reads aggregated lines from standard input.
#######################################
logsum::statuses() {
  local tab=$'\t'
  grep "^S${tab}" | sort -t "${tab}" -k2,2n
}

#######################################
# Keep the busiest paths of aggregated data.
# Arguments:
#   How many paths to keep.
# Outputs:
#   The P lines on stdout, busiest first, ties in path order. Reads
#   aggregated lines from standard input.
#######################################
logsum::top_paths() {
  local top=$1 tab=$'\t'
  grep "^P${tab}" | sort -t "${tab}" -k3,3nr -k2,2 \
    | awk -v top="${top}" 'NR <= top'
}

#######################################
# Print aggregated data as a text report.
# Arguments:
#   How many paths to list.
# Outputs:
#   The report on stdout. Reads aggregated lines from standard input.
#######################################
logsum::render_text() {
  local top=$1 tab=$'\t' data
  data=$(cat)
  printf '%-8s %8s %12s\n' status requests bytes
  logsum::statuses <<< "${data}" \
    | awk -F "${tab}" '{ printf "%-8s %8d %12d\n", $2, $3, $4 }'
  printf '\ntop paths\n'
  logsum::top_paths "${top}" <<< "${data}" \
    | awk -F "${tab}" '{ printf "%-24s %8d\n", $2, $3 }'
}

#######################################
# Print the same data as tab-separated lines.
# Arguments:
#   How many paths to list.
# Outputs:
#   S lines, then P lines, on stdout. Reads aggregated lines from standard
#   input.
#######################################
logsum::render_tsv() {
  local top=$1 data
  data=$(cat)
  logsum::statuses <<< "${data}"
  logsum::top_paths "${top}" <<< "${data}"
}
END_OF_FILE
mkdir -p bin
cat > bin/logsum <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# Summarise a web access log: requests and bytes per status, top paths.
#
# Usage: logsum [-n N] [-f text|tsv] [-o FILE] [-D] [-v] LOGFILE

set -o errexit -o nounset -o pipefail

readonly PROG=${0##*/}
readonly EX_USAGE=64 EX_DATAERR=65 EX_NOINPUT=66 EX_CANTCREAT=73

# shellcheck source=lib/logsum.sh
source "${BASH_SOURCE[0]%/*}/../lib/logsum.sh"

#######################################
# Print the usage text.
# Outputs:
#   The text on stdout.
#######################################
usage() {
  cat << END_OF_USAGE
Usage: ${PROG} [-n N] [-f text|tsv] [-o FILE] [-D] [-v] LOGFILE
Summarise an access log: requests and bytes per status, top paths.

  -n, --top N        list the N busiest paths (default 5)
  -f, --format F     text or tsv (default text)
  -o, --output FILE  write the report to FILE, replacing it atomically
  -D, --dry-run      say what would be written; write nothing
  -v, --verbose      report progress on stderr
  -h, --help         show this help and exit
  -V, --version      show the version and exit

Exit status: 0 success, 64 usage error, 65 malformed log line,
66 log file missing or unreadable, 73 cannot write the output.
END_OF_USAGE
}

#######################################
# Print a message to stderr and exit.
# Arguments:
#   Exit status, then the message words.
#######################################
die() {
  local status=$1
  shift
  printf '%s: %s\n' "${PROG}" "$*" >&2
  exit "${status}"
}

#######################################
# Parse the command line, read the log and write the report.
# Arguments:
#   The command line: options, then one LOGFILE.
# Outputs:
#   The report on stdout, or in the file named by -o.
# Returns:
#   0, or one of the statuses in the usage text.
#######################################
main() {
  local top=5 format=text output='' dry_run=0 verbose=0 log
  while (($# > 0)); do
    case $1 in
      -h | --help)
        usage
        return 0
        ;;
      -V | --version)
        echo "${PROG} ${LOGSUM_VERSION}"
        return 0
        ;;
      -D | --dry-run) dry_run=1 ;;
      -v | --verbose) verbose=1 ;;
      -n | --top | -f | --format | -o | --output)
        (($# > 1)) || die "${EX_USAGE}" "$1 needs an argument"
        case $1 in
          -n | --top) top=$2 ;;
          -f | --format) format=$2 ;;
          *) output=$2 ;;
        esac
        shift
        ;;
      --)
        shift
        break
        ;;
      -?*) die "${EX_USAGE}" "unknown option: $1" ;;
      *) break ;;
    esac
    shift
  done
  (($# == 1)) || die "${EX_USAGE}" 'expected one LOGFILE (try --help)'
  log=$1
  [[ ${top} =~ ^[1-9][0-9]*$ ]] || die "${EX_USAGE}" "bad count: ${top}"
  [[ ${format} == text || ${format} == tsv ]] \
    || die "${EX_USAGE}" "unknown format: ${format}"
  [[ -r ${log} ]] || die "${EX_NOINPUT}" "cannot read ${log}"

  local report
  ((verbose == 0)) || echo "${PROG}: reading ${log}" >&2
  report=$(logsum::aggregate < "${log}" | "logsum::render_${format}" "${top}") \
    || die "${EX_DATAERR}" "malformed line in ${log}"
  if [[ -z ${output} ]]; then
    printf '%s\n' "${report}"
  elif ((dry_run)); then
    echo "${PROG}: would write ${output}"
  else
    printf '%s\n' "${report}" > "${output}" \
      || die "${EX_CANTCREAT}" "cannot write ${output}"
  fi
}

main "$@"
END_OF_FILE
mkdir -p tools
cat > tools/stylecheck <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# Check the parts of the style guide that no other tool checks.
#
# Usage: stylecheck FILE...

set -o nounset -o pipefail

#######################################
# Report the style violations in one file.
# Arguments:
#   The file name.
# Outputs:
#   One "file:line: message" line per violation, on stdout.
# Returns:
#   1 if any violation was found.
#######################################
check_file() {
  awk -v file="$1" '
    function report(line, message) {
      printf "%s:%d: %s\n", file, line, message
      found = 1
    }
    /\t/ { report(FNR, "tab character") }
    length > 80 { report(FNR, "line is " length " columns; the limit is 80") }
    FNR <= 3 && /^# / { header = 1 }
    /TOD[O]/ && !/TOD[O]\([a-z][a-z0-9_.-]*\):/ {
      report(FNR, "TODO needs an owner: TODO(name):")
    }
    /^[a-z_:]+\(\) \{$/ {
      opened = FNR
      func_name = $1
      commented = (prev ~ /^#/)
    }
    /^}$/ && opened {
      if (FNR - opened > 6 && !commented) {
        report(opened, func_name " is long and has no header comment")
      }
      opened = 0
    }
    $0 !~ /^[ \t]*$/ { prev = $0 }
    $0 !~ /^[ \t]*(#.*)?$/ { last = $0 }
    END {
      if (!header) report(1, "no header comment describing the file")
      if (file !~ /[.]sh$/ && last != "main \"$@\"") {
        report(FNR, "the last line of a script should be: main \"$@\"")
      }
      exit found
    }' "$1"
}

main() {
  local file status=0
  for file in "$@"; do
    check_file "${file}" || status=1
  done
  return "${status}"
}

main "$@"
END_OF_FILE

cat > test/logsum.bats <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bats

bats_require_minimum_version 1.5.0

setup() {
  ROOT=$(cd "${BATS_TEST_DIRNAME}/.." && pwd)
  LOGSUM="${ROOT}/bin/logsum"
  cd "${BATS_TEST_TMPDIR}"
  printf '%s\n' \
    '10.0.0.1 200 /a 100' \
    '10.0.0.2 200 /b 200' \
    '10.0.0.3 404 /a 50' \
    '10.0.0.4 200 /a 10' > access.log
}

@test "--version prints the name and the version" {
  run "${LOGSUM}" --version
  [ "${status}" -eq 0 ]
  [ "${output}" = "logsum 1.0.0" ]
}

@test "--help succeeds and writes the usage to stdout" {
  run --separate-stderr "${LOGSUM}" --help
  [ "${status}" -eq 0 ]
  [[ ${lines[0]} == "Usage: logsum "* ]]
  [ -z "${stderr}" ]
}

@test "no arguments is a usage error, reported on stderr" {
  run --separate-stderr "${LOGSUM}"
  [ "${status}" -eq 64 ]
  [ -z "${output}" ]
  [[ ${stderr} == "logsum: expected one LOGFILE"* ]]
}

@test "an unknown option is a usage error" {
  run "${LOGSUM}" --colour access.log
  [ "${status}" -eq 64 ]
  [ "${output}" = "logsum: unknown option: --colour" ]
}

@test "a missing log file is status 66" {
  run "${LOGSUM}" no-such.log
  [ "${status}" -eq 66 ]
}

@test "a malformed line is status 65 and names the line" {
  printf 'only three fields\n' >> access.log
  run "${LOGSUM}" access.log
  [ "${status}" -eq 65 ]
  [[ ${output} == *"line 5: expected 4 fields, found 3"* ]]
}

@test "the text report lists statuses in order and the busiest path first" {
  run "${LOGSUM}" access.log
  [ "${status}" -eq 0 ]
  [[ ${lines[1]} =~ ^200\ +3\ +310$ ]]
  [[ ${lines[2]} =~ ^404\ +1\ +50$ ]]
  [[ ${lines[4]} =~ ^/a\ +3$ ]]
}

@test "the tsv report honours --top" {
  run "${LOGSUM}" --format tsv --top 1 access.log
  [ "${status}" -eq 0 ]
  [ "${#lines[@]}" -eq 3 ]
  [ "${lines[2]}" = $'P\t/a\t3' ]
}

@test "--dry-run writes nothing" {
  run "${LOGSUM}" --dry-run --output report.txt access.log
  [ "${status}" -eq 0 ]
  [ "${output}" = "logsum: would write report.txt" ]
  [ ! -e report.txt ]
}

@test "--output writes the report to a file" {
  run "${LOGSUM}" --output report.txt access.log
  [ "${status}" -eq 0 ]
  [ -z "${output}" ]
  grep -q '^200 ' report.txt
}

@test "the library aggregates without the command line" {
  source "${ROOT}/lib/logsum.sh"
  run logsum::aggregate <<< '10.0.0.1 200 /a 100'
  [ "${status}" -eq 0 ]
  [[ ${lines[0]} == $'S\t200\t1\t100' ]]
}

@test "sourcing the library twice is harmless" {
  source "${ROOT}/lib/logsum.sh"
  run source "${ROOT}/lib/logsum.sh"
  [ "${status}" -eq 0 ]
  [ -z "${output}" ]
}
END_OF_FILE
