make check printed its five commands and the twelve ok lines, and nothing else: ShellCheck, shfmt and stylecheck are silent when there is nothing to report, which is what a gate should be. The line counts follow. The command is 77 lines of code and the library 42 — 119 for the tool, more than the guide's hundred — and the checker and the tests are the same size again. The report shows the two statuses in order and the busiest paths, and the tab-separated form with --top 2 shows two. The dry run wrote nothing and the file did not exist afterwards. And the failures each printed one line and the status §22.8 promised: 64 for no argument and for a bad count, 66 for a missing file, and 65 for a log line that is not a log line, with the line's number.

What the capstone shows

The tool is over the guide's hundred lines, and §22.11's criteria do not fire. Its data work is one awk, its data has no structure beyond two flat tables, its numbers are integers, its input is a plain text format, its errors are statuses, and it has no shared state. It is longer than a script because it is a program, with a contract, tests and a library — and it is the shape a program should have if it is to stay in shell and be maintained: small functions with header comments, logic in a library and I/O in the command, and every rule that a tool can check being checked by one. Each of the five checks caught something while it was written: stylecheck a main with no header comment (and, in exercise 4's patch, two lines over 80 columns), shfmt the one-line case clauses and the spaces inside (( )), ShellCheck an unused constant and an unfollowed source, and bats an off-by-one in a line index, because its lines array does not include blank lines. The tools found what review would have, and found it in seconds.

22.13 The Style and Architecture Table

Rule
What it says, what checks it, and the detail that bites
Google Shell Style Guide
Nine parts; bash only; "small utilities or simple wrapper scripts"; rewrite past 100 lines or non-straightforward control flow. The course follows it except for #!/usr/bin/env bash, shfmt's ((…)) spacing and its portability premise (§22.1).
Which tool checks what
ShellCheck: quoting, backticks, $? tests. shfmt: layout. awk length > 80: columns. A custom lint: header, function comments, main, TODO owners (§22.1, §22.12).
Indent 2 spaces, no tabs
shfmt defaults to tabs: -i 2 -ci -sr -bn, or an .editorconfig. <<- bodies stay tab-indented. shfmt -d exits 1 on a difference (§22.2).
80 columns
Not enforced by shfmt. Split pipelines with the pipe first (-bn), long strings in here documents, long paths on their own line (§22.2).
Names
Functions and variables lower case; constants and exports upper case. pkg::name works in bash and not in dash. A local named PATH makes date "not found" (§22.3).
readonly and declare -r
Inside a function declare -r is local; readonly is global. Assigning to a constant skips the rest of the line, not the script. A readonly library needs a load guard (§22.3).
Comments
Header on every file; a function comment with Globals, Arguments, Outputs, Returns unless short and obvious; comment why; TODO(name): (§22.4).
Layout
Shebang, header, set, constants, sources, functions, main, main "$@" last. A call before the definition fails, and the script can still exit 0 (§22.5).
Idempotence
State what should be true, test, act only if not: mkdir -p, ln -sfn, cmp -s then install, grep -qxF ||. Not atomic and not locked (§22.6).
Dry run
Writes through run, which prints (%q) and counts; reads always happen. A prediction from current state, not a proof (§22.6).
Library files
.sh, not executable, a load guard, a package prefix, definitions only. Source relative to ${BASH_SOURCE[0]}. No set, cd, exit, trap or output at load (§22.7).
--help, --version
Both to stdout, exit 0, one line for the version. Errors to stderr, non-zero, pointing at --help (§22.8).
Exit codes
0; 64 usage; 65 data; 66 no input; 73 cannot create output (sysexits.h); documented in the help (§22.8).
Layers
Parse, validate, compute, act. Compute is pure filters; I/O in main; testable without files (§22.9).
Refactoring
Record a golden copy first; small steps, each compared and re-linted; deliberate behaviour changes separate and named (§22.10).
Stop using shell
Ask §21.7's questions when a script passes 100 lines of logic, when a requirement names data, and when a fix needs a workaround. Keep the seam narrow; the old tests decide (§22.11, §21.8).

The order of use, for a new script: write the header and the skeleton with main, put the logic in functions with comments, run shfmt, ShellCheck and the style check on every save, and write the contract tests first. For an old one: record what it does, then separate the layers, then apply the rest.

Exercises

1. Apply the guide. big-before.sh lists the files in a directory that are larger than a size. Rewrite it so that ShellCheck and shfmt are silent, no line is over 80 columns, it has a header comment, a function comment and a main, and it prints exactly what it printed before on a directory of ordinary file names. Note the guide's reason for each thing you change.

cat > big-before.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/bin/bash
# big files: prints every file in a directory that is larger than a given number of bytes
function big(){
	dir=$1
	min=$2
    for f in `ls $dir`; do
	size=`wc -c < $dir/$f | tr -d ' '`
        if [ $size -gt $min ]; then echo "$size $f"; fi
    done | sort -rn
}
big $1 $2
END_OF_FILE
Solution

The rewrite is below, with both scripts run through the three checks and on the same directory:

mkdir data
printf 'x' > data/a.txt
printf 'xxxxxxxx' > data/b.txt
printf 'xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx' > data/c.txt

cat > big-before.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/bin/bash
# big files: prints every file in a directory that is larger than a given number of bytes
function big(){
	dir=$1
	min=$2
    for f in `ls $dir`; do
	size=`wc -c < $dir/$f | tr -d ' '`
        if [ $size -gt $min ]; then echo "$size $f"; fi
    done | sort -rn
}
big $1 $2
END_OF_FILE

cat > big-after.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# List the files in a directory that are larger than a size, largest first.
#
# Usage: big-after.sh DIR MIN_BYTES

set -o errexit -o nounset -o pipefail

#######################################
# Print "size name" for each file over the limit.
# Arguments:
#   Directory, minimum size in bytes.
# Outputs:
#   One line per file, largest first.
#######################################
big() {
  local dir=$1 min=$2 file size
  for file in "${dir}"/*; do
    size=$(wc -c < "${file}" | tr -d ' ')
    if ((size > min)); then
      echo "${size} ${file##*/}"
    fi
  done | sort -rn
}

main() {
  big "$@"
}

main "$@"
END_OF_FILE

printf '%s\n' '[*]' 'indent_style = space' 'indent_size = 2' 'binary_next_line = true' \
  'space_redirects = true' > .editorconfig
for script in big-before.sh big-after.sh; do
  printf '%-14s shellcheck: %-3s  shfmt: %-3s  over 80 columns: %s\n' "$script" \
    "$(shellcheck "$script" > /dev/null && echo ok || echo no)" \
    "$(shfmt -d "$script" > /dev/null && echo ok || echo no)" \
    "$(awk 'length > 80' "$script" | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"
done
echo "== the same answer:"
bash big-before.sh data 2
bash big-after.sh data 2

big-before.sh  shellcheck: no   shfmt: no   over 80 columns: 1
big-after.sh   shellcheck: ok   shfmt: ok   over 80 columns: 0
== the same answer:
24 c.txt
8 b.txt
24 c.txt
8 b.txt

The original failed ShellCheck and shfmt and had a comment line of 89 columns; the rewrite passes all three and printed the same two lines. What changed, and the rule for each: the shebang names bash by env, since the script is bash-specific and /bin/bash may be 3.2 (§22.1); the header comment says what the file is for and how to call it (§22.4); the backticks became $(…) and `ls $dir` became a glob, "${dir}"/*, so that a file name with a space no longer splits into two — a behaviour improvement the ordinary-names test cannot show; every expansion is quoted; the variables are local; the [ … -gt … ] became ((size > min)); the function big(){ line became big() {; and the executable code at the bottom went into main (§22.5), with main "$@" as the last line. The .editorconfig the checks used is the four lines in the block, and it is the whole of the formatting decision.

2. Make it idempotent. setup-before.sh prepares an application directory. Run twice it fails on the second mkdir, appends its PATH line to profile again, and would overwrite a configuration the operator had edited. Rewrite it so that a second run changes nothing, and show it, including an edit made between the runs.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
mkdir app
mkdir app/v1
echo "export PATH=$PWD/bin:\$PATH" >> profile
ln -s app/v1 current
echo "colour=blue" > app/config
Solution

Each line becomes a test followed by an action: mkdir -p for the directories, a grep -qxF guard for the appended line, ln -sfn for the link, and a [[ -e … ]] guard on the configuration, so that the default is written only if there is not one:

cat > setup-before.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
mkdir app
mkdir app/v1
echo "export PATH=$PWD/bin:\$PATH" >> profile
ln -s app/v1 current
echo "colour=blue" > app/config
END_OF_FILE

cat > setup-after.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
mkdir -p app/v1
line="export PATH=$PWD/bin:\$PATH"
grep -qxF "${line}" profile 2> /dev/null || echo "${line}" >> profile
ln -sfn app/v1 current
[[ -e app/config ]] || echo "colour=blue" > app/config
END_OF_FILE

report() { echo "  profile has $(grep -c . profile) line(s), config says: $(cat app/config)"; }

mkdir before after
echo "== the original, run twice"
(
  cd before
  bash ../setup-before.sh 2>&1 | sed 's|^.*: ||'
  bash ../setup-before.sh 2>&1 | sed 's|^.*: ||'
  report
)
echo "== the fix, run twice, with a hand edit in between"
(
  cd after
  bash ../setup-after.sh
  echo "colour=red" > app/config
  bash ../setup-after.sh
  report
)

== the original, run twice
File exists
File exists
  profile has 2 line(s), config says: colour=blue
== the fix, run twice, with a hand edit in between
  profile has 1 line(s), config says: colour=red

The original's second run failed twice (File exists, from the two mkdir commands) and left profile with two copies of the line. The rewrite, run twice with an edit between, left profile with one line and kept the operator's colour=red. The last of the four decisions is the interesting one, and it is a decision and not a technique: a default file is written once, and an existing one is the operator's, so it is never overwritten. Idempotence does not say which state the script should converge to; it says that running again converges to the same one, and deciding whether a re-run should restore defaults or respect edits is part of writing the script.

3. Refactor with a safety net. grades.sh averages each student's scores and gives a letter. Separate the logic from the I/O: extract a function that turns an average into a letter, prove the boundaries with no files, and prove the refactored script prints exactly what the original did on a fixture.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
declare -A sum count
while IFS=, read -r name score; do
  sum[$name]=$((${sum[$name]:-0} + score))
  count[$name]=$((${count[$name]:-0} + 1))
done < grades.csv
for name in $(printf '%s\n' "${!sum[@]}" | sort); do
  avg=$((sum[$name] / count[$name]))
  if [ $avg -ge 90 ]; then letter=A
  elif [ $avg -ge 80 ]; then letter=B
  elif [ $avg -ge 70 ]; then letter=C
  else letter=F; fi
  echo "$name $avg $letter"
done
Solution

The golden output is recorded first, from the original. The rewrite has grades::letter (a pure function of one number), grades::averages (one awk over standard input) and a main that reads a file name and joins them, guarded so the file can be sourced:

cat > grades.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
declare -A sum count
while IFS=, read -r name score; do
  sum[$name]=$((${sum[$name]:-0} + score))
  count[$name]=$((${count[$name]:-0} + 1))
done < grades.csv
for name in $(printf '%s\n' "${!sum[@]}" | sort); do
  avg=$((sum[$name] / count[$name]))
  if [ $avg -ge 90 ]; then letter=A
  elif [ $avg -ge 80 ]; then letter=B
  elif [ $avg -ge 70 ]; then letter=C
  else letter=F; fi
  echo "$name $avg $letter"
done
END_OF_FILE
printf '%s\n' ada,95 ada,89 grace,72 grace,70 linus,50 linus,89 > grades.csv
bash grades.sh > golden.txt
cat golden.txt

cat > grades-after.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# Average each student's scores and give a letter grade.
#
# Usage: grades-after.sh [CSV_FILE]   (default: grades.csv)

set -o errexit -o nounset -o pipefail

#######################################
# Turn an average into a letter.
# Arguments:
#   The average, an integer.
# Outputs:
#   A, B, C or F on stdout.
#######################################
grades::letter() {
  local avg=$1
  if ((avg >= 90)); then
    echo A
  elif ((avg >= 80)); then
    echo B
  elif ((avg >= 70)); then
    echo C
  else
    echo F
  fi
}

#######################################
# Average the scores of each student.
# Arguments:
#   None. Reads "name,score" lines on standard input.
# Outputs:
#   One "name average" line per student, sorted by name.
#######################################
grades::averages() {
  awk -F, '
    { sum[$1] += $2; n[$1]++ }
    END { for (s in sum) print s, int(sum[s] / n[s]) }' | sort
}

main() {
  local name avg
  while read -r name avg; do
    echo "${name} ${avg} $(grades::letter "${avg}")"
  done < <(grades::averages < "${1:-grades.csv}")
}

if [[ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} == "$0" ]]; then
  main "$@"
fi
END_OF_FILE

bash grades-after.sh | cmp - golden.txt && echo "identical to the golden output"
echo "== the letter function, at the boundaries, with no files"
source ./grades-after.sh
for avg in 100 90 89 80 79 70 69 0; do
  printf '%3d -> %s\n' "$avg" "$(grades::letter "$avg")"
done

ada 92 A
grace 71 C
linus 69 F
identical to the golden output
== the letter function, at the boundaries, with no files
100 -> A

 89 -> B
 80 -> B
 79 -> C
 70 -> C
 69 -> F
  0 -> F

The first three lines are the golden output, and cmp confirmed the rewrite prints the same. The second half is the test the original could never have had: grades::letter at every boundary — 90 is an A and 89 a B, 80 a B and 79 a C, 70 a C and 69 an F — with no file and no working directory. The boundaries are the point of that test, since they are where a >= written as > would go wrong, and the original only ever exercised whatever averages its fixture happened to contain.

4. Add an option to the capstone, test first. Add --status CODE to logsum, which counts only the requests with that status. Write the test first and watch it fail, make the change, and finish with make check clean. Keep every line under 80 columns.

Solution

The test is appended to the suite first, and fails. The change is then a patch to the two files: a new library function that filters the log by status, a new option in main's parser and a validation that the code has three digits, and a line in the usage text. The block builds the capstone, runs the failing test, applies the patch and runs every check:

mkdir -p lib
cat > lib/logsum.sh <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# Functions for logsum. Source this file; it does nothing on its own.
# A log line has four fields: address, status, path and bytes.

# Loading the file twice is harmless.
[[ -n ${LOGSUM_LIB_LOADED:-} ]] && return 0
readonly LOGSUM_LIB_LOADED=1
# shellcheck disable=SC2034  # read by the script that sources this file
readonly LOGSUM_VERSION='1.0.0'

#######################################
# Count requests and bytes per status, and requests per path.
# Globals:
#   None
# Arguments:
#   None. Reads the log from standard input.
# Outputs:
#   Tab-separated lines on stdout, unsorted:
#     S status requests bytes
#     P path requests
#   A diagnostic on stderr for each malformed line.
# Returns:
#   0, or 1 if any line did not have four fields.
#######################################
logsum::aggregate() {
  awk '
    NF != 4 {
      printf "line %d: expected 4 fields, found %d\n", NR, NF > "/dev/stderr"
      bad = 1
      next
    }
    { requests[$2]++; bytes[$2] += $4; hits[$3]++ }
    END {
      for (s in requests) printf "S\t%s\t%d\t%d\n", s, requests[s], bytes[s]
      for (p in hits) printf "P\t%s\t%d\n", p, hits[p]
      exit bad
    }'
}

#######################################
# Keep the status lines of aggregated data, sorted by status.
# Outputs:
#   The S lines on stdout. Reads aggregated lines from standard input.
#######################################
logsum::statuses() {
  local tab=$'\t'
  grep "^S${tab}" | sort -t "${tab}" -k2,2n
}

#######################################
# Keep the busiest paths of aggregated data.
# Arguments:
#   How many paths to keep.
# Outputs:
#   The P lines on stdout, busiest first, ties in path order. Reads
#   aggregated lines from standard input.
#######################################
logsum::top_paths() {
  local top=$1 tab=$'\t'
  grep "^P${tab}" | sort -t "${tab}" -k3,3nr -k2,2 \
    | awk -v top="${top}" 'NR <= top'
}

#######################################
# Print aggregated data as a text report.
# Arguments:
#   How many paths to list.
# Outputs:
#   The report on stdout. Reads aggregated lines from standard input.
#######################################
logsum::render_text() {
  local top=$1 tab=$'\t' data
  data=$(cat)
  printf '%-8s %8s %12s\n' status requests bytes
  logsum::statuses <<< "${data}" \
    | awk -F "${tab}" '{ printf "%-8s %8d %12d\n", $2, $3, $4 }'
  printf '\ntop paths\n'
  logsum::top_paths "${top}" <<< "${data}" \
    | awk -F "${tab}" '{ printf "%-24s %8d\n", $2, $3 }'
}

#######################################
# Print the same data as tab-separated lines.
# Arguments:
#   How many paths to list.
# Outputs:
#   S lines, then P lines, on stdout. Reads aggregated lines from standard
#   input.
#######################################
logsum::render_tsv() {
  local top=$1 data
  data=$(cat)
  logsum::statuses <<< "${data}"
  logsum::top_paths "${top}" <<< "${data}"
}
END_OF_FILE
mkdir -p bin
cat > bin/logsum <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# Summarise a web access log: requests and bytes per status, top paths.
#
# Usage: logsum [-n N] [-f text|tsv] [-o FILE] [-D] [-v] LOGFILE

set -o errexit -o nounset -o pipefail

readonly PROG=${0##*/}
readonly EX_USAGE=64 EX_DATAERR=65 EX_NOINPUT=66 EX_CANTCREAT=73

# shellcheck source=lib/logsum.sh
source "${BASH_SOURCE[0]%/*}/../lib/logsum.sh"

#######################################
# Print the usage text.
# Outputs:
#   The text on stdout.
#######################################
usage() {
  cat << END_OF_USAGE
Usage: ${PROG} [-n N] [-f text|tsv] [-o FILE] [-D] [-v] LOGFILE
Summarise an access log: requests and bytes per status, top paths.

  -n, --top N        list the N busiest paths (default 5)
  -f, --format F     text or tsv (default text)
  -o, --output FILE  write the report to FILE, replacing it atomically
  -D, --dry-run      say what would be written; write nothing
  -v, --verbose      report progress on stderr
  -h, --help         show this help and exit
  -V, --version      show the version and exit

Exit status: 0 success, 64 usage error, 65 malformed log line,
66 log file missing or unreadable, 73 cannot write the output.
END_OF_USAGE
}

#######################################
# Print a message to stderr and exit.
# Arguments:
#   Exit status, then the message words.
#######################################
die() {
  local status=$1
  shift
  printf '%s: %s\n' "${PROG}" "$*" >&2
  exit "${status}"
}

#######################################
# Parse the command line, read the log and write the report.
# Arguments:
#   The command line: options, then one LOGFILE.
# Outputs:
#   The report on stdout, or in the file named by -o.
# Returns:
#   0, or one of the statuses in the usage text.
#######################################
main() {
  local top=5 format=text output='' dry_run=0 verbose=0 log
  while (($# > 0)); do
    case $1 in
      -h | --help)
        usage
        return 0
        ;;
      -V | --version)
        echo "${PROG} ${LOGSUM_VERSION}"
        return 0
        ;;
      -D | --dry-run) dry_run=1 ;;
      -v | --verbose) verbose=1 ;;
      -n | --top | -f | --format | -o | --output)
        (($# > 1)) || die "${EX_USAGE}" "$1 needs an argument"
        case $1 in
          -n | --top) top=$2 ;;
          -f | --format) format=$2 ;;
          *) output=$2 ;;
        esac
        shift
        ;;
      --)
        shift
        break
        ;;
      -?*) die "${EX_USAGE}" "unknown option: $1" ;;
      *) break ;;
    esac
    shift
  done
  (($# == 1)) || die "${EX_USAGE}" 'expected one LOGFILE (try --help)'
  log=$1
  [[ ${top} =~ ^[1-9][0-9]*$ ]] || die "${EX_USAGE}" "bad count: ${top}"
  [[ ${format} == text || ${format} == tsv ]] \
    || die "${EX_USAGE}" "unknown format: ${format}"
  [[ -r ${log} ]] || die "${EX_NOINPUT}" "cannot read ${log}"

  local report
  ((verbose == 0)) || echo "${PROG}: reading ${log}" >&2
  report=$(logsum::aggregate < "${log}" | "logsum::render_${format}" "${top}") \
    || die "${EX_DATAERR}" "malformed line in ${log}"
  if [[ -z ${output} ]]; then
    printf '%s\n' "${report}"
  elif ((dry_run)); then
    echo "${PROG}: would write ${output}"
  else
    printf '%s\n' "${report}" > "${output}" \
      || die "${EX_CANTCREAT}" "cannot write ${output}"
  fi
}

main "$@"
END_OF_FILE
mkdir -p tools
cat > tools/stylecheck <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# Check the parts of the style guide that no other tool checks.
#
# Usage: stylecheck FILE...

set -o nounset -o pipefail

#######################################
# Report the style violations in one file.
# Arguments:
#   The file name.
# Outputs:
#   One "file:line: message" line per violation, on stdout.
# Returns:
#   1 if any violation was found.
#######################################
check_file() {
  awk -v file="$1" '
    function report(line, message) {
      printf "%s:%d: %s\n", file, line, message
      found = 1
    }
    /\t/ { report(FNR, "tab character") }
    length > 80 { report(FNR, "line is " length " columns; the limit is 80") }
    FNR <= 3 && /^# / { header = 1 }
    /TOD[O]/ && !/TOD[O]\([a-z][a-z0-9_.-]*\):/ {
      report(FNR, "TODO needs an owner: TODO(name):")
    }
    /^[a-z_:]+\(\) \{$/ {
      opened = FNR
      func_name = $1
      commented = (prev ~ /^#/)
    }
    /^}$/ && opened {
      if (FNR - opened > 6 && !commented) {
        report(opened, func_name " is long and has no header comment")
      }
      opened = 0
    }
    $0 !~ /^[ \t]*$/ { prev = $0 }
    $0 !~ /^[ \t]*(#.*)?$/ { last = $0 }
    END {
      if (!header) report(1, "no header comment describing the file")
      if (file !~ /[.]sh$/ && last != "main \"$@\"") {
        report(FNR, "the last line of a script should be: main \"$@\"")
      }
      exit found
    }' "$1"
}

main() {
  local file status=0
  for file in "$@"; do
    check_file "${file}" || status=1
  done
  return "${status}"
}

main "$@"
END_OF_FILE
mkdir -p test
cat > test/logsum.bats <<'END_OF_FILE'
#!/usr/bin/env bats

bats_require_minimum_version 1.5.0

setup() {
  ROOT=$(cd "${BATS_TEST_DIRNAME}/.." && pwd)
  LOGSUM="${ROOT}/bin/logsum"
  cd "${BATS_TEST_TMPDIR}"
  printf '%s\n' \
    '10.0.0.1 200 /a 100' \
    '10.0.0.2 200 /b 200' \
    '10.0.0.3 404 /a 50' \
    '10.0.0.4 200 /a 10' > access.log
}

@test "--version prints the name and the version" {
  run "${LOGSUM}" --version
  [ "${status}" -eq 0 ]
  [ "${output}" = "logsum 1.0.0" ]
}

@test "--help succeeds and writes the usage to stdout" {
  run --separate-stderr "${LOGSUM}" --help
  [ "${status}" -eq 0 ]
  [[ ${lines[0]} == "Usage: logsum "* ]]
  [ -z "${stderr}" ]
}

@test "no arguments is a usage error, reported on stderr" {
  run --separate-stderr "${LOGSUM}"
  [ "${status}" -eq 64 ]
  [ -z "${output}" ]
  [[ ${stderr} == "logsum: expected one LOGFILE"* ]]
}

@test "an unknown option is a usage error" {
  run "${LOGSUM}" --colour access.log
  [ "${status}" -eq 64 ]
  [ "${output}" = "logsum: unknown option: --colour" ]
}

@test "a missing log file is status 66" {
  run "${LOGSUM}" no-such.log
  [ "${status}" -eq 66 ]
}

@test "a malformed line is status 65 and names the line" {
  printf 'only three fields\n' >> access.log
  run "${LOGSUM}" access.log
  [ "${status}" -eq 65 ]
  [[ ${output} == *"line 5: expected 4 fields, found 3"* ]]
}

@test "the text report lists statuses in order and the busiest path first" {
  run "${LOGSUM}" access.log
  [ "${status}" -eq 0 ]
  [[ ${lines[1]} =~ ^200\ +3\ +310$ ]]
  [[ ${lines[2]} =~ ^404\ +1\ +50$ ]]
  [[ ${lines[4]} =~ ^/a\ +3$ ]]
}

@test "the tsv report honours --top" {
  run "${LOGSUM}" --format tsv --top 1 access.log
  [ "${status}" -eq 0 ]
  [ "${#lines[@]}" -eq 3 ]
  [ "${lines[2]}" = $'P\t/a\t3' ]
}

@test "--dry-run writes nothing" {
  run "${LOGSUM}" --dry-run --output report.txt access.log
  [ "${status}" -eq 0 ]
  [ "${output}" = "logsum: would write report.txt" ]
  [ ! -e report.txt ]
}

@test "--output writes the report to a file" {
  run "${LOGSUM}" --output report.txt access.log
  [ "${status}" -eq 0 ]
  [ -z "${output}" ]
  grep -q '^200 ' report.txt
}

@test "the library aggregates without the command line" {
  source "${ROOT}/lib/logsum.sh"
  run logsum::aggregate <<< '10.0.0.1 200 /a 100'
  [ "${status}" -eq 0 ]
  [[ ${lines[0]} == $'S\t200\t1\t100' ]]
}

@test "sourcing the library twice is harmless" {
  source "${ROOT}/lib/logsum.sh"
  run source "${ROOT}/lib/logsum.sh"
  [ "${status}" -eq 0 ]
  [ -z "${output}" ]
}
END_OF_FILE
cat > Makefile <<'END_OF_FILE'

cat > status.patch <<'END_OF_FILE'
--- a/bin/logsum
+++ b/bin/logsum
@@ -26,4 +26,5 @@

+  -s, --status CODE  count only the requests with this status

@@ -58,5 +59,5 @@
 #######################################
 main() {
-  local top=5 format=text output='' dry_run=0 verbose=0 log
+  local top=5 format=text output='' dry_run=0 verbose=0 log want=''
   while (($# > 0)); do
     case $1 in
@@ -71,9 +72,10 @@
       -D | --dry-run) dry_run=1 ;;
       -v | --verbose) verbose=1 ;;
-      -n | --top | -f | --format | -o | --output)
+      -n | --top | -f | --format | -o | --output | -s | --status)
         (($# > 1)) || die "${EX_USAGE}" "$1 needs an argument"
         case $1 in
           -n | --top) top=$2 ;;
           -f | --format) format=$2 ;;
+          -s | --status) want=$2 ;;
           *) output=$2 ;;
         esac
@@ -92,4 +94,6 @@
   log=$1
   [[ ${top} =~ ^[1-9][0-9]*$ ]] || die "${EX_USAGE}" "bad count: ${top}"
+  [[ -z ${want} || ${want} =~ ^[0-9]{3}$ ]] \
+    || die "${EX_USAGE}" "bad status: ${want}"
   [[ ${format} == text || ${format} == tsv ]] \
     || die "${EX_USAGE}" "unknown format: ${format}"
@@ -98,6 +102,9 @@
   local report
   ((verbose == 0)) || echo "${PROG}: reading ${log}" >&2
-  report=$(logsum::aggregate < "${log}" | "logsum::render_${format}" "${top}") \
-    || die "${EX_DATAERR}" "malformed line in ${log}"
+  report=$(
+    logsum::filter_status "${want}" < "${log}" \
+      | logsum::aggregate \

   if [[ -z ${output} ]]; then
     printf '%s\n' "${report}"
--- a/lib/logsum.sh
+++ b/lib/logsum.sh
@@ -9,4 +9,15 @@
 # shellcheck disable=SC2034  # read by the script that sources this file
 readonly LOGSUM_VERSION='1.0.0'
+
+#######################################
+# Keep only the requests with a given status.
+# Arguments:
+#   The status to keep; empty keeps everything.
+# Outputs:
+#   The matching lines on stdout. Reads the log from standard input.
+#######################################
+logsum::filter_status() {
+  awk -v want="$1" 'want == "" || $2 == want'
+}

END_OF_FILE

Step 1 printed not ok 13, the new test failing, and nothing else in the suite did. Step 2 applied the patch, and make check ended with all thirteen tests passing — the last three lines of its output are the tail of the bats report, and the checks before them, ShellCheck, shfmt and stylecheck, were silent. The command then printed the report for 404 alone. Two things in the patch are the ones an implementation is likely to get wrong the first time: the pipeline in main was longer than 80 columns, which stylecheck reports, so it is split one stage per line with the pipe first, the layout shfmt -bn enforces; and the filter sits before aggregate in the pipeline, which has a consequence worth knowing: with --status, a malformed line whose second field is not the requested status is filtered out and not reported, so --status trades some of the strictness of the default run.

You started this course able to write a script that works on your machine, on your files, with your arguments. You now know what happens to a line between the keyboard and the kernel, which is the difference between a script that works and a script whose author has not yet met the input that breaks it.

Twenty-two sections, and the useful summary is not a list of builtins.

What you can now do

1. Say what a line does before running it. §2.1 showed that tokenisation happens before interpretation, so that if=5 is an assignment though if is a reserved word. §4.1 fixed the order of the expansions and §4.8 the rule that each happens once. That is the skill every other one rests on, and it is why the course opened with the parser and not with a feature.

2. Make a script fail loudly, and clean up when it does. (( count++ )) returns 1 when count is 0 and ends a set -e script (§11.5); ${prefix:?} exits the script even inside a function; a trap set before a lock is acquired deletes the winner's lock (§17.8); a script that exits on a signal must re-raise it to report the right status (§12.5). Each of those looked correct, and each was found by running it.

3. Keep data from becoming code. Five of the six arithmetic contexts run a command substitution buried in a subscript, and only [ -gt ] does not (§18.4); an empty element in PATH means the current directory (§18.7); declare "$line" runs the subscript in the name (§18.11). The defence is the same in every case: know which contexts evaluate their input, and never put data where one is.

4. Write for the shell that will run it. A bashism under dash can exit 0 ([[: not found makes an if take its false branch), and (( count < 5 )) opens a file named 5 (§19). ShellCheck's --severity=warning gate lets SC2086, the unquoted variable, straight through, because it is info (§20.1). Neither failure prints anything a reader would notice, which is why both were measured.

5. Price a script by counting processes. A loop over ten thousand paths that runs basename took about eleven seconds on the macOS machine, the expansion ${p##*/} fifty milliseconds and one sed six (§21.4); {1..1000000} holds a hundred and eighty megabytes and the C-style loop nothing (§21.4); a while read from a pipe makes a system call per byte and from a file one per line (§21.5). The fixes are almost always the same, and they are in §21.4 to §21.6.

The twenty-two sections, one line each

Worth keeping as an index of where an argument lives rather than as a summary.

§1 when shell is the right tool, the two bashes, and the shebang. §2 the grammar: words, reserved words, lists, pipelines, and grouping. §3 quoting, word splitting and IFS. §4 the order of the expansions. §5 parameter expansion in full.

§6 arrays and associative arrays. §7 conditionals, arithmetic and pattern matching. §8 control flow. §9 functions, scope and libraries. §10 redirection and file descriptors. §11 exit status, errexit and error handling. §12 traps, signals and cleanup.

§13 a command-line interface with getopts and completion. §14 input and output: read, mapfile and printf. §15 text processing in the shell. §16 processes, subshells and the environment. §17 concurrency, parallelism and locking.

§18 security and injection. §19 POSIX portability. §20 static analysis, testing and debugging. §21 performance and when to rewrite. §22 style, architecture and the capstone.

What this course is not

The commands themselves — grep, sed, awk, find, tar — are the Linux course's subject. §15.8 says when to reach for one and §21.5 what it saves, and does not teach their options.

Version control, containers and pipelines belong to the courses on Git and on DevOps. §20.11 shows a script inside CI and §22.12 the Makefile a CI job would run, and neither goes further into it.

The languages a script hands its data to — Python above all — are their own courses. §21.8 and §22.11 say where the seam is and how to cut along it, and the Python in this course is a thin example of the shape.

What to do next

The same thing this course did.

Take a script you rely on, record what it does, and make it prove it. Run it under ShellCheck; write the golden output for a real input; count the programs it starts; run it as a stranger would, with a file name that has a space in it and an unset variable and an empty argument. That is the whole method, and it needs nothing but the shell.

It is worth saying plainly how much that method changed this course. A ${prefix:?} that recovers with || did not: the shell exits. A dash script that opens a file named 5 prints nothing wrong. A report that totals a missing file prints a total of zero and the words "Wrote report.txt" and exits 0 (§22.9). A subshell function costs fifty times a braced one, and a declare -r in a function is local. A [ -gt ] is safe where (( )) is not. Each of those looked right and was wrong, and only running it said so.

There is no reason to expect that to stop, which is the most useful thing this course has to hand over.
